Can you infect the world?
Plague Inc: Evolved is an "updated" version of the mobile game Plague Inc. developed by Ndemic Creations. The game's objective is simple, infect the world and kill everyone
The game is really simple to get the hang of but hard to master as trying to infect the whole world isn't easy. To infect the world, you must select a country of origin, then select a method of transmission (either from livestock, blood, rats, etc...), symptoms (such as vomiting, insanity, etc...) and also the ability of the virus (cold and hot resistance, resistance to drugs, etc...)
Not only that, but scientists and doctors are trying to stop you from spreading the virus through a cure which you have to stop by any means. The game is fun to play and includes a lot of stuff to experiment on including the virus from the Dawn of the Planet of the Apes film
However, the gameplay is mostly the same. Pop red bubbles to spread the virus, pop orange bubbles to gain points to evolve the virus and pop blue bubbles to slow the cure from processing and you have to just assume that the virus will infect the world. The game isn't easy and can get repetitive very quickly however the game is fun to play in short bursts
Plague Inc: Evolved has an interesting yet terrifying premise, infect the world, which is both scary yet oddly educational and fun to do... let's just hope this never happens in real life

I bought this the day it came out. I gotta say I was pretty hyped for it; while I didn't know about the kickstarter and couldn't afford the Early Access, I thought the trailer was absolutely adorable. The art had a simple and colorful appeal to it, and the gameplay looked sound. Playing the game was about the experience I expected after seeing that trailer. You hunt down prey to stay full, and can forage for herbs which act as curatives for your health. I was surprised to discover that you could even mine and fish!
I haven't gotten married or had a litter yet, but did score a mate, and that process is very Harvest Moon-esque, relying entirely on gifts. I romanced Scout as they seemed like the easiest, being really into hunting means they'd really like prey! I have no idea what any other character would like as gifts, or if it's just like real life cats, where they all like to be gifted prey.
I've also started on the main storyline, completing two of the game's collection goals and puzzle dungeons. That's right, there are puzzle dungeons! From what I can tell, they are relatively small, and all underground and locked until you need to explore them; once you get the treasure inside, they lock again. It's a neat way of stopping the player from sequence breaking.
One criticism I do have is that if you die, you lose ALL your items, not just "one or two" like your local doctor cat might tell you, and that the doc only heals you halfway. But, once you get a storage unit in your den, this becomes less of a big issue.
Another criticism I have is that the seasons and the days themselves are very short. I blazed through my first year in about 7 and 1/2 hours because there are only 10 days per season, and I might be wrong but I think the time ratio is faster than 1 in-game hour per irl minute. Since you're a cat and they're aren't really time constraints anywhere, it's not that big a deal, it just makes the game seem smaller; I was genuinely shocked and saddened when my first winter was suddenly here, wondering if there might have been a better way to spend that lost time behind me.
All in all, I think it's a cute game that pretty much nails its theme. Good job.

I think this game's community is practically gone at this stage, too few updates changing too little in such a long measure of time. Just about the entirity of the updates that have happened can be summed up in 'several new gun parts, unimplemented mechanics development and minor bugfixing'
It saddens me to see such a game with such potential just die out becuase the dev doesn't have a team backing them.
The multiplayer is completely dead, the community died for it about a year after nothing happened, the servers are completely empty, the multiplayer tasks simply can't be completed anymore, etc etc.
The screenshots & video of the game on this page are VERY outdated, they've since removed several items, including prebuilt one-part weapons, glowsticks and the RFID radar
The hacking is practically useless beyond the resource gathering robots (you can't hack either of the two humanoid robots, and the only other robot you can hack is a swarm drone(only once you shoot about 5 hives worth of them down and have a rare chance at finding a disabled swam drone nearby), only for it to promptly run out of ammo after missing your enemies for two minutes and then disappear when you reload your save)
-EDIT: You can now hack all the robots, but the only way you can do it is if you spend 30+ hours getting EMP rounds and an EMP-capable gun, finding a lone robot(virtually impossible now that the entire map is now coated in long range robots that can snipe you through walls), spamming it with EMP, getting REALLY close to it(the robot is still DIRECTLY shooting at you, even though it's stunned), hacking it(which takes longer than the EMP's effects if you're not trying to kill yourself), figuring out the hack commands before the robot shoots you twice, then sitting back as your new robot slowly stumbles after you and gets killed because of it's terrible pathfinding AI, leaving you with barely any health(the lower your health the slower you move and the less you can jump, below 50% health you're basically dead), no EMP rounds to defend yourself(bullets do barely anything, good luck killing a robot that can run 30 times faster than you at a range where they can kill you in one shot).
The guns in this game are actually pretty cool, you get to assemble your own weapons part by part, not just find things to stick on/over it like most other games of this type. My main problem with it is that the guns themselves each need unique names(which i'm terrible with) otherwise you physically can't build them, a problem that could be solved with a grand total of less than 10 lines of code.
The power system in this game is actually pretty fun, though i feel like it needs a few more things relating to it (like modules that draw power but can help you in decent ways (like scanners, radars, HUD-mounted displays(ammo count, threat level, etc), active armour, low-powered energy shields, that kind of thing), so far it only powers you running and jumping
The jumping is.... well... meh...
You wait for a long time by a platform and charge your jump(if you're not too heavy to get up where you want to get up to), you then jump fairly high.
The main objective of the game is simply to survive, an objective that gets pretty boring after 2+ hours on the same character in singleplayer. You find an RFID radar multitool and then you just steer clear of enemies, you loot things, then you loot more things, then you avoid some more robots, and that's it....
The basebuilding is a bit of a joke... every part of your base will have physics 100% of the time, so if you don't build it in the right order of placement then you just simply can't, becuase one part will be a couple inches too close to another part and you can't place the rest down. The turrets are completely terrible, they're only really good if you build a stubbly little platform and put them on top with literally nothing around them(their targeting AI makes them not care if they're hitting base parts when there's an enemy robot near one of them, two of my bases have fallen becuase the turrets carved their way through the foundations and dropped the entire base on themselves, instantly destroying everything.
Looting in this game isn't fun in any aspect, it's basically the all-known DayZ looting system, but with more crates to look inside. No point on the map has decent gear spawns(the nuclear powerplant sometimes has a few uncommon crates in it, and some tall 50-story buildings that you can't get up without timing your jump just perfect sometimes have uncommon crates but that's about it,) i haven't seen half of the items ingame since there's simply no real tangible way to get them.
I've looked over the ENTIRE map, every structure and loot spawn, and i found a total of 3 uncommon crates and 5 ammo boxes (with maximum Luck skill(supposedly increases loot spawn rates))
I don't think that this game is... well... 'bad'... i just thing it's underdeveloped and it needs help.
Unfortunately it doesn't seem like the developer is talking to the community(So free help for the dev is off the table) and i'm not convinced that the dev's going to be hiring any freelance help any time soon.
I simply can't recommend this game in the state it's in, the bare bones of the game aren't even really there to begin with, and with the slow pace the game's getting upated it seems like it won't be your money's worth for a long while off.
Definately keep an eye on it though, i'm hoping i'm wrong about my prediction
-EDIT:
It's now halfway through 2017 and there's only been 1 update this year, I used to be able to get 120/130fps max settings, now i can only get 30fps if i drop to med settings. It's now impossible to play unless you get lucky and spawn next to the nuclear power plant + 4 nuclear cells(I spent a week grinding cells and I only got 3 with max Luck skill), otherwise you can't outrun the hundreds of bullet sponge robots that know exactly where you are at all times, it was fine when there were only a few robots hunting you down, but with how rare ammo is and how robots can shoot through walls (if they're close enough and their guns phase through the wall, yes, this happens), mixed with many MANY times more robots spawning now, you simply can't survive without maxing jump skill and camping on a roof and restarting the game to respawn loot for yourself
Yes, it actually doesn't seem like the game's getting a really REALLY small bit of good development, it seems the game's actually getting really REALLY REALLY small bit of completely gamebreaking development now...
TL;DR : The game is dead(Launched 25 Jul, 2014, and as of 02 Nov 2017 it's only on V0.0.6.46, so you could technically say it's 6.46% done in the space of about 5 to 6 years(including pre-release development time), at this rate if you buy it now your grandkids might live to see the finished game)
The most recent update pretty much broke the game, it now can't run on anything that isn't a top-end gaming rig, and when it does it'll run like it was on a 2006 Dell desktop, stay away.

pros:
*the impressive artwork, epic scenery as well as epic boss battles, with beautiful music.
*the level structure is kept simple and easy to understand.
cons:

*the controlls are confusing at the beginning of the game (i wouldn't had of known that i can dodge, or how/that can i use the god powers without looking it up).

Love it. The environment, the feel of the game, the music and the epic views are just plain beautiful. The gameplay itself, as in the story line and the level structure, is kept quite simple, but sadly quite repetitive at times. My personal conclusion is that, it is more of an art and puzzle game with hack & slash elements. But i do recommend it, because as i said - i loved it. Probably because i am a fan of norse mythology, but probably also because it is quite relaxing, with impressive artwork and music.

Style over substance. A beautiful art style can't save this boring drudge of a game that is both dull and frustrating.
Levels are largely devoid of enemies, with the only challenge coming from simply avoiding stage hazards. This would not be a problem if the levels were simple linear paths, but as the goal of the game is exploration you'll find yourself getting lost and turned around more often than necessary in the mazelike levels. With most levels containing no enemies whatsoever, backtracking and exploration turns out to be a drag that will leave most players bored to tears.
The in-game map DOES NOT show your current location, which means that you'll constantly be pausing and checking the map trying to guess where in the level you are, with no landmarks to guide you. Needless to say, this makes collecting the upgrades for 100% completion (or even just to finish the game) an absolute nightmare. Imagine being plonked into a level filled with dozens of identical islands, getting lost, and checking to map to confirm that, yes, the level is simply full of identical islands with no frame of reference. Good luck finding your way to the exit, let alone collecting all the upgrades.
The most interesting feature of the game is it's five boss battles, which are for the most part challenging yet fair. Points off for the final boss being complete BS, however.
Give this one a miss.

Jotun is a boss battle focused game where I found the level of challenge to be very reasonable, unlike a lot of other titles that have come out since Dark Souls seems to have, ahem, rekindled interest in difficult games.  While many games since this resurgence depend on the player having twitch reflexes, Jotun is a much slower paced game where careful observation and pattern recognition are more important than reflexes (at least for beating the game normally and not trying to go for the achievements).
It’s an incredible looking game with hand animated bosses which make me wish more modern games used traditional hand animation.  The presentation is great overall.  To be honest, I wasn’t too invested in the Norse mythology based story, but it does a great job of establishing tone and giving the game a basis for a unified aesthetic.
Jotun does have one notable downside, but it’s not a deal breaker.  The game’s structure is that there are 5 areas visited from a main hub.  Each area (except one) has two “exploration” levels that need to be completely first to unlock the boss level.  Each of the exploration levels has a different gimmick of some sort, but for the most part, these levels involve a lot of walking around and some very light puzzle solving.  With one notable exception, the levels are mostly devoid of enemies to fight and the walking around can get a bit tedious.
Ultimately these levels aren’t very long, but I did find myself getting a bit bored on a few of them – though nowhere near enough to overshadow the parts of the game I liked.  I definitely recommended the game regardless, because even if you do get a little bored with the exploration levels, it’s not a huge time investment anyway.

Beautiful game, beautiful music, cool story. I only played for a few hours, but got so bored I decided not to play on. Jotun is the story of a young girl that has died on the seas, being sent to Ginnungagap to prove herself. She does this by going through several worlds, collecting runes, and conquering the Jotun that live there. All of this is for the purpose of "proving oneself to the gods". There isn't really any dialogue, just narration that I assume is in the nordic language. I wouldn't know for sure though, I don't speak it. The narrators are suitably... husk sounding. Tough sounding. Maybe it's the language, I dunno.
The game is beautiful. Straight up beautiful. 'Nuff sed.
The combat feels clunky at times. You have an axe. You have blessings from the gods that give you various buffs when active. You have a fast, weak attack and you have a slow, strong attack. The strong attack feels too slow. I took kendo for a year and the amount of time you spend with your axe above your head for the strong attack is unrealistic. If your weapon is above your head, it's not protecting your body. This is just unreasonable. It also does less damage than the weak attack does in the time it takes to use. I'd only ever use the strong attack when my enemy was in the air so I could hit them as soon as they land and then switch to weak attack. Freya's blessing also speeds up the weak attack so it becomes even more useful. You can get Thor's blessing to power up your strong attack but... too slow.
The game is in 2D but the characters have 3D hitboxes. This becomes especially frustrating in boss fights with enemies that stand (so, almost all of them). because the hitbox when they're standing is half the size of the one when they're on the ground. Which, sure, it's realistic, but it can become difficult to judge whether or not your strike will hit because the hitbox is so weird. The devs were nice enough to show us a shadow of our character when it's behind a boss, but they weren't nice enough to show us shadows of things falling from the sky that are behind the boss. So quite a few deaths of mine were caused by attacks I literally could not see coming. Not to mention that if your character is where a titan will stagger, it will get knocked back into those hazards you were avoiding. Extremely annoying.
Overall? Great game even if some fights are exceedingly frustrating. Definitely recommend.

In short:
This is overall a really good game. It has challenging bossfights, but the challenge feels very 'fair'. It always consists of elements that are already known to the player. It also has a great atmosphere and art style and pacing, which help make the player feel like a tiny part of a world made for creatures much larger than them. This makes the entire experience feel like a set-up towards a series of boss fights, which, as far as I'm concerned never disappoint.
Longer version:
In terms of gameplay, it offers two very different parts. On the one hand, there are the levels which are all well designed and full of beautiful artwork. They feel very distinct, and all have their own challenges in terms of both combat and exploration. The main character has a somewhat limited repertoire of attacks, but the types of enemies and environments the game provides never let it be boring.
On the other hand, there are the boss battles, which are very challenging. The bosses are all great hulking giants that get more and more dangerous as the fight progresses. Along with the fact that the levels leading up to the bosses generally incorporate some elements of the bossfight, this results in a game with a very natural feeling learning curve. The levels more or less serve as tutorials for the bosses, and the early stages of the boss serve as tutorials for the later stages.
It is in the later stages of the bossfights that the gameplay really shines. At any given time in the game's more difficult parts, there will be many different moving parts on screen, and correctly managing them is key to defeating the boss. At these times the game speed feels really appropriate. Sadly, this means that during some of the more 'relaxed' parts of the game movement and attacking speeds feel somewhat slow. This is only a minor gripe, and there's usually enough interesting things to see and do te keep a player invested.
Lastly, it's very impressive how art style, music and narrative are used to enhance the feel of the gameplay. The atmosphere is somewhat oppressive and intimidating, which really aids in an epic feel when beating bosses.

Factorio is still in beta, but I already want to acknowledge it as one of the best games I've ever played. I really have just fallen in love with this game, sad to say.
I've always had a special place in my heart for games that I thought were innovative and possessed extremely well-refined game mechanics. Games like Tribes, Team Fortress Classic, Starcraft, Minecraft, Dota, were all very enjoyable to me because it gave the feeling that there were tons of little mechanics to learn and that there was tons of depth to these games. I think Factorio is at that caliber of game and in some ways I find it more interesting than anything I've played in the past.
Apologies in advance for the engineering jargon and rambling. To use some engineering words, the game about industrial manufacturing and production. Simply put, you need to gather resources and make products with it. And most importantly, you need to automate everything. You are given goals that seem like they are out of a typical neverending MMO: mine 800 iron, create 1000 steel, etc. This seems like very boring goals, even burdensome, but it is really the opposite. The fun part is that you are given all the tools needed to mass produce the resources. You do not need to mine 1000 tons of steel by hand, you merely need to build the machines that will do the work for you. Now the focus on the game is engineering a base that is as effective as possible.
Let me explain another example: You decide that you want to build special circuits to upgrade your factories. To do this, you need to build some circuits out of iron and copper. You need to manufacture plastic by gathering oil and processing it. You need to assemble your raw resources in a series of factories and combine them in the right order. You need to spend the time and resources to research this technology. And you need to consider whether you should have spent the time on other more important things like building up military defenses.
More than anything you start to think of transportation. How do you get all your products to the right location? Do you want to ship everything by train? Do you want to make an elaborate conveyor system? Do you want to deliver everything with robots?
The part I find genius about this game is that it forces you to think like an engineer. You start to think of things like flow rate of your resources, efficiency of your production, cost-benefit of building certain factories or researching certain technologies. It all sounds really boring but it's not! You just constantly try to improve your creations while you are playing, and that gives the game a massive amount of depth and replayability.
I also love the real-world implications that are layered all over. Did you decide to have everything coal-powered and dump pollution all over your base? You are going to get attacked relentlessly by hostile creatures. Were you going way too overboard with solar energy and renewables? You are going to get really unreliable energy supplies. Did you spent enough resources on military or did you go overboard? Did you really need to build those atom bombs and ICBMs??
I think I've explained enough about the game mechanics, so let's focus on other aspects. The music is great and really adds to the feel of the gameplay. The story -- it's technically nonexistent the same way story is absent in Terraria and Minecraft. I don't really have a problem with that since the gameplay more than compensates for it.
How about the graphics? Yes it's a 2D game that looks a little basic but I think the art is fine. I will counter any criticisms of the graphics with this argument: the game performance is perfect, which is absolutely important. You can have a hundred different factories with thousands of components and the game still runs smoothly. And this is simply not the case for a game like Minecraft, which ran terribly once there were too many entities created.
Overall, I have almost no complaints about Factorio. I'm sure not everyone will enjoy this game, but at the same time I think it appeals to a lot of gamers. I want to say I think it's flawless as it is in beta. It's an extremely well-designed game and it blows away similar games. It's a game I can easily spend hours at a time playing and has a huge amount of replayability.

Momodora III is a short action platformer. It is the third game in the Momodora series, but you do not have to play the other Momodora games first. I recommend you buy Momodora Reverie Under the Moonlight instead of this game if you haven't played it. Reverie under the Moonlight is the fourth game in the series, but it's a prequel and doesn't require you to have played the others. If you've already played Momo IV (or it doesn't interest you), then I recommend you play the first two Momodora games first. They're free; play them first! Now onto actually talking about Momodora III.
Momodora III's combat system is a lot like the system in Momodora II. The combat system mainly consists of melee attacks. Enemies also drop money which you can use to buy items to improves your character. The 'ceremonial fabric' item is incredibly overpowered, especially in hard mode, so don't use it because it will ruin the experience. The combat feels much better than in Momo II. The gameplay is fun, and the bosses are cool. It's a little easy at times, but I definitely still found it enjoyable. The game's graphics are very nice and colorful. The music is good too. My biggest complaint is the game's story. It features some NPCs I liked, but there's no real point where the story is explained to the player. Towards the beginning, you meet a girl named Mariel; she is the only way the story is explained in the game. You should know this so you don't spend 1/2 the game waiting for a proper exposition. The steam page does a better job at telling you the story than the actual game. There is an online manual
. If you go there, you can read the story and about the characters; I recommend you read it before you play. Momodora III was pretty short and didn't feel like it had a real beginning, middle, or end. The game is linear (like Momo 1 but unlike 2 and 4). There are lots of secrets, and getting all the achievements is fun and not too hard. I recommend it if you've played 1 and 2 and enjoyed 2. Personally, It's worse than 2, but it's still fun and improves on a lot of things which weren't the greatest in 2. Momodora III is also extremely cheap!
If you enjoy Metroidvania games than you should definitely play this. It's a short little adventure that's worth playing.

Ok, so following all the bad reputation this game has, I had to try it out.  I understand for backers are angry because they probably paid more than they should for this game.  Albeit, it's not the prettiest game.  When I start up the game, the prologue stage was pretty good, arguably the best stage of the game.  But when you get to the actual stages of the game, that's when the reviews start to either like or dislike the game.  The stages are not reminiscent of Megaman.  The only thing that reminds Megaman fans of the famous Blue Bomber is that you get to choose the order of stages to tackle on first, fight "Robot Masters" or Might Numbers in this case, and get special weapons from the bosses.  Other aspects of the game are not reminisent of Megaman.  The dash mechanic, personally, is a kinda cool mechanic in this game.  Depending on which enemy you absorb when dashing would give Beck a buff.  Buffs can vary from movement speed to penetrating shots, it can help Beck out in lots of ways.  Unfortunately, only certain enemies that you absorb can fill up your "E-Tank" or "AcXel Recover," your healing for a stage.  The stages are pretty hard as well and have nothing special about them or present anything new that we haven't seen before.  The dialogue and voice acting is a bit cheesy, to which I affiliate with Infanue and any of his previous projects with Megaman, so I kinda expected it.  The music in the game kinda sounds the same throughout the game.  There are no notable tracks when you are playing except for 2 or 3 music tracks.  If you want to hear semi-decent retro music, turn the Retro BGM option in the General Settings Menu for a better listening experience.  Overall, the game is ok.  It's not good but it's also not that bad as people claim.  If I was a backer and paid more than 20 dollars to back the game, I would be pretty angry, so this is a review from someone who watched the development of the game from a distance.  If you are looking to buy the game to be expecting it to be a spiritual successor to Megaman, do not get this game.  If you are buying this game expecting it to be a different experience from Megaman, you might just get that from this game.  Shortly, this game is ok.  It's that game that just falls in the middle and hopefully more people can see that.  But if they don't, they are entitled to their own opinion.

I played this game pretty much right after it came out (I was a backer) and frankly loved it. Then I look at the steam/internet reviews and am thoroughly suprised. There is a lot of disapointment that I feel is kind of misplaced.
Yes the dash mechanic takes some getting used to, but honestly I love that you have unlimited air dashes. It let's you try to save yourself if you miss a platform by dashing back to the previous couple platforms. Once you get used to it you can move fairly freely wherever you want.
All the bosses' weapons are unique and interesting to use. I stuck with the main gun for most of my playthrough but there were places where using the right weapon in the right way can really save you and make you feel super satisfied. Ray's weapons in particular were great, they added whole new ways to play with her character and introduced a new dimension of difficulty in choosing which weapon to equip and when. The weapon swapping is cluncky (you have to tab through a menu while in game to choose your weapon), but I feel like it was an intentional choice by the developers to add difficulty to the weapon mechanics.
The difficulty was just right for me. I just finished both Beck and Ray's paths on normal and found myself having to retry every couple of stages 2 or 3 times. This is exactly the feel the classic Mega Man games gave me, challenging with patterns you have to memorize, but when you fail it's your fault. I'll probably give the harder difficulties a try later and am expecting that same challenge.
The graphics are a great 2.5D, there's a few places where you have to get used to enemies in the background and the parallex scrolling can throw you off, but other than that the graphics are nice and smooth without getting in the way of the gameplay.
The story was pretty intriguing, but I played with the Japanese voices on and am fluent enough to understand what was being said. Some of the lines were translated poorly/changed the nature of the characters, so I can understand being upset with the English version of the story. Even then, the basic premise is really cool. Your view changes as you gain more information about the world and the characters come to life. If there's a sequel(I hope) they could do some really interesting stuff with character development.  I haven't listened to the English voice acting, but it wouldn't surprise me if it was bad.
Finally, one of the best things about this game is there are few to no bugs or cheap methods for getting through. You can really feel that the developers made sure it was complete before releasing it, which is something I haven't felt from most mainstream games in a long time. Some people seem to be complaining about the mechanics and controls, but they were the best part for me. The fact that you absorb weakened enemies, and the sooner you absorb them the better, gives the game a different kind of challenge and urgency. Once you start on a room or hallway, you have to keep going, rushing into a new enemy's line of fire while trying to absorb one you've defeated means you have to constantly be on your toes.
All and all this might become one of my new favorite games, beating out quite a few of the old Mega Man and Mega Man X games. I think people started having unrealistic expectations for this game due to how over-funded it was, but games are hard to make, and there were a lot of stretch goals the developers achieved with that extra funding. It's well polished and a blast to play. I agree it's rather short, but with the challenges and different difficulties I can see myself playing it for a long time.

I can't recommend this game enough.

The game's so ridiculously hard to take seriously (ironic, huh?) and ridiculously hard in general that I just cannot recommend it.
Serious Sam 2 is basically what happens if someone took a Serious Sam game and tried to make it appeal to 2nd graders. Which is ironic considering it's obscene difficulty even in lower difficulty modes. The guns have no oomph, projectiles are so miniscule that they're impossible to dodge; the game looks and feels like a kiddie shooter. It's *probably* worth buying when it's on sale for modding or multiplayer; but games like Quake and Doom out-do this game so hard that it's really hard to turn to this game for that.
Also, it's probably worth noting that bad voice-acting, ridiculous weapon models, and out-of-place enemy design PLAGUE this game. The rando pseudo-Cortana that eggs Sam on sounds like she belongs in an iPad coin-pusher game, the guns look like they would be the heaviest things to blast someone with but the sound effects are so ♥♥♥♥ing stock and weak that they're just a nuisance to use, and the enemies are either ripped from a doom 3 mod, or made in 5 minutes with SculptGL.
Really the only thing this game gets right is the level design, but it's kinda hard to enjoy it when you're getting 300 1-hit-gib enemies thrown at you with your only tool being a shotgun with a really slow RoF. (Circle-strafing doesn't work; AI's been programmed to predict movement)

Plague Inc: Evolved is an "updated" version of the mobile game Plague Inc. developed by Ndemic Creations. The game's objective is simple, infect the world and kill everyone
The game is really simple to get the hang of but hard to master as trying to infect the whole world isn't easy. To infect the world, you must select a country of origin, then select a method of transmission (either from livestock, blood, rats, etc...), symptoms (such as vomiting, insanity, etc...) and also the ability of the virus (cold and hot resistance, resistance to drugs, etc...)
Not only that, but scientists and doctors are trying to stop you from spreading the virus through a cure which you have to stop by any means. The game is fun to play and includes a lot of stuff to experiment on including the virus from the Dawn of the Planet of the Apes film
However, the gameplay is mostly the same. Pop red bubbles to spread the virus, pop orange bubbles to gain points to evolve the virus and pop blue bubbles to slow the cure from processing and you have to just assume that the virus will infect the world. The game isn't easy and can get repetitive very quickly however the game is fun to play in short bursts
Plague Inc: Evolved has an interesting yet terrifying premise, infect the world, which is both scary yet oddly educational and fun to do... let's just hope this never happens in real life

I am reviewing this having twice tried to play the game. I find it thoroughly unenjoyable, yet I keep coming back to try it again to remind myself why I dislike it. My only theory as to why I do this is that EA Games has mastered the use of Stockholm Syndrome as a marketing device.
Of the myriad faults I find in this game, the worst offender is the gameplay. You control a soldier who appears to suffer from an impairment of the inner ear. He bobs and weaves in a manner which falls quite short of what I can only assume is intended to be "realistic". This bobbing and swaying, in conjunction with the wild bucking of any firearm you so much as point at an enemy, resulted in my experiencing a wave of nausea much akin to that one might experience during a screening of ‘The Blair Witch Project’ or ‘Cloverfield’ ( these being two films I also don't recommend). This sensation encouraged me to try and take cover and move around as little as required, however as you walk at a speed rivalled by the still life paintings of Norman Rockwell (which is to say, very, very slowly) you will likely find yourself holding down the movement buttons out of necessity to keep up with your better balanced compatriots.
Speaking of your teammates, I would like it noted that I find the decision to send a group of people stricken with acute cognitive delay into combat to be highly questionable both in efficacy and ethic. While at first I found their penchant for calling out enemy locations only after being struck by several bullets to be endearingly inept, but I soon realized there were more tragic circumstances as to why my teammates were performing so poorly. This epiphany came to me when I witnessed the entire team hunkering down, unable to progress due to a sole enemy soldier, blocking their way as he stood amidst his fallen comrades. The enemy soldier refused to retreat, presumably due either to his being  left in a fugue state after having his peers gunned down before his eyes, or to outright confusion at the sudden cowardice offered by this pack of bloodthirsty operatives he had singlehandedly pinned down behind some barrels nearby. I winced and sported a sympathetic if pained expression when I hear my team speak up,
"Help us out here… I think there's one left!"
I would like to take this opportunity to commend the American military for its equal opportunity hiring practices. It was very clear that these developmentally impaired patriots were doing the best they could muster in the battlefield. It wasn’t their lack of fire support or situational awareness, rather it was their heart and indomitable spirit in the face of adversity that won me over and brought a tear to my eye.
Finally, I would steer people away from this game because of the "story", told by means of a cut scene every other firefight/10 minutes of gameplay. It would be offering undue charity to pose that the plot "makes no sense". Indeed, I suspect it may have been created using a computer program developed  in the passing of Tom Clancy in an attempt to generate ridiculous politically charged plotlines for retail media (I have also theorized that Tom Clancy himself may well have been this computer program all along). At any rate, the plot is childishly non sequitur, having the player span the globe fighting Russian troops (!?) to secure a mysterious weapon developed by the Japanese during WWII. All of which renders what are earlier presumed to be attempts at realism thoroughly obsolete.
If you're interested in a different take on the standard FPS, by all means give this a shot, but be warned: The plot, in all probability, was the result of a mad lib, you move about like an inebriated penguin with the gout, and your team offers new meaning to "special" forces.

Battlefield Bad Company 2 is definitely one of the best looking games in the franchise when it was released. Destruction is in this game and is used to great effect and does feel like a novel innovation that was great on release comapred to Levoution which is an abomination to the franchise and is best left forgotten. Gunplay feels weighted, could be better in terms of response but the diverse selection of weapons and maps makes it a worthy purchase. Though some problems appear;
PC version, however, does feel much better due to mouse control, uncapped framerate and overall ability to see stuff beyond 90 degrees of vision.It however suffers from a massive influx of cheaters due to the outdated nature of Punkbuster.
Hit registration simply doesn't translate that well in aspects of lag compensation which is to say - it's far more balanced in showing the animations in synchronisation to their hurtboxes than BF2 and BF3/4 but is still considerably ♥♥♥♥ awful for what they intended as a 'open-ended sandbox FPS of the next generation'. Expect to hit a target only to find his flinch animation and the client-side verification didn't actually register the hit due to traffic choked/malformed packets or lag switching.
And it has a terrible single-player - which became a thing for the Battlefield series for some inexplicable reason until BF1... I admire the attempt of the campaign but it's worse than Battlefield Bad Company 1's and is excessively linear. Lasting less than 5 hours at best, on absolutely highest difficulty sports some comedic character development, miitary satire and not much else. The ending is a cliffhanger that has not been concluded yet and no development schedule or listings have confirmed BC3.
No longer worth the purchase due to a high influx of cheaters, outdated gameplay and arguably the worst hit-registration seen in any game yet.

The game itself is a fairly solid and fun game... with a little bit of repetition in the gameplay and levels... you can expect to see most of the enemies you will encounter within a couple levels and encounter various types of them throughout the game as it escalates. The PC release of the game has some issues... some that specifically I will go further into detail later in this review.
The story is the best part of the game. If you can deal with all of the PC issues of this port and you are a Star Wars fan then the story is definitely one worth getting through. You play as a secret apprentice to Darth Vader and it has some nice tie ins to the original movies... It takes place inbetween episodes 3 and 4 respectively. This edition also contains several other add ons to the original and while fun and some cool levels they felt tacked on to the story and unessential.
The gameplay is pretty fun and from the first level (which I will not spoil for you but has a very cool playable character) where you really see what kind of power you will harness in the game to the later levels where you are a finely tuned killing machine is fast and rewarding. I played through on the hardest difficulty setting which I would not recommend... It is not well balanced and some parts are almost entirely reliant on luck... although playing on the normal difficult level after felt like a breeze in comparison. This is a game that you are supposed to feel like a bad♥♥♥♥♥and it really keeps upping the ante with the abilities you gain access to in an RPG style of progression that rewards you for exploring and playing well.
The graphics while dated are not terrible but are plagued with some issues I will go into detail. Overall the cutscenes are pretty good though. Like I said previously there are some audio and visual glitches in the game when it was ported. The audio cuts out partially in the last two levels (and also in earlier levels for some dialogue in my experience). These nearly ruined the experience for me as it was very removing from the game which at first I was really enjoying and I got caught up in trying to remedy this. There is a slight patch someone made (unnofficial) on the steam forums but it may or may not work correctly. I still experienced some slight problems and was never able to repair some visual glitch that happens almost every time I use force push (which is fairly often) Also occasionally I would find my character caught on invisible objects or have enemies spawn in randomly out of nowhere due to me clipping into an area where I was not supposed to be for a battle and I am unable to view the enemies nor navigate to them to kill them and thus wind up being killed by blaster fire from an invisible enemy.
I cannot recommend the PC version of the game to anyone who can get the console version. The Devs have all but abandoned this at this point and there is no hope of the problems that are hurting this otherwise decent game of being fixed at any point. While it is a fun game and I enjoyed playing it there are many better games out there today. If you are a big fan of Star Wars than by all means pick it up but do so  with caution and you may want to consider waiting until it goes on sale.

When I was pretty little I was obessed with warrior cats and the previous game by the developer "Warrior Cats: Untold Tales." So of course, when I heard about this game, I was overcome with a wave of nostalgia. The fact that I really like games like Stardew Valley (which this game takes some inspiration from) was a bonus.
Although, having played a similar game from this developer, I was a little dissappointed when I began playing. I remember things like significant predator encounters, the chance of deadly cars on the roads, random npc encounters, quests to gain jobs and perks, the ability to build your own colony, and special perks unique to each colony in the previous project. Those things had a lot of charm which I found this game lacking a bit of.
Thats not to say this game doesn't do a lot of things right. The npcs are way more fleshed out, with full personalities and likes and dislikes that the player has to pay attention to, as opposed to just spamming them with "shiny objects" to gain affection. The music is beautiful, and the graphics and animations have a lot of heart. The game has a nice storyline so far, and although it is lacking the apprentice quest system, it has a very nice stardew-inspired quest system in it's place. Kits dont just sit there and do nothing. Overall, the gameplay is better. It's clear that a lot of hard work went into this project, and I wouldn't be surprised if some of the things I mentioned earlier were added in future updates. There's still so much to be descovered- these are just my first impressions!!
Overall, I totally recommend this game.

What you need to know is, this is the kind of game that grows on you as time passes. In the first few days, I didn't like it at all, and actually wrote an unfavorable review. But, after the first season, I saw past the cons and discovered how much the game had to offer. (Some people say that the game gets repetitive, and sometimes it does, but you have to remember that it will be updated, and every time you repeat something, it usually takes you closer to your next goal.)
PROS:
+Beautiful graphics
+Interesting gameplay
+Diverse amount of characters
+Lots of polish, clearly had much work put into it
+Very pleasant soundtrack
+Creative ideas and designs for characters and settings
+Much better A.I. for the NPCs than in some other games.
CONS:
-You seem to have less purpose than you did in the developers' other, although less professional, great game called Warriors: Untold Tales. (Which this game draws from for its battle mechanics and foraging techniques.) Part of what made that game fun was the nostalgia it invoked in fans and the sense of duty and belonging in the clan. You would work hard to support your friends and family, giving you a reason to hunt and survive every day. Sadly, in this game, there's not much in the way of achieving rank and honor, or supporting anyone else. No one relies on you to feed them. This takes away some of the objective and motivation from the game.
-Difficulty with the main story mode. The main story mode starts out easy. You must capture a few different types of prey, which are all common. But when you unlock the first pillar, the others demand you find vaguely rare prey like catfish, and with the really short days, trying to balance taking care of your mate, finding time to return to base and sleep, and foraging, the tasks become drawn out.
Overall, this game is wonderful. Don't get it if you only play FPS games like Call of Duty and Halo, but for anyone who's willing to experiment, this game provides a quite entertaining time, and you won't want to stop playing. (Speaking of which, there seems to be lots of playtime involved.) This game gets an 8.5/10 from me.

I was really looking forward to this game, and I have to say, I'm disappointed.
It's a well-made game, and you can see a lot of effort went into it, but it's just - nothing. It's not substantial. There really is not much to do. It plays fantasticaly, the graphics and music are great, but the gameplay is extremely lacking. Once you're past the tutorial, there's no direction, no guide, no goal. I understand the idea of an open ended game, but this isn't like Stardew Valley, where you know from the beginning you're supposed to be rebuilding a farm, and the game allows you to go about doing that however you want. In Cattails, there's just nothing. There is an optional story, I think, but it doesn't seem to have much of an impact on the game. You can ... hunt ... fight ... get ... married ?
And don't get me wrong, all those mechanics are great. This game is just not worth fifteen dollars, and I was not prepared for the lack of content. If you're fine with super open-ended gameplay where you really just ... wander around ... and you think that's worth fifteen dollars, then by all means, get Cattails. If not - wait for a sale, or avoid altogether.
Also, a lot of people are comparing this game to Warrior Cats, and while I get it, don't come into this game expecting a Warrior Cats-like experience. You don't have a specific role or purpose in your colony - there's no sense of community. Conversations are repetitive and impersonal. So, if you're looking for the experience of being in an Erin Hunter book, don't look here.
edit: relax everybody. i know i haven't played very long - and that playtime was even over the course of two days. either way, my main point was that this game is not worth 15.00. i have read and understand your criticism - take or leave this review.

You can be sure of three things when playing a game from Supergiant games: It will be fun, the art and world will be absorbing, and the ending will be heavier than Havel’s armor from dark souls. Transistor is the shortest game I have played in a while, being generously 10 hours, maybe 15 if you want to play through a newgame+, but it earns keep. Its story and world are the most unique I have ever seen in a game, with a climax and ending that left me just stunned. The sound design in this game is also phenomenal, between the narrator, the soundtrack, and all of the gameplay elements, it meshes extremely well to help guide you through the game’s disorienting settings. Transistor brings several new ideas to the table, while also providing a decent amount of depth. The difficulty system is one of the best difficulty systems I have seen in a game, giving you full health for each fight and encouraging you to add limiters which ultimately makes each battle push you to your limit. The combat takes place in a weird mixture between realtime and turn-based, with both combat styles have their advantages and weaknesses. However, the crowning jewel of this game is its customization of abilities. There are 16 different powers in the game, which by itself would create a lot of different combos, but every single power can also be used as a passive, with up to four passives being available at one time, AND each active power can be MODIFIED by up to two powers. There’s a bajillion different ways to play this game, and the real fun lies in figuring out which abilities work best with eachother. It may be short, but the time you spend in this game will be some of the highest quality video gaming you will ever encounter.

Transistor is a action-strategy game playing from an isometric top-down view from the creators of Bastion. The combat system is what I can only call a blend of Megaman Battlenetwork and Boktai or Hyper Light Drifter. It is an isometric hack-n-slash in between the turn based planning times. There is a huge customization aspect to the game, allowing for near limitless amounts of ability combinations and ways to play. The story is not directly told to the player, which I didn't like at first, but as you progress through the game it becomes apparent what is going on. It is a short game, with the average play through taking about 4 hours. I enjoyed it so much through that I went for 100% completion and sunk 27 hours into it. For a game that costs as little as $5 it was worth every penny.

I will start off by saying this:
This game is absolutely incredible.
You are a mighty viking warrior who had succumbed to the darkness of death, only to awaken onto the grassy plains of the Nordic afterlife. You are given a second chance into greatness, to prove that you are to be welcomed to the halls Valhalla by defeating the Jotun that stand in your way. The lore is spoken to you in the Nordic tongue and it really brings that sense of viability to the game.
The game is unique in it's way of visuals. Instead of using computer graphics, they use animation. You can see the sketchlines used in creating the massive bosses that you are put up against. I admire their 'wholesome' aspect because it felt like it came through someone's no. 2 pencil and their imagination, instead of regurgitated computer 3D renderings.
The soundtrack left me in awe as I was thrust into a fast-paced battle with beings that are more than 100 times my size.
The game itself isn't very long, but I got a decent few hours out of it. There is level hazards, other than the massive, towering bosses that you face against, and sometimes I felt like "well, that's a little unfair", especially during the final fight, where I find it borderline impossible to be able to surive the onslaught of everything, as well as dodge MASSIVE hitboxes, but despite the small irritations, I can't wait to see if there is more games like this from them. I hope the makers of this game do it again. Maybe with a different mythology! I'm a fan!

I really enjoyed playing this game. For anyone old enough to remember adventure book games, Choice of Robots is a must. I would also recommend it to anyone who likes RPGs or who is looking for a great story.
There is so much more depth to this game than many of the 'your choices matter' type of games. One review I read before buying CoR, recommended playing it exactly as you really would if it was real life. This was great advice as once you reach the end (well before that actually), the RPG mechanics become clear and it is a great experiment to see where you would end up. In further playthroughs you can try to shape the story depending on what ending you want to achieve and see if you can make it happen.
The story is immersive and interesting but I don't want to discuss it in any detail as I honestly think knowing too much beforehand will spoil the experience, especially in light of what I said above. What I will say instead is this:
By the end of CoR you will believe in the power you and your robot have to change the world. You will believe in your own autonomy as every decision you make ultimately shapes the kind of person you are to become. By the end you will like yourself more or less than you did before you started playing.
+ Great story
+ Fantastic RPG elements
+ You get to design and build your own robot
+ Interesting experiment to see whether you use your power for good or evil
+ Value for money. It's easily worth the £4 price tag and is an absolute bargain when on sale
- Text only format (this didn't bother me at all but it will be an issue for some)
- The high standard of writing does peter out a little towards the end

At the time I've written this review I've beaten all eight Mighty Numbers.
I am baffled by all the bad reviews, and while I can see why the kickstarter backers are angry it's no reason to be unfair to the game.
Now there are valid criticisms. The game could certainly look better, and the "cutscenes" if you can call them that are an abomination. The voice acting varies from great to terrible in the english version, and the story isn't great, but also not terrible.
But any criticism of the difficulty you read here is basically bs. Yes it's hard, sometimes unfairly hard. Some sections will probably kill you at least once before you know how to avoid them, or in the bosses cases, how to avoid their insta kill attacks.
But that's exactly what you'd expect from a megaman game. The only reason these games take a while on your first playthrough is because you have to basically learn the levels. And this game here is probably easier than any megaman game (outside of 2 on easy).
The controls are fine, it feels overall precise, but the dash messes that up a little. If you get used to it it's fine, and you can control the length of your dash a little. You have to get used to the dashing into enemies after they are stunned, but it took me little more than the intro level for that.
The only issue I have with this is that I really don't use any of the bosses weapons. They are not really that useful most of the time, and even in boss battles I have beaten all of these opponents with the standard weapon, not using their weakness.
Overall I'd say this game could be a lot better, and if I were a backer who paid more than the 20 bucks the game costs on steam I'd be angry too, because with that budget it should at least look better. (Looking at the trailer, the voice acting may be intentionally cringy).

A game that simultaneously tries too hard in some areas and doesn't try nearly hard enough in others. It mimics many negative aspects of 90s platformers, such as blind jumps, death pits, bosses with instant kill attacks, bosses that force you to wait until they can be damaged, and unforgiving checkpoints, while pretending the last 25+ years of advances in game design didn't happen. The English voice acting is passable and just the right amount of silly for a game with this kind of Saturday Morning Cartoon style.
The explosions look terrible, and the plastic-looking graphics without clear outlines make it difficult to tell what's in the background and what's in the foreground, bringing back bad memories of the awful art style of the PS1 Mega Man X and Mega Man 8. Mechanics that desperately need explaining are only explained in a menu you have to seek out yourself, but otherwise the number of tutorials and forced dialogue isn't nearly as bad as PS1 and PS2 era Mega Man X games. The game's movement physics feel fine at first, but the dash mechanic makes platforming slippery and clumsy.
The game has rare moments of smoothness and actual fun when you get into a flow during stages by shooting enemies and dashing through them, but the rest of the game is an un-fun slog that looks ugly even for a PS2 game and feels like garbage to play.
I regret backing this and wish it wasn't too late to get a refund, but at least it was only $40 of my money.

Oooooh, boy. Normally I love these hidden object games and am happy to suspend my disbelief for the genre's usual missteps (like cartoonishly large objects that defy the law of gravity, random anachronisms, lackluster characterization, and the whole "I've found the crucial piece of evidence I needed to solve my husband's murder, but first I need to find three more butterflies and an artichoke!" thing). But the story here is dull, the puzzles in between are easy but tedious and repetitive (time for a matching game! time for a slightly different matching game! hey, let's do that first matching game again!), and some of the Japanese characters are so stereotypical they make Mickey Rooney's character in Breakfast at Tiffany's look like a nuanced, sensitive performance.
Other issues: a hint meter that's really slow to recharge (which normally wouldn't be an issue for me but some of the artwork is so bad you literally can't distinguish one blob from another blob), a repetitive soundtrack, and the occasional need to click an object in exactly the right spot (which is annoying if you're trying for the achievements involving precision). Basically, this is a really lazily- and poorly-assembled game in almost every way. I spent around $1.25 on it and that was still way too much.

Easily among the Worst Games I Have Ever Played. Yes, I meant to capitalize that. It's not a terrible game in the sense that some old beat 'em up you like is a terrible game, but it's fun in a mindless, nostalgic kind of a way. No. This is just a HORRIBLE game.
The opening crawl is unskippable, a flashing silhouette of the game's unspeakably charmless protagonist reminding you to be patient as you watch a three-sentence lead-in fade into nothingness. But your journey is only beginning, young padawan.
You'll then take control of Lord Vader, arriving on Chewbacca's homeworld of Kashyyk to kill a "Rogue Jedi," whatever the frig that is. Vader stalks through the forest planet at an absolutely mercilessly slow trudge (no, you can't sprint), blasting force pushes that knock down literally everything into terrible, splintering masses of pre-realist-destruction, or slashing through the exact same model of Wookie (Wookiee? Wooky? Am I even a person anymore?), over and over again, until your eyes melt out of your head and chastize you for using them in such an unclean manner. And I won't lie - there's something that gets very "No Russian"-y about mowing down innocent creatures that have literally no chance of stopping you, made all the more surreally disturbing by the fact that it's the same model, making the same dying animal sound effects.
When you reach your quarry - a miserable, scrunched-up octogenarian spouting off "the force has corrupted your mind" cliches like they're going out of frigging fashion - the "boss fight" is literally just force throwing him at absolutely ludicrious distances and velocities, then waiting a few seconds until the old turd dusts himself off so you can do it again. Rinse and repeat several hundred times until you've knocked his health bar to a squinch and you get a prize! Nope, not a gun materializing from your screen and blowing your brains out for being so dreadfully stupid as to sit through that, but A QUICKTIME EVENT!
Once you've "Pressed E to Run the Old♥♥♥♥♥♥Through," you stumble across the last thing you expected to find in Star Wars: a young innocent that Darth Vader senses that the Force is strong in! How the 80-year-old man you just piledrived through Kashyyk City Hall sired a child on an alien planet with no females in sight is beyond me, but then again, so is how dozens of people got paid to make this steaming pile of what I can only assume are the liposuctioned remnants of George Lucas' neck fat.
A few dreary cutscenes later and you get some semblance of a tutorial, narrated by a robot assistant that, by its own cheery admission, is programmed to kill you (no follow up to the threat of death by the droid, incidentally).
After another mercifully brief and utterly confusing cutscene where you're introduced in earnest to Vader's moody protege-and-I-guess-step-son, "Starkiller," his spaceship's pilot, "Hot Australian Girl," and a rebel commander-or-maybe-Jedi-or-who-cares, you arrive on a bigger spaceship to - not even joking - kill a rogue Jedi. How rogue he has gone, I don't know, because when you show up there, everybody is shooting everybody, including you. Yes, Stormtroopers and "Militia" alike, further clouding the murky narrative you just spent between $3 and $50 on. But hey! At least you're in control of the protagonist, and more importantly, you can run (even if it is actually just a dash move that you have to keep jabbing at the key for until your finger considers launching an armed insurrection).
And run you shall - through the boring, console-optimized landscape of low-poly environments and splotchy textures and the same three models of enemies. Fortunately, there are loading icons every few yards to punctuate the inanity of your experience and remind you you're not actually stuck in a time loop, flickering in and out almost imperceptibly as a horribly engineered game tries to cope with the fact that a system might be able to accommodate more than a few hundred linear feet of lifeless, repetitive environments.
Combat is awful - take everything you've grown to love about titles like "Arkham Asylum" and then forget it. This game drinks the tears of games with good combat, lavishing in them like a Thomas Harris serial killer and dancing nude to an 80s synth pop song while you huddle, terrified and apalled in the corner, rocking back and forth wondering what went wrong that lead you to this point. "I should've listened to my parents," you'll think as you press the slash key to slash, over and over again. Get bored of slashing and want to run ahead? Nope, the genius developers have thought of that with an old trick from 1993 called "invisible walls." You can also force-throw things in an attempt to break up the monotony, but whatever eye♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥they hired to design these environments apparently snorted so much meth that they made literally everything throwable, so more often then not you're throwing one of the forty-six throwable objects on screen you DIDN'T mean to throw. Oh, and the selection is camera-agnostic - meaning that you'll have to align your character's bearing, not the camera's, to select the thing.
But all of this has a silver lining - I got so fed up of looking for whatever object I was supposed to force-throw to complete a *cough* "puzzle" that I ended up quitting the game, uninstalling it, and vowing to really rethink my life choices. Which I will get to just as soon as I wrap my head around how an army of infuriated nerds hasn't found Haden Blackman and bludgeoned him to death with their limited edition copies of this game.

PC version, however, does feel much better due to mouse control, uncapped framerate and overall ability to see stuff beyond 90 degrees of vision.It however suffers from a massive influx of cheaters due to the outdated nature of Punkbuster.
Hit registration simply doesn't translate that well in aspects of lag compensation which is to say - it's far more balanced in showing the animations in synchronisation to their hurtboxes than BF2 and BF3/4 but is still considerably ♥♥♥♥ awful for what they intended as a 'open-ended sandbox FPS of the next generation'. Expect to hit a target only to find his flinch animation and the client-side verification didn't actually register the hit due to traffic choked/malformed packets or lag switching.
And it has a terrible single-player - which became a thing for the Battlefield series for some inexplicable reason until BF1... I admire the attempt of the campaign but it's worse than Battlefield Bad Company 1's and is excessively linear. Lasting less than 5 hours at best, on absolutely highest difficulty sports some comedic character development, miitary satire and not much else. The ending is a cliffhanger that has not been concluded yet and no development schedule or listings have confirmed BC3.
No longer worth the purchase due to a high influx of cheaters, outdated gameplay and arguably the worst hit-registration seen in any game yet.

This review is for the game ''Battlefield: Bad Company 2'' an action first-person shooter video game.
Developer:EA Digital Illusions CE
Publisher:Electronic Arts
Series:Battlefield
Platforms:Microsoft Windows, iOS, Kindle Fire, PlayStation 3, Xbox 360
Release dates:March 2, 2010
Plot
You take control of Preston Marlowe,one of the ''Bad Company'' member,for most of the narrative story(only exception is during the first mission which is set prior to the main campaign).As the main protagonist you will have to complete a series of objectives and kill most of the enemies in order to complete each chapter,while your A.I allies will help you in doing so.
The campaign circles around a secret scalar weapon for which you will pretty much circle around the globe.From Russia you will head to Bolivia,then to Chile,a little later to Ecuador,and lastly you will land in U.S Texas.In every country you will engage the Russians,sabotage French weather satellites in order to retrieve intelligence and ultimately struggle to capture Colonel Arkady Kirilenko,the main antagonist of the game and the leader of the Russian Army.
Kirilenko,after escaping a couple of times,finally manages to siege the weapon,Operation Aurora,and uses it at the city of Quito.Apparently the weapon emits a powerful electomagnetic pulse rendering every technological equipment useless.Knowing that Kirilenko with the help of a large cargo aircraft and his battling squads of South American and Russian troops flies towars the United States.His attempt to fire the weapon again fails,though.
In the end you destroy scalar weapon and the explosion destroys the aircraft,forcing your squad to bail out.Kirilenko attempts to escape one last time only to be killed from you and then be saved from Sweetwater(one of your squad members).The squad lands in Texas but much to the squads displeasantness they are assigned another mission,to stop the incoming Russian invasion that was passing through Canada and Alaska.
Gameplay
Primarily a first-person shooter but allowing the use of vehicles,tanks,helicopters.Wide variety of customizable weapons such as assault rifles,machine guns,small arms like pistols with the use of modifications such as iron sights,reflex sights or telescopic sights.Health can be regenerated when not being hit.You can jump,sprint,crouch and swim but not for too long.
Recap
A fine game in my opinion.Game's engine (Frostbite 1.5) allows for destructible environments which is really cool.The story is very consistent.And gameplay's quite difficult.Only downside is that game is kind of small.Mutliplayer has endless replay value though.A must buy in my opinion.
P.S I didn't review the game's multiplayer because it's kind of dead.Everybody is playing newer versions of the Battlefield series such as Battlefield 3 or the newest title Battlefield 4.
Have fun and don't forget to support the Developers!

I've looked at the 'Farming Simulator' games with a sort of confusion for years, who would play this sort of game and why?
Well let me tell you who and why. Me and because it's some of the best zen gaming I've ever played. There's no shooting or getting shot at, no rushing against a time limit, no impending doom or limited ammo. Farming Simulator is chilled out gaming, sure you can have huge farm with tons of stuff going on and rush around managing it or you can just cut some trees down with your trusty chainsaw (of which there are a few to choose from) load the logs into your pickup and sell them at the yard.
There's loads (and I mean loads!!) of farm machinery to buy and even more available for free via a very simple to use modding community. I now know my tedders from my wind-rowers.
Seriously, at the current sale price you'd be a loon not to give this a go if you've ever wondered about driving a combine or a tractor.

I know, I know, I know. It seems realllly boring at first and makes no sense. I'll be the first to admit it's not for everyone. But if you are as detail-oriented and obsessive as me, you're probably familiar with the satisfaction that comes with accomplishing a difficult and complex organizational task. Add a militaristic twist on this and you'll enjoy this game a lot. One thing that I particularly like about this compared to most other building games where one building type clearly leads to the upgrade of another is that there isn't necessarily one ideal or most efficient form of the factory you're meant to be building in this game. You can really get creative with how you arrange your resources depending on your play style and even entertain other creative objectives or goals in the process. Loads of complex fun and satisfaction when you finally fix that bug in your factory so that everything is completely automated and performs smoothly.

I very rarely buy games for even close to the full price, and I honestly think that Factorio is completely worth it.
I've restarted countless times just to try to make things a little neater, or advance a little quicker, not that I've even come close to 'finishing' the game, and I'm not starting to tire of it yet.
Having a friend to play with makes it even more fun, but also frustrating as they never put things in the right place.
If you're a fan of the style, with enjoyable, tedious, and never ending expansion and improvement, just get the game, you won't regret it.

A breath of fresh air from the last hidden object game I reviewed, Season of Mystery: The Cherry Blossom Murders is a fairly decent, and lovely hidden object game! You play as Irene Pemberton, who moves to Japan with her beloved husband, Richard Pemberton, to enjoy the calm atmosphere of the land of the rising sun. However, tradgedy strikes when her husband is found dead in his office. Police are quick to rule it as a suicide, leaving it up to you to find out who killed Richard, and why.
The storyline is quite good, and paced very well! A murder mystery, plenty of characters, and settings help to keep things fresh and interesting. Clearing rooms and puzzles is rewarded with more story, as well as character interacitons to keep the driving force going, and there is even a skip button for those who are not interested in the storyline. Interactions between characters is very good, and the characters have different personalities and views: Which may not sound like much, but I've seen some hidden object games with horribly bland characters that you wouldn't be able to differenciate between them if their names weren't listed.
The art? Lovely, absolutely lovely. It's easy to tell that love and work was put in to the different characters, to make them look unique and ensure that they don't 'blend together'. Yet another issue I've seen in some hidden object games, and even in other genres! So it's quite a lovely sight to see. It certainly made it more enjoyable to observe interactions between characters, something that would be a lot less fun if characters looked too similar to one another. Takes a lot of the individuality out when characters look like they were made from the same cookie cutter.
The scenery is yet another thing that was gorgeous to look at. Scenes were well crafted, and dare I say challenging with some, to find the objects scattered across them. I've seen hidden object games where the items just absolutely choaked the scene, making it hard to tell what was underneath even! However, here? You'll have issues finding some items, with how they blend in! Which does increase the difficulty, but certainly makes the items take a little less away from the scenery. Looks a lot less like someone took all their belongings and threw them around the area.
The music is pretty good too, nothing overly memorable, but it is nice, albeit repetitive at times. It doesn't sound so much like Japanese music, so much as mystery music. Had they made more of a effort by adding some music with a violin and/or flute, it would set the mood a bit more, as well as provide some extra soundtrack to cycle through. But, if all else fails, there's always muting it and then playing Zen music in the background for that oriental feel.
The objects hidden amongst the scenes is actually well done! And, thankfully, they are randomized too! Sometimes the game'll give you a pretty easy deal, with pretty obvious placements. But if you get that, then expect tough-as-nails placements up ahead, making getting the "No hint" achievement more difficult to get. Playing cards are THE worst offender for "Most annoying to find" in this game... Or any game for that matter. The game does like to also mix up what you look for too, so if you're looking for three apples... Then expect maybe two apples, and the word 'apples'. Thankfully, there's silhouettes for the items when you click on their names on the list. Making it nice for beginners who could make use of it, or decent for those looking for a challenge, who can decide not to use it.
Minigames are also a blast. They certainly have a variety, making it fun to solve them! But there's always the skip button for those who can't solve them, however that forfeits getting certain achievements. There's one puzzle that repeats itself twice, but it's not that big a deal. Just a memory game where you flip the cards/shells and try to match them. The other puzzles are plentiful, and spice things up.
The fact that this game had achievements made me jump for joy. I absolutely love getting achievements in game, and this one was no exception. I got all the achievements in about two playthroughs, of which I would complain that it was a bit too easy... But, that's probably just because I've played these kind of games a lot, and am pretty dang good at them. It really depends on the person who plays, it'll provide a tough challenge for beginners. However with veterans to these kind of games, they'll probably breeze through it. So your mileage may vary there.

I will be playing through again to try to unlock the last few achievements and see if the objects to search for are randomly generated (as I suspect they might be). Granted the story doesn't change, but the items do randomize, not only in terms of the items to search for but also in terms of the extra items that appear.  On the plus side, some of the randomized items will be new to the scene, but on the minus, a specific item will always be in the same place.

Update June 9th, 2016.
Why is this game still being sold on Steam? It is now over 5 months since the developer has posted any information here or on social media about the game and over 7 (7!!) months since the game has received any software updates.
This game is a complete disgrace and tarnishes the Early Access program.
End update.
This game was released in Early Access on 25 July 2014. It is currently still in Alpha and since the developer has never bothered to release a road map it's unknown if, or even when, it is supposed to progress beyond its present state.
Sadly it's now over 5 months since the last software update and the developer, Touz, continues to ignore the Steam community. A brief posting by him on January 6th was a rehash of previous statements he's made but did nothing to instill confidence that the game is moving forward in any significant way.
Current game play is, quite frankly, boring. At one time there were multiplayer servers that allowed for PVP but the online community has vanished.
The singleplayer component is bare-bones and has no goal. Essentially it consists of running around and attempting to find components for weapons and other bits and pieces while trying to avoid enemy AI. That's it. The weapon crafting system is needlessly complex and there is absolutely no reason to build a base as the AI is not programmed to recognize player structures.
The lack of any progression system, storyline or end goal severely limit replayability. This is made worse by the small static map that comprises the player world . Once all areas have been explored there is nothing to draw the player further into the game since there is no 'further' to be had.
If you are interested in this game, I'd suggest you wait. If the developer decides to actually work on the game and make significant improvements it may be worth purchasing at a future date. Right now it would be a waste of money.
