Ignoring the abmisal community management, the unnecessary delays, and the offensive marketing, Mighty No. 9 is an utterly mediocre game.
It's not hidious (except for the explosion effects), but it's not particularly great looking.
It's not boring, but it's not super fun.
It's definitely inspired by MegaMan, but it does practically nothing to advance the genre.
In spite of having every reason and opportunity to do something new and creative, this game plays it utterly safe. It feels like a step backwards from MegaMan X.

There are a lot of reviews talking about how the game is horrible, but I just don't see it.
Mostly I get the impression it's just because of the hate many Kickstarter projects often get in general.
And people made it very clear they wanted to hate the game before there was anything to even play.
so here's my review of the game itself.
I like the dash. it didn't really need to be usable an unlimited number of times before touching the ground, but unless you already know what's up ahead you probably shouldn't be spamming it anyway, just like you shouldn't spam jump dashes in a new level of Mega Man X. You could hurt yourself. Should be common sense.
If you are replaying the level however, you probably want to go through more quickly, and you'll know enough about the level to maybe take the risk, so it saves you time getting back through.
So far just trying to stay in the air hasn't granted many opportunities to skip over much. since you would still need to get higher up than the enemies first anyway. so most of the time, if you can get over an enemy, there would have been nothing stopping you from doing the same with a single dash jump in Mega Man X anyway.
As for how the dash effects combat, I also like it.. most of the time. it's nice to see combat require more thought than just spam your fire button (or charge attacks) while jumping up and down depending on how high up the enemy is. you learn how quickly you can weaken the target, and get in close before it becomes unstable, to absorb them as quickly as you can, and restore ammo for whatever weapon you were using.
Or if you don't like it, you can just keep shooting them to blow them up, and completely ignore the mechanic.
What i don't like about the mechanic, is mostly just in a situational problem. if there are small weak enemies hiding in a crate, and I blow it up with explosives, they are damaged enough to become unstable, but not enough to out right die, so unless I can see them through the explosion effects, I end up running into them and taking damage.
personally I feel unless there's a good reason for it, like it's a boss, or it still has ways to attack, an unstable enemy shouldn't hurt you just for touching you. but that's still a small problem at it's worst.
The absorb mechanic I find leads me to actually using my other weapons throughout the levels themselves, instead of saving them for bosses. since if you are careful about it, you can restore ammo faster than you use it.
The graphics while nothing amazing, don't really bother me, from what I've seen so far, everything seems to be fitting the game's established style.
The levels don't really stick out as better or worse than most Mega Man levels either.
As for the cons
It has a small number of bugs yes. but it also JUST came out, what game comes out bug free these days?
At the time of writing this, there is a bug that happens on very rare occasion, that makes you keep running for about a 3rd of a second after letting go of left or right.
This is the worst I've seen in the game for problems with controls, and I've been playing with an Xbox 360 controller.
Annoying when it happens, but pretty minor.
Another bug, is the boss Pyrogen seemed to have some strange and oddly large hit boxes for some of his attacks than it looked like he should have. so it made finding a way to avoid him harder than it should have been.
Those I'm sure are only temporary, and will be fixed in a later patch.
The first instant kill trap I encountered, you are meant to be warned about. but it triggered before the characters could finish telling me.
It probably should have had the first one trigger in a spot where you wouldn't be in the way, so you know what to and look out for.
The voice acting, is not that good. but look up Mega Man 8 and you'll see this is nothing new. I find mighty No. 9's to be an improvement actually :P
And lastly, there is a part where you have to grab onto the side of a moving platform and hang there to get past some spikes. I don't feel the grab is reliable enough for the limited time you have to grab that, since if you grab from too high, you automatically step onto the platform instead. it needs more work, before unforgiving sections like that should be put in. or maybe lock you out from out right climbing up for parts like that at least.
tl;dr
Over all, I feel it's a good game, it feels like a Mega Man game, just with some new ways to go about things. and I've been enjoying my time with it.
So if you're a fan of Mega Man, you'll probably like this game.
If you are don't like mega man, you probably won't like it.
And if you already hated it before it even came out, then nothing would change you're mind anyway.

Momodora III is short.  It's one of the shortest games in my entire library; I certainly missed a number of things, but it was completed in around 35 minutes.  The price is fine, especially on sale, but I think the sequel is going to have more lasting appeal.
There's a couple cool features here (something about how the shopkeepers stock items- be it based on how quick you are, or randomly decided) and there's a general competence in the game, but Momodora III is probably not the kind of game that will stick with you over the years.  Small but detailed pixel art, simple combat and bosses, equippable items and quick platforming are all endearing; it's a stepping stone for the developer as much as it is for a player. If you want a breezy afternoon game you can knock out in less than an hour (or speedrun), this won't disappoint you.  It just won't wow you, either.

(NOTE: This review was made on an IPad. If it looks funky, that's why.)
So, for those of you who want a quick answer, yes, get this game. You will (most likely) not regret it.
Now for the more detailed analysis; this game, in its current state, is pretty dang fun. I've fiddled around with all the games major selling points and am pretty satisfied. For example, most survival games have guns that are pre-made and can't be modified aside from, for example, throwing a scope or silencer on it. TFD features weapons that can be modified and upgraded using gun parts you loot from the world. This makes acquiring a weapon pretty hard early on (though you can occasionally find an assembled weapon), but it also opens up many possibilities for your arsenal. Don't like the slide on your pistol? Simply switch it out with another, possibly better, slide. Want to decrease the weight of your weapon? Switch out the handle, shave off a little extra weight. And there's plenty more you can do with this, believe me. There is also a base construction system in place. It can be a little finicky at times, but all over all it's pretty easy to build yourself a structure, granted you get the resources to build it out of. Speaking of which, there is a hacking mechanic involved. I say this now because scattered around the map are harvesters that can be hacked to collect resources for you. Despite what other reviews are saying, it's incredibly easy to hack something. There is a bit of a command prompt, but all you need to do to hack a machine is to type in two commands; one right after the other. That's it. You can hack anything that moves (aside from players, of course). The enemies are particularly hard to deal with, but running away from them is a pretty easy thing to do until you have a gun and ammo. And looting, despite what people are saying, is relatively smooth. Not Rust smooth, mind you, but satisfactory none the less. The community is very small and the wiki is REALLY out of date, so you're going to be learning most of how to do things on your own. And the developers have not abandoned this game, they just released a bug-fix update not too long ago.
All over all, TFD is pretty worth the money. Yes, you're going to run into a bug or two; it's an alpha, it's going to do that. This is a hard game. My advice, save often and keep going. For those who enjoy a challenge, this should provide what you seek.
And the all-important rating: (drumroll) 9/10

This game is downright GORGEOUS, the hand drawn works really well. The game mechanics are varied and entertaining and the difficulty is good, leaning towards hard. I like that the game encourages and rewards exploration. The narrative and how it gives steady information about the Nordic mythology is also great.

The journey is the destination, and with Jotuns focus on artistic style, I found it to be quite a pleasant journey. The boss fights were funnily enough the weaker points of the game for me, with the requirement to learn how to beat them through trial, error and repetition being the most "game like" part of the game.

In the beginning you hear an introduction to the story of Thora, a mighty female viking warrior. As you play you take her on her quest for redemption, and as each level is completed, the story continues to unfold. It's an epic tale of bravery, death, treachery, and revenge.
The graphics are beautiful, and the music is great, everything is drawn and animated by hand with very little digital assistance, so it looks and feels like you're playing an old Disney cartoon from the early years - which is a thing you don't see often anymore. And the orchestrated music brings every moment to life.
As you play through the levels, you gain powers from the various gods of Norse mythology - Freyja, Thor, Loki, and others. Their powers will help you in defeating the Jotun Giants, but even with their help, it's not an easy task. It's not hard though, either. At least, not in concept. Each boss is basically "whack at it until it dies", and you don't have to do it in any specific spot.  But each Jotun has it's own mechanic to go along with it - making things not so easy, So defeating them is easier said than done. But it CAN be done.
I think the only negative side to it all is that, as great as this game is - the experience is a short one. There's 5 areas to play with 1 or 2 levels each - 9 levels total, plus the Jotun levels, making 14. I think a DLC package would be nice one day - to include the 4 other worlds they did not make, and add a lot more playtime to it. Maybe a few more powers from the Gods as well. I admit that even though I'm not finished yet, I only have a little over 10 hours of playtime, and already finished 4 of the 5 worlds. Most of that time, I spent in the final levels, attempting to defeat the Jotun. If I were to estimate my final playtime when I finish, it would probably end up being around 12 or 13 hours.
TL;DR: As short as it was, it's a great game, and an amazing experience. Definitely worth it's price tag.

At first I remained sceptical to the idea of an interactive novel such as Choice of Robots being entertaining. After reading, or "playing", Choice of Robots for a couple of minutes I was absolutely stunned. The story drags you in as it builds up momentum the more you read, and you end up pressing the 'next' button repeatedly to learn what happens after. It is a great novel, not a long one, but a good one. It is easy to read, and you often find yourself emotionally attached to the different characters that you encounter throughout the story, making sometimes tough decisions which ultimately changes the outcome of the entire adventure.
Choice of Robots is definitely something I will recommend to people. The fact that it is interactive allows the reader to take a greater part in the story and feel that their own presence is present in the story; you are there, you are the protagonist. The choices you make create the story.
For the low price it is listed here on Steam, Choice of Robots is worth getting. My only suggestion for improvement would be to allow greater interactions with some of the characters, but other than that, Choice of Robots is a solid piece of entertainment. 9/10.

People, including reseasrchers to fight against those threats, are living divided by the countries/areas, and you assign your loyal super-tiny-killers to those areas.

This coordination makes some aspects against the facts predicted over catastorophes in the studies of the graph theory and/or the complex systems.  An example is the speed of distribution of the cure.  After human society devastated by the epidemic threats, there would be no sufficient measures to save ordinary people with such efficiencies.  (There must be a threshould in the proportion of the living and healthy in the population for the human society to be capable of the tasks.)  However, the effects of the cures in this game are applied immediately and thoroughly.  Second example is the number of people becoming sick/dying, which should be accelarated in the final stage of eradication, since there should be no supports from the healthy.  The game ignores these predicts for the playing experience, and it makes this game rather against intellegence of the contemporary researches.  Or maybe this game has taken the presence of military operations in each nation.  Then the developers should have introduced their presence explicitly to make the players help their management of the situation.  The last example is the Z-force, which seems to not to make any colateral damages.  There could be some protests against them if the Z-force made some friendly-fires, or just they kill zombies who used to be very close to the survivors.
Anyway, this game is alright, especially worth when in a sale.  You will spend an exciting time.  However, you cannot just use your prior knowledge in the field.

The combat on the whole though is solid, difficulty curve feels balanced aside from the items that can break anything, melee attack is fast and strong, ranged attack is versatile and safe, the variety of items allow you to build your own strategy. The platforming is a bit weak and minimal, would've liked to see a bit more in that department, Momodora II was pretty good in that regard, and it's way more vania than metroid in this game, very little exploration here period, unfortunately.
The negatives and positives here balance out pretty well to an "okay" game that for the cheap price I'd say is worth it but don't expect anything spectacular. Hopefully I'll like Momodora IV better than this one, was a liiittle disappointed but not too disappointed.

Preface: Im not the biggest star wars fan. I like it and find Darth Vaders character to be really interesting but i find the whole universe a bit shallow and the movies a bit cheaply made. This review looks at the game from a gameplay perspective.
Ok so little backstory on why I dont recommend this.
I had rented this for x360 WAYYY back when it was released, I reached the last mission and had to go to sleep. Parents however returned it without asking me and I never got around to renting it again. I had completely forgotten its existence until I saw a bundle of it + FU2 on the interwebz.
I bought it in an instant.
Im still debating if that was a mistake or not. I got around to finishing a game from my childhood but the PC port is SOOOOO terrible I thought of uninstalling a myriad of times.
Sound files are missing, in combat you might as well be deaf on certain levels. Music is playing around 70% of the time, the other 30% its turned off. Im not joking sometimes, even in combat, the only thing u hear is your character jumping and swinging his lightsaber. Its like fighting storm troopers in space. I mean literal no gravity space, not on a deathstar or on a planet. Apart from this, the volume of the characters voices seems to go up and down constantly and I got the hint that it wasnt the same voice actor at times. Very big hit to my immersion.
The game allows for a decent amount of powering up your character, but honestly you already feel pretty powerful without most of the upgrades. You basically one shot people with the Force Throw ability. Also, the game allows you to change costumes, but in doing so you have to load to the last checkpoint, and when the mission ends your costume is reset. So i changed costume the first time and never bothered again since it would be reset by next mission.
Another god annoying thing, some character models seem to strech. Like the apprentice of Shaak Ti, her right eye and right lip side stretched like she was having a stroke. By the final missions you will have noticed this on most characters happening at least once.
The graphics are locked to 30 fps by default, only way to circumvent this is by googling for a fix. A guy made a couple .exes that set the fps lock higher. I applied the 60 fps lock and it worked for about 80% of the game. At around the final mission it reverted back to 30 fps, but i was too annoyed at the game at that point and just wanted to finish it and uninstall to care about fixing the lock.
Also, its a very damn short campaign. Granted there is a certain modicum of replayability. Dont let my game time fool you. I left the game open on occassion to attend to RL stuff. The campaign can be finished within 5-6 hours max.
EDIT: forgot to mention how terrible the camera work is. I honestly feel The Last Guardians camera is a masterpiece compared to this game.
TLDR: Nostalgia is a cruel mistress. Terrible PC port. Get this on sale only and only if you are a star wars fan. If you are looking for devil may cry in space, look elsewhere.

I wish I hadn't replayed this on PC to be honest. Played it when the game first came out back in the day on a console, going back and playing this on steam? I can't call it good. It's a poor, clunky port at BEST. The gameplay doesn't handle well, you often find yourself incapable of moving at important moments in a Third Person ACTION GAME. The way everything is based off of targetting would be good, if not for the complete lack of any real camera control. The targetting itself just seems to randomly select items varying around from enemies to random pieces of junk and droids. The controls don't lend themselves well to actually making use of your environment, which was clearly the game's design. It's effectively unplayable deeper into the game. The difficulty scaling would be fantastic as I enjoy a challenge, and it seems the game is built on forcing (Ha) you to make use of all your powers and mix it up intelligently to proceed in some of the harder areas. Unfortunately, these mechanics handle like absolute garbage. There is absolutely no precision and control for moving grabbed objects is near non-existant. Ultimately, it would be a great game, with a pretty damn good story, all wrapped up in a Star Wars package, but as far as this♥♥♥♥♥♥poor PC port is concerned, everything that is great about this game becomes its biggest weakness. The port seems to have broken mechanics necessary to play the game.

Without a doubt, this is a game that everyone has an opinion on, and a lot of it rides on the fact that tens of thousands of backers gave Keiji Inafune $4 million to resurrect Mega Man. How did he do? Well, it mostly plays like Mega Man, aside from the dashing mechanic. The music rocks like Mega Man. The levels are not necessarily up to Mega Man par, the boss fights and their themes are decent, and there definitely aren't enough of levels in the game. The cutscenes, despite having a very talented voice acting cast, are kind of lame, especially since the characters can only make one static expression at a time like bad claymation. There are plenty of holes in the story. Also, while the Mighty Numbers all have personality, Call has less emotion than Mr. Data from Season 1 of Star Trek TNG, and Will White has none of the lovable qualities of Dr. Light. Hell I could see him becoming a villain, all honesty. Mega Man did fine without story for the longest time beyond quick 8-bit cutscenes here and there. Some say the game runs choppy, but I've not experienced that. Haven't gotten into the challenges, but then again we did without those for 8 classic Mega Man games.
Was it worth $4 million? Probably not. Is it a worthy successor to Mega Man? Sort of. It's a rough first entry to a new series, and it could definitely use some polishing and refining. Especially if you're going to tell some kind of story. But in and of itself, it's not a _bad_ game, it just _should_ have been better.

I was one of the kickstarter backers and pledged $20, Mighty No. 30616.
Ignoring the issues surrounding the game's development and release, having finally played the game I beat all 12 of the main stages and found it to be a largely unsatisfying and unenjoyable experience.
The dashing system is at odds with the combat, and the level design, boss design, weapon design, sound design and graphic design all fail to build on the hallmarks of the Mega Man franchise that this new series was supposed to spiritually succeed.
With a number of questionable design decisions and presentation faults, Mighty No. 9 ultimately deliver an unenjoyable experience.
Edit: To clarify, I've played the DRM free version available to backers for roughly 2 hours, the length it took me to beat the main game.

I have completed the game several times now and I must say that this game is really well made.
Just because it's made by Inafune, just because it's a spiritual successor of Megaman, doesn't mean this is another Megaman game. I fear that most of the negative review has levered their expectations to "Another Megaman game" rather than "new side scrolling platform game"
Many claim that the dash-absorb system is bad - I've played the beta and must say that it is frustrating at first - that's if you play it like "another megaman game". But once ou get used to it, you will enjoy this system very much. The dash-absorb system is what makes this game fast-pace and fun to play with.
Bosses designs are excellent - distinctive, charming. Each one is very unique and difficult to beat. They can definitely put some challenge on you if you are not good with action games. After defeating the bosses you get their forms and most of them are fun to use - except a few that I nearly never use.
If you have installed the Ray DLC, then Ray is another fun to play character. Because of the setting of xel deterioration and battle style, Ray's battle tactics is absolutely different from Beck. It is even more aggressive and fast pace than Beck. If you defeat the bosses you get their weapon and they are different than what Beck is getting and again - fun to use!
The game simply is amazing if you don't keep your Megaman expectations on when you are playing. It's definitely challenging, although sometime really difficult and frustrating. And that is exactly what a spiritual successor should do - it provides challenging difficulties and great satisfaction after you complete it, just like Megaman. You can't just copy the whole Megaman system into this game, because the will lose its unique identity if you do so.

I bought this game figuring I'd play it for a bit and move on after I built a couple castles. How wrong I was. Even with the extremely limited toolset this early in the process, the possibilities are endless. I haven't been able to stop playing this game. The physics and how they are apllied to certain contraptions can be a little wonky once in awhile, but it's forgivable this early in an early access game (It doesn't hurt that they are usually pretty entertaining to watch too). I'm standing by like a giddy little school girl in anticipation of the next update, and I'm sure I'll feel the same way for weeks or months to come.
A quick idea of what the game is all about: I finally built a working catapult and needed to test the bad lad out. I went out a ways and put up a wall to see what kind of damage the catapult would do to it. I put up a 5x5ish block wall and cranked the catapult back. The first shot went over the wall. Cool, at least it's working. I went to make a larger target. I went 10x10ish this time...and my beautiful creation crumbled upon itself immediately. Damn structural integrity. In the long run, I had to build a 10x5 then 2 10x10's then a 10x5 just to support the massive wall long enough so that I could load and ready the catapult just to destroy the wall.
Just a tip for some people who complained about the rubble being in their way. You can turn the amount of "Active Rubble Fragments" or something like that down in the options of your saved game. That, or just saving the game and reloading worked for me.

Plague Inc: Evolved is an exciting strategy game with many methods and difficulties. There is no single "correct" way to become a life-hating disease dictator, allowing you to try a variety of new scenarios and approaches for each of ten disease types. At higher difficulties, random events can make or break your entire evolutionary course, though not without cause or justification.
Despite the difficulty of certain viruses (mainly the Necroavirus, in my case), I never felt the urge to look up a walkthrough. The game never got frustrating or repetitive, no matter how many times I clicked retry. Each time, I simply had to think harder and try new paths.
Being a science type, I love the non-frustrating complexity that comes into play in this game. There are so many different things to try in terms of symptoms, transmissions, and now scenarios. Even after you've completed each disease, there's so much more to do. Highly reccomend it.

A great game series, with the previous 2 games being free on rdein's itch.io.
Momodora III is the third game in the series, and has everything you'd want in a platformer.   Great soundtrack, tight controls, and a lot of upgrades and great boss fights.  The game has beautiful pixel art, and the soundtrack is absolutely amazing.
The only problem with the game is it's length, but since it's only $2 and you get 2 hours, you can't complain too much.  The game is short, so running through it multiple times isn't time consuming at all.
Overall, I recommend Momodora III to anyone who likes action platformers.  The whole series is worth playing, especially since the first two games are entirely free and are equally as fun.  Check them out first and they'll give you a general rundown on if you'll like the game or not.
Oh, and small bonus to the game for achievement lovers. The game is pretty easy to 100%, I did a 100% run and a pacifist run and I got every achievement without much struggle.

Hru Momodora III jsem si koupil ve Steam letním výprodeji 2016 za 0,99€ ( 27,- Kč ) a musím říci že svých peněz rozhodně nelituji. Naopak jsem rád že jsem si tuto hru pořídil. I přesto, že hra samotná je velmi krátká ( Mě osobně trvalo pouhých 58 minut tuto hru dohrát. Ano, 58 minut ! ) tak je to skvělá zábava a když se ji naučíte tak i bezvadná odreagovačka. Co se týče hratelnosti tak doporučuji použít Gamepad, hra je pro něj jako strvořená. Jinak se hra ovládá naprosto hladce. Po grafické stránce sice hra není nic extra ale grafika samotná je jednoduchá a příjemná. Co se týče soundtracku hra nijak extra nevyniká ale i tak dokáže navodit tu správnou atmosféru která je adekvátní momentálnímu prostředí. Příběh ve hře je poměrně zahalen tajemstvím, sám jsem nevěděl co se přesně celou dobu děje. O postavách se toho bohužel taky moc nedozvíte. Avšak jako kompenzaci po dohrání nabízí možnost "new game +", "speedrun" a hraní za druhou postavu což hru činí o něco těžší. 8/10 bodů, skvělá ale krátká hra. Až budu mít možnost tak si jistě pořídím následovníka této hry "Momodora: Reverie Under the Moonlight".

I bought Momodora III during the Steam summer sale 2016 for 0,99€ and i certainly do not regret it. I´m actually really happy that i´ve bought this game. Despite the fact that the game itself is very short ( I personally finished it in 58 minutes. Yes, 58 minutes ! ) it is a great fun and when you learn how to play it it can be a great game to relax. When it comes to gameplay i recommend to use a Gamepad. Otherwise the controls are smooth. Graphics are nothing extra but they´re very simple and enjoyable. Soundtrack isn´t any special either but it does do the job well, it gets the right mood corresponding with the current level. The story is kind of a mystery, i personally didn´t really know what was going on half of the time. You won´t get to know much about the characters either. To summarize it all, i enjoyed the game a lot but i was sort of dissapointed by the fact that the game is so short. It does offer two different characters ( Playing as the second one is harder ) and when you finish it you can do a "speedrun" or play "new game +". 8/10 points, great but short game. I´m most probably going to buy the next game of this series "Momodora: Reverie Under the Moonlight" when i get the chance.

I was very disapointed with this game, to say the least. I wasn't expecting too much, but even then it failed to deliver.
tl/dr; the combat is probably the worst part of the game, and in a survival game like this, that's a huge dealbreaker.
The best thing about this game I can say is probably weapon crafting. While it's a pain early on, you could probably make some pretty nice weapons later on. I say probably, because I've never actually lasted longer than a few minutes, so I've never gotten to experiment with the weapon crafting.
The enemies range from either absurdly stupid to absurdly powerful. There are "creeper bots" (they walk up to you and explode) but they're hardly a threat. I don't think I've even been damaged by one of them. There are Hive Bots, which are small, flying robots that swarm near their hives, but they are easily avoided. The real threat are "Hunters" I believe they are called. They spawn randomly and just wander around until you get near. And once they have locked on to you, you might as well be dead. They can kill you in about 2 shots and don't ever seem to miss. AND they travel in groups most of the time, spawning quiet frequently. Maybe they would be easy to kill with a decent weapon, but finding a gun isn't so simple. You usually find PARTS of weapons scattered through the world that you can craft together, but finding all of the essential parts takes awhile, and even if you complete a weapon, ammo is scarce. Melee weapons are a joke, the exploding bots kill themselves, Hive bots can be easily avoided, and Hunters will destroy you the moment you get within range.
Even if poor combat wasn't enough, the world in this game is just so empty. The only place of interest is the giant spire which sometimes (I stress the word SOMETIMES) has good equipment. There aren't any bosses, food isn't a concern, base building is crude and, in the end, pointless, hacking is slow, confusing, and again, pointless. In the end, there just is nothing to do in this game.

When they lauchned this title, it was pretty damn popular for a while. Right now, as far as i can tell, the multiplayer is pretty much dead but if you can bring friends with you you'll definitely have a blast. The game is basically a 4-players coop overhead shooter where you have to complete several linear missions that you can replay whenever you want. There are multiple difficulty level and i can tell you that the highest difficulties really are awfully hard so no matter how good you are at the game you can still make it challenging. There are 4 different classes, each of them feature 2 playable characters (for a total of 8 characters) that have different stats as well as some unique perks and items based on their class. There is a progression system where by you get experience for every mission you play and unlock stuff as you level up. Getting to the maximum level really isn't much of a challenge but the game features a prestige system (as far as i can remember, prestiging doesn't give you any advantage whatsoever but i might be wrong). The game does have its flaws, for example I would say that the level design is fairly weak as the missions are extremely linear and you're usually not rewarded at all for exploring. Also, the game is obviously not meant to be played by a team of less than 4 people, you will have a hard time if your team is not full. That is about it in terms of bad stuff i have to say about the game, which is very surprising considering this is a free-to-play game with no microtransaction at all, meaning it does not make any money whatsoever. Don't let an abysmal final entry draw you away from the series.  RCT1 is as good a game as it always has been, and I daresay it's one of the greatest ever made.  When Steam offered the nomination for the "Test of Time" award, I thought very briefly of X-COM... then ignored that thought and went straight here.  Then I took that award back, so I could give it to the game again.
==
Made by a single person, and with NO ENGINE (the entire game is written in Assembly), Chris Sawyer's Rollercoaster Tycoon 1 and 2 fall under the definition of a masterpiece.  They play well, run smoothly, and have all sorts of great features that other tgames wouldn't catch up to for years.  When SimCity 2000 and 3000, and even 4 were simply running cities with fake-people sprites occasionally walking around, RCT had something only Bullfrog had succeeded in-- a management game with AGENTS.
When they're idle and bored, they find something else to do, and the guest count can reach well beyond even 1000 guests.  They're never inactive, the performance never tanks; it pulls off the simulation of thousands flawlessly.  IN 1998!
What makes this game stand out so much from older titles, however, is the clean interface and visuals.  The isometric graphics still hold up rather well.  The performance is at a stable framerate constantly, and while I'm not sure where this cap sits, it's at least 40 FPS and never drops.  The interface is neatly organized, and every time you click a menu, it IMMEDIATELY pulls up that menu with an accompanying sound.  It also behaves like Windows, with windows appearing per menu that can be dragged around the screen freely.  It actually LOOKS like a game instead of an alien interface, something that can't be said about other classics like X-COM and Theme Hospital.
Perhaps what draws me to the game the most, however, is how you're genuinely building a world in it.  It doesn't have much in terms of background music, and at first, the park
empty; however, you start placing your rides, give them selective background music, and extend your park.  This music adds up to build an atmosphere.  Then, your new guests will make noise.  You'll hear the clanging of capitalism and greed every time a customer buys something, and your guests are louder depending on how many there are.  Coasters going downhill with passengers will have them scream.  You'll also see them very well-animated-- they'll walk around, they'll pull out umbrellas
, they'll throw up if they get sick.  Yeah, their 'tasks?'  All based on their own selfish desires.  They'll want to be happy, need to be awake, need to use the bathroom, and can't take motion sickness.  Their actions all change based on these stats, and it's in your best interest to accompany them all.
In reality, I'm making the game sound more complex than it is to play.  These mechanics are slowly introduced to you, and I played this at a very young age without a tutorial; it just doesn't suffer from the usual complexity problems of these old games.  If you need it, there's a tutorial that consists of watching someone play in real time, essentially a demo of Chris Sawyer taking over the mouse and playing for you.  You can hit Escape to take control at any time, but assuming you don't you'll get to see where all the options you need are.  In reality, however, the game won't take too long to figure out for the most part.
As far as replayability value goes, you just shouldn't be concerned.  There's several challenges to go around, playing with the game rules in various ways by giving you a task and either a piece of land to build on or a prebuilt park in its early stages to improve.  You will NOT run out of content-- in all my years of playing this game, I still have yet to clear through all the scenarios, and Forest Frontiers will always be a special memory to me.
====================
BUY THIS GAME.  It hasn't aged at all.  It's still better than any modern sim... SimCity 5, Cities Skylines, and Planet Coaster all fall short in some areas that this game nails, despite all being good games themselves.  Its compatibility is near-perfect (and if by some odd chance you run into an issue, there's a lengthy guide detailing workarounds and solutions), and a hexeditor widescreen hack is out there if you need it.
If I don't end the review here, I would ramble endlessly about all the things this game does right, but as it stands the best way to do that is to experience it yourself.  The Steam release is a simple port, true, but nonetheless the game looks and runs perfectly.  It still
a highly innovative and organized game, and few things stand in the way of showing off its strengths.
Pick it up, for your own good, and try it yourself; whether it's the full track editor allowing you to build custom rides and coasters, the atmosphere-building sound design and gameplay design decisions that help it feel like a living world, the management of your finances and distribution of staff to keep the park at max efficiency, or the morbid prospect of drowning panda-costumed staff and throwing coasters into the lake, or perhaps any combination of the two, this is a game you simply must play.
Old but gold, should win the test of time award!
Just as great if not even better than your childhood memories.

While it is a very short game, 3-5 hours long, it is a visually stunning experience. Crisp hand drawn world pulls you in from start to finish.
The only problem I had would have been the general clunkiness of moving around and hitting the bosses, once you've adjusted yourself to how it plays there isn't much of a problem.
The story is very cool, having always had an interest in Norse Mythos it was fun to hear what I presume is old norse being spoken and hearing about the Jotun and Gods was always interesting. With no silly cliff hangers, a solid 'the game is over' ending which I liked a lot.
Remember this is mainly a boss rush game so you won't find very many enemies hanging around other than boss fights, most levels consist of two little to medium sized areas you can explore to find collectables or runes/sigils then once a few areas are cleared you are able to fight the Jotun of that area. I believe 2-3 of the 10 areas had enemies you could kill, the game is more centrered around Norse mythos and the world they have hand created.
I have high hopes for there next game ' Sunder '.

An excellent little platformer, was more than enough to scratch the Cave Story/platformer itch I've had for a while. Granted, don't go in expecting the breadth and depth of gameplay and challenge that something like Cave Story offers. This is a short but sweet platforming experience that will net you a handful of playthroughs if you follow the typical pattern of doing a blind playthrough, one masochistic hard run and then focusing on getting the reasonable achievements.
The graphics are pleasant and nostalgic, the soundtrack is particularly fantastic and the gameplay is tight and satisfying.
In terms of the story these are the games that appeal to me the most, ones that don't shove the entire plot into the players face from the get go and instead leave the player initially clueless, requiring them to explore, speak to NPC's that offer snippets of information in a natural way, read item descriptions, etc. Truthfully there is very little substance here storywise, which is expected from a game this short, but it leaves plenty of room for the player to draw their own conclusions and just generally muse on the characters and the state of the world, which helps fill the time while you're flying through the levels mercilessly slaughtering anything that isn't a friendly NPC with your leaf.
My one caveat is while the boss fights are varied in both the designs and attack patterns, it's simply too easy to stand next to them and continuously wail on them until they die. Certainly this becomes more difficult on hard due to having less health or by not using certain items but it's still feasible. Granted some of the bosses move regularly and in a way that mitigates this but they could have all used an extra attack that heavily punishes standing still and continuously spamming. The addition of a flying boss that forced the player to fully utilize their ranged attack with small windows of opportunity for melee damage would have been beneficial in the sense of adding some diversity and increasing the value of certain items for at least one boss fight. Regardless, all the boss fights were reasonably enjoyable.
All in all if you are a fan of platformers, you'll enjoy this and for the price there is really no excuse for not trying it. I'm certainly looking forward to seeing what the sequel has to offer.

Transistor is the sophomore effort from Supergiant Games of Bastion fame. While similar to Bastion in both gameplay and tone, Transistor truly has it's own voice. You are Red, traversing a cyberpunk future city where something has gone horribly wrong, accompanied by the eponymous broadsword Transistor.
As you progress through the game, you unlock a variety of different skills which can all be used in three different ways. E.g., a skill might have the active effect of a ranged attack, or a boost effect to make another active skill faster, or a passive effect to make Red walk faster. This lets the player tailor the abilities they want to use, and offers a bigger variety in gameplay. Additionally, Transistor features "limiters" like the idols in Bastion that both increase experience gain and game difficulty in a variety of ways.
Be aware that Transistor is rather short, which was fine by me. It's not longer than it needs to be and never feels padded
All in all, Transistor builds and improves on what Supergiant started with Bastion.

Most fun I've had in a Video Game without graphics:
Choice of Robots is probably the most intriguing narrative experience I've found in choice / graphic novel genre games. Unlike most games, it does everything well. It would be difficult to say what it does best, but the storyline is definitely an incredible selling point. I like to spin out every scenario in a choice game, seeing what different routes exist, and never rush through. But, honestly, after 73 hours in the game I am sure I still haven't seen every possible twist in this script.
I definitely got my money's worth from time in game and enjoyment with the game. But, more than that... I found myself deeply interested in the subject matter. I've researched robotics some when I was a teacher, got my students involved in designing robots, and of course was really excited to learn about Honda's Asimo back at the turn of the Century. Now, robotics is the frontier of Science.
This narrative takes every single idea you might have thought about the Science of robotics and weaves it in to the many scenarios. There are defenses of the "value of humanity," robotics, as well as many other social constructs. And, there are many poignant comments on immigration, America's role in the world, and Capitalism. I got the feeling of seeing America through the eyes of an immigrant.
But, one of the intriguing things about the layout of the storylines is the very first choice. You start with choosing what dream you will be having at the first of the story. The four choices are all incredible perspectives on the topic of robotics. Though each one lends itself to particular endings, most of the achievements can be achieved through either of these starting points. I just finished my last achievement today with the help of an "Achievement Hunting" friend. Thanks Vance!
The game all revolves around the stats you are building with your choices in each of 4 main traits: grace, empathy, military, and autonomy. These take you into the psychology of robotics. Other factors play into your stats screen as well, such as humanity, wealth, fame, and relationships. But, these are just like tools to help you in achieving your goals with either a robot that thinks, loves, is willful, or militarily useful. You don't feel forced towards any value judgement in your choices, unless you are trying for an achievie that requires high humanity in the end. So, you get to really play with the experience of having the robot hunt down your enemies, or become your greatest friend.
Whatever you choose, it's all there in the game. Btw, I haven't found another choice game I like as much as this one. Tin Star had a passable story, but it had flaws in the achievement setup, for example and lacked replay value. But, I recently got The Daring Mermaid Expedition, and want to start that next. I only hope it provides as much fun as Choice of Robots.

I never knew that text only games, a genre of games that I thought had died in the 1980's, could come back 30 years after their time to hit me so hard in the gut.   This is like the time I thought pixelated graphics had died in the 1990's and then I played Papers,  Please for less than 90 minutes only to realize that a game with even the simplest graphics could still have the power to stare into your soul and reveal truths about yourself even you didn't want to admit about yourself or never even knew about yourself.  Games like Choice of Robots and Papers, Please are the kinds of games that prove beyond any shred of a doubt that video games can be the highest of high art and can have asgreat or an even greater emotional impact on you than books, music, TV, and movies, and other art.  I will be playing this game for a long time and I will be gifting multiple copies to many friends in the immediate future and for a long time to come.

Jotun is a isometric action boss rush game based in norse mythology.
The plot is simple, you are a female viking who died at sea during a storm and have been given a second chance to go to valhalla, but first you must kill several giants in order to prove your worth. Short, sweet and to the point. The game itself is dripping with norse mythology, every aspect of it is based in the mythos of the nords, from the HP increases to the locations you explore. While you can't teach someone about norse mythology using this, you could certainly get a kick out of it yourself if you know about it on a basic level and learn some new things, and for those who love norse myth to death, they'll be as giddy as a schoolgirl on prom night seeing all the references and depictions.
The game has relatively straightforward combat, your axe has two attacks, a quick slash and a ground pound, on top of that you also gain various abilities from the shrines of the gods, each one giving you a little one up in combat. Each boss you fight has a unique set of abilities and attack patterns that you must learn and avoid while laying the smackdown on them in order to progress. Between each boss fight are levels where you wonder around and collect the various goodies inside along with the rune needed to unlock the boss door, typically these have some basic puzzle or minor enemies to kill in order to progress, nothing too straining.
Visually, the game is stunning, the entire thing was hand drawn and it really shows, for better or worse. A few times some of the animations are a little ugly, but the vast majority of the game is downright praise worthy. The soundtrack as well is beautiful, turning what would be a slightly boring none boss level into a relaxing experience as you sit back and enjoy the sounds of violin among other classical instruments.
The game does have a few minor issues. The levels between the boss battles vary in quality, some of them are great, while others are just a chore to get through, especially in the case of one of the later levels which is a real slog. Some of the animations look a little unpolished or are a tad jarring and i wish there was more content than there actually is. There are a total of six bosses, all of them fantastic, but the game can be completed if you really push yourself in around 7 hours, if your not, 5 hours.
despite that, what your paying for is entirely solid and fun, with only one or two minor issues that don't ruin the overall experience. I enjoyed my time with the game from start to finish (minus that one level) and would recommend it to anyone who likes boss rush games, norse themed games or just in general want a quick, beautiful experience.

Computer hochfahren, Chatprogramm öffnen und schauen was Emily so macht...
"Emily is Away" ist ein Spiel, welches sich komplett in diesem Chatprogramm auf einer nachempfundenen, alten Windows Oberfläche abspielt. Wir chatten mit Emily mit der wir gemeinsam auf die High School gehen, bzw. gingen, da sich das Spiel in fünf Kapitel aufteilt, wobei jedes Kapitel für ein Jahr von 2002 bis 2006 steht. Im Chat selbst können wir eine von je drei Antworten bzw. Sätzen auswählen. Neben scheinbar belanglosen Entscheidungen (z.B. hey oder hello) machen wir auch Entscheidungen, die den Verlauf der Geschichte entscheidend ändern (z.B. auf welches College wir gehen werden). Dadurch erhält das Spiel auch einen recht großen Wiederspielwert, so werde ich es noch mindestens einmal mit anderen Entscheidungen spielen.
Der Chat mit Emily fühlt sich trotz Pixelgrafik erstaunlich real an, hin und wieder sickern Emotionen durch und gerade das Ende fand ich sehr...interessant berührend (um hier nicht zu spoilern). Toll fand ich, dass unsere "inneren Gefühle" nicht immer das schreiben ließen, was wir eigentlich wollten...
Generell entdeckt man in dem Spiel viele lustige Details, die man so nicht erwartet hätte.
Die Spielzeit ist mit rund 40-50 Minuten recht kurz, bei solchen Spielen aber durchaus verzeilich. Außerdem sind die Achievements einfach zu erreichen.

„Emily is Away“ is a game which is set in a chat program on an old windows. We chat with Emily who is or rather was in our class on the high school because the game is separated into five chapters representing a year from 2002 to 2006. In the chat we have to choose one of three chat messages we want to send. Sometimes there are quite irrelevant choices (like “hey” or “hello”) but there are also relevant choices (e.g. which college we want to choose). Because of that it has a pretty high replayability.
The Chat with Emily feels despite pixel-look surprisingly real, sometimes you will recognize some emotions and especially the ending was emotional. Another cool aspect is that our “inner feelings” sometimes won’t let us write what we want to write… The game is full of details you would not expect.
The play time is with 40-50 minutes quite short, but absolutely okay. Moreover the achievements are easy to reach.
I recommend this game to everyone, just try it, it’s free.

Serious Sam 2 is a game developed by Croteam and published by the wonderful peeps at Devolver Digital. Serious Sam 2 continues from Serious Sam: The First Encounter and Serious Sam: The Second Encounter
As Serious Sam, you get to travel across different places, fighting against creatures of all shapes and sizes. The gameplay is like that of old classic games, such as DOOM and Wolfenstein where you shoot enemies non-stop in huge arenas whilst getting keys, objects, health and ammo
The game runs on Croteam's very own engine, Serious Engine 2 and I must say the graphics were really nice. The arenas are huge and sprawling, full of Egyptian scenery
The music and sound effects are faithfully brought back from the original Serious Sam: The First and Second Encounter with new music and sound effects thrown into the mix. The sound effects are good but you can hear the difference in sound quality, sometimes poor to sub-par. Music too was the same, the music quality varied from poor to sub-par
The only thing that bugged me was the enemies, they were annoying to say the least. Always running towards, knocking down your health like there no tomorrow and Serious Sam runs so slow that even my late grandmother could run faster than him. The game doesn't feel as face paced as other arena shooter games I've played
Serious Sam 2 takes a huge turn from Serious Sam: The First and Second Encounter being more colourful and crazy from the first two games and taking a more cartoony vibe and not the realistic vibe Serious Sam: The First and Secound Encounter
In all honesty I prefer the realistic vibe from the previous two games rather than the cartoony vibe that is in this sequel, however, Serious Sam 2 is a funny, full-filled gory adventure every fan of Serious Sam should play

Momodora is a fast paced adventure game where you have to save your village from the fiends of hell and to do so you, as either Momo or Dora, one of the two playable characters, embark on a journey to hell itself in order to save your village.
Is the game fun? Heck yes it is!
Is the game challenging? You can if you want.
Is the game frustatingly hard? Nah! It's just the right difficulty ramp. Unless you like it spicy and jam up the difficulty.
What else can i say about this game? If you loved Cave Story, get this game! If you liked Kero Blaster, get this game! There's even a Pixel kameo appearance in one of the levels. Now i'm out of words to describe how just great this game is. So spare me the pain of making up more reasons to convince you and buy Momodora III already.

I do recommend this game. Does that mean I think this game is perfect? Far from it. I feel it's a good game, it just missed the mark so many times. In this review, I'll refrain from mentioning the drama of Kickstarter, how much money went into the game, and Mega Man. At least until the very end.
-GAMEPLAY-
Let's start off with what really matters, the gameplay.
Movement is crisp and well polished. It never felt floaty to me, which a lot of 2.5D platformers tend to suffer from. Beck comes equipped with the standard abilities of a fighting robot. Jump, shoot, and dash. The dash is Becks' main ability, allowing him to destroy weakened enemies and absorb their essence. It adds a bit of creativity to an old formula, though it does take a bit of time to get use to... Often I'd find myself dashing through a weakened enemy, only to get damaged as I headbutted into one at full health. Some enemies give Beck power-ups when they are destroyed this way, raging from increased armor, speed, or allowing your shots to travel through enemies. It's a cool power, but I feel like it wasn't fully realized.
Level design is a bit on the basic side. Some areas do look nice, though for the most part they played very safe. While there are a few branching paths, there isn't really any reason to go looking for them, aside from speed-running. There are no collectibles, no hidden items or powers, very little reason for you to try to explore. Which really hurts replayability. Is it necessary to have collectibles? Not really, but it would have helped with how forgettable the level layouts can be.
Difficulty wise, the game managed to keep things interesting, at least for me. Now, the main source of my deaths were from spiked walls and floors, which did cause some annoyance. Beck's dash ability, while handling well, does not work great in tight spike-filled halls. As well as the occasional 'dashing too far and falling off a cliff' sections. The bosses of the game gave me a bit of trouble the first or second time fighting them. Using your basic attacks, they do provide quite a bit of challenge. Although, as to be expected, once you know their weakness you can take them down easily enough. The only one that managed to get me a 'Game Over' was the final boss. Though, after learning the pattern, and which extra-weapon to use, it was just a matter of avoiding and knowing when to attack.
-GRAPHICS-
Now, for the graphical quality. Graphics should not matter as much for a game like this, where gameplay is king, but... I feel like this is where the game got hurt the most.
The over-all graphic style is nice. It's cartoony, it has some nice character and enemy designs, for the most part. Aside from that, however, everything just feels... Dated. The lighting is extremely flat and bland. Aside from one dark level, where your shots help light the way, the lighting was just overall dull. Explosions are as boring as they could be, just bright orange and yellow sploshes. The atmosphere really has no depth, which ends up making each level kind of feel the same. Animation wise, it's alright. At least during gameplay. Nothing fabulous or anything, just alright. Now, animation during cutscenes? There isn't any. No facial animations, little to no movement, it's kind of mind-boggling. It makes me wonder why they did not just opt for comic-book inspired segments, instead of just static characters talking to each other, with zero mouth movements... Or movement in general.
-STORY-
Segueing off of the cutscenes, the story. Which, in my opinion, they both did great and terrible at the same time.
The first terrible thing they did, or rather didn't do, is explain the world. You get a short, less then a minute introduction to what's happening, and then BAM, you're in. They desperately needed something, anything here. A ten to fifteen animated opening, explaining the world and its characters would have done wonders for the story. Just throwing you in with hardly any explaining does not get you invested in the story whatsoever. They do explain some things, although they do it in the most sinful way possible... Exposition. Reminding characters in the game what happened, or is happening. It's a major pet-peeve of mine, especially when all what was needed was a short opening clip.
Where I feel they did really well on was the characters. Well, most of them. They all have pretty good designs, although they all suffer from cookie-cutter personalities. The greatest fault is with the character Call. Her personality is just so bland and boring, it's really a shame. They gave her such a great, cute design, yet her personality is that of a generic, stoic robot. Where the characters shine, however, is the interactions during the levels, and dialog between each other. Without giving much away, after you a Mighty No., they join back with you and actually help you in other levels. For example, if you defeat MN6, Aviator, he will show up in Pyrogen's level. He appears, stopping a giant tower from falling on top of Beck, if he isn't careful. Each boss you defeat can show up in another boss' level, sometimes hinting what weapon you should use to fight them. It's clever, and it makes you feel like you're actually part of a family...  If only the family was not so cookie-cutter, 'Saturday Morning Cartoon' feeling.
-SOUND-
The music in the game is, of course, amazing. Manami Matsumae never fails in creating a great soundtrack. It's a shame that, by default, the background music is nearly muted by the voice and sound effects! You really need to lower voices and effects by about half in order to appreciate the soundtrack. Sound effects are well done, if not a bit generic. Voice acting wise, it's pretty bad. Not the worst by far, but aside from two or three characters, the delivery is rather bland. "Great googly moogly".
-FINAL-
Personally, I despise the numerical rating system, so instead I'll steal ProJared's!
I give this game a 'Mega Man Powered-up/10.'
Graphics are dated, voice acting is pretty bland and cringy, it doesn't really innovate anything new, it just sticks to being safe. Although, what is there is undoubtedly charm and a tight platformer with really good gameplay. It has the potential of being the spiritual successor we want, it just missed the mark so many times. Hopefully, unlike Powered-Up, we do get a sequel, and we can see them improving this franchise.

I feel like this game is good, but it's missing a lot of things.
Pro's of the game:
-It's Star Wars, and it's still The Force Unleashed, even if it differs from the other versions.
-You get basically all of the extra outfits and DLC (Afterall, it is Ultimate Sith Edition)
-It has a lot of fun features. You just run around, slice everyone up and use different force powers to unleash chaos. I feel like it can be challenging at times, but depending on what difficulty you choose, it's never unmanagable.
-I imagine that most computers, even potato computers can run this on at least low settings.
Con's of the game:
-Ported. The controls aren't very smooth, and using the force to throw people into eachother or do complex stuff is sort of hard.
-Capped at 30FPS unless you use mods
-No windowed mode. You can only play it in full screen
-They took out a lot of the content from the other versions. For example, I don't think the levels with the Jedi Temple exist. Also, they either changed some of the levels or made them different. They replaced a lot of the enemies in the other versions as well. There aren't Navy Commandos, or medics, or really a whole ton of the same enemies from the PS2 version. Also, I might be wrong on this as well but it seems like there are less collectibles to find, such as the Lightsaber crystals.
-Graphics aren't really extremely good, even on high settings with "High Detail" mode on, but it was made a little while ago.
Overall, I'd say it's a fun game but don't buy it for the full price. I recieved this for free from a friend, and I wasn't dissapointed but it was a slightly different experience than what I remember on the PS2 version.

Too much of the game is walking around at a punishingly slow pace, with a poorly scaled map your only guide, and then once you get into the boss fights (which are the only real combat) you wind up floundering; the scale and animation, while impressive and visually stunning, make it a real challenge to both see what you are currently doing and guess what you are supposed to do next. TLDR; this game has a lot of heart, and not enough game.

You are a Viking earning your way in to Valhalla after all, this is not meant to be a simple task. Thank you for this experience, and I can't wait to play your next title(s?).

They usually last 4-5 minutes, testing you to have cat like reflexes and use your 6 abilities when appropriate. The game isn't very long, but it feels like it's the right length with little to no backtracking or stupid collectibles. If something is done well enough I don't mind it being short. Some people have complained about it being too difficult, I don't think it's that bad and I don't consider myself a hardcore gamer.
Really though, it all just feels good. it's a game that feels like the developers enjoyed making it. it's simple, but it's enough to have you pumped enough to take the punishment of the last couple bosses.

The Momodora series seems to make major leaps with each installment. The third game was the first to be sold commercially, and very much deserves it.
Graphically, it continues the progression from Momodora to Momodora 2, with more detailed backgrounds and larger enemies. The gameplay, too, follows on the previous title's advancements. This time you can choose between Momo and Dora, the protagonists of the first two entries, with Dora’s quest serving as the game’s hard mode. With either one, you collect items that allow you to use different powers against an array of monsters and bosses.
The level structure is something of a compromise between that of the first and second Momodora games. You have discrete levels, but can teleport back and forth between them at any save point. At the end of each, a boss awaits. Not only are these powerful enemies more frequent than in prior entries, they have much more interesting patterns and better hit detection. They're more fair, and much more fun.
While it lasts, this is a top-tier game, but it's extremely short. Though no platforming master, I was able to beat the easier scenario in under three hours. Still, that was under three hours of excellent action-platforming and some enjoyable light exploration, offered at a very reasonable price.

An interesting read with significant decision-making, done in a minimalist style with just text and some buttons. If you want graphics and sound, look elsewhere, but if you have the attention span to read and participate in a story, try this one. The style focuses on scenes and chapters rather than rooms, so expect to read about a series of events and choose one of several scripted actions rather than selecting "go north" or "get flask".
I've now played through this twice and had very different outcomes and scenes along the way. It looks as though your very first choice selects one of four overall plots, but they overlap. Your decisions affect a set of robot stats, your own "humanity", your wealth and fame, several relationships, and a spoilery thing, but there are also specific details that get worked into the text like your robot's exact appearance -- which in turn affect stat growth. I think I stopped a robot uprising at one point because I'd put effort into the Empathy stat for instance. (The text implied I'd barely had enough in that playthrough.) The feedback, eg. "++Military", is helpful for understanding the effects of my actions.
Noticed one apparent bug: I'm pretty sure Silas tried to kill me for unclear reasons, died, then was back and in a good relationship status in the last chapter. I also found it odd that another character got shot but wasn't marked as dead, and saving another, obviously important character had no noticeable effect. Would also have been nice to see the final tally of the wealth and fame stats have some acknowledgment beyond the stats screen. The game has no "Undo" button like some text adventures, and I have mixed feelings about that. It adds weight to your choices but is a little like the "Fallout 4" experience where you select a speech option only to find your character does something you didn't quite intend.
So, I give this one a thumbs-up. I'm curious to see how modern text adventures do on Steam.

This is a decent game with quite a bit of content as far as game mechanics goes.  There's plenty of upgrades and different pathogens to choose from.  The issue comes from one giant flaw in my opinion; there's only one strategy that really works.
The game is basically a race between your pathogen's ability to wipe out the humans, and their ability to cure it.  As soon as they notice the symptoms of your disease, they will begin to work on finding a cure.  This can happen very early on and the more people you infect/kill, the harder and more fervently the humans will work to cure it.  There are in-game "upgrades" you can purchase with your points to slow the humans, but they are laughably under-powered; reducing their progress bar by a measely 5-10% and costing you dearly in points. This might sound like a challenging mechanic to be conquered in an epic battle of wits, but it's not.  The gameplay is very limited as far as thwarting the humans or slowing them down, only offering a few one-time-use options for reducing their progress bar.  This is in leiu of the fact that should even one of the numerous island nations close their borders before they are infected, you just lost the entire game. This happens VERY often.  Unless, as I mentioned above, you use the strategy below.
The ONLY strategy I have found that really works is keeping your disease hidden from the humans by keeping it from presenting with any symptoms until 95%-100% of the population is infected.  You then use all of your banked points and flood them into symptoms until your disease is incredibly lethal, and then sit back and watch.  If this sounds boring, that's because it is.  You are literally just sitting there looking at a screen for 10 minutes clicking around a few times.  Pretty dissappointing for a game with so much potential.
I really gave this one the old college try, but it retains its entertainment value for far less time than I spent playing it.  $15 is better spent elsewhere.

Don't believe the hype. Mighty No. 9 is fantastic. This isn't the kind of retro throwback game that's absolutely faithful to the past, like (the still very good) Mega Man 9 & 10. This game is more comparable to throwback titles like Donkey Kong Country Returns and A Link Between Worlds, where a very familiar gameplay foundation (Mega Man, in this case) gets you comfortable, but the game is designed around some new mechanics that lead to some very engaging and memorable level design. I also really dig how the bosses appear during the stage to give you trouble, most notably Countershade, where the whole level feels like a Metal Gear Solid style boss fight.
Though the presentation is firmly rooted in saturday morning cartoons, it bears mentioning that the graphics aren't that great. If that's not a deal breaker, and you aren't already predisposed to not liking it for some other reason, you'll find a lot to love here. Mighty No. 9 is charming and fun, and if you go in with an open mind, I'd be shocked if you didn't enjoy yourself.

It's actually pretty fun and its a damn shame the majority of people decided to go into it looking for a bad game.  Obviously when you go into something looking for a flop you'll find any reason to call it a flop. The controls feel really responsive and the dash is super fun.  Dashing into multiple enemies at once and absorbing all of them always feels great.  I considered the music of the game to be pretty good too.  In the time I spent with this game I saw no bugs at all.  The general opinion is that graphically the game is terrible but I was personally fine with the visuals of the game and found it to be average.
I generally loved all of the boss fights in the game(I especially thought the Brandish fight was pretty fun) but if I do have a major complaint with the bosses would be that a couple of them have instant kills which always just feels cheap and unnecessary.  After they hit you the first time with these instant kills you do notice they have very obvious tells but they really didn't need to instant kill, it makes the said first death feel frustrating because how could you possible have known?  Trial and error in boss fights this way is never fun.  My only other complaint with bosses belongs to the final boss and it really just feels like an oversight that the devs didn't think much about.  Both forms of the final boss are purple, and when you damage enemies to the point that you can dash into them they turn purple.  See the problem here? Said obstacles can block your path in certain point in the level and you to get past them but the thing is that some of them seem to reform immediately and some don't leading me to really be confused on how the rules on these things work. Allow me to start of by saying: I am a huge Star Wars fanboy/nerd, quite obsessed with its universe.
Still, I have to be honest. Booting up the game the controls are by using your arrow keys (setup menu) and pressing enter and escape. The actual game menu is much jankier, requiring you to use backspace when upgrading anything just to find out what it does. Then you have to go back using esc to go down using arrow keys to again go to backspace to look at the info for the next perk. This is teedious and the buttons could not be farther apart/less functional.
Of course I take into consideration that this game is a bit older, but there are plenty of older games that are a lot less buggy with controls that are actually thought through.
JUMPING INTO GAMEPLAY:
It took no more than 0.1 second before over half my screen glitched out so much I had to reboot the game.
Upon rebooting I found this is actually normal because everything past about 150feet/5meters away looks like a computer freezing up, creating a thousand windows upon any movement following the taken path.
OKAY THEN, I keep playing. Darth Vader! AWESOME! Taking the path/perspective of a Sith is marvelous!
Now, use the same three hacking movements 500 times in the first level, which is an introduction to the game and therefore very short. Very repetitive (which if well done would to me not have been a problem, I should add. Taking for example God Of War as game that has done this a lot better a number of years earlier.)
Blocking doesn't work very well and is often not necessary because SOME bolts are automatically reflected. Others are entirely ignored (not an attempt to deflect made.) Adding to lightsaber combat (you using a lightsaber) the attacks are horendously slow, whether going off of canon movie or book legend reference. Often times (usually) the enemy hits you even though you started the attack first. It's like playing with lag and having to make up for it by hitting a lot earlier. Sadly it's not because of the system I'm using but because the in game attack is actually that slow (this isn't upgradeable if you were wondering).
Then jumping into the first 'boss fight' I was only able to see about 60% because a branch was blocking your view which can't be changed, also blocking the amazing Jedi throwing TIE-Fighters at you.
Sadly the amount of poorly thought through controls and glitches make this a very annoying game to play.
To those purely into this for the Lore, give it a go. Maybe you won't mind or have more luck. To great disappointment of my geek heart I shall be asking for a refund.

Jotun's a pretty impressive game.
To start, this game is ♥♥♥♥ing gorgeous. Just look at the screenshots for this game. It’s incredible. The game mainly consists of exploring environments to find a rune and other secrets. The game has little combat in the levels and instead focuses on making each level have a unique design and hazards to show off the art in the game. There will be many times in a level that you will be walking along only for the camera to zoom very far out from you to show off a beautiful environment. It feels very cinematic and impressive but never happens at a time that would make it annoying.
The animation is also great. It’s less impressive on the smaller enemies that face only in eight directions, but the animations on Thora herself and the larger creatures and bosses are great. Most of the larger enemies are all hand drawn such as the bosses and definitely help put life into their movements. The game does a good job at telegraphing their attacks as well with their shadows so it’s you never get hit from not knowing where an attack will land.
The bosses are awesome as well. While the stages focus mainly on the environment, the bosses are where combat shines. Each boss has a unique fighting style and their own set of weaknesses. While most bosses can be beaten by using your axe, each of them has an alternate way to be dealt with.  Speaking of the axe, the axe feels very heavy and cumbersome, but is reflected with the slow and heavy hits that the bosses deal. The game encourages using your lighter attack to sneak in hit when you can and use that heavy charge attack to counter. The game never makes you commit to an attack so it usually never feels like you take an unfair hit.
The music is very atmospheric. I’ve always been a sucker for adaptive music, and the music in this game adapts wonderfully. The music is much more subtle in the stages and picks up when you get near secrets or when a major event happens. The music in the bosses picks up as the boss progresses and flows very naturally.
There are quite a few problems with it though. For one, a few of the stages can get really boring. While they are all impressive aesthetically, Thora moves at a rather slow speed and it can get tedious to run around a level looking for a secret. It’s also hard to tell where you can and can’t go at times, but the game does a good job at telling you where to go. Lots of levels also require a lot of waiting for enemies or environmental ques. There’s also a lot of RNG in later bosses. While this isn’t usually a problem, it’s really damn annoying when trying for the no damage achievements or speedrun achievements. The controls on the God Powers are also a little annoying. Rather than let you switch with number keys you have to switch left and right through them. It’s annoying when trying to heal or shield in a pinch.
Overall, the only complaints I have are very minor. The game is a rather short and pleasant experience with lots of harder challenges to try for once the game is done. It takes getting used to but the first level is makes the adjustment very easy. I’d definitely recommend going through the game at least once and trying for the challenge achievements. (Skip on Valhalla mode if you have too much difficulty as it is extremely hard)
