Transistor is a game I couldn't reccomend more to anyone. There are so many positives about this game that I'm intimidated to even write this review without practically writing an essay, so I'll summarize as best I can with some good old fashion jot notes.
-The story. The
The narrative in this game is amazing. Playing this game will force some emotion out of you, because if it doesn't I'm concerned because you're either a sociopath or actually just dead, and that emotion will most likely be sadness. The good kind of sadness. Not "my dog passed" sadness, more like "my dog who was in this tragic war wrote this extremely heartfelt letter to me, and it offered me a form of closure, a-la Every Drama/War Movie" sadness, and no that's not the story arc in this game. Another great thing about the story is the depth, and the optional nature of it. The actual story of Transistor is very straightforward, but the
of Transistor, that gets much more complicated because this is sci-fi and virtual realities and deep layers are a thing
-The gameplay, and more specifically the combat system. I find it hard to explain this combat system in a summary, but basically it manages to be basic and complex at the same time. Essentially, you have and unlock "abilities", and every ability can either be a move you use in combat, a passive that affects your character, Red, or you can attach it to a move you use in combat to alter the way that move functions, i.e. putting a short stunning attack on a long beam attack to make the long beam attack stun enemies. This makes the combat like a little puzzle where you find what combination of moves make for the most practical loadouts in terms of speed, damage and reliability. And you need to find it because outside of Turn(), the planning phase, you are extremely vulnerable and need a good setup to deal with enemies or you may start temporarily losing your moves, given how this game treats death.
-The visuals. The art direction in this game is insane. It's this weird and wonderful mish mash of sci-fi robotic buildings and signs, mixed with a light dash of this organic flow that we find in the real world, in things like plants and trees. This is most prominent in areas around the early/mid game, where everything you look at seems to have this mix to some degree in the buildings, environment, and even enemies. The color palette is also gorgeous and sets a very dreary yet dream-like atmosphere
- The music. The music is astounding especially the, what I'd call, "main songs" in the game. The songs that have Red singing, as they go from amazing background music that sets the mood, to "oh my god I'm going to cry I understand the context of this what the hell game why did you do this to me". The music is just flat out great.
I could write so much more in praise of this game but apparently this as a character limit, so I'd have to stop around here. But my god this game is worth every penny, and if it sounds even remotely interesting to you I highly reccomend you give it a shot, it's a short but replayable game with a lot to offer, and is easily one of, if not my favorite game.

Whew, it's been a while playing this game and I've waited with a review for this until I've become unbiased enough to actually claim whether this game is good or bad. Roughly 3000 hours spent on this game (It's much, I suppose, though I know people with way more) and it's safe to say I've gotten a decent dose of it and seen what's in the game.
Modern Warfare 2, the sequel to CoD4: Modern Warfare, which was a masterpiece in its days. Modern Warfare 2 soon became this too, a masterpiece for the casual and professional players and those who only played games for campaigns. The firefights you'd have as a rookie Soap fighting your way through the tight corridors of the cargo ship in the Bering Strait to the stealth mission as Roach up in the siberian heights. This game takes you through most of it and doesn't hold back. The campaign is simply amazing, it retains the intensity and brutality of Modern Warfare and shoves it all in your face. Throwing knives, Claymores, Breaching Charges, it has everything. As you make your way through the campaign, you can't help yourself from creating a special bond with the characters, whether it's a good one with Ghost or Price, or a bad one with Makarov or Shepherd.
Multiplayer in this game is probably the biggest aspect, as many people are troubled over it. This game has its flaws and there are a lot of them. If you haven't played Modern Warfare 2, you'd probably still have heard of the noobtubers and trickshotters in this game, which most people despise. People tend to shun the russians and generalize them by saying they all either cheat, use g18 akimbo or noobtube.  Those are the biggest flaws of this game, but there are more, hidden flaws within the game that most people might not notice. One fairly well-known bug with the Holographic sight is that it affects weapon in a strange way. In the FALs case, it gets stronger, with a infinite (or sharply decreased) bullet drop, resulting in a two-shot kill even on the biggest maps, like Wasteland or Fuel. Or perhaps you want to put it on the M16A4, where you'd realize if you compared it with and without the Holo, that it decreases the spread on the weapon, giving it more accuracy. I can list many more problems with this game, but that would ruin most of the fun, wouldn't it?
My whole opinion on this is that every game has its flaws, Infinity Ward just made the flaws very small and insignificant (most of them, at least) while the bigger flaws like G18 and noobtube stand out way more. The game also did gross on ~$250 000 000, and they spent $150 000 000 of it on advertising the game, rather than actually working on it, if they could've prioritized better they could've have made this, awesome game, even better. A masterpiece throughout time, a gaming canon. Yet this didn't happen, due to poor advertising and publishing by the two companies responsible, Activision and Infinity Ward.
I love this game, I really do, but I just can't help criticize it due to all the mistakes and flaws it has. You will find some hackers if you play it nowadays, and the tubers and g18's will always be there, but if you try to thoroughly enjoy the games and times you have without them, you will love this game.

Overall it's a great journey and if Momo3 is your first, grab 1 and 2 (like many have said before me) before you consider buying 4 just to get the full experience. Please ignore my time played, since the game was not released until the day after backer codes were sent out, I played the DRM free Humble Bundle version. I have completed the game, and the boss rush, and Ray's campaign.
This is a bad game. I would say it is worse than many other bad games, because while they are merely terrible, Mighty No. 9 comes close to being good several times. However, anytime it approaches being fun, some poorly designed aspect of the game slaps the fun out of your hands. As a result, it is much more painful and unenjoyable than many, technically worse, video games.
The game does not teach the player the controls. This is especially baffling because it has a tutorial level, however the tutorial level simply leaves out three critical moves requires to get through the game without tearing one's hair out. Indeed, if not for a single pop-up in one level that mentions a single one of these moves, no one would have any reason to believe they exist. The game does not teach the player the crouch dash, the backflip, or the quickfall, and all three of these are absolutely critical for this game. The crouch dash lets the player get by some obstacles, the backflip lets them damage some otherwise infuriating enemies, and the quick fall?
The quickfall is absolutely required because of how imprecise the dash is. Precision platforming is a nightmare in this game, and the ledge grab and quickfall are clumsy attempts to mitigate this. The dash in general sucks, actually. Huge parts of the game can be skipped using it, and while skipping more of this game is a plus, it makes it more obvious the dashing mechanic was something that the game wasn't designed around outside of the bizarre, out of place speed-running focus.
And yes, the game has a speed-running focus. But rather than grading the player on speed and damage taken, it grades the player on combo. The focus is on the player knowing where every enemy is and exactly how many shots it takes to be able to dash them - shooting them more than is required results in a lower score. this mechanic does not belong in this game. Indeed, it feels like half the game was designed around it and the other half was not - the game feels schizophrenic in this regard.
The game has no menu. It's pause menu is a joke, and does not allow the player access to their weapons like in every other Megaman game ever made. It allows you access to options, and to your e-tanks. Your E-Tanks are stupid, by the way. Other than being randomly given one if you die and respawn outside a boss, E-Tanks can only be gotten via combo. and they go away if you die. This means that a crutch intended to help less skilled players can now only be used by exper players. MN9 foregoes one of the most basic elements of game design. Game Design 101 is ignored, here.
In other ways MN9 ignores Game Design 101, you need not look further than conveyance. Conveyance is a simple concepy - make the player understand what they need to do. As an example; in Megaman games, disappearing and reappearing blocks are always introduced in a way that falling has no penalty - usually to get up to a ledge or ladder. Then, once the player understands the blocks, enemies and pits are added. As well, in Castlevanias, Medusa Heads are always introduced on stable ground, and then added to platforming. MN9 ignores this simple rule. Most times such challenges are presented to the player and they immediately must parse the poorly communicated task and execute it, or they die.
These are all the general problems, but there are many, many specific ones as well. The bosses are boring. One level is a giant hallway. Call's singular level is the most abominable, terrible, boring, frustrating level this reviewer has ever played.
I cannot recommend this game. Under any circumstances. While not technically abysmal, the frustrating moments make it one of the worst gaming experiences I've had in recent years. Play Shovel Knight, or Freedom Planet, or 20XX, or Shantae, or Ducktales Remastered, or Axiom Verge, or Odallus - anything is better than this.

Mediocre number 4.5
I really wanted to love this game. I really wish I could pour my heart out about how great the Level design, music, and bosses are..But I just can't. This game has so many glaring problems and it's so...unoriginal.
Mighty Number 9 plays by the traditional megaman formula for the most part, you jump n' you shoot. You blast through enemies while you make a mad dash towards the right. But something's a bit different this time. Every time you kill an enemy, you have to dash through them to actually kill them. Doing so gives you a power-up based on whatever extra stat that enemy had. In concept, this is a fantastic idea and an excellent way to revitalize a now age-old system. In execution, it becomes a somewhat tedious task that never really feels all that rewarding. It's just kinda..something you have to do. I don't hate the mechanic, I also don't love the mechanic. It's meh. Mediocre. Boring.
The level design is very flat and boring as well. A lot of the levels are pretty forgettable, and are relatively short. On the other hand, some levels seem to drag on forever and they just become so cumbersome that you just want to ♥♥♥♥ing bash your head into a wall. This game's sense of difficulty is skewed as all hell. The enemies are really weak and they'll probably never kill you. If you ever die from this game, it will be from one of the mediocre boss fights or one of the really cheap level layouts. There's instant death spikes everywhere in damn near every level. I feel like i'm playing a Dimps sonic game with all these insta-death pits and spikes all over the goddamn place.
The character designs are pretty horrible. All of the doctors look ♥♥♥♥ing stupid, and they're all♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ The english voice acting is slow and terrible, and it'll get on your nerves in a matter of seconds. There's a plot to this game, but it's so watered down and predictable that you probably don't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about it anyway.
Now don't get me wrong, not everything about this game is bad. Honestly, that may be the fact that bothers me the most. There are moments that are really memorable, and some that are really damn fun! There's some amazing boss-fights (although they are few and far between), and there's a lot of potential here. If perhaps the game was tinkered with just a bit more, it could have honestly been an amazing game. There's occasionally great level design, occasionally good dialogue, occasionally good character interactions but..never always. There's never anything consistent with this game. Nothing here is amazing, but nothing here is truly BAD either..Making the experience over-all pretty lackluster.
It's boring
And that's why I can't give this game the review I really wanted to a few months back. It's not what Inafune promised us, It's not what the fans wished for after years of a dead genre long since passed, it's not what 4 million dollars should have delivered.
There's a lot that could be here, but I guess it was all just a Comcept in Inafune's mind.
RECAP:
Mighty No. 9 Is an overall boring platformer that can't decide if it wants to be a rehash and update, or a new twist on the genre. It's stuck in the middle of new and old, and never goes anywhere with any of it's concepts.
FINAL SCORE:
4.5/10 , Half the Mighty No. 9 it should have been

4/10. I do not recommend this game for PC.
(Big emphasis on the word here: PC). Please continue reading to find out why, or stop here. Please note and know that I am a huge Star Wars nerd, owning nearly all books, games and movies. I live, sleep and poop Star Wars, so if anyone can look past flaws and still love it for being Star Wars it would be me.
Greetings!
As some of you saw, Steam had a Star Wars game promotion that included a hefty chunk of some of the Greatest Ever Star Wars games for a very good price, something like 23USD. Without the bundle it was a 160USD so I decided to pop, mainly for Battlefront 2 on PC as I was informed that Online Multiplayer is still functional, so I couldn't resist since BF2 is one of my favorite games of all time. Moving forward, I decided I might as well review some of these Star Wars games that I have played a lot of on the console but never on PC, The Force Unleashed is one of those games. While even on console, reviews were hit and miss. I know that when it first came out, my friends and I were blown away by the graphics and the game mechanic for using the force, which even today is still a fun ability to use.
I won't drag this review out and will get to why I can't recommend it and why I encourage you, if you haven't played this great game, to do so and to do it on a XB360 or SonyPS3. This game was made for console through and through. It looks better on console, it plays better on console and has acheivements on console. Not only this but it is 100% locked to using console graphics, even if you try to force better graphics through Nvidia Control Panel. It also does not use my Ram and the Frames Per Second are locked at 30! And lastly, my biggest complaint here is the games audio. The music, sound effects and voice is ported so badly that it almost brings me to tears. At default the music is so faint and the sound effects sound like your a mile away from the action, yet the voices are loud and have a distortion to them. There a many instances where audio is supposed to be played and doesn't from navigating menus to actual NPC voices, at times missing crucial points about the story. I haven't got there yet but I heard there is no audio at all on the last mission, I can't confirm this claim but with the issues I've encountered so far with the audio, it wouldn't surprise me. Let me just give a quick recap here..
-FPS locked @ 30
-resolutions also locked
-graphics are awful and locked (Can't be changed, even if using Nvidia control panel)
-Audio is atrocious and quite broken, even with adjustments, there are huge chunks that are missing from the game. The audio is really the nail in the coffin for this game.
-in game captions either spring up too fast or stay around for too long
-no acheivements (not a big deal but notable)
-requires outdated software to run
-doesn't appear to even use Ram (I have 32GB and turned Page Filing off. Page Filing was something done many, many years ago when programs required more ram than the market could provide or for those that couldn't afford more ram. It saves a portion of your HDD or SSD to be used instead.This game runs off that partition which explains a lot, if you have PF disabled it won't run.. )
-long loading times and cutscenes (not surprising since this game doesn't use ram)
-zero "safe" mods to increase replay value or to fix the serious issues it has
-more.. just stopping here because its unnecessary
I have played some bad ports from PC to Console and vice versa but this one takes the cake, eats it and sh(ts it out. I could be exaggerating it because I am a passionate Star Wars fan but really, this game on PC is an insult to fans and PC players alike. Save your money and get this on console. You'll have a much better experience overall and you'll get to see why even why this game had some bad reviews, many of us, myself included, still loved it and find it to be one of the best ever made.

After playing Jotun, I can honestly say that it's amazing.  The art style is great, the music is beautiful, and the controls are nice and responsive.  If you're a fan of Legend of Zelda, you'll love Jotun.  There is so much to explore and so many enemies to defeat.  The bosses are difficult enough to take a few tries, but not impossible to beat, which encourages thinking of new ways to go about defeating them. It breaks my heart a little to give this one a negative review, but since this is Steam, a platform for GAMES, I feel I must judge Jotun as a game first and foremost. And as a game it is disappointing.
I'll start with the positive aspects. The music is phenomenally good. The art & visual design are wonderful. The landscapes are beautiful. The voicovers immerse you perfectly in the world. The story isn't spectacular, but good enough for the game and the extra tidbits of norse lore hit the right spots. Overall this is a great piece of art.
But as a game, this is a failure born of obstinacy, I feel. The game alternates between tedious exploration and brutally difficult boss fights. Some levels feel completely gimmicky with forced obstacles (I won't agree with others on storms being part of these, I actually loved the idea of hiding from freezing storms). But this aspect could be forgiven if there was more of a game around them.
Unfortunately, the only other element of the game is the boss fights. The devs seem to take pride and make it a point of worth for the game that the boss fights are tough. They're for true gamers to overcome, not casual folks who just want to relax. If this is indeed their philosophy behind the game, it's a stupid failure on two accounts: first of all just look at the achievements: not even half the playerbase managed to defeat the first boss and the percentages drop sharply after that; second, it means they narrowed their potential player base in such a way that they restricted the money they could make off it. I wonder if they thought/hoped this difficulty and the associated hardcore achievements (defeating each boss without losing life or using god powers) would lead to more game replayability as players keep tryign to beat the bosses, but judging by those same stats, it failed outside a small core of extremely hardcore players. Replayability is nigh null. Once you defeat the bosses, there's nothing to do but do it again, maybe in a harder setting (like the new Valhalla mode which I won't even touch since I can't beat all of them on normal yet).
If the devs made combat more interesting and spread it over the beautifully crafted realms, this game could get more playtime and more sales. As it is, on some levels you just walk around dodging rocks, and as a game that's just boring. Then you finally get to fight when you meet the boss and you just get stomped with alacrity. This is unbalanced and unfun to say the least.

Jotun is an isometric 2D action adventure whose story, mechanics, and ascetics are based on Norse Mythology. For those who doesn't know Jotun means giant and you will be facing half a dozen of them throughout your journey. So right from the title the game embraces the well it draws from. Another nice touch is the narrator and your character speak is Icelandic which is the closets language to Old Nordic we have still around today. Also Jotun rewards exploration there are powerups through the different levels and worlds, but you're not given them for progressing through the story you have to find them. It terms of the of combat mechanics there is a lot there, but what there is polished. I could say that about Jotun in general what it does it does well and doesn't overstay its welcome.

Jotun is mostly about exploration and problem-solving boss fights with an underlying flavoursome story based on old Norse religions.
For the exploration, the two dimensional art direction is beautifully delivered, the locations have puzzles in and about themselves - though slow in nature, there is always a way for the environment to keep you on your toes.
The boss fights, each one presents a unique challenge to the player that requires a degree of thought and careful planning. The only problematic boss fight I found was the second to last battle with Kaunan, the Fire Jotun - I had to try a myriad of methods in order to beat him and I recommend for casuals to prep their butts for that particular fight.
As for the story, it follows the tropes of Norse myths and is told to the player through a narrator speaking Icelandic with a relevant language's subtitles, which is quite therapudic and lulls the player into a sense of peace and tranquility before they're roasted alive like sheep.

The camera and gameplay design on the final two bosses is just horrible. The camera frequently zooms and pans at the same time, which makes you lose track yourself or your sense of direction. The combat roll is counter-intuitive; if you try to attack after rolling away, you'll be blocked from picking your attack direction. You'll be spamming your dodge button to cover distance instead of dodging attacks since some of the bosses can cover a lot of distance in a short time.
The second to last boss spams an area of effect attack such that you can hardly move, while the final boss never stops attacking; he launches homing javelins and area-of-effect attacks concurrently.
Because of the combat design, there are 2 (arguably 4) achievements that are based on pure luck, which is ridiculous. By pure luck, I mean your subject to the game's random decision to whether the final bosses will have escapable or practically inescapable area attacks.
The art design is good, but the gameplay and camera/perspective feel under-developed.

I really tried to like this game, it felt like it could be something special even if it was really F-ing hard. But as the game is now, I can't play it without feeling increasingly frustrated at nearly every aspect of the game.
Yes, its a good game, it held on to me for almost a week, but my patience for it has ended, and I just can't play this anymore.
Pros:
- Crafting - Done in two ways, one by assembling tools & guns through your inventory screen (provided you have the parts), the other through some machine that cannot be moved or made (luckily there's more than one).
- Loot & Materials - All found in small flashing crates in almost areas. Most of the loot is pretty easy to find, but expect copies along the way. You can also, if you have the scematics, use the craft machine to recycle items in your inventory. And there's at least 3 Harvesters (that I'm aware of) that you can control & gather Wood, Ore, and Concrete for you.
- Jumping - Once you figure it out, you'll be able to jump at ridiculous heights, helps when you need to access an item & simply want a safe spot (I'll explain why in Cons).
- Building - As the trailer shows, you can build stuff. You can build pretty much anything in Wood, Concrete, or Brick. The Turrets however require a bit more to build & start up (but they are your base defenses with pretty epic range), and get their own drives.
Cons:
*Note - This is being developed by apparently one guy*
Bots (Enemies) - Every survival game wouldn't much of a challenge without enemies, but these enemies are relentless, annoying, and frustrating. Hunters (looks like Terminators with helmets) move a somewhat slow pace, but have ridiculous range, their mere presence WILL make you run for your life cause there won't be a viable way to fight them at start, and they can shoot you twice & you're dead. Suicide Bots will walk up to you and blow up (after having a seizure).
Bots Spawns - Random spawning is also understandable, but most times you'll as if the game intentionally TRYING to kill you as if you're the end of days or something. You can be walking along and then 1 foot away, an enemy spawns (sometimes you'll get a group).
Bugs - The bugs hurt the play experience a lot. Some enemies will clip on ladders then one second later they're back on the ground, then back at the top again. The menus during multiplayer will randomly stop working, making something simple become abyssmal level frustrating. Since the Hunters will war with the flying hive bots, you can expect some ridiculous lag. When building stuff, you can expect some decent lag, but the more you place & build, then more it goes from ok lag to WTF lag. And best of all, Bots can walk THROUGH WALLS that you built! Making your defensive walls pointless.
Building - Since the Dev tries pretty hard to add realism like gravity to the game, don't expect anything like Minecraft building in this game. If just one piece of your structure is even SLIGHTLY off, expect all your hard work to go to hell, and even better, you lose ALL of the used materials if the building falls. And it gets worse, sometimes you'll hit a point where the Auto-Placement will go where you don't want it, making custom projects almost impossible.
Multiplayer - Despite the game having 352 positive reviews, hardly ANYONE is online to play. Most people I've seen was 4 people in one room (including me). Most times though, the lag & menu bugs will increase rapidly while playing multiplayer (big bad for multiplayer only gamer types).
One Map - Thats right, just one map. The items' placement is random, but buildings, repair station, recycle machines, everythingelse in completely preset. And though there is a ridiculous huge tower out there, the point of it has not been discovered or explained - as that is, the huge tower is completely pointless & serves no other purpose than to take up space.
The Hunters always getting the drop on me, even while having a Radar was getting to me.
My health getting low forcing me to move slower than Yoda with a cane.
No real plot or story in the game.
But bots being able to walk through walls while being able to spawn in unfair spots, that pushed me over the edge.
Sorry to say, but you'll find less frustration in Dark Souls. I'm starting to regret even buying it...
Rating: 5/10.

This game was the first interactive novel I ever played by
and boy am I hooked now!
A 300,000 word experience into the world of robotics, artifical intelligence, consciousness, and what it means to be human. Focus on how you develop your robot, and what values you think are important -- will you make your robot more empathic, able to understand humans and work with them closely? Or will you focus on strength and military, making your robot more suitable to the army?
Of course, the choices you make for your robot also affect which companies or people are likely to back or fund your project, and it can have influence on your romantic relationships as well... depending on the fact if you're going down the love bot route or not. Work your way through (robot) wars, ruined friendships, deaths, and try to answer the looming question what will happen to artifical intelligence as it transcends a certain level. Does your robot have a soul? Would you love your robot and let your robot love you, if you could? What choices will you make in the face of The Singularity?
+ Plenty of choices that actually affect the people around you and the outcomes of the story
+ Highly customizable robot
+ The philosophy behind the themes of AI, consciousness, life and death
+ A bit of political play on a large, global scope
+ Plenty of friendships/romantic relationships to develop around you
- No save points
- A bit rushed towards the ending
If you love these kinds of themes and also happen to like visual novels, you're likely to enjoy this game as well.

An honest review from a long time Mega Man fan.
In all honesty, it's been a long time since I've played a really good Mega Man title. I'm not going to insult Capcom's legendary Blue Bomber, even in the two less than popular Mega Man 9 and 10 on Wii Virtual Console and multiplatform digital release, because I grew up with this diminutive hero. Mega Man was one of my all time favorite characters, and to see Capcom near ignore him after those two titles, and even with the sequel series Mega Man X, Mega Man Zero, and Mega Man ZX / ZX Advent taken into consideration. And I even enjoyed the spin off series of Mega Man Battle Network and Star Force.
When it came to hearing about Inafune's Mighty Number 9, I couldn't resist backing this idea, the collaboration between Inafune and his team, and even with all the delays, which I might add did annoy me considerably, I remained patient and optimistic. Now that the game is out and that I've had a little bit of time to delve into the game for real, I find that I rather enjoy the style of gameplay. It reminds me of Mega Man and Mega Man X both. The work put into this game took time, and for me, was well worth it. The gameplay is smooth, frantic and exciting,  and those are the hallmarks of a solid Mega Man title. Mega Man fans, don't let your nostalgia blind you to the new designs, and certainly don't hate Inafune and Comcept for trying something new. After all, trying something new can be beneficial.
Yeah, the battles with the Mighty Numbers themselves can be hard, and that's the point of Mega Man, to be challenging. Mighty Number 9 is a good game, and while not 10/10 perfect from the standpoint of games from the past, it has its own charm worth looking into.

So, a few months back I decided to play the
series. I wanted to go retro and revisit a dungeon crawler type of game I grew up on (late 80s early 90s) and through a bundle deal I grabbed both games.
Legend of Grimrock (LOG) is a first-person action role-playing game with realtime game mechanics. The Player manages a party of up to 4 NPCs which they move through a grid-based dungeon. LOG draws heavy inspiration from games like WIzardry, Ultima Underworld: The Stygian Abyss, and Eye of the Beholder to just name a few. This game was published by "Almost Human" and released for Microsoft Windows in April 2012.
You are a prisoner and the games starts out where you and three- (3) other prisoners are dropped off on top of Mount Grimrock. The group is being escorted by Knights! All of you have been sentenced by "a court" for crimes against the King, and have been sentenced to be thrown into the pit of Mount Grimrock. Whoever escapes will have their crimes absolved.
However, no prisoner pardoned in this manner has ever returned [DUN DUN DUNNNNNN] . Once being sealed within the mountain, the party of prisoners make their way through levels of Grimrock Dungeon. There is a guide.. A disembodied voice which comes to them in their sleep promising that a way of escape!  Find notes,  clues to puzzles and hidden stashes of equipment!
Learn the story behind Mount Grimrock! The story of the "Undying One" ... That is all I will say on the matter... Play the game!
Gameplay consists of using a Keyboard/Mouse to navigate through the Dungeon, solving a combination of puzzles and combat. Characters within the party gain experience for slaying creatures and beasts within, allowing them to increase in level and progress skills which enhance combat abilities and allow the casting of new spells, and equipment is obtained through exploration and solving of puzzles throughout the dungeon.
I had a blast with this game. It met my expectations of an Action Role-Playing, Dungeon Crawler set in an atmosphere of constant dread and mortal danger. I will definitely play LOG 2.
- Graphics are OK.. Respective to the year of release... Could use retexuring and re-releasing!
- Great atmosphere and story, IMO,
- Awesome soundtrack,
- Boss fights were not so challenging (for me) one you learn the "fighting dance", Google it!
- Highly repayable if you have the time.
- Via the Dungeon Editor - Plenty of Dungeon & Quest MODs attached to the steam workshop!
- For me 75 hrs to complete base game + Item Collections + Achievement Hunting,
- 1st Playthrough achievement progress: 36 of 40 (90%)
- Normally $15... I'd wait for a sale....

Legend of Grimrock has build up a huge reputation
among Dungeon Crawler fans in the RPG genre.
Once for its modern approach to revive a genre,
which seems almost forgotten.
But also it recieved many credits for its professional implementation.
And indeed, Legend of Grimrock is very professional....
a very professional plagiate.
While many seem to be dazzled due Legend of Grimrocks
better visual and audible appearance,
let's not forget that this genre lived up to the most
in times we were chained to limited capabilites.
EGA, VGA, Soundblaster or even the Atari ST.
But that didnt prevent those games from becoming gaming legends.
Why? They had and possed something original,
which was implemented in a very enjoyable way
in terms of gameplay, which hasn't been introduced before.
And that is the bonus those games recieve,
for inventing something new,
which is appreciated among gamers.
Now, Legend of Grimrock has nothing original.
Not only that this is disapponting,
but you do realize this just too late in the game.
I did, when facing the end boss. This was most disappointing.
The developers did let go of all good deeds
and implemented this machine like end boss,
in a kind of arena fight,
which does not bear any of the genius a dungeon master had.
They tried to stack up the difficulty and shower you
with a sense of danger by spawning endless smaller enemies,
which tend to block your way constantly,
while you try to evade and dodge the machine hunting you constantly.
After dying and fast loading dozens of times
all joy in me was gone due this unprofessional concept
of the last and first end boss fight.

Like the two freeware gems that came before it, it's a little game with big personality, and a few rough edges that are more endearing than detrimental (think of a cute little terrier with a flopped ear).  Despite its simplicity and brevity,
positively throngs with variety; the painterly vistas, fine chiptune soundtrack, and whimsical enemy roster are constantly shifting, and there are even a couple side-missions wedged in there -- one of which is a hidden boss, no less!  The story of this and the other games interlock, but the narrative is still fairytale-vague; there's enough detail for atmosphere and series branding, with the rest left up to your imagination.  That's fine with me, though.  I've always loved the "rustically cosmic" viewpoint of fairytale and myth, and if it's good enough for me, it's good enough for you!
The physics were okay in the previous games, but one thing I really love about
is that Dora and Momo have a real sense of weight to go with their speed this time around.  They don't hop in unswerving Castlevanian trajectories or anything, but there's a fine heft to their little pixel bodies.  You feel like you are actually steering kawaii lumps of tireless, monster-bashing meat, not flicking around passionless digital ghosts that would feel perfectly satisfied in either state of inertia.  This game has nailed it where too many indie platformers falter!
is the very model of a low-cost neoretro platformer.  Though it can be completed in under 25 minutes if you rush, you shouldn't let that concern you, as the game's potential brevity completely belies the amount of fun that can be had from it.

Serious Sam 2 was the much awaited sequel to the original Serious Sam. While it was a solid attempt by Croteam it was very held back, and as a result didn't sell well. Today it has since been forgotten compared to the originals and the later sequels which tried their hardest to distance themselves from this game.
What went wrong? Well for starters Croteam released this game too late. It released in latter end of 2005 around the same time as games like F.E.A.R. The graphics to Serious Sam 2 also resemble Unreal Tournament 2003/2004 while the industry was shuffling towards more grounded visual styles. As a result while the devs worked hard on making the game look visually nice and colorful, it didn't really attract newcomers to the franchise.
However Serious Sam 2 had a negative reputation in the eyes of fans because of its style and Croteam's poor decision to build the game for the original Xbox. It suffered from similar problems as games like Deus Ex Invisible War. Serious Sam 2's visual style is very cartoony and bizzare. The guns don't look very interesting and neither do the enemies. Unfortunately due to the small mobs the enemies are also much more bullet spongey. And due to being an original xbox game, the size of the maps and the amount of enemies you fight are also very small. It's a game that feels much more generic as a result compared to the originals and feels more like you're playing something like Halo.
But it isn't fair to truly rag on this game because it did try to stand out compared to the originals. For starters the variety in maps is more interesting in this game. Ranging from a jungle where you start out, to a futuristic city scape, to a town with a very chinese architectural style, to a hellscape with buildings made from bones. Likewise deathmatch was greatly improved with this game. It also recieved several really nice modifications like Insamnity which fixed the issue with the enemies.
I have to thank Croteam for re-releasing Serious Sam 2 since I suspected they wouldn't due to the negative reception it has. And they did take the time to fix it for modern operating systems and widescreen resolutions. While Serious Sam 2 is a very average game, it would be unfair to say it deserves to be forgotten.

Transistor is a beautiful game that has simple but well developed mechanics.  Its story is direct, nothing out of this world, yet still with enough feeling to be felt.
For those of you coming from Bastion, Transistor's play style is slightly different. You carry the Transistor, a sword to which you add different abilities you pick up along the way. Each of this abilities are either your direct attacks or support moves, allowing a total of four in the game. You can combine abilities with one another, allowing for extra effects or boosts to those moves already. This allows for different approaches in combat which may mirror or not your preferred tactics.
The Transistor gives Red, our protagonist, the ability to plan for a "Turn", during which you may move around the field and plan attacks against your enemies. This makes Transistor just a little bit less hectic than Bastion, while still retaining a real time approach. The Turn is fantastic and much needed in the game, and I would recommend making the most of it if you play this game.
Red is a singer in the game, and her voice has been taken. While she can hum throughout, it is her link with the voice within the Transistor, and their interactions through terminals which make the adventure endearing. Transistor's soundtrack is beautiful. Its tunes are best felt in-game, and the lyrics tell a story within it too. I would say buying this game with the soundtrack is definitely worth it.
Transistor's art style is inspiring and admirable. It is a visual treat to play this game, and even the cutscenes are wallpaper material. It gives the feeling of a futuristic and artistic city, trying to be effective in its architecture.
For me, Supergiant Games has been a two for two with no regrets in their first two games. I have a preference for Transistor, perhaps more because of its narrative. Regardless, both games are worth your time, and if you didn't enjoy Bastion because of its gameplay, you may prefer Transistor's tactic-oriented one.

Stay away, simple as that.
The game itself after almost a year of development has gone basically nowhere. Same three bots since the begining, looting system is currently a chore to pick up anything that's inside a box/bag, game lags on lowest settings possible, in the dark sections of the game it's basically pitch black even on the highest brightness settings.
The Robots:
The Hunter is broken, always has been. In the begining it one shot you and could detect and walk through walls. One year later the only change is now it takes two shots to kill you. With how the damage system works the more damage you take the less mobility you have. One shot takes you from 100% down to 18% essentially crippling you. Leaving you to wait to die or take an hour to find a repair station to fix the damages. Personally I liked it better when they insta-killed me instead of me stuck there waiting to put the second bullet in me.
The Kamikaze bots are stupidly easy to deal with. They walk slowly, stand in place to explode, and take five seconds to explode. Making it insanely easy to just walk up to them to activate their self destruct and then casually walk away.
The Hives I don't know if they've been changed or not because I kept getting shot down by Hunters before I could get anywhere near one of their nests. They're insanely hard to shoot down and hack considering their high mobility.
Overall they can detect you before you even know they're there and you end up just getting gunned down.
Loot System/Items:
The loot system is rudimentary at best. picking up individual loose items is a breeze but picking up items in boxes or bags is time consuming and grating to grab items out of. Oh by the way the ammo comes in a box that you have to open first then take the ammo out of adding a needless step to looting. When grabbing items from a box/bag you have to click it then select the item then take an amount of said item. There is no double click to grab the whole stack or singular item. Items now no longer come in completed products. You now have to go out and find the seperate parts to craft said tools to do anything.
Weapons:
Melee weapons are a joke in single player. Good luck getting close enough to whack a Hunter to death, the Hive Drones are out of the question, and "Why would you even?" with the Kamikaze bots. Guns now need to be built which is the only way to effectivly defend yourself against the Hunters and Hive Drones. So have fun hunting down every single part. Also you can't break down items into their base components or continue to craft on an incomplete item. Making anything you've finished crafting with only the parts you had effectivly useless.
Hacking:
Hacking is overcomplicated, if you don't know coding before hand you're going to be referring to a guide before you memorize the basic commands (if you can even stomach playing that long).
Power/Mobility System:
I like the power system in this game, you need capacitors to store charged up power and you need reactors/solar panels to generate power. The more weight you carry the more energy you consume. If you run out of power you have to slowly waddle around or stand around a bit to generate some more power (unfortunatly you're not going to be able to stand around much). The jumping system sucks, let's just sit here for two minutes while I charge up my jump to get over a two foot high ledge. Basically making jumping a chore and something to not bother with considering most of the map is flat anyway.
Optimization:
This game is terribly optimized. It lags on the lowest settings possible. The brightness setting literally doesn't even matter for it does basically nothing for the pitch black sections of the game.
After all of this my only advice is never buy this game or wait for another year to see if something significant has been done. After a almost a year in development this game has basically gone no where and it won't get anywhere fast. Just avoid the game and find something else to buy/play.
(Edit) The reason I have 16 hours on this game is because when it first came out the game had a fun masochistic challenge to it, even though the AI had quite few advantages. In the beginning we had a little thing called the RFID Tracker. It allowed us to see enemies on the map due to their RFID chips installed. So you could effectivly avoid enemies before they could even auto lock onto you or run out of the range of their auto lock before it was too late (F.Y.I This item isn't in the game anymore.) . The PvP aspect had you set in teams of two to survive against three other teams. Unfortunatly when the PvP was first introduced you couldn't win with your partner being alive, it was coded to be last man standing. So you either ended up murdering your team mate in the beginning with the basic tools given to you or have a battle royale at the end. Game was fun at first but with nothing new to up the ante, fix issues, or add more interest to the game it gets dull and repetitive.

Jotun has a beautiful aesthetic and great voice acting which really capture its epic Norse theme, and the story is quite good enough for the very minor role it plays in the game. However what this game is really all about is the boss fights, and this is where Jotun really shines. Naturally reviewing difficulty is highly subjective, but I found the boss fights to be extremely rewarding, pleasantly challenging, and perhaps most importantly, fair. By fair, I mean that the game has a skill based combat system. When you are defeated, it will be because of your own mistakes, not because of the RNG. Whilst the bosses do have many distinct attack patterns to learn, the game avoids forcing you to fail to do so. I believe, however unlikely it is in practise, that you could defeat each of the bosses first time. There are no points where you have to fail simply to learn to avoid some arbitrary gotcha. In between fights, the game has you engaging in light combat and puzzle solving. These are nothing special, but given that they appear to be there mostly for pacing reasons, to space out the boss fights, I feel that they do a good job. You're never likely to get stuck on any of these puzzles; they'll just hold you up for long enough to give you some breathing space in between the boss fights.
All in all, I highly recommend this game to anyone who wants a satisfying challenge and likes the 2D indie aesthetic of the game. However if your primary interest is in narrative or role playing, this probably isn't the game for you.

Jotun is a top down Norse adventure game (with occasional bosses) where you attack slowly and then mash the dodge button immediately afterwards. You rush in, do damage, and rush out. The gods do grant you powers though to make this combat system significantly more interesting, though. A lot of the gameplay is exploration (and timing and reflex based "puzzles"). The game is about 4 hours long to beat if you aren't great with the bosses (with some but not a lot of secret searching) and, in my opinion, ends right when it needs to (before the gameplay gets boring).
The art is pretty and awesome, though a bit rushed looking, it will either look beautiful or mediocre to you depending (look at the screenshots for which camp you fall into).
The game runs great on Linux, better than a lot of Unity games. My recommendation is pick it up at half price.

The graphics and visuals in this game are stunning, all high res hand made drawings that give a cartoonish and fairy tale atmosphere to the game. In some points during the gameplay, the camera will open wide and get far from your character so you can observe the amazing landscape.
This is kinda odd, but Jotun is not a hack and slash adventure about killing hordes of monsters coming to you. Most of the time you will be exploring the environment and just walking through the landscape. So, I would say that the game is usually very slow paced with peaks of action on the boss fights. Dont get into the game if you dont like to slow down and explore, cause thats what you will be doing most of the time.
The boss fights are the moments were the action peaks and the game gets intense and challenging. Mosts boss fights are a fight and a puzzle at the same time, were you have to learn and observe the bosses' moves and patterns before attacking. Also, the difficulty degree gets really high on the late bosses. It kinda reminds me of Dark Souls a bit.
My experience with this game was good, I enjoyed in the exploring parts and had a thrill during the boss fights. I just dont recommend you to play this game while you are sleepy, cause the slow paced walking parts and the backgroung music are going to get you down soon. But, overall its a very solid game.

Ear candied, eye candied, finger grinding fun "with a clean interface."
Subject to the same tolerance levels and precision as gun smithing and mesoscale engineering, acing ESJ Groove City will leave your fingers ready for neurosurgery. As in, you'll be able to do neurosurgery afterwards, and you'll also need a neurosurgeon to have a look at your carpal tunnel.
If you're anything like me, once something goes wrong three times or more, you'll curse like an ape and smash the keyboard if nobody's looking. ESJ Groove City is quite hard at times, and some maps had me trying again and again, but I came through will all five of my identical keyboards intact because ESJ was playtested on grumpy gorillas and has workarounds:
First off, there's the bright and clear colors, sharp gradients, clear outlines and sort of "broad stroke paint brush" slash vector-art style that's very easy on the eyes figuratively as well as literally.  Lots of pretty with a simplicity that doesn't add too much fine detail, which would just infuriate my already taxed primate brain.  Pretty by design, easy to process, pleasant to look at.  If you have synetshesia I would recommend licking the screen while playing.
Secondly, fantastic electronic dance style music. You'll be too distracted and appeased to remember why you were trying to gnaw off the FN keys in the first place, and then you'll notice your fingers just kept playing anyway because it's so satisfying just to move around to these beats.  Music and level colors/designs/mood are also very well matched. Feels like you're kicking it off in some huge dance hall.
Third, whenever you die, a random and fairly subtle ♥♥♥♥♥♥ sound plays. Stylish, clever - brain hear sex, brain think pleasure, brain no get mad for dis!  It's a weird positive feedback that for some reason still doesn't make you commit serial suicide too often. Whether this was intentional or not, it works very well.
Easy to learn, challenging gameplay, no negative feedback or flow breaking interruptions (except when you die a lot because it's kinda hard), pleasing to the senses, and it seriously feels like this game shares some synapses with whatever processes cookies and pink foam candy. Modest price. Very recommended.

ESJ: Groove City is an easier, shorter sequel to the original Electronic Super Joy game. It can be beaten and 100% completed, achievement-wise in under two hours, and isn't a very hard game to conquer in full.
It's a fun hardcore platformer with a nice amount of comedy built into the levels. It's the same zany humor you found in the original ESJ for sure. My only gripe is how short the game is. This could have easily been a simple DLC to ESJ, yet they chose to make it standalone. The length of the game doesn't take away from the fun to be had, however. You will be frustrated at the few difficult sections, and it gives a challenge to the player, all while creating a silly objective to gain.
Overall, the game is great if you can get it on sale, at least 50% off would be a fair value. If you enjoyed the original ESJ, or even Super Meat Boy, this is going to be a great addition to your library.

- - - -I will update this review as the game updates. Most recent review update: 3/3/15- - - -
This game is incredible and exactly what I paid for. A game stressed upon physics that has near limitless capabilities, based upon construction, destruction, rinse and repeat. 8/10, but since it came out only a few days ago, I'd say it deserves those extra points for being this fantastic right from the get-go. If you want an awesome game, buy now. If you want a game you'll(or at least I'll) play for the rest of your life after a few months period of updates, Buy. Now. All in all, there are some drawbacks, but it's almost 98% positive fun gameplay. That is, if your "Fun" includes architectural design and physics used to demolish everything in sight.
+Positive+
+Even the medium graphics are incredible. If you have a tough system, please play on the highest graphics possible, for the beauty of the scenery is astounding. +30 points
+The physics engine is to DIE for. I've been craving a game of this caliber for my entire life. Want a bridge that splits in the middle and slides into sockets? Do it. Want a machine gun catapult? Do. It. Want a rope suspended bridge that rebounds against cannon balls? Do. +70 points
+The versatility of what you can make is awe-inspiring. You could make a system of pulleys and winches that operates 20 catapults surrounding a castle to demolish it in one fell swoop(or alternatively, miss with every single one and destroy your beautiful catapults.). +40 points
+Realizing what I've said earlier, I'd like to build upon it all. Since windmills are most definitely usable, you could make. A fully automated, wind powered line of catapults that reloads itself and launches projectiles infinitely until it runs out of ammo. +(does this even count)10 points
+It just came out and it's this good already. Also, frequent updates. +50 points
+Barbarians are cool and the fact that they were added in earlier than they should have is good to see their mechanics beforehand and find good ways to build defendable fortresses before their AI gets revamped. +10 points
-Negative-
These points generally have more written, but that's because they need more explaining.
-Long loading times, but this is expected if you've played Space Engineers, and isn't really a problem once you've got a world loaded. -5 points
-Lag. If you have a system with generally low specs, you might want to consider getting a new computer to play, or taking countermeasures to weaken the game's stress on your speed. However, having a low-end computer myself, the lag is not unbearable, and fully understandable considering the powerful physics engine. -10 points, though this is only a user-related issue. If you have a strong system, BUY.
-One of the core reasons there is so much lag is the worlds. Sure, the forests look beautiful, but I'm in creative mode. Shouldn't I get a choice of a very small world with no forests? The trees and the rest of the world are a source of great lag, while I am trying to build a trebuchet to demolish this finely structured building in front of me. Smaller worlds are needed. -30 points
-No legitimate hands-on tools/weapons. What I mean is this: Space Engineers had player-wielded machine gun rifles, yes? Then these engineers should get swords. I want to sword fight on my castle as it crumbles. Obviously this shouldn't be stressed until multiplayer comes, or DEFINITELY when true NPC raiding parties come. Also, the raiding parties should not be limited to swords, they should get at least simple siege weaponry i.e. a catapult they pull with them. Also, when these NPCs do come around, ideally they should be able to take keeps and/or spawn in keeps with the map, so they can be raided and taken over. -5 points
-There is a moderately bad bug involving broken stone cubes, I believe it is due to parts of the stone cubes that DO break getting partially lodged in the unbroken parts, keeping them both elevated and preventing you from placing blocks for repairs unless you damage the block further yourself(which can cause more damage to the surrounding area) and dig a hole underneath, place a block so that the physics reload and the fragments fall, and fill the hole back up, all so you can make repairs. Also, sometimes the fragments that are stuck midair cannot even be broken. This is but a small bug however, and I pretty much covered the whole thing in that paragraph. -5 points (Partially fixed the bug. You go, guys!)
After all that, still +155 points.
The best part of all of it? Mindless destruction. And why that is the best part is that it's not even mindless. It takes full consciousness and mental focus to build a machine capable of laying waste to fortresses from afar. Thank you, thank you for this wonderful gift of a game. And I thought SPACE Engineers was good. Compared to this, I'd say SE is half the game this is/will be.

I look forward to seeing how this game is going to grow to it's final release.
I'm a fan of survival/crafting games, and I think this one is going to be great. I love the seting of being one of the machines left over after an apocalypse that killed all of humanity. It's a refreshing break from hordes of zombies, mutants, or aliens.
The Hunger/Thirst/Sanity mechanic common in other games in replaced with Power supply and consumption in The Fifth Day. Everything you do consumes power from your character's Capaticor stat. The rate of consumption depends on the action; walking consumes power quicker than stanging still, running quicker than walking, etc.. When your Capasitor stat reaches 0 you you stop being able to do anything. However, you also have a built in power generator which charges your capasitors when you are standing still. Located throughout the world are Power Stations where you can acquire more capasitors, remove them from yourself to quickly charge to full on the Power Station. I've also found solar power farms that I was able to recharge from.
A very cool feature I enjoy about the power consumption thing is that when you hold the space bar to jump you'll build up energy to apply for the jump to be higher. Very useful if you want to jump up to the top of a building to check for entrances or get a better view of the area. :)
The crafting system is easy to use, but I have dificulty finding the ingredients to make stuff so far.
I love being able to hack other machines, like Harvesters, to do my bidding. :) I wish that Harvesters would drop their payloads into one common container instead of littering the place with them.
Needs a larger map. I hate invisible walls. :(
One thing I hope the devs will change is how the player character looks. At the moment it looks like a human in a black suit with a silver faceplate. However, all the things that keep killing me are cool looking robots. I'm a leftover machine too. Why don't I look like a cool robot? Being able to find new parts to attach to myself and alter my looks and functions would be awesome. :)

Was a backer, had high hopes, was let down, like everyone else.
However, I would like to rather highlight what can be changed to make mighty number 9 better without a complete rework.
1. Make the Boss Tells proper again.
Mega man was great in that the bosses followed their rules strictly. Each Action had a proper start up animation, which doesn't cheat the player's learning process. If a boss ducked, he will dash and stop. NOT DASH AND THEN MAYBE JUMP AND THEN MAYBE SOMERSAULT AND THEN MAKE A SANDWICH. If you made rules, just stick to them.
2. What's with the dash-into-staggered-enemies mechanic? Get rid of it!
Seriously, it serves no purpose. It doesn't give you upgrade points, it SOMETIMES gives you a (redundant) power-up, but most of the time it just takes your focus away on your main enemy interaction: SHOOT THE S**T OUT OF THEM. Either shoot them up or make the dash his main attack. Not to mention that STAGGERED ENEMIES BLOCK SHOTS. They can take so much damange. Which really frustrates players because...
3. The bat enemy is not fun. Because it breaks rules.
All the enemies follow one rule that doesn't break the flow of the game. They attack you, and that's it. Bats, however. They stick to you, and DOT you. And NEVER releases you. Challenge is one thing, but it makes the fight complex. Just one of these things sticking to you while in a fire fight and you're dead. It's frustrating and they always have the first jump advantage of being out of shooting range. And there's THREE. ALWAYS GODAMN THREE. The staggering mechanic causes the FIRST bat to block ALL the shots. If you HAVE to show a prompt to teach the player how to deal with them, you gon' done it wrong, sir.
4. ENGLISH. VOICE. THIS IS WHY I VOTED JAPANESE FROM THE START BECAUSE ENGLISH VOICES IN A JAPANESE GAME HAS NEVER WORKED. EVER.
This is more of a gripe. The cringy english dub cast is back, ladies and gentlemen. You can just mute the voices and the game will play better. (Seriously, if Inafune took the money used to hire these clowns and put it into the game, maybe the game would be better.)
Also, why does Beck keep going OOPS and OWHH when he lands? I thought I was getting hit by something only to realize its his landing voice. BAD FEEDBACK creates a disjointed experience.
5. Ledge gripping is more of a hindrance and really should be just replaced with wall climbing.
You know what made Mega Man X more fun? Everything, you say? Well, you're kind of right, but wall jumping made mobility in MMX really fun and challenging. Ledge clinging, however, makes wall jumping selective, and can even obstruct jumps because Beck will just cling when you wanted to link your jumps. GUESS WHAT YOU JUST FELL!!
Just make it a proper wall-climb mechanic. Don't tell me Inti Creates don't know how to do it.
6. The animations really needs to be sharper
Its an action game. Naturally, the expectation would be towards sharp, responsive animations. This is something the animation crew probably could fix, but as of now it really feels like a sloppy mess. Its hard to see if you are jumping, or about to jump, and before you know it you are already in the air. It lacks the feel of momentum. Not really a make or break point, but something you wouldn't expect Inafune to overlook.
7. What happened to the magical Intro Stage?
Every reviewer has probably raised it, but the intro stage teaches NOTHING. Beck moves right, shoots stuff (not to mention the default fire button is on the MOUSE. HOW INTUITIVE) and dashes into enemies. All with pop up prompts.
THEN COMES CUTSCENES THAT REALLY ADDS ZERO VALUE TO THE GAME. Its cheesy, its redundant and PLAYER REALLY DONT CARE. I wanna shoot stuff! I wanna dash all around! Beck can dash infinitely as much as you can spam, and you show me some dude that I don't care about. I got a buster, I got a dash ability, I WANNA TRY THEM OUT.
All in all, I would have gladly played through a Mega Man ZX clone and be happy. The mechanics in Mighty Number 9 are all in conflict with each other. It's difficult to play through even a single stage, and the cut-scenes just break the momentum of the game play. Unless there's some reborn patch being made, nope, don't buy it.

One of the best and most immersive dungeon crawlers I've played.
Legend of Grimrock offers an experience that I haven't really encountered in many RPGs, that is making a detailed and immersive dungeon crawling experience that is full of traps, secrets, puzzles and enemies, as well as also being a pretty good RPG in its own right.
The gameplay is rather odd as it is grid based, yet everything plays out in real time (akin to other first person, old-school RPGs) which it can take a while to get used to. This grid based movement does tie into how a lot of this game plays out, since combat is in real time, you'll find that you'll need to plan things out before you engage in combat since it is unideal to be fighting in confined areas because you can't dodge (yes, you are indead dodging in a grid based game).
On top of this, you are also controlling 4 custom party members who move in unison but can be repositioned so they only take damage from certain sides, which is important since you will ideally want melee classes in the front with ranged and mage classes in the back. Speaking of magic, this game has an interesting spell casting system which involves making symbols by clicking 9 different rune symbols to cast a spell, you won't know how to cast a spell until you either find a scroll which tells you, or if you make a lucky guess. While all this may sound daunting, it is surprisingly a lot more simple and enjoyable than it seems.
Of course there is more to this game than combat. The dungeon also features a lot of devious traps, interesting puzzles and a bunch of secrets which all lead to worth while rewards. This is where I think this game truely shines as it honestly feels like I'm exploring an actual fantasy dungeon, which Is a feeling I don't get from many RPGs. It is super satisfying when you solve a difficult puzzle using your wits, or finding a loose stone in a wall that opens a secret door.
This game even features a level editor with Steam workshop, while I haven't used it much myself, I've seen a few pretty good maps, with some even featuring custom content.
Overall, this is a really fun and enjoyable experience that I think a lot of RPG fans will enjoy. A Definate thumbs up from me.

Playing this on a 3.3 GHz iMac, with the AMD Radeon R9 M395, El Capitan 10.11.6.
This game promises to recreate the great dungeon crawler games of the past, Dungeon Master & Eye of the Beholder, and it does so brilliantly.  It takes all the elements that made those games so much fun, and gives them a nice little polish for today’s gamer.
The graphics may not seem cutting edge to a lot of modern players, but they perfectly recreate those classic games, as does the sound, game play & UI.
I have not had run across any glitches or bugs playing on my Mac, which is not always the case with PC games that are usually programed for Windows first, and ported to the Mac as an afterthought.
There have been only two parts of the game that have dampened my enthusiasm for playing it.  The first is that some of the puzzles make no logical sense.  I have had to resort to game guides at a couple of spots that I could not figure out, and when I read the solution I was like “You have to be kidding me!”  It was something like, spin around three times, click your heels together while saying “There’s no place like home”, while poking yourself in the eye with a vorpal blade, and finishing by throwing yourself down a pit of death.  Maybe not quite that absurd, but I would doubt that anyone will figure out every puzzle without resorting to a game guide.
And there are a couple of spots that even when I knew what I had to do after reading said game guide, it was crazy hard to actually complete the puzzle.  I am currently stuck in a room filled with fiery Uggardians and pits in which I have been unable to get past.
Don’t tell me I need to “Git Gud”.  At my age, I’m as “Gud” as I’m ever going to “Git”!
Still, I would highly recommend this game.  It satisfies the nostalgia urge in anyone who ever played Eye of the Beholder on their old Amiga or Atari ST. (both of which I owned.)

Top-down Norse-themed exploration/boss rush game.
You are tasked with exploring fantastic locations and tracking down runes that unlock the game's bosses. Each location has a unique flair and hides a few secrets, but can lose its appeal if you get lost or die too often. Your character has a dodge roll and attacks with an axe - tools which you'll use against the location's obstacles as much as against opponents.
The exploration is complemented by tense duels with powerful giants, that reward fast reflexes and good tactics. Each Jotun has its own weaknesses, and it's possible to find health upgrades and limited-use spells to make the fights easier. There are achievements to encourage you to fight with self-imposed restrictions, but the mechanics aren't quite precise enough for those challenges to feel fair.
The game is visually striking, and dishes out tidbits of Norse mythology at various points, although the plot and characters are next to non-existant.
Basic, but good at what it does.
amazing looking 2D game steeped in Norse mythology. And the bossbattles with the Jotun are amazing.

It took me a couple of levels for this game to really click with me, but I stuck with it--largely due to the beautiful hand-drawn art and Norse mythology theme--and I'm glad I did. If you took the exploration/boss fight emphases of Shadow of the Colossus and the combat of Hyper Light Drifter (and yes, I realize Hyper Light Drifter came out after this game did), you would probably end up with something very much like Jotun, which I think is great. The levels are also well designed, and the mythological theme isn't just pasted on over the top of the mechanics. It informs the level designs, boss fights, character designs, etc.
I won't say it was all perfect. Some of the levels felt a bit too long for their own good, but it never got to the point of being intolerable, and it was only a couple of levels. Overall, if you're looking for a fast-paced brawler, look elsewhere, but if you want an exploration-focused game with good boss fights, killer visuals, and a strong mythological flavor, you're in the right place.

Overall, though, two thumbs up.

Star Wars: The Force Unleashed is a game that was originally released for the Xbox 360 and Playstation 3 and was ported to PC and Mac.
The game follows the character Star Killer through the Star Wars Universe performing tasks for Darth Vader. There are various planets in the game however some are bundled with glitchy sections. For example, I experienced times in which I fell through the world leading to my death which was infuriating due to the checkpoint system they have meaning sometimes I would be forced back way earlier in the level.
The story in 'Force Unleashed isn't a work of art but it wasn't too much of a bother for me. The game follows a simple formula of sending you to a location, killing every living thing and defeating the boss. What makes this interesting is the various ways to kill your enemies. As you progress through the game you unlock new abilities and you can upgrade them with Force Points which are gained by completing the current mission, finding hidden holocrons and killing things.
As mentioned before, there are bugs and many are annoyances however some can be quite funny.  One particular bug prevented me from completing the game right at the very end. Revealing details of this bug may ruin your experience if you intend to play this. However I can say this: near the end of the game you will encounter boss fights in which you can't take your time otherwise you will run into a bug and won't be able to progress.
Overall, despite the bad port job and other negative things I recommend this game but only to a fan of Star Wars and only if it was on sale.

Transistor.
One could try to compare it to the studios previous title Bastion, and in regards of optic and sounddesign both titles are masterpieces. But they couldn't be more different in Gameplay.
After this little introduction to the actual review:
Graphics:
The artstyle of the game is mesmerizing and creates a impressively coherent world, one that you can loose yourself in. The isomorphic camera stays centered on the main character, Red, who, by the way, looks every way the dignified beauty, despite fighting her way through the deserted districts. There are almost none parts where you get the the feeling you don't recognise whats happening on the screen in front of you.
Sound:
Just like in Bastion, there is a narrator, that leads us through the game in the shape of our weapon, the Transistor. The voice is pleasant to listen to, but the clear highlight of the sounddesign is Reds muted singing along the hypnotic soundtrack. Her voice is simply beautiful and at some points you will likely find yourself standing still, just to listen to her humming. The effects of the attacs are nothing extraordinary, but well thought through and fit in with the rest of the game.
Gameplay:
Here it gets interesting, this is where the large divergence happens. Whereas Bastion was kind of a hack'n slay, Transistor takes a, at least in my opinion, more elegant route. You traverse the city Cloudbanks as Red, and whenever you encounter enemys, the game closes of the part of the map, in which the fight occurs. Then you start to plan your turns. That means, you essentially stop the time and select which skills and movements red should perform, each of them consumes a part of your "turn-meter". If you activate your turn, Red performs all actions almost immediatly. After that you need to evade the enemy in real-time, until your "turn-meter" filled itself. Then you can plan your next turn, until you defeated all of your enemys. For your victorys, you get energy, which which you can equip more powerfull skills. Each of these skills can be combined with others to create a individual playstyle of your own. You can even influence the difficulty by activating limiters.
Summary:
One of the best games I played so far, be it the story, the graphics or the sound. The tactical part with the turn-planning appealed to me in a very special and unique way. If you like a game, in which you can loose yourself and don't mind using your brain in the fights, I can only highly recommend this little gem.
Thanks for reading, and Cheerio,

Screw what people say, with all those "Not Recommended" comments.
This is, to be honest, one of my first reviews... And, it actually kinda saddens me that this game is getting so much hate.
Yes, The Fifth Day is incomplete. It's obvious. But, it's not bad... Actually, I find myself loving it when I find another person to play it with, as Multiplayer makes the Death Game so much more fun.
Simple, you start out with nothing (Sadly), and work your way around the map, avoiding hunters and other dangers while keeping your power up, until you can find a Hacking Tool, a harvester, and a construction tool. Then, you multi-task exploring for ammo, weapons, weapon parts, etc. and managing your base, its power, its defenses, and the supplies your harvester(s) collect.
Yes, it's obscenely hard in single player, especially when you have nothing to work with... But that's the point.
It's not supposed to be a solo experience.
It's supposed to be either a team of people, working together to make a base, and survive who knows what, or a fight for your life as you hunt for supplies, watch out for hostile players, and hope that there are still harvesters around to claim so you can survive on your own.
Please, if you're thinking of getting the game... Get it. Support the game devs, expand the community, and wait who knows how long for an update. (Yes, it's updating... But think how hard it is to make this kind of massive game, with all those A.I. trying to hunt you down and destroy you. Along with managing the hacking gimmick... yes, you can hack everything except for other players. It takes a hellish amount of time to master, but if you can get hacking something to make it friendly before it kills you down, then you stand a chance for experimentation.)
Just don't buy it.

This is the first Steam game I've ever bought. The first digital only game I've ever bought as well. Why? Because there was something about those first two frustrating Momodora games that just kept me playing, no matter how many times I died or almost punched a hole through my monitor out of anger. "I will defeat you!"
And to my (pleasant) surprise, one of the major problems I had with the first two games was finally fixed... I had controller support! This series has always desperately needed that, because &$%@ keyboards, yo!
To my (unpleasant) surprise, this game feels like a gigantic downgrade from the previous ones. The gameplay is fairly uninteresting, and while trying to play it safe and compromising between the linearity of the first game and the open Metroidvania style of the second, it just comes off as kinda bland. It's still okay, and more than worth the small asking price (on sale, that is), but a little disappointing for fans. Also, as many have already stated, it probably should have come bundled with the first two games, since they're already free.
I recommend this in hopes that the next game in the series shakes it up a bit more (and it definitely looks like it will). The series deserves more attention, and I'll be giving it a download as soon as it's available.

Utterly unremarkable in an oversaturated genre and quite bad as a sequel.
While the first ESJ scored with its fresh approach to style, story and gameplay, Groove City ends up feeling like a rushed level pack blown up to be a separate entry in the franchise. The point is, even the first game's DLC has more quality than this sequel does.
+ still nice visual style and sound direction
- most of these are just rehashes from the first game
- way too short (I had beaten the game twice within 1.5 hours)
- meaningless collectibles that occasionally even hinder your view of the action
- merely beating the game has become far too easy
- while beating it with zero deaths has become too frustrating thanks to an overabundance of missiles
- in general, difficulty only comes from missiles in Groove City
- and even more generally speaking, Groove City sorely lacks variety overall. Many elements of the first game have either been ditched entirely (no double jumps or ground pounds) or don't make it past what can only be described as short cameos (ice only appears in a single bonus stage) and barely anything has taken their place. It's like the developer completely ran out of ideas.
+ the story has its good moments
- but for the most part it follows the first game's path too closely, simply imitating it instead of building up on it. How about a villain that has no more than a minute of screen time?
- There are no boss battles to speak of. The final stage has you dodging a few obstacles for less than a minute and you're already done.
- You'll hardly come across anything worth remembering. The generic levels just kind of blend together.
+ It has a level editor. Yay.
- Too bad you can't even share your levels.
