I was all set to downvote this with everyone else, And then I played it. And HATED it. It was mainly things like cheapo one-shots right at the end of each stage. It also has boss one-shots midway into victory.  Either scenario tries to cheaply rob you of progress you've rightfully fought for, right at the end. That is extremely irritating. I was ready to downvote the game even harder.
But then, a turning point started. I got a handle on dodging all Pyro's attacks. (I somewhat remembered the strategy from the demo.) The spacing and timing took some figuring out, and precision, but was exhilirating when it worked. I went through a similar process with Cryo, staring at irritation, then noticing a workable pattern. (Although I still don't understand how to get past the flailing jet-spray. I just sort of got a couple of lucky dodges at the end, and barely won.) In either case though, it took sort of a Zen-like concentration.
It was at that point when all of the good parts started melting together, forcing enjoyment.  The music, which I switched to retro mode, seemed channeled right out of classic Mega Man.  Dashing combos are frenetically fun, and refreshing. Extra lives and buffs are tucked behind slightly hidden breakable walls. The buff power up system grants temporary extra powers mid-stage, which I find really fun. The buffs also appear to affect boss powers differently. It feels like a new layer on the classic. However, I do NOT like the "speed-run" focus. Then again, I suppose that's just an optional challenge to improve on. I go through at my own pace and ignore speed rank for now. That immediately increased my fun. I noticed a lot of qualities from the classics, besides one-hit traps, which are significantly more overtuned than Mega Man. (Although, in fairness, Mega Man did have those ♥♥♥♥ing disappearing blocks.) The movement, jumping and enemies generally feel on par to me. There are fun new twists somtimes, like the underwater gas-cloud enemy. The DLC feels similar to proto-man's appearances, with some Zero stuff mixed in. Without giving anything away, I particularly enjoy Countershade's stage, which totally fits in the classic MM feel, to me.
This is my own experience. I'm sure others will feel differently, which is okay.
The actual game: 8.5/10

I'd like to start by rebutting the claims that Jotun is a puzzle-platformer. It's an action adventure game in the same vein as Shadow of the Colossus in that, most of your time is spent travelling through different areas (the key difference is that there are minor enemies in this game).
Story:
The story is told by your character as a narrator throughout the game. It starts off confusing as all hell but by the end, you understand what's going on and why you're doing what you are. There's no big twist or anything and the story itself is somewhat mundane.
Gameplay:
It's fairly typical isometric gameplay which is well executed. You complete between one-three levels to unlock God Powers and the bosses which is where you will spend most of your time and, if you want the achievements, lose most of your patience. Throughout the levels, you're awarded for exploring every inch with Golden Fruit and God Powers (Extra Health and Extra Power Usage). There are five separate worlds which are vastly different in both appearance and the hazards they present.
Bosses:
The bosses themselves can be completed without too much trouble. When you're going for the kills without using powers it will get much more difficult. There are also challenges to get the bosses killed without getting hit and within very tight time frames.
Length:
The game itself for a first playthrough will probably take 2-4 hours depending on how much you explore but the achievements will add to that time considerably. I spent over three hours getting the last boss killed with no God Powers but I didn't feel bored doing it, extremely frustrated maybe but not bored.
Art & Sound:
The artwork is neatly presented and instantly represents the world that you're exploring. Music was fairly minimalistic throughout the game aside the bosses but this worked to the games benefit as it made the battles seem much more chaotic. Both A&S were fitting to the games setting and well executed throughout.
tl;dr - Good game, good artwork and sound, fairly easy unless you want all the achievements, in which case it's frustrating.

Jotun is a beautifully drawn adventure game about a viking warrior named Thora on a quest through the nine worlds to prove her place in Valhalla. When I started this game I was expecting a brutal action adventure in the Souls-vein, however Jotun is not that game. It is not like Titan Souls or Salt and Sanctuary, you don't have to "git gud" to enjoy Jotun. In fact if that's what you're looking for, Jotun will leave you disappointed.
This game is mainly about exploration, atmosphere and environmental puzzles. Combat is very simple and very sparse. You could almost classify this as a boss-rush game, since the absolutely towering bosses comprises most of the combat in the game. That would be doing it a disservice though. I came out loving the atmosphere and the setting. If you like Norse mythology at all, you will love this game. The game is steeped in it, telling you stories of the gods and the worlds they inhabit. Narrated in a similar fashion to Bastion in what I assume is faux old Norse (sounds like Icelandic to me), key points in each level will provide you with interesting lore accompanied by a dramatic camera zoom-out. I rarely care for exploring a game world for any other reason than finding secrets or loot, yet here I found myself scouring the maps for additional lore.
If you like Norse mythology, get this game right now. If you want a Souls-like experience, you might want to play something else.

This game suffers from an awful first stage - both the art and gameplay vastly improve after a rather lukewarm opening. Whilst the movement controls remain a little clunky throughout, the beautiful environments, amazingly animated bosses and varied gameplay mechanics introduced in each new area make it equally enjoyable and memorable.
The game has a distinct style, both in looks and the moment to moment action that make it truly unique. It's essentially a game about exploration and solving environmental puzzles to unlock the 6 titular bosses. These same puzzles and hazards from the preceeding stages are further expanded upon within these climatic battles to make each feal quite different. There are few fodder enemies to bother you inbetween boss encounters and it comes across as a top-down, Nordic Shadow of the Colossus. It's not without a few niggling issues though. The lack of a true map only artificially lengthens the game and doesn't really add anything. The two-button combat also lacks depth. However, due to the combat being limited to 6 rather short (if fun) major encounters, it doesn't outstay its welcome either.
Expect around 4-6 hours of gameplay total without much replay value. That being said, I do totally recommend it for the price. The handdrawn art can be breathtaking and the game is paced reasonably well, with the relaxed exploration making a nice counterpoint to the hectic battles that provide the backbone of the experience.

Electronic Super Joy was a remarkable example of an indie platformer done right. It combined excellent level design, punishing yet fair difficulty, an amazing soundtrack, and an absurd amount of fun to make it an excellent addition to anyone's Steam library. As a fan of the original, any sort of worthwhile sequel or add on or DLC would have been more than welcomed. Electronic Super Joy: Groove City is, unfortunately, none of those things.
Understandably that is a high bar to live up to, but Groove City doesn't even come close to trying. It is sold as its own game,  and described as a sequel but it really isn't either of those things. Groove City is thirteen separate levels (with a couple of additional "hidden" levels), the entirety of which can be completed within thirty to forty five minutes. This would barely feel like a full length DLC package, and the fact it is sold as its own game seems misleading as there isn't nearly enough here to consider it its own anything. It would be like if an ice cream shop sold the sprinkles separately and also told you they were totally ice cream, just trust them on this one.
Brevity is not always a bad thing, but the main issue here is the levels themselves just aren't that good. The levels in Electronic Super Joy were extraordinarily designed, with this brilliant and wicked challenge that kept you coming back for more. Here, everything is decidedly more ho-hum. It feels like this was a pack of levels deleted from the first game for not being up to snuff, packaged together here as a sort of "lost levels" kind of deal. The original game was brilliant in its design. Here everything is obvious. There are no clever, memorable levels along the way, and there are only one or two here that would really feel in place with the original game.
So the game suffers from being short, and then what is here really isn't worth the price of admission. Not everything is bad. The ending couple of levels are entertaining and the music is still bonkers off the charts excellent, but those things alone don't save the game. If you're looking for more Electronic Super Joy to play, just go replay the original again as more fun is to be had that way. This is neither super nor joyous.

Just go play the original Electronic Super Joy, it's more worth it than this one. You can pretty much 100% the game under 40 minutes. It's way more easier than the original, so there's that. There's also a level editor, that I actually didn't tried. So far, I didn't see people using it, that's a bit disappointing.

Like the previous Momodora games,  this is a challenging action platformer with physics and palettes reminiscent of Cave Story.
It feels good to play and has pretty nice level design. It's short, but some variable story events, challenge achievements and a New Game Plus mode add replayability.
An equipment system lets you customize your abilities and allows for some fun combinations.
There's a weird design choice that takes getting used to, but works out somehow: Your own attacks are drawn on top of everything else, so reckless rapid-fire attacking is prevented by the need to keep your screen clear.
Enemies aren't hard to dodge, but getting hit is really punishing. In hard mode, you die in 2 hits. You have to play carefully and strategically. The level design means you have to stay on your toes and can't cheese everything, even when you've unlocked some powerful item combos - with the exception of the 5x damage item, which serves as an easy mode for boss fights and can be avoided to preserve the challenge.
Momodora 3 brings nothing spectacularly new, but it delivers a memorable good time for very cheap. If its genre is your kind of thing, just play it.

Momodora III is the third game in the Momodora series, the rest of which are available to download for free with Momodora III being the first of the games on steam. Momodora reminds me a lot of Cave Story, and in a good way. Like Cave Story it uses pixel graphics to paint a beautiful and varied enviroment, has a great soundtrack, tight controls and people refer to it as a metroidvania for some bizarre reason. I never understood that line of reasoning: Metroid is a metroidvania, Castlevania: Symphony of The Night is a metroidvania, Bunny must die is a metroidvania, Cave Story is an Action Platformer with some light exploration elements and so is Momodora III. Having said that, like Cave Story it is a good Action Platformer with some light exploration elements, it's also fairly challening. Oh yes, by the end of the game I was certainly no stranger to the purple-haired lady on the Game Over screen. Fortunately the game offers three difficulty options: Casual, Easy and Hard. This coupled with shops, pickups and plenty of hidden treasure means that the player has all of the means possible to make the game as easy or hard for themselves as they want.
At first, the story in Momodora III seems mostly non-existant. You spawn in front a small shrine and you go on to steal a key to open a door to move on, there isn't even so much as a quick exposition for the player. There's a quick description of the backstory in the manual along the lines of: "Demons from hell are attacking your village, go do something about it." but it really doesn't give much. However, there's definitely a greater narrative in the works and there are a lot of things going on that the player is never shown unless they go through the effort to look for it. Maybe there's more in the previous games that would help the player understand what's going on, I honestly don't know.
The game has two playable characters: Momo and Dora. As far as I can tell there really isn't any difference between the two of them gameplay-wise. Okay so, playing as Dora gets you a shop where there normally wouldn't be one for Momo but the item sold can be gotten for free in the very next level, so why even bother?
Overall though, I don't have anything real bad to say about Momodora. Well... okay except for one thing: It's short. I mean Really short. The game can be completed in about 30 minutes and that's counting side quests. My first playthrough clocked in at a little over half an hour I believe (not counting time between deaths). Although, depending on your point of view this could be a good thing, The game is great for speedrunning and even if it's only 30 minutes it is definitely 30 quality minutes with nice graphics and a beautiful soundtrack.
If this sounds up your alley I can definitely recommend Momodora III.

Momodora III is an action platformer, pure and simple. No puzzles, no fetch quests, no level system: just action and platforming. The player is given two different characters to choose from, along with a wide variety of upgrades and power-ups hidden throughout. The gameplay is simple, but effective.
It's the style of the game, however, that really makes Momodora worth playing. The simplistic 8-bit graphics are vibrant and well-animated, with lush, ethereal environments to explore. The music is fantastic, offering a collection of energetic synth melodies at times, while giving haunting chords others.
The story is scarcely given, but it does exist. It's the blending of it all that creats the experience, not any one facet. And clocking in at about 50 minutes, the game is short and sweet. Go buy it.

I really, really wanted to like this game. I loved Megaman and was very hyped about this release... for the first 2 years anyway. After waiting 3 years for its release, however, I am extremely dissapointed with Mighty No. 9. Many people are complaining about its voice acting, graphics and story. To me none of this matters. What made Megaman great was its incredibly tight gameplay and exciting action.
Unfortunately, No. 9. fails at that too. Controlling Beck feels clunky and as I played this game I found myself wishing over and over that I could have Megaman's charge shot back. I also found myself extremely disliking the new dash system (whereby you have to quickly run into your enemies corpses to collect their energy). Worst of all, the game seems incredibly easy except when it is being cheap. In other words, the only time that I would die was when I was not expecting something at all. In Mega Man games I would frequently feel like when I died I was just not fast enough and I would do better the next time. In Mighty No. 9 I would find myself getting frustrated the only times that I died and felt like you could only avoid death with prior knowledge of the room. The boss fights also fall into this same pattern. The difficulty made this game feel like a boring trudge, interspersed with some moments of panic.
If you are considering buying this game I would reccomend you instead go rebuy Mega Man X (not 10 although I understand that is good too). That game, while dated, still exceeds Mighty No. 9. in every way that I can think of.

Mighty No. 9 is an interesting case. The development process was full of problems and drama to the point of inverting its own substantial hype.
What we ended up with is, in my opinion, exactly what I wanted, and what I always saw us getting. The controls are perfect, and the jumping feels right. Boss abilities are a full transformation - which, as a fan of Mega Man Battle Network, I appreciate enormously - and use regenerating ammunition that replenishes as you defeat (and absorb) enemies. The game in every way rewards skill and punishes failure.
If you don't like Quick Man stage, you may not like this game. Death comes easily.
As for the rest: the designs are really nice, and the transformations are more varied than one might expect. The Japanese voices are great, even if what they say is slightly different than the 'translation'. The graphics are decent; nothing extravagant, but not low-poly either: an almost toylike look, which I approve of even if it's not particularly inspired.
Overall, I like this game. I'd say it's easily worth a shot, especially if you aren't caught up in all the drama.

The progression has been wonderful as well, easing you into the game, and then ramping up as you delve deeper into the maze.  Don't let this niche title slip under your radar.

This game suffers from an awful first stage - both the art and gameplay vastly improve after a rather lukewarm opening. Whilst the movement controls remain a little clunky throughout, the beautiful environments, amazingly animated bosses and varied gameplay mechanics introduced in each new area make it equally enjoyable and memorable.
The game has a distinct style, both in looks and the moment to moment action that make it truly unique. It's essentially a game about exploration and solving environmental puzzles to unlock the 6 titular bosses. These same puzzles and hazards from the preceeding stages are further expanded upon within these climatic battles to make each feal quite different. There are few fodder enemies to bother you inbetween boss encounters and it comes across as a top-down, Nordic Shadow of the Colossus. It's not without a few niggling issues though. The lack of a true map only artificially lengthens the game and doesn't really add anything. The two-button combat also lacks depth. However, due to the combat being limited to 6 rather short (if fun) major encounters, it doesn't outstay its welcome either.
Expect around 4-6 hours of gameplay total without much replay value. That being said, I do totally recommend it for the price. The handdrawn art can be breathtaking and the game is paced reasonably well, with the relaxed exploration making a nice counterpoint to the hectic battles that provide the backbone of the experience.

In short,
is an exploration game that offers a beautiful and enjoyable, but casual, experience. Some of the more intensive gamers might not find pleasure in the pace or challenge in the fights, but those looking for a game that's a simple and interesting experience will find it here.
Visually, the game is very impressive. The art is vibrant and colorful, and each level has its own tone. I can recall only a couple instances where the simple style came across as cartoonish; the game is otherwise very well-colored and shaded. Despite being hand-drawn, the animations are very fluid and detailed.
The game is drenched in Norse mythology, and those who love the myths will undoubtedly enjoy seeing their characters and locales faithfully brought to life as much as Thora does, from the grand dwarven caves to the branches of the World Tree. The game's characters speaking in Icelandic, a language very close to Old Norse, helps lend it a quality both mythic and strangely authentic.
The narrative is straightforward: defeat the Jotun, impress the gods, and earn a place in Valhalla. The gameplay is similarly simple; Thora only has an axe for a weapon, along with a handful of god powers activated at the touch of a button. Mechanics-wise, the game offers nothing other games haven't done before, but it offers a wide variety that allows each level to stand out.
The boss fights are similarly varied, with each boss bringing their own strategies to the table. The scale of the arenas and the visual bombast make the fights feel appropriately epic, but once the player figures out their attacks and how to avoid them, it becomes pretty easy to defeat them; hopefully the upcoming
will offer a greater challenge in that regard.
The biggest issue I found with the game was Thora's speed. Her slowness makes a certain amount of sense -- she's a normal woman in a land scaled for giants and gods, so it's going to take her a while to get anywhere -- and it gives the player enough time to take in the gorgeous sights, but it can be frustrating whenever the player needs to backtrack. The limited mobility also adds some frustration to the Jotun fights, especially since the player needs to get close to deal damage but usually needs to move away to avoid damage.
The game is also very short. I played it twice in a little over nine hours. I don't mind games being short, and I don't think this game suffers for it, but potential buyers might want to consider if a 4-5 hour game is worth the full price.

This game is amazing. It's about automation and growth with the motivator of survival and escape.
In the bare starting scenario you start with a pickaxe. You mine some stone and build a furnace. You mine some coal and some iron ore. You put those in the furnace and you get some iron plates. Those you turn some of those into gears, then build yourself a coal powered miner, some conveyor belts and coal powered 'inserters' (picker arms that can pick things up and put them other places or insert them into, say, your furnace). Then you build a self powering coal mining operation. You use the extra coal to put in other furnaces, miners, and picker arms to build a small coal powered iron mining operation.
And it continues and scales up and up. Eventually you get robots that can fly around and place things. And then you get the ability to create blueprints, so the blueprints direct the operations of the robots and you can stamp out entire factories in one go.
A friend said it's a lot like programming. And he's kinda right. It is.
All the things you build work in predictable ways and interact with each other exactly how you'd expect. Exactly how you get from raw materials to product is carefully thought through and well balanced. The people who designed and built this game knew what they were doing and executed extremely well. This makes my top-ten list of games, possibly even in the top 5.

I want to start by saying that I loved the first game. ESJ was, and remains, one of the tightest platformers I've ever played, and challenging enough that I'm still going back to work on the bonus levels. That said... what happened?
This game is frustratingly short, and can only claim difficulty on par with the first game by the metric of dying in the same place a bunch. Most of this game is a breeze compared to even the earliest of ESJ levels, but you'll still die because this game is so floaty. The slam mechanic in the first game kept platforming quick and skillful, allowing you to get back to the action faster by trading speed for time to line up jumps. You were likely to die, sure, but if you didn't, you had precious seconds that weren't wasted falling. Now, there is no slam, and every drop feels too long. The other powerups seem to have disappeared, and the level mechanics of old are practically unused. A handful of sticky walls, a couple of irritatingly placed max-length jumps... nothing like some of the platforming challenges of ESJ.
Of course, the game needs to feel long, because as I said, it's frustratingly short. 100% completion clocked me at 77 minutes, and that's mostly the time I spent trying to get Black Stars before I realized that they count whether you live or die. The rainbow stars are interesting, but ultimately pointless as well. Meanwhile, I have 13 hours and counting in ESJ, and I'm nowhere near 100%, just on the overall time achievements alone, much less beating the bonus levels.
The music is the saving grace, as good as ever. But honestly? If you played ESJ and want more, you're better off replaying the first game and maybe just layering this soundtrack over the top to make it feel slightly different. This game doesn't do enough to stand out as a sequel, and could have been an added levelpack to the first.

i somehow missed the golden age of dungeon crawlers so when legend of grimrock came out it was both a new game and a novel idea to me.
and it's insanely big fun!
exploring a dark dungeon, fighting enemies in tactical combat, collecting both gear and treasure, hunting down secrets and distributing skill points to your party members to make them more powerful.
i love it! you simply can't ask for more.
for a 2012 game it still looks reasonably good and the lighting system adds a lot of immersion in an otherwise dark dungeon. sound is decent as well while  the music is rather subtile. and that's perfectly fine since you want to hear secret doors opening in the distance and enemies waiting around the corner.
however the whole game is pretty old school by the book. there is no autosave, no fast travel or any of that stuff you somehow expect in newer games. if you want to go somewhere you have to walk there yourself and if you don't save for an hour and you die you are screwed. this game does not hold your hand and it is not afraid of punishing your mistakes. if you get yourself in a bad situation chances are you will see the 'game over' screen within a few seconds.
you need to put a considerable amount of effort, thought and work into this game if you want to make it to the end.
if you don't want that and you are more of the casual type then you will not enjoy this game.
also you never end up being untouchable in this game so there's a constant challenge from start to finish. you always need to watch your back and plan ahead before acting or your party will be face down in the dirt in no time.
i finished the game in 18 hours on my first run, the second run was done in just over 9 hours despite being on higher difficulty and with the automap disabled. sadly the maps are fixed and not randomly generated so it's up to you to adjust the difficulty and change the composition of your party if you want to keep the game interesting for a second playthrough. luckily you can download player made dungeons or even create your own little hellhole with the editor.
if you like the challenge of a game actually trying to kill you instead of babysitting you all the time then this is a really good choice.

This "interactive novel" is a work of art and love... I recommend its reading for everybody and especially so for sci-fi minded people and for all who're interested in artificial intelligence and robotics.
I was interested in the theme of this game / interactive book from the start but I postponed its reading with false arguments (which basically boiled down to this one : "why read a game that may not be so well-written when there are so many sci-fi books around, books which probably have better characters, plot and structure? i.e. : if I want a book, I should take a book.") And I was wrong. Because the writing of this game is much better than most books I've read. The plot has surprises and several turning points. The characters are interesting and/or endearing. The main theme is very well addressed, and there are lots of secondary themes that are well developed as well. In fact this isn't just good, this is great.
In addition to all these qualities, the author seems to be very erudite in many fields (or has good counselors and took the time to listen to them). In addition to computer science and robotics, this book consistently makes reference to both popular sci-fi culture (Isaac Asimov, Lois McMaster Bujold, and many others, ...) ; and to the classical culture (Shakespeare, Marc Aurelius' meditations, Buddhist tales, and many others, ...). There are even a few fun references to popular videogames and their subculture that are well timed and well phrased as well...
Political issues and strategic outcomes seems to be thought out with lots of intelligence and a surprising finesse. I'm truly impressed by this work, now!
The endings seems to be widely divergent (though I've not explored them all yet), and this book seems to have been written with love and lots of attention to detail. I've finished the story a first time, then a second time with a very similar path with just a few variations, now I'm trying to test a different approach to see what happens...
TL;DR -> Score: 9.8/10. Read it / play it. Now.

Titanic21´s 21st review!
I know, I know. The consol version is better. And I can totally agree with that. I remember those times I battled my friend on his Nintendo Wii in two player mode, I completed this game two times or more, I tried to collect all Lightsaber-Chrystals (and failed), I enjoyed the graphics as much as I could and I remember any of those missions. Oh, good old times...
And so I bought this on Steam.
"Wait... Two player mode? Where are you? Nowhere, but that´s okay, how should that even be possible, two players playing on the same keyboard simultanously... (...) Just gonna jump right into! Mh, the Menu looked better then... I don´t care. (...)  Okay, there we go. Mh, controlling Lightsaber with mouse, didn´t expect anything else. Unfortunately I can´t set the direction of my cuts this way, but that´ll be allright. Yes, killing Wookies using force is still as fun as I remember. (...) Oh, what´s that? A holocron? No, it´s a chrystal to transform you Lightsaber´s color with! In the shape of a holocron... No, I am sure there where animations for that on the Wii version... So now I should be able to go back to the Rogue Shadow to get my new, better Lightsaber... What´s that? No Rogue Shadow? Sad, sad... Well, let´s move on, I gotta finish this! (...) So, done here... That was shorter than i thought... It took me longer on Wii, I am sure. Is it the difficulty? Oh wait, they actually took out some story... probably that´s for saving memory, I get along with that. (...) No, I am not disappointed, of course! It was still fun to play and I don´t think this is overpriced, as they say. (...)"
If you didn´t get it, here´s what I want to tell you:
The reason why the reviews are so different is, that a lot of people bought this after they had played the console version. and yeah, I do agree, it´s way better. But although the PC-Version is so weak and has a lack of content, compared to the one for other systems, what we´ve got here is still one of the best, if not THE best game from the "Star Wars" franchise in existence. So in my opinion this is worth it´s money, but getting this in a sale is better, of course. If you have access to the console version, play it instead. If you don´t, get the Steam version. I have to admit that if I hadn´t ever played this on Wii, I wouldn´t ever understand the ammount of negativ reviews.
I know this review doesn´t discribe the game itself, but I hope it will help you making your choice instead, for the case the mixed reviews make you doubt. As usual, I can´t promise that you´ll like the game, this is only my opinion.
Thanks for reading and have a nice day then ;)

Rating: 6.5/10
Overview: Third Person Hack and Slash
The Good:
+The story is pretty decent even if it feels ‘shoe horned’ into the Star Wars universe. The story does provide good context and keeps the game together.
+Every level has a unique look and feel to it.
+Find collectables scattered through out the level to upgrade powers, abilities and combos.
+Sound Effects
+Cool force powers and effects
The Average:
The combat feels average at best. Even though you have a lightsaber and really cool force powers, none of it feels powerful or impactful. The enemies feel like canon fodder and the targeting systems is too unpredictable. Given that you can lift and throw many objects in the level it becomes frustrating when it targets the wrong thing. Sometimes when I wanted to throw my lightsaber, it would target the piece of debris rather than the enemy standing right in front of me.
Boss battles suffer because of the combat. What should be epic fights turn into frustrating experiences.
Levels are very linear and play out almost the same way every time making for a somewhat repetitive experience. Kill a bunch of enemies, move to the next open area and do it all over again. There is not enough gameplay variety or puzzles to mix things up.
The Bad:
- lack of graphical options
- Changing audio does not effect CGI cut- scenes
- Graphical and sound glitches, crash to desktop
- Final Boss battle has a glitch forcing you to reload over and over again until you no longer experience the game stopping glitch
- Without spoiling anything there is a final section of a level near the end of the game that is incredibly frustrating.
Conclusion:
A game that has a lot of great ideas but fails in execution. What should have been an amazing experience feels frustrating. If you love Star Wars then you may get enjoyment from this, but there are plenty of other third person adventure games out there worthy of your time.

As many have already mentioned, this game looks heavily influenced by cave story, so if you enjoyed it, you might want to give this a try.
However, despite looking a lot like it, this game isn't as good as cave story. I loved this game, but I'll start with the cons.
The history is generic, the characters are not that unique, the 2 playable characters are exactly the same (same attacks, health, everything) and the game is really short (took me around 1 hour to clear it for the first time). Not to mention that most of the bosses only have 2 attacks and huge HP, so it gets boring.
Now that I got that out of the way, let's get to why I do recommend this game. It may be a simple game, but the price is fair for what it has to offer, and it's really fun. There are 3 difficult levels: Casual, Easy and Hard (casual can be skipped, since the health regen it's absurd to the point that not even the last boss can outdamage it). Some events can be triggered with different actions, so you will most likely lose something on your first playtrough, giving it more replay value. The level design is not that impressive, but it's good and there's a couple of hidden passages that you may miss if you don't pay attention. For the completionists, it's also easy to get every achievement.

Hard to give a thumbs up or down on this one - Momodora III is a well presented platform/action game, has a solid soundtrack and appears to offer a good challenge. But for all that, I find myself wondering if my time and money were well spent - its short length (less than 2 hours on my first playthrough, on Hard) isn't a negative by default, but Momodora's gameplay is soulless.
There's plenty of classic platformers around Momodora's length, but these encourage careful progress, skillful play and an understanding of stage layout and enemy behavior. In short, they're worth revisiting, and become more satisfying when one understands its intricacies. One quickly realizes that Momodora doesn't ask for anything so strenuous. Here, players can just make a mad dash for the next healing point (3 screens away, guaranteed), save, and do it again until the end. Stages and enemy placement and behavior are as simplistic as they come, and bosses attack slowly (usually with one heavily telegraphed attack). There is no difficulty curve - if you can get through the first five minutes, you'll make it to the end.
So Momodora will take less than two hours of your time, and less than five dollars out of your pocket. You'll see some pretty pixel graphics and have a soothing soundtrack (in ogg format) stashed in the game files, but the game you play will probably be forgotten by the time you head to the toilet. Is it worth it? The obvious wasted potential poisons the experience of the game itself - this could have been quite good, but when the credits came around I wondered if the developer was more interested in making the assets than the game. I recommend against it - I have enough games in my library that I certainly could have spent the time on better games. I imagine most people can say the same.

Momodora III is a 2D action platformer inspired by Cave Story and developed by rdein. As the name says this is the third Momodora game but the only one to be released on Steam while the previous two installments can be downloaded and played for free. In this game you play as Momo or Dora, two priestesses sent to investigate events surrounding the village of KoHo.
To start of, this is one of those games that can’t be judged by cost. Most people might think of this game as a below-average indie platformer but they are in for a surprise. Momodora III is one of the best hidden gem platformers I have played in recent years along with Cave Story.
One of biggest attractions of Momodora III is the simple pixelated graphics which I am biased towards so my opinion of the graphics will differ from the you, the reader. The environments of each stage are polished to the brim and each stage has its own unique atmosphere conveyed to you by its appearance and enemies. The character sprites look top notch for a 2D game and each enemy is graphically different from the other. Though there isn’t much dialogue in the game, the designs of the characters give them some life, especially their different attires.
Another important aspect of platforming games is the soundtrack, which Momodora III excels at. There aren’t words to describe the music other than it is simply beautiful. Each stage has its own music to go with it and all of them are jaw dropping to listen to. The music just gets you immersed into the game and flows well with the atmosphere it's trying to convey, further enveloping the player.  Soundtrack isn’t something that I pay much attention to but this game does it so well that I just had to include it in the review.
The gameplay is quite basic for playformers of this day and age. You have to traverse through areas as your specific character, jumping and moving on platforms to make it to the end of the stage while avoiding obstacles. Each stage has its own specific set of enemies and their abilities as well as appearance correlate with set stage. In order to counter these enemies you have 2 types of attacks, normal and ranged making for a simple yet enjoyable combat system.
You also have item slots which you can customize depending on the stage or your play-style. Items can be bought or found in different stages. Like most platformers, after you reach the end of a stage you face a boss. The bosses have their own attack pattern and by memorizing these patterns they can easily be beaten. The bosses are very memorable because of their uniqueness.
This game also has three difficulty settings Casual, Easy and Hard so you can choose the one that you most prefer. On the easier difficulties you start with more hearts and items, on Hard it is vice-versa.
The only bad thing about this game is that it is really short and I am giving special emphasis on its length as it is possible to beat the entire game in 30 minute! However, with its cute graphics, fun gameplay and cost of $4 Momodora III deserves a recommendation from me.

An enjoyable dungeon crawler that take inspiration from old school games like eye of the beholder and dungeon master.
The game features a lot of well-designed puzzles which will take you time to solve, there are also 7 treasures hidden in the levels of Grimrock to collect and of course every level got numerous secrets that hide helpful supplies and equipment to help you overcome the many challenges waiting ahead.
The combat is what you expect out of an old school inspired dungeon crawler – you will usually lead your enemies to an area where you can dance around the them in order avoid being hit while attacking them.
You can unlock a hidden challenge mode called "Toorum Mode" by fulfilling the requirements for the steam achievement called " Buddies with Toorum".
This mode let you do a solo run with a unique character with unique class that include with some unique sets of skills and abilities.
To do this, after unlocking the achievement you need to start a new game with character creation on and then you need to change the first prisoner's name to Toorum and press enter (don’t make any other changes to the character and do not add any other prisoner to the party).
There is also an option for an "Old School Mode" that disable auto-mapping completely, so prepare a stack of grid paper and a pencil for that retro feeling.

Completely frustrating game.
Frankly, this game has made me realize I can't trust Steam reviews anymore, at least not in the aggregate. This game by any modern standards is terrible. Awful, clumsy interface. Level design that will make you pull your hair out. Controls are clunky. Ugly graphics, even considering its age.
Why do people rate this so highly on Steam? Purely nostalgia. This is why I can't trust Steam reviews anymore. I understood that the graphics would be outdated, sure. But the gameplay, interface, level design, and controls should all have stood the test of time, right?
No. I have to do so much tedious labor to do the simplest of tasks, such as leveling the ground, getting rid of trees (hint, you have to do it one click at a time), and making sure that the roller coaster pieces fit not only the slope of the ground, but each other. Simply, there is a lot that the programming should have taken care of for you. Did I really need to click on several different menus in order to 1. raise the slope 2. raise the tiles 3. place the tile or track 4. make sure it all exactly fits back at the beginning. Otherwise, start all the way over with a clunky arrow system to select the exact track you want to change out, rather than simply clicking on the piece you want to change. I can't count how many rollercoasters I've begun just to delete the entire thing because it would be easier to just start over than to figure out how to make it all fit in the end. Oh, by the way, the game timer will tick away as you figure out how to finally make the rollercoaster pieces come together.
Level design is either very repetitive, or done in such a way to be completely frustrating. One level has a park that's a lovely garden. But in order to achieve the usual goals (park rating above X, number of guests above Y at a very specific date), you have to destroy all the loveliness. In other words, destroy the park and build yet another cookie cutter theme park that makes for good business in order to reach the level's objectives.
Worst of all, you have to play every single repetitive little level in order to get to what you really want - a sandbox mode. Look, the reason why we all play this game is not to make fake money. It's to have a theme park that looks the way we want it. Right? So why not just give us the sandbox level to start with? I understand that the game developers want a learning curve. But right now, the thirty or so levels all feel like agonizing tutorial levels that I cannot skip.
Interface involves so much unnecessary clicking. In addition, the little pictures that indicate different menus are not very intuitive. Poor design.
And of course, the graphics are an eyesore. They're not just outdated. They're just plain ugly. I can play a very old game, such as the original Super Mario Bros. or Sonic the Hedgehog and appreciate the graphics for what it was in its heyday. Even if I can't, the lack of good graphics is compensated by good gameplay in a true classic. But as discussed above this is not the case in this game.
I haven't yet tried the sequel (RCT2), but my guess is that's where the game developers actually fixed all the problems that drive me crazy.
If you want a good theme park simulator, find another game. There are plenty out there.

Not your typical Hack n Slash. On the contrary, Jotun is a beautiful game with hand crafted backgrounds that really make you think you're tiny. Basically the game challenges you to complete 5 zones with 2 levels and 1 boss each. The levels are usually constructed maze like. Your goal is to find the "boss runes" to unlock the area's boss. You can also find "skill runes" that give you certain power ups to use during combat (limited use), "refreshing pools" that refresh your life and power-ups (only once per activation) and "hidden golden apples" that permanently increase your life. Skill runes include healing, invincibility, faster running, distraction clone, increased melee damage and homing arrows.
Once you have used up all your power-ups they will be unavailable until you hit a new fountain or until you defeat a boss (or are defeated by a boss). Sames goes for your life bar. The levels themselves usually do not involve a lot of enemies, if at all. Mostly you will be fighting elemental hazards, like lava, lightning, cave-ins or big birds that swoop down from time to time, amongst others. This makes the game very unique, but those looking for a combat focussed gameplay should veer clear of this one, because you will not be fighting a lot.
Speaking of fighting, you only have 2 attacks anyway. A low damage quick attack and a high damage (veeeery) slow attack that can be cancelled by you or by taking damage. The combat really isn't what makes this game great...outside of the bosses there's just too little to do in that regard.
The bosses themselves are gigantic Jotun, Norse giants so to speak. Each boss has its own attack patterns and stages. So the lower health a boss gets the more difficult it becomes for you to defeat him. You have to learn the attacks and know when to pop you power-ups to go for the kill. They are extremely fun, but can be a bit frustrating at times. Technically you can also gather all world power ups including health before engaging any one of the bosses. They do not give you special drops or powers or whatever, however. After you defeat the 5 area bosses Odin awaits you.
The music, the art style and the Norse narrator are what make this game great. It's not very long. I got about 4 to 5 hours in and I've not rushed through it, but explored every nook and cranny. You are paying for a nice theme and an artistic vision rather than a game with deep gameplay. If that is worth the full asking price to you, has to be your decision. For me, unfortunately, it's not, since there are just too many games out there and Jotun in my opinion is not worth more than maybe 5-10 bucks at most in such a competitive land scape. I'm nevertheless glad that I played it.
For the final boss you might as well be fighting RNGesus.

I received this as a Christmas present when it was slated for January.  I would have to say if Inafune wanted this as a spiritual successor to Mega Man, he must have meant MM1 and none of the others.  The emphasis on it feeling like a score attack (there's a reason it was removed after the first Mega Man, it was a platformer, not an arcade game/score attack game), no invulnerability to One hit KO mechanics while in invincibility frames from taking a hit elsewhere.  Sadly if you're looking for a platformer, I can't recommend it.  You can pretty much tank all the damage through a stage, excepting one hit KO mechanics and pits.  Level design and bosses are gimmicky due to being based on infinite air dashes (which was necessary to assimilate airborn enemies I guess?) and assimilating enemies to kill them faster.  Don't get me started on the bland, contrastless art style.  Tack on the massive delays and overhyping for an ultimately extremely mediocre game, and we've got Mighty No. 9, suffering from Duke Nukem Foreveritis.

Keiji Inafune and his team at Comcept set up a Kickstarter to create a spiritual sequel to Mega Man, a franchise he put many, many years' worth of work into (but didn't create - I sure see that bit of misinformation being spread around a lot lately).  It took much longer to do this than they anticipated, in part because they spread themselves too thin trying to port it to as many platforms as possible.  Their plans and business decisions were frequently ill-advised along the way, but in the end they delivered what they said they would.
And now we're making Inafune a pariah because we were inconvenienced a bit, or had to wait longer than we wanted, or because the game doesn't look like a handful of concept art mock-ups shown during the pitch.  I see people howling for blood, wanting to know what the money was spent on, apparently unaware that game development is REALLY EXPENSIVE and the 2.6 mil or so they actually cleared after Kickstarter fees and backer reward costs isn't anywhere near enough to make the HD, hand-drawn adventure they naively believed they were getting.  I've seen Mighty No. 9's graphics compared to a PS2 game by people that apparently never actually played a PS2 game if they honestly think that's true.  I've seen truly remarkable individuals boycott the game altogether because they hired a community manager that's openly a feminist.  I've seen it bashed by professional reviewers for being too much like Mega Man.  As ever, Kickstarters fail to understand that their pledge wasn't a pre-order, nor a guarantee that they'd get whatever they were envisioning when they hit that donate button.  Yet here we are, awash in another sea of crowdfunding bitterness.  I'll be glad when that particular fad passes, if only so I don't have to keep reading about this silly, entitled drama over and over and over again.  It's a 20 dollar game about a robot boy that fights other robots, not a moral line in the sand.  Mighty No. 9's fate was sealed long before it ever released, brought low by a bunch of manchild angst and internet slacktivists eager to turn EVERYTHING into a cause.
So, all that said, how's the game?
Frustrating, occasionally brilliant and surprisingly addictive.  The dash mechanic gives a certain fluidity to the Mega Man-derived combat that even the X series only hinted at.  This comes at a cost, as a lot of environmental hazards are basically rendered harmless and certain sequences intended to be setpieces fall a little flat.  The antagonists sport some great designs (Dynatron and Battalion in particular are awesome), but you'll likely find the powers you gain from defeating them less effective than your standard blaster in most situations.  The presentation and design of certain stages are cleverly done, yet others verge on being an afterthought.  Yes, the graphics - much like the engine rendering them - are outdated, yet I was pleasantly surprised throughout by some neat lighting effects and fun little details that are there purely to add some character.  You get the sense that if the game was ever permitted a sequel, we might have something really special on our hands.
Seems pretty unlikely right now, and that's a shame.  Inafune wasn't out to swindle anyone.  He was just overwhelmed, as so many before him have been when trying to realize a crowdfunding dream.  If you're a fan of classic Mega Man and have an open mind, give it a shot.  You might be surprised.

When it comes right down to it, fans that loved the prior two Serious Sam releases either absolutely love or abhorrently hate Serious Sam 2. Stepping away from the dime-a-dozen FPS graphic design, this title takes on a vibrantly colored cartoony approach that was prevalent in many top-end adventure games at the time; Crash Bandicoot, Ratchet and Clank, and Spyro, to name a few. Though none of these are FPS games by any means, these are the footsteps that Serious Sam 2 followed in both graphically and with its quirky, more mature, sense of humor, while still keeping the core gameplay that trademarks the series.
It's easy to notice that CroTeam had a much larger budget for this title. One of the best and most noteworthy features is the addition of an actual, well flushed out storyline that's completed by a massive amount of cutscenes. Sam "Serious" Stone gets summoned to the Sirian Great Council, where they give him the task of finding five medallion pieces that are being held by different races on five different planets. Once Sam has the amulet, then his arch nemesis Mental will be vulnerable. Most of these planets are populated by friendly races that help Sam along his journey, as he battles wave after wave of foes, and Sam sometimes aids them by releasing any of their people who've been held prisoner by Mental's army. At the end of each planet, the player is tasked with fighting a monstrous boss battle, each with a different mechanic that's more than just spray n' pray.
There's almost always a cutscene at the beginning and end of every level, and there are a total of 42 levels that are split into 7 chapters. Indeed, Serious Sam 2 was the largest title to date at the time of its release in 2005, and the total run time of the game is roughly 9-10 hours if you play on the easiest difficulty. This is a monumental upgrade from the 3-4 hour runs that either The First or Second Encounter offered. Though still linear in nature, every level is distinctly its own, from sprawling forests, snowy mountain tops, hellish volcanoes, an alien city, a game show, and so much more. Despite its straightforwardness, there are still tons of hilarious secrets to uncover, and the game also throws in the odd nod to other spectacular FPS titles like Unreal and Duke Nukem.
As stated previously, Serious Sam 2 does keep the core gameplay of the series alive and well. Players will face onslaughts of nearly constant monster spawns in massive open areas, while jumping and dodging attacks rather than rely on cover-based shooting. On easier difficulties, the player's health replenishes overtime, but harder modes make one rely on health and armor pick-ups. Once the enemies are cleared out, it's on to the next foe filled area until the end of the level is reached. However, new to the series is a life system, and instead of dying and getting a game over, players may now respawn rather than restarting at their last save point. Extra lives can be earned based on a score system where points are earned by killing enemies. There also aren't as many power-ups, but Serious Damage has been left in play.
Not only does this title offer the most diversity of the series in terms of maps, but it also is chocked full of new and old enemies alike; more than the previous two installments had combined. Just looking at the game, its enemies, and its weapons, it's really easy to tell that CroTeam got a lot of inspiration from the Halo franchise; in fact, some of the humanoid soldier enemies look a lot like Spartans. The futuristic, alien-like design of some of the weapons look very much like what would be used in the aforementioned acclaimed series as well. Since Halo 1 and 2 were extremely popular at time time, there's no doubt that the influence sunk in to Serious Sam 2, but it works in its favor; making it feel both new yet familiar all at the same time.
Despite all the good things that can be said about Serious Sam 2, its major downfall is how long some of the fights become. There are times when the player will question whether or not the hordes of enemies will ever stop spawning, and it does become monotonous and tiresome despite the vibrancy and diversity of the enemies and levels. It's not necessarily a game that someone would want to sit down and pound out hours playing all at once, but rather split up into days and even weeks to avoid the grueling wave grinds. It does give one an opportunity to use every single weapon in their arsenal to their advantage, but it still doesn't relieve the overwhelming sensation that these mechanics are in place to elongate game time.
The excellent soundtrack should also be given a shout-out here, as each map is filled with brilliant music catered to its landscape. Not only do you have amazing music for the small duration of time that you're out of the fight, but there's also epic battle music that's sure to get your blood pumping as you riddle enemies full of bullet holes and plasma burns.
It's true that the whimsical, off-beat side characters and quirky cartoon nature of Serious Sam 2 will not appeal to everyone. However, it's without question that visually the game is the best in the original trilogy of releases. The flushed out storyline and addition of numerous cutscenes have made a major difference that definitely doesn't go unnoticed. Though some have complained that this release doesn't feature as much gore, the franchise never had much until the HD Encounters were released; with that said, Serious Sam 2 does have quite a lot of blood in it. Sam has also kept his crude, tongue-in-cheek humor and it's even more prominent now with the large amount of dialogue in the game. Without a doubt, for fans new and old alike, this is the Serious Sam that you should be playing.

I'm reluctant to write this review, but even at a sale price, I'm not sure this game was worth the money.
This choose-your-own-adventure text game starts with an interesting setting and gives you some interesting options for a psychological subplot while you go through the main storyline. You have a decent amount of control about the type of robot(s) you will build, and what kind of business or other ventures you will engage in. However, the interactions with other characters are somewhat limited, and become increasingly detached as the story leaps ahead years from page to page. If you've traded your humanity for success, that's a plausible enough story mechanism, but if you're doing a more "humane" run-through, it takes away from the immersion. Overall the last half or one-third of the story feels rushed, and even though the scope of the story is usually quite grand by that point, I found myself uninterested in it.
The writing in this story is tolerable, but not particularly good. What breaks the game for me, however, are the continiuty errors. For example, in one play-through, your lover ends up disappearing, causing you great emotional distress. Then, a few sections later, in a passing line, the story notes that this same lover has left you because of a particular political choice you made. Nowhere was it mentioned that the lost love returned safely, so it makes zero sense for them to have reappeared without explanation only to leave you again. This sort of continuity error takes away all value from the "choose your own adventure" aspect of the game and sadly makes me unable to recommend it.

Finished after something over 25 hours - (second outing).
Enjoyed it a lot as it's a proper old-school dungeon crawler but with a more modern outlook - so that's a win from the start. Traps and assorted puzzles can be challenging, but not frustrating, and enemies are varied and nicely done.
Graphically it looks really good, and with that and the excellent sound design it creates a great and indeed claustrophobic atmosphere - (play it with headphones in a dark room for maximum effect!) .
Overall I definitely recommend it, the story does draw you in - (literally in the dungeon context) - and you actually do find yourself caring about the four characters you control, the resource management aspect added to the stats and skills and so forth serve to really add to the experience; dungeons also - (given that they are linear) - have a surprising amount to do and find, which was nice.
If you add all of that to a great and definitely old-school mapping system - (which you can turn off) - and a really good and intuitive level editor, you have a great package!
Complaints?
Not a lot to be honest, some of the creature attacks could have done with being a little more varied - (I'm looking at you spiders), and some of the specialisations weren't I thought catered for quite as well as they could have been - (rogues, to be honest, didn't really seem to have much to be "roguey" about other than, very effective, ranged shots), and I guess that I was disappointed in the hit\miss ratio of my tank - I felt that she should have had a better accuracy given her level.
To be honest though, none of these things are really more than niggles, and certainly in no way to be taken as game-breakers.
In summary, it's a really good modern take on an old gaming trope with a great retro feel, a good story and neat little touches, it looks good and sounds good and is a fine example of how less and simple are sometimes much more fun and effective than michael Bay-ing the nuts ouf of a non-linear open world uber romp - (which is cool too, but you know what I mean).
Looking forward to II, when I have the cash!! :D

There is one path to go through, through the entire game, with small easily missable tidbits on the side throughout. It is very linear, but that doesn't detract from what the game wants to tell you. It can be off-putting though, if you simply want to explore the beautiful city then you cannot. I didn't have any issue with it, personally, but others definitely do. The game has a story and a setting that it wants to present to you, and that's exactly what it does as you progress forward.
Combat might feel overwhelming, shallow, or repetitive. It can take practice to get used to, and you do need a halfway decent combination of Functions, especially as you progress farther, to do worthwhile damage and survive without losing Functions very often. But that's one plus of the combat: it's highly customizable. You can make various sorts of builds. Every Function has 3 effects, 1 that can happen at a time, depending on how you have it equipped. Is it a main skill? It is an upgrade to a previously existing skill? Is it a passive? Play around and experiment. Look at the numbers in the Access Point screen when you're equipping stuff and read what they do. I'm a big fan of Void(Bounce,Purge) followed up by Breach(Ping,Breach), and Spark(Bounce,Load) is also really nice. I hear that it's worth trying Jaunt(Purge,Split) and Help(Switch,Load) but have yet to do so, myself.
You can find some very fun and very satisfying combinations, and you can also, eventually, buffer yourself to survive the hardships a bit more easily. Similarly, you can equip Limiters to make the combat both more challenging and more rewarding. Combat is surprisingly complex and deeper than it seems, and the moves are versatile. It gets especially crazy later on, as you're trying to shuffle around with the best combination out of what you have and with turn planning to survive difficult encounters. It's exciting and thrilling, but can feel unfair until you learn. As for repetition, there isn't anything to be done about that unless you change up your build often. I didn't find it repetitive nor did I feel that it dragged on, but that's simply because I was enthralled and learning every step of the way and personally do not mind combat even when it does feel repetitive in games. Other people definitely feel differently.
The game starts off with you thrust into the middle of events and from there the plot and details evolve as you travel and progress further and further and both hear, read, and see more and more, as more facets are revealed. It is a somewhat straightforward story, but there's a surprising amount of depth if you choose to dive into it, through unlocking all of the character bios, finding all of the machines, getting all of the dialogues, and just thinking about it, really. You aren't given all of the pieces and must figure out, or theorize, about a large amount of things, yourself. What you are given is fed to you in delicious little pieces that slowly fit together more and more. Is the ending confusing? Are other things confusing? Are some things seemingly random? Yep, yeah, and yes. There is a reason, implication, and symbolistic meaning for all of it. However, similar to Dark Souls for the sake of memes and comparing this game to one of my other favorites, you can very easily miss the "point" of the story and wind up feeling confused and left unpleased. You'll either love it or hate it or think not much of it, really. I for one absolutely adored it and found it very memorable, particularly the Process and learning about Cloudbank and the Camerata's involvement. I'll see you in the Country, friend!
How quickly you level up is dependant on how many, and what, Limiters you have equipped, how many side encounters you fight through, and I think also how many enemies you let respawn to kill again but don't quote me on that last one, I'm not positive at all. I do feel that you receive new Functions in an appropriate pacing, and I enjoy how you have a choice between two Functions and two Limiters each time you level. There are some areas that can be considered difficulty curves, and you can really find yourself in a rut if you keep perishing and losing Functions and barely surviving. It's absolutely worthwhile to visit the Beach whenever possible and practice things there and complete all of the tests, or at least try to. Some of them can be quite tricky. NG+ is also interesting. You keep your level, your Functions, and your Limiters of course, and enemy encounters are scaled up accordingly (harder enemies from the end of the game placed in the beginning of the game, for example, and small things like Creepers are less squishy). All in all, the game's pacing feels right and I feel that it builds up appropriately where needed if you take the time to listen and care to what you're hearing. It's pretty fair and balanced overall, with some things being notably worse or better than others but not gamebreaking or neccessarily gamechanging. It's all on how you use them and how you end up going through the game, which may be weird to say since it is so linear.

One of the worst games there is on steam and one of the worst games I have ever played period. The only reason to bother with it is for the story and with the cutscenes being available on youtube there is no reason to buy this terrible game. Bad gameplay aside, I wasn't able to finish it because of its numerous technical issues. On the last level you fight 4 waves of elite soldiers. 1 wave would have been plenty, but for some reason at this point they decide to flood you with them. It is one of the worst stages I have ever seen in any game because as soon as it starts you get knocked down over and over again. Most of the time there is no way to even dodge it because there are about 4 different types of enemies firing at you from all heights and angles that all have knock down shots so you stay on your back most of the time. You can't stop and fight because the second you do you go into a knock down loop and are lucky to get out of it. The knockdown in this game is particularly bad because it takes its time letting the ragdoll physics take over and ragdoll you around on the floor until your guy does a Shawn Michaels hand-spring back to his feet which is also very slow.
So since I couldn't do this part without dying from staying on knock down lock down, I lowered the difficulty to easy so I could take less dmg and just get the game over with. Since about half way through the game I had started to rush and just try to get this mess over with. I lost any urge I had to keep looking for skill point cubes and just went into hurry mode long before even the last level. So with the bad guys gone on this level, you have to use force pull and open some grates to jump down into a lower area. The problem here, like many other parts in the game, is that the force powers don't always respond right. So I couldn't open the grates and started jumping around. I got completely glitch stuck in a part of the floor that was raised a little and had to exit to the main menu and select continue game. It started me back at the beginning of the level so i would have had to defeat those 4 waves again. I just alt+f4'ed right the ♥♥♥♥ out and uninstalled this immediately. It wasn't the first time I had gotten stuck in the game in a place where I should'nt be able to but did because their quality testing on this game was non-existent. This was just the final straw.
About 3/4 through the game the sound also started messing up. I came out of a cutscene and only half of the sound effects were working. I restarted the game and it fixed it but on the next level it started it again so I just played until the last level like that because at this point the game was just so bad that I didn't care.
The boss fights are also some of the worst boss fights I have ever seen. This is I assume supposed to be a casual game for any and all Star Wars fans but the only ones who are going to be able to beat most of the bosses are people with a♥♥♥♥♥♥load of skill and patience. Any casual gamer or kid playing this has no chance of beating most bosses unless maybe they put it on easy. The boss fights were poorly conceived and even more poorly implemented.

So far I've beaten the tutorial stage and 3 out of the 8 initial stages (i'm assuming there's probably a final boss stage, a la old megaman games).  So far, these are my impressions:
The controls feel sluggish and only partially responsive
Character animations are awkward and look weird (remember how smooth the old megaman games felt?  Think the opposite of that)
Gameplay is very shallow - you have only 2 attacks, the gun attack and the dash attack to absorb enemies
You do absorb powers from bosses you beat, but they aren't very inspired or interesting to use
Platforming is very simplistic - no clinging to walls like in Megaman X
Random spikes in difficults revolving around enemies placed to murder you with cheap insta-kills
The boss battles (for me) have been extremely easy - even more so because the game tells you which power will be useful against which boss (the previously defeated boss offers "advice" on the level their power is useful on).
To be fair, the game isn't terrible.  Enemy placement seems to be mainly geared towards speedrunning, if you're into that sort of thing.  Overall, it feels like a game concept that was made before the first megaman game, and improved upon to create the megaman series.  Also, the voice acting, graphics, and cut scenes are atrocious.
EDIT:  Well, i've finished the game.  The final boss actually did show that some thought went into her design, and she was tough but fair with pattern recognition as the main key to winning... i've upped my score by one to reflect this.  However, I'll also say that the level to get to her was a gigantic pain in the♥♥♥♥♥and was not fun in the slightest.  Furthermore, the other bosses and levels (that I hadn't played when I first wrote this review) did nothing to counter my original criticisms.

Having played longer, I've edited this review.  Still very positive.
Is this game what I was expecting?  Not really.  Closer to the original MM games rather than the more refined controls that came later (See 20XX if you want a MMX-style game that's really fun).  Personally, if there's not a charge weapon of some sort, there should be some auto-fire, and I'm not fond of the dash-absorb concept, but the latter is consistent with the character concept and I imagine I'll get used to both.
That being said, it's a very fun game.  Unlike other games I've played, it really is "tough but fair."  The graphics are bright and crisp, a nice change from the current generation of overly cluttered dim corridors.  The powers are interesting, the fact that beaten bosses help you out on some levels does boost replayability a bit.  The voice acting reminds me of the cartoons I watched as a kid, and I'm actually okay with that.
Overall, a decent successor to the original Megaman games.  Just watch out for the instant death areas.  There are a lot of them (luckily, you can set the number of lives you start each level with, from 2 to 9, which is a fair way to adjust difficulty in a game like this).

With Jotun what we have is a surprisingly simple to play game with great compexity, stunning artwork  and surprisingly challenging yet simple fights.
There was so much to be pleased with in terms of the design. Whether it's the great artwork, the use of norwegian with subtitles, the scenic views or the brilliant manipulation of the camera to show off some brilliant vistas. You will have to agree Jotun is a beautiful game which captured it's norse origins superbly.
The gameplay itself is easy to pick up and yet the game is still challenging. Trawling through the minor realms is pretty straightforward, I haven't died yet while hunting the various treasures. You'll learn the story as you progress and feel the emotion behind your character as you progress. each realm you enter has its own particular obstacle which on its own isn't that tough if you're smart. Whether it's occasional lightning strikes, dodging freezing wind or  smacking around a bunch of dwarves you shouldn't find the game that challenging at these parts. Just enjoy the story and the world you find yourself in.
It's not the world or the pretty pictures that Jotun is all about though. This game is about bossfights.
Your goal in Jotun is to impress the gods through combat with mighty enemies, entering the realms was done purely to unlock that areas related boss. These bossfights are spectacular and where Jotun really shines. The camera shifts to emphasise exactly how tiny you are compared to these behemoths and it's brilliant. Remember those previous realms though, those easy obstacles from before are gonig to make you curse when they get stuck together alongside a giant hellbent on squashing your face.
Sadly there isn't much replayability to Jotun. There are some really tough and fun achievements to hunt that add some replayability but after that you're pretty much done. I don't anticipate playing more than 20 hours tops on this game before everything is completed or I give up trying to kill Hagalaz without taking any damage (I haven't even tried yet and I know that's how it's going to end).
I give Jotun 8/10
What is lovely is that current owners fo the game will get access to the DLC for free, which is a lovely thing for the game devs to do and makes me feel all warm and fuzzy inside. The price is already low and I believe worth spending on the game if you're interested.

On the other hand, I am sorry to say that the rest is so bad and shallow that even a full scale article is not enough to tell what falls so short. But briefly, level designs are incredibly boring and lazy. To solve the puzzles or to obtain items/god powers, only thing you have to do is wandering around aimlessly in literally empty places or dodging things like winds or rocks. There are not any real or difficult enemies or threats around, only annoying mechanics.
Apart from that, boss fights are supposed to give you some tough time but believe me, they are also not difficult, they are just tiring and annoying. Visually it looks gorgeous and you are expecting something epic but after a couple of fight you come to an understanding that if you are ready to spend some frustrating time with dodging things, you are going to beat the Jotuns eventually.
Overall game lacks depth and excitement. Story is like non-exist, it is a linear, uninteresting and uninfluential story with linear gameplay. This game is dealing with one of the most interesting concepts in the world like Norse mythology and you are expecting something more clever and epic but it only gives you some shallow level designs and annoying mechanics. It may be visually beautiful but I don’t think that it is worthy of your time or money.

In general, Groove City is just a H-I-I-I-G-H value for a cheap price. Go ahead and purchase!

I don't know if I recommend this game actually. but since I have to pick between yes and now, I guess I recomend it.
It looks and sounds amazing. I have nothing but compliments on those aspects. They put me right into the right mood and into the world they built.
The gameplay is where things get a little fuzzy. Platforming is good. All the right elements are there, the character size, the camera system, speed, platforms size and distance. Everything comes together nicely and jumping around is fun and challenging.
The level design (or room design?) has its highs and lows. Sometimes you enter a room and a couple of steps ahead there's a spike pit. Seeing how fast the character move this is a very easy death right there. You just entered the room and is still pressing the dpad, you fall over simply because you didn't have time to process the room layout.
Minor nitpick: The first screen of the game tells you to press A to start (as in the xbox button). I am using one so that's nice. But after that is all arrow keys this, shift button that.
Combat is the main problem I have. Even some ingredients that made platforming great are getting in the way of a good combat system. The character speed and size on screen, combined with the range of melee attack, forces you to get uncomfortably close to the enemies at the same time making that very hard. A wrong touch at the dpad and you are taking contact damage or too far to do any damage. Add to that a ridiculous amount of screen shake, projectiles flying around, ghost companion, and the confusion is all set. I find myself squinting at the screen the whole time to find my character and it's just not enjoyable.
Honestly I'm finding it hard to get over the combat aspect of the game. I keep closing the game and then opening again, because everything else is so engaging. I only played for 40 minutes, and I don't know if I'll keep playing.
So, reiterating: I'm not such a great fan of the game at the moment.  But it is very affordable! and others might be ok with the issues I am having. So, if you like what you see at the trailer I suggest giving it a shot.
