There is one path to go through, through the entire game, with small easily missable tidbits on the side throughout. It is very linear, but that doesn't detract from what the game wants to tell you. It can be off-putting though, if you simply want to explore the beautiful city then you cannot. I didn't have any issue with it, personally, but others definitely do. The game has a story and a setting that it wants to present to you, and that's exactly what it does as you progress forward.
Combat might feel overwhelming, shallow, or repetitive. It can take practice to get used to, and you do need a halfway decent combination of Functions, especially as you progress farther, to do worthwhile damage and survive without losing Functions very often. But that's one plus of the combat: it's highly customizable. You can make various sorts of builds. Every Function has 3 effects, 1 that can happen at a time, depending on how you have it equipped. Is it a main skill? It is an upgrade to a previously existing skill? Is it a passive? Play around and experiment. Look at the numbers in the Access Point screen when you're equipping stuff and read what they do. I'm a big fan of Void(Bounce,Purge) followed up by Breach(Ping,Breach), and Spark(Bounce,Load) is also really nice. I hear that it's worth trying Jaunt(Purge,Split) and Help(Switch,Load) but have yet to do so, myself.
You can find some very fun and very satisfying combinations, and you can also, eventually, buffer yourself to survive the hardships a bit more easily. Similarly, you can equip Limiters to make the combat both more challenging and more rewarding. Combat is surprisingly complex and deeper than it seems, and the moves are versatile. It gets especially crazy later on, as you're trying to shuffle around with the best combination out of what you have and with turn planning to survive difficult encounters. It's exciting and thrilling, but can feel unfair until you learn. As for repetition, there isn't anything to be done about that unless you change up your build often. I didn't find it repetitive nor did I feel that it dragged on, but that's simply because I was enthralled and learning every step of the way and personally do not mind combat even when it does feel repetitive in games. Other people definitely feel differently.
The game starts off with you thrust into the middle of events and from there the plot and details evolve as you travel and progress further and further and both hear, read, and see more and more, as more facets are revealed. It is a somewhat straightforward story, but there's a surprising amount of depth if you choose to dive into it, through unlocking all of the character bios, finding all of the machines, getting all of the dialogues, and just thinking about it, really. You aren't given all of the pieces and must figure out, or theorize, about a large amount of things, yourself. What you are given is fed to you in delicious little pieces that slowly fit together more and more. Is the ending confusing? Are other things confusing? Are some things seemingly random? Yep, yeah, and yes. There is a reason, implication, and symbolistic meaning for all of it. However, similar to Dark Souls for the sake of memes and comparing this game to one of my other favorites, you can very easily miss the "point" of the story and wind up feeling confused and left unpleased. You'll either love it or hate it or think not much of it, really. I for one absolutely adored it and found it very memorable, particularly the Process and learning about Cloudbank and the Camerata's involvement. I'll see you in the Country, friend!
How quickly you level up is dependant on how many, and what, Limiters you have equipped, how many side encounters you fight through, and I think also how many enemies you let respawn to kill again but don't quote me on that last one, I'm not positive at all. I do feel that you receive new Functions in an appropriate pacing, and I enjoy how you have a choice between two Functions and two Limiters each time you level. There are some areas that can be considered difficulty curves, and you can really find yourself in a rut if you keep perishing and losing Functions and barely surviving. It's absolutely worthwhile to visit the Beach whenever possible and practice things there and complete all of the tests, or at least try to. Some of them can be quite tricky. NG+ is also interesting. You keep your level, your Functions, and your Limiters of course, and enemy encounters are scaled up accordingly (harder enemies from the end of the game placed in the beginning of the game, for example, and small things like Creepers are less squishy). All in all, the game's pacing feels right and I feel that it builds up appropriately where needed if you take the time to listen and care to what you're hearing. It's pretty fair and balanced overall, with some things being notably worse or better than others but not gamebreaking or neccessarily gamechanging. It's all on how you use them and how you end up going through the game, which may be weird to say since it is so linear.

I remember playing this back when it came out and thinking it was just awesome. The technical prowess of Digital Molecular Matter and the likes was enough to look past an at times overly melodramatic story, cringeworthy dialog and voice acting performances, clichéd characters, and an often irritating targeting system and gameplay mechanics.
Unfortunately, close to 8 years down the line, I'm forced to realise that breaking stuff and making it look pretty is basically much all that TFU does well. As opposed to some games with a lot of heart that retain a certain charm even after a few years, The Force Unleashed doesn't seem to have aged all that well. The only thing it had going for it was that it looked good, and by today's standards that's just not true anymore. Sadly, this only serves to emphasise all of its original flaws. It also feels ridiculously overpriced at the time of writing this.

Jotun is an isometric action game where you play as a viking woman who has died at sea. Because her death wasn't honourable she has to prove herself to the gods by defeating the Jotun in combat.
The game's art style and sound design are both fantastic and do wonders for setting a tone in the world as well as the various Jotun fights. The combat is slow and feels very deliberate when executed. This makes fighting the giant Jotun feel like it has a better sense of scale. You feel as if you are this tiny person fighting this formidable giant who is much stronger than you.
The thing I liked the best about Jotun is that it teaches you almost all of the mechanics required for the bosses organically in the exploration phases prior to the actual boss fights. You are given an environment to learn and practice in, so when you eventually get to the Jotun there are no surprises. I say almost because there is a mechanic in one fight that isn't introduced prior to said fight. Not sure if I missed something, but that aisde Jotun does an excellent job of introducing and teaching the player through playing the game.
Jotun is a beautiful game that is mechanically sound and prefers to teach it's players through it's design. I think it is a fantastic game and if anything I've said here has you interested I would recommend picking it up.

Jotun succeeds strongly and wholistically in relating a memorable overview of Norse mythology while weaving and foiling that with a woman's personal narrative in that culture.
Nothing feels superfluous. There exist independently gamey elements, but they seem to have been chosen and work perfectly for just exactly what they're chosen to do.
The visuals are clean and emotive with camera panning conveying strong vistas and a sense of scope while the main character's animation feels smooth and just the right amount of visually off to place her as outsider on this ethereal plane of beings.
Sound design is epically rumbly and deep, establishing weight and import to the right objects and events.
The game pacing works right along with that visual scope. It is plodding and deliberate. You feel small and alone against enormous beings. Your motions and attacks feel slow but powerful; that is your connection to this place.
Huge sections of world are effectively empty - Punctuated by the appearance of powerful forces and rare monstrous beings. (For real, one third or less of the levels have any actual enemies to fight besides bosses.)
I could probably start running in circles describing how one elements leads into or support the other, but it should be clear by now that this was a fun, engaging experience with Norse myths. If you want to spend a few hours living the legends, jump in.
The possible cons that some gamers should consider:
1. Short (Think twice if you're the bro always asking for X hours out of each gaming dollar spent.)
2. Easy (I think all the exploration and combat fits perfectly to tell the story and theme, but the slow, deliberate fights are mechanically trivial.)

As someone mentioned, "The 7 day demo looks better than the final game, WTF happened?" Here's the answer to that: Because this game is incorrectly named. It's actually called Mighty No. 2. This game is NOT the Mighty No.9 we are looking for.

Before the review a little disclosure: Not only am I backer ($120 tier) but I’m also No. 56008.  But I’m here to review the game only.
STORY
The Xel absorption angle does bring something new to an otherwise basic plot and it sets up the game just fine.  Could the worldbuilding and character development been done better? Sure, but personally I usually don't care for stories in my platformers as it usually doesn’t add anything to the experience.  But I did sit through this one for review purposes, and though I have no issues with it in terms of storytelling, I did find it distracting.  For a game that's practically built around speedrunning, the cutscenes during the stage and in-between just grinds things to a halt.  Thankfully you can skip them, but then there's still audio dialogue that play at certain points of a stage.  I was fine with it for the most part and the text dialogue that played with the audio never blocked anything important, but I can imagine a few of you will be wishing for a way to turn it off.
GRAPHICS/ART DIRECTION
It’s the thing that people notice right away and scrutinize.  So I’ll be blunt: it doesn't look great.  Technically speaking the graphics most likely aren't going to impress anyone, especially when you can find mobile games that can match or even exceed it.  Overall it's not terrible, outside of those laughable effects obviously, and the "Dreamcast" comparison is a tad extreme.  In fact there are some moments where I was genuinely impressed; the hallway just before facing Countershade comes to mind.  I would say it’s stuck somewhere in the middle: definitely not good enough to compare to anything current gen (even indie games), but not bad enough to consider it a deliberate homage to older platformers.
The 2D character designs by Kimo Kimo look fantastic, with everyone having their own unique styles.  However the in-game character models, though they look similar, look so lifeless and fake that they lose all appeal.  The lack of facial and mouth movement are an issue, but I find the fact they all look like they’re made out of plastic or rubber is what kills them.  Yes they’re robots but they also had so much life and attitude on paper, whereas in-game they look like automated dolls.  This issue is mostly noticeable with the human characters, with Dr. White having a naval mine for hair and Dr. Sanda looking like an actual balloon that should float into the air at any moment.
The look and design of the levels doesn’t fare much better, sharing the same lifeless and fake issues.  And as if they were attempting to fill in the emptiness of the levels, there are times where they go overboard with the background and stage effects.  It’s clear they put plenty of effort into the backgrounds of the level and it does impress at times, but you know they’re doing too much when it gets difficult to see what you’re doing or it just starts to hurt your eyes.  Just thinking about the cross hatching beams in Aviator’s stage or the highway busyness in Brandish’s stage makes my eyes water!  This becomes a huge issue when trying to determine if an enemy damaged enough to safely absorb, which has resulted in numerous instances where I would prematurely dash into them.
As for framerate, I ran into some noticeable dips during my playthrough.  At one point it was practically game breaking during Brandish’s stage as it made it almost impossible to jump between cars safely.  However resetting the game seem to solve that particular issue but the occasional dips still remained.
MUSIC/VOICE ACTING
Mega Man has been known for its music, but sadly it’s just passable for Mighty No 9.  It’s not bad, but I wouldn’t necessarily call them good either.  Outside of the main theme, none of the songs are memorable nor do they pump you up for what’s in store.   This is most notable when facing bosses, where in past Mega Man as you meet the end stage boss a song plays that gives you sense of impending doom.  As for Mighty No 9?  The soothing beginning of the main theme starts to play out when you meet your foe.  It totally ruins the mood and the actual boss theme that follows doesn’t help to bring you back into the mood.
The voice acting for the English audio is Saturday morning cartoon bad, and looking at the dialogue, I’m fairly certain that was their intent.  I choose not to cringe every time I hear someone talk however, so I quickly changed it to Japanese.  It’s pretty standard typical anime sounding, so it’s not bad.  I do have a major gripe with the subtitles though, or should I say “dubtitles”.  Instead of translating the Japanese dialogue, the subtitles are taken from the English dubs transcript, and as a result there are many instances where they don’t really match with each other.  There’s even one instance where Aviator simply laughs in Japanese but the subtitles shows an entire sentence of dialogue.
GAMEPLAY
Dashing is the main attraction to the game as it helps you to traverse the stages and is needed in order to use his Xel Absorption ability.  You can absorb enemies far faster than simply killing them with your arm cannon and doing so grants Beck with power ups that help with taking care of the next wave of enemies.  Furthermore, enemy placement and level design practically demands that you use dash every chance you get.  And at first I have no issues with this, but the novelty of it all wears out fairly quickly and I grew tired of pressing the dash button far more than the attack button.  You also realize an odd conundrum: the ability to dash constantly gives you too much freedom as you can at times just skip past enemies, but dashing being the best way to take out enemies also feels restrictive.  Thankfully getting new weapons from the bosses alleviates some of the monotonousness, but you’ll most likely find that only 2 or 3 of them are useful outside of boss battles.
Level design wise, as I mentioned it can get pretty empty at times.  It shares many of the same features of a level you may find in a typical Mega Man game: go through a hallway full of enemies, fight a mini boss, another hallway of enemies and then the boss.  However there seems to be something lacking with Mighty No 9’s levels as if there’s not enough variety or enemies spread about the stages.  There are instances where things do get hectic as you navigate through obstacles and enemies, but it’s few and far between.  I would like to acknowledge Countershade’s stage, though practically just one big hallway, there’s a unique twist of having to find the boss as he snipes you from a distance.  It’s original, which is sadly missing from the rest of the game.
The game is difficult in typical Mega Man fashion, where cheap deaths are plenty and pulling your hair out as you try and figure out a boss’ attack pattern is the norm.  I’m fan of that so I’m totally ok with all of that!  My main issue with the gameplay are with the controls.  They’re simply not intuitive enough and pretty inconsistent.  I can’t count the times where my dash would overshoot me one minute and then have it not push me far enough the next.  Anyone who has tried to dash under the turbines in Dynatron’s stage can probably relate to this.  There have also been numerous occasions where I’m hanging off a ledge and drop down when I was trying to jump up.  I’m all for a game being challenging and punishing me for not being precise, but it’s hard for me to find any enjoyment when the game doesn’t let me control Beck the way I want to.
CONCLUSION
Could I recommend this game?   Even at around $20 I don’t think I can.  For newcomers, they can buy the Mega Man Legacy Collection at the price and it does a far better job at showing how fun platformers can be.  And for Mega Man fans who’s looking for their next fix, I feel that there are too many flaws with the game to allow them enjoy it.

Jotun is a charming little game that mixes environmental exploration and boss fights. It shines through its narrative immersion and offers breathtaking art and music. The game is relatively easy and short, and it is more about experiencing a beautiful journey than it is about overcoming challenges.
For a game that's basically a boss rush, Jotun is quite easy to beat. I killed every one of the 5 jotuns quite handily, usually with no more than 2 retries. The end boss was a bit harder, and took me 5 tries. It took me just about 5 hours to complete the game 100%. Don't expect Titan Souls or Shadow of the Colossus in terms of difficulty here, as the game does not require much in terms of thinking and skills.
Combat in Jotun is basically just move, hit and dodge-roll. Once in a while, you'll trigger a special power, but they're not that crucial to your success and don't really bring in any tactical play. Similarly, environmental puzzles are not complicated, they just take a bit of work to complete.
One interesting characteristic of Jotun is that it masterfully gives the illusion of great danger and urgency, when in fact, gameplay-wise, it's not a hard game at all. But the mise en scene and overall atmosphere make every fight and challenge feel epic and dangerous. It may sound negative, but in fact, the result is very pleasant and exhilerating, especially the boss fights.
I think Jotun's greatest strength is that every action you take, and every location you visit feels important and connected to the game's progression. You certainly don't mash buttons in this slow-paced game that sometimes feels a bit like a walking simulator. It's all about economy of player action, in order to serve the narrative experience.
Jotun's narrative immersion is supported by a breath-taking art-style, an atmospheric soundtrack and a great narrator. Jotun really is unique in this regard, and feels like no other game. All of this culminates in boss fights, which are awe-inspiring and memorable.
Overall, I recommend Jotun. Go try it now!

Mighty No. 9 Will forever be haunted by its delays and failure to live up to everyone's expectations. I'm not going to defend the delays and other bull that came along with this game. But the thing is it's a great game. Worth more than its $20 price definitely. But it's reviews, at least from non-pro critics are really just being tainted by Self Entitled Pissants. They all ruined the experience further with their negativity and mob-meme mentality. So many reviews are short, jokes, or by people who barely actually touched the game. If their issues are based on the game being unplayable to framerate issues than I hope those get fixed so that they can hopefully actually play the game and re-do their review. I'm running a 8-10 year old custom build a friend built for me when I saved up about $800 from a summer job and I luckily could play it at full settings no issues. The only time I had issues was when I went to test something for another reviewer, and yes, at least in Cryosphere's stage in windowed I would get some frame issues around the mid-boss, but that was it.
Enough of the anecdotal stuff.
Visuals: I like the visuals as they are. They are cute and cartoony. They remind me a lot of how Megaman looks in Sm4sh. They could be better, but what would really be the point? The game doesn't have a bad visual style and is pleasant to look at.
Sound: The music and sound effects are great. Though I know the Mighty No. 9 Rap by Mega Ran will get flack, I like it because its so bad it's good. Its a lot like the Pumpkin Hill and other Knuckles levels music from Sonic Adventure 2. The voice acting(In English) is enjoyable if you take it for the hammy acting that it is. It's not exceptional but, its a Megaman inspired game. At least it's not Zero wondering what he's even fighting for.
Gameplay: The gameplay is fun. It's not Megaman, it's not Megaman X, it's not Megaman Zero, ect. If you want those go play those or the really good fan game of them. Or even go play 20XX on Steam. It's a great Megaman X inspired game with Roguelike qualities and co-op multiplayer and leaderboards. That all being said Mighty No. 9 is its own game and shouldn't be judged so harshly for not being its predecessors. It is it's own enjoyable experience with it's own new things. It's a mix of a score and time attack at the end of the main campaign. At first I didn't like the score thing or the weakening enemies to dash at them and had no interest in the game. But I actually loved it. It really made me want to push to get better at the game. I love speedrunning so I'm gonna give this one a shot. Now the game can be almost punishingly difficult at time, what with not letting you keep its equivalent of E-Tanks on death, but its more than manageable especially if you don't turn off the feature that occasionally throws you some pitty power-ups for mucking up. A little patience and perseverance will go a long way.
Story: Nothing special or spectacular. Basic Megamany stuff. But Dr. Whites secret does have me wanting mroe DLC or a sequel.

I was not a backer for this game, but I must say if you are looking for a Megaman game, this will not fully fulfill your wants or needs.
Do not go straight into this game thinking it should be a new megaman, because that might just set you up for plain disappointment.
There are a few things this game does right and does them pretty damn well.  The combo system and the new way to take out enemies is both something fun and something that takes getting used to. The ranking system is very similar to the one in MMZ games and allows self improvement and to see how well you can run the game and how good you are getting.
Now don't get me wrong this game has a $20 price tag and you can probably finish it in a good 2-4 hours depending on how good you are at adapting to the new mechanics of the game.
Now lets get to the nitty gritty of the game.
Pros:
- New basic system of how the game plays but keeps a good core of Megaman to it
- Infinite air dash <3
- Combo system can feel rewarding if that's what you're into
- One of the level designs is completely new to MM games and feels fresh although it can become tedious
Cons:
- LOTS AND I MEAN LOTS OF INSTANT DEATH TRAPS
- Said traps are often before a boss room and can lead to frustration
- No wall kicking... so when you get hit by an enemy and fall below the platforms you are dead :(
- Climbing up walls/platforms can be a little weird
- Most levels and designs for the levels aren't anything new.
- Very few soundtracks... you hear the main theme like 30% of the game...
- The credits... is really long because of the kickstarter backer list
All in all the game is not terrible as a lot of people out there have put it to be, it's just they are putting a lot of faith and dreams into what they thought would replace Megaman.  If you go into it with a fresh mindset the game in itself is quite fun.

A  short, cute, fun action/platformer.  Momodora III won't take you more than 90 minutes tops to beat but it's a game with no fat or padding out and has decent replay value.  The most unique aspect of the gameplay is that you can find/buy various items that act as accessories and can have multiple ones active at the same time.  Even though the game is short, you can new game plus and carry over your accessories so use can whatever you unlocked the first time through right off the bat.
Graphics, sound, and controls are solid.  Save points are frequent enough that death isn't a huge setback.  There are three difficulties, with the easiest basically rendering you invincible.  Bosses look good and have some decent ideas but are mostly beaten by getting right up into them and whacking away rather than any particular strategy.  You can play as either Momo or Dora, with Dora being the easier of the two.
In short, a fun little pixel game that reminiscent of Cave Story in multiple ways with a decent bit of replayability.  Definitely worth the cheap asking price if you have any interest in the genre.

In my opinion, Legend of Grimrock is quite good but has some glaring flaws. The UI is extremely obtuse and clunky, especially for spell-casting. If you input stuff too fast, it loses track of what order it was inputted. The story is also very lacking in depth or charm, player characters and enemies alike are non-descript and typical fantasy cliches. Legend of Grimrocks' strength lies in its intelligent level design, solid combat and mostly good puzzle-solving. You get rewarded pretty handsomely for having attention to detail, so if that's your thing - you'll love this game.
Personally, I enjoyed my time but find myself kinda bored after a while. There's so little writing, combat is rhythmic but not particularly engaging or fluid, levelling up doesn't feel exciting either. Most of the hook is exploring and discovering secrets, which is great but just not my thing as much. Your mileage may vary; if you like old-school dungeon crawlers, you're in for a treat. Legend of Grimrock nails that aspect, just personal enjoyment factors stop me from appreciating it as much as most. For me, it's enjoyable but imperfect.

Everything about this game is well executed and polished, however, it's all done in a way that each thing will feel good or bad to you in a highly subjective way.
The sound track and visuals are, arguably of course, the best part of this game. You can love them, hate them, or just be meh, but you cannot deny that they are well crafted and implemented.
The story is great and well thought out, however, it is drip feed to you through characters who clearly know more and just don't explain anything. As well as through background information as a reward for experimenting with the skills.
The Skill system revolves around using skills you aquire as either active, an upgrade to an active skill, or as passive. There can be up to four passive slots, and four active slots. Each active slot with up to two upgrade slots. Most slots need to be unlocked through leveling. As you progress the game you start earning limiters which can allow you to make the game harder to gain more experience.
The combat is in real time, but most situations and skill combinations require you to use the planning mode, where each skill and movement costs a predetermined amount of a bar. The more of the bar you use the longer before the planning mode is usable again. There is no health regen in combat and all enemies are faster than you so using this effectively is almost mandatory. When you lose all of your health, you will go into planning mode and as long as it is not on cooldown consequtive hits will activate planning mode again. If it is on cooldown you will not die, but one of your four skills will be removed and you will return to full health. The slot will open up again at the end of the fight, but the skill will be unavailable until after the next. If all skills are removed then you hit a game over state and reload to before the fight.
I will say that I don't personally find turn based combat enjoyable, and the quasi-turn based combat in this game is no exception, but I was able to find a "build" that allowed me to mostly play real time. It is a sub-optimal way of playing the game but it can be done.
There are not that many enemies in this game but they are very unique and different.
While the game is not a long game I believe it has enough for a second playthrough with a newgame+ mode and the limiters which add a choose your own difficulty to the game.
All in all, I thoroughly enjoyed the game and would recomend it if the combat system doesn't sound like it will put you off.

I bought this game during an ofert together with Bastion. The tragic storyline can easily be associated with real life situations in a world where everybody has opinion but not many really listen or pay attention. The city of Cloudbank is attacked by a virus called Process, a virus created to solve the problems the city faced but out of ambition, an elite group called Camerata turned things for the worse. The main character's voice was stolen and we gain information as we progress through the voice of the mysterious man locked inside the Transistor.
I absolutely enjoyed the music the game has to offer, together with the grace of Red and charm of the Transistor it gives the game a unique touch. The different melodies can summon a variety of feelings ranging from love, peace and nostalgia.
The achievements require a certain degree of skill and planning. Some of them are achieved as the story progresses, most of them are optional content of the game, which I totally recommend doing. It took me about 15hrs of casual gameplay to completed all achievements, but it didn't feel a burden at any point of the game. Should you require any help, there are some achievement completion guides provided by the community which are truly amazing.
I loved the narration and philosophy towards life transmitted by our sidekick inside the Transistor, the strategy required to complete some of the fights (I recommend you playing with several limiters at a time for a tougher experience), the visual art combined with the music creates a wonderful catching atmosphere that will keep you hooked all along.
The caring and sweet rapport between Red and "X" feels very natural, everythings flows in such an elegant and charming way that it comes as no surprise to feel happy for them and wish they can be together as some point of the story. If you put yourself in his shoes, Red is a beautiful, chaming, fair, independent and smart woman who is perfect for the role of main character.

This is a review for Mighty no 9 and I have to say that it was unfortunate what happened with this game.
Here is a quick score if you don't feel like reading the rest:
Story: 1/2
Level Design:1/2
Characters:0/2
Sound Design:0/2
Gameplay:1/2
Total Score 3/10
The fact that this game was pushed back 3 times and raised 4 million dollars (and needed another 2.4 apparently)
Adjusted Score: 1/10
Story 1/2
-Spoilers-
The game is about a world where robots fight in a coloseum.  One person (Dr. White) creates a robot capable of absorbing other robots and adjusting their programming (Trinity).  He is immediately fired for making a dangerous weapon and goes to another company and makes the same robot but in "cute" form (Beck).  Trinity takes control of 8 other robots and they go haywire while Trinity absorbs the entire robot coliseum.
There is a small tangent about the female Beck (Call) and how she could be a battle droid who loves to kill but that never gets resolved.   And yes that is the entire story.  And I had to piece it together just to get that.  The story is bland, short, and you really don't care about anyone involved.  And since the world is not flushed out it feels like your going from random location to random location with no real rhyme or reason.
Level Design: 1/2
I have to give them some credit because this is where all the money went when making this game.  Some levels are really cool designs and moving backgrounds that make you feel more involved in a 2d scroller.  My favorites were the mansion that forced you to backtrack through the level to find and fight the boss, the high way where you had to jump car to car and the boss even destroyed a couple of the cars you tried to jump on, and the oil field where enemies in the distance would light oil patches on fire while you traversed the game.  None of these are original but about 1/3 of the game levels were well designed.
On the other hand; pacing is horrible.  You can tell the game was made for speed running as killing enemies mean nothing really, there are bottle neck areas made to kill you and ruin your life totals no matter how many you have, and sadly the levels have very little actual design with the game in mind.
-Example for Contrast-
MegamanX had levels that required you to do tasks that the boss would do later that level, the rainforrest for instance:  You had to dodge creatures in the trees that shot at you from above (like the boss) and then had to go through a cave with falling projectiles (like one of the boss attacks).
Mighty no 9 on the other hand had no real plan on how the level would prepare you nor did they really have a pacing set.
In other words levels should get harder as they progress and challenge the player in a meaningful way something this game did not understand.
Characters:  0/2
I really tried on this one to find something of value.  Beck is completely bland, no charisma, no spunk, nothing.  The main hub characters have white outlines (I don't think the concepts were finished) the voice acting was bland at best and down right awful for a few characters (Call).  The jokes they made were painful and were directed at an age group that would never be able to finish this game.  The bosses were megaman rip-offs and not even the good ones.  There is even a Zero in this game and HE IS TERRIBLE!  The bosses are easier than their levels with the exception on Trinity and the final boss should not be the only exception.  And as far as character growth goes I quote Monty Python "You came from nothing you go back to nothing, what have you lost?  Nothing!"
Two exceptions to this rule:  Avi is ok at best but when you have to rehear the same joke 23 times due to a bad level area you get sick of him quick.  And cryosphere yells "pew pew pew pew" when she attacks.  Not enough to earn a point with me sadly.
Sound Design:  0/2
If you are a fan of any MegaMan game you know that the music makes the levels, I still hear X music today and recall the exact level it's from and visualize the boss in my head.  Here, the music falls into the background and when I say that I mean you don't care about it.  You could honestly hear white noise and not tell the difference.  The damage sounds and the hit sounds are there but you don't feel them when they play, and the voices are there but they feel off somehow.  (It could just be the bad scripts)
Gameplay:  1/2
The core of any MegaMan game is going to be the gameplay mechanics and MightyNo9 is no exception.  The idea is you hit enemies enough times to destabilize them and then dash through them to earn points, heals, buffs, ect.  The bosses will also require you to do this to finalize damage that you have already dealt (if you don't sections of health will heal back)  The concept isn't bad... but the execution leaves much to be desired.  Honestly in the game, dashing through enemies tends to put you in more danger rather than killing enemies.  It also forces you to plan your boss fights thoroughly and you will take a lot of extra damage just trying to stop them from healing.
The attack has a sever handicap as well, the button can only read x amount of times before it locks up meaning your main attack tends to be in 3 shot bursts (not good).  The number is roughly 30 taps every 10 seconds.
Also for a game that really wants to be a speed runner the movement controls are a little loose.  I've died several times because my joystick went back into middle position and moved me one pixel the wrong way.
Final Factors:
-Price-
For $20 you get a game that gives you about 6 hours of entertainment, and I use that word liberally here.  But it is pretty and the gameplay is fun if you have friends to sit with you and grief the whole time.
-Pushback-
Ok the argument here was that they were trying really hard to give the game online play everytime they pushed it back.  (3 times)  They did say other things were causing them to fall behind but the online was the big argument.  I did not play a single online game and did not care to try.  Very few gamers would in this case.  Further the option for coop was online challenges not the actual story so I ask what was really the point then?  Why bother adding it at all other than to justify your mistakes and sticker price?
Pushing back a game is acceptable once.  We are a forgiving people, and we believe this will make the game better unfortunately pushing the game back 3 times means the hype will either be way too high that it cannot be achieved or there will be no hype at all.
-Kickstarter-
I know everyone will hit this so let's get it out of the way.  MightNo9 raised $4 Million to make this game.  If this was not bad enough the creator said in the release stream "People keep talking about the 4 million we raised, however what they don't understand is that that was only 60% of our costs."  So this game cost somewhere around 6.4 million to make.  I have to ask what did you spend it on?  Because I don't see where all that money went too in this game.  Further this is a huge insult to a community that gave you 4 million dollars to help create their dreams again and help you with yours something they will never get back.  If the creator can't show appreciation for everything his community has done for him he doesn't deserve to make games again.
Conclusion:
In conclusion the game is alright at best.  It feels like indy developers tried to recreate MegaMan and just forgot to play any of the MegaMan games.  The characters are attrocious, the animation was worse and would have been better as dramatic anime stills.  The levels had no feel, rhythm, or care brought into them other than the background art.  The gameplay can feel clunky and the most important skills your character has will get him killed more than help him.  If it goes on sale buy it.  But even then don't give this developer any more money.

UPDATE 1: Wow, can a day make a difference. Now having seen all of the main levels of the game, excluding the end game, I need to revise my decision. Playing through the sniper, mine, power plant, and airship levels, I realize that the level design here is awful. Currently in the middle of the game right now. I'll probably update this once I'm finished with it, but here are my impressions. If you are a fan of side-scrollers, you will probably like this game. I haven't noticed any problem with the hit detection and the controls are responsive. Obviously, this game is in the vein of Mega Man and is probably going to be the only experience to match that erstwhile series. I really enjoyed the dash/kill mechanic. It adds another dimension to positioning in combat and gives players who are highly skill-based something to aim for.
On the other hand, this game is ugly. Or, more to the point, the aesthetics of the game DO NOT mesh well with this 2.5D art style. You can tell the the artists were more used to working on sprite-based games, and the polygon decision was an exceptionally poor one. In fact, this is my biggest problem with the game. It is not pleasant to look at by any stretch of the imagination. The voice acting is a close second, though. I don't think ANYONE wanted to hear Mega Man X4 style dialogue, ever. Yet here we are.
In the end, the mechanics of the game are solid. Imagine, if you would, a delicious cake that someone smashed with various pieces of silverware. Sure, it looks like hell, but it will still taste good. If you are new to the genre, don't start here. If you are, however, experienced in this kind of game, pick it up; it is worth your time, even if it doesn't look like it.

While not as diverse and and fleshed out as the base game, Groove City is a fantastic mini-sequel that offers a lot of content for such a small package. Unlike the previous entry, the game is very much your basic platformer, and does not have any buttstomping, gravitational changes, or the like. However, this helps refine the game itself, and the challenge is not nearly as daunting yet just as enjoyable.
Of course, Groove City is every bit as challenging, but the challenges are purely of platforming prowess, and there are plenty of secret areas that once completed can unlock further bonus levels with even more kick than the main missions. It's not that hard to miss a lot of them, and at a little less than two hours I have finished all the main levels, found a good few secrets, and only managed to unlock two of what I believe is a possible secret levels. That and the now implemented score system adds a lot of replayability for those who don't find the game hard enough.
On top of all this, Groove City comes packed with a level editor, and if you're the soul who loves ESJ and wants even more, you can make to your heart's content. The level editor is fairly well contructed, and it did not take me too long to construct a few basic levels, so definitely check it out if that's you're thing.
All in all, Groove City retains all the charm of its predecessor and adds a lot in exchange for what was taken away. Definitely pick this up if you're into the immense charm and challenge that this series offers.

ESJ:GC is a nice game, the pixel art is attractive and the soundtrack is very much enjoyable, there is just one major issue I have that has ruined my experience. The way the camera snaps when your character reaches a certain part of the screen, rather than always following you with smooth scrolling, has caused so many deaths that would have otherwise been avoidable.
The camera will often snap sideways at vital points. It is especially frustrating when it occurs in mid-jump, right before reaching a ledge. It adds an unnecessary level of difficulty to an already difficult game that just should not have been there in the first place.
Because of how the camera system has been implemented, and with how often you have to repeat small sections of the game due to failure, this is one of the only games that has managed to disorient me and cause motion sickness. It may not happen to everyone but because of my unfortunate experience I just can't recommend a game that works against the player in such an absurd way.

Overview: If you're new, pick up the first Electronic Super Joy. If you're returning,  this still has more of what you have come to love, plus a level editor, but finishes a little prematurely (insert checkpoint moan here)

It is about half the length of the first game, the levels, although possibily easier to speed run than the original, are absolutely more punishing (and rewarding) for those that are completionists, striving to get each star and finding the sometimes devilishly tucked away hidden rooms increase the difficulty significantly. It also has a level editor, so you can create and play custom levels, where you can really extend your play time.
Sadly Groove City does not have the double jump or smash abilities used in this game. This can make the game feel more focused, but after having them in the first, not having them in the second hurt the game I felt. I also LOVED seeing the short potions where color was implemented instead of the monochromatic style used primarly in the game. I would have loved to see atleast some levels done in that fashion or even the entire game.
Ultimately this game gives you more excellent gameplay and music, but misses out on some opportunities that could have taken this game to even greater heights.

A short but beautiful game.  It is at its strongest when it centers on exploration and puzzle-solving, but its reliance on randomness added to the world's threats subtracts from the experience.
This game is beautifully designed, with every frame very clearly hand-drawn at a level I would expect from a golden age Disney cartoon.  For the main character, most of your enemies, and the scenery, this works phenomenally.  I did notice some choppiness to the animation in two of the bosses, but in all the style works to the game's credit.
This game starts off deceptively simple, but quickly ramps up the difficulty.  There is very little handholding involved, but they make sure you understand a mechanic before they will let you progress.  New powers are not given, they are earned through exploration, though admittedly the shrines that give them are fairly easy to find once you realize the pause menu has a map on it.  When you earn a power, there is no text that explains it, the game instead opts to demonstrate its use.
Throughout the game, Thora will occasionally give a voice-over explaining an aspect of Norse mythology, or the story of her own life.  With the exception of one level, this is well-executed, not seeming overbearing and taking place while still giving you control, allowing you to progress as she speaks, if you wish.  I did feel that the swamp level overdid it, its puzzle being to make you traverse the level to reconstruct the creation myth, but this is a small gripe.
The game's biggest struggles lie in its mechanics.  The strong attack is nearly useless, save for puzzle solving.  By my observations, it does precisely the same damage as if you just hammered the light attack for the same span of time, with the added drawback of rendering you immobile for a rediculously long period of time, praying no one around you hits you and interupts the attack.  The isometric view makes for beautiful landscapes, but hit boxes, particularly for bosses, tend to vary wildly.  In one move, a boss' entire body will be a solid object, allowing Thora to hit him even if she swings for his head which should be far above her.  In another move on the same boss, Thora will have to walk under him, swinging at his ankles again.
By far what prompted the most swearing from me, however, was its random elements.  You may be getting your powers from the Norse gods, but you will spend most of the game praying to RNGesus.  Many of the environmental dangers run off of RNG, such as random lightning strikes in a cloud level, and the bosses seem to choose from their skill sets at random.  This tends to lead to the Dark Souls problem of repeatedly throwing oneself at a boss fight, praying they don't use the one move that wrecks your face quite so often this time.
In all, though, a very enjoyable game, and one I am happy to have bought and supported.

There's still one area that bothers me... a long row of spikes that you look like you should be able to get over... somehow... hm.
There are some serious issues - there are some bombs which insta-kill you if you land just outside them, but not if you land in their center (???!WTFAAAA???) and the difficulty levels are sadly lacking a "normal" setting - only casual, easy and hard. I guess it supports speedruns, which is important for some people, but they have no souls.
And the game-teaching can be a little obtuse at times - I got about halfway through before I realised you could equip items, or rather, how you did that.
Overall, 6/10, 1 point more if you enjoy this specific genre.

I never played the old-school dungeon crawlers of yore and my reaction towards this game is not fueled by any nostalgia I might have felt towards this long-forgotten genre of first-person dungeon crawling, so this negative review is neither colored by a feeling of “they’ve changed it and now it sucks” or “they haven’t changed enough which is why it sucks”.
And make no mistake, I did not have fun playing this game. I’ve only played around 2 hours, and I simply cannot make myself do any more of this. First and foremost, there’s not much of a story to speak of. You have a little bit of exposition for why your party is in this particular dungeon, but from then on, there’s really not a lot of narrative building up here. The first couple of levels are completely devoid of anything informing the player who built this place, why it had been built and the floors don’t tell self-contained stories themselves, since there’s very little differentiating any given tile from another one. Maybe there’s more to come later on, but the game up to now is so godda
mn insubstantial that I’m not eager finding out.
Speaking of tiles, I didn’t mind the tile based movement. It’s obviously there to harken back to older games that worked the same way, and I can appreciate modern developers wanting to go back to game design ideas they had fun with in their youth, even though there is a valid argument to be made that sometimes, design conventions disappear because we’ve found better methods for engaging the player, but I don’t want to be an arbiter on that front. But what I can criticize is the way combat interacts with said tile based movement. From what I understand, in these old games, combat used to be turn based, whereas in Legend of Grimrock it’s actually done in real-time. This causes numerous problems for me.
For one, having to click on every single attack button instead of having dedicated hotkeys is quite a hassle, especially with the magic system, which requires multiple clicks and never allows for quick magic attacks. And I get that it was also designed with tablets in mind as well, but I’ve got this lovely keyboard full of buttons I could be using and yet I have to use the mouse for combat. This is especially galling since it uses an a
ss-backwards binding scheme, where you attack by using the right mouse button. Clicking the left mouse button causes you to grab whatever weapon is equipped in order to swap it out with something else. I can’t count how many times I ended up grabbing a sword instead of attacking. Don’t make me unlearn over 20 years of gaming experience just because you can’t program key rebinds into a game.
This is only further exacerbated by the fact that the obvious strategy to beating every monster I’ve encountered is by kiting around them. Simply lure them out of a corridor into a space with at least 2x2 tiles and you can entirely wreck the AI in this game if you stand diagonally to the monsters and wait for them to make their moves – going even so far as to turning left and right multiple times while the game tries to calculate the shortest route and deciding which of the identically short routes is the more optimal one – while you hit them during their turning animations. Then just hop along to the next diagonally oriented tile and repeat that process until you win.
This hectic approach to combat robs the game of any tactical considerations it might could’ve had, since you’re entirely focused on kiting the enemies while remembering to right click on every attack once the cooldown has worn off. Fights all feel the same and the only times they do differ is when the game sends you into an obvious death trap, whenever multiple mobs start wailing on you at once from multiple directions, so make sure to save before you open up a door, since a lot of this game is trial-and-error.
A typical RPG convention also rears its ugly head, and that’s the fact that it doesn’t matter that your enemies stand on the tile right next to you, if one of your party members isn’t specifically trained in the art of hitting sh
it with a stick or sword or lance, they’ll miss every single swing. RPG developers, I get it. You have to abstract mastery and proficiency somehow. But seriously, I absolutely hate it whenever I see a “skill” as simple as aiming a swing for an enemy being something that needs experience. Every human on the planet has basic hand-eye-coordination and can hit a human-sized object without fail every single time. Cut that sh
it out, it’s annoying. Do dice rolls for real skills that need actual training or simply for critical hit calculation. But don’t have my tank miss half of his swings for no reason other than bullsh
it RPG conventions while it doesn’t seem to matter how many points I’ve poured into evasion whenever enemies attack.
While you’re not in combat, you’ll be doing a lot of puzzles, though the ones I’ve encountered were fairly straightforward. The game’s limited visual design means that there isn’t a lot hidden from the player. One of the very first “puzzles” is finding a loose rock in a wall and once you’ve done so, the same mechanic keeps appearing basically everywhere with tons of “hidden” rooms being accessed by rocks in the same location every single time, all looking exactly the same.
All of this combined, the lackluster and repetitive combat, the unengaging puzzles and a general lack of narrative to draw me in made me lose interest in this game fairly quickly. Chalk it up to this type of game just not being for me. I usually try to play my way through every game I play before I make definitive statements, but every so often I encounter one that utterly does not gel with what I want out of games and the end result is that I simply stop giving a sh
it and instead start playing something else. And Legend of Grimrock is one such unfortunate case, where nothing about the game managed to draw me in and made me want to endure the rest of it in spite an aspect I might’ve enjoyed. Because that last bit, that aspect that I might’ve enjoyed, is simply not there.

Mighty no.9 is a game that had a huge expectation from people, it's Mega Man's spiritual successor made by its same creator. I'm a hardcore Mega Man fan that played almost all of the games and among all the series, for me, X is the best. I backed up this game on kickstarter, played the betas and was always looking at the development progress. After waiting through several frustrating delays I must say I'm satisfied with the result.

It was made to incentivize the player to move fast and blast through the stages, which is how I believe most Mega Man fans played the Mega Man games. Still, you can complete things at your own pace, it's not mandatory to do things fast. There is no charged shot like in many of the most famous Mega Man games, but that is compensated by the increased interaction with the dash move in this game. Your aggressive and fast play style is rewarded by increased buff timers that help you even more to blast through things. It feels good. The dash is also not just a mere gimmick, it is the game's very main theme that the hero can absorb and manipulate data from other robots, it's his special quality, that's why it is so fundamental in this game.
I have seen people complaining about level design and that's laughable. There's nothing wrong with the level design in this game, MN9 isn't Mega Man, it was stated since day 1 of the kickstarter that this was supposed to be a game Keiji Inafune wanted to make but couldn't while he was with Capcom, people are making the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ mistake of expecting this to be a Mega Man sequel when it's not.
Almost everything is oriented towards the dash mechanics in this game: enemy position, spawn timer, hidden items, safe zones, etc. and again I'll say that this is different from Mega Man, it's supposed to be, but it still resembles Mega Man; you still have to jump, shoot and dash avoiding spikes or ramming into enemies without neutralizing them first. Without giving many spoilers, I'll mention that one of the levels breaks the linear "go from point A to point B" kind of design Mega Man always had. In this particular level you need to chase down a sniper that hides at different places, so you'll find yourself going back-and-forth to find him while avoiding his bullets and traps along the way. In my opinion that's a creative idea, it matches the boss theme very well and puts you outside of the same old thing you did for decades. A bunch of losers that never did anything in their lives complaining that the creator of the games they love so much doesn't understand his own games, while claiming that they do, is simply hilarious.
The soundtrack was done by the same team who did the classic Mega Man games' soundtracks, so they follow a similar style but are not exactly the same. I wouldn't say the soundtrack is the best thing ever made, it's clearly behind the greatest Mega Man soundtracks but it's most certainly far from "bad" as some people are claiming it to be out of senseless hate.
As far as Mega Man games plot goes, they are extremely bland and simple, especially when you are looking at the classics. Mighty no.9's story is pretty good and follows the same pattern of the Mega Man X series: not super simple but also far from deep and complex.
Mega Man games always suffered from few characters you could identify with or cheer on but for Mighty no.9 the bosses aren't merely bots you are going to exterminate, you actually rescue them so they can go back to being your allies, which in my opinion is just perfect. That's something I always dreamed of for Mega Man games, I always wanted more of the bosses, especially in the X and Zero series and always loved the short and bland interactions characters had before killing each other. In Mighty no.9 the bosses you defeat will give you support in the other stages, be it by killing nearby enemies, destroying traps or clearing a path, they will be there to help you. In my opinion that makes the game much richer, it's a reward for the work you did in previous stages and you get to see more of the other characters.
Mega Man games were always known for not being very easy and people always had to spend a good amount of time trying over and over again to learn patterns, tricks and secrets to things. It's the same with this game, the stages are full of annoying parts that you need to move fast and with accuracy. Overall I think the hardest parts are the stages (good and old ♥♥♥♥ing spikes!), not bosses, but that doesn't make them super easy as a lot of them have 1-hit kill abilities and you'll probably die a few times to get the timing of their attacks right. It took me over 7 hours to finish the game's main mode in normal difficulty (still have DLC left to play).
There are a bunch of optional modes such as a special co-op stage where two players control 2 different characters, each with their own characteristics and abilities. Challenges that will test your skills, online competition over scores, boss rush and more. So if you are an achievement hunter or simply the kind of person that enjoys going for the hardcore stuff, there's plenty of content for you.
I played the game using Japanese dubs and English subtitles and I must say it's really good. They picked a bunch of talented, well known and expensive voice actors for this game. I can't say the same for sure about the English dub, but from what I followed during development people who preferred the English dub were pretty happy with the result too.
And last but not least:
If you are a huge Roll lover from Mega Man like me this is the closest you will ever get from playing as Roll in a 2D Side-scrolling Action game. If you don't like Call then you are probably ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.

This game is amazing. It's about automation and growth with the motivator of survival and escape.
In the bare starting scenario you start with a pickaxe. You mine some stone and build a furnace. You mine some coal and some iron ore. You put those in the furnace and you get some iron plates. Those you turn some of those into gears, then build yourself a coal powered miner, some conveyor belts and coal powered 'inserters' (picker arms that can pick things up and put them other places or insert them into, say, your furnace). Then you build a self powering coal mining operation. You use the extra coal to put in other furnaces, miners, and picker arms to build a small coal powered iron mining operation.
And it continues and scales up and up. Eventually you get robots that can fly around and place things. And then you get the ability to create blueprints, so the blueprints direct the operations of the robots and you can stamp out entire factories in one go.
A friend said it's a lot like programming. And he's kinda right. It is.
All the things you build work in predictable ways and interact with each other exactly how you'd expect. Exactly how you get from raw materials to product is carefully thought through and well balanced. The people who designed and built this game knew what they were doing and executed extremely well. This makes my top-ten list of games, possibly even in the top 5.

I used to play The Force Unleashed so much when I was younger, and it made its debut as the first Star Wars lightsaber combat game on the Wii.
And the The Force Unleashed II spat right in its face, and everybody hated it.
But, honestly, we all like to hate The Force Unleashed II... but wasn't this game bad since the beginning?
I don't know how this game performs outside of the Wii or PC, but I can say the difference between these two versions is night and day. The Wii has worse graphics and level design (as usual)... but the PC has a lot more issues than I was expecting.
For one, the game is buggier than the Amazon rainforest. Throughout most of the game, I was battling the game crashing, floors disappearing, sound effects cutting out, and even lightsabers being turned on in cutscenes where they obviously shouldn't be on. By the end of the main story of The Force Unleashed, the game was so broken that there was no music- not even any sound effects- save for Starkiller's lightsaber and footsteps.
This could be a symptom of PC getting some of the worst ports of games that were originally intended for consoles. This is especially evident when playing QTE's, since the layout for the buttons isn't laid out for a keyboard and mouse. It's mapped out more for the four buttons on a 360 or PS3 controller, so I found myself failing several times because of where Q, E, and Left-Click were placed on the prompt.
And since this is the first time I've played the HD version, I can say it's much shorter than the Wii's campaign. I know that the Wii story had a lot more unnecessary padding, often involving random trips to the Jedi Temple to fight a random Sith lord before the story decided to start picking up again. But the biggest flaw in this game's story (and really with its gameplay), is its horrible pacing.
The story feels forced. Every beat, from being betrayed, to meeting the girl, to the conflicted interests, is all something like a cop on the run who's out for revenge after being betrayed. And the game rushes its cutscenes so quickly that it leaves little for the already paper-thin characters to feel empathetic or feel any drama going on in the plot.
The pacing in the gameplay is also very off. Many times, I was just thrown in a large area with tons of enemies and upgrades placed around at random, and traversing around could be a massive pain in the a**, because the game can be so chaotic that it becomes stressful to try and manage what enemies to get or what upgrade to grab first.
Also, like three characters die in the story and come back to life. Seriously. Rahm Kota, Starkiller, and PROXY should be officially dead for what happened to them, and yet the miraculously come back to life later in the story. Even Kota reveals that he wasn't blinded at all by the end of the game, which seems odd, seeing as how he took a lightsaber to his f***ing eyes!
Another new feature to this PC port, is that it isn't just your average Force Unleashed copy... it comes with DLC! Packed with costumes you'll never use, ever! Seriously? Why would I want to just dress up as Jango Fett, if all I do is talk and play like Starkiller still? I know it doesn't matter to some people out there, but literally anyone can make a skin mod. I find this part of the DLC lazy as sh**.
But along with the mounds of useless character skins, there's also three levels tacked onto the main story. I thought all three would be a continuation of the dark side ending, but I was wrong. Only two do. And the game purposely has you play them in the wrong order. The game has Hoth listed before Tatooine, even though the events happening suggest that what's going on on Tatooine is happening before Hoth.
The new skins and lightning color didn't impress me. Hoth was pretty decent for what it was worth, as was Tatooine. They were both just average. But for f***s sake, who decided to make the Jedi Temple, and why is it even relevant as DLC? It's just a random deleted level from inside the Force Unleashed's main campaign with some incredibly unintuitive design and horribly simple puzzles. In the words of my uncle, while getting robbed at gunpoint, "F*** this!"
The Force Unleashed for the PC is bad. And boring. And predictable. It's got some incredibly simple combat within long, linear levels that don't award a player for their exploration, but more for accidentally running into a randomly-placed secret. It feels so unfinished, I expressed at one point that I was playing an unfinished beta. Do not play The Force Unleashed on Steam. It might be better for the last generation of consoles, but stray far from this game. I'm giving it a 4/10.

Every game of Plague Inc seems to pan out in the same way. Despite attempts at variation, you essentially plop your plague down in a country of your choice, wait a bit, alter the DNA to *sort of* encourage it to spread where you want it, and the rest is spent balancing deadliness, infectivity and humanity's resistance.
In essence, it’s a very ‘procedural’ game, modelling the replication of your badass bug on its travels throughout the world. Crucially though, what it isn’t… is ‘strategic’.
Sure, you can navigate your plague towards different environments – arid, cold, rich, rural etc – by making decisions about how its DNA will mutate, but whatever your choices, your goal is the globe, and that’s what you’ll end up covering.
Similarly, you can see which countries are working hardest on a cure and try to kill those countries off slightly sooner, but in the end, the ‘procedural’ element wins out, and your decisions don’t make much of a difference.
A strategy game where your decisions matter this little isn’t much more than a simulator – or even a slightly interactive video with some bubbles to click.
Give the app a go before you open your wallet – it’s much cheaper!

Those games are quite a while around, Dungeon Crawlers. They form in a way the basis for CRPGs in the eighties and they somehow never get out of vogue. Especially games which are riddle and skill based.
This game has some good skill based riddles, or some other riddles to solve, a lot of fighting (albeit the creatures and their varieties are quite limited). A simple and easy to use magic system, which is glyph based - and a skill based character progression.
Technically the graphics are fine, well made including the animations of the critters in this Dungeon, and the sound could be well called "atmospheric". Gameplay is simple and the game has a balanced learning curve. There is a lot to explore and even more to find...
There is a "hunger" system included, which forces you to find edibles, you also have to mix your potions, and find scrolls with spells to cast so you can learn the magic ropes. Amunition is another scarce resource, especially bombs don't come as easy to find so use them wisely.
There are three of the four known "basic" classes of RPGs available... Fighter, Rogue and Wizard, there are no priests but this is giving the game also a more challenging outlook. To heal up you can wander around, or search one of the saving crystals that are found in the dungeon, or you have to mix potions.
A well meant hint, don't be sloppy with your resources, like food, potions, amunition and equipment - you'll be rueing it in the endgame if you do.
Another good thing about the game are the secrets, there are some of them... you'll have to find them inventorise them and well, yeah, another unlock in achievements may be the reward.
People who like RPGs, Dungeon Crawling, Skill Tweaking and getting some nice Dungeon Master, Eye of the Beholder, Bards Tale, Wizardry... Nostalgia will love this game.

The game progresses at an even pace and you have time to adjust to your new scenarios, and it can be fun to come up with very different party makeups which gives this game it's legs for multiple run throughs.

It's a fun game.
Anyone who has followed the development of Mighty No. 9 knows how many issues came up. The development was plagued by delays and poor communication with its Kickstarter backers. So while I understand many people's frustration with the title, the game itself is good, though not exceptional.
Pros-
-Simple, fun, run-and-gun gameplay
-You're encouraged to dash into weakened enemies to absorb them, rather than destroy them outright with your blaster. It's an interesting twist that speeds up the pace of the game, and in some cases leads to really clever level design and let's you be creative with the variety of weapon types you unlock.
-The characters, while not deep, are cute and entertaining in small doses
Cons-
-Cutscenes are too long and drawn out. You're better off skipping them, since the important information will be relayed to you during the stage anyway, and every stage has an "Explain" option in case you've forgotten something.
-Music is forgettable, though that's only my opinion. Coming from Megaman vets I was hoping for a more exciting soundtrack. In fact, I can't even remember what most of the stages sound like.
-Content is lacking. No hidden upgrades, no item shop, no secret areas. Besides a few shortcuts, what you see is what you get.
Overall, I'd say it's definitely worth checking out if you're a fan of the genre.

It's pretty mediocre... But better than nothing?! Yeah! Yeah? Yeah...
Yeah, it was pretty mediocre.
It's not a horrid game! It functions at a basic level of being a fun run 'n gun game, and it has a couple pretty good points to it. Some levels are fun and when you get a good flow going shooting and charging enemies and zipping through the level there's a good game in here, but it's bogged down by so much unnecessary or poorly executed stuff that with all the hype and a perfect storm of initial concepts coming together into this potentially great new series, it's a big letdown that it ended up being this ho-hum attempt at a new, exciting franchise to surpass its predecessor.
The thing is, I'd still rather go back and play any Mega Man game, from the original series, or X, or Zero, or ZX, as they all did a much better job at what this game tried to do, and for nearly 4 million dollars raised not from a publisher but from fans with faith in a veteran design team, and constant delays and complications, that's kind of a sad thing.
I'd start criticism with the fact that enemies die so easily to the point that even big guys are unthreatening, maybe to emphasize a fast, flowing playstyle, but that the fast playstyle doesn't work at all when juxtaposed by insta-death obstacles in most of the stages that the camera sometimes does a terrible job giving any warning about until you've already fallen into them. The dig site area in particular had some pitfalls that the camera doesn't move to warn you about until you're already just about falling into it, and are easy to fall into while dashing along unless you know they're there from previous trial and error deaths, which is never a good sign.
The power plant stage also had a crappy insta-death fan obstacle you have to crouch-dash under. After automatically crouch-dashing through non-lethal tight spaces for the rest of the game realizing you have to hold down to dodge the fans for this single instance, it was very poorly communicated, and the blunt tip of "try dashing" really doesn't remedy the poor design of that obstacle, I still thought it just meant to do a normal dash for two lives lost. It seems like they barely playtested some of this stuff, or did so then didn't bother to do anything more than put up a crappy hint box in front of the obstacle.
Conversely to enemies, some bosses soak way too many hits in the late game which not so much challenged but rather just made my hand cramp up. I didn't have an issue with the patterns, in fact I enjoyed quite a few of them, but hammering the button over and over for really long, repeated phases gets monotonous and physically irritating.
The soundtrack is fairly forgettable, a couple decent themes but a lot of generic or goofy stuff that I don't expect many people remembering the game for.
Cardboard characters, especially Call. She's the most dead-eyed, droning, colorless character I've seen in almost anything period. For all the hub-bub they had about voting on and finalizing her character design they did nothing with her other than a short, tedious key card hunt stage with an agonizingly slow boss. There's some dialogue where she's questioning why she feels nothing in regards blowing up other robots unlike Beck who absorbs/repairs them but it goes nowhere, expands nothing, it's just fluff that doesn't serve any purpose for the game other than I guess letting you know Beck is a cool, special dude?
The dialogue in general is distracting from gameplay because suddenly you've got subtitle windows popping up in the middle of the action, or like in the prologue blocking you from gameplay before you can even get into the action. For another genre maybe it would be okay, but a run 'n gun game having that kind of stop & go is a really bad idea.
So I hope you can understand a little better why I find a lot to be bad about this game.﻿ Get it on a sale? I guess so, there's some fun to be had here, just, you'll have to do some wading through bad stuff to get to it, you may come out more disappointed than you'd hope.

Freaking Inafune. I wanted to start off this review spitefully and say that "No one wanted this game to succeed more so than I did," but that's simply not true. And it's so much worse because of that. If it was just me, if I was the only one disappointed by Might No. 9, well that would be something; but this game is a disappointment to so many people. It's glitchy, uninspired, and downright un-fun to play. During Brandish's level, Beck can't seem to stay on a damned car without sliding off and landing into the road of doom. You could chalk up that happening to a slip-up on my part, which I did, but when something occurs umpteen times, it becomes a trend; a trend of poor controls.
The boss fights are just kind of boring and unchallenging as a whole, the power-up's you recieve don't even feel like they're worth all that much, it seems a lot more advantageous to stick to your default weapon. Call has (and I cannot stress this enough) the most BORING personality in a video game ever. You could have just has Siri's voice do all of her lines and it probably would have conveyed more emotion.
When I first heard about this game coming out, I was so excited. I've been a fan of Megaman for so long. When Megaman's fall came I was so distraught, but it had seemed as though Mighty No. 9 would be the true successor. I mean he had the pedigree, he had the idea, he had a good enough look. Instead we waited so long for a false messiah. Megaman is dead, and I can only hope Beck won't be far behind.

The main mechaninc of the game of shooting and dashing could be good, but lack of attack options at the start makes so that you can only fight one ene at a time: if you don't absorb an enemy, it still stop bullets, so your choices are either ignoring the dash and lose the bonus or coming close and getting exposed to other enemies you couldn't hit before. Basically, it's a shooting game that forces you have to hug your enemies to death. A strong short range attack or a charged shot could have made the mechanic work much more smoothly.
My number one cause of death is hitting those purple insta-kill spikes. Most of time, because they were out of the screen when I jumped or because a small attack bumped me onto one. The plataforming sections come out as cheap because of that.
Right now, the game doesn't recognize XInput (X-Box) controlers, but works fine with DInput. The controls can only be configured on the ingame pause menu (not on the main menu), which is an unimportant but annoying.
Overall, for a game delayed almost a year, it still has a lot of obvious problems that should have been solved before release.

This review is based on early accessed version and I'll edit this once I deem fit, blah blah blah.
In short: Not now. (Unless you have a lot of money and you don't know how to spend it, then, fo for it).
This game looks very promising, and, don't get me wrong, I do like this game (Umm, maybe I'll like later versions). However, there are so many things to remind you that this is not a good choice to spend your $20, for now.
Pro:
-The  "Every thing can be destoryed" idea is interesting.
-There should be some other pros, but I forgot them...
Con:
-Bugs. Yes, this is in early access. But, hello, for a $20 early access title you won't expect to find bugs every single minute, which I'm not exaggerating. Most of them are just minor glichs which we're already get used to, thanks to Ubi, EA and many others, some of them are serious bugs which will pervent you from building what you want to build, which is the whole point of this game.
-Missing content. Some stuff you can clearly see in trailer can not be found in game (Corner celling and Wall flags, for example). This is not a big problem since I believe the developers will add them in future patchs. But, don't you thing they are a little bit dishonest?
Maybe it's just me who have got these problems. Since it's seems everybody else are absolutly love this game. Please correct me if you find the game is fine and the only thing gone wrong is my mind.
First, the graphic. I know many people concern this question. But, what would you expect from a medieval building game made by indie developers who are only be known becase the space engineer? No offense, developers, the graphic is fine, and it's actually better than fine, despite I started feeling sick after serval hours working with stones (It's mainly my fault beacuse I'll get the same feeling when mining in Minecraft). However, it is a bit of problem if you want to built an enormous castle using only stone. Their is no "lighting" in this game, I mean, no light emitted from torch or other light sources. So it looks the same no matter how you arrange your torchs, every thing is grey (gray) and ugly when you stand inside your stone building.
Second, the physic. Most people want this game because of the fancy "every thing can be destoryed" stuff. However, I wouldn't recommand to take this serious at this stage. Ok, this is actually not a big deal. But, hello, I know there are many people in the world will find this annoying just like me XD. Either woodlock works fine, but when I connected them together (SIMPLY connect them with a wood stick, nothing else), both locks suddenly decided to not let wood rotation anymore! Be noticed, the "woodlock" here means lock wood to one axis, not lock it completely, I'm sure. Oh, one more thing, aiming your catapult is much harder than sending human to the moon.
