Star Wars: The Force Unleashed is a very clunky 3rd person hack and slash action game with good combat mechanics and excellent use of the force powers.
In terms of story, it fits well into the Star Wars lore – the characters are interesting, and there are no let downs on the endings part. The 3 DLCS, that can be access by creating a new game, also adds to the Dark side ending of the main story.
I really wanted to give this game thumbs up but I cannot, this game got some serious issues that keep it from being a great game.
Let start with the technical Issues of the PC port, this game suffers from the "console peasants port syndrome", the frame rate is capped to 30 and it shows.
Try unlocking the frame rate to 60 and you'll see the difference, the combat will feel more responsive (30 fps makes the game control less responsive) but as a result it will break the force grip mechanic, causing the objects you grip fly upwards without control, so you can only have it unlocked up to 40 without it breaking the force grip.
Some sound files are missing from this port thus making 2 levels, the Raxus Prime and Death Star levels, without them.
This game got barely any graphical options, if you can call what you have call graphical options at all.
Also for some reason Cloth simulation is not active by default, which will lead to some visual bugs.
Another problem is the narrow FOV, that means that you will not see all the enemies that are attacking you, making the combat less fluid.
The camera and the lock on systems are bad, you cannot lock on an enemy, it happens automatically and that means that when you try to use the force powers it will attack the nearest target….so if an enemy stand near a rock or a crate then the force push, grab or lightning will attack the object instead of the enemy and Sometime you cannot even lock on an enemy because it won't recognize it as a target.
From the design decisions perspective, first the star destroyer boss fight is infuriating and badly designed, because the camera sometime will lock on automatically on thing you don’t want to or wont lock at all on a tie fighter and this will make the boss fight very, very, very long.
Also the time it takes to recover from a knock down is too long compare to other beat'em-ups or hack and slash, thus making you vulnerable or falling down a pit and dying, dying to an environmental hazard or dying by being stomp by a giant boss.
and don't start me talking about those annoying QTEs at the end of the combat/dual.....there is no penalty failing at them, so what's the point in having them at all?!? I understand having them in the middle to spice things up. I understand having them in the middle to spice things up but in the end they could just replace it with a cutscene and you wouldn't feel the difference at all.
So no I won't recommend it on the PC - go play it on the console, but if you want a good Star Wars game with Jedi powers and nice story? Then try the Jedi knight series on GOG only because the steam versions are broken.

Just came back from beating the game today, to offer support for the game.
Momodora III is an easy, short platformer. You won't find any real challenge here, and it won't keep you busy for hours and hours (unless you replay it again and again). But for $3.99 or less when it's on sale, if you are like me and your first game was Mario Bros' on the NES, then you should find this a fun little trip into your earliest gaming memories.
It's a little work of love, it feels fairly well polished and has a great feel to it while playing it. The soundtrack is great, the person who did this, did an amazing job.
I'd also like to mention you find numerous little items you can buy or find while playing, take each one for a test drive to see if you like the item, and what it does. They all offer neat little perks like reduced damage, healing when you kill enemies, and one changes your attack animation into something longer reaching and cooler looking.
Got a "New Game +" option at the end, and it warned me:  "Things will be a bit different this time". Hopefully a bit more challenging but not too much, I enjoyed the casual and fun gameplay alot. Highly recommend this game for anyone who was born in the 8-bit era like me. Just don't expect a challenge, there is none that I know of. Play it for fun and you won't go wrong.
Update:   Came to check and see if I had reviewed this game because my memory sucks and I couldn't remember. Yes, yes I have.
The New Game+ offers no challenge over the original playthrough and if anything, having all the items and skills from the previous playthrough lets you absolutely slaughter it as if you were a God. Not saying that isn't fun because it totally is. Just, there's no challenge to be found in New Game+'s.
Also, buy this game. Seriously, if you like 8-bit retro games and platforming, buy it. I actually got to talk to the developer a bit, he is a really friendly guy, who cares about his work. Support him so he makes more games like this.

---
You feel lucky that robot technology has never been hotter, thanks to the ramp-up in robot technology in the last war. You're able to provide for both of your robots, thanks to the money you make from working for Josh.
Puppet, the more adventurous of the two robots, appears to have tried more tastes than Springtrap already. Like siblings, they seem to have settled into niches in competing for your attention: Springtrap now tries to be more humanlike, while Puppet occasionally flaunts his freedom to be strange.
"Did you try dirt?" Puppet asks Springtrap. He walks behind the younger robot, who is putting out plates. "Dirt tastes very interesting!"
"I don't think people are supposed to eat dirt," Springtrap says uncertainly.
"Sure they do!" Puppet says. "It's called 'pica,' and it helps people get essential vitamins and minerals. I read about it on the Internet."
Springtrap gives you a worried look. "We're not going to eat dirt tonight, are we?"

Even if text-based choose-your-own-adventure stories aren't your thing (and I've never met anyone who didn't at least entertain the idea), you'll still enjoy the little moments like these among the many different paths this story has. :)

An interesting experience of how technology affect our lives and how it's changing and evolving in turn can change us. Our morals, our beliefs, etc. Circumstances change along with our technology, and just as our computers change and adapt to us, we adapt to them, raising a question of just how different we can be from each other. As robots come closer to being human, it also changes just what we think of as being necessary to claim to possess humanity. This game doles out some emotions, weighing relationships with humans against relationships with robots, and as the story progresses, it can be that you only know the robots are robots because the game reminds you of it.

At the end of the day Choice of Robots is a solid entry into the text adventure genre and it's one of those games that give the genre modern validity.

I'll buy any game that includes beautiful hand drawn 2D animation, but what really makes the underlooked "Jotun" special is the time and effort it takes to tell an engaging tale steeped in authentic norse mythology. The authenticity is brought out in part by the Icelandic voice acting, which was very well done IMO.
On top of this, its a pretty great game on its own with atmospheric Boss battles that are extremely tense and challenging, while maintaing a fairness that managed to keep me from ever feeling frustrated. Perfect difficulty, welcomed puzzles to break up the action (and unique free roam environments that have since been given a slight rework by providing the player with a faster running speed so that it doesnt feel so much like a slog), and a beautiful soundtrack, art style, and mythological setting, really make this 5 or so hour game very fun and immersive. Highly recommend playing this one on a late weekend night during a storm. Im going to go read up on some norse mythology!

i have several categories for my large collection of steam games.  mostly they are practical, like "in progress" or "play soon"... and indeed i do take advantage of my "favorites" folder, like many, i would imagine.  the point is that i also have both a "storage bin" and a "trash bin".  there are only 3 games in my "trash bin" so far, and this is one of them.  the sole reason it is in there is because it made me vomit.  literally.  few games make me so nauseaus that i can't handle it, but this one of them.  i don't remember which one it was, but it was an xbox release of Doom that also did this to me and i don't have a clear explanation for it, nor am i suggesting that it will do the same to you.  but IF  you are the type to be sensitive to certain patterns and motion sickness, you MAY want to stay away from this.  aside from that, the frantic and violent gameplay was what you can expect from this genre.  i'm not here to criticize one's freedom of choice as to what they find entertaining, i'm solely basing my review on the fact that my poor stomach couldn't handle playing this game for more than a few minutes without great duress.  and i did try multiple times.  alas.
from what i remember, the actual gameplay wasn't too bad.  normal run around shoot em up type stuff.  i think it was revolutionary at the time it was released.  but then, when i think back, it was this or MDK or Postal or Doom, etc...  revolutionary is as revolutionary does.  this is probably why i am not a professional game reviewer.

Well, here we go.
I can't really say the game in itself is bad. It's a good action game, some musics are good, and the challenge is here. Gameplay wise, it has what you'd expect from a Serious Sam. But.
First, what the hell are those characters and the way they speak. In all other Serious Sam games, Sirians are mentionned as a technologically advanced race, and have this mysterious aspect. Who were they ? Where did they go ? And why ? But here in Serious Sam 2, they're ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ cartoonish human-like aliens with a ridiculous accent.
And it's not only the Sirians, all your allies are incredibly ugly.
Then, the humor. It is fun, sometimes. But this sometimes is really sometimes. You'll have to expect jokes like a bird ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ on Sam's shoe, a guard being awoken by Sam's fart, stuff like that.
The cinematics are bad too. They're too static. They could have been better. Sometimes it's like a diaporama, because they were too lazy to animate anything. Combine this with the ugly characters, and you get something really cringy. Also, they're often brought without logical reason, just because you killed the last enemy. They don't let you get to the end of the level, they just throw the cinematic.
Now as I said, gameplay wise, it's a self respecting Serious Sam. However, the thing that bothered me here, is that some levels are too long. Or rather, too repetitive. Monsters spawns last too long even when it's obviously too easy to spawn kill enemies, and the game can get really boring because of that. Imagine Kleers spawning continuously, with sometimes a Bio-mech to bring some more power, and this for a good minute or two, when it should take around 30 seconds, if not 20. This isn't the right way to make a game challenging.
If you're thinking of buying this game, just forget Serious Sam 1. You're still playing Serious Sam, but the universe is not the same. It's like they made it for a much, much younger audience. I don't really want to give it a thumb down, but I definitely can't give a thumb up.

This is a decent game with  responsive gameplay.  The levels are reminiscent of classic Megaman, including the difficulty spikes with insta-death zones. The game tries to drive the player to gain points and quck times, but points and absorbion percentage does something for the player. The bosses are farily made well overall, and all have noticable tells that help dodge their moves; although the difficulty of avoiding damage is something else. Something new that I liked was how the bosses beaten are scripted to assist in part of a level; it isn't a game changer, but it just helps a little bit in passing a hazzard or two.
This game is just about worth the $20 price.  I would suggest either getting it on sale if just for yourself (although I would say that for any game on Steam), or buy a physical copy to swap or lend to others.

All the 9/10 4.5/5 scores this game is receiving is probably the reason we do not hear much from the devs of this game anymore (2017). Why does this game receive so many positive reviews? One word - NOSTALGIA
Besides nostalgia, there is literally nothing positive about this game. Controls are abysmal, spells are pathetic, combat is outright stupid.
Controls
This game forces you to use the mouse in the dumbest possible way. I really miss playing games with arrow keys and numpads after playing this game.
Spells
Most of the time, they are just the same stupid thing with different colors. Like fire does not burn, ice does not freeze, lightning does not stun, etc. Just a damage figure with different color; and I stress most of the time. Let's not forget the pathetic click runes everything you wish to cast spell - AND - the game does not even show you spells that you already know; so if you stop playing this game for a couple months and you didnt keep all the scrolls in your inventory, you probably will have to Google how to cast the simplest of spells.

Spend your money on maybe Wizardry if you like games of this genre. If you like retro classics - just get Buldar's Gates series. If you want a properly remade retro game, there is Pillars of Eternity.
This game is only for the most diehard of fans of this genre who like self torture.

Legend of Grimrock is an RPG dungeon crawler that's heavily reminiscent of that old 3D computer screensaver of an infinitely spanning maze made out of brick walls.
Grimrock is definitely not a game everyone will enjoy. It's full of puzzles, really tough fights, and very scarce autosaves. As much as I don't like doing it in these sorts of games, Grimrock is definitely the kind of game that requires save-scumming in order to be proficient at it. Some dungeons will have you playing for upwards of an hour in between save points. If you die, you're forced to load up a save. If you got immersed in the game and forgot to save, then I wouldn't blame you if you packed up the game for the night and played something else; it's something I've done a few times already.
Save scumming also takes the risk/reward out of the game. Why should I have to decide whether or not jumping down this pit (which may or may not contain weapons, crafting regeants, armor or food) is a risk worth taking when I can just save, jump down, and then load back where I was if I don't like the situation? Adding save crystals that can be reasonably reached within 15 minutes of gameplay between each other would really discourage this kind of issue.
Beyond the issue of save-games, Grimrock is an exceptional game I'm surprised I haven't heard more of. The screenshots make it seem a lot less interactive than it is. The entire time, you're going to be on your toes wondering where the next enemy is going to come from. Every scittering footstep, every heavy stomp, and every peep from shuffling metal boots will put you on edge. Grimrock is meant to be a place where the guilty atone for their sins, and it really does feel like the dangerous derelict mountain prison that it's meant to portray.
The combat is interesting in that it consists of real-time combat with four individual fighters; it is NOT turn-based, as the trailers may have you believe. You control 4 characters (but they all move as one unit, so it feels more like you're controlling one person with four heads, if that makes any sense) who all cast spells and do actions independent of each other. The characters in the front get hit more often, but are allowed to use melee weapons. The characters in the back can't use melee weapons, but they get hit less often. When one of your characters is killed, it cuts your damage down significantly; getting lowered to only two or even one fighter in a corner is basically a death sentence.
Grimrock rewards planning and strategem. Having an escape route in case you get overwhelmed, crafting potions and putting them in characters inventories beforehand, and keeping your eyes peeled for traps and puzzles goes a long way towards your own survival. Most of your deaths in the game are going to come from when you're trapped in a corner or hallway against an enemy that you can't fight head-on, or from being overwhelmed by lots of small enemies.
The puzzles are probably my favorite part of Grimrock; lots of times, I've been stuck at a puzzle for a while just thinking to myself "this has to be impossible" for the longest time until I finally find out a solution. Some puzzles are mandatory, but the most difficult ones are usually optional and reward you with sick loot. I'd wager a player could get maybe three full playthroughs on Grimrock without a walkthrough in order to complete the majority of the puzzles.
Grimrock is really an excellent RPG, and perfect for anyone who is looking for a tough-as-nails game with less sitting around on your hands and more action-packed... uh, action.
Classes are way too ♥♥♥♥ing linear to enjoy it. There's no way to deviate your builds too much from the generic roles.

It's a branching path story game that decides what story to give you based on your alignment of a couple sliders. The choices are obvious as to which alignment they affect (building a metallic robot increases its military, and decreases its grace; giving it wings gives it grace and reduces its military usefulness). But, the story has to keep prompting you to interact with different parts of the decision tree, so you get weird things like being a multi-millionaire and choosing to employ humans in your factories in Detroit, but then you go to war with China, and now you're sorry you ever let the Chinese get near these things. What? When did the Chinese gain the ability to rip off my robots and make them militaristic? Oh, because I used cheap chinese lithium ion batteries? That's ridiculous. If my company is successful, and there's design changes happening, and materials are getting upgraded, let me source better batteries from somewhere else. Don't make me pick a motorcycle battery when my company is supremely profitable.
It's not open to be whatever you want it to be. You're allowed to type only on fields that don't matter: your name, your robot's name, your robots pronouns. You can't affect the story, you can affect the flavor text. If you choose one of the built in options you will rarely have a tie in back to the originator (Isaac Asimov names are one of the built in options, so you can get references back to those books in later dialogue if you themed correctly). But if you manually type in a name, Suddenly the game has nothing pithy to say about how your name and your situation relate back to the book.
It's not a very visually delighting game. Black text on a white background. Only one button is styled. The Next button. All other buttons are your OS' default look and feel. It's lazy design, and it hurts that it's not free.
The author chose to point out on every page of the UI that he is a Ph.D. which bears out my experience with most Ph.D.s. More concerned that everyone knows you spent a lot of time in school, than putting that knowledge to work. Good job on your Ph.D. now do work that isn't already bested by a group of people posting on free Choose Your Own Adventure forums.

Played a few minutes, but don't think I will continue this one. I'm wanting an experience that feels somewhat like a classic text adventure, like Zork, where I'm thrust into a world and situation, and making decisions solely on my reactions to the plot. Unfortunately, this game is not properly delivering.
I have two main gripes about the presentation:
1) Too many of the choices read like quiz answers in fashion magazines, where instead of the answers just containing my possible actions, they also impute motivation into my character that may not reflect how I'm interpreting the situation. Made-up example: instead of the choices being "Cautiously open the door" or "Kick the door in", they are "Cautiously open the door, hoping nothing scary jumps out and eats my face," and "Kick the door in. I am a superhero, afraid of nothing!". (I may open the door cautiously because I'm a practical person, or kick it in hoping to surprise what is on the other side. A game should not tell me my emotional state; it should offer me simple, basic choices and allow me to feel my own emotions).
2) Some of the questions are not based on how I am reacting to the situation, but are asking me to make fundamental decisions about the nature of the story universe. While this is fine and a common replayability device at the start of interactive fiction games (e.g. "will you be a GOOD WITCH or a BAD WITCH"?), it's poor storytelling to force such decisions on you when you're already well into the plot. The question that I am quitting on is asking me who it was that just called my cell phone while I was speaking with a professor. Instead of the call being from a specific person and giving me a choice of actions (answer it, send to voicemail, etc) I'm supposed to decide who the call is from, choosing between three people I know. That's ripped away any immersion I had felt to that point and reminded me that I was a reader, not a participant.

Every game of Plague Inc seems to pan out in the same way. Despite attempts at variation, you essentially plop your plague down in a country of your choice, wait a bit, alter the DNA to *sort of* encourage it to spread where you want it, and the rest is spent balancing deadliness, infectivity and humanity's resistance.
In essence, it’s a very ‘procedural’ game, modelling the replication of your badass bug on its travels throughout the world. Crucially though, what it isn’t… is ‘strategic’.
Sure, you can navigate your plague towards different environments – arid, cold, rich, rural etc – by making decisions about how its DNA will mutate, but whatever your choices, your goal is the globe, and that’s what you’ll end up covering.
Similarly, you can see which countries are working hardest on a cure and try to kill those countries off slightly sooner, but in the end, the ‘procedural’ element wins out, and your decisions don’t make much of a difference.
A strategy game where your decisions matter this little isn’t much more than a simulator – or even a slightly interactive video with some bubbles to click.
Give the app a go before you open your wallet – it’s much cheaper!

This game has a hawk your size, sitting on top of the head of an even bigger eagle, both carefully eyeing you to decide whether you look tasty. If that's not enough for you:
While the actual game mechanics are somewhat rudimentary, it is MORE than made up for by its excellent artwork, atmosphere, style and the variation those mechanics are capable of demanding of you. Set on the foot of the World Tree from Old Norse mythology, you're going to be travelling to several different worlds. Bar none, all of them are imaginative, unique, breathtaking and surreal in their own right.From walking among the stars, sliding across the ice hunted by a giant drake underneath or walking on top the lush, dew dappled leaves of a single giant tree, each environment presents different gaming aspects, from fighting overwhelming numbers, puzzling, pathfinding and timing. While the mechanics are indeed rudimentary, they never become boring in their versatility.
The music, little touches in the animation and the breathtaking landscapes make each of them uniquely memmorable. The game is in Norse, but even though I couldn't understand the language, the calmth and quiet determination in Thora's powerful narration means you don't need to. The foreigness only adds beautifully to this otherworldly adventure, while you browse the subtitles to know what's going on when arriving at vistas.
It's a bit short, but nonetheless an extremely rich adventure that I could reccomend to anyone who wants to be inspired, amazed and impressed.

The best way I can describe this game is that of a storypiece. The gameplay is fine, but the thing that carries this game is the amazing visuals, voice acting, and theme that create a cohesive piece of art. It's definitely still got some gameplay elements that people would like, such as combat, skill use, resource management, and exploration...but people who go into the game thinking it focuses on these elements are going to be sorely disappointed.
Yeah, it has some puzzles, some combat, and some resource management and exploration, but not enough to satisfy people who are looking solely for GREAT puzzles, GREAT combat, GREAT choices, GREAT exploration. It has a little of everything, but what it does excel in is the storytelling and visuals.
The art is absolutely gorgeous and some of the Boss fights are just breathtaking. It also has some of the best camera angle controls I've seen in a game. The camera is often used to make your character seem just as insignificant as you really are in the realm of Gods, zooming out to give you a sense of scale of the scenery and Gods you will be seeing.
Honestly, it's going to disappoint people looking for difficult gameplay or solid controls, but I will say that there are maybe 2 bosses that felt very challenging. (One of them perfectly encapsulates this game and I wish other boss fights would be as cool as he was)
Anyway, if you feel like playing a couple of hours (I spent 5 completing it at a normal pace, some exploration and sometimes just rushing through a zone) of a single player game that focuses on the experience of making you feel like an underdog, with a beautiful art style, I recommend picking this up.
If money is tight and you're looking for replayability and things to do besides the main game storyline, I'd say look elsewhere.

This is a mixed review, but overall it's a game that is worth playing. I will mainly point out what I felt wasn't that great about it, so this might read like a negative review while it isn't.
First of all it is a nice homage to the dungeon crawler days of Dungeon Master and Eye Of The Beholder. It's mainly based on the first and while I'm a bigger fan of EOTB I played my fair share of DM. I like the fact that you are restricted to tile based movement, but can use a camera to look around. If there was just a bit more to look at...
My first complain would be that the presentation while being nicely drawn/crafted (especially the monsters), lacks in variety. In the 13 levels there are four different wall 'sets' and those don't even have enough variation in itself. I take this is due to the small team, but it certainly feels a bit sad to not have more variation. That being said there is a good amount of different monsters, but they have a common problem as well...
The fighting system feels very close to DM (also the magic system), but the enemies feel a tad too damage 'spongy'. It's not that much, but over time the feeling that each enemy takes too long adds up. That changes slightly in the last levels when enemies require a bit more tactic. It's not too bad though and after getting used to it the skill system does really provide a decent way to build your characters.
The puzzles are my main complaint. There are too many reaction/time based ones and while most of them are optional, some aren't. This means that you have to remember patterns and execute them without a flaw. This also happens in DM and EOTB, but it's far less and they are more forgiving. Granted most of the time if you fail a time based puzzle you 'only' lose some health, but it also adds up to the point were you just don't want to do it anymore.
The last complaint is the final boss. He deals a lot of damage and can insta-kill you, but at the same time he doesn't have that many hit points or any ranged attacks, so with a tiny bit of tactic he's really easy to beat.
That all being said, Legend of Grimrock is a very well done throw back to Dungeon Master and I enjoyed experiencing the 13 levels.

Short, cute, fun.
You play one of two characters, Momo or Dora.
Dora allows you to buy a ghost spirit, and that basically attacks for you earlier in the game, or at least earlier than Momo does. So, it sort of makes it easier. In this game, you gotta find out a lot of things by yourself. Such as finding some hidden items, finding some hidden areas, and knowing what works best and what item combinations fit your play style.
The game is short, to the point where someone beat it in less than 7 minutes. With that being said, its not surprise the stages are short. If you know what you're doing, you can easily beat the game in a short period of time. If it's your first time and you're a scrub (like me) it might take you a while.  You don't have to rush though. It's nice to take the time to explore, try to find items, kill enemies or just enjoy the soundtrack. (which is great, you can buy it on the composer's bandcamp.)
Since the stages aren't too long, the bosses must be difficult and take a while to beat, right?
Uhm, not exactly.
The bosses were quite easy for me on my first time playing, some not even hitting me. It just depends on your skill level, or if you know what the bosses do. Some people say they're hard, I say they're quite easy. The story isnt really explained all too well in the beginning, since the game is short there aren't many ways the game directly tells you what the story is, aside from the good ending of course. Some bosses have a very simple pattern, some have attacks that are easy to avoid. Some are harder than others. Heck, even some of the earlier bosses are more difficult than the later ones.
The achievements and speedrun records will keep you busy. Try to get both endings, try to speed run. Heck, it even changes stuff up a bit and you can do a pacifist run. Aside from the exploring you can, trying to 100% it, or just trying out new item combinations that you didn't before, this game will keep you busy. You can waste so much time just trying to beat your own records, or even attempting to beat the speed run record.
I'll try not to spoil too much, so lets get ahead and finish this already somewhat long review.

I could say this game is both for the fans of Megaman and not at all.
It's strange to say that but that's the only way I could definitely describe this game. It has terrible level designs for the first parts of it but it does gradually gets better, and I'll get into that a moment later. You don't really get too invested in the characters while playing but there are some heartfelt moments throughout. It had it's goods and had it's bads.
The levels weren't exactly polished for what they were trying to go for and caused many people plentiful amounts of rage, myself included. Once I learned how to use the mechanics, turned off the voices, changed the BGM to 8bit and learned the medkit system, it started to become more fun.  If it were more fleshed out, I think this would've been a pretty good game to call a Megaman spiritual successor.
There were two bosses that really stood out to me, Brandish the counterpart to Zero from the Megaman X series and Countershade the ♥♥♥♥ing sniper wolf of this game.
Brand who is trying their best not to give into the evil of Trinity is trying to avoid Beck through the whole stage and does not want to fight you. In the end you force him to do so and try to free him through the fight. He's able to ♥♥♥♥ing reflect your bullets with his blades and tries to get closer to you and mess you up. As the second phases happen he unleashes one off the coolest attacks that you'd probably see in a Dark Souls game. And it was ♥♥♥♥ing amazing.
Countershade had one of the coolest sniper battles in gaming in a while, the best being The End from MGS3 and it pulls a few similarities from it. During the stage, you're trying to track down the sniper and they show you a foreshadowing of his shots to help you avoid his path, and they can change dependent if you're near a reflective orb or not. I found myself struggling at this point since I was a bit impatient with the game from the get go, I had had a sudden realization and decided to use Brandish's power. He was able to reflect the sniper shots and made it a whole lot easier. As I progressed, he started to become more and more careful with his positions and laying down traps (if you happen to beat a certain boss before playing the stage, they help you clear the traps and many bots will do the same on different stages). It forces us the players to slow ourselves down, think and move strategically. And it all ends with a rad boss fight in the oval office, like an old western movie but instead of a revolver, you're avoiding sniper fire that ricochet of the walls. That's cool, you can't say it's not.
Once beating the other stages, with the help of the other Mighty Nos. you had gone off and defeated, you are greated with two stages at the end. One of the options allows you to play as Call, who is weaker, more aerodynamic, and stealthy compared to her counterpart, Beck. You're forced to play more stealhfully and consider your choices more wisely this time around. Brains over brawns. I won't say much about this fight but god damn, I enjoyed it. It really respected the players intellegence this time around.
The Final boss fight wasn't as awesome as I wanted it to be, but it did have a nice colour stage and I love me some colours.
I think at the end of the day, it tried it's best to be it own thing rather than being a Megaman clone, and I respect them for that. Our own expectations and two years of delay had probably ruined the experience for us. I don't blame you. If this were any other game, I think it would've been rated and taken a bit more differently. I enjoyed it for what it was (the last part that is) and what it was trying to be.
Pros.
Brandish
Call and her stage
Few good boss fights
Countershade and his stage
Bots fighting for you on each boss stage you haven't completed (it was really touching to me tbh)
Good 8bit versions of the OST
Cons.
Probably everything other than what I listed.
------------------------------------------------
Verdict: Don't play this game expecting anything, just try to push through the first bit, enjoy the 8bit soundtrack and turn off the voices! Other than that, I think you'll have a fun time. Buy it when it's $10

Mighty Number 9 is the supposed "spiritual sequel" to the excellent Mega Man series that, despite having four million dollars to its name for the creation of a single game, fell utterly flat on its back and failed to even partially deliver on what was promised. The finished product, which was released just over three years after the Kickstarter began, looks closer to what a couple of highschoolers would make in their free time as a fanmade indie game homage that was produced over summer vacation. It's hard to believe that this is the work of people who not only worked on the Mega Man series itself, but people who supposedly have a passion for said series. In comparison, Mighty Number 9 is like the cardboard Gundam cosplays, but worse. They're barebones, created by fans, and the only similarity is having the name of the source material plastered on the front. Only, in MN9's case, the Mega Man name isn't on the front, it's instead been buried deep, deep within the earth, because Comcept has very likely killed off the last chance for Mega Man to make any sort of comeback in the future.
I would add more examples to this review, but unfortuantely, just like Mighty Number 9, I must leave it unfinished and cut short due to time and budget constraints.

Might Number 9 is a good game. The graphics are nothing great but I find charm in the way that the cutscenes unfold with the looping animations, it has a very calming Atmosphere to it for me. I found the Story interesting the way it unfolded I mean there isn't much to say without spoiling the Story just felt like classic Astroboy.
- The Music
Having played the music in BGM mode I never heard a somg in this that wasn't  good, I've heard complaints about the newer version soundtrack and thats probably justifiable but for me I liked the game.

The stages feel like classic megaman, if you are looking for a game like megaman Zero, or Megaman ZX  this isn't that kind of game, the stages are simplistic and there are some stages wehre a weapn can open up a new path (Batallions missle and the mine) But its very much just a basic megaman game like Megaman 1.

Honestly, I don't care about the drama, no one should care about the drama its over and done with. Judge the game as it is now and not what some lady did that aggervated a huge ammount of fans.

First of all, I read the reviews before I bought this game. It was a little daunting to spend the $20 with seeing the overwhelming huge negative reviews. At this point, I've played the intro mission and have 1 boss down. I don't normally write reviews, but I think it's important to give this game a positive perspective. I can't say I've played every single Mega Man game, but I have played quite a few. Of those,  my favorite series has always been Megaman Zero.
So, to give it a comparison to the Megaman series (however this game is not one of those games), it does do exactly what the game description claims. It takes many elements from the whole series that maybe these developers enjoyed. There is no wall jumping, but to say this game has no platforming challenge is coming from people who aren't playing the multiple stages. Also, there's no charged shot so you have to constantly be looking for the moment to dash and absorb enemies. Levels, in general, seem more compact and shorter than most Megaman levels. Though it still holds to have a "miniboss" and from what I can tell, each level will have it's own challenges.
I think people are overlooking the fact that the "Zero" series received mixed to negative reviews and was incredibly punishing. It also went the speed run route and gave you a score/rank at the end of the level. What Mighty No. 9 does, is give you an element of the score to assess if you are going to get the rank you are aiming for. Many a time, I was attempting S ranks in Megaman Zero, only to see I achieved an "A". So, I'd have to reset before the auto-save to reattempt. Mighty No. 9 let's you just replay if you want to go for a better rank, which the majority of Megaman games don't let you do.
If we go with the original Megaman series, that game had precision jumps that required you to hit that exact pixel to make the jumps, plus enemies that were placed simply to disrupt you. In those cases, you had to hit a jump just right, shoot just right and still maybe you wouldn't make it.
And with the Megaman X series, although still a blast to play, is recycled from iteration to iteration. Not to mention they've all done things or attempted certain content that just failed. I think Mighty No. 9 is just attempting to establish a foothold to hopefully lead to further refinement in future games. Honestly, to compare this to Megaman is doing this game a disservice since you're comparing a game with 20+ years of development/changes to something brand new.
I won't say Mighty No. 9 is perfect though. The voice acting is meh, and I couldn't really go into full detail about the story. But it seems like that might be mediocre. Also, the stat boosts seem a little awkward to me. Yet, for a game trying to do it's own thing while paying homage to series that's almost went dead (other than re-releases), this game is worth playing. And is certainly worth the $20. It has challenge, replayability and even co-op. Which, I can't say we've ever seen in a Megaman game. To include online leaderboards, it's just a game that can be played multiple different ways by different types of gamers. Either way, it'll probably be a rewarding experience.

The game is... well, so far (at only about an hour in) it's bad.
It's  not terrible, but it isn't "okay" either. It's like a 4/10 if I had to number it that way.
Let me quickly get the good stuff out of the way, since there is less of it than bad. The options menu is good. You can change the controls entirely. There are a full range of graphics and sound options. The music is pretty good. The art is pretty cool (the 2d stuff) and the splash screen stuff (like boss intros) is nice. The controls themselves (outside of the bit I will talk about below) are very tight and responsive, and I can't complain about them much.
Now on to the bad.
-The graphics are bad. The colors are bland and boring, and everything looks like it is slightly foggy. I can't explain that at all, but it is mildly depressing to play in.
-The 3d modeling looks amateurish. This is a really frustrating thing too because it is likely the reason the game took so long to release.
-Beck (the main character) isn't interesting and looks like a generic robot.
-The enemies generally don't look like anything interesting. Enemies blend into the backround, and the backrounds themselves are bland and uninteresting. The whole game looks like it was done in Unity, though it says Unreal in the beginning splash screen.
-In several sections of the game, the lighting is bad enough that enemies are almost impossible to see, and projectiles are hard to see as well.
-The game doesn't explain what the "buffs" are over Beck's head, and it isn't intuitive enough to let you figure it out simply.
-The "AcXelerate" mechanic (the charge) is not fun, since it stops if you run into anything that can hurt you, and there is no way in the beginning to charge vertically up, so it's more a short-range glide than a charge.
-The "AcXelerate" charge mechanic is supposed to let you kill enemies faster, but enemies only "glow" for a short time, which is the only time you can "charge" through them and collect them/kill them quickly. The trade-off for this mechanic is that enemies are tougher, so if you don't charge them, it takes forever to simply shoot them to death. This makes the game boring because charging is too risky with so few lives to be using it as an aggressive attack move (since it does no damage). It's...  frustrating, instead of fun.
-Level hazards are very harsh and in the worst spots they can be in, considering the movement mechanics.
-Beck says the same one-liner over and over and it's super annoying. All the characters say the same one liners over and over again.
-The voice acting for most of the characters is VERY bad. Like, Sonic '06 levels of bad.
-Beck's projectiles don't travel the full length of the screen, so you can't spam the shots and hit enemies as they appear on screen.
-The levels are a bit too tough and far too long for how tough they are. You Don't get anywhere near enough lives to finish most of the levels without being really good or just really lucky.
-Most of the game seems to be based on pure luck, rather than skill or strategy.
-The interface is a bit weird, overall.
But really, what bothers me the most out of all of it is that there doesn't appear to be a wall glide/wall jump. Instead, there is a ledge grab mechanic. As in, they have specific ledges you can grab in verticle obstacles that you can hang on to with your hands. You can't shoot (in the beginning) from these ledges. You just hang there. This makes the game slow and boring rather than fast and fun, and worse, it makes most of the fights seem like there is little you can do if an enemy is too high in the air (which is often) or if they are just on top of a ledge and there is nowhere to shoot them from.
I wanted to like this game. I backed this game on kickstarter. I am glad it isn't vaporware (I was worried there for a bit that it would be) but I am not happy with the final product. If I COULD get a refund, I might, because this is just a frustrating sack of stuff that I, as a fan of Megaman X, didn't ask for and didn't fund this kickstarter for.
The bottom line is there are a lot of much better platformers out there for around the same price that are a lot more fun. This isn't fun at the moment, though I will change my review if they change anything substantial in the game or I find out that I just didn't understand how things worked and it suddenly becomes fun. Until then, I'd avoid this one.

Jotun: The Tradition of Storytelling
Long before the internet, even before the printing press, stories were shared by the human voice. Most cultures have a rich tradition of oral storytelling, when communities gathered to hear news from the village over or explore the worlds of gods and legends.
Traditional oral storytelling appeared in many forms, from campfire tales to travelling poets reciting sagas and epics. This communal experience fosters an intimacy and always reveals something about the teller and audience. Myths and folklore shared in this manner take on the cultural influences of the speakers, and are shaped and changed in the telling.
Though the original version of oral storytelling has largely disappeared, the tradition lives on in films, comics, and video games. One such game, Jotun from developer Thunder Lotus Games, represents a return to this tradition of storytelling.
Jotun tells the story of Thora, a Viking woman disgraced in death who travels through the afterlife to prove herself to the gods and earn a place in Valhalla. The game is heavily influenced by Norse mythology, as Thora encounters a number of gods and legendary creatures along the way.
Thora herself narrates her journey, in Icelandic with English subtitles. She is essentially the tale-teller, the speaker recounting the story of her travels. The Icelandic narration strengthens the experience, helping to draw the player into the tale and adding a layer of authenticity. Hearing the story directly from Thora also creates intimacy with the player, a crucial element of any storytelling. The narrative structure of Jotun, along with Thora's voiceover, reflects a modern interpretation of classic storytelling. Jotun's visual style also supports this argument while adding additional layers of meaning.
Jotun's art style is beautiful, with hand-drawn characters and backgrounds and smooth, stylish animation. The game appears to be a classic Disney film brought to life, full of cartoony style and colourful, memorable characters. Just as traditional storytelling influenced Disney, so does Disney influence Jotun. Tales change in the telling, and tellers change with the times.
The visuals also convey the mythic heritage of Jotun, with massive enemies filling the screen and dwarfing Thora. The world of Jotun exists at a certain level of abstraction, with just enough detail to convey the setting yet still remain dreamlike. The world is created in broad strokes, much like a storyteller weaves a tale.
Much like storytellers respond to their audience, so does Jotun respond to the player. Exploration is rewarded, often with tangible rewards like new powers for Thora. However, the intangible rewards offered are more interesting. There are hidden locations that will provide additional details of mythology and folklore. These are the real storytelling rewards and are definitely worth seeking out.
Jotun isn't the only recent game that represents a return to traditional storytelling but I think it's an ideal example. The combination of narrative journey, intimate voiceover, hand-drawn visuals, and rewarding exploration combine in a package that both draws inspiration from and offers commentary on traditional oral storytelling.

Electronic Super Joy was a gem of a game. Electronic Super Joy: Groove City is not.
It's basically more of the same - which is to say that it features tight, responsive controls, a brilliantly energetic soundtrack and a kooky sense of humour - except they've added in sections in which you have to jump JUST before you hit the ground. And when I say JUST before, I mean that the timing window is literally a fraction of a millisecond, otherwise it's back to the checkpoint with you. This would be only barely tolerable, were it not for the fact that you need to execute these jumps multiple times in a row. Never EVER before have I seen a timing window so utterly ridiculous. I am normally inclined to rise to the challenge of tough games but this is not an unduly tough game so much as it is an insane game mechanic amidst an otherwise reasonable challenge. This does not provide a cohesive sense of difficulty in the way that something like Dark Souls does, which accentuates the frustration when these appalling jumping sections occur. It's a pity that this one piece of awful, awful design had to spoil the other 99% of stuff which was just fine.

Mighty No. 9 is a pretty good game, and, IMHO, does itself justice as a megaman clone. Unfortunaately not a lot of the people reviewing it agree with me, and I can't for the life of me understand why. I mean, sure, it got delayed a crap ton, but it's out and people should be happy that it is.
The art style for the game is pretty lighthearted, as first impressions go, and the story doesn't contradict this too much more than most Megaman games - Zero excluded, seeing as the stages always felt pretty dark to me, and the story was far more dramatic, but I digress. Basic story, without spoiling anything, is that your typical futuristic megaman world is maintained peacefull by a mixture of humans and robots. Robots are even given an opportunity as combat machines in the Collosseum to battle it out. No idea if they're paid or anything, but there's a healthy way to vent out violence. Suddenly, for some weird reason, every robot in the world - for some reason, pardoning your character and your navigator - lose their electronic minds and start murdering everyone, everywhere, without question. Even the FLOOR CLEANERS are killing people. Enter Beck, on his way to a fight in the Collosseum, who ends up walking right into the middle of all of this.
Game mechanics are relatively simple, and, much like Megaman, they stick to the generic 8 boss system. Beck - 'Mighty No9' - is the final model in a set of 8 other robots, each built for a different purpose. Beck is unique among them, as he has the ability to assimilate enemies into himself, and sort-of do a mind control thing that's never really explained. By assimilating other bots, he gains more power. To do this, you have to land a few hits on an enemy and then DASH near them - which is really weird, but it works - and the enemy will be absorbed, granting you various buffs and such. Of course, you're still able to just kill everything, but that takes FAR more effort. Just don't bother. Now, because of this ability, Beck, when he defeats a boss - and yes, you HAVE to assimilate every boss, or they'll become invincible and just regen the damage you dealt - will clear whatever's making them nutso out of their head and gain a new power, just like any other megaman. Now, normally these new powers are all combat abilities for dealing with another boss, but have an effect that's used to unlock secrets in other stages. Not so in this. Each ability has a combat side, but a few of them have other perks as well - one gives you a melee attack that blocks/reflects most ranged attacks, another gives you increased jump height and a glide, and yet another turns you into a bulldozer, boosting your run speed and causing you to damage enemies you run into without taking damage. There's far more than just combat abilities in this, though they also have a means of dealing damage - that's usually the cherry on top.
The game also includes something I've only seen in the Battle Network series, and that's multiplayer - as in, ACTIVE multiplayer, not just trading things back and forth. You have Co-Op challenges, where one person plays Beck and the other Call, and you have Race Challenges (which are more than just a race, but I'm not going to go into detail) as well as solo challenges that go beyond the normal scope of the game. Many of the challenges are simple, or just minigames, but there's more than a few that are pretty tough to beat - namely, one that requires you to go through the ENTIRE GAME, start to finish, every single level and boss, without dying once. Trust me, that's a daunting task - most of the levels in the game have pretty annoying deathtraps to get through that require either incredible luck or a decent amount of skill. My personal favorite part of the game, though, is that once you complete a leve and beat the boss, you can go back and play that level again - exactly as it was the first time. Including the boss fight. Most of the games in the Megaman series had this, but the boss would be removed and the levels changed accordingly - this is the first time I've seen the game KEEP the boss fight at the end.
Overall I really enjoyed the game, even in spite of all the cheap ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t the game throws at you that gets you killed. I will say this much, do not - DO NOT - fight Mighty No. 2, Cryosphere (the ice element, if you don't know what 'cryo' means) until you have AT LEAST gotten through 3-4 of the other bosses.

I would recommend Rosenkruez Stillete and its sequel instead. Although they are doujin games, they have more of what made Megaman fun to play than Mighty no. 9. People seem to be blinded by nostalgia when it comes to this game, wanting it to be almost a copy of Megaman and then stating it fails to capture what made Megaman great. Now that that is said, here are some Pros and Cons:
Pros:
Great level design
Controllers are very responsive
Bosses alter levels when you beat them
Absorbing Powerups from enemies is fun
Challenging and makes you think
Great Music
Cons:

One thing you'll notice is I didn't mention the graphics. Reason being, I don't care for them. They didn't "downgrade" the graphics like some people claim, they just simply stylized them to their liking. Its a hit or miss if you like them or not, though most people don't because they compare it to the 7 day tech demo.
The game overall is great in my opinion. It retains good platform qualities and the Megaman stage design that games like Megaman Unlimited failed to do. The game rewards you for playing fast and thinking fast but challenges you at the same time. Every power-up has its own uses, and they come into play at the final stages of the game where you will need to use them in a variety of situations, instead of them just being there with no real use. While the voice acting (Sandas)  might be cringy, its not unbearable, the game obviously was made to try and appeal to a younger audience while also trying to appeal to the old Megaman fans, which it didn't do so well. As it stands alone, its a fun and great game. Comparing it to the classic Megaman, its not bad at all, as it feels like it belongs. My final verdict is 7.5/10.
Note: When people compare this to Megaman, they usually have the thought of Megaman X in mind. This game was to be designed with Classic, not X in mind, hence why people hate on it a lot because they were stupidly expecting X-like game.

Salutations Everyone and welcome to my review of the Legend of Grimrock. Legend of Grimrock is a first-person dungeon crawler by Almost Human games. In this dungeon crawler, you either take a preset team of 4 or, more commonly, create your own band of 4 to take through the depths of Grimrock to earn your team's freedom.
Before we go further, let's discuss options. The options menu offers many quality options for textures and shadows that let you tailor Grimrock to your machines needs, but as the game's ports to IOS and Android work well, your machine does not need to be powerful to run at maximum settings. Aside from that, there are two sliders for audio. One slider is for Music and the ambient noises of the dungeon, and the other is for sound effects such as sword swings and punches. Both can be muted should you wish, and the sliders actually work. Finally, there is a multitude of extraneous options such as complete mouse control and hiding damage texts which is entirely up to personal preference/machine.
After the options menu, we go on to the story of Grimrock which is simple. You play as four prisoners who are dragged to the top of mount Grimrock for crimes commited. The judges absolve you all as your are pushed in for those who survive Mt. Grimrock are given their freedom. As such, it is your objective to reach the bottom of the mountain while you receive assistance via a being that speaks out to your in your character's dreams. To avoid actual spoilers, I'll end this portion here, but the story is generic so that you can create backstories of your own for the party. You react how your characters react thus giving a "truer" role-play experience, akin to those found on tabletop.
From there, we go on to the most important aspect of Grimrock, character creation. During character creation, you determine the race from four types and each character then gets his/her class from one of three types. This gives you "12" options for race/class combinations which can expand out further in gameplay proper. Naturally, certain races are better at certain class because of raw stats; however, due to the rpg nature of Grimrock, the end result cares more about class than race. The only thing that race truly decides are the traits that grant bonuses that are unique to the race/class. Finally, you determine stat distribution of bonus points into the four stats of Strength, Vitality, Willpower, and Dexterity. For those experienced with RPG's you'll realize that dumping all stat points into a primary stat is a good thing for specialization is key to making Grimrock a breeze. In reality, the benefits are minor compared to how you level up in the main game, but optimizations can mean the difference of 20 health points or mana points by the end of the game.
All this talk of optimization in Character creation is nice, but the game isn't about building characters. The game is about racing through a dungeon, fighting monsters, and solving puzzles. The movement systems is based on a grid. Specifically, you can move, forward, backward, turn left, and turn right. You can do this as quickly as about one move action per half second. This is good as it is your primary tool for staying alive. In addition, each member of your party gets one "hand" action per second that regenerates based on when the action was used. All of this together makes up Grimrock's frantic combat system where you duel enemies that either out-number or out-power you. Note the game has several levels of difficulty and the difficulty simply changes how quick the enemies will move and attack. Otherwise, it has no effect on stats of the enemies.
To compensate for the strength of the enemies, you get frequent level ups which grant skill points to boost a character's level in one of six skill paths. Each path works by granting traits, abilities, and buffs based upon how far along the path you are. Those clever enough to realize it will focus on one path to get access to high-level powers and skills to kill all opponents, but a secondary path is also recommended to compensate for either a low defense or offense that comes from specialization. Those who don't do this will find the late-game to be near-impossible which is a definite flaw in the game's design, but it is easily correctable via the multitude of throwable bombs found in the game. Aside from that, the other flaw with combat is that several weapons are unavailable except through the many secrets of Grimrock. For instance, you cannot find a missile weapon until at least level 3 behind a secret that is easily missable to those who haven't played before. As such, it is a poor mark on an otherwise good game.
Aside from combat, the rest of Grimrock is based on exploration which rewards savvy players. Many of the puzzles in Grimrock have simple solutions that are hidden behind layers of prose, or they are simple logic puzzles that can be solved via trial and error. As such, the puzzles are fair and easily solvable to most people. However, there are a few, optional, puzzles that do not fulfill this format which give no indication on how to solve them properly. However, this isn't a humungous issue as everything hidden behind them is either food to handle hunger (the game already gives you too much and an infinite source) or it is equipment that is made obsolete by other, easily find-able, items. Furthermore, many secrets are simply hidden switches which can be spotted as they are made to stand out if you are actually looking, and these tend to have the best items. All in all, puzzles are mostly fair and secrets are important to the power of any Grimrock run, but they aren't 100% necessary.
In short, Grimrock is a fun game that will take about ten or so hours to complete. For its price, it is worth the buy, and its charm leads to a lot of replays and runs. Each run can be vastly different from one another, and that is the benefit of any run of Grimrock for it never becomes too boring. You can only make it so by actively seeking only the best builds and stomping all enemies into the ground with little challenge. As such, I implore you to make your party and delve into the dungeon!

I really wanted to like this game, but I just cannot. The art style really struck a chord with me, and I am a sucker for norse mythology. I still listen to the soundtrack, and absolutely loved the Icelandic voice-overs. If this had been a cartoon, I would have stuck with it for an entire season with no reservations.
As a game, Jotun just does not deliver much in the way of fun. The trailer on Steam is highly deceptive, making it appear as though you will be involved in tense boss battles by using lots of quick edits. The reality is that enemies are few and far between, and the majority of the game is a walking simulator. A very slow walking simulator.
The slow pace is reflected in the combat as well. Thora only has two attacks with her axe, a standard swing, and a slower, heavier swing. Pretty common in many games, but how it changes is just how absolutely slow Thora swings when using the heavy attack. It takes about eight seconds. Eight seconds of standing still, vulnerable, with your hands over your head like an idiot. It is nearly unusable in combat, and only useful to clear obstacles out of your path. This leaves us with only the basic axe swing for the majority of combats. The hit boxes feel a bit suspect at times as well. There were several moments where the animation went through an enemy only to not have it register any damage.
The camera is also a pain. It will zoom in uncomfortably close at times, and other times will zoom out to show a beautiful landscape and leave you a tiny dot on the map, making it somewhat difficult to get around corners or not get stuck on scenery. The camera moves at a slower pace than the character, leading to times where Thora was very nearly walking off the edge of the screen. Having to stop and stand still while the camera meanders into place just so I can prevent from walking into a lightning trap just slows down an already glacial game.
I really wish the developers had made up their mind on whether they wanted to create a puzzle/exploration game or an action game. Had they taken combat out entirely and left the axe only for puzzle solving, I feel it would have been a tighter game and invested the player more into the world. Had they sped up the combat, movement, and camera the game would be quicker, but also more grounded with the idea of Thora as a seasoned warrior. As it is now, Jotun feels like a walking sim with poor controls and frustratingly simple, yet ineffective, combat.

[TL;DR at the bottom]
Jotun is a tough one – at first glance you got a rather simplistic Norse Action-Adventure Game with an exceptional focus on its boss fights. Before we get into the juicy details, let’s start out with the art design and the soundtrack, which are generally highly praised – and justifiably so. Especially the art of the game looks absolutely gorgeous and may remind some of “Banner Saga”, as well as adding to the immersion through smart camera movements, more often than not to show the detailed backgrounds or to help the player find their way through crowded combat situations.
The Soundtrack, while being above average is nothing I’d highly praise. The voice acting on the other hand is quite good, even though the game is quite sparse with any kind of dialogue, which results in the player only getting to hear it during single-sentence remarks of the player character, Thora.
Now the story is very straight-forward, you’re playing as Thora, a Norse woman who recently died at sea and is given a second chance to prove herself by defeating the Jotun, elementals who roam the different level you get to “explore”. Exploration now is not something Jotun sets a focus on, as each of the different levels (2 per Jotun) is very straight forward, while each of them introduces a “gimmick” such as poison gas, or puzzles to complete.
My personal favorite among those gimmicks is an ice-storm which simply forces you to stop each time it appears, so that you not freeze to death. That being said, practically each of those gimmicks is not much more than a simple annoyance for the player and even the “puzzles” don’t exceed the difficulty level of playing the first level of Tetris. Added to the linearity of the level design, each of those required 2 stages before each boss becomes much more a chore rather than anything else. The only improving factor being the drawn backgrounds and the rare remarks of Thora, trying to introduce the player to a bit of Norse mythology.
Which, of course, laughably fails, if the only thing you do to create a bit of immersion is to let Thora say “The raven (unpronounceable name). Between its eyes sits the eagle (unpronounceable name).” – while it may look cool, and probably has a nice reason to be there, at that location you may generally find interesting to learn more about, the player is just left there, getting a name and the smallest bits of history thrown at him.
The best example of this may be in the fifth stage, a swamp in which you recreate the Norse creation myth. Great in theory, until you realize that you have to travel for 2-4 minutes between each of the five spots you have to activate, each of them tells you a couple of sentences about that myth and in the end you realize that you’ve basically learned nothing from it, since you forgot half of it by the time you’re finished.
So the story, while intriguing at first, fails to convey anything of what it presents in its level design. Thora’s story also doesn’t evolve into anything other than what it was in the beginning: She drowned and now fights for the right to enter Valhalla.
Another thing I absolutely need to mention before going on is, that there are basically no enemies in the different levels, with only very few examples, such as giants who do nothing else than throw a single rock at you every few seconds, or dwarves that run from you on sight, until you reach a certain point, where they all engage you. What that means is: Nearly all of the levels you need to complete are effectively empty, with the exception of the aforementioned environmental hazards.
So: In essence Jotun is just a glorified Boss rush. Are the bosses any good?
To answer that, we first have to talk a bit more about the combat.
So what did I previously mean by “simplistic”? Well – you are quite limited in your combat options, having only a rather fast (and absolutely useless) attack and a slower one, which requires you to stand still for several seconds. Additionally you can discover different shrines throughout the different areas you can explore, which reward you with abilities such as Healing, Blocking and so forth, which are all quite useful.
A giant flaw in the combat system is the fact, that the Hitboxes of each enemy, as well as your own axe is very wonky and is the most important reason for the acclaimed “high” difficulty of this game. Example: One of the bosses you encounter is a fiery-giant. With one of his attacks, he swings a giant sword at you, bending forward in the process.
Now: He is arched over, yet still is upper body is way over your own player character and as a rule of thumb you may have learned from the previous bosses: You only focus on the legs of any of those giants. Yet you can still hit him. The same principle applies later to the last boss as well, who throws lightning spears at you, which circle around in the area, while still loosely tracking your position.
After fighting that boss around 6 times, I still have not a specific clue how the hitboxes on those work. Generally you do not have invincibility frames, yet if you role at a specific time, only the dead-center of those spears seem to hit, while at other time even the particle effects around it cause you to take damage.
What I blame here are the clunky animations. While they may look fine, gameplay doesn’t seem as fluent as you’d need it to be for a game which heavily relies on quick reflexes, especially when using your Shrine-abilities.
The Jotun themselves are nothing to write home about either. I personally consider myself average of skill and it took me around 1-2 tries to complete each of the Jotun. Each of them basically only has 1-2 attacks to begin with and as such none of them is particularly interesting and really only impressive on the first look, thanks to the beautifully drawn graphics.
The last boss however was the most disappointing one – only having the ability to throw either one, or.. and now pay attention! – three spears at you. Great. At around fifty percent each of the bosses has a second phase, which basically is the same as the first one. Here however, the last boss just summons copies of each of the previous bosses with a singular attack. Adding to the wonky hitboxes and that you suddenly have to watch out for 2-6 different enemies makes the last boss an absolute chore, or much rather, has you praying, that you simply do not get hit.
TL;DR:
+ Graphics/Soundtrack (mainly voice-overs)
+ Smart camera movement
+ Option to return to the Hub-Area anytime you want, without having to backtrack
- Story might as well be nonexistent
- Linear, empty and all around tedious level design
- Level-“Gimmicks” are mainly an annoyance (e.g. Ice Storm forcing the player to stop every few steps in an otherwise       completely empty level)
- Very bad presentation
- High difficulty is mainly artificial (horrible hitboxes, overscaled damage and more..)
- Way too short (Completed it myself in around 2 hours, with most things discovered, though that is not the average)
- No replay value
- The price
After finishing the game in just over two hours, I can confidently say, that Jotun simply isn’t worth 14,99 Euros, or your regional equivalent. It’s an overpriced Boss-rush which suffers greatly due to its presentation and flaws in its combat system, most noticeably the hitboxes. My plea to you: Do not be tempted to buy Jotun just because of its pretty visuals or because you’re interested in the subject of Norse mythology.

I was hoping this would be like the excellent Jedi Outcast or Jedi Academy games but it is nothing like them. This is a buggy console port with clunky controls, a god awful camera, and unsatisfying combat.
The controls are bad with either keyboard/mouse or controller. General movement is much better with a mouse and the camera actually works fine with mouse, but doing combos and especially moving/throwing objects with force grip is easier with a controller (though still clunky). Force grip in this game is kind of important. There are always objects around you to grip and throw at enemies or grip enemies themselves. You also need to grip and manipulate objects to progress which is much harder to do with a mouse. Some moves and combos require you to press two buttons at the same time, one particular move requires three buttons, which are far easier to do on a controller. Also my mouse sensitivity became super high when I gripped light objects which made throwing them accurately next to impossible. So I'd recommend using a controller as it's less bad. However, with a controller that leads to the next problem...
The camera. It's the worst. It doesn't work properly with controller. It consistently fails to rotate to where you're facing when you turn. You have to manually do it yourself ALL the time. Having to rotate the camera when you're in the heat of battle is annoying. Actually, having to turn the camera anytime is annoying. I don't know why it works fine with mouse but not with controller but it's irritating as hell.
Then you get to the combat and it becomes repetitive and frustrating especially with the poor controls. Turning is less accurate with a controller so you'll miss your targets a lot more when using force powers. I said earlier that using force grip is easier with controller but focusing on the object you want to grip can be a challenge because you have to be looking right at it which is harder to do with a controller.  In later levels you will constantly face off against a bunch of enemies  all at the same time that can resist your force powers, snipe you, use homing rockets, stunlock you while everyone shoots you, and it just becomes a chore. You can get knocked down with a rocket and it takes like three seconds to get back up for some stupid reason and someone else fires a rocket right as you stand and you're knocked down again. Suddenly you don't feel like such a bad aѕѕ sith anymore. There are also quicktime events when fighting stronger enemies and bosses, because timed button presses are always fun and exciting and never get old.
You can't manually save your game. The menu has a save option but it doesn't work. You only have checkpoints and sometimes they're poorly placed and right before a cutscene so if you die you gotta watch it again and again because the cutscenes are unskippable. Sound/voice is also missing from some levels. Even using the recommended fix doesn't solve it. I had to copy the sound files from the disc version of the game (don't ask me how I got it) and transfer it to the game's folder to actually fix it. Great job devs. Oh yea this game is also locked at 30fps. You can download a fix to raise it but it causes issues with force grip which is already bad enough.
The 3 bonus levels you get with the Ultimate Sith Edition (accessible after you finish the main game and start a new game) aren't anything special. It's more of the same and the storyline is completely absurd for two of the levels. Just to give you an example:

Alright, now having sunk quite a bit more time into this game, I think its high  time i gave it a proper review.
The Sandbox is literally just that, a sandbox. It hands you a bunch of elements (quite a few actually, with the ability to make more), gives you a blank canvas and says "well, im going to go over here for a tic. Go have fun". The elements it offers you are all scripted to interact differently with eachother, and will often transmute themselves to a different element (lava dropped in water becomes stone, wood burning produces ash).
And once you get beyond the simple stuff, you can move onto the complexities of "emitters" and the wonderfully blank/sentient creatures that you can play with.
With all these tools combined you are left with a game without a plot, and without any real set goals... and its Fantastic!  (note: there ARE a plethora of "story mode" levels, as well as a campaign mode that serves as a more in depth tutorial)
So all in all, i think this is a delightful little time waster as long as you dont expect AAA blockbuster content from it. THis is not a CoD clone, this is not Half LIfe 3, this is just a cute little toy you can play with and kill some time
...the price is a tad steep tho. So get it on sale

I decided to completely edit this review because of it's hostility, just so you know alot of the not helpfuls and the discussions are / is probably because I was a real cynical prick with my previous review.
I have only played this game for a short time so I dont know if I just missed alot or just need more time to get used to it, but here you go (dont depend too much on this, take this more of as an "addon" for the other reviews)
I firstly want to say that, the physics are pretty awesomely made, besides the thing that the water keeps having spasms on the top layer and cant be kept still without freezing it completely, which is really annoying when you want to make oceans or lakes or ponds just for the looks.
Also, the graphics / the art are amazingly done, however there again, the resolution has not been edited in a single way so youre basically just gonna play a resized / larger pixel version of the Ipad game.
What seriously disappointed me, were the humans.
They basically either sit or move around slowly, without any walking animation which would be okay, if it wasnt for this really annoying and stupid max cap of 6 humans.
Also, you dont directly get everything in the game.
Alot of elements, and almost every tree and ai etc, has to be bought with "mana", which you only get from finishing quests, and from what i know this game doesnt feature a way to bypass those yet, so if you ONLY want a sandbox experience without having to do alot of quests, then this isnt your best choice either.
The game actually has ALOT of potential to become better, however as of now, it simply isnt worth the 9,99 for early access.

Alot of the potential comes from the devs which seem to be pretty cool, and want to hear from bugs and cool things to do from / with this game all the time, they are really interactive with the community so I dont think this game is a "Refund-now" case.

So heres my summarized score:
Gameplay: 2/10
Graphics: 8/10 (9/10 if it wasnt for the mentioned scaling / no resolution situation)
Music: 4/10
Potential: 8/10
Devs: 8/10
Overall: 5/10
Also, these are some things the devs should fix to make this game be better and recieve a good score:
First off, scratch the human maximal capacity. This is what mostly ruined the game for me. I can only spawn 6 humans, I mean theyre just like 6 pixels that stand around or randomly walk into two directions, I think we should be able to spawn as many as we want to.
Second, add some better deaths. I throw lava on a human i expect to see him run around burning and turning into a charred corpse or atleast just run around and then fall down, but he just simply disappears. It made me think if that was intended or if it was just a glitch in the game.

Third, give us an option to, for example have normal water that doesnt have spasms on the top layer, shooting blue pixels up the sky every second. Just some still water so I can create a lake or pond and have it be there instead of disappearing in mere minutes.
Fourth, an option to unlock everything with just one click. This game is supposed to be a sandbox after all, so I would like to have more freedom of what I want to do, instead of being forced to do certain stuffs and quests so I can buy me a pine tree to grow.
Fifth, More Modding Support, like creating custom creatures or elements.
Sixth, more human varations. Right now theres only one man and one woman and the workers.
Thats all I can think of. These are the truly gamebreaking things in this game for me.
You fix / adress these issues and I'll probably give this a good review, considering the graphics and future updates stuff look / sound really good.
