If you have been around those areas of the web dedicated to free games you have probably seen a lot of what are termed "Falling Sand" games. Basically you have a blank screen and can "draw" pixels on it. For example you set your brush to 'sand' and hold the mouse button down: many pixels appear on the screen and fall down with gravity. Other elements behave differently and elements react with each other; you have things like fire, ice, water, TNT, acid, steam etc.
The main difference between this and other falling sand games are the missions. It's like if you got a falling sand game and added stuff like from those incredible contraption machine games (or Bad Rats haha). There are quite a lot of missions in total, plus a user gallery which is already quite full since this has been released on iOS for a while.
In this Falling Sand game you've got your familiar elements like fire, virus, sand, water etc., then you have some electronic/logic type stuff like power, metal, LEDs, detectors etc. for building minecraft like creations. You then have some more "god game" type ones (that do feature in some of the online falling sand games too) like clouds, plants that grow and people. You can turn the people into a variety of job-themed things like builder or miner that alters their behaviour so you get a kind of lemmings thing going on. Some of the elements don't do anything though, like purely decorative ones, basically like bitmap stamps.
I have The Powder Toy which is free, for windows which is a better simulator with more elements and a higher resolution but I still bought this because there's something cute about the lower resolution, the fact it plays sounds when you add elements, and the interactive things like people.
There's nothing else like it on Steam and I recommend it.

Every single aspect is either irritating, uninspired, or just plain bad design.
-Gameplay: The new mechanic here that differentiates Mighty No 9 from Mega Man is Beck's ability to endlessly dash through enemies and absorb their powers for a short time, killing the enemies in the process. Not a bad idea. But the execution of that idea is where the game fails. The ability to dash forever with no limit trivializes all platforming, which was horrible to begin with because the level designs are so basic and bad. -Writing and voice-acting: Feels like the game is aimed at children with learning difficulties. Voice acting is some of the worst I've ever heard, interrupts gameplay way too often with crap you don't care about, and there's no way to speed up the dialogue, only skip it.

I know this game is getting a lot of heat, but I thoroughly enjoy it. Before I go further, here are a couple of caveats that may affect my perception: 1. Though I've been following the game since the Kickstarter, I didn't back it, so I didn't have any money invested in in prior to purchasing it, and 2. I'm a huge Mega Man fan, having played the series since the first one came out in the late '80s, and with Mega Man 2 being my favorite video game of all time, so I might be a bit biased toward MM-style games.
Now that that's out of the way, like I said before, I really liked the time I've already invested in the game, and I plan to continue coming back to it. I like the character designs (which I know is personal taste and a lot of people hate them), the levels were well designed for the most part, the controls were responsive (playing on a Steam controller, for what that's worth), etc. It's not going to win game of the year or anything, but I thought it was good for what it was, essentially taking elements from the classic MM and X series, mixing in a bit of Azure Striker Gunvolt, and adding a pinch of new ideas.
That's not to say that everything was great, though. The levels, while generally well designed, don't do much to stand out from standard platformer level design (and the sniper one was very monotonous), the voice acting was very hit and miss (more miss than hit), and I ran into a few technical snags, though not nearly as many as some people seem to be encountering. I had one significant frame-rate drop on the ice level, and one time while switching weapons while hanging on an object (right before the boss, nonetheless), I fell through the objects on the level and had to completely restart (that level, not the whole game).
As I said before, it's not going to set the gaming world on fire or completely revitalize the genre (not that there aren't quite a few other Mega Man-inspired games already available), but for me, it was a good time.

I have never written a review before, but as a person who grew up on platformers, Momodora III is quite possibly one of the best games I have ever played. The game mechanics and the character movement through stages are like butter. Like, room temperature butter. And what I mean by this is that when you jump to another platform you don't slide off of it by .5348958349054 mm and die, like in some certain platformers I have played before.
Paired with an amazing soundtrack and cute graphics, after beating the game it really left me wanting more, and by this I was really wanting more on the premise of the plot and story. The downside to this game lies in its brevity, however as a balance to this its small price tag is definitely worth it.
Overall what really makes Momodora III a great game to play is its simplicity, however it is not simple. It has the perfect combination of challenge, variety of items, and skills. On top of that I just love super kawaii pixelated graphics and good music. So if you like all of these, this is definitely your game.

MomoDora III is an exciting platformer with no cheap or gimmicky deaths.  The controls are tight and responsive and if you die it is your fault. There is no time limit so you can take your time and slowly defeat enemies and learn the layout.
The story is that Death has turned evil and Momo or Dora, being shrine maidens, must purify her. Momo or Dora must battle her minions through various stages with huge boss fights to defeat Death. The cool thing is whenever you die you will see Death laughing at Momo or Dora.
Momo and Dora both have an extremely short reach with their melee weapon, but it goes into an arc. They also have a ranged attack and Momo and Dora both control the same from what I saw. The enemies are not difficult but serve as cannon fodder for money. You need money to buy items from vendors or you can find them after a boss fight or in a secret treasure chest.
The game does not support two players, the boss fights are simple when you learn their patterns and the game is linear, too linear. Once you know the layout you can zoom through the game in under 30 minutes.  I also wish that Momo and Dora had different colored weapons and a different ranged shot. All these can be overlooked and still be enjoyed.
To sum it all up, I whole heartedly recommend this game to people who are looking for a new experience or just want to test out their platforming skills. It is worth your money and you are guaranteed to like or love it. I will be looking forward to the other games in the series. Good Job, rdein.

Oh god did I flip when I saw this existed. So far I'm probably about half way through and it's rock hard. I'd say compared to the original game, it's a step up in terms of difficulty.
I will say that there are some differences between both games, and the original seems to be a lot better in terms of its platforming. Groove City is a lot less smooth and fast, it doesn't move as constantly as the first game, perhaps due to the difficulty. Seems like it's far easier to get stuck on obstacles. On the other hand, it's a real challenge and for the most part, I feel it's pretty fair.
The gravity seems a little off in this game and as far as I've played, I haven't seen any powers (e.g. double jump or smash) which is a little disappointing. There is also a few parts that seem a little unfair, basically there are two of these 'chase' enemies on either side of a platform, very close to each other and you must jump between them and tap the jump button before you land to jump before they hit you. This seems to be completely random as to whether you make the jump or not. Even so, all obstacles I've encountered so far have been solved with enough practice.
The music is great as usual, amazing stuff, very cool to bounce to.
I like that it does try to innovate and introduces mechanics not seen in the first game, for example the stars, secret rooms and alternate paths through some obstacles. The black stars that produce missiles are a pain but then, missiles are going to be a pain regardless, especially without the stomp ability.
Considering the extremely fair price and the enjoyment (and at times, frustration) it provides, it's definitely worth picking up.

On May 26th, 2012, Plague Inc was published to the Apple Store by Ndemic Creations. Later that year, on October 4th, it hit the Play Store and the game's popularity blew up like wildfire as more people were able to try it. Youtubers started doing Let's Play... videos of it and people started to share it with their friends. The game became popular enough by 2013 that Ndemic Creations decided to expand the game to PC and release it under Early Access in February 2014. Since the PC release, the mobile versions of the game have managed to stay in pretty close tow with what the Steam Edition has. The mobile versions of Plague Inc do not have multiplayer, nor modding support. However, I can respect Ndemic for not abandoning the original versions and making sure that they still get love, too.
Evolved was originally Plague Inc, but with amped up graphics and with the expansions added in. It released for $15 and was an okay release. In 2014, I recommended this game on sale. As of May 2016 and under full release, I feel this game is worth it at full price. This release does everything the original does, but has player customization and freedom that only PC can give you. These features have been added since the Early Access release and have done nothing less than improve the game and give you more replayability.

I want to start by re-itterating what I said in a previous review for an early access game, I don't usually write reviews and I want to make it really clear that I am neither for nor against this particular game, it has positives and negatives like all games.
Now as far as early access goes, this game has stood up pretty well in my opinion, it looks very pretty (even on my crappy computer) and also on my friend much more powerful PC. The other little game additions like hacking, which I personally think is a fantastic idea, really makes the game feel that little bit more unique, and once you get the hang of it enemies become far less of a problem! Further positives are the way the game is playable, you choose to either go full frontal assault, or try to build up your defences first, or just loot and pillage like a stealthy ninja, entirely your choice and all completely plausible. A final positive is the loot drops, a lot of games try to do loot drops well and you end up either majorly disappointed or getting the same repetitive items that you have no use for, the drops aren't rare nor are they frequent, and that adds that realistic post apocalyptic feel.
Negatives now, enemies. There are only two, one who is easy to avoid and simply blows up (easiest way to kill it is walk up, say hello like a gentleman, them promptly leg it in the other direction), and a different enemy that is frankly OP! Laser guided, radar using, gatling gun motherf***** that you get even a little to close too and it will shoot your face off without even so much as a thought. Which brings me to my next point, health system, I don't get why when you take damage you are forced to slow right the hell down! 100% health you can run and walk normally, 20% and you can barely move forward unless you get to a charging station, which is impossible when you are being followed by the bloody terminators. FInal negative so as not to seem like I am dwelling, the tardiness in updates. I completely understand that this is a solo project manned entirely by one person, and that making a game can take years of development, but updates are necessary for a game to be judged and eventually improved, which is why I am feeling a little disappointed with the current game version of the game.
Now like I said, I neither dislike nor adore this game, It has so much potential and is a nice change to the repetitive rubbish that are most current games who are all, apparently, the same FPS shooters over and over again. I full support this game and it's developer and I hope he or someone else manages to finish this game in the near future as I would love to continue playing it with a larger map and more options!
(As a not to people wondering why I put this review as positive, I see far too much negativity where reviews are concerned of people wanting money back and complaining blah blah. It's not helpful, and it won't make the game move ahead any faster. Positivity will be picked up ((Hopefully)) by the developer instead of the negativity that I can only imagine is a major put off).

I played both BF:BC2 and the Viet Nam expansion.
In BC2, you join a group of homicidal maniacs who are living a psychotic delusion where they are fighting for the US military in an effort to stop the Russian Federation from taking over the world by renting out cheap housing in cities devoid of any civilians and moving their military hardware into it. In reality, the group are actually assaulting random military bases, and then attempting to escape when the soldiers retaliate. They eventually imagine that they recieved orders to intercept an EMP device that threatens to destroy the world by creating awesome surf. The four crazy men do everything from hijacking unarmed scientific vessels to interrogating homeless men that their drug-fueled psychosis has led them to believe are Russian Commanders.
The multiplayer component is an extension of the world that these men crafted for themselves to stop them from committing suicide at the prospect of spending the rest of their lives in a mental institution eating stale apple sauce. The US and Russian militaries both buy their guns from the same shop and are free to use which ever weapon they wish from either country. One of the classes you can play is a necromancer who may bring a soldier back to life no matter how horrid his injury, provided he does so within a certain time window.
There is another class that may repair any vehicle by pointing a magical impact wrench that materializes replacement armor on a vehicle, even as it is being shot at. Paradoxically, attempting the same with a human being results in the opposite effect. This same class has a tool which launches one of those blinking lights early morning joggers wear, except this one attaches to the hull of a vehicle and magically guides missiles toward it, provided you stare at the blinking light long enough.
Oddly, there appears to some sort of temporal distortion, where events seem to happen a split second after they are supposed to, leading to hilarious moments where two people can knife each other to death at the same time.
The Viet Nam component is similar, but has a different background.
A group of insane racists invade a country and begin eating all of the food. The inhabitants respond with incredible effort to push back the superior force. The invaders respond with undeserved indignant rage, and create in their minds an imaginary binary distinction within the territory, one of which allies itself with the invaders in the hopes that the maniacs will turn their attentions to the group that they frequently refer to by the color "red". The color apparently causes great anger to manifest within the invader's ranks.
The invaders are so unstable that the only way to soothe and direct them is to play counter-culture music very loudly in all the bases and vehicles belonging to the invader. This does not quell their racism, as they will continue to shout racist remarks whenever they see their enemy.
This game and its modes and expansions are very interesting, but I still find it weird. I have about 300 hours playtime outside of Steam, so i can recommend this game confidently.
Please note that the game has team balance issues, and that Viet Nam has only a few active servers.

- An underwhelming product that fails to live up to the promises made in the Kickstarter; a project funded on the name of the producer and a beloved franchise alone, that deviates detrimentally that is neither a successor to
nor a solid product in of itself.
- With Capcom shelving one of gaming’s most iconic characters that has been with a lot of gamers from childhood, many were quick to hop on the chance of aiding in funding a dream. A Mega-Man successor with Mr. Inafune at the helm, we couldn’t possibly desire more. Sadly, that dream was nothing more than a fevered stumble that lead to a rather uninspired, ugly mess. A clear mismanagement of funding, overreaching goals, trying to launch on too many platforms, poor communication between the community and the development team,
is a train wreck.
The graphical fidelity is unpleasant at times, with low resolution and poor animations all over the place ranging from the environments to the character themselves. The culprit, I suspect, is because they decided to try and create one unified project that could easily be released on all of the platforms, and since the Nintendo 3DS is the weakest link, that’s the bar it was set to. While there are some okay settings for the PC version, the limitations placed by the developers makes it look awful.
The music is there, and while I do applaud the inclusion of a retro version, it’s not something I’d image myself enjoying outside of the game, if not shutting it off completely to play my own, or another game’s soundtrack. This is mostly due to how un-engaging and boring the level design and combat system is. Everything, from the ground up, was built around the mechanic of dashing, which trivializes too much of the platforming. It feels like they were trying to create a score attack/speed-running/MM game, and it feels haphazardly implemented.
The speed at which the game fumbles about is also of concern. Too often does it feel like you have to wait for enemies or platforms that move between levels of just a tad bit too slow to annoyingly slow. There are even segments you have to wait for the 2.5D elements to stop goofing around before you progress, there was even an instance where I was moving too quickly and was killed when part of the background tumbled forward to "cinematically" kill off a couple enemies. If you want to implement a story, this doesn’t feel the way it’s meant to be done. It slows the pacing of the already sluggish game down with a mix between comic panels and real-time cinematics, coupled with phoned-in acting performances that are often better skipped.
I’ll mostly skip the drama that occurred between the community and its handlers; not because it’s unimportant, but because it’s an arbitrary exercise in dismissal of a review. Even mentioning it can ultimately reduce what you say to “Opinion discarded”, I will say that it was horribly done and led to a Mighty PR nightmare that resulted in the developers working in a creative vacuum devoid of adequate feedback, which can be seen with how there was absolutely zero changes between the beta stage and the final release version.
This, ultimately, leads to the verdict, and it has a couple of varying outcomes depending on what you expect from it. As it stands, it’s not a good Mega Man game; it’s bland and unengaging. As its own product, it’s lackluster and disorganized. I didn’t have a modicum of enjoyment throughout the torturous attempts to play it, and attempted it with an honestly open mind. It can be fixed over time, but who knows at this stage, it’s anyone’s guess at the moment. It all boils down to bad design decisions that can be a learning lesson for budding developers; start small and then grow big, let things progress at a manageable pace, don’t try to take on too many projects at once and do not set out to make a franchise (counting your eggs before they hatch). If they stuck to a few core systems and had better communicate between their targeted audience, things might have been different.

Star Wars always needed a hack and slash game. Force Unleashed was the game we needed, and deserved, after a 5 year hiatus from Jedi Knight. Ignoring, of course, that it has no multiplayer. That's probably a good thing, though, considering how wonky and broken saber duels were in JK2 and 3.
Sam Witwer, the dude who voiced Darth Maul in Clone Wars and also Rebels, and also Crashdown from Battlestar Galactica 2003 (and unfortunately the protagonist in the upcoming PS4 zombie game), plays Galen Marek i.e Starkiller, Vader's secret apprentice. He finds Marek in the beginning of the game and raises him as his own, then uses him to apparently infiltrate/create the rebel alliance. TFU is kind of a Sith power fantasy where you go around beating the hell out of Jedi masters, falling in love with an imperial officer, and pulling Star Destroyers out of the atmosphere with your force powers. But it's awesome.
The combat in this game is unfortunately not as complex, or at least the moveset not as large as you would hope for after gems like Ninja Gaiden or games like God of War. You get your standard Force powers - crush, push, pull, mind trick, lightning, and you get to develop those skills by putting points in to them by earning points and by finding Holocrons, which also lets you make some sort-of-combos. You also find saber crystals throughout the game which change your saber color and change what passive effect the saber has when used. Combat eventually gets boring as with all games that have combat, but on the bright side you get to toss Stormtroopers around like toys, or kill those walking trash can droids.
Graphics, considering they are from 2008, are as good as you can expect from a console game that's 8 years old at this point. The PC port doesn't appear to have been given any special attention, though - even maxing out the graphics still shows that they used the same low-res textures for most of the game.
Unfortunately, as a GFWL game, this is one of many titles that didn't get the Steamworks treatment and never will. No achievements,  no workshop, none of that. It also has a fair share of technical problems and I can't even get mine to work on Windows 10 properly, not to mention it would crash at random on Windows 7 when it had nothing to do with performance.
I'm sure it's overpriced right now, so I really wouldn't recommend buying it if it's anywhere over $10.

RCT Deluxe is one of those rare old gems that, no matter how much people try, has yet to have a spiritual successor fully recapture its essence or innovate in a meaningful way, and the reason for that is in the game's fundamentally brilliant design: it's a concise, well-balanced blend of extreme customization and structural rigidity, two seemingly-conflicting ideals that are perfectly intertwined. Coaster design, park layouts, scenery, and other aspects offer near-infinite variety, but the isometric view and deceptively simple and intuitive grid system offers a very acute precision to coaster refinement that allows a player to master the art of designing and redesigning coasters.
The game's primary focus is on the creation of your very own amusement parks in one of dozens of locations, each with their own distinct goals. To be successful, one must learn how to keep their guests happy by providing them with an assortment of pre-built rides, stalls, and utilities as well as custom roller coasters and other rides that the player must design using a user-friendly ride editing tool. This and other tools offer the player complete control over the ride's track, trains, thematic elements, and price. The player must be considerate of their guests' ride preferences, as every section of track and the overall route will affect three ride statistics: excitement, intensity, and nausea. Learning to design coasters with these stats in mind is a fun and challenging puzzle in itself, and it has a major impact on a park's overall success.
Beyond the fundamentals, after the game eases the player into the basics of park management, each new unlocked park objective teaches a new skill and provides new challenges for the player to test their ability to adapt. The absurd amount of campaigns, contents, rides, scenic options, and other items allows for literally hundreds of hours of fun just to get through all the campaigns at least once, and no two feel alike. Furthermore, while certain methodologies and techniques are sometimes encouraged, the game allows for all sorts of individualistic play styles and different approaches to the same hurdles, so it always feels like strategic and creative problem-solving, not memorization or repetition. Challenges are always present, but they are fair and well-crafted in their structure, so you are always encouraged to improve.
Visually, the game has aged extremely well, and the sprites and assets all look and function beautifully. The game is coded in Assembly, so modding will likely not be an option, but the game's performance is always top-notch. Be sure to check that this version of the game is compatible with your OS before you buy it, but I would highly recommend this game to anyone. It has superb replayability and is always as fresh and exciting as the first time you played it as a little kid. If anything, it's probably more enjoyable today, given the ability to revisit and appreciate the complexity of the game's design with the mental sharpness that comes with adulthood.
Granted, there are occasional small issues with path-finding and staff location assignment as well as the occasional imprecision of the algorithms for calculating ride stats. However, none of these concerns are close to game-breaking, and a bit of extra forethought and experimentation can avoid most if not all of the effects of these, thus the limitations of the game encourage you to work more effectively within those limits. For example, careful planning of main paths, kiosks, queue lines, and facilities can ensure that guests' needs are catered to, and assigning staff locations based on footpath traffic and ride exit access can ensure that rides and paths are always maintained in a timely manner. As of this review, I've clocked over 100 hours into this game, and I absolutely cannot wait for the next 100 hours.
My final rating is 9.8 out of 10. This game was a labor of love, and it really shows.

I have played a few of these Choice games, including Champion of The Gods and Choice of the Deathless. Choice of Robots is by far the best one of the lot. Detail. Reactivity. Replayability. Maturity. Heart. Robots is superior to every other interactive novel out there in every way, and I don't feel that is an exaggeration.
In Choice of Robots, you make a robot. Surprise. You determine its appearance, materials, power source, and ultimately influence its personality (though not entirely). As you guide your "young" robot through the strange customs and idiosynchrasies of modern human life, the manner in which you teach your robot about the world and its place within it will have repercussions in future events.
I have played through this a total of four times, and each time, the ending I received was COMPLETELY DIFFERENT. Not only that, the game achieves the apex of interactive novel aspirations, in that it succeeds in making you feel like the ending you got was the "real" ending. In all of my playthroughs, I felt nothing less than total satisfaction with the ending. And in one, special playthrough, I came within a diode's width of choking up from the feels.
The game has a healthy amount of differing statistics, and these are CONSTANTLY increasing, decreasing and being tested depending on the choices you make. There is an excellent balance of player-determined and statistic-determined story changes, giving you enough autonomy to guide the story in the direction you want it to go, but not so much that it breaks the fourth wall and makes you feel like a bored author.
There is a reason this game has 99% positive reviews. Why not go find out?

I'm enjoying this game and will probably rack up at least 70-80 hours in it all told, but I have a few pro's and cons to go over as despite a big upgrade from the previous Farming Simulators, this isn't altogether a perfect game, although they did improve on a lot of the previous mechanics and expand on it.
Pro's:
+ The greatest draw to this game is the open world and freedom to do whatever you want.  You can either play the campaign for realism or free play to just drive around in cool vehicles right away, or personally, I enjoy spending time logging mixed with farming, which has been expanded and improved in this game.
+ Tons more vehicles than the previous game, in virtually every aspect
+ A slightly better AI system than previous
+ Mod support including easy access to mods from a built in mod menu, including tons of free mods added from Giants software themselves.
Con's:
- The AI is still a bit wonky, I had cleared out all trees near the edges of my farm and expanded the borders of fields with plows, but then the AI would do weird things like not harvest or plant in certain areas or would get themselves stuck on rocks, etc.
- No AI still for things like straw collectors/balers or tipper drivers.  The AI is still "stupid" and is unaware of other AI vehicles, meaning two AI vehicles meeting on the same path will get confused and get stuck requiring manual intervention.  This happens a lot say with cultivators and seeders, if they meet at the edges of the field when they try to turn, even if they're not overlapping each other.  AI vehicles also get confused if something is in their path, even if it would be easy to just go around or avoid it (like a trailer parked on the outside edge of a field that seems out of the way enough).
- Money seems harder to make in this game than previous, and harvest missions almost seem like the fastest way to get money early on, and not develop your farm.  If all you want to do is just work on and develop your farm, they should have made it easier to start out imo.  This is especially problematic because you start out with old tractors that have really high repair costs and will drain your income.
All in all I was hoping this game would expand on the AI aspect to really allow you to play more of a farm management role instead of a farmhand itself, and while the AI is slightly less stupid than previous and other comments have pointed it out, it still has a long way to go and still requires you to do quite a bit of the work.  It should be called more accurately as a "Farm Vehicle Simulator" than "Farming Simulator," and had I known the AI was still fairly bad I wouldn't have picked up this title, and by the time I really figured it out I was past my 2 hour refund mark.
All in all, I still gave it a recommendation.  What I wanted out of this game may be different than others, and I'm still enjoying it despite the limitations.  It's a game I'll sink 80+ hours into I'm sure before I move on to something else, but at the same time wish it was something more than what it is.

This game feels like "I wanna be the Guy" meets "Super Meat Boy" meets "LIMBO". It's not a good mix.
The gameplay sums up to very basic walking and press sensitive jumping.  You don't get any new skills or mechanics that add to gameplay whatsoever throughout it. You go through what I'm assuming is a collection of the worst possible obstacles there can be in a platformer - trial and error segments, slow moving and seemingly random homing projectiles, unavoidable trash pickups, screen corners of death, you name it. If you've hated it in a platformer, it's probably in this game.
The graphic design is l̶a̶z̶y̶ ̶a̶n̶d̶ ̶u̶n̶i̶n̶s̶p̶i̶r̶e̶d̶ ̶p̶i̶x̶e̶l̶ ̶a̶r̶t RETRO style. All segments containing actual gameplay have all elements (characters, homing missiles and landscape) painted completely black with a few exceptions of a couple white pixels and trails. This makes for incredibly confusing distinguishment of elements on screen and becomes frustrating as friendly characters are aesthetically similar to characters that murder you and so on, so forth for everything else.
The soundtrack is a selection of a few generic trance music tracks. They all sound the same and become unsettingly repetitive after a while if you ever do get stuck at a segment and having to listen to it loop - and watch as the 2 frame background characters bob their heads to it.
The game also suffers from the "thinks it's funny" syndrome. It randomly pops up background characters being vulgar and other lowbrow tactics to get a laugh out of people. While I am a person who would very much laugh at the Pope being into Strippers and Scientists yelling over nipples and everything in between, it was far too obvious it was just trying to seem random to get easy laughs for ratings.
Overall this is a very poor game that seems like it was coded in a few days over a couple bottles of vodka. I've played tons of platformers and can safely say this one lacks severely in every aspect. There's no penalty for dying and overcoming the bullcrap obstacles renders no satisfaction whatsoever as they're not difficult as some just demand patience or dare I say luck.
What angers me the most about it is not the poor taste humor or bullcrap gameplay, but the fact that someone out there is laughing because he got this crap on here and is charging money for it.

I managed to get all the collectible achievements about halfway through the game, after which point there seemed to be no point in collecting more. On May 26th, 2012, Plague Inc was published to the Apple Store by Ndemic Creations. Later that year, on October 4th, it hit the Play Store and the game's popularity blew up like wildfire as more people were able to try it. Youtubers started doing Let's Play... videos of it and people started to share it with their friends. The game became popular enough by 2013 that Ndemic Creations decided to expand the game to PC and release it under Early Access in February 2014. Since the PC release, the mobile versions of the game have managed to stay in pretty close tow with what the Steam Edition has. The mobile versions of Plague Inc do not have multiplayer, nor modding support. However, I can respect Ndemic for not abandoning the original versions and making sure that they still get love, too.
Evolved was originally Plague Inc, but with amped up graphics and with the expansions added in. It released for $15 and was an okay release. In 2014, I recommended this game on sale. As of May 2016 and under full release, I feel this game is worth it at full price. This release does everything the original does, but has player customization and freedom that only PC can give you. These features have been added since the Early Access release and have done nothing less than improve the game and give you more replayability.

This is a survivial game set in a post apocalyptic setting where humanity has been wiped-out by machines.  You are an android and you must avoid or fight the robots that you encounter.
Although you do not require food or water to survivel (you're a machine) - you will need weapons, ammo and supplies.
There is an impressive home/base building system in this game.  You can build small shelters to massive installations (building system is similar to Rust).  The gathering of the building supplies is unique.  Instead of "you" spending time collecting wood, concrete, metal, etc - you find and program flying machines called "Harvesters" to do this for you.
The enemy in this game are robots  that seek your destruction.  they come in a few different varieties.  One is a walking bomb.  Another is a flying swarm.  The other is essentially "Terminator".
You spend a lot  of your time exploring and searching through the ruined buildings for useful stuff - and you have to really manage your weight/energy supply in this game.  The more loot you carry - the more energy you use to move.  If you run out of energy - you must wait for your supply to recharge.  this becomes a problem if there are robots coming after you.  The enemies are a real threat - you can be one-shotted by them.
The most impressive part of this game is the structures you can build.  The downsize is that other than gun turrets and a power station - they are largely empty and only serve as protection against bots or other players (if play multi-player).  There really is no decorations or furniture - again you're a machine.
Overall in the short time I have played it - i like what I saw.  I think this game has potential.  The map is decent size but not massive.  I could not see multi-player supporting more than 3-4 players on a server.

Even in it's current state, the developer's have put in a huge amount of work into this. Fully destructible structures that allow people to admire what we have been longing for for decades in the gaming industry (excluding the Red Faction series)
The construction engine in this game allows for some rather unique and powerful designs to be born from the players mind. Although rather complicated to get everything working as the construction uses a lot of different parts to come to life, once accomplished things such as trebuchet's that launch wooden poles which the player has to put in can be fired, catapult's can be made with counter-weight's, an entire village and a castle on a hill can be made, fort's with their own defences and human-activated bridges can be built to grant passage between a bridge, a gap and the fort itself, even a car can be made! But that's not counted as it's due to the player having super-human powers =T
I have so far only been able to make a poopy little immobile light catapult that launches a single boulder, but I have seen people on the youtube's build catapults that fire 5 or more different boulders! Of course, without the proper craftsmanship required to build such a thing, it will break due to physics and weight affecting everything.
The destruction in this game is also astonishing! Being able to crumble structures in a way that I have never seen before really makes me want to continue playing this game. Being able to watch a humongous chunk of stone fall off the top of a tower and crumble a tichy little house beneath it just makes me want to keep replaying that moment at different angles and analyse how awesome it all looks! Of course, everything breaks at given points, but it looks so dynamic and realistic you probably won't notice that for the first hour or two of playing the game because you'll be too into destroying everything and watching how neatly everything crumbles and cracks and breaks around the point of impact!
The only current downside to the game for me is the flying. It feels too much like Space Engineers gravity-less flying and the momentum kind of gets annoying too. I personally like to fly around like in Garry's Mod, move when you want to move, stop when you want to stop. Other than that it's a very useful feature.
The graphics in this game are also really nice. They have a realistic medieval feel to them and actually look like what they are supposed to be. Stone looks like actual stone, wood looks like wood, ceramic roofs look a bit too modern, but I guess they can also be seen as Roman roofs if you would like to think of them in that way. The trees (which can also be broken and knocked over) look like really nice trees. The only thing so far that makes my computer want to go super saiyan is when the entire castle map which can be pre-loaded is destroyed and the rubble is moving. Apart from that, the game (at least on my intermediate powered PC) runs very smoothly at 40+ fps.
So,
Amazing game, brilliant and realistic physics, awesome construction engine, runs smoothly, good graphics and has an awesome soundtrack!
Would definitely chuck boulders like the Hulk into castles from different angles and simulate people screaming in fear again

It's a decent game, and a good recreation of old grid-based dungeon crawlers.
THE GOOD:
- Great graphics and runs fairly well for such a low-budget game
- Quick saving/loading in an era of Halo checkpoints
- Dungeon editor is included
- A few old tropes are averted to interesting effect: the game is now real time, you have front- and back-row teammates, you can game traps to a certain extent
However, there are some design flaws.
THE BAD:
- Character progression is very shallow and rather trite: basically you pick a weapons skill and then circle strafe enemies while hunting for secret gear with very little other thought into builds
- There is practically no music other than the theme song (which, nonetheless, is great)
- The interface was like a touchscreen game, although the game was ported to iOS 3 (!) years after its PC release. What I mean is there is a distinct lack of hot buttons, everything depends on a mouse click, and this can be very annoying especially later on with faster enemies.
- The final boss is just ridiculous, taking the real-time aversion to its limit in a way that I'm sure you don't want to deal with, whoever you are, even if you enjoy action games.
- The amount of button-hunting required to even reach that point is also ridiculous, and be prepared to either backtrack repeatedly or look up a walkthrough to get through the game.
Depending on what you think of the above, make the decision for yourself. Since Steam, for some reason, is forcing me to give me a blue glowy thumb of happiness or red festering thumb of hate for the game, I'll give a blue.

It's pretty much a disaster. The controls are not optimized for PC and the start menu controls do not allow you to change the default. You have to go in game and press escape in order to change them. Even then, the game still continues to use escape and enter as button inputs for menus for whatever reason, rather than allowing you to change them to something simpler.
Once you have figured out how to change the controls to actually play the game, you come to realize that it's not even worth playing. The game runs really slow and suffers constant FPS drops as well as outright freezing. Visually it looks absolutely terrible. Hitboxes are crappy and you start out with no easy way to shoot upwards, downwards or diagonally while many enemies appear exactly in those locations relative to your own. Bosses are frustrating partly due to all of these aforementioned issues (especially the lag) but also more generally. The game also lacks depth as a whole and mainly amounts to just shooting and dashing into bland and predictable enemies when the opportunity arises. It never feels like there is much skill or effort involved  even if the game somehow did run without constant lag.
It seems like the entire game just runs badly on PC in particular while more broadly not being all that great anyways across the board. I definitely regret funding it on Kickstarter. In my defense, there was no way I could ever imagine the profound depth of Inafune's incompetence. He took 4 million dollars and managed to produce one of the worst video games of the 21st century. In my opinion, this game is certainly the worst video game of the 21st century in terms of the ratio of money and time spent to end product quality. There are platformers and metroidvanias on the market with exponentially smaller budgets yet far better gameplay, visuals and art direction. I really wanted a solid platformer but instead this project was bungled in every conceivable way. It's not good at anything, Despite what the developers say, I would argue that nothing WOULD be better as it would amount to money and time saved. There is also a lot less drama and disappointment involved with nothing. The sheer fiscal mismanagement of this project makes me wonder whether the developers are completely incompetent or just contrived from the beginning to set up a scam akin to the plot of the musical "The Producers": banking on a terrible product because there is more profit to be had than from a good one.

Usually I only notice the quality of a game's camera system when it's bad. Good cameras don't stick out. Jotun is one of the rare exceptions from this rule. When you move towards one of its many huge landmarks, or approach one of the massive bosses, the camera zooms out and out and out until your character is just a few pixels large. This provides a sense of enormous, epic scale that so very few games get right. Dark Souls and Shadow of the Colossus come to mind. Never before have I seen anything like this in a 2D game.
The gameplay alternates between calm, peaceful exploration that satisfies the completionist in me, and epic, perfectly executed boss battles. The bosses are just the right difficulty - every one of them took me countless attempts to beat, but it never felt frustrating because every time I had an idea how to make it better next time. And there is always some trick to it that makes the fight a lot easier.
tl;dr: Stunningly beautiful, unique atmosphere, great boss fights, would buy again

Graphics:
So seeing the screenshots here on Steam got me to buy the game. If you are into the kind of retro like graphic, then this game is perfect for you. And the background colouring changes shadow to create the illusion of distance truly makes the game graphical beautiful.
Gameplay:
Before I played the game I read a review of someone having trouble in the game, so I decided to play it on Hard. I spend some time learning the attacks one melee and one ranged, simple yet a great move to avoid over doing the attack part. There is a great mix between using melee or ranged attack instead of just one being completly broken. Enemies are unique and interesting, learning patterns will be required in some rooms in order to move on. Now boss fights! They have certain abilities that really classifies the boss makes it unique and on hard you have to learn the attack patterns which is a huge plus! Instead of just being able to cheese the fights. Movement is smooth and easy going you won't find any problems there.
All in all gameplay is really great and well thought of!
Sounds:
The sounds are great and you won't get tired of them, even if you have to spam attacks. The sounds are retro too and makes for a fun/enjoyable game. Sounds will also hint attacks a lot of the times so you can predict things that way.
Difficulty & Length:
I spend 1.5 hour completing the game on hard, could be done on less if you are used to the bosses. Overall a game worth that time and more if you are interested in hunting achievements, I will be doing that atleast. It's not super hard, but not super easy at the same time, planning will be required!

DO NOT BUY IF YOU HAVE INTEL INTEGRATED GRAPHICS: For some reason it has this weird effect that makes the background textures get all nasty and blurred. Its technically not game breaking, but it does make the game look really, really crappy in parts. I've done a lot of research and there is sadly no known fix. Okay, onto the actual review:
I bought this because I enjoyed playing it on the Wii way back when. If you liked the game before and just want to experience it again, then buy this game. If you've never heard of it before and therefore won't be able to experience through rose colored glasses like I have you probably won't be all that impressed. Its a decent Star Wars game. Not as good as Jedi Academy or Battlefront, but still decent. If you want some hack and slash lightsaber/force action then you will probably have a good time, just don't expect anything revolutionary. In terms of gameplay its just a linear action game with a fun combat system that rewards clever combinations of force abilities and lightsaber techniques.
Gameplay aside, there is just one major con: This is a console port. A really, really crappy console port. The UI literally is not compatible with a mouse; I kid you not you navigate the menu with the bracket "[ ]" keys. Its like it was ported by someone who had never played a PC game in their life.
There are also no graphics settings other than resolution and a checkbox for high detail (I wish I was kidding). If you have an onboard graphics card though you can adjust for anti aliasing, Vsync and things like that.
Last but definitely worst, the game is locked at 30fps. I kid you freaking not. Worse still, there is no way to uncap it in game. Fortunately I found this thread
, followed the instructions, and succesfully,painlessly managed to run the game at a gorgeous 60 FPS. One thing to note, after deleting the local content folder and re-downloading it I just skipped straight to unchecking auto-updates and replaced the SWTFU.exe entirely with the original without entirely uninstalling and reinstalling the game. If for some reason the file is no longer available reply to this review and I'll figure out a way to send you the folder.
All in all, SWTFU is a solid, fun Star Wars game. This particular port sucks, but with some tweaking the gameplay, in my opinion, redeems it all.

There are few things more satisfying than infecting the American population with a disease called "Democracy," then guiding its evolution as it spreads across the globe. I was all swole up with patriotism as I watched the American ideology invading every nation on Earth one at a time, blessing the indigenous with the Democratic way and insominous American dream, and killing them all in the process. Just like in real life. And then on one fine evening, a tear was nearly brought to my eye when writ on my screen was "Victory. Democracy has successfully eliminated all life on Earth." Finally, the commies and the terrorists were gone. There was only freedom now.
In all seriousness, Plague Inc is an interesting game. It's challenging, more complex than you might imagine, and allows for many choices as you choose the next mutation of your disease, customizing it to the situation at hand in order to, hopefully, exterminate all life on Earth. Before a cure can be developed of course, and before you accidentally cripple your progress, such as through making the disease too lethal, killing the infected before they have a chance to infect the rest of the world.
To be completely honest though, I disagree that Plague Inc is worth fifteen dollars. X-COM: Enemy Unknown is thirty dollars, which would imply that Planue Inc thinks itself at least half as good as X-COM. It's not. Command and Conquer Generals Deluxe Edition cost $20 at launch. Plague Inc is certainly not almost as good as CnC:Generals either. It's an interesting game, I like it, but it's not worth fifteen dollars. I'd say a reasonable price for this game is five dollars or less, not fifteen. I recommend Plague Inc, but not at the current price. Wait for a sale.

I think this is the best choices-matter, story-branching, multiple-choice, you-can-make-a-difference game I've ever encountered (so far).  It beats all the allegedly choice-driven games like Life is Strange, Tales from the Borderlands, assorted Bioware games, Alpha Protocol, Arcanum etc.
There are multiple ways of solving problems, or avoiding them . . . and even failing to solve them is not the end (most of the time), bringing on more plot turns and twists. Some outcomes seem either unobtainable or inexplicable, but become completely logical in retrospect once you think about them. There are few to no situation where I felt that a choice was missing, unlike many other branching games.
At first I felt that the 'no graphics; powered by imagination' bit in the sales pitch was cheesy, but after playing through for 5-7 times, I can say that that line was absolutely deserved: the game provides something that big-budget ultra-HD failed to provide to this day, even games from lines which are allegedly known for great stories.
I want to see more games by Kevin Gold. I also think big companies should consider putting hiring and putting Kevin in charge of making stories for their games.

*** REVIEW IN PROGRESS ***
Mega Man is back... under a different name. A flawed but promising start for a new franchise.
PROS:
+ Surprisingly non-manichean story
+ Difficult yet addictive gameplay
+ Quirky, memorable characters
+ Challenging boss fights
+ Optional japanese dub
+ ReXelection abilities
+ Decent voice acting
+ Good soundtrack
+ Call's stage
+ Xel Powers
+ Raychel
CONS:
- Underused Call
- Dull-looking levels
- Unintuitive crouch dash
- Occasionally unfair level design
- Pointless multiplayer component
- Playstation Portable-era graphics
- Unimpressive in-game cutscenes
- No charge shot nor auto fire option
- No proper introduction to the game's world and characters

Frustrating, unresponsive controls, cheap one hit kill deaths in normal play and boss battles. This was meant to harken back to the old days of Megaman, but to do so through theme, setting, and style, not through old crappy game designs that were intended back in the day to extend rental play, keep players busy on the same level for hours so they never notice the game was very short, or to keep players dropping quarters. There are reasons that the industry moved away from these terrible design choices decades ago, yet they are all repeated here.
I will say though the writing is weak in terms of the characters lines and banter, it's art style does bring up memories of Megaman, so in that reguard they got one thing right. Everything else shows a fundimental misunderstanding of why audiences loved the series this game was supposed to replace. The little blue bomber and his struggles against an evil mad scientist, fighting colorful and creative enemies, with cool powers and transformations (MM 6), not cheap deaths with a character who is so heavy and unresponsive in the controls that it's difficult to be as agile as the game acts like it wants you to be.
It saddens me that the creator's belief that we're lucky to have it as it came out is some sort of positive (rather than nothing at all) and that they'll just try better at the sequel is baffling. As a wiser man once said, "But the first impression is most lasting :(," and as such this game is a very poor showing for what could have been an amazing new IP, ushering forth a new age of gaming, with retro IP's and crowdfunding as a way to get out content and not just corporate control.
I backed this game way back when, because I believed in the project. I loved the design and art shown and the idea of a new "megaman" to replace the one Capcom can't seem to "handle," and I would love nothing more than to recommend this game to everyone, however I can not. This game takes a nostaligic idea and attempts to fill a demand and void in our market place, but it does so by returning all the poor design choices and mechanics that older gamers suffered through and hated (and newer gamers won't enjoy or be used to compared to game design now), and trying to stack on top of that new ideas that would make it different enough to be it's own thing, only making it clash violently. This in and of itself is well understood by the creators by the addition of a sort of "pity" mechanic, where by as you continue to fail and die to the poor controls and cheap deaths, the game will throw extra lives and boosts at you to try and balance out these issues rather than taking the time to have better designed the levels in the first place. One wonders what they were doing during the multiple delays and push backs if not balancing these issues directly.
I wish I could say that this game would be worth picking up down the line, because I still believe in this at it's concept and it's core element, but other than the unresponsive controls, everything else I've mentioned above can not be patched to fix, but are built in elements to the game play and would require redesign. I'm not an amazing gamer, but I am an older gamer with years of experience under my belt with many different genres over the years as well as many in the series this one wants to be, but this game was nothing but frustration to me. If you're looking for a "challenge" by way of terrible game design and controls, then this game may indeed be for you, but if you wish to relive "Megaman" fun or want a game to have fun and enjoy, this isn't a good pick for you. I recommend you pick up one of the Megaman compilations that are around. Mind you, these games will have the "NES hard" quality you've heard of or lived through, but even Capcom was smart enough to know those were issues and have added ways for players to deal with them more easily to create a better balance for new and old players alike.

First off let me get this out of the way, I'm reviewing the game as if I heard nothing of the kickstarter and prior knowledge to the creation of this game.
Story:
You take control of a Beck, the 9th robot in the Mighty robot series. Something have made the robots turn evil and you're the only one who can stop them and the other Mighty robots. The story is simply, and I'm fine with that. Many 2D scroller platformers don't have the most elaborate of stories.  My real problem was the voice actors. Some of them just felt off, whether it was just how the sound for their character to how they actually acted out their character. It just didn't feel that well done.
Gameplay:
Mighty No. 9 is a side scroller platformer that involve shooting your enemies into submission and then dashing into them. That pretty much the game, now let go into more detail. You will shoot enemies with you blaster until they glow with a blue, red, green, or yellow aura. At your point you must dash into them to get rid of them. You can just keep shooting them until they are destroyed but this take much longer as a way to dispose of foes. Boosting into enemies is an interesting game mechanic but it tend to lead you into more trouble, such as boosting off a ledge or boosting into an enemies' attack (yes sometime enemies will still attack while they are in this vulnerable state).
Also in term are platforming, Beck have a useless stagger forward animation that occur sometime after landing sometime and this is the worst thing to have in a platformer. When you are doing precision platforming, the last thing you need is to worry about is if your character is going to take an extra step forward after making that jump. I can't tell you how this has been the #1 reason I've died in a platforming section. It really is just an useless mechanic.
Beck gain new abilities (transformations in some cases) from each of the Mighty robot he defeat at the end of each stage. These new abilities to only serve for using them on bosses or to help you get through a certain part in a level.
The stages are short and at the end of them is boss. If you cleared a previous Mighty No stage, you may see that Mighty show up and assist you at certain sections in the stage. That was a nice little add on to the levels. But the levels themselves are not that great. They are completely forgettable, because you can just dash through most platforming sections. The dash let you zip through the air as many time as you can press the dash button. Not to mentions their not that many sections in the level that ask you to rely on your new abilities to maybe find better paths/shortcuts or just to find secrets.
Graphics & Sound:
Graphic are just "meh...."
They aren't great, but they aren't just horrible either. It just with the art style they went with for the graphic doesn't fit playing the game in HD at 1080p.
The music is decent, but none of the tracks are catchy or memorable.
This game tried to be a new Megaman game, but it just mediocre. Not to mention if you're going to base your game off of a big franchise then you better add enough new stuff to the game to really set it apart. Mighty No. 9 doesn't have enough to do this. So if you ever played a Megaman game you'll find yourself constantly comparing it those game and realizing that it doesn't hold up against them. Nor do it have enough original content to set it apart from this. Now does this mean I hate the game. No, it a decent game but for almost $20 you're paying way too much. This game at best is only worth $10, I recommend if you get this game you get it while it only $10 or less. If you get it for that price you'll feel like you got a good game for that price. I actually hope they can do a sequel to this, just because the problems in this games are fixable.

But it was because I had fun in some spots that made the bad parts annoy me so much.
All in all this game get it name truly right. It really is a Mighty No. $9 game.

There are a lot of gameplay kinks that could have easily made the game much better
EG: Movement
- Some stages are set so that Beck needs to be at the peak of his jump to be able to grab onto a ledge, meaning he has to hug close to the wall to be able to overcome the obstacle. Easily offset with a greater jump height or a reasonably thought out stage layout.
- The "dash" function is unrefined and the player has little control over how minute Beck's dash can be (long, short), thus making controlling Beck much more difficult than it needs to be.
- Xel absorption can only be performed by a forward dash. This is quite unreasonable for the player as seen in Cryo's stage where movement is not only hindered by the slippery floor movements but it leads to a quick, cheap death for the player. This usually takes place because the enemies are in an unfavourable position to be absorbed because it can only be done via a dash, where dashing is highly not recommended.
Boss :
EG - Pyro's only indication his attacks are his verbal lines. Halfway through the battle, White and Beck have a small dialogue which hinders your battle for a moment. This wouldn't be a problem if Pyro's OHKO mode wasn't enabled during the course of this conversation.
Overall this game was mediocre, it was trying to be a Zero series clone via stage ranking and point calculation with a pseudo-X series dash mechanic that is vital yet unrefined, in X series type stages with Classic character control. I'm sorry to say this Mr Inafune: This is your worst game yet. It pales in comparison to my first ever video game (X3) in every aspect of gameplay.
EDIT: I find myself stuck in the Robot Factory at the 4 switches part. I have no idea what to do ATM but the degree of perfection this game asks of the player in exchange for limited actions is not what a good amount of players can perform. For starters I think that absorption of enemies is the main issue with the game and should be removed save for boss fights.

This game is extremely fun to speedrun, and it is fairly replayable because you are bound to miss many of the secrets and hidden items. There are also two characters. I played with the hard character because the easy one was a little bit too powerful in comparison. I didn't wanna cheese the bosses at all.
Also, to the devs: the Arabella Sisters fight has problems when you take out the white one first. You can be completely barred by projectiles due to their random patterns when they come out, and then you get hit by the purple beam attack because you can't jump over the huge wall of purple bullets. That's pretty cruel.
Once I noticed this, I just killed the purple one first because the white one is seriously a pushover in her second phase, and so is the purple one in her first phase. This is kinda imbalanced. And yes, I know that you can redirect the bullets by jumping. That sometimes isn't enough. Unless I'm missing something (I never tried to attack the bullets to cancel them, so maybe I'm just stupid for not doing that), I see it as a problem.
Other than that, I give it a momo/10

Momodora III is a not-so-difficult 2D Platformer where you travel through a variety of areas, beating up bosses, and learning a little about the people you meet along the way. The game doesn't go into great detail about your quest, leaving the task to the player to uncover the story through their journey. I wanted to like this game. I REALLY did. I TRIED really hard to like this game, but at the end of the day I couldn't. I bought Transistor because it was developed by the same people who made one of my favorite indie titles. Bastion. I was sincerely hoping for another unique, emotional story that was both fun to play and entertaining mentally. Unfortunately, Transistor is little of either.
Its unfair to compare it directly to Bastion, as a game should be judged on its own merits rather than compared to other similar works. I will as such review it on its own content, comparing to Bastion only to contrast how some specific things were done differently.
Pros:
+Soundtrack is inspired. I mean that, one of the best I've ever heard.
+Art style is gorgeous if you don't mind unrealistic art. If you're looking for hyper-realism this probably isn't your thing.
That's pretty much it tbh. The game's main redeeming qualities are in its aesthetics :/
Cons:
-Combat is a mess. Supergiant tried to merge active beat'em up combat with pseudo turn based combat and the hybrid baby is pretty awkward. There are like 8 enemy types in the game and every fight is just a different mix of those enemies. Levels essential consist of running from small arena to small arena to fight new groups. If you choose to use the turn based function, during the recharge period you're essentially a sitting duck since you move slower walking than pretty much any enemy in the game. If you DON'T use the turn based then in many fights you're at a severe disadvantage due to being unable to strike certain enemies from behind (they dodge too quickly) or at risk of being overwhelmed by sheer numbers. Also, props to whoever on the dev team decided to make you slower than every enemy in the game, making it impossible to outrun anything chasing you without a dash command.
On top of that, combat is extremely unforgiving. Most of the time you have no way to heal during fights (although you DO fully heal between arenas), and if you die the game revives you in the current arena with a penalty- one of your four selected attack commands is disabled. This means you will need to try to finish a fight, but short one quarter of your core fighting tools. If you die again, you lose another command. Die a third time, lose a third command. You'll finally get a game over if you die a 4th time, which extremely likely if you ever end up down 3 commands.
The command system its self is an over complicated mess. Each of your commands can be equipped to use actively or it can be equipped to a passive slot on either your character or one of your active commands. While in theory this allows for a large range of customization, its like saying you can customize your drink at a fast food restaurant. You could get cola, grape, or orange... Or you can get cola AND grape, cola AND orange, or grape AND orange! At the end of the day you're gonna pick a long range attack command, a short range attack command, and then your choice of two utility or movement commands. They're all pretty much interchangable, especially since equipping commands together will usually combine their effects. I'd have much rather seen a pool of truly unique attacks that had a variety of uses, but that's kinda the theme here. Lots of bland, not much variety.
-Story. Ok, gotta talk about Bastion for a sec to frame this critique properly. One of the things that made Bastion so wonderful and that caused it to become so popular was that it had a super unique twist for story telling. The world it built was very different from anything else before it and the mysteries of the game were something the characters were discovering together. The hero of Bastion would explore places, the narrorator would explain them, and when you encountered new creatures or locations they'd be described promptly (in colorful manners). The world was RICH and your actions directly affected the story as it happened. You, as a player, were working with the game characters to figure out the game's mysteries.
Transistor TRIED to repeat that bit of storytelling genius. They checked off all the boxes of good qualities I listed above. Mysterious bad stuff happened just before the game started: Check. Main character never speaks and has a narrorator companion who tells the story and describes the world: Check. Player can interact with the world: Check. There's one MASSIVE difference, however. In Bastion, the mysteries of the game that need answers are mysteries to the characters AS WELL AS the player. You and your characters BOTH learn about the world as you explore. In Transistor, damn near the entire plot is already known to everyone in the game and the player is late to the party. Transistors's narrorator constantly hints at things without actually explaining them. Too many times you're left scratching your head without answers that the characters CLEARLY have and simply aren't discussing. Its such a basic storytelling trap that its one of the first things they teach you NOT to do in creative writing classes.
Aside from that, where interacting with the world in Bastion felt extremely organic, in Transistor it feels extremely forced. In Bastion, if you rolled off a ledge the narrorator would comment on your clumsiness. If you spent time smashing up obstacles in an area he'd talk about how you really cleaned house. Beat a level at full health and he'd talk about how you stomped your way through some ruins without taking a scratch. He just constantly commented on what YOU were doing, the story was clearly focused on what YOU had going on. In Transistor the focus is put less on the player's character and more on the enviroment. Your only ability to interact is limited to kiosks scattered around the city. The narrorator will comment on the enemies far more than on anything you do.
-Game is extremely short. Like 4 hours or so if you don't have trouble with the combat. Its also extremely bare bones, essentially running thru a series of corridors from battle arena to battle arena with the occasional lull for a plot device. While I don't mind short games in general, I DO want to feel like there's enough content and enjoyment in them to justify the price tag, and in my personal opinion Transistor comes up short on both of those marks.
Overall, I'd give it a 3/10. Game is pretty but not very fun or interesting. I wouldn't get it even if it was on sale. That said, if you've not played Bastion yet GO DO SO. Other than the difference in setting (fantasy vs sci fi) Bastion does everything Transistor tries to do, except better in every way.

RollerCoaster Tycoon: Deluxe is the First installment of the RollerCoaster Tycoon Franchise. This game was made I believe late 1990's or early 2000's, with pretty good graphics and programming, made by one guy (Chris Sawyer).
I remember when I first started playing this game when I was 7 years old, I had no idea what I was doing, but I had fun messing around until I went bankrupt or something. Now I know how to properly manage a park, and respond to the guests' demands, as well as making sure I make a nice and steady profit.
This game still holds up really well IMO, and is nice to kill some time when you got nothing to do or anything like that. The game is also very realistic, people react to what happens in the park, not entirely, but functionally. Here's to name a few things:
1. If a RollerCoaster crashes (Accidentally), some people will leave the park and the ride's popularity will plumet to 0%
2. A ride's intensity and price will affect whether a guest will ride it or not (Some guests like intense rides, some don't)
3. When you begin building more than 3 (Good) RollerCoasters, guests will start to no longer want to pay more than $1.00 for less thrilling rides.
Just to name some things---
(Also, Employees get paid less than minumum wage on this game, so be glad you don't live in a RollerCoaster Tycoon world, or you'll be living with $35-$50 a month)
Overall, it's a good game
If you like RollerCoasters, Tycoons, and CHEAP games, then give this one a try.

I haven't had much fun with this game. I like the theme, I like the graphics, but to me it was not much fun.
The game is divided in five areas, one per each giant, plus one final boss battle. There is one exploration level per area, another one with more action and a fairly short boss battle. It is the boss battles where I had most trouble with. Bosses tend to move great distances, and then stay static so that you can catch up. And that is because your character, Thora, moves relatively slow, and attacks slower than that. Battles for a mediocre player like me end up as being a lot of movement, and not too many attacks. I get confused selecting one of the seven powers and using them (select through two buttons, use with another one), so I ended up not using them efficiently. Because of all that, the boss battles drag longer than expected, thus making me frustrated whenever I fail to impress the gods.
I did not like the fact that after the first area, you are given free access to the other four ones. There is one, the fire giant, that is supposed to be harder than the rest, as the developer stated in the forums. It becomes easier to beat whenever you can spam enough powers. And to add to the odd feeling about the game, this giant falls over abruptly after an unknown number of hits and can push you into molten rock, into a cheap unnecesary death.
And those are the small things that pile up into this non recommendation.
However, I need to give Kudos to the developers from being active in the forums!

While it doesn't live up to they hype that was expected, given the budget and time in development, I'm going to ignore that for this review.  How is the game?
It's fun.  The control mechanics are solid, and they work well, although they're not what you would expect from a Mega Man successor.  Dashing is something that you constantly do, but you have to be careful, because dashing into enemies or projectiles hurts more than just walking into them.  Sometimes it's better to walk into a shot than try to dash away, but I think that depends on your skill level.
The absorption mechanic was given too much focus in the game, I think, and I find myself wishing that it was more like Metroid Fusion, where you do absorb the enemy (according to story), but you're not using a dash mechanic to do it.
The whole game has a bit of a speedrunning feel to me, which is something that I enjoy.  I usually don't bother counting how many shots it takes to defeat enemies, but this game makes me want to in order to get a better score.
I've only played through a few stages so far, but they are lacking in overall creativity.  In the City (opening stage), I would expect what I got.  It's linear, and is there to teach the basics.  Fine.  But then in the Waterworks, the only pieces that stood out to me were the poor water gravity (you can actually just air dash across an entire section of the stage without dropping down to deal with the enemies) and the annoying water jets on ice platforms.  Everything else in that stage was relatively bland.  The bosses themselves are good.  You can's just go in gung-ho and blast them down, because you're either leaving yourself open or you can't reach them with your blaster.  You need to learn their patterns, which is a good thing.
Anyway, on its own, I think the game is worth playing, and it is a fine game.  But if you really want gameplay that feels like Mega Man... this isn't really it.  The stage gimmicks are too weak, and the mechanics are too different.  Go play 20XX for some solid, challenging, Mega Man platforming.

I backed this Kickstarter way back when because I'm a really big fan of Mega Man, particularly of the X and Zero games. I hadn't really followed the thing carefully over its extended development time, but when the key finally showed up in my inbox yesterday I was eager to give it a whirl.
And I'm sorry to say that this is kind of crap.
It's fairly basic Mega Man gameplay, but there's this weird emphasis on dashing through enemies as soon as you bring them to low health. That's okay I guess. It means you're constantly moving forward and are playing a pretty fast paced game. That's not bad.
The level design though? That's ♥♥♥♥ing bad. It's filled with stupid death traps that you can only avoid by using otherwise worthless platforming gimmicks (Crouch dash???). If you look at an (infinitely better) game like Ori and the Blind Forest then you'd know that the key to good 2D platforming is to give the player powers that give them OPTIONS in combat and platforming. You don't put a gameplay mechanic in that is only useful to avoid a pair of death traps in one stage at one part of the game.
Bosses meanwhile are basic. Are they hard? Yes. They have insta-death attacks and the ones I fought were in special rooms with fire walls or instant death pits to limit your mobility. And that just doesn't make for fun fights. In the X games or the Zero games you could bounce off walls, dash away to catch your breath and generally could focus on what the actual boss was doing. When I'm trying to just stay out of a death pit I'm not focused on the boss.
Meanwhile: Graphics? Nintendo 64 level. Music? Completely forgettable.
This is no successor to Mega Man. If you want something Mega Man-ish, then your best bet is probably going to be Shovel Knight, Ori, Valdis City or any of the other umpteen other 2D platformers that easily surpass this massive disappointment that Inafune has given us.
