I hear a lot of people saying that this game is either too easy or too hard, and I really think these people aren't understanding a major element of the game: the items. There's a large handful of items that you can equip three at a time that affect your attacks and your characters' abilities. With these you can make your character
, or a one hit wonder. The game can be played as you like it, and if Momo is too hard for you, you can play as Dora instead, who has one extra heart, seems to do a bit more damage and starts with the Dream Ring instead of having to find it. I've also heard people say this game is short (as Momodora games always are) but it took me about nine hours to finish doing everything and getting all the achievements, which I'd call reasonable for a game like this. Just running through once though? Yeah it won't take long.
The bosses were all somewhat basic as usual, some even reusing patterns from Momodora II, but I still thought they were pretty fun. The areas are all vibrant, unique and visually sharp, the graphics are as smooth as always and the sound design as well, however I'd say I enjoyed Momo II's soundtrack a bit more.
On the downside though this game has
too many instant kills, pits and spikes sure, but also bombs. Explosions are a one hit kill and this gets frustrating later on when a lot of enemies have bombs. The slightest misstep in some areas can send you into a pit or explosion immediately, sometimes right after a room transition. It doesn't really add to the difficulty either, as checkpoints are usually nearby anyway.
I also didn't care for the secrets. I really did enjoy finding the secret boss and how it was done in general but I found it all by accident absentmindedly and I wouldn't have if I hadn't just gotten lucky. There's also an achievement for saving a character before she dies that I frankly had to look up because I couldn't figure out what I was supposed to do (one item having a massively misleading description didn't help either).
All in all I really enjoyed this game, it's a lot better than the previous games and shouldn't be judged by them alone.

Short, sweet, and fun. The pixel art is gorgeous and clean, with excellent use of color. The soundtrack is fantastic, but it unfortunately doesn't appear to be available for download anywhere. Difficulty and level design are, for the most part, very well considered. There's enough optional collectables that power up your character in different ways that you can tailor the difficulty to whatever degree you prefer. The game can be Dante Must Die-hard or Kirby-easy; it's all up to you. Level design is very Clasicvania-esque in that it expects you to take things somewhat slowly and to carefully consider your approach to navigating obstacles and fighting the common enemies. Boss fights are fun and well designed, but have a little too much health for how simple their attack patterns are. Though, as mentioned above, there's an item you can abuse to make boss fights ridiculously easy. Replay value is going to stem entirely from how much you enjoyed the game. It offers a New Game+ where you keep your items, but as far as I could tell nothing really changes between the playthroughs (though feel free to tell me I'm wrong). But that's okay. It's short and fun enough that I can definitely see myself busting out Momodora III on a rainy day. It doesn't offer any real incentives for a replay, but neither did any of the classic titles it's clearly inspired by.
If you're a fan of classic Mega Man, Castlevania, or Cave Story then consider picking this up. It's definitely worth the $5 asking price.

The reason why I don't recommend this game is because this game is from the old era of games where gimmicky combat was all about the player either being lucky or exposing some of the cheaper elements of the game in order to triumph.
There are many other choices to make if you support consoles, but unfortunately as a PC user most of the third person action titles with a camera that isn't isometric seems far away from ever happening because of PC being a secondary platform, and because most PC gamers prefer using a keyboard. Games like dragons dogma, dark souls, skyrim, devil may cry, dynasty warriors, toukiden, and eventually God eater and for honor, seem to be the only few types of run around jump action titles that exist with melee combat on the PC genre. However, all of those games have mechanics that will actually support your playstyle, this does not.
Some examples of these bad elements include bosses endlessly countering attacks, randomly losing 40 percent of your health from attacks, missing with your sith thunder attack, faulty attack priority, getting locked into enemy combos, slippery slopes while exploring, bad camera angles, cutscenes everywhere, and a throw system that trumps the combat system because of the ai.
Granted, games of this time have always been full of gimmicks when choosing the hardest available difficulty, however, in action games, it's almost necessary to do so to enjoy the variations of combos the game has to offer. Though the ai makes a point to walk through half of your combo to the point where it feels like you're playing a dragon ball z game, and it's almost an implicit need to throw and blast everything rather than even try to punch anything. That's a big no no if you're trying to make an action game... it'll end up being like dragon age... where mages and archers destroy the game for any type of melee. Moreso with the latter.
It's not a bad game though... the visuals, movement, enemies and effects are still a strong point, the visual fluidity and normal difficulty pacing in the game makes for some of the more fast and curious platform games I've played in the past and adds action from other games that lack the speed or traversal appeal that this game boasts. It's one of the main reasons I've bothered picking it back up despite already playing through most of it on 360. But despite how much I do like the game after I bench some of the more irritating elements, I would never recommend this game to anyone who is looking for a fair and honest challenge. Because let's face it, outside of exploration, the main reason for playing it is to kick butt Jedi style. Not kicking yourself for the game being too cheap to play how you want.

I played this years ago on the Wii.  The PC version is based on the PS3/X360 version.  Of course, the Wii version had lesser graphics, but there were also quite a few difference in the levels, due to being a less powerful console and using the Wiimote.  So, I always wanted to to play it on PC, and I finally got around to it.  The Sith Edition adds three new levels to play outside of the main story.
Overall, I like this game and had a lot of fun playing it. Graphics are good, although not the best I've ever seen last gen.  There aren't a lot of settings in the game, but you can turn on anti-aliasing and other features in your video card settings to improve the looks.
The game is not without its faults. I had a lot of trouble with the targeting system.  There is a targeting button that helps in some cases, but it doesn't solve the problem completely.  Many times I died were due to targeting.  That's not to say the controls are bad. The controls are pretty good for the most part.  YMMV.  I also found that some sounds were missing in the last two levels. If you run into this problem, search the Steam forums for a fix.
The real highlights are the story, characters, voice acting, and production values.  This could easily fit as the true "canon" between Episodes III and IV.  It gets thumbs up from me.

I love the original Electronic Super Joy to no end, but this feels incomplete like an early access beta because most of the things that made ESJ 1 fun are gone.
Mainly,
, reducing the gameplay to very basic jumping and running.
The level design is missing the variety that made ESJ 1 fun, and there's just a handful of enemies. The obstacles are very heavy on tiring chains of instant jumps, so these few enemies managed to overstay their welcome in a 30-minute game. It's kind of sad. I would probably enjoy these levels if they were between other stuff, but this way there's just too much repetition for my taste.
There's also been some bugs. The final boss fight feels half-baked - there's invisible death fields and the cloud platforms have strange hitboxes. There was also a game-breaking issue with screen resolution, but it has fortunately been fixed.
The text has been stripped (ha ha) down in comparison, and while the absurd innuendo follows the spirit of the first game, there's much less of the cheerful "Hey! Keep it up! Groovy! ..." comments that created its atmosphere, so it feels like the party you're traversing has moved from enthusiasm to a drunken lull.
If this game contained the stomp move and more variation in obstacles, I'd love it, but this way it falls flat. It's inexpensive though and still pretty good, just disappointing in the context of the first game.

Groove City is a wonderful addition to Electronic Super Joy, with a handful new levels and more music by EnV.
The difficulty is placed somewhere towards the later half of the first game and picks up from there. No double jump or smash abilities in this installment makes it more focused on skillfully dodging and utilizing your movement.
I am a bit saddened that this 'sequel' only lasted me an hour or so, but it was still a very pleasant experience to return to the mad world that is Electronic Super Joy.
Highly recommended for fans of 2D platformers, though you might want to wait for a sale, or grab it before October 9th as there's currently a promotion running at 45% off.

I bought the game for 0,22€ using a coupon and I'm glad I did because I honestly don't feel like the original price of 4€ would be worth it. The game offers about an hour of gameplay and to me it didn't really feel as challenging or rewarding as the first one. If you are looking for a game like this I would recommend playing the first ESJ before this. I prefer the leaderboard system in the first game where top times were your goal and not so much getting a ton of points.
The level design didn't feel as fluent as it did in the first game and I feel like a lot of the stars where just placed randomly with no real reason behind it other than getting more points. This is my personal opinion and I won't say it's a bad system but I simply found trying to get got times and top spots in the first game more fun.
You should only really buy it if you loved the first one, but just as a warning, don't expect to get that much real gameplay  out of this one unless you like collecting stars. You will most likely get all of the achievement fairly easily and beat the game in just one sitting.
As a conclusion I think the music is still as groovy and perfect as it was in the first one and there has been a lot of updates to the visual style but the lack of new mechanics and the short time that it takes to complete it brings it down. Nevertheless, in the end I did enjoy it because I love these kind of games :)

It made me seriously think.
I don't play too many extremely narrative-heavy games, as I really prefer emergent gameplay sandboxes, but the concepts of robot ethics in this game drew me in, and had me seriously weighing the choices, asking me which of three or four things I valued most highly.
There are four major robot attributes, and four general paths for robots based upon them, from robot revolution to lovebots.
On the negative, however, the writing vacillates between clever and overly sparse.  Some of the romances in particular feel overly rushed to "get to the good parts", and involve little more than direct options of "make this person boy/girlfriend?" "yes" "YOU ARE NOW DATING!" Maintaining it is mainly a matter of "I will dislike you if you make choices related to specific topic I am focused upon", such as Elly's humanitarianism, or Tammy's paranoia about the government.
The character that is overwhelmingly the most focused-upon, besides your own, however, is the one character you can't date, your prototype robot.  You can get her to love you and spend forever with her, but even making love-bots mainly means creating a new character to be a "younger sibling" that has far less development.
Likewise, in spite of the fact that your romantic interest could be there at "birth" for your robot, your robot considering you "father"/"mother", and your romantic interest actively being involved in remodeling your robot, there is almost no interaction between your robot and your romantic interest.  (I.E. If I'm "father", why is Elly not "mother"? Why doesn't Elly try to impress some of her humanitarianism upon the robot? She instead chooses to just sit back and judge the way you raise the robot all by yourself.)
That said, however, it's dirt cheap, and I seriously stayed up all night just mulling over what it was telling me, trying to puzzle out the right answers, or else trying to find some way to wiggle through the requirements, and find a way to get everything (or at least, a greater share of what) I wanted.

My playtime alone should speak volumes about how much I think of this game. I'd say about 700 of those hours were actually spent sitting in front of it, building various factories.
This is a great game for those wanting something very involved, very detail oriented, yet something that can be played at a sedate pace.  It has some mild survival elements, due to having to defend your factory, and it has that ever-popular randomly generated world feature. The logistics mechanics of the game are the best I've ever worked with, they are the meat and potatoes of the game. Even well after you've 'beaten' a game of Factorio, there's forever more tweaks, and optimizations you can make to your layout to make it that much more effecient, or that much more aesthetically pleasing, or for the masochists in the crowd, both at once. Combat mechanics are fairly solid. If you don't like part of how the game works, there is a -huge- modding community (things like making ores last forever, PvP, or making the game even more complicated, or even adding in super-strict survival elements), or you can make your own. Basic tweaks are not overly hard to do. The game is still actively in development, and so far the updates have yet to negatively impact overall gameplay. The multiplayer works pretty well flawlessly. I have yet to have more than the occasional stutter, and I'm reasonably sure that was my ISP and not the game. The game is well worth the purchase price in it's current state, even if the developers were to abandon it today, and they show no signs of stopping any time soon.
All of that considered, though, the game is still not for everyone. This is not a game where you're likely to sit down and 'finish' a map in a single sitting. At least currently, the tutorials are sorely lacking (though the devs are aware and more are in the plans), and at the very beginning the game is not super-intuitive at the very start, especially if you're new to the genre. Once you play for an hour or so, though, you can get the underlying logic of the game, and things get easier.
Overall, I highly recommend the game to anyone who wants something they can sit around and tinker with for days on end. It's great with friends, and playing with the train system can almost be a separate game in it's own right. It's at least worth a try, and if you don't like it, there's always the Steam refund policy.

More Like Artificial Difficulty No. 9.
All I can say is sloppy, sloppy game design. Was Keiji Inafune actually working on this?
Yes, I'm aware that this game looks like a PS2 game and yes I'm aware that the English voice acting is very poor (believe me, you'll want to use Japanese audio as it's far less grating on the ears) and that the story is lame and frequently gets in the way of the gameplay (thankfully, the cutscenes can and should be skipped), but those aren't my main concerns of this review since those issues can be overlooked to some extent.
My main issues with this game are the abundant artificial difficulty and waiting. For the first level, there are falling pillars (insta-gib if you get hit by one of course), so you need to wait for them to clear or be skillful enough to dash underneath them (which is the less safe option and very difficult to time). There's also mortar from above. Again, you need to wait  or move through them, since you have no invulnerability frames during your dash.  If you get hit, you'll be briefly stunned, which pretty much guarentees insta-death if you're on a platforming section. Now combine those two gameplay elements together and you'll get frustration galore.
Even then, the platforming sections aren't all that interessting since the level is incredibly spartan of any sort of detail. With so many memorable locales in platformers recently (such as the magical landscapes of Trine), Mighty No. 9's drab environments are utterly forgettable.This wouldn't be so bad if the levels were well-designed, but from what I've played, they're not, being mostly linear affairs with little incentive to explore the environments (not every game needs to have sprawling environments, but Mighty No. 9 is not a good example for the strengths of linear platformers).
Then there's the boss, Pyrogen, a.k.a. the king of artificial difficulty. He's got all of three attacks (and while they're telegraphed, they're not super distinct from each other and you get very little time to react- especially if you're not playing the game with English VOs). Even if you dodge the attack, the AoE of his attacks are silly large, so you can still be damaged unless you get a pixel perfect dodge. If this were it, it wouldn't be that bad, but during his second phase, he gets one-shot attacks (on normal difficulty, mind you) and no other behaviour changes. Considering how annoying his attacks already were, this just pushes him into the realm of absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t with a cherry on top. He's just frustrating and completely unfair, when his AI doesn't bug out and have him jump against the walls (which are covered in fire because more "difficulty").
Now, I don't mind hard bosses. I love the Dark Souls series and its challenging bosses (like Ornstein & Smough, Champion Gundyr, etc.), but those games are different in the sense that you don't have insta-failure if you make a mistake (unlike pyrogen's second stage) and you have time and space to observe the bosses attack telegraphs and react accordingly (some exceptions like Capra Demon aside). You don't have that luxury of space in this game nor do you have relatively slow bosses. Also, since you have no invulnerability frames in this game, being aggressive (which the dash encourages) is punished. Finally, bosses in Dark Souls are a lot more interesting to fight since they have a wide variety of attacks with different windups, timings, and counters instead of a few extremely similar moves that seek to annoy the player because of how similar they are.
It's a damn shame though, since dashing through enemies and building up a combo can be really fun, but the game throws so much waiting and fake difficulty at you that it's really difficult to get into a good "flow" building up combos.
As for performance, it seems to be mostly fine. I've gotten some crashing and freezing issues, but nothing too obscene. Graphics options are what you expect from this sort of game (window options, resolution, anti-aliasing, etc.) and performance seems to be a rock solid 60 FPS on my rig (i5-3570k, 780 Tis in SLI, 16 GB DDR3 RAM@1600Mhz, 1440p resolution). That being said, this game has a lot of visual tearing, so enabling V-Sync is a must. Oh, and the menus are kind of a pain to navigate, especially considering that there doesn't see mto be mouse support in the menus.
So yeah, for 20 bucks and 4 million dollars raised on Kickstarter, I'd expect a lot more than what we got from this game. There are better and cheaper platformers out there (such as Dust: An Elysian Tale). Mighty No. 9 isn't terrible, as the mechanics are competent (if highly uninspired) so it might be worth a buy if it's really cheap, but I can't recommend it at this price.

So, as we know, Mighty No.9 is a spiritual successor to the great MegaMan from Comcept, Mr.Inafune's own company he started after breaking off from capcom. Yesterday, as well, Backers got their copies of the game. And after playing it for the entire day yesterday, I've decided to go ahead and write what I thought about it.
Initial Reaction: I can't give a 100% honest detailing of my reaction to playing the game, having had access to the special demo during its developement, but I can say that when I first played it I thought to myself "This is definetly Megaman" and was extremely excited for the full game's release. That having come to pass and full access to the content my opinion hasn't wavered, I love the way the game looks, feels, and plays.
Gameplay: As expected, it feels like the classic MegaMan games Keiji Inafune helped develop at Capcom. You run and shoot things until they die. (Or absorb them, as an alternative in No.9) The controls feel just fine, if a little bouncy, and easy to understand. (likely caused by how the models bounce around during movement, so it can be a little misleading on the feel of the movement) The only thing I can really bash is the Ice Physiscs. (No big surprise.) The game is fairly difficult but not impossibly so. Just enough to give long time fans of games like this a run for their money and then some.
Glitches I've found/Other complaints: Save for the ice physics, I've found in Aviator's stage the Flying Hool-hoop thing you can grab onto can sometimes early release you on the wrong layer, and you'll fall endlessly... Easily remedied by leaving the stage, though be prepared to make your way back there, not too bad I suppose. And the game runs fairly slow at times if your system is as old as mine is, being unable to handle the amount of activity on screen at once. FInally, some stages feel kind of empty, like Pyrogen's. Its background is fog at an oil plant. Completely empty back there save for parts of the stage where enemies are standing on things in the back.
Summary: I've found it to be a great game, Inafune and his team delivered what they promised, and I'm happy with it. I'd happily recommend it to about everyone who don't hate MegaMan's gameplay style. And The DLC for Ray is worth it too as its more content to play through. (You'll see what I mean if you get it.)

Disclaimer: I backed this game for $60.

The first time I completed the campaign, I cried. It's that good.
A game isn't good if it doesn't play well. That being said, Transistor's core gameplay is very well thought out, with clear checks and balances that makes the game not too easy, but not too hard either. All of your abilities use up a certain amount of "power slots", with more powerful ones using more power. Speaking of abilities, all of the abilities can be used as either a primary ability, an ability modifier, or a passive buff, with each ability applying its own twist. Using abilities in different situations also advances the lore (I'll get to that later). Each ability set as one of up to four primary abilities also acts as a life. When your HP drops below zero, one of your abilities gets temporarily "burned out," leaving it unusable for a portion of the game. The resulting possibilities are almost endless. You can do what I did and load up on all four primaries, with two or three ability mods and a passive, or you can load all of your abilities as passives with one devastating primary, or any combination of the two. The enemies aren't very diverse, but as you advance said enemies will grow stronger, introducing very clever new variables that you must account for.
As far as raw graphics go, Transistor isn't gonna blow you away with HDR, real-time reflections, or extremely-high-quality models. Since the camera is locked into a third person landscape perspective that keeps stuttering to a minimum, Transistor will still run extremely well on pretty much any computer (it's also available on mobile devices, if that's your thing). The design and art style is what truely gives Transistor life. The overall design speaks of mainly Japanese influence, but if you look around there are a lot of nods to software development. For instance, each ability is known as a Function, and the name of each ability is written as such (for instance: Crash(), Ping(), Help(), etc.). Each ability animation  is crisp, yet vibrant in its own way. The only real issue I had is that the developers chose to use fluid animations for the player character, but went with slide-by-slide animations for enemies and other entities.
Okay, I'm done now with the spoilers.
The music of Transistor is absolutely phenomenal. The underlying chords usually provide a dissonant yet pleasing tone, while the electronic percussion and guitar/keyboard lead instruments provide some very interesting melodies, harmonies, and rhythms. Another item of notice is the fact that some instruments are used completely out of their usual genre. I mean, come on. Who has heard any EDM that uses an accordian melody and uses it well? If you're a music nut like me, do yourself a favor and buy the soundtrack.
All in all, Transistor is a rollercoaster of a game. While it's not the best-looking, it more than makes up for that with creative design choices, a stellar soundtrack, and a gripping storyline.

Transistor is the second title from Supergiant Games who gave us Bastion. It has similarities with Bastion. Both have narrator, but unlike in Bastion where narrator comments everything that the kid does, here narrator is a guy trapped within the Transistor. Transistor is this sword-like thing that you use as a weapon during the game. Also story of the Transistor is in some way similar to Bastion. In my opinion they took the story of Bastion, tried to make it more mystical and complicated, but failed in that attempt.
So about the Transistor. Game is set in the city of Cloudbank. Some theories say that Cloudbank is a virtual world, something like Matrix, where city changes based on opinions of people etc. There are some OVC terminals, and sometimes game will ask you how weather do you want and based on votes, that's how weather is going to be for that day, and stuff like that. You can't really change the city in this game by yourself, but your task is to stop the Process from spreading more and to prevent it from destroying the city. Story in this game is very mystical, and you won't get a thing till the end, since there is not much to hear about except that Process is destroying the city. This game doesn't have a good story though imho, so don't expect much.
Other than the story, this game is great. Artstyle is simply beautiful, soundtracks are great, nothing less to expect from Supergiant Games. As for gameplay, it's awesome. It's turn-based combat, and you have these functions that are actually people who died during the game, and you absorb them into the Transistor, and then you can use them as functions(powers). They are called like "Breach()" for example, you can see why are they called functions, because this is a virtual world, and attacks are just functions in some programming language. Combat works like this: You press button to start a turn, then you execute your functions, but you have limit, and every function takes different amount of "space" during that turn. For example you can execute just 3 "Breach()" functions during the turn(that's my favorite and most used function). After your turn is executed it takes 4,5 seconds for you to be able to execute turn again and you can't attack in that time, you can just run from enemies. Like in Bastion, you have some tests here, that you can do for achievements, and you can also make game harder by activating some stuff. After finishing the game you can play through ng+, but it seems that dialogues are a bit different, but just some minor lines. Game itself is about 5 hours long, little longer that Bastion. It's fairly easy, just like Bastion.
Another great title from Supergiant Games, offering us awesome gameplay, with some beautiful artstyle and soundtracks, and a bit boring story. Great game, but Bastion was better.

I played this years ago on the Wii.  The PC version is based on the PS3/X360 version.  Of course, the Wii version had lesser graphics, but there were also quite a few difference in the levels, due to being a less powerful console and using the Wiimote.  So, I always wanted to to play it on PC, and I finally got around to it.  The Sith Edition adds three new levels to play outside of the main story.
Overall, I like this game and had a lot of fun playing it. Graphics are good, although not the best I've ever seen last gen.  There aren't a lot of settings in the game, but you can turn on anti-aliasing and other features in your video card settings to improve the looks.
The game is not without its faults. I had a lot of trouble with the targeting system.  There is a targeting button that helps in some cases, but it doesn't solve the problem completely.  Many times I died were due to targeting.  That's not to say the controls are bad. The controls are pretty good for the most part.  YMMV.  I also found that some sounds were missing in the last two levels. If you run into this problem, search the Steam forums for a fix.
The real highlights are the story, characters, voice acting, and production values.  This could easily fit as the true "canon" between Episodes III and IV.  It gets thumbs up from me.

If you liked the original ESJ, then you will like this. Keep in mind that, while it IS cheaper, and it IS a sequel, it is a LOT shorter. There are barely any levels. There are only 8 achievements and they are all straightforward and easy to get. BUT, there is more content on the way, and very recently (as I am writing this review) a level editor was released. This is good. Level making/sharing = endless fun.
This game is a lot like the first one: bright colours, sexual noises and jokes (there is still a PG mode), head-explodingly-good music, and... MISSILES. There is one big difference though: You can't smash. Which means a lot more dying to the missiles. But this change is also good because it lets you focus on "proper" platforming, just you and your jumping against the world, no way of defending yourself.
There are only 15 levels (including the two secret levels) but they are well made, challenging, and all unique (there are no worlds like in the original). And of course, the music is awesome. There are 7 new songs (I think) and one or two of the best from the original game have been re-used.
Another difference is that you get a score for each level, based on how fast you finish, whether or not you did it without dying, and how many stars you collect. These aren't like the stars in the original game, there are lots of them, and they give you 10 points each. If you are someone who likes getting high scores, you will spend a long time replaying levels to get a better score. There are also black stars, which award you 69 points (it's true) and then spawn a missile.
And of course, there are normal missiles. Sadly, they still exist.
There are also several small secret areas, with large rainbow stars which give you a heap of bonus points. Most of these are concealed in walls that look slightly different or suspicious. There are 2 secret full-length levels as well.
At the moment, there is a lot less content here compared to the original ESJ. There is also no endless mode. But the new level editor means that you could potentially have endless levels to play, and if you like making your own levels, you will have even more fun. Being one of the first to share some maps, Michael Todd (the dev) played my levels:
Overall, I highly recommend this game.

Just came back to this review after a few hours of having cooled off.  I wrote my original review right after rage quitting, which wasn't fair to the game. I'm changing my oppinion on it, but I'm leaving what I wrote before, because I think some of the complaints and feelings have merit.
As a tldr foreword, I'd rate this game as flawed, but worth playing.
Sound and art are excellent, level design is hit and miss, and combat can make the game a slog at times.  A more detailed review is below.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
What went right-  Again, the aesthetic is just gorgeous.  I love the accuracy of the setting, and the voice acting is superb.  I think I would have liked to have heard the voice actress display more emotional range, such as having dialogue other than backstory and grunts, but I recognize how that could be difficult to implement.  While I see how this could have been a turn off for some, I actually really appreciate that the dialogue is in icelandic.  I assume it's Icelandic, anyway.
What went wrong-  I still think the combat system could use some work.  There're two main gripes I have here.
First is mobility.  Without using Freya's Speed, you move painfully slow in relation to the Jotun. While this isn't always a huge deal, as I said before, in 3/6 fights it makes a huge difference. The dodge roll is also kind of an issue, for two reasons.  First, depending on the frame of the swing animation, the dodge roll comes in a bit late as a cancel, which makes the game feel less responsive.  Second, the distance is pretty short considering the huge size of the Jotun.
The second issue is the combat mechanics. The major issue with these is tutorialization. Until it was pointed out, I didn't know that projectiles could be attacked, or that Freya's Speed sped up combat animations. Aside from tutorialization, a couple of the boss fights suffer from both too little player communication, and too much stagnant AOE.
By player communication, I mean animation and environment cues to the player. For example, when a boss in dark souls might hold up a sword for a second before swinging, letting the player know he/she needs to dodge. In a few of the fights these cues seem too short to reliably get out of the way, or don't give enough directional information to understand where to dodge.
By stagnant AOE I mean that sections of the combat space are made too dangerous to stay in, with effects lasting longer than they should. Since spaces of the map are made dangerous, sometimes even with proper player response to animation cues it becomes impossible to dodge an attack.
In conclusion, better tutorialization of mechanics would have drastically effected playabillity, while certain combat mechanics could have been implemented better.  I feel for example, that cooldown timers may have been a better idea than limited uses of powers, as after you use all your powers in a fight, it becomes nearly impossible to complete.  This would also have allowed stricter control of fight pacing.  Lastly, a "Restart" option in the menu would have been a godsend, as after taking too much damage, or running out of power uses, I'd end up just having to wait for the Jotun to kill me, which hurt the pacing.
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
Some really stupid design choices mar an otherwise nice game.  There's only two main parts of Jotun.  The art/aesthetic and the combat/user mechanics.  The art and aesthetic are beautiful, and the game is well voice acted.  The combat mechanics would have been okay in 2001.  The hit detection of a lot of the ranged weapons is just atrocious, the combat roll feels slow and clunky, as does combat in general.
The only *real* combat in the game is the boss fights against the Jotun, and while some of the fights feel alright, 3/6 do not. This is partially due to the way they implemented the god powers, and the power attack with the axe.  The power attack takes eons to wind up, leaving you open to whatever attack the boss might use, so you can only reliably use it during a boss's cooldown window.  Which happens to be very short.  God help you if any environmental effects interupt you.  This in itself wouldn't be the worst, except that the most reliable damage in the game (thor's god power) only affects your power attack.
I won't say too much about the last boss fight so I won't spoil it, but it's the biggest ♥♥♥♥ing mess of the entire game.  This is where that shoddy hit detection comes in, along with a mid boggling decision to allow certain projectiles to fly around forever, or until they hit you.  You can't use your defence power against them, because they interupt you even if they deal no damage, and you have so few casts off your other damage mitigating ability that it barely helps you.  So instead, these projectiles just follow you around until they inevitably strike you because of the shoddy dodge roll.
4/10.
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

Thunder Lotus almost nailed this game. Everything aside from gameplay was superb.
Art direction, atmosphere, icelandic narration and level design were fantastic.
Gameplay had highlights in the boss battles, which are the main selling point of the game and were just hard enough to feel satisfaction when they were defeated but (aside from Odin) were easy enough to beat with only a couple of deaths each, so ragers fear not. Each boss had interesting mechanics that made most of them a joy to fight.
In spite of that, for a game that is advertised around defeating giant gods, the combat was dull. You have two attacks, one quick (pronounced useless) and one slow (pronounced infuriating). You have one combat-based God power that just powers up the slow attack, which can easily miss.
The rest of the gameplay was also lacking, namely tedious character movement and low interaction. I could smash some iceblocks for example, but attacking the giant dandelions did nothing. This is a small gripe I know, and granted the dandelions were just part of the scenery, but chopping them would've been satisfying and is indicative of the rich world being made to feel barren due to a very limited number of interactive moments.
Despite the shortcomings, I still recommend this game when it's on sale. It was short enough to avoid being ruined by the gameplay and the atmosphere was striking enough to make me consider learning icelandish! I will be keeping an eye on this developer because if they can improve their gameplay, they will surely produce some stunning games and impress the gods!

This is a very special game that is quite beautiful and inspiring. You play as a viking woman warrior who drowns and is taken up to the realm of gods. There, she must find special runes to unlock the gates of valhalla. In order to do so, she must traverse five very different worlds (each broken into two separate levels) and fight giant Jotun or guardians. The five worlds are very different and oftentimes entering into a new area feels like playing a different game.
The game's protagonist fights with a weak, somewhat fast attack, and a strong, very slow attack. She can also aquire, hidden throughout the levels, magic spells that can heal or make her faster or throw magic spears. The fighting is pretty basic stuff.
Where the gameplay shines, however, is in three areas. First, the art is absolutely amazing. It's like beautiful handdrawn art that has an at times abstract quality to it. The is game is a true masterpiece. Second, the levels. Each level is unique and interesting. Different gameplay is employed in each level and different strategies must be used to get through them. Also, most of the spells and life enhancing items are cleverly hidden so there is extra challenge in order to find everything. Finally, the bosses. These guys are not only drawn and animated beautifully, but they are huge. It's like playing Shadow of Colossus in that most of the battles are learning the bosses' patters and weaknesses. It's extremely challenging to tackle these giants but immensely rewarding once you come out victorious. And those hidden spells that you can find? You'll find yourself scouring every corner of every level to find EVERYTHING because you'll need them for the bosses.
I'm so glad I got to play this game. In my mind it is a work of art that was a blast to play. I think the developers did an outstanding job and I would highly recommend this game.
On a technical note: game ran smooth at 60 FPS and 1080p resolution. I played with a controller and it worked fine. I didn't try keyboard controls, but I couldn't see myself playing this with a keyboard. I never had a glitch or crash and saw no bugs to report. The game is about 6 hours long and there isn't much replay value after you beat it.
This is an amazing and beutiful game that suprised me when it said it was hand drawn. It has fun and difficult bosses mixed in with viking mythology.

Excellent little gem.
At times frustrating, yet almost always thoroughly immersive. There's a fair amount of fulfillment just in completing the core game: beautiful maps to explore, Shadow of the Colossus-esque fights that feel oh-so-rewarding upon victory, a neat & tight-fitting soundtrack, and the devs have used achievements to mask optional hard modes (time trials; restrictions on power-ups...) which extend the gameplay well, with seemingly crucial elements of bossfights being optionally foregone.
However, It can become somewhat tedious to finish exploring for the last of Idunn's apples, or that last God statue, because the cinematic nature of the maps enforcing the protagonist's small stature is primarily done with scale and time. If you complete a zone and want to return for a missing object, it's really just an autorun experience. Likewise, the act of returning to bosses for achievements can become a pain in the butt; a small wait quickly becomes a significant test of patience. Although there is some effort taken with awareness that the player will die multiple times in pushing for victory, the cinematic flair works against it at times; it'd take a special kind of powergamer to play it start-finish, but in brief installments of each zone it works wonderfully.
Regardless, good game.  I doubt I'll forget their unique, artful depictions of Jormungandr, the serpent that encircles the world, Ratatoskr, the squirrel that carries insults along Yggdrasil, or the wyrm Nidhogg that chews at its roots any time soon. Worth your attention at full-price, even more in the sale -- the devs have routinely entered their games into Humble Bundles (including a Monthly), and ran a free weekend recently offering permanent ownership of this title. I'll be following their next release(s) and hope my words have persuaded you to look into (at least!) this one. :)

My playtime alone should speak volumes about how much I think of this game. I'd say about 700 of those hours were actually spent sitting in front of it, building various factories.
This is a great game for those wanting something very involved, very detail oriented, yet something that can be played at a sedate pace.  It has some mild survival elements, due to having to defend your factory, and it has that ever-popular randomly generated world feature. The logistics mechanics of the game are the best I've ever worked with, they are the meat and potatoes of the game. Even well after you've 'beaten' a game of Factorio, there's forever more tweaks, and optimizations you can make to your layout to make it that much more effecient, or that much more aesthetically pleasing, or for the masochists in the crowd, both at once. Combat mechanics are fairly solid. If you don't like part of how the game works, there is a -huge- modding community (things like making ores last forever, PvP, or making the game even more complicated, or even adding in super-strict survival elements), or you can make your own. Basic tweaks are not overly hard to do. The game is still actively in development, and so far the updates have yet to negatively impact overall gameplay. The multiplayer works pretty well flawlessly. I have yet to have more than the occasional stutter, and I'm reasonably sure that was my ISP and not the game. The game is well worth the purchase price in it's current state, even if the developers were to abandon it today, and they show no signs of stopping any time soon.
All of that considered, though, the game is still not for everyone. This is not a game where you're likely to sit down and 'finish' a map in a single sitting. At least currently, the tutorials are sorely lacking (though the devs are aware and more are in the plans), and at the very beginning the game is not super-intuitive at the very start, especially if you're new to the genre. Once you play for an hour or so, though, you can get the underlying logic of the game, and things get easier.
Overall, I highly recommend the game to anyone who wants something they can sit around and tinker with for days on end. It's great with friends, and playing with the train system can almost be a separate game in it's own right. It's at least worth a try, and if you don't like it, there's always the Steam refund policy.

I wasn't expecting to review this game because I don't like the combat system inherent in this genre, and leaving it a bad review for that reason would have been silly.  It would be like leaving a bad review for Sim City because there was too much city building.  However Legend of Grimrock has won me over!  Let me explain how:
First and foremost, there are a multitude of secrets to find in Legend of Grimrock, for the observant and clever gamers out there, most of which will offer significant item rewards for finding them.  The power of your characters is heavily gear reliant, so finding valuable items in secret stashes is always very exciting.
Puzzles are an integral part of the game, and most have optional portions beyond what is required to net you one of the afore mentioned secrets.  They are all well designed, requiring thought and in some cases deft timing.  Trap pits lead to actual places, many of which house treasures of their own.  Did you get through the whole puzzle without falling once?  Jump down anyway!  Maybe you'll find something cool!
Finally, this game is very atmospheric.  You will feel the tension as you delve ever deeper into dungeon, knowing that powerful monsters could kill you if you are not careful and prepared.  Ominous (sometimes helpful) messages left by your predecessors will give you a glimpse into their thoughts.  The skulls you occasionally find will give you a glimpse of their ultimate end.  There are also certain traps... well, let's just say I have seldom been so thouroughly panicked by a game.
This one is a true gem.  Even if you don't care for the genre, you'll want to give Legend of Grimrock a try.

This is a great modern game that succeeds in giving players a old school dungeon crawler feel while still manages to be creative.
The Good:
1) "With a 95% positive rating, its likely you will enjoy this game." - Captain Obvious.
2) Good Graphcis
3) Good Music
4) Good RPG experience
5) Creative and smart puzzles/riddles. What's a good dungeon crawler game if it didn't have good dungeon designs?
6) Old school mode. I never had a chance to unds how playing a game while having to draw my own map was like. No longer the case with this game.
7) Extras. Above sound track and concept art, there's actually reading material and quite abit of lore builing. Love the world map and descriptions of each races etc.
8) Good combat, a true test of gaming dexterity and skill.
8a) You will soon realise timing is crucial. If you timed your attacks well enough you can put enemies in a partial stun-lock. consider enemy recovery time and your characters' cooldown etc. Very fun to learn how to exploit this.
8b) I'll say that the combat is clumsy in a good way. You have to draw complicated runes to cast powerful spells. Potions can only be used from inventory. Weapons must be changed in inventory and dragging the icon. Attacks will only be made by right clicking on the correct location where the images of your weapons are. Your archer will have to swap between crossbow+quarrel and bow+arrow (thats 2 item swaps which takes alot of time). You have to pay attention to enemies' attacks and movement and then move your party accordinly to dodge attacks. All of that and much more are all in real time. No pause of combat. Opening maps and inventory only makes you open to enemy attacks instead of pausing the whole game or combat. All these makes this game awesome.
The Bad:
1) Story suck.. I don't actually mind since good story are usually more of a bonus. But the most rememebered and talked about games are the ones with great story. So I find this more a pity than anything else.
2) Replay value. Kinda low since any difference in a 2nd try would be too little to justify the trouble to have to do the entire adventure all over again... Toorum mode was interesting though.
All in all, good game sold at a low price. You're totally losing out if you gave this game a miss.

I hardly ever, ever, ever write reviews. It's true, you can check. So when I write a review for a game you should take into account that it hit me that hard.
This is a book. A CYOA (Choose your own adventure) book. Albeit a complex and much more complicated one.
If you are not a fan of reading long scripts of text for 1-3 hours (Took me 2.4 hours my first run) then that's alright, but I would still encourage this.
This game accomplishes something that most sandboxes and games that "emphasize story" have barely come close to doing; making your choice matter. This isn't a case where the story is the same with minor differences from your choice, but a real evolving adventure. One tale could have you create Skynet and cause the end of humanity. You could create the new iPhone-esque style robots with a company. You can conquer the world with a robot army. You can forgo the world and all people and create a robot child of your own to raise peacefully. You can live, love, fight, squander, become rich, become poor, become ill, overcome obstacles, and more.
If there was a way I could hit that recommend button multiple times I would, but for now just settle with a thumbs up.
In simpler terms, 10/10 I would find love and make a family once more, and prove my humanity still.

How does one live with one's self after inadvertently starting World War III? This was a question I often asked myself while sitting in isolation at a military prison in the Caribbean. At least it was quiet there, and I was finally left alone with my thoughts.
Every choice we make has unforseen consequences. Some good. Others bad. But then I guess it's just a matter of perspective. One person's "good" is another person's "bad". Many people died because of my actions. Or was it my inactions? But still, others profited from those deaths.
I lost my freedom while covering for a friend... all because she was into jazz music and gave me the one thing I looked forward to beyond my work in robotics.
And of course the robots. They were thrust into a world where many were not ready for them, while others sought to exploit them. In truth, I think I just wanted a friend. Someone to talk to. Someone to experience things with. Someone to be in awe with when something new is discovered. First it was one robot. Then I built another. I was not prepared for the responsibility that would be required, but I'd try to adapt. Later in life, I would learn that the responsibility for bringing robots into the world was very similar to raising your own biological children. The same rules applied, one choice at a time.
I've wined and dined with robots. I've danced with robots... I even broke a robot's heart.
Sometimes, I look back to earlier in life, and actually feel regret for hooking up those very first wires to control the gears and servos. But then I quickly find myself disgusted that I would even have that thought because of what good came out of those unfortunate events. Besides, why imagine possible paths to descisions I've already made? There are still secrets yet to be answered. (And some I'm not sure I want the answers to.)
No. I will move forward and be free. Despite the pain and uncertainty our choices may bring... what matters now is moving forward in the present, learning from the mistakes of the past, and plan for a future filled with peace and kindness.
A robot taught me that.

As a backer for the kickstarter I feel shame for backing it in the first place. Bought on the hype that Keiji Inafune would deliver another Megaman masterpiece was truely a pipe dream. I should have known that Megaman died when legends 3 died.
Anyway to the actual review, Mighty No. 9 is a Megaman Clone (if not just a Megaman game with a different name). There is the same ole platforming, shooting and boss fights. The boss is beaten, get their powers and then can use that to beat another boss who is weak to that power. My main gripe is how mediocre this game is despite having a 4 million dollar budget.
The one factor that makes this different from previous Megaman titles is the ability to absorb enemies that give Beck (Mighty No. 9) stat boosts. These stat boosts range from increase in weapon damage, increased speed, or taking less damage. I felt that this mechanic was very poor and didn't impact the game play that much. Most of the time I would use the dash to speed through the level (since it would kill enemies faster) but I never conciously wanted stats boosts in most situations. There are fringe moments where the game forces you to get a certain stat boost to continue the level but that describes why the mechanic is bad. I should want to get these boosts most of the time instead of ignore them.
The aesthetics of the game were ok. As a backer I thought i was going to get some good 2D sprites like the concept art given. The problem with that thought was it was concept art. The art was changed to a 3D style that I felt looked poor, mediocre animations as well as very static facial expressions (something I would not expect from a 4 million dollar budget). Probably the reedeming factor would be the environments in the game. Many were colorful and fad a lot going on in the background.  The music as well was mediocre with many forgettable tracks. I can say this without doubt as I write this review just minutes after finishing this game.
I would say that if you are new to the Megaman franchise, I personally recommend you get any of the Megaman anthology games (be it classic Megaman, Megaman X, or Megaman Zero). But if this game still peaks your interest then I suggest you get this game when its on sale. If you are a Megaman fan though, avoid this game. I feel that supporting this game would just only entice Inafune to make another disapointing Megaman game if given the funds.

So let's just ignore all the controversy for a moment and actually look at the game itself, and only the game itself. Is it any good? Yes and no. Mostly yes though.
Let's go over the bad stuff first, and note what can be dealt with in that regard.
THE BAD
-English voice acting is pretty bad. Easily fixed by using the JP voiceovers.
-Graphics overall are underwhelming. This is one you just have to deal with sadly.
-Weapon selection is clunky as hell. No MM style weapon menu where you can just change modes while paused.
-Game fails to teach you about your Action Shift, which gives you a special jump with i-frames for dodging. Seriously, I wish I'd known about this far earlier.
THE GOOD
-Controls feel spot on for the most part. Everything does what it should and with quick response times.
-Fights are fast and emphasize a faster shooting approach than traditional Megaman, where bosses were invincible for a ridiculously long period between hits.
-Level design is pretty well thought out for the most part and emphasizes running, jumping, and shooting equally well.
-Some of the bosses are pretty darned fun and unique, such as No.8 who was probably my favorite of the bunch.
-Most of the weapons are fairly useful, although some get used far more than others. But this also depends on playstyle.
Could it have been better? Yes. It also could have been a LOT worse.  Also, who knows? Maybe the sequel will be what truly gets the series going. Megaman 2 was the game that put THAT blue bomber on the map afterall.
Anyway, if you see it on sale at some point, definitely worth a look at that point. Full price...Only if you have the 20 bucks to burn.
Regarding the DLC, only worth it if you enjoyed the base game and want an even more challenging mode. Ray is incredibly fun and fast, but like Protoman in MM9/10, meant for Expert players. She takes WAY more damage and is racing the clock, as her life constantly drains when she isn't killing things. That said, if you enjoyed the base game and want a fast, aggressive skill based character to try the game with on a second play, go for it.
This is coming from someone who did grow up with Megaman. And that said...Is Beck the successor we're longing for? Not yet. But he's got potential.

The enemies are sometimes anthropomorphic onions, so a bit of Parappa the Rapper. You kneel over at checkpoints that you can warp around to, a feature directly ported from Dark Souls 2. This game's difficulty is taken from the classic platformer Microman. You can equip items to your character just like in Skyrim. There's blocks that fall down, just like Tetris.
In fact, I would find it hard to not compare things in this game to other games. Maybe that's because comparison is actually a really bad way to objectively review anything on an individual basis.

Fortunatly because of the amazing checkpoint system, you now get to fight ragdoll-god once again and continue trying hopelessly to escape that corner while getting ragdolled for another good portion of your life.
So, is the game good you ask?
YES! You should certainly get this game.

Before I start, I'd like to ask that you read my review before downvoting it instantly just because it's negative. With that said, I don't think that ESJ:GC is a
game, just unfinished, and its current content is more like what you'd expect in a minor DLC or free update for the original game.
But first, let's start with the good parts. The soundtrack ranges from good at worst to amazing at best, which isn't surprising as the composer is the same as the first game's. The story and one-liners are about as quirky as in the first game, and you may or may not see that as a good thing, although for me personally the novelty of butt jokes, battlepopes and robot strippers has worn off a bit. Most of the few levels present were decently designed, with some skillfully timed jumps required at parts.
Now we get to the bad parts. One thing that I noticed right off the bat was that the ability to ground pound had been removed. Considering the original game had 4 total moves (left, right, jump, ground pound), this change is pretty significant. There's no way to get rid of missiles now, you can only jump around them, and the screen can get ridiculously cluttered with them unless if you purposely suicide after each checkpoint. I also found myself taking too long to fall at times and dying because of it, where in the original game I could have just ground pounded downwards.
Some platforming elements from the first game are either used only a few times, like the sticky walls, or not at all, like the wings. There's only one "boss", and all you have to do is avoid his attacks for around a minute. There are only a few varieties of enemies present, you could probably count them all on one hand.
These are all minor problems compared to the main issue, however: the game is just too short. I'm not particularly good at platformers, and even though I died several times, I was able to beat the entire game in slightly over an hour, getting all achievements in my first playthrough. There's no replay value at all. There is an included level editor, but this seems to be the dev's way of saying "this is all I'm doing, you finish the game". It seems to me like the dev didn't want to release these levels as free DLC for ESJ like he has in the past, but instead slapped a level designer on it and called it a new game.
I can't really complain about the price personally, since I bought this for 27 cents, but I know there are people who will want to buy it at full price. My word of advice: don't. It's basically a small level pack disguised as a sequel. Ask yourself if you think $5 is worth an hour, tops, of entertainment. You can make your money go much further than that on Steam. Of course, if you have a coupon or it's on sale, feel free to go for it if you want to burn away an hour of your time.
In conclusion, ESJ:GC has the potential to become just as good as ESJ if more (free) content is added, but as it is now, it's just a skeleton of a game that happens to have great music.

Transistor is the second title from Supergiant Games who gave us Bastion. It has similarities with Bastion. Both have narrator, but unlike in Bastion where narrator comments everything that the kid does, here narrator is a guy trapped within the Transistor. Transistor is this sword-like thing that you use as a weapon during the game. Also story of the Transistor is in some way similar to Bastion. In my opinion they took the story of Bastion, tried to make it more mystical and complicated, but failed in that attempt.
So about the Transistor. Game is set in the city of Cloudbank. Some theories say that Cloudbank is a virtual world, something like Matrix, where city changes based on opinions of people etc. There are some OVC terminals, and sometimes game will ask you how weather do you want and based on votes, that's how weather is going to be for that day, and stuff like that. You can't really change the city in this game by yourself, but your task is to stop the Process from spreading more and to prevent it from destroying the city. Story in this game is very mystical, and you won't get a thing till the end, since there is not much to hear about except that Process is destroying the city. This game doesn't have a good story though imho, so don't expect much.
Other than the story, this game is great. Artstyle is simply beautiful, soundtracks are great, nothing less to expect from Supergiant Games. As for gameplay, it's awesome. It's turn-based combat, and you have these functions that are actually people who died during the game, and you absorb them into the Transistor, and then you can use them as functions(powers). They are called like "Breach()" for example, you can see why are they called functions, because this is a virtual world, and attacks are just functions in some programming language. Combat works like this: You press button to start a turn, then you execute your functions, but you have limit, and every function takes different amount of "space" during that turn. For example you can execute just 3 "Breach()" functions during the turn(that's my favorite and most used function). After your turn is executed it takes 4,5 seconds for you to be able to execute turn again and you can't attack in that time, you can just run from enemies. Like in Bastion, you have some tests here, that you can do for achievements, and you can also make game harder by activating some stuff. After finishing the game you can play through ng+, but it seems that dialogues are a bit different, but just some minor lines. Game itself is about 5 hours long, little longer that Bastion. It's fairly easy, just like Bastion.
Another great title from Supergiant Games, offering us awesome gameplay, with some beautiful artstyle and soundtracks, and a bit boring story. Great game, but Bastion was better.

Since it's been so long since Bad Company 2 came out, it's hard to believe that it actually had a rocky launch, what with the legacy it's left behind and the praise it's since gotten from the Battlefield community as a literal stronghold of nostalgia. Now that it's on sale for steam for so cheap, I have to highly, highly recommend this Origin-free offering to anyone on the fence who hasn't already bought it on impulse.
Not only is the campaign often considered superior to that in BF3 (and especially BF4: we can all agree DICE rushed their way through that one), the multiplayer experience is simply phenomenal. Technical details, such as hit registration, bug-ironing, and netcode, are all spick-and-span polish, unlike a certain disaster in recent memory. Even this late in the game's lifespan, the mechanics of multiplayer, though simple (there is no prone, for instance), lend themselves well to fun teamplay (of course, this depends on the variability of pubs). There are still plenty of servers available (vietnam is less populated than vanilla), so don't be afraid to pick it up. I guarantee you'll get plenty of mileage for the little you spend on it.
More details/specifics I can list off the top of my head:
+ Multiplayer is free of the flaws we've come to associate with BF4; highly polished.
+ Map design is much better than BF4; debatably better/as good as BF3 (which I have not played, admittedly).
+ Excellent balance.
+/-: Mechanical changes (i.e average TTK is much lower than in BF4, no prone, alternate gameplay styles favored because of alternate map design, helicopter piloting is much less responsive and more difficult)
- Less player customization. The only camos are available as alternative weapons in the SPECACT. For example, in the SPECACT, you get an MG3 SA with map-dependent camo in addition to your standard unlockable MG3, and can access it without having to level for the normal MG3. There are a few vanilla weapons that have camo on them by default, however, such as the m24, and some weapons do change color scheme depending the map (SCAR-L is tan in desert/jungle, grey in arctic).
- Less weapon customization.

So I just completed 100% of the achievements (Pre-Valhalla Edition) for Jotun and figured it was time that I write a review for this game that I love so much. From the outside, Jotun looks like an adventure/exploration game with little combat during levels and tricky epic boss fights. While this is true; for me, the meat of this game comes in boss mastery and completely centered around combat.
Jotun starts with Thora (the hero) dying without a chance to enter Valhalla due to an inglorious death. Odin, the Allfather grants you a chance to enter Valhalla through great deeds by collecting runes and defeating the Jotun (giant elemental beings tied to Norse mythology). To battle a Jotun, you must complete two levels through exploration and some puzzle solving (unfortunately little combat). These levels are associated with the elements of the corresponding Jotun and vary in terms of what is needed to complete them. Each level will have a rune, an apple (increases max health) a Godshrine (gives you a God Power or additional uses of said God Power) and a few vistas or other points of interest where the camera zooms out giving some beautiful shots. Once the runes have been found, it is time to face the Jotun.
These Jotun bosses are giant elemental beings that will test your resolve, quickness and combat strategy. Fighting these beasts for the first time can feel like an impossible task and defeating them feels like a massive accomplishment. In fact, when beating these bosses for the first time you wonder how any of the achievements for them are even possible. This is where this game goes from good to great!! Each Jotun has 5 achievements associated with them. 1-Initial defeat, 2-Shun the Gods (use no God Powers), 3-Perfect (take no damage), 4-Time trial, 5-Special conditions (ie. don't attack in melee, defeat at under 10% health etc.) Learning all the bosses patterns/quirks and figuring out strategies to complete these tasks can be daunting, but because of reliable combat mechanics and tight controls is very rewarding. Combat is simple with a regular attack that can be used twice for a slightly faster combo, or heavy attack which is a painfully slow wind-up followed by a massive blow. Throw in a dodge-roll and six God Powers (speed-up, heal, shield etc.) and that's it. What makes the combat so great is that you know exaclty what you can get (and are going to get) out of your character. Learning how to use this to maximum advantage is all you have, and what makes this game SO DAMN FUN!!
Now with the Valhalla Edition, all of the Jotun are buffed to the max (more HP, do more damage, more powerful abilities etc.) I have played through each boss of this mode (no special conditions) and it is insane... really looking forward to the challenge of defeating these bosses without using God Powers and without taking damage!!
To sum up, if you're looking for a good action/adventure with outstanding visuals, good music/atmosphere and decent combat... you'll probably find it here. If you're looking for the above with testing combat achievements and you enjoy boss-mastery type games you might just fall in love with this gem like I have.

For those of you who would rather watch my video review of this game, here ya go:
So the main part of this game is fighting the bosses, which for the most part is fun. But before you can fight a boss you have to complete the two levels that accompany each boss. These levels are there to let you explore this world that they have created and enjoy the artstyle, however it isn’t anything special. Each of these levels usually has one mechanic that is drove into the ground bythe end of it, making you glad that the level is over. This is problematic because the hand drawn graphics make you want to explore and see more of the level, but the mechanics either make it hard to explore or just down right tedious. I found that I was often having to pause and look at the map to reorient myself, which I don’t think should happen in a game like this because I want to be focusing on the art and the world. I want to be looking at this world that they have painstakingly hand drawn. Instead I am constantly opening up the map. Pausing in a game like this should be a sin, but the layout of some of these maps is so poor that it is a necessity. This part of the game is so incredibly boring, that I often found myself ready to quit when I was forced to do them.
But once you have suffered through two levels you can reward yourself with a boss fight. The boss fights are without a doubt the best part about this game, but they still have their flaws. One of my biggest problems with them is the combat itself. Combat consists of three attacks: fast, slow, and charge. However all three of them feel sluggish. Once you get past how slow your character is, the boss fights themselves are not particularly impressive. Each boss goes through a moveset, once it is taken below a health threshold it gets a second moveset. It is basically a memorization game. Which isn’t that big of a deal, but for a game whos main draw is the boss fights, I figured that the fights would have been a bit less formulaic than they were. I was hoping for a more reactionary fight, where the boss actually responds to what I am doing, but unfortunately that is not the case. On certain fights you can pretty much just stand in one spot and wail on them and get the best possible outcome. Not all fights are like that, some of them force you to constantly move around and dodge attacks, which was pretty fun.
With all of that in mind, I cannot recommend this game. It has good visuals and a few good boss fights, but overall the game is pretty boring and a majority of the boss fights are nothing to brag about.  It feels like a lot of people are getting swept away with the visuals in this game and are forgetting about the gameplay, which is slow, generic, and unimpressive.

TL;DR at the bottom.
Lets just start with this: The reason I haven't written this review yet was because I couldn't take my face out of the game itself.
ALSO This game is early access (and I mean "it got released today" early) and if you do not know what that means, it means that it is in early development and will grow in the future.
Aside from one sentence remarks, let's start with a basic summary.
Most people probably know that Medieval Engineers is Keen Software House's second "Engineers" game (for those who don't know, Space Engineers is the first and I thought it was spectacular). This game has a whole new level of interesting and unique features, and both Space Engineers and Medieval Engineers are going to feed each other ideas. For example, ME had  "Voxel hands" first, then SE got them. So, back to this game and ONLY this game. This game has smooth gameplay, solid building, few bugs that I can see, and is very beautiful graphics wise. Two of the main features you come across very early in gameplay are the destruction physics and compound building.
1. Destruction physics: The detsruction of buildings reminds me a lot of "Red Faction: Guerilla" and it's GeoMod engine. When a catapult projectile is dropped on a building, it will crack and shoot dust up. When a catapult projectile is charged up and launched, it does major damage. When a full building block (or a whole building itself) is dropped on a building, it is just turned to rubble. The destruction is solid and satisfying to cause.
2. Compound building: This is a feature I hope gets implimented into SE. I am positive it will. Here's what it does: Let's say the whole in-game building system is on a grid of 1x1x1 cubes (let's call it a unit). So 1 block of stone is a whole unit, 1 stairs block is 1 unit and so on. Well, If you have walls that are placed to the edge of the unit, then you could not place 2 walls to make a corner in a 1 block unit. With compund building, you can. So you can do it with almost any block.
Now, PROS and CONS:
Pros:
1. Gameplay: Solid, smooth and fun. Pretty straight forward. 10/10
2. Graphics: The worlds are beautiful and very scenic. Even the buildings themselves and the medieval textures are very realistic and quite spot on. There is 1 bug where placing multiple blocks in 1 slot makes textures glitch in the spot that the material overlaps. But not too big of a deal. 9.8/10
3. Building: The building is solid and fun. Easy to do, but takes some getting used to. 9.8/10
4. Controls: There are alot of controls to learn and shortcuts to master, but it is not too hard to get a grip on. 9.5/10
5. Complexity/simplicity balance: One thing I look at in any building/crafting game is how simple it can be for simple people, while also being ABLE to be very complex for very creative people if they so choose. This game does it. You can simply build houses, or use medieval machinery to build crazy contraptions quickly and actually quite easliy, and of course there will updates and optimizations. 10/10
Cons
1. *YOU CAN IGNORE THIS ONE FOR NOW; VERY EARLY ACCESS GAME* Not very much content, so if that is what you are looking for, you should wait a few weeks, months maybe.
2. Map size: As far as I can tell, the maps are not very large, and are not procedurally generated. HOWEVER this might (and probably will) change in the future.
TL;DR
Very good game with solid gameplay, beautiful graphics, a lot of controls but easy to use, and smooth overall. Not many cons other than the map size. Very early access so there isn't much content yet, however, I recommend this game for sure.
I hope this review helped you make a decision. :)

Grimrock plays like Eye of the Beholder with better graphics and actual depth of field. If you liked EotB, that's a good thing. If you hated it (or have no idea what EotB even is), this game is PROBABLY not for you. It doesn't feel like a modern game. It feels like an upscaled version of a game from the DOS era. The puzzles are vague and cryptic, there are no "directional arrows" pointing you where to go, very few map notations, you have to memorize (or write down) spells and recipes, and your supply of... everything is limited. If you do stupid things, you will die.
The good stuff in the game is obvious (and I've mentioned some of it). There's challenging puzzles, the ambient noises are useful (you'll want good, bi-aural headphones), the classes/builds allow for enough flexibility to build the way you want, the magic system is great, the tileset is pretty, and the controls are sharp. Combat actually feels dangerous, and requires you to be aware of your surroundings at all times. It's exactly what you would expect from a well-reviewed game in the same format as EotB.
I really enjoyed Grimrock, but it's not without flaws. The enemy AI is bad. Really, really bad. You can kite everything. It's practically required at points (and therefore I'm fairly certain it's an intentional "feature"), but it feels and looks really stupid to dance around a 2x2 square stabbing wildly whenever the enemy walks into your line of sight. Some of the hidden switches (those specific to getting treasure, NOT clearing the floors) are very hard to find. It's not a bad thing necessarily, but if you want to get the best gear you'll likely need a guide. Inventory management is cumbersome, because you cannot have more than one character's bag open at a time. Before you begin, you don't know what kind of gear you're going to find, meaning you can dump a bunch of early points into, say, Armour on your Fighter, but not have any heavy armour to take advantage of it. This problem is particularly bad for mages, who rely on you finding hidden scrolls to learn new spells (or cheating and looking them up online...), and can have 20 points invested in a tree they only have the first couple spells for. You're never sure if you missed the scrolls, or if they're just further along. There are some weird things with items, too. Occasionally you won't pick up an arrow you fired, leaving you to go hunting for it after the battle (not fun). You can't use a mortar and pestle from inside a container, meaning all your Alchemy materials have to stay in a character's inventory (10+ bottles, 6 reagants, and the Mortar takes up about half that guy's bag). You find weird things all over, some of which you will want later and some of which are just garbage. It's impossible to know which ones are critical to your mission (or hunt for treasure), though, because there isn't any tagging. And it's not like the game ASKS for this sword you found to be in your inventory. There's no prompt saying "No entry without sword." It's a silent check that you either pass or fail, and without a guide you might never know it was even there.
You'll notice none of the issues I had with the game are anything close to being "game-breaking." They're just minor, quality of life things (and most of them are things that, if changed, would dramatically decrease how difficult the game is). It really is incredibly well polished, especially for an indie game.
If you're curious, I'd put the game at about 20 hours in length if you go exploring. It's far easier than EotB, both because the updated graphics give you better depth perception and because it has a built-in map+healing crystals. It's still challenging, though, it's fairly priced, and although not without flaws I would recommend Grimrock to anyone who likes old-school CRPGs. Just be sure to read the manual before you start, and always keep an extra torch or five handy. You never know when you'll need them.
