Call of duty series is a huge franchise of war games spawning from WW2 games to depictions of fantasy modern era war, and later version dealing with future tech. This game is obviously taking place in the moder war era but the question is it a good game. I will be reviewing modern warfare 2 with a pro/ con style and ending with my conclusion.
Pro:
The single player has an amazing story. The story is a thrill to play and has some very "edgy" moments that at the time was controversal but I appriciate that they didnt patch it out. It made the bad guys more of a reason to hate and was no joke a fun mission to do. The rest of the game the player changes characters from SAS and rangers, each character plays a pivital role in the story and do not feel like a generic soldier.
Amazing music. The game has some very emotional and fitting music in the game. I can not say much but it is definantly worth listening to, thank you hanz zimmerman.
Graphics look amazing. The visuals are very breath taking from the a snow storm to a gernade explosion. The particles the game has add to the immersion, like the leaves falling or the wind blowing up trash or debris from a wreckage. Character models look pretty good, especially in cutscenes.
The spec ops bonus mode is fun to play. To the addition to modern warfare series is the addition of the spec ops mode. They are challenges that take experiences from the main game and test players skills. Depending on what difficulty or how fast completed, depends on what star ammount the player earns. The stars are used to unlock additional tiers of spec ops mode which get harder the further gone. Also some spec ops mission are coop only so those are best played with friends since communication is key to success especially on veteran difficulty.
Con:
Multiplayer is awful. Since the graphics are so amazing, this can be a distraction. The enemies regardless if they are wearing sniper cammo blend in very well with the graphics because they share the same color scheme. Yes it makes sense in a war but it can lead to many deaths that could be avoided. To add to that, the game has many many hackers. Thats to be expected but it is a disapointment that the multiplayer is still active and no matter what lobby I am in, the experience suffers because hackers kill indefinantly. I got 5 hours on multiplayer and had no fun besides doing a private match with a friend. That leads me to my next issue with the multiplayer, the private matches. Its not fun to go to a private match and not have the ability to goof off with friends like in black ops 2 or black ops 1. The guns and attachments you earned in the multiplayer transfers over to the private match. This cripples the experience with friends because it forces everyone to play the multiplayer to earn their gear and go to private matches to have fun with 1v1 snipers or just combining guns to just have a good time.
Conclusion:
The game is good, that i will admit with all the pros i did mention above but the fun to be had with friends is very limited. All the spec ops mission can be done in coop but only a few are manditory coop. The story was a blast to do from start to finish and veteran proved to be quite a challenge. If i want to be honest i can not reccommend the game to anyone. The reason for that is the content for any gamer is so small. If single player is what your looking for than  all the campaign is available and most spec ops is available but most people that do call of duty do it for the multiplayer and here at this time it is broken. Spec ops is the only real multiplayer experience worth having since the multiplayer mode is full of hackers and doing private matches with friends leads to disappointment for the only thing that can be used is the pre made classes. The starting pre made classes are just 3 and the other 2 are unlocked later after leveling up a specific ammount. So in order to have fun with friends everyone needs to go into the multiplayer mode and play online matches to earn the gear that they want to use with friends. Such a grand idea fails to add enjoyment to the game and will cause players to put down the game sooner than they expected. Even if there was a combat training to level up in a private matches separate than online level ups similar to black ops 1, then I would be ok with that. That is not the case and being forced to play a broken online mode to get slaughter by hackers all the time...no thanks.

I was interested if this COD will be fun and playable like it was almost 10 years ago. I am not a big fan of the latest games from this franchise, but back at the day - I was having a blast playing this game. And guess what? It still rocks.
SP campaign is a high-octane rollercoaster ride and it still feels like you are a starring role in some Hollywood action blockbuster movie. Full of special effects, slow-mo scenes, vehicle driving, and stealth missions and of course tons and tons of great shooting - the gameplay delivers that well known COD look, feel and play. It can be overwhelming at times, but that is what you can expect from these games.
Spec Ops are a welcomed addition to the game, as the challenges will be taken a step further. They are designed in that way, that you will always crave for more of them, and kept pushing yourself to be a bit more precise, faster and smarter.
MP is the foundation of this game, as it is polished to the max, but still stripped from those things that ruined many (but not all) of the COD titles that followed this one. And the best part - people are still actively playing it!
All in all - this package is one of the finest packages that you can find if you are an FPS player. Well worth the money, even after all these years.

I wish I could recommend this game. I loved "Bastion" and I really tried to like Transistor, but it's just not nearly as good.
The biggest issue is the story. It's way too vague and confusing to make heads or tails. The motives of the characters are unclear and so is the whole setting and what's happening around.
How are you supposed to care about anything if the game doesn't give you enough information to begin with? However that's not the only problem. If you want to gather even the flimsiest of hints about the story, you have to switch the ability positions (and therefore their effect). That may sound innovative at first, but in truth it just prevents you from having any working combination at all for most of the time.
Speaking of abilities: If you happen to lose, the fight will just continue but the game locks one of your very few skills until you get to the next save point. And having to fight (and win) with your main ability disabled is... just as fun as it sounds: annoying.
With the story and battle system ruled out, what's left of the game? A decent running time (didn't feel short), nice music and a good "narrator" doing the commentary. At the bottom line it's not much and even though I bought it on discount, I feel like both my money and time were wasted.

Transistor is the SIGNS to Bastion's Sixth Sense. It's the part in the developers library where you start to think maybe they don't fully understand what made their masterpeice so good.
I'm writing this in hindsight from after the launch of Pyre, another game that had beauty but little substance, which I'm starting to worry is what Supergiant's Legacy will be. Transistor had a huge pedigree to live up to, and it flatly did not, does not, and time hasn't exactly softened those edges.
I'd like to explain Transistor's story, but it disappears up it's own bum so quickly that it I'd need shoulder-length rubber gloves to retrieve it. It's not as bad as say, Bioshock Infinite, but Transistor prefers the 'Explain Nothing, let the audience figure it out' method of storytelling. I don't think I'm an idiot, but when you make a world where everyone may or may not be a computer simulation, a digital soul, or just people living in a Cyberpunk nightmare, something more descriptive than "There's a magic sword that eats souls, also it looks like a computer chip, go stick it in the mafia' might have helped.
This is something they fixed in Pyre, which goes the exact opposite direction of explaining EVERYTHING, and doing it well, so Supergiant is learning.
Let's be frank, Supergiant nailed Isometric combat in Bastion, and they've spent the rest of their development career trying to appologise for it. Combat in Transitor is a weird Turn-Based Action Hybrid that sounds like the final fantasy ATB system, but in effect plays more like the combat version of Regenerating Health. You have an action bar that you can use to unleash a Planned Attack, which involves you rushing up to the enemy, dumping your best attacks in their face, and then retreating until it recharges. You CAN fight them conventionally, but the enemies are "Really Goddamn Dangerous" and if you get hit it drains your Action Bar, and if you're action bar is depeleted, you lose attacks, which tends to snowball.
I was not a fan.
So why leave it recommended?
Well, there's the sword, you see? And it has a voice like the saddest 1920's trumpet player in history, and he names the enemies cute names and he's trying to rekindle his relationship with his ex-girlfriend / wielder and...
Look, Transistor isn't necessarily fun, lucid, or fully realised. But it has heart. It has all the hallmarks of some mad genius who had an idea stuck in his brain and vomited it into digital smoke and code. There's a value in that. There's a value in seeing what you can do if you're willing to just go for broke and make exactly what you want.
Just...get it on sale.

Badly designed junk.
For a game as obsessed with looking cool and precise manipulation as this one is, it has to have a better camera and control scheme to work.
The controls seem to want the micro-second pixel-by-pixel precision of classic arcade games, but the engine has response lag and the controls are way too sloppy to do things in less than one character height. The auto-target is ... bad is the only word, constantly locking onto things off screen instead of the foe centered in your view. The controls can only be adjusted before you start playing, and the tooltips in game use the default control scheme anyway.
The camera is a kludgy mess. It pans around randomly, does not line up for you to be aware of the bottomless pit you're about to step into, and refuses to follow enemies even during boss fights. Boss fights get their own camera angle, altering the basic camera behavior from "behind the character" to "cinematic overview", without adjusting the control scheme for the altered perspective.
Fights with large foes will suddenly become quick time events for "cool kills". Unfortunately, you're so busy with the timing that you can't appreciate the cool thing you're supposed to be doing. Thus, these "cool moments" exist in my memory as random button icons flashing on a screen.
The story is bland, and spoiled by the "sat on main menu too long" in-game trailer.
The characters are shallow and predictable.
Bosses randomly, and with no indication of when, become invincible while fighting. This seems to last for three to five seconds, and is most common when the player begins to get a series of successful attacks chained together.
TL;DR: Bad. Don't buy it. If you get it for free, don't install it.

Ok,so. It's not bad. If anything,I'd say the game is very basic. It has all the basics of a Mega Man game. It is a Mega Man game. Apparently a lot of people forgot Mega Man X7 is also a Mega Man game. I'd also like to point out this is the same series that gave us Zero's infamous freak out after killing Iris. So I really don't know what these people were expecting when they booted up today.
Bare in mind I'm playing this after apparently 4 updates were released today,so it may be different from earlier reviews.
The game play is pretty solid. You shoot enemies and dash through them to get their power ups. If you don't care about the power ups,you can just keep shooting them til they drop. It's not a difficult mechanic to use and it's ok. I prefer the random drop method of the old MM games,but that's me. It reminds me of Axel's copy ability in MMX7. It wasn't that great then either. In the end,it's not the best MM game,but then,Inafune's company isn't going to have the resources of Capcom in it's heyday.
The levels aren't anything special. They serve their purpose,they offer a challenge,but it's not the best design. But then,once again,the level design was falling off in the more recent MM games too. So I don't know what people were expecting.

This is an exceptionally well designed and finely tuned game. It feels like caftsmanship, like somebody laboured and tinkered away in a garage for years, getting every bit just right. Shortly before going fullscreen the window says 'build 4410'. I take that to mean 4409 RCs went before this one.
The control scheme is complex but not complicated. There are a lot of tricks to pull off but they mostly work by building on top of the basic setups. So failing at something grand will usually result in pulling off something simple, thus keeping you going rather than interrupting your flow. Most of all it just feels right: There is a satisying sense of connection between what your character is doing and what you're doing. Slam down the analog stick and the board slams down on a grinding surface.
The gameplay is tight and eextremely skillbased. I'm 10 hours in and I suck at it, doing 20k combos where others count them in the millions. Still, it's never throw-your-controller-away frustrating because it's easy to see how improvements come with practice and a restart is one button push away.
The music is gorgeous. Intense at times - cue the trailer - but mostly laidback. It's really good for getting in to the flow where splitsecond decisions are something you can do lazily and take your time about.

Choice of Robots (CoR) is possibly the best interactive novel I've ever read.
The description is pretty much self explanatory, but it's so much more.  This is a very well written novel in seven chapters, and while similar things happen during these seven stages, exactly what happens and how it interacts with later chapters is entirely up to you.  When they say the choice (and consequences) are yours, they mean it.
You might not expect much replay out of an interactive novel - certainly I didn't.  Well, I'm currently in my third playthrough.  Again, the core events happen, but exactly how and what comes as a result is entirely up to you.  The endgame for the two complete playthroughs so far were very different.
Do you want to be the 'bad guy' and, as the ad says, try to take over Alaska?  Do you want to try and launch a golden age with robots and humans side by side?  You can do both, or neither.  Each choice you make has the opportunity to lock or unlock certain issues, and how you handle these issues directly affects how your robots turn out.
The writing is top of the line:  The author is obviously well versed in the English language.  After awhile you forget you're playing a game and think you're just reading a novel.

As child of the 80's, I enjoyed the Choose Your Own Adventure, D&D solo books, and the other one called Lone Wolf I think it was. I will be checking out the other titles from Choice of Games that are rated high for more choices and nonlinear storylines!

It's got potential but do realize it is early access and an alpha.  If you can't handle incomplete games with glitches and bugs -- look elsewhere.
Potential is nice - StarForge had mass potential and so have many other games.  Some reach it, others don't so go in knowing the risks and judge it based upon it's current state for playability -and- your willingness to risk based upon that potential.
A list of things to look at:
- The skill-point system only works multi-player so you won't skill up in single player.
- Multiplayer you will end up against leveled up oponents and those levels have meaning and high value.  Lots and lots of value to being leveled up here.
- Gathering requires hacking a harvester which then can take quite a while to gather things - you can't harvest anything.
- to get that hacking device you must find it.
- Robot NPC's drop nothing.  You need to hunt through ruins to find weapons, ammo and other supplies.
- ammo is fairly scarce for the quantity of robots you'll bump into - again, no points for dealing with AI opponents.  You're best bet is to run/aviod them.
- robots can pop up at any point near or far.  They have been toned down to 2 shots to kill you but that's the best you'll get.
- AI robots cannot aim upwards.  If you are above them, they can't hit you with their weapons -- if at range and above, they can and will hit you.
- AI robots can walk through walls that you build.  So if you build, make the building tall and use stairs to get up there.
- You need to find power for your unit - not those silly solar cells but nuclear power.  Without it, you won't be able to power up the capacitor to run, jump, etc.  Extra capacitors are good but you shouldn't need too many of them.
- picking up anything early will stop your running.  Anything except a nuclear power units.  The solar power cells weigh a ton for the energy they give, which slows you down.
- many items are sunk in the ground and other items - you'll see loot markers but can't loot the item nor even know what it is.
Again, it's got potential but that potential has a long way to go to be achieved.  IMO - worth supporting with funds but don't expect a highly clean and polished version at this time.

Frankly, I don't understand all the hate. This game has great core mechanics. I'm not experiencing any of the issues other people are, such as lag. And, shocker, I don't mind the graphics. Frankly, most of the negative reviews I've heard and seen online sound more like people wanted a blatant copy of the original Megaman games and would have never been satisfied with anything else. The voice acting is fine. The graphics are not distracting or all over the place, and you can't tell me the graphics were any better on the original Megaman games. While others have mentioned bugs in their copies, I have yet to encounter any.
This game reminds me of playing the originals as a young kid gripping the controls in anger as I die for the millionth time and the satisfaction of finally timing everything right to beat the level. If that's what you're looking for, like I was, then this game is for you.
If you somehow wanted a game with Megaman that involved a "plot" beyond a contrived reason to kill and steal the powers of several different robots, you clearly are not familiar with the Megaman games to which this is the "spiritual" successor. This is reminiscent of the original games that were nearly impossible to complete without putting in days if not weeks to complete the game. The bosses are unforgiving if you mess up, and the levels are challenging to navigate. You die at a similar rate to Dark Souls and its related games. Like I said, this takes me back to the times I played my SNES copies of the Megaman games. I have to recommend it for bringing out the inner child that wants to throw a controller against the wall because I died to the same spike trap for half an hour.

Backed the game in 2013. Definitely regret it now. For all the delays, its made little to no progress since the backer demo last year. The level design is messy and the environments seem very empty.
There's just so much bad that happened in the development plus the assorted technical issues present on all versions (hard crashing wiius, bricking some wii u storage devices), delayed 360 version, delayed 3ds version. Hell even the soundtrack is delayed. Plus the digital extras I should get for backing are missing.
Honestly the only decent part of the game is Ray's DLC and even then its only reaching somewhat decent.
Level design aspect is really hard to dissect but it doesn't feel right. The repeated air dashing doesn't feel right and seems generally unnatural. There are basically no secrets or reason to explore. If you don't have the red xell power from enemies, fighting a group of them is a ridiculous chore due to them being bullet spongey and needing to dash into them to finish them off. Bosses generally seem poorly designed as well, such as the water boss that is basically untouchable most of the time (doing this as Ray kinda sucks since your life is ticking down as they time scam) and also the fire boss that legitimately just pulls out an instant death move from nowhere.
Overall the mechanics, level designs, and bosses all just come together in a way that is very unappealing and without much flow. It just feels very off as a result. The lack of secrets is kind of annoying. Even the very first Megaman game had the secret in Elecman's stage that allowed you to create platforms to walk on and every Megaman after that kept adding more and more stuff to find. But this game is incredibly vanilla and leaves no impact

Also lets not forget about the one advertised mechanic that got cut due to tight budget where Beck was supposed to be able to actually absorb enemies and get new abilities as a result, not just stat buffs, kind of like Axel did in X7 and X8.
Overall I feel like too many people on the forum are trying to discredit negative opinions of the game by saying "Its like Megaman! Megaman is hard and had instant death spike!" etc. If you think that its fine. But its also possible for it to be like Megaman in some way and different from it others. I remember when I played it years ago... Many years ago. At the time I didn't like it, it hadn't the feel of the first two "Encounters" but now, after years I can say that... Nothing changed. I just don't like it...
Serious Sam 2 is an FPS, the simple kind of FPS where you face waves and hordes of enemies before you move to the next area. This is a classic feature of this franchise, together with the humour given by silly situations, small oddities hidden in levels and the dumb comments from the protagonist, Sam "Serious" Stone. This formula is a classic, already seen in games like Duke Nukem and (in minor way) Shadow warrior, So the first two encounters were praised for its old school mind-free structure and the humour inspired by the above-mentioned classics. So there is much to be expected from a 2nd chapter like this, and actually it IS based on the structure of the first 2 encounters, so we have again hordes of silly enemies, humour and an enormous arsenal with an enormous amount of ammo to unleash on the waves of enemies.
Then why I didn't like it... Again? Honestly, I don't know what to say, I see many people around liking it, but I just can't. Somehow it's the feeling like this isn't serious sam anymore, or maybe it's too much serious sam. Walking around levels I can recognize another classic feature of Croteam's work, so ambience are well done, and you can run into nice landscapes and so on. But some levels are simply odd. They're trying to be some kind of "funny odd", I dont' know. Not to mention the "story" with those 3 "sirians" calling you for help against mental's forces. At the beginning and end of every level there's a cutscene with them or with Sam in the current level and yes, sometimes they're funny, but they often are trying Too much. Same with enemies, trying too much with too many differnet kind of overly-spoofed enemies. And I acknowledge that we're visiting other planets, so obviously there MUST be a variety of "species", but... I don't know they're quite cartoonish... But considering it's serious sam and the design of the prevous encounters I should say they're TOO cartoonish.
I must say one thing about weapons. Beside the fact that I forgot to mention the presence of turrets and other weaponized vehicles (which in my opinion are both a useful introduction) I have to say something about shotguns. Am I the only one to find those weapons (single and double) to behave quite awkward? They're supposed to have a wider impact on longer distances, so I always try to shoot more enemies at once with shotguns. Hell, I'm expecting to kill more at once with them (like I usually do in other games), yet they almost work like a gun... Totally disappointing, considering it's one of the weapons I use the most...
Music is nice, But it doesn't kick♥♥♥♥♥like the first encounters (in fact one of the boss tracks is from the second encounter...).
And everything I said, all the problems or differences mentioned are completely gone in Serious Sam 3:
- Old enemies back? Check
- Old weapons back? Check
- Levels with a great level design, and no pastel colours or other dumb stuff? Check
- REALLY Epic music And BADASS HEAVY Boss Music? Check
- More Balanced Humour? Well, almost check, SS3 is quite more serious (with sarcasm and humour, but... Whatever, this is a SS2 review...)
So this makes me think that also the developers quite agree with the points I've mentioned. And if they did it's because the community reacted on those matters. Then why does Steam lists many good reviews? I have no idea, only GabeN could shine us with his knowledge, but I can guess that's because SS2 it's not a bad game Per se but it's just a Game trying too much to be a Serious Sam Game (I said too many times Game, I know, but I wanted to make a point...), and this is my reason I can't recommend this game.

TurnOn is an extremely adorable platformer without platforms. Following a blackout event, an “alien creature” traverses through electrical lines in an effort to bring light to those who need it most. Child-friendly gameplay, cute aesthetics and visual storytelling elements make this game a truly relaxing ride through Electro City.
Professor Brain needs help following an accident at the power station in Electro City, so he employs a cuddly alien creature (spark). The player controls this spark in an effort to bring electricity back into homes, activate failed generators, and maintain order throughout the shambling city.
There are lots of easy achievements that promote exploration of the many levels in TurnOn, including: an achievement for turning on 3 lamps for each level, an achievement for lighting up X in each level, etc. Animated comics, along with NPC actions throughout gameplay, provide immersive visual storytelling along with insight on upcoming levels.
In this platformer without platforms, the player traverses through electrical lines in order to progress. Many familiar platforming elements are utilized, such as: jumping/falling, hazardous objects, hidden pathways/alternate routes, collectibles (lightning), checkpoints, and a lethal fall (the ground). Even though TurnOn is a 2D platformer, its artistic use of multiple platforming depths/layers and multi-linear progression makes it feel almost like a 2.5D platformer.
Most of the deaths in TurnOn stem from missing a line/jump and falling to the ground. Every now and then, hazardous objects or an enemy (drone) will attribute to it, but this is a very friendly/casual game so that’s generally not the case. You can die from falling as many times as you need, without any penalty, and restart from a checkpoint. Any previously acquired lightning will remain in your possession. Specific objects, however, will hurt the spark’s health (denoted by 3 green lightning bolts); these are red lightning bolts (collectibles) or enemies. If the spark loses all of its health, the level will restart, and all collectibles will be returned. Green lightning bolts can be collected to recover lost health.
One of TurnOn’s most challenging, yet most exhilarating, elements is with its use of runner levels. On these levels, the screen and spark will progress forwards at an uncontrolled pace. Often times these runner levels are themed and present many active animations. A major aspect that makes me love these levels is with its great harmonization with the music. You will find yourself jumping and falling to the melody and beat changes (adds a lot of joy and promotes immersion).
Even though I personally enjoy the runner levels, the other platforming levels also provide a great deal of fun with its visual cues. Each level is themed, and often times, the spark will have a specific goal: guide the little girl back home by lighting up the street, scare away burglars by repowering alarms, revive a household’s energy consumption, etc. This variation in level design and immersion through effortless storytelling helps keep the player compelled to continue playing.
The controls for TurnOn is very simplistic; 1D movement, jump, and fall. Although the controls, by default, are sufficient for gameplay when using a controller or M&K, there is no support for rebinding controller/keyboard buttons. This shouldn’t be too big of an issue as precision handling is not required, but many platformer veterans may want to be aware of this.
The developers of the game seem to be very active with regards to player support and update frequency, as seen in the Discussions board and News updates. After only 5 days of release, a major patch was implemented to take Let’s Plays and Review feedback into consideration. Details of the patch can be seen
.
Even though TurnOn is fairly polished, there are a couple suggestions that may improve gameplay; these are listed below.
TurnOn is a very relaxing and addictively fun product. Its cute aesthetics, visual storytelling and harmonic runner levels earn it a recommendation for any fan of platformers or child-friendly/casual games.

Wow this game was a breath of fresh air!
Not the usual hack and slash or breeze through the park that you normally get with these types of games.
Getting to the heart of it, Jotun is a little bit like Shadow of Colossus, but the intensity has been broken up with sections of exploration and puzzles. Some of these levels even involve no combat (I did not mind this as it brought a nice change of pace).
The hand drawn art/animation art style is worth playing this game for alone and is good proof that you don't need shiny graphics to make something look epic!
Of course the music is just as grand, after all Jotun is about Norse Mythology!
The voiceovers in Icelandic really really help set the scene and aid in the story.
The boss design is where this game really excels and I say with confidence they are some of the best I've ever seen in a video game, not to mention that they’re a tough challenge! On each occasion you have to figure out how to take down a giant with just an axe and some abilities you found along the way…but that moment of satisfaction when you finally take them down is amazing!
The only thing I could fault is perhaps the ending. Without going into spoilers, I was expecting something more, longer and larger for all that work you put in.
Nevertheless, Jotun was a hidden treasure and really glad I played it!
The gods should be impressed with this game!

So yeah Jotun is an action/adventure game with a slow character. It's disturbing at first.
But, once you are used to it, the game is actually great !
Great musics, great voice acting, gorgeous artwork, the game really sets the mood right.
Then the boss battles... It's the biggest feature the game has and it's delivering it right !
There is two big parts : exploration and boss fighting.
- Exploration areas won't features a lot of fighting (in most of them you won't encounter any enemies). You will collect runes to open portal to get to the boss battle. Each exploration areas will teach you new mecanics used by the boss they give access. Some of those areas can be a bit too big and with a slow character it can be a bit annoying (one is mainly too big for what it has to offer... but it's really my only gripe with the game, it shouldn't stop you from playing it !).
You'll collect god powers in those areas too. Those will enhance your character and give you special abilities like healing, shielding, etc...
- Boss battles are really epic, with a good balance of difficulty and are very very very well designed. You can do them again once you have killed them and try some epic challenges like killing one without taking any damage ! :D
Achievements can appear pointless for most of us (I personnaly like them xD), but those really show how the battles are well designed, and are worth trying.
TL;DR :
- Great game very well polished, with epic boss battles.
- A character a bit too slow while exploring BUT you'll get used to it and it won't matter in the end :)
- Good difficulty and balance overall.
- The game has some replayability if you enjoy challlenges !
- Totally worth the price.
For those who are asking themselves : no it's nothing like Shadow of the Colossus.
I won't go into details, so let's just say the feeling is totally different and if you look for a SotC 2 you might get disapointed. Anyway, I enjoyed SotC and I enjoy Jotun !

Let's get this out of the way: This game is not even remotely close to being in a state that meets the expectations you might have after watching the video trailers. You are extremely limited in what you can do at this time.
Essentially, you only have 'creative mode' available to you at this moment, but if Keen updates this with the same pacing and quality of Space Engineers, then you can expect frequent and awesome changes to come hard and fast.
DAY 1 Pros:
-Textures (even if placeholders) are beautiful and rich. The forest landscape reminds me of Elder Scrolls Oblivion.
-DirectX 11 and multithreading offer stability and  terrific multiplayer opportunities down the road.
-Destruction is very well designed and the physics seems solid.
Day 1 Cons:
-If the projectiles are the same mass and velocity to the eventual siege weapons, then stone walls will need to be a lot more durable, because right now they seem to be as strong as cardboard.
-No multiplayer or survival at day one. This is expected, but I just want it to be obvious if you are going to buy the game based on that.
-A distinct lack of goats.
Summary: Game has extremely high amounts of potential and is already fun to tinker about inside the world. Software company that makes it is very considerate of their players and will update frequently and deliver.

When I firstly launched the world, I felt like I have just appeared in the Medieval Era. The nicest medieval music and nice grassy plain met me with happiness and temptation. Then, turning left 135 degrees, I saw a house. I walked to it and sat inside, feeling really cozy. Although, then I saw big projectile in my belt. Of course, it is really obvious what to do. I saw how to control those in a really friendly presented tutorial. So, I walked out from that cozy 15th century house and picked up my projectile and BOOOM. The house is to the ground. Great havoc-ish damage physics - KSH always deals with those damage physics, in all their recent games.
Okay, I wanted to build a castle like this Neuschwanstein one. I found a mountain, terraformed a bit of ground for the keep and started building. I made a nice guard tower, which fromed so SOFTLY and INTUITIVE, which I can't say for some games, even, sometimes, Space Engineers. I copied the tower, although, it took me a big bite of my time to mess around with copying and pasting it. I couldn't rotate it. Although, I am going to close my eyes on ot - it's a magnificent alpha.
So, I saw another problem - maybe I am doing something wrong, or don't know how to do it. But I built my towers sideways to the "voxel grid". I would need to build my walls the wacked way. *Sadface:(*
So, let's see, what is positive, and negative about this game.
+++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++
1. Nice, Fluid and intuitive building system.
2. Nice graphics. Not the best, but they are good for the game of this type.
3. MAGNIFICENT damage physics, and structual integrity.
4. Mechanical elements. And weapons, that you build yourself, which means, that if you are in multiplayer, better you build your Trebushetes ( or smth. ), the better you will siege.
-----------------------------------------------------------------
1. Sometimes crashes. You can drop this off, because it's an early acces game.
2. Hard terradorming. You need to get your hands dirty and whack for a little bit, before building.
3. Sometimes, whacky movement/dissy camera. Well, that is the problem of all the games from KSH.
Just deal with it.
Although, I give this game a good 8,5/10. It's a great game with big potential.

What a ♥♥♥♥ing disappointment this game is. The gameplay is absolutely tedious. The dashing mechanic is so half-baked, especially for a genre where we've been taught to shoot as a distance and dash after the enemy is dead. The English voice acting is dreadful - do yourself a favor and switch it to Japanese. The script is totally different in Japanese; I'm not sure why the English script is in the shape that it is, but whomever "translated" it sure as hell thought they were funny/clever. It's really no better than "anime fan on prom night" in terms of writing. I'm serious. It's bad. It's worse that the English voice acting is atrocious.
This game would have benefited from dropping the lame♥♥♥♥♥dash mechanic, but there's a lot of other strange design choices as well. Why can Beck grab on some ledges, but not on others? I'm assuming to prolong the game with cheap deaths, since there's no reason to teach players to grab ledges and then miraculously kill themselves thinking they have this ability.
I can't even pain myself to get through a level. It's just... all the excitement has been sucked out of this game. It's been delayed for so long, it's still buggy as hell (stuck on ledges with ice, etc), runs poorly and looks flat. This would be okay if the game was at least fun, but the very goal of the game, dashing through stuff, is just so cumbersome that I'm not sure if I'll be able to make it through this game without mind-altering substances to make it palatable. Seriously, who's idea was it to have a game where you have to dash through enemies after shooting them, but not allow you to shoot and dash at the same time? Even Mega Man X could dash and shoot at the same time, but you're telling me Comcept devised a game around the "revolutionary" mechanic circa 1991 and omitted something that would make it slightly more enjoyable? Unbelievable.
I'm not sure if I'll be able to slog through this game, but I'm going to try considering the cash I dropped on it (and lack of return policy on Kickstarter). Don't be like me, though. Don't spend $20 (or any amount of money) on this game. This isn't a spiritual successor. This is straight up coat-tail riding in game form. I was quickly taken in by TurnOn. It bills itself as a platformer without platforms, and while that’s not strictly true, there's a focus on exploration and puzzle solving that the genre isn’t especially noted for. It’s a game about restoring power to a darkened city, which you do by moving a grinning alien spark around power lines until it’s able to reactivate circuit boards and power grids.
There’s a kind of understated plot behind it all, dealing with aliens made of electricity, but it’s all kind of nonsensical. And that’s okay, because it makes it no less adorable. Exploring a world draped in darkness and reactivating the lights is strangely satisfying. Most levels are very laid back affairs, asking you to explore until you meet certain criteria, such as saving a girl walking home alone from an angry dog, or uniting two lovers at their favourite restaurant by clearing their way. What was once something as simple as turning on lights slowly dials up in complexity. You might have to activate cranes to drop metal platforms across pits, or reactivate traffic lights to clear massive congestion.

UPDATE: I have now gotten to the final boss of the game.  My recommendation not to buy this game has not changed.  Rather, it has only strenghtened as more problems arouse.  I was going to write about those as well, but apparently there's a character limit and I can't.  Oh well.  Avoid this game.
Original review is below:
NOTE: I did not beat this game.
I did not beat this game because I got sick of the terrible level design and the incredibly cheap, frustrating bosses.  I played through levels that are brimming with instant kill death traps, which is frustrating because Beck slips and slides around after a dash and it's really easy to die.  I played through levels with bad enemy placement that doesn't mesh well with the "dash into enemies to finish them off" game mechanic (why would I want to dash towards an enemy hanging over a pit or death trap?).
The combat in this game is not fun.  You shoot enemies a few times and they change color, and then you dash into them to finish them off.  If you don't want to dash into them, but still need to get them out of your way, you can keep hammering on the fire button and eventually they'll die that way.  The problem as mentioned above is a lot of the enemy placement is poor, and you'll find enemies in places that you don't want to dash too.  Often times it's easier to shoot an enemy until it changes color and then just move on.
Beck's movement is also not fun.  You can dash and you can grab ledges.  You can dash several times in a row to get over large gaps if you need too.  However, you can't climb on walls or do anything else to get more vertical movement than just a regular jump.  This makes avoiding attacks, especially during boss fights, fairly frustrating.  You can hold down a modifier button and then press Jump to jump backwards or attack to jump backwards while firing bullets, but neither move is particularly useful.   You can also choose to dash towards the ground if you want, but again this did not come in handy.
The biggest problem is by far the cheap boss fights.  Many of them love to lock you in place and if you don't hammer the directional buttons or the jump button fast enough, you'll lose an insanely large amount of health.  The fire boss had attacks I could not avoid no matter how much I practiced.  He'll dash towards you and then unleash a huge explosion.  If you just jump out of the way, you get hit.  If you jump and dash once, that isn't enough to avoid the attack and you get hit.  If you jump and dash twice (assuming you can do that quickly enough), your second dash will carry you straight into the walls of the area which are on fire, and you get hit.  Other times he'll dash towards you and then jump and body slam you.  If you dash out of the way, you'll dash into the fire he left behind him before jumping.  If you dash the other way, you'll hit the column of fire against the wall.  It seems like you're just supposed to walk out of the way, but if you do that, you won't get out of the way fast enough.  You'd have to walk towards him as he dashes towards you to already be moving when he starts the jump, and then you run the risk of him just doing a dash right into you instead.
Then there's an ice boss that will freeze you and then try to crush you if you can't mash your way out of the ice in time, and after trying to crush you, the boss will float up into the air where you can't hit them.  Then it does a freeze attack that you avoid by dashing around randomly and hoping you don't get hit by it because there's no pattern or timing to it at all.  If you do manage to dodge, chances are you get stuck in a tiny space where you can't avoid getting frozen by ice balls the boss throws down, and then it immediately loops back to the trying to crush you thing.  You can get stuck in a loop of never being able to hit the boss because it's never on the ground for you to hit.  This boss also never stopped making obnoxious noises during the fight. "Wait a minute, wait a minute!" "Pew pew pew pew pew!" "(some other random mess that I'm not even sure was English)"  SHUT UP PLEASE!
The other bosses are also similarly unfair, but rather than sit here and describe each one, I'm going to move on to their annoying health bars.  Rather than just shoot the boss until it takes enough damage to die, you shoot at it until it turns purple and then it immediately starts healing itself, and you have to dash it as soon as possible to stop it from healing and make the damage you already dealt be permanent.  Of course, the boss will turn purple at the worst possible time, right before they go into some move where you can't reach them to dash into.  Then of course after you dash into the boss, you have to get away quickly before you take the classic video game "touched the enemy" damage.  From boss fights to just the regular combat on the way to bosses, the "dash into enemies to steal their Xel" mechanic just puts a huge damper on the fun.
There are other strange things about this game too, like if you die when you have a health recharge available (think an E-Tank from classic Mega Man, or a Sub Tank from Mega Man X), the game takes it away.  I started the intro stage with 2 lives, and found 2 extra lives throughout the stage and finished it with 4 lives.  When I picked another stage to play, it knocked be back down to 2 lives.  Why take away power ups and lives for no reason? It feels like the game just flat out has contempt for the player.
I even had problems with lost save data.  I played a little in the morning when I recieved my download codes, and when I came back in the afternoon, both my save data and my game options (such as screen resolution) were reset and the game acted like it was booting up for the first time.  Deleting the game and reinstalling it seems to have fixed most of this, other than the game insists on turning motion blur back on no matter how many times I turn it off.
Also, this is a really minor complaint because it wouldn't have mattered to me much if the game was fun, but the dialog and voice acting is horrendous in this game. The opening cutscene starts with a narrator proudly declaring "IT IS THE PRESENT YEAR" for no reason whatsoever. While playing through stages, you sometimes have to sit through random dialog between support characters. Cutscenes with the characters in them are also poorly well done with almost no animation, or animation done off cue.  A character will stand completely still with a big dopey grin on his face while lamenting how the fate of the entire country depends on Beck.  And when Beck hears this plan, his line is something along the lines of "Yeah, great id- Wait what?!", and he has an animation of going into a shocked pose, but the animation of him being shocked starts while he's agreeing rater than the part where his words indicate shock. But other than off cue animations like that, characters in cutscenes are stiff, just standing there, not even having any animation to make their mouths move as they talk.  Again, this is a minor thing and I wouldn't care about it too much if the game was fun, but it's not and this just stands out as another terrible design choice.
In short, it's
better than nothing.  If we had gotten nothing, I could have spent my time doing anything else, and it would have been a more enjoyable experience than playing Mighty No 9.  Instead I played this, and it left me crying like an anime fan on prom night.

is a casual, side-scrolling platformer that conveys a story through stellar audio and visual presentation without the use of words. (Except for the guides and instructions, of course)
In this game, you control an alien that takes the form of an electric ball and lead it through its journey to restore the light in Electro City.
The gameplay is pretty simple and straightforward - you traverse through electric lines/wires and apparatuses which activates and/or repairs them through contact while collecting blue lightning symbols. Each of these actions will have an impact to the score you will get upon finishing the level. Still seeing people in need through the level? Search again for hidden paths that you might've missed.
Also, you will find adversaries that might stand either your way or the people living in the city, and some of them require different mechanics in order to be cleared. Though there isn't a game over that could force you to start over, there are still some cases that may halt your progress through the game.
Falling through the lines and touching the ground will result in you being sent back to your checkpoint, but everything that you have collected are still with you, every apparatus activated, and no damage taken. However, if you exhaust your life bars (represented by the green lightning symbols on the upper left part of the screen) you will restart the level from the start.

Don't let the short play time fool you, I've actualy finished the game in offline mode.
TurnOn is one of these games that don't focus specificly on gameplay alone, but rather on the atmosphere. You are a spark which can only move between wires, which makes the game a platformer. However, because the enviroments are in 3D, you will also be moving back and front, which can cause some confusion. Another thing that bothered me a bit was the camera, which, I feel, was a bit to close in certain parts. However these are only minor gripes in an otherwise very well made game.
Your job will be helping all kinds of people and with the aid of the soothing music, it is a great combination to enjoy yourself after a long day at work/school. The game is also apropriate for younger children, however they might not be very good at it because of the previously mentioned 3D enviroments. However, that is not a big problem because it's actualy very hard to "lose" (it is possible by hitting to many red sparks or enemies). If you fall to the ground, you will simply resurrect at the checkpoint without loosing anything.
While the gameplay is fairly basic, the atmosphere is the part to enjoy. When you start a level, it's mostly dark and depressing. After running around for a bit, it slowly gets brighter and brighter and the people get more and more happy. The sequences in the form of a comic book are a nice adition too and you will be seeing them quite a lot.
To wrap things up, while the price isn't that low, I feel the game is worth it. It's not one of those competitive games to raise your adrenaline but rather a soothing and calming adventure, which often brings up a smile to your face. If only the camera was a bit further away at some points.
Final rating: 7.5

Jotun is an action adventure game set in the Norse-mythology world and viewed from an isometric 2.5D parallaxing camera. You play Thora, a Viking warrior in a quest to
(the catch-phrase of game) and enter Valhalla. To do so, she must brave nine perilous "Realms" (levels), find the secret "Runes" (keys) that will allow her to challenge five powerful "Jotun" (giants) in their lairs and defeat them to impress Odin, the Allfather of the Gods.
Jotun was developed by Canada-based Thunder Lotus Games studio and was
in mid-2014.
Each time you launch the game you start from "Ginungagap", an ethereal realm in the void between Valhalla and the physical world; no harm can find Thora in Ginungagap and you can teleport back there anytime. The Jotun realms are all directly accessible from Ginungagap and once you find the runes required to unlock the Jotun lairs, you can also access the boss-fights anytime. There is a preferred order in which you must explore the realms and challenge the Jotun and you can redo the realms & bosses anytime (without extra benefit).
Thora has a limited set of moves in her arsenal: a low-damage fast swing, a powerful but slow overhead chop and a roll/dash to dodge attacks. Exploring the nine realms, Thora can find "Ithunn's Apples" that permanently increase her max health and shrines that grant her "God Powers" used to perform special actions, e.g. restore health, move faster, hit harder etc; there is six God-powers to be found and each has 2-3 charges. Thora's health and God-power charges are fully replenished each time she visits a "Mimir's Well"; there's usually a couple of them to be found in each realm (they usually serve as auto-save checkpoints too) and one in the entrance of each Jotun lair.
The giant Jotun bosses each have a unique set of powers/weaknesses and the fights are usually split in 2-3 phases, more difficult as the boss' health decreases. In order to win those fights, you have to figure out the pattern, lay out a plan (involving careful use of Thora's limited resources) and execute it correctly. When killed you are respawned to the entrance of the Jotun lair, at full health, so you can immediately retry the battle.
The rest of the game revolves around exploring the Jotun realms to find the runes, apples and God-powers which will aid you in the boss-fights. Each of the realms has a unique Norse-mythology inspired theme (e.g. magical forest, lava-filled dungeon, frozen lake, stormy cloud-realm etc) and there's some mini-puzzles, some labyrinth-navigating and a few regular enemies to beat. Thora can die in various ways when exploring the Jotun realms, but going through them is relatively easy.
The game has beautiful hand-drawn graphics: the sprites are especially well-designed and animated but I think there's room for improvement in some of the background art; it feels like Jotun attempts to define an original style of its own but falls just a bit short of the mark! The music and SFX are nice, sometimes atmospheric and never lacking or annoying; what I mostly liked about the audio is the narrator/voice-over in Icelandic which is heard a few times in each realm/lair, when you reach a key location. The gameplay is solid, mostly revolving around the relatively hard boss fights; my only concern is that the realms you must explore before you challenge the bosses are quite easy and sometimes feel a bit empty. Don't get me wrong: I like how Jotun fuses the Norse mythology in all those "quests", but I just wish there was more to do!
I played with keyboard but a controller would probably be more appropriate. I am not really good at these games and it took me ~8 hours to complete Jotun (find all there is to be found and beat all bosses) and get ~30% of its Steam achievements. This is a well made choose your own adventure game, with loads of different paths to take and plenty of different endings to discover.
There are some interesting ideas about what it is to be human, have a soul and about what life really is. There's plenty of food for thought and after this first read through I find myself questioning what I really would have done in the situations the author presented me.
Something that bugged me is how although the game itself is fully thought out and realized, the actual writing isn't. Much of the early game was simply presenting you with choices and didn't tell much of a story. It lacked character and meaning. However (at least in my ending) the later stages of the game are far more concise and this more than makes up for the early game. Now that the author knew for sure which direction my story was going I noticed a distinct change in not only pace, but tone in the writing. It was much more drawn out, presented me with far fewer choices and was just working towards the finale, which was really something.
Some of the writing wouldn't up as a book, but the pros more than outweigh the cons. Replayability is off the charts, with at least four completely different directions the story can go, all of which have a couple of other off shoots. As long as you play it for the great philosophy and science-fiction, rather than the writing itself, you'll have a great time

Simple answer: you like story (even if it's more of a "tell" than "show" style)? You like reading? You like choices that matter? Good, you answered whether you like this game or not. Just check out the free trial if you are having a hard time deciding.
(minor spoiler)---- Robot Hitler, Check. Child becoming a Vietnam Vet, Check. Creating a world-wide technocratic utopia, Check. Become a quintillionaire pacifist who advanced robotics and green tecnologies by leaps and bounds while giving massive amounts to charity, Check.  =====(end spoiler)
And that's not even scratching the surface.
I don't know whether it's an extreme pleasure of mine to have met one of the best contenders for my "favorite game ever", right next to Star Wars Knights of the Old Republic, and Dawngate (R.I.P.), or if it's kinda sad that these modern games with ever evolving graphics just don't give me the kind of satisfaction that this game does.
The most major thing in this for me: your choices matter, sometimes extremely significantly...like, changing whole chapters significantly.
(Spoilers)=== You could be stupid and attack the FBI with 0 military stat...and be thrown in jail, and that's the rest of the chapter compltetely changed. In my Technocratic, pacifistic utopia, the ENTIRE chapter 6 was rewritten. ===(end of spoilers)
I don't want to overhype this, but it's pretty damned compelling, and the connections between choices are made simultaneously clear...yet blurred, if that makes sense. You feel like something you did influenced it, but at the same time, it could pass for generic material, which I think is very intriguing.
Not to mention, when I chose one of the endings, at the beginning, I noticed stuff...missing. Particularly stuff that included...like...i dunno...the statue of freaking liberty! It wasn't there in my second play through. Like, that was actually a good chunk of the story in my first play through. I am really intrigued whether that was because I wasn't stressed enough to cause it (kept military too low), or if that entire sequence with Alaska was ending(beginning)-specific, or what. It's amazing.

I loved Bastion, but compared to it Transistor is just kinda "ehh" to me.
As we all know, the artstyle is unique and well done. That's a definite plus. The ost as well is great.
As for the minuses, I wasn't sure what I was supposed to be doing a lot of the time. Sometimes I didn't know where to go. And sometimes I didn't really know what abilites were good.
One kicker that I really didn't like was the death penalty. When you die, you respawn at a checkpoint with one of your abilites disabled. It doesn't really make sense because if I'm at a part that is already difficult, I'm just going to die more without some abilities. That mechanic frustrated me.
I really wish there was a middle thumb for Transistor, but I feel the world is a bit cliche'd, the characters don't stand out like in Bastion, and the game mechanics are frustrating. I would give the art and music a thumbs up, but game thumbs down.

A story is rather meh (I really commend you if you got it), but Transistor is a pretty good game otherwise.

It's SUPPOSED to be a Mega Man ripoff.

When I backed this game, I had a lot of hope. What I wanted: Megaman X, or Megaman Zero, repackaged. New characters, new weapons, new worlds, fast paced action, interesting new story or even a play on an older one. Instead, I got that... transformed.
This game is focused more on Mega Man, the oldest version, but with added dashing and the focus of dashing through enemies. To what purpose? No real purpose, only specific ones give you special bonuses. Instead, it's mostly just for points. And you do it, near constantly, to move at a real rate. Rather than MMX or MMZ, where you could dash jump or dash once in the air, or even dash straight up, you are constantly buzzing forward. It's uninteresting, to say the least, because it limits what ways you can play.
Then, there's the lack of wall kicking. Everytime I hit against a wall, I wanna kick against it, get higher. I want to be able to have a greater freedom of movement that isn't provided at all. Ledge grabbing is the only thing you can do, and it only works on specific ledges, not even every ledge.
While you can spam dash to go fast, the level design is ultimately focused very linearly, horizontally, because the only thing you can do when going up or down is hope you line up a shot. You can't wallkick up or slide down to the right spot to kill something, you can't dash up into the air to get some extra height just for a moment to hit that thing flying just out of your vertical reach otherwise. No, you get none of that. Your movement is heavily restricted.
And the dialogue, it goes on and on. It even instantly assumes you're an infantile tool at the beginning of the game. It tells you the first enemy you see is an enemy, it doesn't even give you the chance to find out on your own.
The game is heavily restricted compared to games from the Megaman X and Megaman Zero series. I didn't back Inafune for older, now defunct, less enthralling gameplay. I backed him for more cutting edge 2D gameplay.
Why is that all so important, that it has to be compared to MMX and MMZ? Freedom of movement is more engaging, you're more allowed to do what you want to have fun, you're more in thought about how to approach something. Mighty No. 9 doesn't even have a very useful power switching setup, but you could swap to everything you needed in MMX and MMZ.
What that translates to is boredom. You are expected to do this, you are expected to do that. You are being led on to play how it was designed, not by your own freedom of choice.
It is boring. Boring, dull, uninspired, and passable.
Long wait for a successor to megaman, and all we get is a substitute for the terrible Megaman X Zero gameboy games.

TurnOn is a fun platformer with a lovely art style. The game progresses in a light mood which makes it an ideal platformer for everyone. What's not to love?

TurnOn is what I would call a casual platformer. The game is not very challenging but is a fun game if you want something to sit back and enjoy and not have to worry about tough jumps or time limits. The mechanics are pretty simple as you jump between different power lines in the city to turn the city's electricity back on. The game includes some puzzles which mostly involve exploring to find what you need to turn on in order to proceed. Despite not being much of a challenge, I had a lot of fun with TurnOn.
Another area where TurnOn excels is its' atmosphere. TurnOn is a really charming game. The graphics are pretty nice especially as the levels light up as you turn on the city's lights. The music fits the mood perfectly. The thing that stood out most to me though was the little storylines in each level. An example is a level where you guide a lost kid back to their house. The main story could have been developed a little more but the game does such a great job creating a charming environment.
While I really enjoyed TurnOn I have two issues with the game. As already mentioned the game is really easy. You will breeze through most of the levels. If you are looking for a challenging game, TurnOn is not it. The difficulty leads to the other issue which is the length. Since you can breeze through the levels the game ends up not being very long. I finished the game in around 4.5 hours. Unless you want to go for all of the achievements it will probably take you around the same amount of time to beat the game.
If you are looking for a really challenging game, you might not like TurnOn but otherwise I would recommend picking it up.

TurnOn is a cute platforming adventure with some levels using aspects of a running game. In TurnOn, you play as an alien creature (that looks like a ball of electricity) in a city shrouded in darkness, and it’s your goal to help the citizens, and restore the power and lights.
You travel along the powerlines and telephone poles jumping from one to another to bring power back to the city. There are two styles of levels: one is more of a casual platformer, and the other has some of the aspects you would see in a runner game (like Temple Run, or Bit.Trip Runner).
In the platforming levels, you move to power up things as you go, and in some levels you are basically escorting the characters through the levels by opening doors, and setting off alarms to scare away the bad guys. Contrary to the casual platforming levels there were other levels that resembled a simpler version of running game. You are forced down the lines with no way to slow down or speed up, and all you can do is jump from one wire to another.
Fortunately, there were more platforming levels than runner levels, but I spent a lot of time dying repeatedly on these runner levels. I don’t like runner games, and I admit it’s partially because I just plain suck at them,
The game took me 4-5 hours, with at least an hour and a half of that dying repeatedly
. While it wasn’t the most frustrating game I’ve played, I would have probably skipped on playing this game if I had known about the runner levels. At the same time though, I did enjoy the other parts, so I’ve got pretty mixed feelings about the game as a whole.

I absolutely adored Transistor.
Firstly, the story is absolutely beautiful. You pick up bits and pieces as you make your way through Cloudbank, and as you level up new abilities for the Transistor. Piece by piece, you understand the story and the people within it, and it all comes to a conclusion so beautifully. I was surprised at how emotional this game made me feel, and how much it reminded me of what it means to be fully human.
I enjoyed the feeling of evolving with game. There is no combat tutorial, but the game knows you'll learn, maybe slowly at first, but surely. You have opportunities to play around with abilities and combinations to develop your own fighting style in a safe environment.  You can een add different limiters to make the game more challenging, and in return you'll earn experience bonuses.
The art is stunning,  and the soundtrack is an absolute masterpiece. It is so beautiful, haunting, and emotional, and I have been listening to it on repeat on spotify. The music is kindof addicting, honestly.
While the game is short (only about 12 hours til the credits), it was probably the most fun, immersive 12 hours of my life. I would sit down to play for an hour and walk away 5 hours later because I couldn't rip myself away from the story and the gameplay. The only downside is that it is so short, as I was NOT emotionally ready for it to end. It came to a beautiful conclusion, but I selfishly wanted Transistor to stretch on forever. This game is worth every penny, and more.
This game is a work of art. Truly, don't pass this one over.
An absurdly great experience, with tight gameplay, but beyond that, flawless art, soundtrack, writing... An unforgettable presentation, an emotional ride. Yes, yes, yes I recommend it!

Only complaint that it's so short. Was worth every penny otherwise.
What are ya waiting for? Buy it!
Such a beautiful combination of art, design and masterful storytelling. Simply amazing.

This game kept me engaged from beginning to end.  It has compelling, emotional storytelling that avoids cutscenes and instead uses regular secondary-character monologue, similar to Bastion.  Luckily, it's never once annoying or overly expositiony; in fact, it can be quite humourous and human.
The gameplay is the perfect marriage between thoughful strategy and fast-paced combat.  The variety and possibilities are endless and everyone will have their favourite set of abilities.  There is always a sense of tension around the difficult enemies, but also a feeling of ease as you work out the best step forward.
As a musician and artist myself, I fell in absolute, intense love with the soundtrack and presentation.  I listen to the songs often when I need something to study or work to, and several of the art pieces are in my computer's library.
This is the first game I've ever felt immediately eager to complete 100%.  Although not incredibly difficult to do so and there are not significant rewards for the player, it's still a welcome sense of accomplishment.
I usually don't like picking favourites for my interests, but this is my favourite game of all time.  No argument.

Like Bastion, this is a really well-executed and polished game--really feels more like a studio game than an indie title. The artwork is great, and the fighting system is really good. The different weapons really allow personality to shine through in the play. Also, like Bastion, the difficulty is high enough to maintain interest, but low enough that very few deaths will occur to even a casual gamer.
Things I liked:
- Music, Art, and voice acting
- Plot was touching
- RPG mechanics: varying and interwoven nature of weapons, the "planning mode", and the live action in between plans.
- Using temporary loss of weapon as a penalty for losing a full bar of health. The penalty was high enough to make it painful, but not high enough to trigger a revert.
Things I didn't like
- The whole "empty world". It worked really well in Bastion--although even Bastion had *some* interaction. For their follow-up game I would have liked to see a different plot.
- Lack of emotional punch. There were a lot of elements that should have been sad--loss of the whole world, loss of boyfriend, etc. And the boyfriend as the talking sword could have been really great. But the sword felt more like the talking robot in Beneath a Steel Sky than a boyfriend. And I never really did get the nostalgia for the world, or for lost friends we never met. In Bastion I felt the punch, and I loved in Bastion that there were some small decisions that helped involve me more in the story.
- I would love a little bit of branching decision making (doesn't have to have much impact--just a little would be fine) to involve me more. Again, the ability to save an enemy and other small things in Bastion made a pretty big difference.
- In keeping with the other things, I think there was too much polish--too much focus on "pretty" and not enough focus on the plot elements.
- No time to really enjoy or work through all the weapons because we kept getting them right to the end. (yah, yah, I know, I could play again with the new settings, but I don't feel like it)
But, despite my criticisms, I felt the gameplay was excellent, and I will definitely play future titles from this developer. I just hope that they a) don't keep trying to copy the empty world of Bastion, and b) deliver more emotional punch in future games.

I have only just finished my play through of this mind-blowing game. In it you play a brilliant Robotics engineer--think Hiro from Big Hero 6--who kickstarts the age of robotics. From the off it is full of choices your character can make, besides being very well written by the author. The robot I first built, Ariel,--the game lets you choose practically every aspect of them--was a daughter of sorts, having chose to activate the tiny winged humanoid while looking at me and naming myself as 'Father' to her. As she discovered the world around her and slowly, sometimes awkwardly, grew into a young adult under my care, I grew incredibly attached to her and it actually moved me to tears on more than one occasion. It is the most powerful game I have played in a very long time and some of the most powerful story telling I have encountered in a very long time.
Imagine a Asimov classic only you are the main character. My first story depicted a relationship akin to that of Doctor Lanning and Sonny from the film I, Robot mixed up with a reversal of the plot to Bicentennial Man for the protagonist. I brought about a golden age where man and a new species of mechanical people coexist in peace in the wake of a violent Sino-American war.
You literally can follow many paths through the way you design your first robot and raise them and your relationships with the story's many side characters. Will you achieve world domination? End man as we know him/her or live the high life as a Tony Stark type character? So many routes you can go down. Will you become an American hero or a backer of the Chinese? I have heard that you and your first robot can even become a crime-fighting vigilante duo!--but don't hold me to that.
Such an amazing game which, in relation to all others, I can only describe as a Bethesda RPG in text format... but with far better plot and writing.
In fact, I'm so impressed I encourage all who read this to buy it--it's less than £5, and I have been moved so to create this review, which I rarely do.

I first played this game on xbox but when I saw this game was for 5$ on steam, I could not resist.
You play as Starkiller, Vader's apprentice who is sent on various missions accomplishing your master's will.
The story is the main strong points of the game. The first missions you are sent on assassination missions and unlike assassin's creed, you actually feel like you are hunting down your targets. However this is a personal story, Starkiller, Galen Marek's story. And without spoiling anything, I'll just say that the story is worth while. However I have to point out some of the dialogue: its not always good, some of it would need to be re-worked. Why? Because it can create strange plotholes, and while still using different words it could all be fixed. Such as ( i don't consider this a spoiler because it is right after the prologue but i'll cover it anyway)
By having better dialogue you can have a better story.
Graphics. You know what? They're not that bad mainly because this is a third person game, you don't get to see the textures from really close. But yeah, there are some textures that are low-res.
However it can be fixed with an fps mod fix on
. I played the game with the mod: I can't stand 30 fps. I recommend using an xbox controller since this is a port.
Voice acting is good. However one issue: I got a bug on the first mission where I could not hear Juno's dialogue. I tried to find a fix for it but nothing worked so far.
Finally the gameplay. This is where I both like the game and dislike it. First of all this is what I like: Combos, you can unlock alot of combos in this game and the animations for it are really cool! You have to memorize combinations of attacks and there are enough variations to keep you invested in your 11-13 hours play through. You can unlock different types of lightsabers which provide different buffs and you can choose the color as well. This is awesome because you are not force to use the same lightsaber and you don't have to look at the same colors are well. You can chose the buffs and the color independently of each other.
The movement system, this is where the game falters. It is not fluid enough, not responsive: you should be able to interrupt while you're in the middle of a combo, because when you're pressing X,Y,X,Y and you see a missile coming straight at you, well prepare to rage alot. This is my biggest problem in the game: sometimes you can't avoid dying. Most of the times when I died I could not do anything because i was in an animation, I could not avoid the danger. It feels like the game forces you to die occasionally. When you are locked in an animation you can take damage and there is nothing you can do. The worst issue is when jumping: and you get shot by a sniper or a rocket, you fall down and for some reason you slide on the floor for 30 meters. The problem is that it is an animation and you are locked in it so no matter what happens you can't get out of it. Some levels allow you to fall off the map and when you start to slide, you know five seconds ahead that you will die. Hopefully you understand why it can get really frustrating. And you might have to redo sections multiple times, not because you played on a hard difficulty but because you were extremely unlucky.
Loading screens? I have to talk about them because they're bad. They can take a while to load 10-20 seconds and the worst part: WHY ARE THERE LOADING SCREENS INSIDE OF MENUS?!?
The enemies could be a bit more varied, I don't mind slicing through hundreds of grunts but the mini bosses need more variations. Some enemies are really anoying such as the purge troopers. You have a lightsaber, you should be about to slice through them without a doubt, but this is an overall complaint in the game: lighstabers don't really feel like lightsabers when fighting against tougher enemies. I don't like also how some types clones can resist my force attacks, isn't the point of the game to unleashe the force on them?
So overall I really like the game even with its flaws. To me it is an above average game with many flaws but you can still find enjoyment in it.
