While I like the idea of dungeon crawlers Legend of Grimrock is simply too rough around the edges to recommend. At the time of writing this review I have completed the first three levels of the game with a Human Warrior, Minotaur Warrior, Human Rogue and Insectoid Mage party.
The tutorial is a series of images that explain the most basic concepts of the game. The tooltips when you mouse over attributes or skills give you essentially flavour text. They don't really explain exactly what affects they will have which is a crucial part of RPGs like this where you really can't afford to waste points.
I was constantly Googling trying to get clarification as to what exactly certain attributes or skills would do. A lot of times I got linked to the Steam forums where players seemed to be debating amongst themselves exactly what the affects were. The reason this irked me so much is that this is the prototypical old school RPG where you can easily spend points on stuff that is essentially useless and with no ability to respec it makes it really easy to make mistakes and which then feels like you have neutered your character.
I'm about three hours in and so far the combat has essentially boiled down to right click on all four characters to have them take a swing, wait a couple seconds and repeat. There is no real strategy in how you attack, at least not yet.
My melee classes have a weapon and a shield because it seems that high evasion is an absolute must for frontline fighters. However this means that they basically can do nothing except right click every couple seconds. Rogues in theory could have a bit of variety because you don't need a shield if your in the back row and could have two things equipped but the problem is that you can't attack with both. Any attack puts both equipped items on cooldown. This caries over to the mage who after they cast a spell has to wait again.
For all of these reason combat becomes incredibly repetitive and boring. Perhaps it gets better later on and you get more ability to strategize but I am three hours into the game and it feels incredibly dumbed down to me. I'm sure some people reading this review are saying "you're suppose to move a lot in combat" and while I tried doing that it was no fun at all. Since you have to move on a grid it's essentially like chasing a younger sibling around the kitchen table. You can literally run in circles and the enemy can't hit you and while it is a valid strategy running around in circles for hours is by no means fun in my books.
You know how a lot of people talk about how games make "quality of life" improvements because developers realized that many of their game mechanics were simply there to elongage the time the user spent playing and actually really agitated the user? This game took all of those lessons and ignore them and instead went back to the old school Dungeons & Dragons mindset.
Simple things like mages burn through their energy far faster than rogues or warriors so they become useless faster and require constant rest or trips to the life crystals to restore their energy.
Health regenerates so slow that after a battle you often have to sit and wait to heal back up. Otherwise you're spending a couple minutes running back and forth between the afformentioned life crystals.
Perhaps all of this wouldn't be an issue if the game dropped health or energy potions but in my three hours of playing I have only got enough ingredients to make four health potions and you will burn through them almost instantly.
The straw the broke the camels back for me was the spiders on level 3. I had the best armor I could get at this point in the game as far as I am aware. Full light armor for both my warriors and they both had over 100 hp but the spiders would still hit for 20+. So I could take a max of three spiders back to back before my party was completely wiped and I had to take a couple minutes to properly heal.
The kicker was that these spiders can poison you and of course poison means damage over time. Problem is the same ingredients you need to make health potions are the same ingredients you need to make antidotes and even if I made antidotes instead of health potions I would only have made four of them. I easily fought over 20 spiders and got poisoned over a dozen times. It would not have made any difference and I still would have had to run back to the life crystal a dozen times just to cure my poison because the game did not give out proper resources.
In my mind these kind of games should be about battle strategy and how you use medicine during a battle is part of the strategy. But after four battles if you're completely tapped and the only strategy then is to cheese by running around the kitchen table well then I think that means something went wrong during the design of the game.
Like I said in the first sentence of this review, I really like the idea behind this game. Crawling through a massive dungeon while overcoming the challenges inside. I just didn't think the challenges would be limited resources and knowledge of playing ring-a-round the rosie.
Didnt even know i was a fan of old school dungeon crawlers. Finding secrets got me hooked on this game. Watch a trailer or a gameplay video first so you dont get dissapointed with the combat system.

tl;dr: This is a great game and I would recommend anyone even remotely interested in Norse Mythology to buy and play this game.
Hail Vikings! Take a stroll through the realms of creation in the Norse Mythology as you battle Giants! (Or Jotuns as they are called). This game is part Dark Souls, part Legend of Zelda, and combines some of the best mechanics of both. Use the powers of the Gods to collect the Runes of Power. Search for Golden Apples to improve your health. Fight your way to Valhalla.
Pros: The game itself is very good, taking a page from Dark Souls the bosses are brutually hard (with some exception) but incredibly fair. Every attack has a set pattern and telegraph that makes learning the bosses fun and makes it obvious what you have to do, so that failure to perform the right actions leaves you vulnerable, something that you have -complete- control over. The exploration levels are drenched in lore from the mythology. And the visuals (The MF visuals! OMG) are amazing and fluid. They make everything feel so mystical. And the settings are breath taking.
Cons: Some of the environmental hazzards or 'puzzles' get a little boring once you know the pattern. The Nine Rivers in particular is guilty of this, but it doesn't take away from the majesty of the game, just makes it slow going.
Overall: 9.25/10 Great Game, Awesome experience.

It’s hard to figure what needs to be said about Jotun that hasn’t already been said. The game heavily explores Norse mythology as players take control of Thora, a fallen, female viking who must now trek through the mystifying lands in the hopes of reaching Valhalla. However, she must first appease the Gods by defeating each of them in combat, gaining their specialized abilities to utilize against greater deities further ahead.
The game is presented beautifully as it contains hand-drawn imagery, extravagantly orchestrated music, great voice-acting and easy gameplay mechanics that’s simple to control. That being said, this game isn’t as forgiving as some may think. At first glance it may be viewed as appealing, childish game with artistic flair, but it is in no means an achievable success in one quick playthrough. In simple terms, this game is not the easiest. Your character is equipped with basic attacks that seem deliberate, along with a heavy attack that drags on before making contact against your opponent. So while engaging in a new fight, the player must evaluate enemies’ movements and lay out strategically planned attacks while retreating more often than not. Sadly, you’ll notice that you die several times, but this is the point as it’s a learning process and becomes increasingly fun as you get better at it. You must die to learn your opponents moves and adjust your gaming style accordingly. The Gods may be predictable but they like to change the playing field a bit.
From my own experience the first boss was daunting but beatable; the second boss, however, some more figuring out on how to get rid of its remaining 25% health. Jotun is seriously one of those games that’ll beat you down and kick you once you on the ground, but for those stubborn gamers who thrive for that success: giving up is not an option. Frustration will accompany unsuccessful attempts, so be prepared!

The gaming market is dominated by fast paced, action packed games, which are fun, but sometimes it's nice to slow things down. Which is where TurnOn comes in. A casual platformer developed by the four man team of Brainy Studio, TurnOn features some great relaxing music, colorful art style, and creative level designs.
TurnOn is a narrative story told through comic-like cutscenes and during the game’s levels. After a power station accident, an alien becomes sentient by fusing with the power stations’ systems. Players take control of the little ball of alien electricity as it makes it way throughout the city trying to restore the cities’ power. Players travel along the electrical wires throughout the power station, residential, and commercial districts of the city. Players must solve puzzles like helping a little girl get home safely and fighting crime by setting off alarm systems to scare off looters.
The levels of TurnOn are wonderfully colorful and dynamic. The power lines allow players to travel seamlessly from the background to the foreground. This gives each level the feeling of being three dimensional despite the games 2D art. What slightly contrasted this great feature was that the electric alien of the game would not change in size when moving from the foreground to background in some parts of the game. It was minor, but it still made the character seem out of place compared to everything else, which would shrink and grow in size as the game’s camera moved back and forth. The game’s puzzles in each level were not overly challenging. It mainly just took a bit of exploring and common sense to realize which power box to jump into to activate more lights or to stop traffic lights for someone to safely cross the street. The slower paced and relaxing puzzle levels of TurnOn were juxtaposed by racing sequences. During these, players would jump between four different wires at a time, trying to collect as many hovering lightning tokens for points, while avoiding falling to their deaths or hitting the red tokens, which when three were hit, you died.
TurnOn’s art and music were two awesome parts of the game. The lighting in the game feels bright and vibrant due to its contrast with the blackout of the city. The background is painted with a darker color palette of blues and purples, that still give the game a fun and cheerful feeling, without making it feel dark and gloomy. People also populate many of the game’s scenes, usually in distress about one situation or another, all related to the cities’ blackout. This helps the city feel alive, and being able to watch them cheer or enjoy their lives again with your help adds to the satisfaction of completing each puzzle. The music of TurnOn was one of my, dare I say it, turn ons. The casual gameplay and vibrant colors are complimented by the smooth jazz throughout the game. The music during the puzzle scenes adds to the relaxing mood and made this game one of my favorites to come home and play after work. The racing sequences of the game had faster pace music to compliment their gameplay. The developers definitely hit the mark with creating a great atmosphere for their game with the music.
TurnOn is a very enjoyable and relaxing platformer that is great for adults and kids. The colorful art style and smooth jazz music fit well together, while the simple gameplay and dynamic level design made it fun. I did run into two bugs during my playing, but both of the them were easily fixed by simply reloading the level from the previous checkpoints and neither occurred more than once. The developers were quick to respond to my email about the bugs, so I am sure that these minor kinks will be fixed soon.
Pros:
Colorful art style
Relaxing music
Dynamic levels
Fun gameplay
Controller support
Steam Achievements
Comic-like narrative
Kid friendly
Simple controls
Support for 18 languages (check Steam for list)
Cons:
Few bugs (minor and easy to get around)
Character does not change size with movement from background to foreground sometimes

With illusive dignity, I'm going to present the review of the crown jewel of Call of Duty franchise. Call of Duty Modern Warfare 2 inflicts the most immersive and passionate experience. Like what kind of situations you need to be very focused and accurate to overcome an intense battle. Let me share my thoughts on very few aspects. By the way, my review is based on only campaign.
Story, obviously one of the momentous features of this title. They have really focused on the story to make it passionate and flashy. Though, the story is definitely one of the eminent stories for me. Well, the story has been continued with Captain Price and Soap from last installment with an intense storyline. Got some heinous and impulsive moments as well. Besides, this story has perfect sequences what i have never seen in any other stories. Tell you what, this is what i call a perfect and superior story. This is like some kind of ravelled and immersive story which is affiliated with invasion-battle theme. This story started to become more lovable at the final chapters. So i guess you'll love this, just like i did.
Gameplay, the other fundamental feature of this title. As you know it's a first person shooter type game. If the gameplay gets some deficiency then we would totally defy the story. Because gameplay has to be brilliant and epic. So i guess, there is nothing wrong with the gameplay as i have completed on Veteran difficulty. So i had to be very strategic and wise to overcome my way to the conclusion. I couldn't court the world and eliminate hostiles so effortlessly. Because you have to be focused and wise to make any position. Sometimes you can't stay at open for few moments. Hostiles wouldn't need second chance to take you out on this difficulty. You need right equipments and weapons to neutralize situations. You got couple of guns around you like sniper, assault, smg and riffles. But i used sniper and grenade launcher most of the times. Also you can use flashbangs, claymores and grenades for better combat strategy. You don't need any medics because your health regenerates eventually and quickly. But things will be different in every difficulties. I recommend you to play on Hardened mode.
About Special Ops, this is another game mode alongside campaign and multiplayer. You can complete dozens of missions on very few locations which are included in campaign mode as well. There are difficulties in this mode also. But you can always go easy. Alongside, you'll earn more stars for higher difficulties. This mode is important for your achievements mostly.
I haven't played a single match because didn't get any match yet. There are couple of modes to try but still i'm on zero ground. So i can't say anything about multiplayer. But i guess we should choose Call of Duty franchise for campaign mostly.
Visuals, would totally ignore this about a Call of Duty title. Still decent and good visuals. I guess, it doesn't matter when the storyline and gameplay tearing up alongside. But i had some deficiency with the visuals. I felt bit headache because of it. But just a few times. Guess won't happen with you.
Have no bleat about the performance. I'm getting solid 60 FPS with highest presets on Intel Core i7 7700K, R9 390 STRIX and 6GB Ram. Besides, i got crashes for few times but no bugs, errors nor any stuttering till now. Just to be informative, Download takes 7.4 GB and then installation requires 11.4 GB of space.
Creators pulled out some inspiring and iconic background scores for better strategic and straight combat experience. All those background scores are perfectly matched with their given situations and moments. Definitely loved all of them.
So geezers, I'm genuinely recommending to all FPS lovers. Allow your veins to experience an immersive and strategic invasion. I personally guarantee that you won't be disappointed at all if you make it worth of your first try.

Legend of Grimrock is a great example of an indie game that finds a niche that bigger devs and publishers have no interest in and does it well. It takes the gameplay of old dungeon crawlers like Dungeon Master and Eye of the Beholder and puts a nice coat of paint on them. It's surprising how well the idea holds up with only a few little quality of life improvements.
Of course, Grimrock isn't for everybody. Most people are probably going to find it a little tedious to slog through same looking hallways while having to save scum in case a monster closet opens up on them.The tile based movement and "click on a character portrait" combat is less than smooth, but if you're the kind of person who likes Resident Evil with tank controls than you probably understand how restrictive design can be a good thing sometimes. It creates a frantic combat atmosphere as you try to coordinate moving around with attacking while setting up rune combinations to cast spells.
For a certain kind of person, there's something engrossing about wandering lonely, abandonded hallways, solving puzzles and finding secret treasures. There's no soundtrack here, just the moan of an empty dungeon and the occasional skittering of an enemy that might be safely locked away or just around the corner waiting to pop out at you. There are no loot drops, if you want better weapons and armor you better make sure your puzzle solving is up to snuff as everything needs to be earned and a lot of things are squirreled away pretty deviously. Generally the game is pretty fair and you can get through with a minimum number of secrets found (I discovered a little over half) one puzzle that required backtracking for specific items that you might not think important to carry was annoying, but most puzzles that you need to solve to progress won't make you tear your hair out.
If you're interested it may be better to jump to Grimrock II, which I've heard improves a lot on the formula here, but on its own this is still a solid game and a unique experience if you're not familiar with this style of game.

Like Bastion, this is a really well-executed and polished game--really feels more like a studio game than an indie title. The artwork is great, and the fighting system is really good. The different weapons really allow personality to shine through in the play. Also, like Bastion, the difficulty is high enough to maintain interest, but low enough that very few deaths will occur to even a casual gamer.
Things I liked:
- Music, Art, and voice acting
- Plot was touching
- RPG mechanics: varying and interwoven nature of weapons, the "planning mode", and the live action in between plans.
- Using temporary loss of weapon as a penalty for losing a full bar of health. The penalty was high enough to make it painful, but not high enough to trigger a revert.
Things I didn't like
- The whole "empty world". It worked really well in Bastion--although even Bastion had *some* interaction. For their follow-up game I would have liked to see a different plot.
- Lack of emotional punch. There were a lot of elements that should have been sad--loss of the whole world, loss of boyfriend, etc. And the boyfriend as the talking sword could have been really great. But the sword felt more like the talking robot in Beneath a Steel Sky than a boyfriend. And I never really did get the nostalgia for the world, or for lost friends we never met. In Bastion I felt the punch, and I loved in Bastion that there were some small decisions that helped involve me more in the story.
- I would love a little bit of branching decision making (doesn't have to have much impact--just a little would be fine) to involve me more. Again, the ability to save an enemy and other small things in Bastion made a pretty big difference.
- In keeping with the other things, I think there was too much polish--too much focus on "pretty" and not enough focus on the plot elements.
- No time to really enjoy or work through all the weapons because we kept getting them right to the end. (yah, yah, I know, I could play again with the new settings, but I don't feel like it)
But, despite my criticisms, I felt the gameplay was excellent, and I will definitely play future titles from this developer. I just hope that they a) don't keep trying to copy the empty world of Bastion, and b) deliver more emotional punch in future games.

In OlliOlli your primary goal is simply to ride your skateboard to the end of each obstacle-filled level without crashing. Crash and you have to restart the level. Essentially the game plays like a runner-style game with your character constantly moving forward, although the high level of precision needed for the later levels almost makes it feel like a rhythm game. Secondary to beating each level, you can focus on getting high scores and beating challenges for each level, such as scoring a certain combo or getting all the collectibles.
OlliOlli has a simple but unique control scheme where you perform tricks by holding and releasing the left control stick and pressing A to speed up and stick landings while your character continually moves forward. It definitely took me some time to get used to the fact that pressing A does not make jump while wiggling the control stick does but, once I got a hang of it, I found that this type of control offers up a lot of freedom and works quite well.
Overall, I enjoyed OlliOlli's gameplay a lot. It's a fast-paced steep challenge that I enjoyed as a fan of precision platforming
While I enjoyed the distinctness of OlliOlli's five worlds, Urban, Junkyard, Port, Base (soviet Russia), and Neon (retro-future Tokyo), and the crisp clean menus, I found the simple pixel graphics of OlliOlli during actual gameplay to be somewhat lackluster. They aren't bad but they also didn't stick with me and it was occasionally hard to distinguish what was purely an obstacle and what I may be able to grind, which was problematic.
OlliOlli is yet another indie title with a fantastic soundtrack. The music seems to take influence from a number of sources and has elements of electronic, jazz, and hip-hop. It's upbeat, catchy, and kept me going as I crashed over and over again.
The sound effects are fine but much less memorable.
OlliOlli is a fun runner-style sidescrolling game with a steep challenge that features a unique control scheme and a great soundtrack. You don't need to care for real life skateboarding at all to enjoy this one. I would recommend it to anyone looking for a high precision sidescroller to test their skills.

Papers Please is a masterpiece that everyone should try out. How a visually crappy game like this could pull of such great story still boggles me. Ultimately Papers Please is all about routine, you quickly pick up the rules of how to play and what to do, and then are giving some interesting choices , do your job well and protect the interests of an oppressive society, or do your job poorly and be executed. Your family’s lives, your life, and the lives of the people you encounter are in your hands. You somehow have to juggle those and the daily circumstances to make it all work out. You really feel the pressure of the times, and the urge to do the ‘right’ right. The consequences seem dire and the choices really tough.
In conclusion, it’s not an expensive game, it’s impossible for me not to recommend this. It’s got a very good story, great characters, shabby graphics but they work, a decent enough soundtrack, and some good replayability.

For anyone who has played this 'game', the other reviews are hilarious and you'll smile and laugh.  I find there to be a lack of a serious review and for some reason I chose to play this game without really digging for details (hey, it's free, what more could I want to know!), so maybe I'll help someone save themselves a quick 15 minutes.  First of all, typing this in 2016 as a 31 soon to be 32 year old, it's a quick injection of nostalgia - specifically seeing the options you have each year of what your profile pic options are.  Windows XP fans and heavy users of various instant messaging addicts will find this a great jaunt down memory lane.
So for a free game, that's short, has the above, as well as "beyond the game enjoyement" you can get from joking around with those who have given this a try; why did I thumb it down?  Simply put, I didn't get what I thought I was going to get.  Here was my mind set after looking at the short description of the title and the handful of screens: "Oh neat, a story-based game with a branching path that takes place via yon olden instynt messygyng soufghtware!".  I was in.  My mind was on fire after the first year (takes approximately 2 minutes) thinking that this was going to be a story about internet bullying, domestic abuse, depression, or maybe a neat way of looking at how two people's lives can be completely divergent yet friendship-is-forever-come-on-everybody-lets-hug-it-out-type thing.  Instead, it's about a girl who I talk to once a year for 5 years, made clear that I thought she was only a friend, may have taken advantage of her despite specifically trying not to while still being a friend (I even said leave the booze at home, for crying out loud), who suddenly is done with me and yet I am forced to, somehow, have feelings for her?  Congrats to Mike & Emma though, those people at least sound like they have their heads on straight!
In all seriousness, I went in thinking that the story was going to be worthy of some legit social commentary, and it may well be for some of you depending upon the choices you make, but I expected more.  One thing that I would love to see is some serious expansion done by the developer.  They could be collecting lots of data about how people play this game and expand upon it rather quickly and interestingly, including interacting with the others on the friends list.  The possibilities are both boundless and daunting - but then again.....that's what I thought when I launched it, and look how that wound up....

Star Wars: The Force Uleashed is a fairly average 3rd person hack and slash set in the Star Wars universe. The story is, while a bit bland, fairly good overall and goes in-depth into the events between the 3rd and 4th movies in the Star Wars franchise. The game features a set of force powers and effects the make the player feel like a powerful badass apprentice to Darth Vader - flinging stormtroopers out of ship windows, shocking them with lightning, and slicing/skewering them with your lightsaber all work to support this feeling. But this is where the game stops being good, at least on the PC port.
The default controls for the PC are clunky at best, making the "god of war style" combo system this game touts difficult to pull off at times. The flaws in the controls are made even worse in instances where precision is needed - precision that makes the difference between beating a level and yelling at your scream in frustration as moves that you would like to pull either dont go off or miss your intended target entirely (leaving you open to a brutal counter-attack as well).  This is particlarly evident in the boss battles (take your pick which one). The game stops being a behind the shoulder 3rd person beat em' up and jarringly shifts to a 3D isometric "Mortal Combat Style" fight, where you cant gain an advantage or effectively perfom combos becuase you're not really sure where exactly you're hitting (and even if you do hit, the bosses have a very annoying habit of countering or blocking everything you do). In one particular level you are supposed to bring down a star destroyer from space and crash it into the planet you're on. This task is borderline impossible due to the horrible controls and lack of  any precision aiming available to you.
The poor optimization is also evident in the jarring loading screens randomly placed in levels, and before and after the "high quality" cinematic scenes. Poor audio syncing also results in the cinematics being a pain to both watch and listen to. Sometime in the beginning of a level you will see yourself standing at the starting point for a few moments, at which point the screen goes blank and THEN the beginning in-game level animation will go off. Also, the music and sound effects for the game tend to cut out at random moments (even during 3D cinematics) and will not return unless you restart the game entirely.
Overall I only recommend this game if you're a Star Wars fan, and even then I'm not sure I can say its a good recommendation. 4/10

I bought The Fifth Day after watching one of PsiSyndicate's lets plays for it. He stated in his video that the game was poorly made, very buggy, and had little to no content. Still, I purchased it in hope of a half-way decent survival&building game.
Once I launched it I was greeted with a pleasant surprise. The game's visuals were beautiful and captured the asthetic of a cold, lonely wasteland well and without any FPS drops or crashing on maximum settings. Once I started walking around the desolate world I came across a new breed of enemy, robots. The bots were well modeled and effectively frightining, as one of them slowly turned around; scanned me and shot one round. Killing me in my place. I must say I jumped as the shot rang out.
Gameplay mechanics such and building and combat are fluid and difficult enough to provide a challenge, not a headache.
To start building you must find a hacker tool (They mainly spawn in cities and towns), and a harvester. (Harvesters are found in pits around the map) If you do find a harvester, you must hack into it using the tool mentioned above. Once hacked you command the machine to collect resources and drop them near you (The way the harvester flys around and drops supply pods is impressive for a game this young). Once you have enough resources you build using a recipe book found around the map. The building itself is rather alot like the game "Rust" by Garry Newman, You craft templates and place them in a locking format. I prefer The Fifth Day's building more because it has no glitches with the terrain and more templates to produce more complex structures. Combat is wonderful, the weapon models sway with your charecter, the firearms themselves feel powerful and fun to fire, and the recoil is set properly to give you the satisfaction of a well aimed shot.
The AI is not the smartest out there, but still provide enough of a challenge to keep you on the edge of your seet as you walk through the deserted countrysides and cities.
All in all I give The Fifth Day a 10/10, for breathtaking visuals and atmosphere, no bugs or glitches, well designed building and gunplay mechanics, interesting and new hostile enemies, low hardware requirements, and low price.

Transistor is a work of art more than it is a game. The visual aesthetic of the gameplay, and especially the cut scenes, is both striking and unique. Transistor has, by far, the best original soundtrack of any game I've played. It is the only game soundtrack that I listen to separately from the game itself, and I've spent more time listening to the soundtrack than I have playing the game.
More importantly than any of those individual assets of the game is how it all integrates together. How the gameplay visuals, the amazing interactive cutscene, and perfect music blend together yields a product that is truly greater than the sum of its parts. Each aspect stands on its own, and without any of them the game would still be fun to play, but it's all of them together which make Transistor a masterpiece.

A fun, interesting strategy/management game where you play a worker at a border station to get from one country to another. As the game progresses the rules you must follow change based on the socio-political climate between the made up countries. Your job is to look for those who have fake passports/incomplete paperwork and deny them entry.
It's a fantastic game of choice with lots of cool story moments and once you complete some endings you get a few arcade modes to try, all of which are as fun as you find the story, but without the story elements to bother you as you do your passport checking duties. As stated before there are a lot of choices that affect the outcome of the game, so keep an eye out for that and try to get all the endings, as each one is unique and an appropriate end to the game.

[Graphics]
It feels like there was almost no difference with the quality they did with the demo. No graphical/HUD improvements since then. The voice acting was above average in terms of delivering emotions but mouths aren't moving. Character renditions look like hollow shells.

Pretty decent stage BGMs. It gives a good feel on the actual setting.

Mr. Sanda's baby talk is kinda annoying.
[Gameplay]
This does feel a lot like Megaman. Even the difficulty level. However, I do not like how the game treats the players. It starts off by treating you like a total gaming noob (telling you to press A to jump) to 5-8 deaths before defeating your first Mighty No. boss. Boss AI is also a mixed bag for me. Pyro's three attack pattern and Cryo's two (three, if you get iced) attack pattern is not impressive, but still substantially challenging. Also, Beck's battles seem so slow. Maybe I gotten used to X's charged shots. Charged shots give another dimension on fighting enemies. [Controls]
Depending on what you use, the controls' experience is different. I use an XBOne controller and pressing RB to do the dash felt awkward at first.
[Overall]
Eliminating the history of creating this game, this is a very solid $20.00 platformer. A true spiritual successor to Megaman. As a Kickstarter, it is dissapointing af. I would recommend it if you really seek the old Megaman thrill.
But still, there are a lot of poor character (personality) designs for me. Get it for the gameplay. Worth your $20.

Well, after about 30 hours of play (not consecutive) and about 3 worlds, here's what I have to say.
Factorio is a game that lets you build huge "bases" that start with mining raw minerals from the ground like iron and copper, then mive them along conveyor belts to be processed, where they can then be put into factories, which will automatically craft more complex items and components for you. You can build refineries and chemical plants to refine oil and create plastic for advanced electronics, create labs to research new tech, build walls and turrets to defend your base from aliens, and build robots that connect to a logistic network, which can be used to transport materials, fight aliens, and even build entire bases and structures from blueprints using signals.
This game is responsible for some of the greatest fun i've had, but i'll warn you: if you're looking for a FPS-alien killing game, get outta here. This game also challenges your mind with base design, because believe it or not, there's such a thing as a bad base design. You have to arrange mines, furnaces, conveyor belts and factories, along with other structures. My first two worlds were absolute disasters, because I did not have the forsight to organize chests and allow my factories easy access to resources. You can only have so many pipes and belts in one area. My third world was better, after watching some youtubers and some thinking. As you play the game, it will only get easier. My advice is to play the tutorial, all the way through. It will help you immensely with learning how to craft items, how basic electricity and research works, etc. I only played through the basic controls tutorial and I regret it. This game also features multiplayer, which is simple to use and can hold dozens of players. I belive one server had over 100 players at once.
Now, last but definitely the polar OPPOSITE of least, mods. This game features a wide variety of mods, such as extra ores, more gun turrets, better aliens, and tons of other things. I tried out a set of mods called "Bob's Mods" which has mods for pretty much every conceivable aspect of the game, from ores to crafting to organization and base layout. As soon as you get the hang of the game and have the controls down, I highly recommend using mods. And the game has a built-in mod browser that makes it very easy to search for mods, install them, and toggle them on or off from within the game. This thing puts Fallout 4's mod support to shame. It's simple and cleanly designed, yet it gets the job done. The only catch is, you have to make an account on their website, which they will prompt you for. I have all of Bob's mods installed and they definitely improve the game, by adding so much more for you to do. I find it is very easy to lose 4+ hours in this game without realizing it, though it may be just me.
I could say a whole lot more, but I figure the 4 10-year-olds who started reading this have moved on already. So i'll make a tl;dr and get it over with.
TL;DR:
PROS:
-Frequent updates
-Challenging and fun gameplay
-Solid programming
-Fairly good community base (getting bigger every day)
-Excellent communication between devs and the community
-Randomly generated worlds, customizable terrain generation
-Near-infinite different number of ways to build your base and beat the game
CONS:
-Combat AI for aliens is somewhat lacking
-Very easy for bases to become clustered and confusing, making it difficult to expand
-Logistics and Circuit networks are explained poorly in the tutorial, if at all
-can become repetitive after dozens of hours of play, without the use of mods
Overall, I would have to give this game an 8/10 or 4 out of 5 stars. It's an entertaining game that stimulates your mind and is a great way to spend a saturday evening. Or an entire weekend. I won't judge. It gets updated frequently, the devs never pull a "Valve" and make changes nobody asked for, and the game requires fairly low processing power to run. I can play it with decent graphics on my 1.5ghz mac, and with something better it runs incredibly smooth. But it has room to improve, like any other game. I highly recommend this to anyone who is looking for something different. Similar to Rimworld.

Keen Software House brings us yet another "Engineering" game. This time however not in space but sort of safely on the ground.
Those who are familiar with Space Engineers will certainly enjoy this game, the controls feel very much the same and the building mechanics ave a lot in common. However, there are some very vital differences, I'll list them later on.
Those who are new to the "Engeneering" saga of KSH may need to put in a little more effort to get the hang of the controls and building mechanics but with a bit of perserverence everyone get's the of this game.
The game is still in pre alpha, this means that everything is subjected to change, and crashes are not always inevitable. The game runs smoothly tough and feels like a proper early acces title. KSH is known for updating Space Engineers weekly, the same will probably happen to Med. Engineers.
The major building mechanic differences:
1) You can choose to build objects "off the grid" wich means they are not snapping to the ground or other objects, this means you can build objects that are moveable by e.g. walking in to them or making moving contraptions.
2) You can now build multiple pieces of wall and a like in 1 bulding square. Buildings get more compact that way, something that is still not available in Space Engineers.
3) Large and small blocks can easily be build on or to eachother without uses of converters and the sorts.
4) Properly breaking objects, walls and the like.
5) Optional (but recommended) building integrety wich means you got to really plan your builds to make sure they don't break under they own weight.
TL;DR:
It's a great and promissing pre alpha game that will certainly warm your heart if you like building, planning, medieval styles and a great dev team that updates their games reguarly and listens to feedback.

**My hours played appear low due to a technical issue - you can read about this and other issues at the bottom of the review.**
At the time of writing this review, The Force Awakens comes out tomorrow! I can't wait to see it. Since you're in the future, did you enjoy it? I'll bet you did. Is Luke a bad guy or something, what the hell is up with that? I hope he's in the movie for more than 5 minutes, or my future self is gonna be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥
Anyway. in the spirit of Star Wars enthusiasm, and since my Star Wars game reviews seem to be more popular than when I♥♥♥♥♥♥on Call of Duty games, I decided to cross this game off my backlog a short 7 years after its release.
So does it hold up in 2015? Yes and no.
Right off the bat, you can tell FU lacks the polish of the other titles I mentioned. Or the polish of any AAA game, for that matter. The first level has you fighting wookies who jump around platforms and fall off of them regularly, or trip over their own legs and have trouble getting up. The stormtroopers on your side of the battle get stuck in foliage and shoot in the wrong direction. (I guess in that sense the game is just like the movies.)
FU is a hack-n-slash in a similar style to Devil May Cry, Ninja Gaiden, Metal Gear Rising, Castlevania: Lords of Shadow, and God of War. Since I prefer those series based on gameplay, it's really the Star Wars branding that makes this game worth recommending to fans. The story is so-so, but the acting is well done and the characters are fun. Vader plays a central role and is voiced pretty convincingly, and the Emperor makes a few appearances. The show stealer is your sidekick droid though, who has been programmed to both help you and also cheerfully kill you in order to keep your senses alert. It's fun to have a friend around that's super excited about stabbing you to death. Another instance of good characterisation is a whacked-out Jedi recluse that has holed up in a junkyard. You fight him in a recreation of the Jedi Temple he built with trash, and you can Force-throw a scrapmetal version of Yoda into his face if you want. It's good stuff.
The game's unfinished feel is in large part due to the physics engine, which is equal parts ambitious and poorly executed. You'll notice it in the first two minutes of the game, and it never changes. The wonky physics are a part of the fun factor though, since this game's MO is letting you create chaos by using a variety of moves and powers to overkill everything. It's not a tightly balanced combat sim, and I suspect that on harder difficulty levels it would lead to lots of frustration. Targeting enemies and objects is done automatically, so trying to grab one particular thing in a mob of action and then throwing it into another particular thing is oftentimes futile. Since the AI is generally stupid and your character vastly overpowered, it still remains fun to try out the generous amount of moves and combos at your disposal and watching the carnage ensue.
This isn't to say that there isn't any strategy to the combat. Certain enemy types resist certain moves, so the game is pretty good at getting you to use your entire move set. It also rewards variety with bonus points, which in turn allow you to upgrade your character with new moves. In this sense it reminds me of the EXCELLENT and oft-overlooked FPS Bulletstorm (please go play that game, here, I'll make it obvious)
*****BULLETSTORM***** ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, it's the best
which is all about being creative with your killing. The combat is a little bit too repetitive, and there isn't a whole lot else to do besides kill things, but the game's 10 levels are both large and visually varied, which keeps things just interesting enough until the end. Plus, the boss battles throughout are well done.
It's a shame that the PC port is so bad. There is a single graphics option - high quality 'yes' or 'no', and 'yes' still looks poor. Texture pop-in is very close, the game is locked at 30 fps, effects are sparse and cheap, and movement feels stiff. The visual style is what saves the presentation, with environments well detailed, lots of color, and a nice costume change occurring regularly for your character. Star Wars games have had a bad habit of looking very similar to each other despite the movies' frequent tonal shifts, and aside from an early Imperial location typical of Dark Forces and virtually every other Star Wars game in existence, this feels like a visually unique product.
One note about lightsaber combat: it's meh. There is a greater emphasis here on power usage, and I had a much better time with the lightsabers in Jedi Knight II and especially Jedi Academy.
Taken as a whole in these modern times, The Force Unleashed just feels rough around the edges. You can tell Lucas Arts is out of touch with the genre - your character frequently "levels up", yet has no level to speak of. A level up just gives you some points to invest in certain skills. The quick-time events that finish off bosses and certain large creatures are repetitive, lack impact, and just feel sloppy. The sound effects and/or music cut out several times in the later levels.
And the set piece design feels just as unsure. Take this example - an early boss fight occurs inside an observation deck on a spaceship orbiting a planet. At one point the deck tears off the rest of the ship, inverts and begins plummeting down towards the planet, as you and your Jedi enemy fall to the domed glass roof. You can see the planet underneath you and the glass begins to burn and glow as you enter the atmosphere while the Jedi is Force-throwing various objects at you. On paper this sounds like a totally epic set piece, but due to a whole lot of factors, just winds up looking dull, even compared to the original God of War's opening hydra fight from three years prior. Lucas Arts are not the masters of these scripted sequences, and it shows pretty painfully.
Bottom line is this: there's not a whole lot of impressive stuff in the game, but I give it a light recommendation because it's a casual experience that remains the only Star Wars game where you can stylishly demolish everything around you with a true feeling of power.

), and a shorter, summarized version here on Steam.
Gameplay: More of the Sam you come to love, albeit slightly watered down. Guns are more or less the same from SS1, the levels are just as huge and sprawling, but nowhere near the intensity of the waves of SS1. Bosses are pretty good overall. Otherwise, game is still a lot of fun, just not as good as Serious Sam 1. 8/10.
Story: Actual cutscenes this time around, usually a good laugh and generally worth watching. Never becomes anything close to dramatic, which is perfectly fine. 7/10.

Sound: OST not as good as SS1, but still pretty good overall. Very comedic voice acting. Sound design just as good as SS1. 4/5.

Joutn is a visually beautiful game. The artwork alone is a reason to take a look at the game.
The gameplay is generally good if simplistic. You have a basic attack that does very little damage but is fast and a heavy attack that does a lot of damage but is slow along with a few limited special attacks. The puzzles for each level are fun but not too taxing and help a lot with the world building. The bosses are challenging and reminiscent of NES/SNES games but with much better graphics/animation. There is a good variety of bosses and in some ways it reminds me of a Mega Man game (i.e. fire man, ice man ...). Some of the bosses are straight forward to beat on the first go, but others require several tries and a little luck. The boss fights can get a little frustrating when the timing is unforgiving, but it is very in the vein of the old NES/SNES games.
The story is kind of boiler plate--fight stuff because it is there--but the mythological framing is perfect. The Norse setting (with the presumably legit Norse dialogue) are a huge selling point of this game. The game does a great job explaining the different worlds of Norse mythology and a little bit about the inhabitants of those worlds. It focuses mostly on the Jotun and there is one level with dwarves, but it leaves out a lot of other parts (no elves, dark or otherwise). I've read a few books of stories, but am no expert on Norse Mythology, and the game does include some things that I had never heard of (specifically the part about the eagle, the falcon, and the squirrel on the Yggdrasil level)
I paid around ten dollars for the game and got about ten hours of gameplay from it. I don't think it has much replay-ability, but I think it is a pretty good value by that calculation.
If the developers read this review: Great Job! I hope you consider extending the game to tell more stories of Norse Mythology or applying a similar story telling framework to other types of mythologies. All in all, the game did a great job showing how video games can augment narrative.

This game is seriously cool. Why? Because it has a lot of things a game should have. Beautiful graphics? Check. Wonderful soundtrack? Check. Intuitive gameplay? Check. Facinating plot, with well written characters? Check. Let's break those elements down one by one.
The aesthetics of the game oscillates between Art Deco grandeur with nods to Gustav Klimt's golden phase and stark white and red minimalism. Somehow the designers of the game manages to make them work together to dramatic effect. There is a plot relavent reason for the contrasting styles in the game and as the story progresses one aesthetic will come to dominate the other. Yet no matter what part of the game you are on, the styles never seem to clash. In fact, this is probably one of the prettiest games I have encountered this year, on par with The Room Series and The Vanishing of Ethan Carter (both of which are highly recommended and on Steam). This is especially true with the cutscenes. You can tell the pictures were painstakingly handpainted and they make for lovely wallpaper.
Okay, I know that tastes in music can vary widely between people, so I will leave a link to the
I personally loved how there are different versions of the songs depending on what state of gameplay you are in. There is the full song for when you are walking around and a paired down version for when you are planning your moves. Which brings me to the next topic.
I have never played a game quite like this before. Imagine a third person shooter in which you plan your moves first. Not like "Okay, let's pause the game and plan my next moves." No. Planning is a gameplay mechanic that you are encouraged to exploit.This is because Red is a small woman carrying a weapon that is almost as big as her and she doesn't move all that quickly. With planning however she could execute all her moves almost instantanously. So one can describe the game as a turn based third person shooter.
The game is very easily picked up after a short tutorial. The weapon itself is loaded with different abilities that can be stacked and comboed for maximum effect. During the planning phase the game will predict the damage dealt to a particular enemy; however, it is only a prediction as enemies move, gain shields, etc. Therefore a bit of overkilling is recommended sometimes, especially for boss fights.
To justify the unusual gameplay there is a very unusual plot. Personally I loved playing the game and guessing what is going on. There is always a degree of ambiguity about the game with even the characters guessing wrong what is going on. In fact the plot is so complicated I recommend playing the game twice. Seriously. Maybe even three times. I cannot discuss much about the plot without spoiling something. Just play the game.
But I can tell you about the game is that it has really good characters. The protagonist, Red, isn't one to take things beaten down. She is one of the few female protagonist with her own agency outside even what the players want for her. She is her own woman. She needs no man. I love her for it. And the narration of Sword Boyfriend is not to be missed. He has a snarky personality with something to say for almost all situations. It is he who provides the narration and background information for the game. And the villians? They are not who you think they are.
Tl;dr: this is an unusally cool game with gorgeous graphics and wonderful characters. Need I say more?

This game, if you can even call it that, is really bad. Like,
bad. I have quite a few reasons why. Let's begin, shall we?
The graphics in this game aren't terrible, but they aren't great either. There are only two animations I have issues with, and those are the fire and the explosion animations. Jesus, they look terrible! It seems like those animations would be used in a cliclé cartoon rather than a video game that's supposed to be something like Mega Man. I would say I prefered fire and explosions from the classic NES games, and that's really saying something. The graphics for the floor get much worse as you turn down your settings, but I couldn't notice a difference in anything else, really.
This game runs really badly for me. Even if all of my settings are turned all the way down to low, I can't play this game without getting lag spikes every five seconds. That gets extremely annoying after a while. My computer isn't bad, because I can run Grand Theft Auto 5 much better than I can run this game. Optomization of this game could be much better. If this was my only issue, I would buy it on Xbox One or something and play it there, but it isn't.
I really hate the gameplay in this game. When you first start, it feels like it'll be like a classic Mega Man game, except for the guy in the lab coat standing right in front of you. I have no idea how he didn't die, considering the streets we're running on are being invaded by robots of all shapes and sizes. Enemies are harder than ever to kill, which wouldn't be much of a problem, except for the fact that you have two not very efficent options of getting rid of them. You can either shoot at the robots until they just die, or you can dash into them (when they're "stunned," mind you) to get rid of them. I hate this so much. It seems pointless to just keep shooting at them, but it's even worse when you have to run directly at them to kill them. What game does that? What game? Another issue I have is the grunts your character makes when you fall off of a box. You grunt when you land from a box? A FREAKING BOX?! Seriously! I'm a human being, and I don't grunt in pain when I jump off of something that's a few inches above my height. This guy is a cyborg. It shouldn't hurt him to land, much less off of a box that's only a few inches taller than him. This game removed the slide as well as charging up the buster, and those two options would have been very helpful.
So, basically, robotics have advanced greaty over the years, which was just perfect when the world fell into chaos and panic, because they were used to keep everything in order! So, people were getting stressed out and stuff because of "peace keeping measurements" (which was basically just bringing in robots), and someone decided to start a "Battle Colosseum." I mean, I can't really see how on earth this would help, but okay, let's just go with it. So, Dr. White (Ha Ha) created 9 robots to battle in this event, and they all placed very highly. To nobody's surprise, an act of cyber terror was unleashed, and nearly all the robots went rogue. They then took over the world. Original story. Anywho, the virus continues to spread, and somehow, Beck, AKA Mighty No. 9, remains unaffected. I don't know either. He was the "weakest link" and now the fate of the world rests on him. Fun times. To be honest, I didn't really care for the story.
One thing I hate about this game is the lack of keyboard support. On the main menu, the game only displays the controller controls, which leads me to believe it would take me a while to learn the keyboard controlls, assuming they aren't displayed in-game.

I really want to like this game. I am a huge megaman fan and have played all of the games besides the battle network series.
From the stand point of a kickstarter backer I am disapointed in the game. I believe that Inafune got caught up in the moment and attempted to bite off WAY more than he could chew and that led to the game falling way short of expectations. If the game had been developed for only a few consoles or only PC like intended the game would be amazing instead of a dissapointment.
Attempting to pull myself from the bias of being a Backer this game is not terrible.
Despite what people say the graphics are not bad. Sure they look nothing like the pre aplha build that Comcept showed after 7 days of development but this is assumed because the game needed to be toned down to be used on the other consoles.
The controls (when not spamming the dash) are tight. Not NES Megaman 2 tight but the precision is there and you can control Beck smoothly jumping and dodging shots is not a problem. Platforming is a breeze.
The story itself is a simple story that is definetly leaving itself open for a sequel. Probably one of the higher points is how the Mighty Numbers interact with eachother throughout the game.
The music while it is not nearly as memorable as the 8 and 16 bit tracks of Megaman and Megaman X is enjoyable but unfortunately can get drowned out by what is going on during the stage.
My biggest complaint with the game is the dash. Clearly the game was designed for speed running. It punishes you for playing safe by not rewarding you with Health Tanks. The dash feels com,pletely different from MMX and it is easily spammable. There was one stage that had an updraft and I was able to dash all the way to the top without touching a platform. And there are many times when I was unable to control the dashes slipping off of platforms and desperately tring to avoid pitfalls.
The game has found itself in a tricky position. It tries to identify as a new megaman game but it tries so hard to be different that it strays from the formula I love just enough. Give this game a try. I believe that this series *knock on wood* has potential. It just gets taking some getting used and despite how the kickstarter campaign went I have no regrets backing this product.
A game with ALOT of potential. Excited to see what the future holds for this game.

Quite frankly, I don't understand the hate for this game at all. I'm a long time Megaman fan and I've played damn near every Megaman game that's come out and I love MIghty No 9. They gameplay is reaaaaaally fast once you get the hang of it. I like the controls, but it is a bit of a shift from Megaman games as far as physics go. I got used to it relatively quick, and I'm loving how it plays. It is difficult and at times frustrating, but once you hit the flow and the groove of the game you sail through stages blowing everything up.
Love the way you can switch forms in this. When you beat a boss, you don't just get one power like in Megaman and Megaman X, instead you get a different set of attacks depending on the form. It adds a little extra depth that I appreciated. I love the way dash system works once I got used to it. It was an adjustment, and I'd reccomend remapping dash to a trigger instead of a bumper o controller.  As far as the length of the game, I'd say it's on par with the Megaman games this game is looking to keep in spirit with. It can be short or long depending on how you do things, but replaying runs has always been enjoyable to me.
I understand that many are upset about the delays and how the Kickstater went, which is can definitely understand, but those delays were due to productions issues...not adding content. It's unfortunate that this game had trouble getting out, but I think people's feelings about the process of getting the game to release has translated into poor reviews. I'm not trying to say people who are upset are wrong, but I hope that the negativity of the process doesn't affect what to me is a very enjoyable game. This is Comcepts first go at releasing their on game, so it isn't guarenteed to go smoothly, but they've added features that Megaman hasn't done before. Multiplayer Megaman that isn't turn based? Chaotic, but awesome.
I love Megaman. I love Mighty No. 9. If you like Megaman or fast paced challenging 2.5d platformers, get it.
Give the game a chance. I still believe in Keiji Inafune and I still believe in Comcept.

A spiritual successor to the classic Mega Man games, Mighty No. 9 stars Beck, a robot tasked with defeating his eight siblings to save humanity.  With each robot defetated, Beck gains a new ability, typically elemental, as well as the robot's assistance in stages.
I have been thoroughly enjoying this game.  The story is very reminiscent of the classic Mega Man games, while the gameplay itself is closer to the more fast-paced Mega Man X games.  In particular is the dash mechanic, a feature used heavily in the Mega Man X games, but no also used to gain points and temporary buffs from enemies.  Naturally, there are plenty of obstacles in the way, particularly the purple, electrified spikes that kill instantly on contact.  Another feature inherited from the Mega Man X games is that defeating the robots in the "correct" order affects the stages, allowing easier and quicker navigation.
The game also features voice acting throughout.  This is a nice addition, allowing play to continue while listening to the characters' commentary, rather than pausing to read the text.  I will say that Cryosphere's ice puns did make me laugh, and cringe, thinking about the what killed the dinosaurs...
THE ICE AGE!
Those familiar with the Mega Man games may well find this a nostalgia trip, wrapped in a new, colorful coat of graphics and animation.  Give it a whirl and see if you have the bolts to save the world. \m/

Gameplay- The Force Unleashed's main goal was to make the player feel like they are a sith lord, being able to use different, powerful force based attacks. In that aspect the game delivers, but this all gets boring after a while, as combat is rediculousy easy, I'm sure anyone can beat the game without upgrading too much. Combat is not satifying at all, as you find yourself killing waves and waves of enemies without trying. During the second part of the game different variants of storm troopers arrive, in order to kill them you have to use a particular technique, this gets boring FAST. Most boss fights are pretty lame as well, as many of the bosses limit or restrict your uses of the force powers, or they require constant button mashing. This makes the boss fights boring and not rewarding, a good example of a well designed boss fights would be the colossuses in Shadow Of The Colossus, all the bosses were unique. Mr Freeze from Batman Arkham city would be another one, as Freeze adapts to your attacks, evades, and movements. It was a multi step fight with out lame QTE sequences or out of placed cutsences, which were everywhere in The Force Unleashed.
Story- The story is mediocre, which is really sad because the Star Wars universe is very interesting. The main character Galen Marek is very dull, and has no emotions, a good comparison to Marek would be Connor from Assasin's Creed III, which is not a good thing. Other characters are not much better etheir, everyone just seemed so boring and unteresting. The missions are not much better ethier, they all feel the same, as you slaughter waves and waves of enemies. level design was flawed, as many of the levels looked very similar and were boring to play through. The Force Unleashed has two endings, both were terrible, the good ending being a little bit better than the bad one, but thats not saying much at all. In the end you find yourself not being able to make any decisions as the game does that for you, but it really does not matter as the build up and the characters along the way were boring and painfully average.
Overall opinion- The Force Unleashed is game made only for Star Wars fans, if you want a hack and slash game, go ahead and buy DMC, it's much better than this. If you desire a game that explores the lore and mythos of Star Wars, this not the game for you etheir. The people that would enjoy the Force Unleashed would be hardcore star wars fans and people that want a easy game where you feel like a god. At the end of the day Star Wars The Forced Unleashed is a disappointing  game, it could have been great but instead it fell short, The Force Unleashed is not a terrible game, but it's not a good one etheir.
Rating- 6/10 Average game.

Meet Steve, a blocky, cube-headed little robot. Taught to love, not fight. He is quirky, cute, and oh so loveable, and I've never even seen him. And meet Olive, my companion bot. She shows a little more complex emotion than Steve, but is just as likeable. Olive wanted to love me, but I wouldn't allow it. I was married, and although I accept robot marriage and robot-human romance, I was not up for it myself. She felt rejected. Steve was clueless, like a happy, yet genius, child. Though Olive was hurting, with her advanced emotions coming into play. One day, we were just taking a walk together, Olive and I. She asks what she can do with her life. I say she must look after Steve, as I am dying. She didn't want that, so I ask what she wanted to do. That's when she replied "Whatever I want," and then ran off without another word. That was the last I'd seen of Olive, after her murder trial, after all her learning and experiences with me, Steve, and my wife. Her and Steve, my creations. My children.

I don't normally enjoy things enough to review them, so bare with me here.
My first 'playthrough', if I could call it that, it was much more of a readthrough, of 'Choice of Robots' took me just over three hours to get through, and likely could have taken much longer, assuming that I wasn't terrible and took so many 'bad' decisions, I'd say my first read could have easily lasted me four or maybe even five hours. It should go without saying, that there is an immense amount of replayability in a game such as this. Which is to mention, replaying this is definitely something I intend on doing, but I'm not sure that I'll be able to recreate the attachment & bond I had with my three foot tall, human-like, winged 'Ariel' with multitool hands, whom was vehemently opposed to conflict as a result of my actions.
See, Choice of Robots is a game where your choices can influence the course of humanity so heavily, that the sense of creating a story just for yourself lends to a sense of wonder and beauty that I haven't really experienced in many conventional books or text-based games in perhaps forever. Even though I could tell from about halfway through that my choices were going to lead me down a seemingly 'undesirable' route, (considering that my presumption was that I would shatter Capitalism and create a Utopia) I still continued to read on and make decisions based on the situation, as the writing and sense of achievement is so fantastically constructed, that I didn't find myself feeling sad, or upset at the fact that I might not get that 'good' ending, instead, I felt happy that in what is undoubtably a story of such scale & grandeur; mine was a story revolving around me, my friends & my family. This is what, in my eyes, we'd call a testament to the brilliance of the writing.
I can't speak of the aspect of how destroying the world may turn out, or how imposing a singularity upon humanity would be, but in my playthrough, the process of building up a robot in my own image, including its gender & naming it, right up to the viewpoint it had on the world, made interacting with my three foot tall companion really something quite special. Taking my creation which, at this point, had evolved into something so much more than just that, to the park, and observing the body language she gave off whilst she learned to properly kick off on a swing to propel herself up into the air was certainly pleasant. But knowing that our actions had turned her from being a military-backed weapon, into a video game loving creature of empathy? That was something else entirely; something I've not experienced before.
If you are even remotely interested in robotics, sentience, world politics and business practices, I'd heavily advise picking up this game. Even if you are just looking for a great story, you definitely won't be disappointed. I think the myriad of Overwhelmingly Positive reviews such as this give evidence to that.
My one gripe with this game, if anything, would perhaps be its length, which I don't even feel justified in saying, especially after just one playthrough. But in my particular instance, it felt as if certain sections were rushed, and that at quite a lot of stages, I didn't get the chance to sit and talk, explore and influence quite as much as I'd have liked to with other characters & situations. But this is completely forgiveable given the scale of the game and the immense replay value.

Serious Sam 2,a campaign game and a FPS shooter is the sequel to Serious Sam: The Second Encounter. The main objective of this game is to bring down Mental and his vile armies. For that, the player has to battle through thick jungles, murky swamps, frozen tundra, and futuristic cities.  The player is able to obtain better gear and epic vehicles as time progresses.  Tired of campaign? No worries, Serious Sam 2 offers co-op and deathmatch chaos. Besides that, its soothing soundtrack and scenic levels motives the player to carry on their endeavour.
+ Easy to control and navigate the character.
+ Cartoony graphics.
+ Beautiful maps and environment.
+ Unique maps and levels, battle accross more than 40 levels!
+ Contains different "species" of enemies including bosses.

I originally played this game back when it first came out and was addicted to it then.
15 years later I pick it up again and still addicted to it. It is one of the better sims out there.
Pros -
A lot of customization available.
A lot of thought put into development.
Just fun to build roller coasters.
Cons -
15 years later and the game still  has some of the same bugs like:
Losing control of your mouse when you quit the game. To regain control you have to right click, which isn't intuitive.
Still freezes when it saves sometimes and randomly freezes, but never crashes.
Mechanics nearest the rides that need to be fixed don't do anything.

Pros:
. Addicting
. Very nice graphics/sound aesthetic
. Hundreds of hours of gameplay, not including replay value
. Feeling of progression through scenarios that the sequel does not have
. The satisfying feeling of seeing people enter and interact with an amusement park that you built
. You can create your own theme park!
Cons:
. Selections of attractions to build feel a bit limited at times
. Isometric view with no shadows makes building/landscaping a bit tedious at times
. Scenario objectives mostly constrained to achieving a certain number of guests/park value
. Most of the scenarios are very easy (however this doesn't take away from the fun at all) while the others are extremely difficult. Essentially, not a great difficulty curve.
The pros overshadow the cons. In other words, the pros enhance the experience more than the cons take away from it.
Extra note: If you've never played before, make sure you look up some strategies or gameplay footage (Zisteau being the best to watch in my opinion) before you do. Trust me.

This is the part where I abuse a game I have just played... The game seems to just have re-occurring maps on different stages, say the first stage, it has rails and stairs, throughout the levels on each stage, of which is a bit weird, as you are trying to improve score, so why wouldn't you give the player a different map per level instead of stage, I know they may take some time to make, but it would add a lot more variation. As I said before I used a controller as this game is easier to play with one, but say I didn't run the tutorial, I would have no clue about the controls, as in settings it says nothing, about controller controls
This game is unique, I have never played something like it, and the style is brilliant, the maps are ok, but improvements could be made, The controls may be hard to learn, but when you learn to play the game it is brilliant, I have saw videos, and a friend of mine said he enjoyed playing it also, I would recommend this game to someone who enjoys pixelated, skating games, and also could go under the Indie genre, but I feel the developers have done a wonderful job!

What else even needs to be said at this point? It's pretty bad. This might not be super insightful, but I feel it necessary to at least say SOMETHING to add to the pile. People ought to understand what they're getting into. None of this is even taking into consideration just how harrowing the development process had been. That's a whole other can of worms I don't care to get into.
To be fair, it isn't ALL bad. Despite the rest of the game, I actually sort of like the visuals. They could have used maybe a little more polish(pizza explosions!), but overall it's probably one of the better parts of the game. Take that for what you will.
The music, on the other hand, is completely forgettable. I've already forgotten the music for the various stages and whatnot. You're never really given a chance to appreciate it, anyway - lots of errant sound effects and annoying voice acting yelling over the action. It's like they're ashamed of it.
The actual gameplay is pretty mediocre, as well. It's Megaman at its most barebones, but with the twist of a 'dash' that lets you charge your weapon to be more useful than 'barely at all'. It also has the added bonus of racking up a combo to try and generate as high a score as possible. It's a neat idea, in theory, for promoting multiple playthroughs of even just a couple of the stages.
In practice, however, the stages are so boring that it isn't worthwhile, and enemies are such a non-threat that you can just tank hits and dash through entire sections of the game to get to the boss. It's at complete odds with its Megaman roots, which actively discouraged just ramboing through rooms mashing buttons. There was a lot more thought put into enemy designs and their placement. To use an example, this game's equivalent of sniper joe *drops* his shield the second you shoot it. It's such a mess.
I played three of the stages, and while they were all unique on paper, its few ideas just don't add up to anything because of the aforementioned problems. There were a couple moments that made me slow down, but it's because of how poorly they're handled. For example, there's a water section where you're meant to fall through a tunnel of instant-death spikes. Pretty par for the course for old Megaman vets. This one laughs at you by putting a section right underneath the camera where you have to dash out of the way of a set of spikes in order to progress, and if you don't know it's there, I guarantee it shaves a life off of your total. The other was a set of buzzsaws you were meant to 'crouch dash' under, but what they meant to say was 'lightly press forward for several seconds to get as close to the instant-death saws as possible in order to dash, just barely, to the other side'.
Of the three bosses I ended up reaching, i'd say none of them were fun to fight. Apart from the sniper I encountered, the other two had embarrassingly annoying voices and they took every chance they could to screech and giggle and whatever during the fight. If it was meant to make me more aggressive and prone to mistakes, it 100% worked. Really, though, I imagine they're all a real slog to get through, and that's because they're ALL(ALL OF THEM) allowed to regenerate their lifebar at various checkpoints during the boss fight. It just feels like a slap in the face. If you triggered their 'glowing so you have to dash into them at this point' mode at a really bad time, chances are you won't be able to reach them or capitalize...and then you'll have all of your progress undone. To call it infuriating is purely an understatement.
I'd say 'let this be a warning to kickstarter backers', but I had certainly been roped in from the start, as well. It's a shame I couldn't get my money back as I saw the decline during development, but here we are.

A surprising freebie on Steam, which is actually a lot more fun that expected.  Alien Swarm follows the genre of the "alien monster" squad shooter, with a 2.5D tactical build.  Take control of one of four squad members with a particular specialty (heavy weapons, healing, etc) and kill bugs.
The game is simple and robust, with a clean engine and UI.  Weapons are definitely manageable with a bit of variety beyond the skins.  Some decent execution of tactics can be encouraged, with fire lines and herding of aliens, which supports the tactically minded quite well.
The game ships with an open editor for custom maps, and modding is given pretty much a big thumbs up to encourage custom content.  Decent graphics quality (given it's a free game) and sound is well-developed with a good selection of stock components.  The game offers a gradual increase in challenge level, up to and including 'hardcore'.
It's short, and there's almost no plot to speak of, but can't complain about that in a decent-quality free game.  The challenge rating can be quite high, which can be a turn off for some players.
Mostly forgotten not long after being released, which can result in long, empty queues in multiplayer, which in turn means some later missions are nigh-impossible without assistance.
Revamping this so it features more in the queue would be a good move by Valve (who made it).
7/10, though that's including it being free.
