Amazing game with a novel and well-executed concept, great art, and interactive gameplay. This game is a great example of an indie game that isn't too complicated mechanics-wise, but manages to keep it interesting and is executed in a way that still makes it great, despite being 'simple'. Papers, Please gives a great narrative about immigration and is much deeper than I thought. A solid 8/10 overall.
+ Interesting and gripping plot. Many possible endings and really makes you face moral decisions about immigration and law.
+ Consistent art that is pixelated but still entertaining and doesn't get old.
+ Gameplay is simple but still varies enough to keep it interesting, and feels interactive.
+ Not too intense, easy to put 30mins into a day without getting addicted.
- Can be frustrating and tedious at times (I'd argue this is by design, though).
- If you're not too familiar with the game, the plot can develop without you really understanding what's going on. Some endings are inaccessible unless you start the game over, or know what to do from the start.
Overall, awesome game. I will be recommending this to my friends both to play and to take inspiration from as a not-too-complicated indie game that has a great and novel concept and delivery.

This game... wow, this game! While my own account only has 18 hours or so shown (as of the writing of this review), I have spent many, many more hours (close to 80-90 hours) pouring over the details of my factory and how it has grown into a town of sorts, that spans a good portion of the continent that I live on.
My factory (or should I say factories at this point?) has a living, breathing history built into it and I can point out how everything formed. It's to the point where you can tell a lot about the person that built that factory just by looking at the layout and what parts they're building, etc.
This game is definitely for the OCD of us, especially if you are a problemsolver; unfortunately, I'm not smart enough to completely automate EVERYTHING but for people that have the time, intelligence, and willpower to do so, it's certainly possible, especially with the components that you can build later on that allow you to set limits and boolean functions to keep production lines running smoothly. I also love the research trees in this game, with a lot of new components and upgrades to look forward.
My biggest gripe right now is the single player "campaign mode" just seems to be more like a bunch of maps thrown together, rather than a flowing narrative with a map that evolves with you, at this time. Well, I must say, this is much, much better than all that Skyrim ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.  Old-school dungeon-grinding, with a bit of new-school twist.

For the record, I haven't played many games like this in, well, almost DECADES...so just to clarify, I'm not really up with what the dungeon-delving kids are into these days, bar the aforementioned Elder Scrolls nonsense and the very, very excellent Darkest Dungeon.  I am pleased to note, however, that this is more than a mere "dungeon hack"...there's lots of puzzles and traps, and interesting and strategic ways to fight and handle monsters, so it's already ten times more intelligent than, say, a Borderlands game (not that that's any great feat, but bear with me).

In case you're wondering how it all works, your party moves through the dungeon in a limited version of a first person perspective (you can only move forward, left, right, and back; then turn to face in a different direction, ninety degrees at a time) and the combat is half-way between a turn-based approach and a more real-time urgency.   What this all adds up to, best as I can tell, is a bit of a best-of-both-worlds approach to dungeoneering: That is to say, it's not TOO much of a game of reflexes and/or hand-eye coordination, but still has more moment-to-moment suspense and atmosphere than one could muster with a strictly turn-based situation.
It also offers a nice middle ground between so-called "casual" gaming and something a bit more involved, not to mention a decent compromise between "lighter" fantasy elements and something a teensy weensy bit "darker"...so if it's a game with that kind of balance you're looking for, then by all means, step inside.

Me personally, I was in the market for a bit of a nostalgic dungeon crawl with some slightly spiffier, more modern graphics, and that's precisely what I got; so for the price of three bucks (on severe sale) I was well-chuffed.  In all honesty, though, it's probably worth the full asking price even if you play it through just the once - it's certainly LONG enough! - and it furthermore has a fair dose of replayability, thanks to customisable characters and multiple difficulty levels and so forth.  It's far from the Second Coming, and gets awfully grind-y at times, but it's pretty darn good for what it is.  Know what you're signing up for, and chances are you won't be disappointed.

OlliOlli is a good example of a clever game idea executed poorly. The concept is simple: you control a skateboarder through various 2d levels and perform tricks based off of jumps and rails, racking up points through carefully executed combos and landings. The controls are fairly straightforward and the levels aren’t too hard to pick up….at least until later on when the difficulty curve goes through a sudden spike.
In the last two areas of the game the developers seemed to want to punish the player as much as possible by requiring absolute perfection on every single jump and grind. This would be alright by me except the timing for a perfect landing or grind seems to differentiate between parts of a level and hitting the directional or landing button before contact at a certain pixel distance will net a different result when it should be exactly the same every time. This made the second level of the final area absolutely impossible for me and earlier parts extremely difficult to pass.
It doesn’t help that for the hard levels, the developers thought putting the most brutal part near the beginning was a good idea. Forcing the player to die over and over again before they even make it 10 seconds into the level is really ♥♥♥♥♥♥ IMO and just results in a lot of frustration for when you finally get past it and then die another few seconds later, only to return to struggling with that first 10 seconds. Finally, I had stability issues with the game whenever my connection to steam servers wasn’t so good and it would crash to desktop several times.
I won’t be getting the sequel to this one unless the engine and level design get a serious overhaul.

This game is truly fantastic. It's one of the last well-rounded shooters, in that it has both a great single player and a great multiplayer.
The single player story is simply concerned about letting the player have fun and have a few laughs. It's a rather lengthy story with varied missions, and most importantly, doesn't take itself too seriously. Unlike most other fps games out there, you actually end up liking the guys in your squad, and they all seem like more than meatheads with guns killing the poorly equipped foreigners. There are certain parts in each level where the game lets you ♥♥♥♥ around and destroy as much of the level as possible, showing off the great destructibility in the game, and letting you have a bit of a rest. Whoever designed the campaign deserved a raise, because it's great.
When the game first came out, the multiplayer had some issues, and that kind-of tarnished its reputation. However, patches for the pc version have completely fixed the problems, and the game plays excellently. The maps range from
to medium sized, the vehicles are balanced, the guns feel great, and it's really easy to find servers. A large draw is the destructibility - maps are completely unrecognizable after a round. No cover is completely safe, and there is a great feeling when you blow up a wall, run through the still settling dust, and empty a mag into an opponent. Warning, BFBC2 is not like COD: you don't snap to sights, you feel heavy while running, and a medic will nulify all of your hard earned kills.
BF3 or BF4 may be more familiar games, as they stick to the conventions of modern military shooters, but BFBC2 is just pure, dumb fun. It's a unique experience that I cannot recommend more.

Since this game is nearly identical in terms of mechanics to the Wargame series, I will be making nearly direct comparissions between the two
I've had my eye on this game since a few months before it was released. Being a huge Paradox and Wargame fan, and an even bigger fan of WW2 strategy games, I had high hopes. I waited until the winter sale when this game was 50% off at $20 before purchasing. Having seen many (positive) video reviews prior to, I was confident I wouldn't be disappointed in this game
The first issue I came across with this game was the way they handled conquest mode. In Wargame, there are a multitude of sectors scattered across the map, each one worth a certain amount of points. To capture this sector you needed a command vehicle to be stationary within the sector. Some sectors (mainly on larger maps) could even allow you to deploy land, air, or sea vehicles. In Steel Division however, the conquest game-mode consist on a single horizontal line at the center of the map, which fluxuates depending on units advancing or retreating close to the front line. This means that the map is initially only "broken" into 2 sectors. Yours, and the enemies. Now yes, it is possible to flank enemy units, and cut them off from their main sector, which gives them a penalty, but my initial point is still valid in that there will only be 2 sectors typically. The way to win the conquest game-mode is to control a larger portion of the map than your opponent, until you reach a specified amount of points (or the timer runs out).
Destruction mode in Wargame was very similar to conquest, in that there were still separate sectors present, each worth a point value, but these points were put towards your logistics. The benefit to these split sectors in Wargame, was the fact that you and your allies could be spawning in 2 totally different corners of your side of the map, which made for some more tactical planning useful. In Steel Division, you are simply given the entire,undivided space to spawn units with your allies. Both games perform identically in terms of victory conditions, and logistics settings in Destruction mode. Unfortunatley, logistics have been dumbed down significantly in this game. In Wargame, you could place F.O.B.'s (or Forward Operating Bases) that served as a hub for your units to get ammo, fuel, and repairs (EVERY vehicle in Wargame has a limited fuel quantity, in addition to limited ammunition). In Steel Division, all vehicles have an infinite amount of fuel, and F.O.B.'s are no longer present. Another strange thing I've noticed with this game (or maybe it is the result of laziness) is the fact that transport vehicles
upon dismounting your troops or towed guns! If a truck is carrying a squad of men in it, the moment you tell them to disembark, the truck just disappears, and
be used to again to transport your troops. The same goes with your towed guns. If you tow an AT gun to a position, and wind up advancing, you're going to want to move that AT gun up too, right? Well...the AT gun crew now has to haul the gun on foot to their destination. I get that transport trucks were sent in as canon fodder in Wargame, but they DID have a useful purpose. If a squad needed to head back to base to rearm, or to advance quickly, you could tell the men to simply get inside of the vehicle and be on their way. That is not the case in this game. The frontline in this game is a
problem with this game, as it eliminates sneaking around your opponet to flank. If the opponent sees the line moving, they know you are advancing. If they see it remains stationary, then they know you are sitting back with your units. It eliminates any sort of strategic planning
My next big gripe with this game was the lack of an armory, or some sort of in-game reference page to read up about the different units within the game. In Wargame, you had an entire menu to browse all units from all nations, and were able to get a brief description about them. In Steel Division, no such menu exists. The closest you can get to this, is to check out the units while creating a deck. Each unit DOES technically have a small (1-3 sentence) section written about them at the bottom their card...but the sentences are "cosmetic" and are only there for looks. Thats right. The little tidbit about the units is so small that you cannot read it, and even if you zoomed in to try and read it, it is not meant to be functional. Why they thought this was a good idea is beyond me. While on the subject of fonts, the font size for things like ammunition calibre in the units info is so ridiculously small, that it really is a struggle to read it, even though it IS intended to be fully functional. Bear in mind I'm a young person with good eyesight, and even I struggle to see this without pressing my face against my moniter.
Now I am used to the plethora of units in the Wargame series, but seeing as how this game takes place in a very specific portion of the Second World War, I had no problem overlooking the lesser quantity of units here. (~1450 units in Wargame Red Dragon, as opposed to ~400 here)
My last gripe I have with this game is the (most likely) ensuing wave of paid DLC they will be releasing. Paradox is known for having a ton of DLC for their games (19 paid DLC for Hearts of Iron 3, 18 for Europa Universalis 4,
for Crusader Kings II). Based on their track record, I have zero doubts in my mind that this game will be receiving a similar treatment. Although these DLC's may fix the issues within this game that I currently have, I still don't think its justified, considering most of their DLC should've been in the base game initially, anyways.

Steel Division is a RTS game set in WW2 Normandy and covers timeline from the D-Day through June, July and April of 1944 ETO. Maps were meticulously recreated using aerial photos from the period up to the point where you can overlay google maps over and it will fit. For someone who is interested in WW2 maps, this is a real treat, as you will have no problems with identifying places from the history books like Ranville, Sainte-Mère-Église, Sainte-Marie-du-Mont, Hermanville-sur-Mer and so on. There is a plethora of maps in many gameplay sizes from small 1v1 up to vast 10v10s featuring entire Sword and Omaha sectors. All maps can be fully zoomed in and out to the point where you will be able to see entire sector of operations, which is amazing.
Game features more than 400 history based units, assigned to number of divisions (US, UK, CAN, POLISH, FRENCH, GERMAN) which fought in Normandy area. Some units are common, some are exclusive to single division giving it more specialized flavor. There are even peculiarities like ex-french vehicles converted and pressed into German Service. Before you get into the battle, you need to compose your division battlegroup - You pick up a division you want to play (mind that a tank division will offer different units and availability than airborne, or infantry division, will play differently and have other strengths, weaknesses and applications). During engagement, not all units are available from the start. Battles are divided into A, B and C phases, where during A phase, only light and recon units are available, while C phase is where you can roll out everything, including the toughest and deadliest heavies. This not only forces player to think about lighter units, that otherwise would have been never picked, but also creates interesting interaction between divisions. For example one division may have large recon detachment and would be a very strong A phase, while others might be composed mostly of C phase tanks, which would force player to play defensively until C phase and unleash hell afterwards.

Steel Division offers 3 single player campaigns (4 long missions each and quite challenging, units carry over from one mission to another), Co-op horde mode - called Breakthrough, Skirmish vs AI (Normal is difficult for newcomers) and large multiplayer component from 1v1 to grand 10v10 spam fest. MP scene is quite stable and lively, with average of 300 players daily, monthly tournaments and a board of competitive ranked elitist drama queens :) (Pro tip - don't use Matchmaker, or you will wait ages to get a game, go to Custom Game and join, or create one and you will be playing in no time). Community is quite helpful, with many guides and even a mentoring initiative. Plenty of content for everyone and knowing Eugen, game will be supported with balancing patches and content DLCs for many more months to come.
Gameplay wise, I would sum it up as Combat Mission meets Starcraft mid road. All distances, ranges and statistics are scaled, so let's say a Panther A, can shoot at 1200 meters with accuracy of 7 and penetration chance of 17. Accuracy and penetration chance rises by 1 point every 100 meters closer to the target and there is also veterancy factor in play. Reason I'm writing this is to show what you can expect after buying the game and to save people disappointment, that the game is not what they expected. In other words, rivet counters, who are after top notch realism need to realize that this is largely arcade game in a historical setting, which sacrifices a lot of details for fast gameplay sake. At the same time Starcraft clickers might feel overwhelmed by the number of different stats and mechanisms they need to master in order to be effective.
This game is heaps of fun if you're into real time strategy or general WW2 setting and a bang for a buck, considering other options on the market. No micro-transactions, no loot box s**t, you get everything you paid for straight away. It's not easy for a casual person and quite challenging, but if you give it a chance and spend some time with it, it's a brilliant experience.
Obviously this review doesn't even try to cover most of game's wonderful features, as it is merely an opinion. Please see below for more comprehensive reviews

I think EUGEN listened to me posting suggestions for a World War 2 version of Wargame. Heh. I like this game, however, the multiplayer community is almost non-existent. I have yet to get on a 10-vs-10 match like in Wargame. The one thing I'm not liking too much is the phases. I wish they would do away with it and do it Wargame style and duke it out with your best units right away. It also results in some balancing issues with the various divisions. From a tactical point of view, the phases also don't really make much sense as I don't think World War 2 was dictated by "phases". They could do it using "era" like in Wargame where certain troops and equipment are only available in later war years. That being said, the game is still enjoyable and I recommend you add this to your WW2 collection. I recommend downloading the mods that allow a Wargame style gameplay.

Really interesting game. What made this game so enjoyable for me is the way that the game puts the player into morally compromising positions. You're forced to think carefully about the decisions you make as they actively shape the world in which the game unfolds, and the wide variety of decision making options throughout each chapter makes you feel fully in control and does a good job of removing the usual feeling of limitation that can be experienced in many decision-based games similar to this. Multiple endings shaped by your decision making and a great storyline ensures that the player gets their money's worth despite the minimalist design, although I can't help but feel that the addition of a soundtrack or illustrations would have made this experience more fulfilling. Absolutely worth the price, but less story-oriented players could easily get bored.

Kind of like a slower paced Bastion with Diablo 3 syndrome where you can only equip 4 abilities at a time, although there's a good reason for this, since every time your health bar is depleted you randomly lose 1 ability that can be recovered after visiting 2 checkpoints. Naturally, lose all your equipped abilities and you die. I thought this was a pretty neat health system.
The game also has it's equivalent of VATS more or less, except in this it's called Turn(), and rather than aiming for an enemy's head, or their left testicle, you carefully plan out a number of moves best suited to the situation, which you will then carry out swiftly upon confirming your turn. After taking a turn though, it does leave you vulnerable until it recovers, during the recovery you can't use most abilities, except for abilities like Jaunt (teleport-dash a short distance away) or Mask (Short term invisibility), so equipping one of the turn recovery friendly abilities is advisable.
You can also mix and match up to 2 abilities per active ability, to grant them side-effects, some work better with others. As well as putting abilities into passive slots for passive abilities. You can also augment the game's difficulty by activating limiters, which make the game harder in certain ways, which also give you bonus exp.
Overall, I liked Bastion a bit more than this, but Transistor is still a fantastic and refreshing game.

Disclosure: Have not Beaten all the bosses, or even challenged them all yet, however I doubt beating them will change your impression and enjoyment of the game positively or negatively, and they are all immensely challenging from what I have seen so far.
This game is beautifully hand drawn, has a great art style and direction, and can be described as a peaceful, yet engaging experience, with a heavy emphasis on exploration, and puzzles with a minor emphasis on battles and fighting.
The single hardest level in the game is the second fire level stage with the giants throwing rocks at you, exploding on you, landing on top of you, creating lava bridges. There seems to be a problem with how long the second half of the level is from the last check point compared to every other level in the game, making it feel like a gauntlet, it's approximately a ten to 15 minutes gauntlet, that I had to repeat 6 or 7 times, which felt extremely unrewarding, and was a huge spike in difficulty from the remaning portions of the game.
But I would definitely recommend this game to anyone looking for a very artsy, exploratory, puzzle game, for it's amazing art style, music, and as of this review, boss battles having a very epic feel to them.
The gameplay experience is well worth it's price tag, and the levels feel well balanced with the exception of the aforementioned fire level. The boss battles are incredibly challenging so far. (Tree being, Lightning Being, Viking Gold Mine Creature being) And I have only actually beaten the first boss. (Tree Being) yet still finding myself enjoying every moment of it so far.
A slight complaint is that the power ups feel a little underwhelming and don't seem to particularly help with the boss battles too much, HOWEVER it also means that the boss battles are essentially always challenging, and my guess is that you can probably go for speed runs with enough practice against the bosses without any power ups which might add for some interesting replay value.
Get this game if you are looking for a unique experience, with a very artsy feeling and some interesting difficulty levels. Be prepared for the level with fire giants to potentially ruin your enjoyment of the game however, as it is a really high difficulty spike compared to the rest of the game.

First Impressions video:
Jotun is a boss fighting game, clean and simple. You play as a norse woman who died in a shipwreck and must now fight Norse gods in Jotenheim. The gameplay consists of walking through beautifully drawn landscapes until you come to a boss that you should probably hit with that giant axe you have.
The gameplay in Jotun is okay. You have a standard attack, a power attack, a roll, and a god power. You have to dodge attacks while trying to get shots in (Dark Souls skillz for te win). There are two issues. The small issue is that the game does not tell you the controls. You have to either guess or look in the control mapping. It's not a big issue, but I didn't know how to use my god power for a couple fights.... which was fun...... The other issue is that combat is slow. It doesn;t have a sense of urgency to it that is prevalent in games like Dark Souls and Titan Souls (which I consider to be similar games to this).
The visuals are the best part of this game. They are gorgeous and interesting. Everything has a level of polish that speaks to just how much time the developers put into drawing the pictures. Good for them.
Overall, Jotun is a decent game with beautiful visuals. Don't expect fast paced action, because the action tends to be quite slow. All that being said, it is quite a game.

I know my way around norse mythology and I'm certainly not used to having it so accurately portrayed in popular media. So if you like vikings and their weird believes, check this out! The graphics are gorgous and the atmosphere is very dense. An extra compliment to the developers on how they manage to convey scale in this hand drawn 2D enviroment. The game mostly relies on the Dark Soulsy story telling method of letting you experience the world instead of forcing exposition down your throat (but less cryptic than in Dark souls).
With its 8-10 hours the game doesn't overstay its welcome and forgoes stretching content in favor of a fuller, tighter game experience. Everyone who loves immersive atmospheric games and marvels at the feeling of felling a particularly difficult Boss should definately try Jotun. It's a great game : )

Okay, so I first discovered factorio around august 2016 and I purchased it on September the same year. Because I decided I could do better as the Youtube let's player I had been watching. (I don't remember who the Youtuber was)
Anyway, my previous review was outdated because I wrote it shortly after I bought it. And now, with my four hundred hours worth of gameplay I figure I can give this game another review.
So first up is PLAYABILITY
Early access by its very defenition can be terrible to play but it can also feel like a completed game. (With some things not in the game) This game though it feels complete, stable and is a complete joy to play. As far as I know, most of the major features are in the game but don't quote me on that bit, because I'm not sure.
There ar a huge amount of mods you can download and enable to make the game even more enjoyable. The game in its vanilla state can be a bit easy once you figured out how to setup your base. It gives you a very satisfied feeling when you put the final touch on your setup and you can quote the Big Man from The A-Team and say 'I love it when a plan comes together' (i love that series)
If the game seems to simple if you're watching a let's player on Youtube then there are a LOT of mods that will complicate the game by a LOT.
Right now it's iron ore - > iron plates - > iron gears
That's the vanilla, but with mods it's a much longer cycle to get the same thing.
Right, so if you're thinking of buying the game, you should be asking yourself: what is the point of it and is it worth it?
The answer to the first question is fairly simple. The 'story' (of what little there is) is that you crashed on an alien planet and you must build a rocket to get the hell out of there!
As you know, an industry has polution and the more polution you have, the bigger of a chance you have that your base will be invaded by aliens also known as biters.
The game map is absolutely HUGE and pretty much infinite for all intents and purposes. There is a map editor to create your own perfect map if you have your own ideas how to make your base.
Right, so I already said that you need to get of the planet by building a rocket right? Well, BEFORE you can do that, you must build yourself an enttire industry. You start with limited tools and do everything by hand and in the end EVERYTHING is automated.
The second question: (is it worth it?) is pretty much an undeniable YES! The game doesn't have a steep learning curve at all and is easy to learn once you figure things out. I would advice to NOT impulse buy this without watching some videos first. I bought a game similar to this one and I got burned because it went 1.0 a few weeks later and isn't anywhere NEAR as good as this one. In fact, it isn't finished as far as I am concerned but that's besides the point.
There is a free demo you can try though where you can get a taste of the game. I never regretted buying the game though.
Now, if I had to discuss the cons of the game:
I wish there was an interactive tutorial that would give you objectives and that would teach you how to build a successful base. (in one game you understand) It would be scripted and would tell you where to place what. Because even now, with so much time spent, I still have to play carefully plan my base out because I keep stumbling on problems.
As for bugs...I haven't actually run into any bugs in vanilla factorio, but I do run a heavily modded game so when I never ran into bugs in vanilla factorio, I mean it. I have had plenty of crashes with my heavily modded factorio though. But then, that's to be expected if mods conflict with each other.

Oh, Factorio, where do I begin?
Factorio is a game about automating all the boring crap you do in other games.  You have to manually mine some ore for maybe 10 or 15 minutes, and then then game is all about automation after that.  In essence, you are attempting to create a giant, automated factory that can produce one of any number of products, from simple Iron Ore and Steel Plates to Uranium Fuel Cells and Rockets.
Factorio is also a game about logistics.  You need to calculate your inputs and outputs, balance your throughput, and optimize your factory layout.  While there are enemies on the map, you can turn them off and play the game without them and not even notice.  They do, however, add an additional complicating element, as you now have to divert resources to defense.
This is one of the best games I have ever played.  It is polished, thoroughly thought out, and has a clear vision.  It's not uncommon for my wife to come in and tell me I need to go to bed, and an hour later she reminds me NO, REALLY, GO TO BED.  It is extremely fun and difficult to put down, largely because it has the good ol' "But I just need to fix this thing real quick" hook.
Best of all, the devs push out updates so quickly, the community often times will tell them to slow down and sleep!  The game is currently in early access, but it feels like a finished product.
I cannot more highly recommend Factorio.  If you've got the $20, you will get a huge dollar-per-hour value out of this fantastic game.  Buy it.

For the most part, you're gonna be staring at one of three screens: the map screen (showing the disease spread), the disease screen (where you can purchase traits with accumulated DNA), and the world information screen (showing the measures being taken against your disease as well as progress towards human extinction). Anything you can think of is shown, even as graphs detailing your statistical growth, the percentage of population infected and dead, and the cure research conducted and needed.
A little thing that's making it more enjoyable to play through is just reading through the symptoms and trying to imagine what unholy suffering I'm causing to the humans, slowly appearing on the map as darkening red dots that stop shuffling about as they poop out their organs. Talk about being morbid and sadistic.
The price tag may put you off, especially if you've played the original mobile versions and/or find the additions potentially unnecessary. Just to be sure, grab it on a sale, and let your inner mad scientist free. A million is a statistic after all. Or perhaps 7 billion even.

OlliOlli features a clever system for performing skateboard jump tricks and grinds that places emphasis on timing and sticking the landings rather than the aerial acrobatics themselves. It then marries this system to a strange and increasingly brutal endless runner of sorts, which puts relatively harsh constraints on the possible tricks in the late-game. A more dedicated or talented player might find the opportunity for impressive displays of skill, but I found mostly found OlliOlli frustrating and tedious.

It's essentially all about trying to complete various challenges in each level while also trying to dish out the highest score doing various tricks & grinds before you reach the end mark or eat pavement. Many of the challenges require multiple runs of the same level and the more challenging ones may become a marathon of trial & errors mainly because the map will likely have to be memorized to an extent so as not to miss certain rails to grind on or gaps to jump and such. Each level has 5 challenges each and as soon as you finish one then that one challenge is completed for the rest of the game. To get the highest scores you have to combo up grinds & tricks as much as you can before landing back on the ground.
While all levels are relatively short most have an absurdly extensive amount of rails and other objects for you to grind on to keep combos going. Some levels allow going from start to finish without even hitting the pavement until the very end which can be a pretty cool challenge of its own. There are no checkpoints but because the game's made for trial & error restarting a level after failure goes by pretty fast.
The game is designed to be played with a controller in mind and although playing with the keyboard is allowed it's unrecommended. The game is played out using only the joystick (WASD) for performing tricks & ollies and the shoulder buttons (left & right arrow keys) for performing spins midair or doing other various tricks & grinds when combined with joystick moves.
Whatever combo that's been made aren't fully counted for unless a PERFECT landing to the ground has been made which can be done by pressing A (down key) just right before making contact with the ground. Grinds can be landed at a PERFECT as well though the penalty is much more minimal if not timed well enough as opposed to missing landings on the ground.
The skater moves on his own so you're really only in control of his score spewing moves and speed while at the same time avoiding wipeouts. Trying to perform various tricks & grinds felt a bit complicated early on, even after the tutorial, but I found myself getting a better feel for it as I kept playing especially when some challenges want you to perform specific tricks which usually become much more simpler than they sound. The number of tricks themselves feel very limited despite it saying "over 120" and they consist of board flips, spins, grinds, and ollies. Some of the animations for the tricks take a bit of time before being completed so learning what to use and when can also be a big deal when trying to stay on the board or not miss a rail to grind on just because your trick took too long. On that note you can actually finish most of the challenges with just ollies since they have practically no animation to wait for.
Personally I disliked whatever kind of music was in here. Luckily I'm able to turn that off and pump up my own tracklist on another window of the
and
The game presents itself with a handful of glitches that can be incredibly infuriating to those looking to do outstanding to perfect runs.
One of those would be that when you try to connect a grind you'll sometimes fall under the rail or just wipeout completely, even midway through the grind. The only time you're supposed to wipeout during grinding in this game is when you get off and land on something that isn't pavement, land on stairs, or hit an obstacle at the end of the rail which are never present between the beginning and the end of any rail.
It could just be on my end but the controls become unresponsive often when performing fast actions. Uncommonly when I try to jump an ollie or a trick from the ground with the joystick nothing will happen which usually leads to a wipeout. There are also times when trying to do an ollie or trick I just suddenly wipeout on the long flat road I'm riding on as if the character slipped without even getting any airtime. The "slipping" doesn't really show that it's a part of the game so I'm lead to assume it's another glitch.
This was apparently ported from another console and it's not entirely well polished either; the game crashes rarely for whatever reason, sometimes I have no control over the menus thus forcing me to restart the game, and there are rare & random but minute frame drops & skips which can be gamebreaking for a game that requires precise timing.

This game is a tile-based hack n' slash with very rudimentary role-playing elements. The closest thing I could compare it to is Might and Magic X, although this game is not turn based and has no emphasis on story. You create and control four characters, moving on a tile, and fight stuff/solve puzzles. You get 2 characters in the front row that can swing melee and get hit by melee, and two in the back that can't reach or be reached.
Let me jump right in to the gameplay. I did not like the combat in this game because it is what I like to call "very clicky". Since the game is not turn-based, you have to fight monsters in real time. Basically the combat involves clicking on all of your character's weapon icons to make them swing or shoot at the enemy, then waiting for the attack to come off cooldown so you can use it again. You can get fancy and swap out characters that are getting hurt too badly with characters in the back, ostensibly "tag teaming them". You can also abuse the fact that you can move on tiles faster than the enemies can, out flanking and out maneuvering them so that they can't hit you but you can hit them. This is pretty much the limit of what you can do in combat. It makes the game feel rather actiony and twitchy, rather than tactical. The latter technique just feels rather abusive and cheesey which made it not fun for me to do. However, I quickly found out that you need to do this in order to not take too much damage.
Now, it's true that you can cast spells in combat to make things a little more interesting, but the spellcasting system is rather flawed as well. You're basically tracing patterns and clicking certain rune buttons that comprise a "formula" for the spell. But since you're doing this in real time, it's very clunky and awkward to do. It becomes more of a clicky reflex thing (how fast can you do it!) than a tactical or roleplaying thing. Something like this could be really cool in a turn-based game, where you're depending on the character's skill and not your own hand speed as the player. Overall this would make a more RPG friendly experience.
The second bad thing about the gameplay is that the puzzles are extremely contrived. The very first one I encountered was solved by clicking a tiny section of wall that looked no different than any other section of wall. I found it only because I clicked literally everywhere on screen for several minutes and got lucky. I guess this is the gameplay?! You'll probably have to look up guides if you play this. I don't see why they can't put some kind of clue or hint or make the section of the wall look suspiciously different. This would make the puzzles at least engaging and make the player feel smart for figuring it out.
So, what about the ruleset and character progression? Well, I actually can't say too much about the rule system. That's because the game doesn't explain how different stats are being calculated. At the character creation screen, you put points in four ability scores that are well defined as to what things they increase. The game even shows a stat block next to the ability scores which changes to reflect the ability scores as you mess with them. The problem is, we don't know what a lot of this stuff does, how it's calculated, or even what a "good" score would be. For example, we know dexterity increases accuracy, but "accuracy" isn't defined at all. Sure, it's obvious it has something to do with hit chance, but we don't know how attack rolls are claculated in this game so we're not really making an informed decision here. This system could be a lot more transparent.
Moreover, you also buy skill points. Mousing over a skill tree shows the first few bonuses you get from increasing that skill, but not the whole chart. So again, you don't really know what it is that you're choosing. The spell skills (earth, fire, water, air) don't even define what type of spells that tree covers! It would be awesome if it showed brief explanation of what kinds of things to expect in each tree, followed by two examples of earth spells. But because the game doesn't do that, you're going in blind again.
This neccessitates that you're going to end up picking some combination of skills and stats that don't work. This game is very trial-by-error type of gameplay. I myself made a minotaur tank who focused on large hit point pools for defense and massive strength for big damage output, and he got massacred right away which of course ended up being a TPK. So you can forget about playing the character you WANT to play. Instead you'll be playing the character the developers want you to play.
My minotaur example helps me transition to the next point: there is extreme imbalance in the stats in this game. From personal experience of dying so much when using certain stats, as well as looking up guides online, I found out the truth about the system. Strength is completely awful for a melee character. "What! That's completely counter-inuitive!" Exactly. Turns out, the damage bonus provided by high strength doesn't scale at all and isn't enough enough to actually change how many hits it takes to kill and enemy. Doh. Stamina is likewise bad for a tank, it's just better to focus on evading damage and protection (armor). Again, counter-intuitive. Turns out the only stat that really matters for anyone who isn't a mage is Dexterity. Likewise, a lot of the feats in the game are totally useless and there are like 2 good ones that you should just take on every character.
Lastly, everything in this game is incremental. None of the skills or feats really make your characters pop out as unique or change the way you approach combat. The game would have benefitted from some really colorful Fallout style feats.
Summary: This game is an optimization, trial and error, incremental hack n' slash lacking any depth or unique character progression. The combat is action based and clicky. I would reccomend this to an action gamer who likes to just look up guides and isn't interested in roleplaying.

This game feels like someone was locked in a basement since the 1980's and then was introduced to the all the newest tools for game making, and then told to make Megaman.
That said, the dashing feels very quick and responsive, and honestly could be removed and reused in another game focused around it. The dashing in this game doesn't work well with the platforming since you can effectively use it to fly, plus combined with crash/collision damage with enemies makes both elements feel counter-intuitive.

Gameplay would be nice but the level design doesn't give it enough room to shine. Dashes and combo system are heavily advertised as a main point of the game but have to damage enemies first and you need to pick up a random drop to upgrade your shots to pierce enemies. This tends to lead to you just blowing up robots instead of dashing into them all for a combo.
Difficulty ramps up a lot quite quickly from what I saw. They introduce a mechanic to the stage in a calm, controlled environment(much like the original Megaman games) but then that mechanic ramps up fast in difficulty. The fire stage for example introduces interactive backgrounds that will kill you if they fall on you. Seems simple until a few screens later where they add falling platforms and robots shooting you from the background that were introduced earlier in the stage as well. It wasn't one and then the other. They just threw you into a bullet hell with falling platforms and backgrounds and expected a lot of trial and error on when you should run or wait. It's basically game over if you get hit by anything and the background falling will even knock down platforms(would be a nice touch if the jumps weren't so tight without them)
It definitely feels reminiscent of a Megaman game but it still needs a lot of polish in design if it wants to come close to it in quality

To make it short this game is basically the small lovechild of Bastion, Shadow of the Colossus with a dash of Dark Souls. If you enjoyed these games you will very likely enjoy Jotun.
The gameplay is tight and precise. There is no complex RPG developement system here but also no unencicary padding. The combat is simple, tight and precise and the rest of the gameplay is very varied for each world and feels very immersive and fitting. The Boss fights are clearly the highlight and batteling a towering creature 40 times your size, that shakes the very ground when it moves is a particularly unique thrill very few games offer!
The graphics are gorgous and the atmosphere is very dense. An extra compliment to the developers on how they manage to convey scale in this hand drawn 2D enviroment. The game mostly relies on the Dark Soulsy story telling method of letting you experience the world instead of forcing exposition down your throat (but less cryptic than in Dark souls).
With its 8-10 hours the game doesn't overstay its welcome and forgoes stretching content in favor of a fuller, tighter game experience. Everyone who loves immersive atmospheric games and marvels at the feeling of felling a particularly difficult Boss should definately try Jotun. It's a great game : )

Later you will also find "powers" which give you effects like speed or more damage or protection. So for the player there isn't that much complexity, which I like, but the game could need a little bit more depth, however the bossfights make up for that.
Every boss has a unique theme and unique mechanics. The nice thing is how the game introduces you to some of these mechanics in the "puzzle" sections before the boss itself which helps to learn how to dodge certain types of attacks and so on, so there is no trial & error. Also the bosses start slow and easy and get more hectic and difficult the more you damage the boss. There was 1 boss which was a bit dissapointing, because that boss had very little attacks and didn't have the quality (in terms of animations, sound design etc.) as the others for some reason. And that's a big deal, because you only get to fight 5 bosses, the game isn`t that long. If you take out all the "puzzle" sections, you could complete the game in 2 hours, but I think it is good that these intermissions exist, to give the player time to breath between bossfights, however they aren`t designed that interestingly.
Sometimes you get to visit interesting locations or see cool creatures, but as the player you are mostly just running around with a very low movement speed and that made these parts a bit boring to me. Also it discouraged me from exploring, but the game wants you to explore. Some powers are hidden really well, but are SO helpful to beat bosses. Thankfully the game shows you the location of these locations on the map, but the map doesn`t show you your location, so you always have to keep track of where you are, but that is artificial difficulty in my opinion. If the game had actual puzzle mechanics and things you could solve or secrets you could find, then the game would probably show you your location, but currently it's just about finding the right path.
Because the game isn`t that long anyway and the "puzzle" parts didn`t feel fleshed out (some were cool) I can`t recommend this for full price, but it is a game you should definitly buy at some point, because the bossfights are just really well made, except 1 as I explained and there is a final boss after the 5 bosses, but that boss just recycles all of the previous bosses. That isn`t neccessarily a bad thing to do, but here it is, because of the low amount of bosses/content in general and because there is nothing after that. In Shovel Knight for example you also fought every boss one after the other in the final level, but then you also got to fight a real final boss with unique mechanics.
One last thing I want to mention is that I think the theme of this game is wasted. This had so much potential, but outside of some random dialouge about the things you visit there isn't a big story or anything. The game ends as abrupt as it starts. I mean visually it had some really cool places, the voice actors did a great job I think and the soundtrack is also really well made, but it's just the theme of the game, it could easily be something else and it would stay the same game.

What a lovely game. Based in Norse mithology, Jotun brings you to a beautiful and wonderfully craften world.
You're Thora, a viking that died an infamous death and has to prove herself through a chain of great challenges to be able to finally reach Valhalla.
You have to defeat all the fallen giants that await you in the "limbo". For this you have first to traverse and explore through diverse levels that will introduce you some obstacles and enemies, that you will need to learn to deal with, as the concepts introduced there are essential for beating the bosses later. Smart design that eases you at a good pace on how to approach things.
The artstyle is absolutely gorgeous, as is the world building. You will find lots of lovely views throughout the game, and all levels give you insight and are linked to the Norse mythology thematically. It really feels like very passionate representation of it.
Throughout the exploration of the levels, you're meant to find the pillars that will allow to access the boss batle, but you will also be able to find health upgrades, as well as new powers that give you some helpful advantages (like doing more damage, running faster, restoring health). Those aren't needed for progression, but they do help you greatly on it, rewarding the exploration of every nook and cranny in the level. In many of the levels you will have to solve puzzles to progress, either navigational (finding the right way and order of going to a certain place) or more standard puzzles of activating certain mechanics in the correct way.
In addition to that, the combat gameplay is fairly simple. You have a strong attack, a light attack, roll, and roll+attack, and you always use the same weapon. It's responsive and it works well, despite not having a great depth to it. The challenge of the game comes with each boss's pattern. Timing is essential and you need to learn how to read their movements. Patience is recommended and just spamming attacks won't help. You apply what you learn throughout the levels before to effectively use it your advantage.
Both the design of the bosses and their animation are wonderful. Each one is drawn in a way that both clashes and fits into the world, taking a very hand-drawn aesthetic to them that makes them stand out in the world while at the same time feeling like it's part of it, with smart use of color and shading. The animation also works in the same way. They stand out from the rest by only having some frames of actual animation, feeling like  old-school hand-animated characters, while at the same time flowing perfectly with the game and what's happening.
The art also conveys very well the same feeling you have in Shadow of Colossus, battling creatures that seem so much bigger and powerful than you. You're just this tiny being, against giants that are almost the size of mountains, and every thing gives the sense of epic.
Adding to the wonderful world and art in display, I have to reference the music. The game has one of the best soundtracks I've heard this year. It's on point every single time. Proper epic, daunting and energetic tracks while takingg on a boss, soothing ones while exploring, etc. Every single one feels crafted to the specific moment you're going through.
Certainly of the best indie titles of the year, even if flawed in some ways. The combat has lot of potential and could be a bit more diverse and have more depth, and the game doesn't have much replayabilty, but other than that, it's great. Definitely recommended.
8.5/10

I doubt any dissenters to the notion that video games are ostensibly a form of art exist within the video game hoi polloi anymore. To those self aggrandizing cultural stalwarts who are - I present to you Jotun, the latest in an exponentially increasing list of beautifully crafted indie darlings that strengthen the art argument just about monthly.
Jotun's story is that of our heroine, a viking woman named Thora, who's life ends unceremoniously in a storm. Unable to ascend unto the halls of Valhalla, Thora must garner the reverence of the Norse gods to secure her rightful place in Asgard, all the while revealing the story of her life in pieces along the way. Thora's life is fraught with Shakespearean tragedy, told in a fashion which is somehow both autobiographical and eulogistic. Developer Thunder Lotus Games out of Montreal couples this with a hauningly minimalist landscape and score, and has created a deeply moving experience.
The gameplay of Jotun is deceptively simple. There are no enemies besides the bosses which the player only encounters by gathering the necessary runes from their respective area. Exploring these areas was an incredibly joyous experience for a very unique reason; the area maps are purposefully vague and do not show your location. The game remedies this in very realistic ways like zooming the camera out when you're on high ground, giving you a better lay of the land and forcing the player to navigate using a form of dead reckoning. Not all will find this as endearing as I did, but I found it added a layer of realism and difficulty to getting around and, at the very least, gives you a much better appreciation of the level design. Boss battles are the classic "notice a pattern and counter accordingly, using the abilities you've acquired thus far" but, in practice, are not so patronizingly easy and in fact can be quite the opposite.
Jotun is everything from beautiful to terrifying to heartbreakingly tragic. The gameplay, art style, and score are resonant and powerful, and the difficulty and learning curve are just right, meaning Jotun feels something like the perfect mix of Dark Souls, Shadow of the Colossus, and Transistor. Jotun could benefit from a length increase, but then again, so could most artsy indie games, and even though I found it's unique take on navigation to be charming, there was a definite need for a mini map, as I found myself pressing start just about every 2 minutes to look at it. Jotun is a fun game that is presented well enough to make you feel feelings and think thoughts which, at the end of the day, is a definition of art. Don't expect Jotun to change the way video games are perceived tomorrow, but absolutely include it in the list of games that will change that perception in a few years.

The novelty of this game has been slightly tainted, in my opinion, due to having played some 100 hours in class since its Android release.
Nevertheless, it's a pretty solid port - you could say it's close to a different game because of all the new features, like Scenario Editor and Co-op/VS Multiplayer. All of them are really nice additions that (with the exception of VS Multiplayer, arguably) help boost the game's longevity, the same way new disease types have done for the mobile version.
For the most part, you're gonna be staring at one of three screens: the map screen (showing the disease spread), the disease screen (where you can purchase traits with accumulated DNA), and the world information screen (showing the measures being taken against your disease as well as progress towards human extinction). Anything you can think of is shown, even as graphs detailing your statistical growth, the percentage of population infected and dead, and the cure research conducted and needed.
A little thing that's making it more enjoyable to play through is just reading through the symptoms and trying to imagine what unholy suffering I'm causing to the humans, slowly appearing on the map as darkening red dots that stop shuffling about as they poop out their organs. Talk about being morbid and sadistic.
The price tag may put you off, especially if you've played the original mobile versions and/or find the additions potentially unnecessary. Just to be sure, grab it on a sale, and let your inner mad scientist free. A million is a statistic after all. Or perhaps 7 billion even.

Well, as you can see from the playtime I've put a lot of hours into this game.  I was a huge huge fan of Dungeon Master, then Chaos Strikes Back, and of course the Eye of the Beholder series.  I even tried my hardest to like StoneKeep, but it was just a touch too formulaic to be considered an 'evolution'.. It was really just a repetition.   At the time, the Bards Tale games were also exploring the rectilinear 2.5D game approach, and I did quite like them, but they were vastly inferior at projecting an atmosphere (I felt).    So, I hope you get an idea of where my review is coming from: I'm a die-hard Dungeon Master fan, who really likes the genre, but is looking for DM with improvemetns.
Legend of Grimrock is a superb game, there is no doubt about it.  "Polised" doesn't even come close to explaining just how wonderful the world is.  The rocks glisten, the toches flicker, and everything has the exact same 'feel' as Dungeon master, from the pressure-plates, and doors opening to the 'worms' (now snails) which offer up repulsive-sounding chunks of meat to keep your party alive.
The big question that you want to ask is "Does it represent 25 years of advancement over Dungeon Master?".  The answer is "mostly".  I'll explain in a bit more detail...
The game is effectively the same as Dungeon Master: You start out at the 'top' of a dungeon. In DM, you were a party of resurrected adventurers controlled by a wizard (who you could see if you battled your way all the way back up the dungeon and used the 'see through walls' spell on the first door!).  In LoG, you're a party of four adventurers, imprisoned for unknown reasons in a big mountain.   The door closes, and this is where the first main difference arises: Choosing your party.
In DM, you 'floated about' as a spirit essence, looking at paintings of dead adventurers, choosing who to resurrect, and who to 'take' but remould into your desires.  This was completely revolutionary.  LoG picks a very AD&D approach instead, and just allows you to stat-roll and custom-build your party.   DM allowed you a lot of freedom over your party. It was pretty much possible to get anywhere and do anything with any party (although a lone adventurer was too hard for me to ever complete the game with).  LoG is essentially the same, however there are some classes which are completely useless, and some races which appear to be awesome (minotaur).  I took a Rogue, but didn't look at the achievements list, so never got assassination, and therefore never got the one thing that the rogue is good for, the backstab Steam Achievement. Pah.
OKay, so you pick your formulaic team (Fighters up front, mage(s) and rogue(s) up the back), and head into the dungeon.   The first level is a training level, as you'd expect. You're deposited naked, so you find some loincloths, daggers and rocks, and use them to bludgeon the locals, as you'd expect...  There are a few traps, and puzzles, but by and large, it's your standard training level.  HOWEVER, the game's true nature comes to the fore at this point...
The training level can kill you.  And is does. Over and over.  You see, there's a trick to playing LoG, which you have to learn RIGHT at the beginning, or you're going to die. and die. and die.  You must never try to go toe-to-toe with an enemy. You will die.   The monsters are always scaled to be a difficult challenge.  To fight you must find at LEAST a 2x2 grid, and strafe, rotate, hit, strafe, rotate, hit, strafe, rotate, hit... and so on.. and so on.. until one of you is dead.    Woe betide you if there are two enemies: This is a retilinear circus of death.. you'll get trapped, and die.  For two enemies, you need a 3x3 grid, making sure never to step into a corner cell if you can help it!  And so, you quickly learn the mathematics of LoG.  Quick count: 3 enemies, right I'll need a 4x4 space to dodge around them in, at least.
If you're REALLY lucky, you'll come across them in a snake-like corridor, and can use their abysmal path finding against them.  Monsters will often sidestep with you, so you can pop-left, shoot, pop-right, and the monster will take the arrow or fireball in the face, then step right again, and now there's some rock between you.. You wait to cooldown, and rinse repeat.
I'll say this again: Never ever ever try to go toe-to-toe with an enemy.  Sometimes you can't help it. In this case, you're probably boned, but try and slash your way out of it as best you can:  There are some 'secrets' which FORCE you to be in the middle of a swarm of things (Fighter's Challenge), and in this case, you're boned.  Over and over.. until you get lucky and reload enough times that a space randomly appears in front of you, or whatever, and you're able to retreat out of the swarm... Something like that..
Supplies are in short supply:  Lack of food is the main impetus to keep moving.  There were many times that my party were getting low, because I'd been searching for secrets, and I just had to plough on into the next level, to get some food.    At first I found it annoying: Cosntantly running low: There are penalties for being hungry!  But then I realised it was to stop people stagnating on earlier levels.   I remember in DM having my entire party encumbered with Worm Rounds because we'd camped near a spawn point, and I ended up dagging them up and down, and up and down, three or four levels down from the spawn point, so I could have a stash.   Similar things happen in LoG. There's a famous 'snail room', but you only get two snails, which is barely enough to keep two party members alive.  However, they do replenish every time you step a certain distance from the room...
As you get deeper and deeper, the enemies stay just as hard.  Okay, I KNOW they're getting harder, but I'm getting better at the same pace.  So, while a snail on level one needs ten dagger-hits, a cthulu-faced magic-wielding lightning-thrower-evil-demon on Level 12 still takes ten lightning-sword hits.   So, the 'experience' changes a little with the variety of ranged vs. melee monsters, but the game stays uniformly difficult.  In DM, there definitely felt to be an advancement in ability, and monsters became easier.. So in DM, that demon would take three lightning-sword hits, if you see what I mean?
Descending through LoG, the 'tunnels' feel slightly different. You start off in fairly rustic 'sewers'?, and then descent into perfectly rectilinear dressed-stone corridors.  They stay this way until the very last level, which goes very industrial, and it becomes clear what the game's emblem is all about.
There's a LOT of side-activity here.  You can plough through without finding many secrets, but the majority of the good stuff is behind tiny buttons, and so on, so it really pays to explore.   However, there's always that looming hunger, so you can't spend too long.  There's about enough surplus food int he dungeon (without snail-mining), to get you back to Level 1 from Level 12 two or three times, if you forgot something, before you really start to run dangerously low.
I'd say my main gripe about this game is the w ay that the skill 'trees' (or just skill List) works.  In DM, you started off beign able to do "14", (fire), and then learned "144" (fireball)... But once you leveled up, you could try for "244", bigger fireball... sometimes it'd work, sometimes it wouldn't.   LoG has nothing like this.     My second main gripe is that magic needs SO MANY DAMNED CLICKS to work.   five perfectly-placed clicks on smal squares, while you're trying to strafe,turn,hit,strafe.... is a REAL pain the a$$!!!!
All in all, I'd say this was a really excellent attempt to remake Dungeon Master.   They've missed some of the fun in a few areas, and instead concentrated on graphical beauty.  Doesn't stop me from recommending this though. It's a great game, so long as you learn the one cardinal rule: Do not go toe-to-toe with an enemy if you can help it!

What can I say?  This game isn't so much a game as one of the most engrossing short stories I've ever read.  I guess I'll start at the beginning.
I am not a fan of text based games.  Take a look at my game library and you'll find it filled with graphically beautiful titles.  I bought this game on a whim because it was reviewed as overwhelmingly positive and it was extremely cheap during the Steam Summer Sale.  Having played it now, I gladly would have paid full price (which is still less than 5 dollars).
I made one mistake (or incredibly brilliant move, depending on how you look at it) when I played, I named my character after me and my robot after my wife.  This made the story all the more impactful and meaningful than I ever could have expected.  I tried to play peacefully, I cared for my loved ones, I avoided conflict and tried to be quiet, but they hammered me down.  Took everything I loved away from and locked me up.  Bitter and angry, I fought back, but I didn't have the skills or know-how and I failed bitterly at that as well.  In the end, the one thing that mattered most was still with me though.  All of those emotions came through in just two hours of play.
Having played it, you then look back and think "I should have done that differently" or "I shouldn't have helped that guy" or "what could life had been if I had chosen her instead of her".  These are all questions you can answer by firing the game up again.
What a brilliant, wonderful game and I highly recommend it!

Transistor is a unique action adventure RPG that takes place in a beautiful and intriguing world.
Pros
- Gameplay is an innovative mix between realtime action, turn-based tactics and strategic planning that feels great.
- Diverse number of different playstyles is allowed by the variety of abilities and how they work with each other.
- Character progression is meaningfully determined by the choices the player makes on every level up.
- Enemies grow and get stronger over time making fighting them never dull.
- Customizable difficulty rewards the player for taking on tougher challenges.
- Art will blow your socks off.
Cons
- Constant voice in your ear might be annoying for some players (if you played Bastion and loved the Narrator then you will probably love this too though!)

This game looks stunning. But like the main character once you get past the looks, all you get is a hum.
Transistor starts out mysterious and ethereal, leaning into it's art style heavily, and that's great, but as soon as it wraps up it's little opening mystery - about 30 minutes in - the suspense, anything even remotely compelling, is gone. From there it's all just repetitive fights, incessant overly complicated unlockables and a soundtrack that drones on and on without ever really feeling like it exists in the same game. Building your powers is a great idea, and the way Transistor does it feels like it has potential, but the pieces come way too fast while the slots to use them in come way too slow.
The game's fights, also, lock you into a tiny area filled with semi-destructable obstacles, making navigation instantly annoying. When the enemy units can float casually through or over the blocks and you can't, it becomes frustrating. When the pause-and-plan functionality feels like its more trouble than its worth, it just becomes a button-spamming simulator, which the build-your-powers system would make you believe it isn't. And when the game decides to make it too hard so you NEED to use the planning system, I turned it off.
Drop this powerset-building mechanic into a brawler - 2D or 3D it doesn't matter - and you'll have an innovative system that works within your game. But everything about Transistor feels like it's holding me back or pushing me away, and while the end result of the unlockables system may be fun, I'm not about to slog through a boring series of samey levels to find out.
If there was an art book of Transistor, I'd grab it. It's a beautiful thing to look at. But the game struggles to align it's systems, and make use of it's best parts.

Great little 2D skateboarding game. Don't know if this would be playable with KB+M - the tricks are pulled off by moving the controller stick around similar to a fighting game.
Chain together grinds and tricks into huge combos while you dodge obstacles and try to complete stage objectives. Lots of timing involved which takes some time to get used to, but starts to feel good after an hour or so.

I really actually like this game. I'll pretty much play any skateboarding game since the EA skate games aren't on PC (thanks EA) but I was pleasantly surprised by how great the controls of Olli Olli are. The tricks feel very similar to their real life counterparts. For example, kickflips in real life are a flick off of your backside front of the nose, and in olli olli it's a flick to the right on the analog stick (which would be your backside if you ride goofy).
That and the variety of tricks are what keep me coming back. The courses are fun, but if feels a lot less like skating in the later levels. The first world is still my favorite.
The one possible con I've had so far is in the quality of the port. The game occasionally will have a runtime error and die on me for no real reason, and it's the only game I play that does it. But when it works, which is usually, it's a great game.

There is fun to be had in some parts, but the graphics are meh, the level desgn is incredibly obnoxious at times, and the writing is pretty bad. I'm glad Comcpet included a Japanese dub. At least then I could pretend I had some cultural distance from the writing.
On top of that, the Ray DLC is something that should've been added to the main game. I don't care whether it was funded after the base game or not. If you develop content for a game that's released at the same time, it should be included in the base game. Now, anyone who didn't originally back the game or spring for the physical version will have to pay an extra $5, which is incredibly tacky.
If you want to play a Mega Man spiritual successor from Inti Creates that's good, check out Azure Striker Gunvolt. It's $5 cheaper, has no content locked behind DLC, has a better art style, and is really fun.

I honestly never was anticipating this game at any point in time, which I suppose puts me in a unique position. I like Mega Man, but I'm no die hard fan of that series, which is why I wasn't too fond of the idea of a spiritual successor with an uninteresting style that is very derivative of the series it so desperately clings onto.
That being said, I was gifted this game a while ago, and after hearing all the Kickstarter woes and drama, I was curious as to how "bad" it seemed like it was going to turn out.
Honestly from the hour I played, which included half of the stages in the game, I concluded that this game is a case similar to Duke Nukem Forever; namely that is so unbelievably mediocre and average at best, but gets extra negative points for being delayed endless times and having development woes/controversy.
Mighty No. 9 is so aggressively uninteresting, so vanilla and pedestrian; it is a sobering affair that makes you realize that all the controversy really wasn't worth it for the end product. If Mighty No. 9 was truly terrible, it would at least have been memorable, but it isn't. At all. The visual design and art direction is low contrast, unappealing and at worst, downright ugly. I don't care if it looks like it could've ran on a PSP, but at least give me interesting locales! An oil facility, a military base, a mine, etc. Do these boring, industrial stages sound interesting to you? Well, they aren't.
God, I really wished this game could be fun to bash, or fun to defend. However,
it is impossible to do either. This is a depressing game, one with no ambition or life put into it. It feels rushed while also being mechanically competent at the same time. It feels slapped together and half heartedly crafted, as if zero care was put into things like voice acting, stage designs, etc.
Inafune, I can honestly say that Mighty No. 9 is not better than nothing.

Alien Swarm is truly the best coop game I've ever played so far. I'm now in the position to compare it to HELLDIVERS.
You can choose between different unique characters. Some relations between those characters are special and this is reflected through some chatting between them.
There are four different classes (Officers, Technicians, Medics, Special Soldiers) with unique abilities. Every character has it's own strength and weaknesses concerning his class and thus weapons/items at his disposal.
There are no useless weapons or items. Even the start rifle is useful for experienced players with high level characters! By the way, no stats of your characters are changed through playing. That's a wonderful feature of this game.
All missions are meaningful connected with one another. The experience is thrilling but without a horror factor. At later stages you get used to fighting against all kinds of alien threats but it never get's boring or dumb.
The game stays challenging through various different difficulty levels and different modes like hardcore friendly fire. Thoughtful integrated Steam achievements are one key element in continually challenging the player.
If you really want to try a good coop game and you like action packed games with an alien theme do yourself a favor and give it a shot. In the beginning I was sceptical too but I never regret I got started with this beautiful coop game.

Okay, so I first discovered factorio around august 2016 and I purchased it on September the same year. Because I decided I could do better as the Youtube let's player I had been watching. (I don't remember who the Youtuber was)
Anyway, my previous review was outdated because I wrote it shortly after I bought it. And now, with my four hundred hours worth of gameplay I figure I can give this game another review.
So first up is PLAYABILITY
Early access by its very defenition can be terrible to play but it can also feel like a completed game. (With some things not in the game) This game though it feels complete, stable and is a complete joy to play. As far as I know, most of the major features are in the game but don't quote me on that bit, because I'm not sure.
There ar a huge amount of mods you can download and enable to make the game even more enjoyable. The game in its vanilla state can be a bit easy once you figured out how to setup your base. It gives you a very satisfied feeling when you put the final touch on your setup and you can quote the Big Man from The A-Team and say 'I love it when a plan comes together' (i love that series)
If the game seems to simple if you're watching a let's player on Youtube then there are a LOT of mods that will complicate the game by a LOT.
Right now it's iron ore - > iron plates - > iron gears
That's the vanilla, but with mods it's a much longer cycle to get the same thing.
Right, so if you're thinking of buying the game, you should be asking yourself: what is the point of it and is it worth it?
The answer to the first question is fairly simple. The 'story' (of what little there is) is that you crashed on an alien planet and you must build a rocket to get the hell out of there!
As you know, an industry has polution and the more polution you have, the bigger of a chance you have that your base will be invaded by aliens also known as biters.
The game map is absolutely HUGE and pretty much infinite for all intents and purposes. There is a map editor to create your own perfect map if you have your own ideas how to make your base.
Right, so I already said that you need to get of the planet by building a rocket right? Well, BEFORE you can do that, you must build yourself an enttire industry. You start with limited tools and do everything by hand and in the end EVERYTHING is automated.
The second question: (is it worth it?) is pretty much an undeniable YES! The game doesn't have a steep learning curve at all and is easy to learn once you figure things out. I would advice to NOT impulse buy this without watching some videos first. I bought a game similar to this one and I got burned because it went 1.0 a few weeks later and isn't anywhere NEAR as good as this one. In fact, it isn't finished as far as I am concerned but that's besides the point.
There is a free demo you can try though where you can get a taste of the game. I never regretted buying the game though.
Now, if I had to discuss the cons of the game:
I wish there was an interactive tutorial that would give you objectives and that would teach you how to build a successful base. (in one game you understand) It would be scripted and would tell you where to place what. Because even now, with so much time spent, I still have to play carefully plan my base out because I keep stumbling on problems.
As for bugs...I haven't actually run into any bugs in vanilla factorio, but I do run a heavily modded game so when I never ran into bugs in vanilla factorio, I mean it. I have had plenty of crashes with my heavily modded factorio though. But then, that's to be expected if mods conflict with each other.

Oh, Factorio, where do I begin?
Factorio is a game about automating all the boring crap you do in other games.  You have to manually mine some ore for maybe 10 or 15 minutes, and then then game is all about automation after that.  In essence, you are attempting to create a giant, automated factory that can produce one of any number of products, from simple Iron Ore and Steel Plates to Uranium Fuel Cells and Rockets.
Factorio is also a game about logistics.  You need to calculate your inputs and outputs, balance your throughput, and optimize your factory layout.  While there are enemies on the map, you can turn them off and play the game without them and not even notice.  They do, however, add an additional complicating element, as you now have to divert resources to defense.
This is one of the best games I have ever played.  It is polished, thoroughly thought out, and has a clear vision.  It's not uncommon for my wife to come in and tell me I need to go to bed, and an hour later she reminds me NO, REALLY, GO TO BED.  It is extremely fun and difficult to put down, largely because it has the good ol' "But I just need to fix this thing real quick" hook.
Best of all, the devs push out updates so quickly, the community often times will tell them to slow down and sleep!  The game is currently in early access, but it feels like a finished product.
I cannot more highly recommend Factorio.  If you've got the $20, you will get a huge dollar-per-hour value out of this fantastic game.  Buy it.
