This game looks stunning. But like the main character once you get past the looks, all you get is a hum.
Transistor starts out mysterious and ethereal, leaning into it's art style heavily, and that's great, but as soon as it wraps up it's little opening mystery - about 30 minutes in - the suspense, anything even remotely compelling, is gone. From there it's all just repetitive fights, incessant overly complicated unlockables and a soundtrack that drones on and on without ever really feeling like it exists in the same game. Building your powers is a great idea, and the way Transistor does it feels like it has potential, but the pieces come way too fast while the slots to use them in come way too slow.
The game's fights, also, lock you into a tiny area filled with semi-destructable obstacles, making navigation instantly annoying. When the enemy units can float casually through or over the blocks and you can't, it becomes frustrating. When the pause-and-plan functionality feels like its more trouble than its worth, it just becomes a button-spamming simulator, which the build-your-powers system would make you believe it isn't. And when the game decides to make it too hard so you NEED to use the planning system, I turned it off.
Drop this powerset-building mechanic into a brawler - 2D or 3D it doesn't matter - and you'll have an innovative system that works within your game. But everything about Transistor feels like it's holding me back or pushing me away, and while the end result of the unlockables system may be fun, I'm not about to slog through a boring series of samey levels to find out.
If there was an art book of Transistor, I'd grab it. It's a beautiful thing to look at. But the game struggles to align it's systems, and make use of it's best parts.

Coming from Supergiant's Bastion, I had high expectations for this game. One thing entirely different about the two is that the combat system in this game is a lot more wild in good and bad ways.
This game comes with a ton of weapons known as "functions". Like Bastion you can arm yourself with multiple functions at once, but the coolest part? Each function can be modded into another (with up to two mod per function late game). You can arm yourself with a total of 4 main functions so the possibilites are huge. You also get frequent points where you can swap these functions and I had a blast playing with all the combinations.
Starting off, you have a small array of functions and things aren't very clear from the beginning. Personally, I fumbled my way through the start understanding the combat system. In detail, there are two combat styles: real-time and turn(). Turn was interesting since it makes the game more strategy based and you really need to plan things out, but with the right combos and you'll tear through everything. Again though, this wasn't very clear from the start and the restrictions were awful. I learned the hard way that if you die you don't reset but lose your functions temporarily (which resulted in me wiping my first couple of saves).
: Really big expansive combat system but poorly explained and limited early on. P.S. Would highly recommend a keyboard for this game. I started off with gamepad and it really ruined the experience.
Story was a bit on the hazy side when it came to understanding. You really want to read everything you get to in order to see the whole picture. That being said, I feel like Supergiant was going for a more poetic, artistic style compared to Bastion's story which was cool
Leave it to Supergiant to nail this once again. Awesome soundtrack overall though no real main theme IMO like Bastion. Additionally, art was really refreshing for this game. Really pretty scenes (keeping in mind this game came out 3 years ago) and cool comic cut-styled scenes.
I give this game a solid 8/10. Part of this may be my fault for trying to play with a gamepad (seriously use a keyboard!) but a lot of the game needs to be self-explored and understood as well which was kind of annoying starting off. Stick with it though and you'll have a blast!

A modern take on oldschool dungeon-crawling roleplaying games,
called to my nostalgic side and reeled me in.  I'm glad too, because it turned out to be quite the experience.  It's about a group of prisoners being sentenced to Mount Grimrock, where their only chance of survival and ever seeing daylight again is to descend through the labyrinthian interior of the mountain, level by level.  Oh yeah, and each level is riddled with deadly traps and swarming with horrible monsters.  Not exactly the type of place that leaves a mint on your pillow.  Enjoy your stay!
++ Oldschool feel
++ Challenging puzzles
+ Graphics
+ Music/Sound
- Storyline
-- Very repetitive Scenery
= A couple things that I hope is improved upon in the sequel, but I definitely recommend it.
is a great value for your money (especially if you get it on sale) and a unique change of pace if you're getting tired of the same old same old.
- Right off the bat, loading up the game, BAM, there it is:  the title screen!  And you know what the title screen has?  Great music!  Unfortunately, that's pretty much all the music you'll hear in the game.  But the good news is that the quiet, interrupted only by a little ambience and the occasional sounds of nearby monsters, makes the atmosphere fantastically creepy!  Other sound effects are usually from traps and monsters killing you, because you are awesome and put the game on Hard difficulty. Good for you!
Let's not forget the oldschool dungeon-crawler experience.  Yep, nailed it.  The movement and combat and overall feel the game is spot on.  It's like a blast from the past for older people like me, no doubt about it, but with modernized graphics.  Well, the graphics aren't exactly setting new standards in the gaming industry, but they are quite good and a whole lot better than the
, am I right?? (Look it up, kiddies.)
As for the puzzles, I found them to be quite challenging at times but a lot of fun to figure out.  I highly suggest putting away those online guides and start your game on hard difficulty and "old school mode" which takes away the in-game map, thus leaving you to your pencil and grid paper to make your own map.  Some people might fight this to be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥(and it can be lol) but it's also much more rewarding, plus you get an achievement for it.
- All I really understood from the start is that a group of prisoners had to find their way through Grimrock -- solve the puzzles, stay alive and gain your freedom.  There is more though, little tidbits of story pieced together throughout the game, but they are somewhat confusing and uninteresting.  I would have preferred more detailed explanations regarding the origins of Mount Grimrock, its creators, etc, maybe even murals or something that triggered cutscenes that gave a deeper glimpse into Grimrock's purpose and history.  Alas.
In the end, the only other complaint I had as I played was that the scenery got boring after a while... since the whole game had just
different wall-types with little or no decoration or ornamentation.  Perhaps it adds to the immersion, feeling like every hallway looks the same, getting lost, and making you go a little crazy like the prisoners probably would be.  Still, it would have been nice if each level had it's own unique look.  But that's just me.
-  Hands down, great game.  Some improvements could be made, of course, but all in all, I'm seriously impressed and Legend of Grimrock 2 is definitely on the agenda.  I highly recommend giving this game a look, especially if you are feeling the need to mix things up a bit.  After all, I don't see many other oldschool dungeon-crawlers floating around.
Trust me, it's worth it.  Just... mind your step. Lots of ogres, no bathrooms in sight.

As you know, Windows 10 hates old games to the point where you can't even run old CD-rom games such as the Sims 1, this game is no exception. The only option is a No CD crack or a digital version.
1. For this game, simply go into your Steam folder (C:ProgramFiles(x86),Steam, Steamapps, Common, RollerCoaster Tycoon Deluxe) and locate the game's .exe file. (or jsut called RCT if you have extentions hidden.)
2.Right click the icon and go to propperties
3. Go to the compatibility tab
4. Run compatibility mode for Windows XP Service pack 2
5. Check the "run as administrator" box
6. Check the "Disable display scaling on high DPI settings" box
7. Click okay, test the game out (for me it worked the 2nd time)
8. Enjoy

OlliOlli reminds me why I spent hours and hours on the early THPS games.
Allows you to do tricks only Tony Hawk can dream of. 8/10

Brings what I loved about Tony Hawk's Pro Skater to a side-scrolling perspective. It gets crazy-hard; I wish there were some more levels in the middle that could be completed after a few tries. The combo system is fun, but difficult to master. There are four directions for tricks, a timing-based landing system, and two buttons for spins. You have to be alert for the entire length of each level (around 2 minutes) to meet the objectives. Getting to the end counts enough to get to the next level, but "pro" levels only unlock when you meet all five objectives.

I find the prospect of having to ride on a board with wheels under it a very, very terrifying experience. There are many ways I can fall off that board, and I imagine all of them have to do with something like falling onto a turd or a water hydrant or onto a set of figurines that are participating in a heated battle of Warhammer 40,000 on the sidewalk, where I will pierce one of my internal organs on a Tyranid and have to explain to God when I get to the pearly gates why I am such an ultra-wuss.
OlliOlli captures some of that terror because it has a difficulty curve that's steep as hell, like learning how to ride an actual skateboard. The tutorial could have been better (for some reason I couldn't actually figure out how to do Perfect Grinds until I just said '♥♥♥♥ this' and played an actual level, where I slowly figured it out on my own, but I think that's more of my blatant inattentiveness than the tutorial's fault), but the real learning experience is pretty much about getting better and faster at the game, and learning how to squeeze in more tricks between grinds for higher scores or for unlocking bigger, better levels. If you want to unlock those "Pro" levels, you gotta ♥♥♥♥ing earn your keep. Once you get in the groove of actually starting to pull off sweet moves and getting in the habit of varying what moves you pull off, the game opens up dramatically and challenges you even more.
Despite OlliOlli's semi-'thrown in the deep end' type of tutorial, it gets its vibe right. The soundtrack is the perfect thing to grind to, and the controls are a bit finicky but the way they are built allows for effortless cool stunts between jumps. It looks cool and I bet you will not be called a nerd if you show people how you can do a 1080 Backside Flip-It to people on the bus without losing. It's Super Meat Boy hard - you will break your knees and ankles so many times before you can finally pull off that grind-flip-grind-twist-grind-perfect landing combo, and it will feel glorious. If you can beat all the Rad levels, I bet you can show someone at the interview for your next job and you will get that job.
Personally (oh no! Personally, the verboten word in video game reviews), I'm not a fan of these endless hardcore trek-up-Death-Mountain challenges, and OlliOlli didn't change my mind. But I like what it's doing enough to recommend it.

So...ive played the wargamming series before...and i didn't like them much. I hoped that some of the mistakes in the wargamming series would not be present here. I was wrong.
I consider myself a RTS player. I broke my teeth on command and conquer, and have played plenty of others so far. This game looked good on the outside...but it soon started to give me reasons to not like it.
Firstly...strictly from a looks perspective...its not very good looking. And the sound quality is terriable. A good example i found was the heavy machine gun noise on the sherman is not continuous...so you get gaps with no sound even though its firing. It just doesnt sound like a war.
Secondly...the units themselves? Eh...i was dissappointed at the choices. I'm aware this is a game attempting to be somewhat historical, but i would have preferred to pick an allied nation and to use units from that nation, rather than a division that felt like it was missing certain units used by that nation. In addition to this, the dead units are just so very cheap. Instead of some sort of uniqueness to a destroyed tank they just give it a black skin. It would have been nice to see tanks with their turrets missing or something.
Thirdly...and the thing that drives me mad with all the wargaming games and this one...is the difficulty. War is no walk over true...but i can't even get past the second mission of the easiest campaign. It is next to impossiable. RTS games should have a gradual increase in difficulty, so that you can learn how to use your units to the best of their abilities. That is not what any of these games have.
The issue i think is the fact that this, like wargamming and Ruse have similar styles of play, trying to go for the grand massive battle, limited units and painful difficulty. This results in one thing. A lack of fun. These games are not fun. They are frustrating. And i hate that.
Want a good WW2 RTS? Stick to something like Men of War...or...play an older game like Blitzkrieg. They are still better.

Recently, I've played a bunch of puzzles games and a good friend told me to play Grimrock because of the puzzles... But to me, it was mostly the gameplay that I really liked about this one. I really loved fighting in this game. It started so slow. I wasn't even sure I was liking it at first, but after an hour or so. Bam. I was in. I was in it for good. Nothing else really interested me. All I wanted was to level up, gain abilities, gear my characters, kill more stuff, walk further, discover more secrets, and of course get confused by the puzzles.
Grimrock is a perfect example of a typical indie game that takes an old 90's (even maybe late 80's) gameplay design and redo it in our modern era. It is kind of a slow game. Every time you move is tile by tile and when you attack or so you click on the attack, do it on front of you, wait for the cooldown and repeat. But in the end, it's only like if it would be a turn based combat system, but sometimes, you can get a turn faster than your opponent. Also, it gets pretty hard. You can facetank the first level or 2 but the gameplay gets pretty crazy pretty fast. You discover new types of weapons and new monsters. You have to kite them in order to survive. They are hard. You have to act fast and think fast too. You are not always fighting in the same environment. It's a really great mechanic. Any limitations you may have, the monsters have them too. You have to learn their pattern, and execute yours.
There is just so much stuff to discover. The whole world is begging you to find the hidden stuff everywhere. You will have to face really hard puzzles just to keep going on the main tract. They always comes with clues, so it's really fair. But some of them are really obnoxious and if you are not in it for the puzzles, you might want to consider looking for a guide. Or maybe just relax and take notes for an hour or two because some of the puzzles really require you to do so.
It might be a good idea to look for character guides too before starting to play. The way you build and play your character really matters. Like you might completely ruin your run if you put stats in stuff you end up not using. The game gets pretty hard later. You have to have good gear and especially specialized characters. So if you consider playing, but you only have time for 1 playthrough. Do a bit of research, look out recommendations, and get the game because it is really fun to play.

This game is amazing, I really like it, I put a few hours into it so far nd I am loving every minute of it. The combat is very well done, and although its turn based, the fact you can move around to avoid damage is very good. Also having the 2 front line characters and 2 back line characters makes it so you can strategically place your characters the way you want. I made to fighters  with one being really tanky and the other one having a bit more damage to go in my front line and a mage and rogue for my back line, and I find it a very good setup. Theres 4 races. Human, Minotaur, Insectoid, and Lizard man, and each has their own strengths and weakness. Human is balanced all around, but isn't the best at one specific class, Minotaur is more tanky, but has low dexterity so they have a low starting hit rate, making them good tanks, Lizard man has high dexterity, but lower strength, making them better rogues, and Insectoid has higher willpower, making them better mages.
Of course you don't have to make a character based off their stats. You could for example make a Lizard man fighter that has high dexterity, but lower strength, or a Minotaur rogue that has more health and damage, but hits less,  or all humans for all around classes. It may not be as reccomended, but would work. Also honestly the game allows you to import your own photos, only the specs make up each race, so you could essentially have 4 anime chicks if you really wanted. Overall it is a great game, and is very fun, and addicting. It has great gameplay, great sound deseign with the ambient soundtrack, pretty decent graphics that are pretty enough, but also not too demanding for those that have lower end pcs can play, engaging puzzles and the enviroment is nice, even if it is just a dungeon it really fits the game, and although there isn't much to the story, it is just enough to fit the style of this game. I would highly reccomend this game. 10/10

If old school dungeon crawlers are your thing, welcome your new favorite game. I never played any of the genre before, but it makes a good first impression graphically. The puzzle designs are a little obtuse at first, but are managable with patience. The combat seems goofy at first, since its a tile-based movement game, but actually lends itself to being quite strategic in the later parts of the game.
One issue I have with some areas is that it can be almost impossible to spot where hidden buttons are on walls in the early part of the game. Unless you know exactly what you're looking for, it can be very frustrating. Later dungeons have secret buttons that stand out a little more, but hunting down those first couple of secret buttons was like pulling teeth. In some cases, they are necessary to progress thorugh the game, which can be very difficult to know what to do next without cheating and consulting a strategy guide.
The game is deceptively deep in terms of mechanics, and it pays dividends to do some research on how the combat works at the start, since levelling up certain characters for certain functions can almost be undone if you don't know what you're doing.
I wish there was a little more variety in the tilesets of the dungeons, but the monster and puzzle design make up for it, I think. I still get chills every time I'm running through a timed puzzle and the trap door in the floor opens up to a "AHHHH" scream.

If you're like me, the controls will infuriate you.  The fun you derive from this game is by creating a smooth flow throughout a level. Obstacles and incorrect timing are what interrupt the flow in a 3d game. In a 2D game, you'll find it's more often the confusing controls and what you can't see emerging from the right side of the screen that will interrupt your flow, and thus, your fun.
The primary problem is that it has a very strange control layout that doesn't quite translate from Tony Hawk's 3D world well enough to a 2D world. I wish jumping was just bound to a single button, instead of having you pull back on the left stick of the controller to "charge" a jump (which is more time consuming - which, in a reaction based game like this, can be killer). And while pressing a button to stick a landing is all well and good, it's extremely hard to time it well enough to get a smooth flow going.  It's almost like they ripped touch controls from a mobile game, and tried to emulate them on a gamepad.
And this is the problem, really: Is this game a complicated endless runner, or is it a watered-down skating game? It doesn't quite know, and it simultaneously fails at both.
I've spent about 15 minutes on this title, and I can't honestly see myself being bothered to try and master it, which is a shame because I like the music and aesthetic.
How this game because an indie darling, I'll never know. And I generally like what Devolver publishes.

OlliOlli is a simple, but fun, challenging, and mildly addictive skateboarding game. It's an arcade-styled game that focuses on stringing together combos of skateboard tricks to grab the high score, and knockout different objectives. Levels become progressively more challenging, as do the objectives. There are several game modes including a "Daily Grind" to compete for global high scores each day, and multiple versions of each level that can be unlocked by completing all that levels objectives. There's no lack of content, for sure. The game play is entertaining and challenging - landing a long combo of crazy tricks perfectly is so satisfying, and ♥♥♥♥ing up can be terribly frustrating. Personally, I find the frustration and fun to be equally balanced in a way that makes the game addicting, but in short bursts. It's the kind of game I play for half an hour at a time because of a spontaneous desire to beat a high score or try one of the Daily Grinds. The only two negatives I can come up with are the keyboard controls are a kinda wonky (although the game clearly states it was designed for controller play) and the price tag is a little steep. But overall, I'd recommend OlliOlli.

I wish there was a "mixed" option for how I feel about this game, I guess I was expecting this to be like a sidescroller version of Tony Hawk but that is so far from the truth. This game is insanely hard and unforgiving, the "amateur" mode is the basic mode you will play, and I'm scared to even attempt the extra mode, the main levels start out relatively fun but the game soon jumps drastically in difficulty. This is not a skateboarding game, this is a game all about speed and timing, I used a controller to play and the game only uses the left stick and the A button, it requires you to push up on the stick to perform an Ollie, you can try pushing different directions to pull off better tricks but most of the time I find that you don't have the time between jumps to actually land any of them and if you mess up even slightly it will ruin your entire run forcing you to start all over again, also whenever you come down to the ground you are required to "land" your trick by pressing the A button at the correct time before you hit the ground, missing that perfect moment will result in a "Sloppy" or "Sketchy" landing which will completely ruin any momentum you have gained if it doesn't cause you to bail immediately. This game would be much more fun with some sort of free skate or casual mode but instead I found it insanely frustrating just trying to get through the basic levels, I was ready to throw my controller through the wall several times. Most levels pretty much require you to grind the entire way and if you miss even slightly you will lose all speed and bail, trust me this will happen A LOT, I had several times where even though I know I hit the button at the right time it didn't register and gave me a sloppy landing resulting in me failing several levels in a row I eventually gave up once I hit level 5 because it requires such perfect timing yet like I said it sometimes does not register so even if you think you're getting good at this game it can still get glitchy and you will fail due to no fault of your own. I eventually gave it another try after a few months and finally got past level 5. If you like insanely challenging and unforgiving games and playing the same levels over and over and over until you get it right then go for it but if you get frustrated easily don't even touch this game unless you have an unlimited supply of extra controllers.
It can be a fun game, but it is def not a casual skateboarding game like most would expect and having to perfectly time a button press just to land your tricks takes a lot of the fun away and just causes more frustration.

Platform: PC Windows
Genre: Action/Exploration
:
Thunder Lotus Games first title Jotun, another positive outcome of a successful Kickstarter campaign, is an epic trot through a world of Norse mythology. It’s a top-down action exploration game that pits you against large foes and beautiful, yet treacherous landscapes. Jotun delivers challenging boss battles, but it also focuses heavily on building atmosphere and anticipation rather than throwing countless of enemies at the player. The considerable amount of downtime before these fights might put off some gamers, but if you’re able to absorb yourself in the world through its beautiful hand drawn visuals, powerful soundtrack, and epically cool voice-overs, you will also find the boss battle well worth the buildup. It might also make you want to read up on your Norse mythology knowledge.
:
Jotun tries to pack as much Norse mythology in every area of the game as it possibly can, but a few creative liberties are taken. Both gameplay and presentation might draw your mind to games such as “Journey” and “Shadow of the colossus” as you explore vast environments with gorgeous vistas and face larger than life boss battles.
Playing as Thora, a young Viking warrior, named after the god of thunder Thor himself, you are tasked with defeating 5 mighty Jotun to earn your place in Valhalla after dying an inglorious death. Thora must travel through five regions and find two runes in each and every one to summon these giants, all possessing a certain elemental property. There are few enemy encounters in these levels but they all present unique stage hazards that keeps you on your toes and prevents the overall experience outside of the boss battles from feeling repetitive.
Each region has two levels and presents its own feel but they aren’t all executed as well. The winter region Niflheim (yes, they are all tongue twisters) has one level with quite a boring and unimaginative layout and the other one has an annoying stage hazard that forces you to stand behind walls quite frequently to avoid deadly storms. The fire region also had a spot where I accidentally killed an enemy that I needed to take advantage of in order to progress, and it didn’t re-spawn, forcing me to restart the level. A very minor design flaw perhaps, but it needed to be mentioned. The Jotun of the storm region, even with its badass design, wasn’t as dynamic and fun to fight as the rest.
It might be a tad bit inconsistent, but besides the aforementioned weak points, it is truly enjoyable exploring every region and level to find health upgrades and gifts of power from the different gods, which you will sorely need. It doesn’t hurt that the soundtrack is beautifully put together and the Icelandic voice-over help set the desired tone.
:
The introductory level in Jotun teaches you everything you need to know about the controls without it feeling like a tutorial. At the end of said level, a tutorial boss is introduced to make sure that you’ve got the basic controls down before facing off with the first Jotun of the game. There are no advanced button combinations needed to become the conqueror of the Jotun, but it is far from an easy task. You have your standard light attack, heavy attack, dodge button, and one button to execute your god powers that will give you different ability boosts that lasts only a couple seconds. Thora’s heavy attack takes a few seconds to execute and her dodge roll has some end lag to it, so timing these correctly can be the difference between success, and sometimes instant death.
It’s a game that gives you a satisfying challenge with dynamic and responsive gameplay, instead of just having complicated controls and it all culminates in a moment where you must prove that you’ve mastered the timing of dodging and attacking, not only to the gods, but to yourself as well.
:
All in all, this is a great debut from Thunder Lotus Games but I can’t help but feeling that it had the potential of being so much more. Even for an indie game I’ve come to expect a bit more content, and the few traces of puzzle exploration felt lacking. The lack of enemy encounters and meaningful tasks to keep you engaged gameplay wise might also hamper a second play through, as I loved taking my time exploring every nook and cranny and savor this living painting of a world, but the second time around, I found myself rushing through most levels just so I could get to the main attraction. Your level of enjoyment might come down to how much you’ll be able to immerse yourself in the game and appreciate the awe inspiring scenery.
Ultimately though, The pros far outweigh the cons, and thematically speaking, I found Jotun to be a breath of fresh air, and I wouldn’t mind revisiting similar scenarios in gaming in the future. Dynamic battles along with a powerful score and occasionally breathtaking artwork all come together to create an ultimately satisfying experience. It might leave you wanting more, but still happy with what you got.

Jotun takes the style of games like Shadow of the Colossus and Titan Souls into a gorgeous world of Norse mythology.
While not a particularly long game, clocking in at around 5-6 hours, Jotun is well-crafted and engaging.  The hand-drawn art style brings the world to life, set to a lovely soundtrack, with an absolutely amazing sense of scale.
Unlike Titan Souls and Shadow of the Colossus, there are other enemies aside from the bosses in Jotun, though they aren't the primary focus.  Jotun is a game first and foremost about exploration and spectacular set-piece battles.  As Thora you start with a limited set of moves - light attack, heavy (charge) attack, dodge roll - but acquire spells to aid you as you travel through the different areas of the world.  Each area culminating in a boss fight that is as much a puzzle as it is a test of skill.
Again, the sense of scale is what sets Jotun apart.  Combined with the art style it almost feels like you're immersed in an old Norse storybook, traveling through the pages as you seek to impress the Gods and on your quest to enter Valhalla.

So far this game has been a viking blast. Here are some of the reasons why I would pick up this game.
1) Art Style: A lot of work has been put into making the aesthetic for this game. It is amazingly drawn and gives a sort of Banner Saga kind of aesthetic to the game. The maps look beautiful and in some parts the devs were able to give a sort of scale using this hand drawn method that I have never really seen in a game before (eg A large ocean view with pillars that look like they are taller than the empire state building).
2) Music: This is what I believe to be one of the most important aspects of a video game and this title does not disappoint. The soundtrack is perfectly in tune with the setting giving the proper mood for the proper moments. It is also great to listen too, making me wish to be able to buy their soundtrack.
3) Gameplay: Although slow in some sections (eg walking around for 15min because you are either lost or cannot find what you are looking for) the game definitely picks up the pace in combat. If you enjoy slow paced combat where you like to think about your next action (similar to the pace of world of tank, even though not related in any way its pacing is similar), however this game is real time so you will not be pausing but the attacks of the enemies and yourself are slow enough to generate this feel. All the attacks of yourself and enemies (especially the Jotun) have a real kick to them, imaging squashing 20 dwarves with one swing. The boss battles (which are the most important part of the game) are some of the best executed ones I have ever seen. You really need to think about the style of the boss and how to create opportunities to defeat it without getting destroyed by a giant shield or lightning bolt. All of the hero abilities are very fun to use and are extremely important to being able to win against a boss (you need to use them or you will not win), something that most games forget to do (aka not using an ability because it is useless later on). The controls on PC are easy to use and rebindable which is also a good thing.
Overall I would recommend you guys to take a look at Jotun, I have been having a lot of fun with it.

Jotun is easily one of the most beautiful games of 2015. The games art-style, soundtrack, and voice work speak for themselves. Being top notch and well done in every regard. One second your fighting a massive earth god and the next your floating serenely through a gorgeous star filled sky, solving constellation puzzles. It's this balance of beauty and chaos that makes Jotun such a fun, unforgettable experience. The only gripe I could possibly have for Jotun is that I wanted more. The games nine levels while incredibly well designed, make the game feel rather short just coming in at about 7-8 hours at the most. This is a rather small gripe, as the entire game is a very enjoyable experience from beginning to end. The story and theme of the game is handled very well and makes you feel steeped in Norse mythology.  Other areas like controls are tight, god powers give the game more strategies and make gameplay dynamic. Jotun is a prime example of what indie games can be, and should be. Buy this game!

Mighty No. 9 is by no means a masterpiece. But it is also by no means a bad game. The development process for this game has been a turbulent one due to the huge number of platforms the game was developed for combined with the lack of planning, and it shows through an overall lack of polish. But the basics of a good platformer are still there.
--
Graphics: 6/10
The graphics are a bit crude overall, and the character models are very rough around the edges, though this is mostly evident during cutscenes, especially since there are no mouth animations at all during dialogue and the characters stay in an idle animation most of the time.
However, while some stages look bland and a uninspired (Pyrogen's stage being the biggest offender), there are stages that do look very nice, Battalion's stage being my personal favorite in this department. Overall, while the lack of polish is evident, the graphics won't be much of an issue during the heat of action (save for a couple stages) and won't detract much from the overall experience.
--
Sound: 7/10
The music for the game can be a bit of a mixed bag. Putting aside the one truly abhorrent track (Dynatron's stage having that honor), the tracks in the game range from slightly above average to blood-pumping spectacular (looking at you, Brandish). Most of the tracks fit their stages very well, and all of them are very reminiscent of Mega Man, blending the Classic and X styles.
As far as voice acting goes, the english version does have that saturday morning cartoon corniness that some may find grating, but I had good chuckles at some moments of brilliance. Aviator and Battalion are my favorites in this aspect. The japanese version is very well done, just as one would expect from a japanese game.
--
Gameplay: 8/10
This is where the game truly shines. The game is very fast paced, and while platforming may be made a bit easier due to the air dash mechanic, the levels are built to accomodate for that. Bottomless pits and one-hit-KO spikes are scattered throughout the stages, so caution and calculated actions are still required. The controls are spot-on, and the dash absorbing mechanic, along with the combo system, make for a very fast-paced game. The transformations acquired by defeating the bosses are the true star of the show though, adding a ton of variety to how the stages can be tackled, all of them being useful at many points of the game.
However, this focus in speed does tone down the exploration factor down a notch, so outside of health items and 1-ups, there aren't any secret power-ups like lifebar upgrades or hidden equipments that require you to use the bosses abilities to be acquired, like in many of the Mega Man games, and this is a feature I truly miss. Because of this, there isn't much of the sense of progression present in those games, especially since all difficulties above normal mode give you all the transformations from the get-go.
--
Overall: 7/10
The lack of polish is evident, as is the fact that many sacrifices had to be made due to the hellish development process. However, the effort put in the game does show. The game is still fun to play, and it has a lot of untapped potential that future titles may benefit from. If anything, this served as a learning experience for Comcept, much as Mega Man 1 served for Capcom back in 1987. I truly hope this franchise follows in the steps of Mega Man 2, delivering a sequel that takes everything good about the previous title up to eleven and adding stuff to improve the game even more.
All in all, while it is necessary to look past the rough edges, platformer fans, especially Mega Man fans, will most likely enjoy the game very much.

Loved that game, therefore sharing my story:
Summary of Completed Chapters
Chapter 1
On the day you first built Sarah, you awoke from a dream about a robot companion to head to the lab. Your graduate school advisor pressured you to make Sarah more acceptable to the military. After some back and forth, you ended up making a plastic winged robot with a humanlike head and humanoid hands.
Then you went back to your place to teach Sarah some words.
Chapter 2
The next day, you hooked up Sarah's biodiesel engine and tried activating her. You then took Sarah to see Josh, who was impressed and agreed to fund your education if you would work for him after you graduated. You discovered you were attracted to Juliet, but you didn't succeed in making a good enough impression for her to reciprocate your feelings. Josh told you that evening about how he'd once been a juvenile delinquent, essentially, but turned around because he was inspired by Asmiov's book I, Robot to make a robot company called "U.S. Robots."
As months passed, you became busy teaching Sarah about the world through high school textbooks and taking her to the park. Your funding from U.S. Robots kept you in Professor Ziegler's good graces during this time.
In time, Mark Ali, a reporter for the San Francisco Chronicle, heard about Sarah and asked for an interview. You agreed.
Chapter 3
You gave Mark an interview, and allowed Mark to come back to your place to interview Sarah.
Mark wrote an article that was generally positive about you and Sarah. When Professor Ziegler found out about the article, he was very displeased, but decided that the most effective way to get you out of his hair was to let you graduate.
Mark's article also attracted the attention of one "robotObsession1987," known in real life as Tammy Cooper. A month or so later, you received your doctorate. Shortly thereafter, your father passed away. You resolved then to work on better medical technology that could save people like your father in the future.
You joined Josh at U.S. Robots as his chief scientist. Elly had already volunteered to be your first employee.
Chapter 4
Your first potential client for U.S. Robots was Galen Medical, a surgical equipment company. They were happy with the state of your technology, and gave you a contract that allowed you to purchase a factory. That allowed you to build a robot factory in Detroit. You decided to use your own robots for your workforce, but leave humans in supervisory roles. When you finally shipped robots to Galen Medical, they were pleased with the robots you delivered. Your business suffered a blow when Chinese companies, aided by Chinese government hackers, began to steal your technology. Your business was dealt a further blow when there was an explosion at your factory, caused by a bomb set by Tammy.
You were visited by a politician, Jacqueline Irons, who asked for a campaign donation. You gave a significant donation, and Irons won the presidency. The newly elected President enacted a series of protectionist bills that ultimately made China angry, and they cut off the U.S. supply of rare earths. The tensions between the United States and China came to a head with the assassination of the Chinese Prime Minister in San Francisco. War followed shortly thereafter.
Chapter 5
Captain Rogers invited you to a military lab. There, you saw that Professor Ziegler was copying your work and passing it off as his own to the military. Captain Rogers asked you to join the country's war effort. You agreed, but specified that you only wanted to provide robots that were nonviolent in nature. An agent came to your place to try to get you to lure Elly there, because she was suspected of being a spy. Elly fled to Canada to escape the American agents. A man identifying himself as "Mr. Sun" hacked his way into one of your robots to ask you to defect. You did not.
In the end, America muddled its way through the war relatively unscathed. Tired of seeing robots used for violent ends, you decided to create a truly beautiful robot.
Chapter 6B
You created a humanoid companion robot named Michelle, but you were fairly bad about allowing her to do anything fun. It seemed Michelle was interested romantically in you. When Sarah and Michelle were attacked in the street, your robots were badly damaged. You pressed charges and dissuaded Tammy from any further attacks.
Chapter 7
In 2049, you went to Surprise, Arizona to surprise your mother with a gift for the holidays. You learned it was your surgical technology that had kept her alive this long. On returning to San Francisco, you had a brief stroke, followed by a vision of a robot companion -- the same one you saw thirty years before. I played wargame prior to this game and that game while fun always irked me with territory control, placing a command unit in a area box and bam you control the area. You also lost control just as sudden and it felt like alot of the game revolved around the command units. This was my biggest issue in wargame, control of territory felt unnatural and led to games where you babysit that one unit. I am so happy this is gone in this game, now territory is determined by units influence. You now control what you actually have logically control over, units push a territory line through numbers and power. There is no babysitting that one unit that will lose your control of areas anymore, instead command is finally doing what they should be. The command makes everyone within their influence better, encouraging you to always have one with your army. The new morale system also means command units have a bew level of importance.
When units are shot at their morale suffer, once it maxes out your unit becomes pinned. Pinned units will not do anything except fall back if ordered, they lose their influence on the battle line as well. On top of this a unit that is pinned will surrender if enemy troops get close. Now a command will prevent your troops from surrendering if nearby, reduce the morale damage and cause your units to fight better. If command gets pinned though you are in trouble.
Another welcome change is that there is no hp anymore, units are still pretty though. Infantry rarely lose members unless they are caught moving without cover or pinned/falling back. But when they are caught they die fast, so quickly stopping movement of your ambushed infantry becomes vital to keep them alive. Tanks also recieved a big change, without hp they instead live and die by armor values.
When a weapon with AP value hits a tank the shot can bounce and do no damage, cause minor debuff or in extreme cases cause temporary disabled tank. Bounced shots may do morale damage but it depends on how big of a shot it is compared to armor. If a shot has higher AP than armor it can penetrate the tank and in most cases that means instant death to the tank, but it might survive with a serious damage instead such as tracks broken, guns damaged and so on.
I love this new system as this makes tank battles feel a bit like world of tanks where armor facing matters a great deal, it almost becomes a small game in itself. As for infantry, they might be unable to hurt a tank. But some units come with anti tank weapons, wich ALWAYS penetrate tanks if it hits. This makes infantry a huge threat to tanks, except that theese AT infantry have a pathetic range of roughly 200 meters. In comparison tanks can have ranges up to 1200 meters on their guns, so the main danger comes when infantry hides in terrain to take out tanks that get too close.

This game, like Super Meat Boy and its ilk, is a game of frustration. If you get easily frustrated from dying and restarting, then this game won't appeal to you.
I love the music in this game, it's a great little sound track. The movement is fluid and getting a good run feels wonderfully cathartic.
Unfortunately, that's about where my fun with this game stops. I don't mind a frustrating game but it has to be me that made the mistake, not the game. Too often, I had to restart because my skater glitched on a certain part of the track or near the end of a rail or just as he passed an obstacle. I was equally unimpressed when to stick a landing perfectly requires good timing but all too often it felt random as to how soon I needed to press the landing button...but that could just be me.
Speaking of landing buttons, herein lies one of my most frustrating problems with this game: the controls. When trick modifier and spin are the same button and I want to jump > spin > land with a modified grinding trick, all that happens is I keep spinning because I didn't leave enough of a pause between letting go and pressing the button.
Next, if you want to jump, you have to press the trick input. It works but it would have felt better if there was a separate button for jumping, tricks and landing.
Lastly, I wanted to mention the level design. While the levels made good obstacle courses, I found it difficult to keep track of my skater on the final stage as a lot of the colours blur in together. I also had a problem with the Junkyard stage as most things were brown and all too often I wouldn't see an obstacle before it was too late.
All in all, I did have fun with this game but with a mixture of problems between controls and frustrating level design, I'll be designating this game to the bottom of my pile of games that I won't be playing again. Just one last objective before I complete it :)

I love the idea, and as someone who was pretty damn good at chaining together combos of grinds w/ manuals for tons of points in tony hawk games, I was excited about this game. Sadly it is very rough around the edges. Let’s first talk about some of the worst controls I’ve ever seen. To jump you hold down, and to do tricks you hold down and make arc motions on the analog stick. Yes, you actually CAN’T use a/x to jump, the uniform jumping game button. You don’t even press up on analog like most games, you press DOWN! Then if you want to land a trick you have to press JUMP (durr duurrr), but if you want to land on rails with grinds, you use down for that. See how confusing and pointlessly dumb it is. You also can’t rebind the controls to A to jump as I tried. So good luck dying 200 times because you press A to jump or press down on analog to land, unlearning everything you have from gaming the past how-ever many years, just so this game can have “a steep learning curve”.
If the controls don’t hurt the fun, there’s the game mechanics. Tons of times when I would press A at the exact right time it would say I completely missed it and will screw up the trick, and because that makes you unable to do anything for 5 seconds I would inevitable fall down and die. Other times I would press it when I did before and it would say perfect/sick, showing how inconsistent the landing feature feels. Then there is grinding. Countless times I would press the grind button above a rail only to fall past it without grinding and lose. Other times you will be unable to tell if you can make it or not because of how the stuff looks to be in the background, and if you try sometimes you get it and other times you don’t leading to frustration at the lack of clarity of the game. The worst part is the grind button makes you go flying down, so even if you should grind and the game for some reason doesn’t let you, it will compound the problem by rocketing you to the ground (super realistic skating feature) so you don’t have enough time to press the land button, meaning you’ll probably die even if you land on pavement. Also the items being in the background means you will hit things you didn’t know were part of the course. Also I had bugs where I would just suddenly fall while grinding as if I got hit, but I hadn’t. Another time it said I was grinding but also made the sound counting me as falling, so I ended up grinding for 3 seconds before the game decided I had fallen. Also there will be times where you don’t know what’s coming up and you jump and land and there isn’t enough room to land and then jump again, meaning you must lose once more because you couldn’t see what was ahead and it was out of your control and already decided, which is dumb.
Then there is the camera. For some inexplicable reason, the camera is towards the top of the screen. I would constantly be falling and not able to see the ground, to see if there is steps, a rail, or ground. I died tons of times just because the game wouldn’t let me know what to expect till I was there and it was too late. It also doesn’t help that every time you land it takes 20 seconds to absorb a landing before you can jump again, leading to parts where you just don’t have enough room to jump again before you auto die. Also in levels with snow where the sidewalk is missing, it will count as hitting you while you are still on the walkway, which makes no sense. Snow in place of a sidewalk is lower and basic physics means that shouldn’t hit you before you get there. What SHOULD happen is if you don’t jump beforehand you fall into it, or if you land on it, but not the way it is currently terribly done.   Also the game won’t register jumps sometimes when you press them. Same goes for tricks like 60% of the time. I would swoop the analog only to have it just jump me, and right after that I’d do the same thing and the game would actually count it. There are times when everything in the game actually works together and you’re grinding and flying through the air at high speeds and making a huge combo. The environments also look pretty drab and same-y, leading to all levels of a given area to look the exact same, with only a little different layout of the rails/steps. It sucks that at least 50% of the time you fall or die or miss a trick or don’t grind or don’t do a trick, that it seems to be the game’s fault and nothing you did incorrectly, which is opposite of what I can say for tony hawk games. I get that they want to facilitate people playing the levels over tons of times but poor game design/mechanics/control is not the way. This one needed more time in the oven to fix things. Replay tony hawk underground on ps2 insead. 4.5/10.

Multiplayer co-op is absolutely fantastic. Difficulty and speed get kicked up just playing together. Even normal is HARD compared to solo, but there are also a lot of things provided to help out your partner. Games can get real intense real fast and if you don't watch what's going on, you get smacked around rather quick. I don't know if they were already aware of it or what (no indication on the forums), but within 24 hours of reporting an issue, there was a hotfix out to fix it. They communicated with me on the forums and kept close watch on the issue asking if their patch fixed it (which it did). The polite and transparent actions on the forum leave me comfortable and confident that this game is not only good but will remain that way.
In short, BUY THIS GAME. It is worth every penny, even without being on sale. I thought its price point was a bit steep, especially since this game is more or less derived from the $2 mobile version, but the added content and extra work put into the game definitely add enough to it to make up the price difference. I'm not only happy with it, but happy enough to be interested in getting extra copies for some friends of mine. nDemic, excellent work!

Seems like a great game so far. I've run into a few bugs but overall it's been pretty enjoyable - moreso than I expected.
There are plenty of open world crafting sandbox games but this is one of the few that is also a complete RPG and didn't just contain a few RPG elements. There's an Explore mode that leaves the story out. It also has multiplayer, which I haven't tried yet.
When you create your character you can choose your gender, race, skin color, hair color, fur color, eye color and clothing color. The color options seem a bit too limited, especially for the clothing. A color slider similar to Terraria may be the best way to go.
Your character will have different stats and be better or worse with certain types of weapons and skills depending on what race you choose. For example I chose Fox, which is really good with magical abilities but has low HP and deals very low damage with physical attacks and I think they each have their own unique abilities that can be learned. There are 8 races to choose from. Wolf, Cat, Bear, Fox, Deer, Mouse, Raccoon and Rabbit.
You have a character level as well as skill levels for every weapon, tool, element and type of crafting in the game. You can learn new abilities depending on what type of skills you've leveled up. Leveling up weapon and tool skills makes you swing faster but does not increase damage dealt, to increase your damage you need to spend ability points, craft stronger weapons or craft and wear other gear that increases damage output.
(It doesn't but might in the future.) Increasing crafting levels makes you craft faster. You find objects containing ancient knowledge to unlock more skills and crafting recipes as you play through the game.
There's a huge list of craftable items that expands as you progress, luckily there are some filters to help you find what you're looking for. To make weapons, armor and tools you have to first craft pieces of it and them assemble them. You can apply various elemental upgrades to your gear during the assembly process, which is a nice touch. You can build your own house or village and craft lots of furniture to decorate it with.
There's a lot of NPCs that you can interact with, most of them are pretty likeable.
Most of them have several options when interacting, such as asking various questions, inspecting them and buying, selling or trading. In Explore mode you can create a village and random NPCs will move into the houses!
It's a simple yet decent story.
When entering the volcano the scout was under attack. If I moved forward to initiate the cutscene, surviving enemies would disengage and begin to wander and then the game would freeze. I had to force close the game. This happened twice in a row. The third time I entered the volcano I waited until the scout killed all the enemies before moving forward and this made it so the cutscene didn't freeze the game.
At the end of the volcano a reward box was spawned but I couldn't open it. It was one of those boxes that vanish when opened, so I think the area being a safe zone with unalterable terrain made it so the box couldn't be opened.
The game has locked up a few times in random locations.
The sounds have been improved!
My resolution issue was apparently due to a glitch. If I fullscreen the game and then press an F button to change the resolution, the game becomes windowed and I cannot resize it using the mouse. Toggling fullscreen off makes it so the game window can be resized using the mouse.
The issue with the mortar was resolved. It now uses a wooden bowl instead of mud to craft, making it craftable in Era 0 (Before defeating the first boss).
So far it seems impossible to create your own safe zones. You can build a house almost anywhere in the game, light it up with braziers and put a bed in it, but it will never be considered safe. So you can't research new abilities or recipes nor can you heal from sleeping in the bed. Also, monsters can spawn in your house even with it sealed off from the outside world.
The water issue was resolved. I can now use the secondary fire button to place water from the wooden bucket.
A lot of the time it's difficult to tell what gender an NPC is. This doesn't really matter much but perhaps it could be displayed when inspecting them. You could just add the symbol by the race.
Crafting items takes time, but it also pauses the game. I believe pausing the game during crafting makes the timers less meaningful. It's silly that I can stand in the middle of a group of enemies and craft 100 units of twine and make a few hundred arrows while they just stand around. Leaving the game unpaused during crafting would provide more meaning to the timers, instead of 'just wasting time', it would require players to plan ahead a bit better. For example, if a player was poisoned they could simply open the menu, craft a workbench, craft a mortar and pestle and then use that to craft an antidote to heal with (provided they had the requisite materials on hand), without taking any poison damage - essentially making the crafting timers meaningless. My suggestion is to either make crafting instant or to leave the game unpaused when in the crafting menu.
The dev is very responsive and open to critical feedback. As you can see, some of the issues I mentioned in this review were resolved in the same day.
Overall it's a great little game that exceeded my expectations. There's a lot of content for such a small game (22.3MB) and I look forward to future updates.
It's a really good game so far and I hope it only gets better.

RPGs have always been my favourite genre of video games, mainly due to how they always deliver something special, more than your average shooter. With shooters while they deliver almost non-stop action and can be fun to play, RPGs are always a nice breath of fresh air, and along with this, RPGs always have more depth than most other genres and tend to be heavy in story and lore. LandTraveller is definitely no exception when it comes to this both in regards to presentation, gameplay, story and lore.
LandTraveller plays as you would expect it to from the store's description and if you've played most other RPGs, you can customize your character in any manner you wish, varying from the creation of how your character looks from the start of the game, to what their specialised skills are and how they interact with NPCs. The majority of LandTraveller's gameplay is handled really well.
There is a great variety of customisation options in ways to design your character’s appearance, most of the stuff isn’t actually going to affect how the character plays, except for when you choose which species you would like to play as. Each species have a different set of set out stats, ranging from thing such as strength and agility, and the decision by the player of which to choose will reflect on the play style the player wishes to assume.
The way in which players can build their character In the way in which they want them to be built is simple, it’s all dependant on how frequently players use a specific style, such as using an axe as a weapon or a sword, the more you use one of these weapons, the more skilled the character will be with that specific tool.
The main gameplay element that LandTraveller promotes is that of exploration. Despite LandTraveller having a rather small map when compared to others of the same genre, LandTraveller fills this map to the brim of content and things to explore quests to take on, a variety of different things to learn in different areas of the map and quests in which it will require pre-work done by the player on this aforementioned in the category of exploration, as this will reward the player with at times making progress with the quests easier as well. I’m not saying you can’t complete quests without exploring and levelling up your character a lot, but the game definitely rewards players that are willing to learn about the world they’re in and are willing to build up their character and get immersed in it.
I have mixed thoughts on the story that LandTraveller has, which I’ll explain in a minute. Without giving too much away, your character is out one day hunting but ends up getting knocked out, they’re then found later and are taken into care for a few days while they’re out cold. And, jumping ahead a bit, you learn a volcano is going to erupt and you have to learn more about it.
As for my thoughts on the story, there isn’t anything particularly wrong with it per se, it acts as a good set up and basis around the entire events like most RPGs should be, but the main issue I have with it is that the character that you’re playing as, at least at the start of the game showcases that they have more knowledge of the world and the events transpiring in general than the player actually does. Since this is a game where you’re building up your own character, the player is certainly put at a significant disadvantage when it comes to knowledge of the world they’re in when the main character knows more about it and presents little of it as possible to begin with to the player. The presentation of the story would have been better if the main character learned about the world and story and effects it would have on the world as the player did to make the player feel more like the character was their character.
The graphics in LandTraveller are done in a gorgeous pixel art style and soundtrack to go with it. These two fit so perfectly together that it would be a crime for the other to exist without the other. This is definitely two of the greatest aspects that I personally think LandTraveller does best out of most other games of its type.
Now comes to the part of my main complaint of the game, I would have sunk more time into the game past the current timestamp that I have on it now, but there is one thing that has prevented me from doing so, and that’s regarding the glitches. Random crashes, ranging from 5 minutes from start-up and 2 hours (the longest session I got out of the game) and corrupted save files, forcing me to restart. These are the main two things getting in the way of making this game reach its true potential and I desperately hope that these issues are resolved. Disregarding those issues, there is a lot of play time to be had in LandTraveller, just like any other RPG, it’s literally just these core issues that are getting in the way of me getting the true amount of enjoyment I want to get out of the game.
LandTraveller has a lot of potential and the majority of how it delivers a lot of its content is done well, with good gameplay elements, set up, graphics and sound. But LandTraveller is greatly let down by repeated glitches, crashes and save file corruptions that are really annoying and greatly hold the game back.
Pros
+ Fun and addicting gameplay
+ Exploration done well
+Great graphics
+Decent story set up
+Great soundtrack
+ Great customisation
Cons
-Character knows more than the player at the start of the game
-Game crashes, at one point leading to save file corruptions
-An annoying glitch regarding the game randomly resetting your key mappings.
Final verdict: 8/10

Set-up in a noir (& blanc) retro-cyberpunk environment, Transistor first shines with its smooth narration and intense visuals. Then, early in game, the combat mechanics reveal themselves and get the player hooked. While the gameplay is reminiscent of anything from action-RPG to hack and slash, it is really something else: no skill tree, no harrowing choice over character built, and a freedom of play style that's guaranteed to suit your taste.
Let me clarify:
The main character can stop time at any moment of a fight, and start planning her moves almost in the manner of a tactical RPG. This time freeze isn't compulsory, though, and juggling between tactical and real time mode adds a lot of depth to the strategy.
Then comes the built. No class, no tree, just slots 4 attack, 2 upgrades per attack, and 4 passive. Players gain new skills as they level up, which behave differently depending on what type of slot they are used. This system offers a great deal of combinations, which will come in handy since some situations will require adaptation. Note that not all the skills will be unlocked during the first playthrough, which adds a lot of replayability to the title.
The combinations of these mechanics results in intense, strategic fights; it compels players to create and polish their own mix, and blends perfectly with a well balanced and cleverly adjustable difficulty curve.
On the top of these two unique gameplay element (and other fun subtleties), the game makes a point of delivering a polished, detailed experience, delving into character relationships, background and motivations to create a universe that deserves attention and exploration. Add to that great voice acting and a fantastic soundtrack, and you'll understand why the reviews are overwhelmingly positive.

So I bought Transistor during the Summer Sale and I'm glad I didn't pay full price for it.  This is my second Supergiant game (the first being Pyre) and, like Pyre, I certainly enjoyed the presentation.  However, again like Pyre, the story is completely confusing and you get dumped into it without much context.  Even after finishing the game, I'm still struggling to understand what happened.  The environment seems vast, but ultimately you take a linear path towards each battle.  Again, like Pyre, the battles are just easy peasy.  I managed to make it to level 11 I think.
Probably the most annoying thing is when you enter a "backdoor" to practice skill combos, you'll eventually exit the backdoor without the option of saving some kind of preset.  I thought I had a rocking combo at one point, that did over 1500 damage, but damned if I could figure out what I did once I left the practice room.
Ultimately, it doesn't matter ... the devleopers must've realized the combat wasn't strong enough on its own and so when you encounter the last several battles, you get these critters that cloak and toss homing missiles(?) at you that basically drain a ton of health when it explodes.  Really cheesy enemies ... and they take a lot of hits to kill.
The best battle was at the end (of course) and I won't spoil it but you do get a taste of your own medicine so to speak.  The banter of the antagonist during the battle is kind of a prelude to Pyre's antagonist.
So I'm going to grudgenly recommend this game mainly on the presentation.  It takes about half as long to finish as Pyre, but I probably could've cut out an hour or more just by not goofing around with the "backdoor".

This is a perfectly functional Mega Man clone. Yeah, there's better games out there for your money--but you've probably already played through the Mega Man Legacy collection (which doesn't even include MM8, which is what this most reminds me of) and beaten Shovel Knight six times. If you're jonesing for more Mega Man content, this fits the bill; it feels like a Mega Man game made for the Dreamcast, and I don't mind that.

In my initial review I wasn't very clear about how I felt about the game beyond saying that "I love it" so I'm going to revamp it after playing for much longer and give better detail about why I like it.
Pros:
It feels like a mega man game: Some people have been saying it doesn't, but I've played every mega man and it is the game that got me into video games to begin with. While everyone is welcome to their opinion, I can guarentee that this is Mega Man like. Infact, I feel like I'm playing the NES ones all over again. I'm currently on the last boss area, playing as Raychel, and I'm being greeted with an NES classic: Three lives, Long stage, boss that won't die. Now don't screw it up or you go back to the beginning of the stage! And I love it.
The stages are interesting for the most part: Generally, the stages are just as you'd expect. Go from point A to point B and kill the guy at the end. I like that formula. There are a few stages that stuck out for me though, including the fire stage where you have to dash past falling pillars, the highway stage where you're jumping from car to car and some jerk is breaking them, and the city hall stage where instead of point A to point B, you're in a giant circle, and you're following a sniper around to try and get him to stop hiding and fight you normally. I liked it a lot.
There are lots of pits and electric traps: Now you might be saying "Why are you counting this as a pro?" well, because when I play something like this, I wanted a mega man game. And part of the fun was figuring out how to get over the pits, and avoid the spikes without dying. And even though some might call this "Aritifical difficulty" it is what I expect out of some mega man games and I welcome it.
The powers: I haven't had much experience with Beck's powers, but as far as Raychel's go they're quite fun and I enjoy them a lot. Beck's I'm sure are a little more.. range based which is good too!
Challenge mode: I played several of the solo challenges and every time I lost I just got frustrated, but that kind of frustrated where you just want to push harder until you finally accomplish it.
Retro music option: You can make the music into bit tunes. I did this immediately and left it that way.
Edit (6/24/16)
Boss voice acting: I actually really like most of the enemy robot voice acting, now that I've played beck more and they actually talk.
Okay that's how I feel about the pros, now for the cons.
Cons:
Graphics: The graphics are a little.. wonky.. Beck's walking animation is kinda weird but honestly I let this go, but I can see it being weird for other people. Raychel on the other hand is gorgeous and I'll cut anyone who says something else!
Locked content: There's quite a bit of locked stuff behind needing to "beat the game" or "accomplish a certain thing". Which bugs me a bit.
Voice acting: The voice acting is... it's terrible, but maybe they'll add an option later to put the japanese voices in which I'm sure are better? I don't know, I haven't heard them. In the future time of robots, your character can make dozens of different decisions that shape their own personal fate, as well as the outcomes of significant events throughout the development of robot AI technology. Stats that affect how robots turn out consist of Autonomy (self-awareness), Military (blind loyalty), Empathy (to have feelings for and/or understanding of humans), and Grace (perfection in movement). With 72 achievements to strive for, there's lots of re-playability.
The two main countries with superior robot technology begin having high tensions and eventually escalate to all-out war. Will you prevent the Sino-American War? Will you defend your country (the United States) at any cost, even if you lose a bit of your humanity in the process? Will you side with China and leave behind your friends and family?
Why choose sides at all when you can create your own empire with your robot army?
Interested in finding love? Will you choose a human companion or the perfect robot partner that you created? Love robots so much that you're willing to abandon your meat bag body in order to achieve Singularity? Can't decide between humans and robots? Well, you can always go for the Trio achievement.
I, indeed, recommend this sci-fi themed choose-your-own-adventure story (game). It was a fun, interesting read full of nerdy references to great inventors and scientists of the past.

Having made it to the end I really cannot recommend this game at all.
I have read that a lot of people gave up before the third level - which is understandable - but if you continue on there is actually some game to enjoy.
You get used to the controls after a while and work out how the force powers work to actually enjoy using them, but it is overall ruined by insanely badly done boss fights the like of which I don't think I have seen in over 30 years of gaming.
The developers seemed to hate the player and while bestowing them with playable sections they had to punish them with the bosses.
I rarely need youtube videos to help me play games but I looked up nearly every fight as it was so tedious to try to work out what you were doing wrong.
And having seen how to do it they then rarely presented a challenge as it was just spamming their weakness until they died.
Ignorance of game mechanics when you haven't been taught is no great weakness on the players part it is the failure of the designers.
I also - which I never do - looked to see if there was an infinite health cheat just to be able to play the game without the tedium of dying and starting again.  Sadly there wasn't and I consider having even looked really bad.
I got it in a bundle and if you can then try it but don't expect too much.  Definitely don't buy it even on sale.

This is a game about checking for discrepencies in paperwork.  It's about trying to break the rules without getting caught.  It's also about whether or not you should break the rules.  After all, what's the reward for being honest and dilligent but a crappy wage and a sick family?
How could that possibly be fun?  Well...  It's an uncomfortable kind of fun, a strange sensation that gives this game an appeal unlike any other.  It's not a game, it's a job, and you will want to try again and again until you get it right because your family's life depends on it!

I underestimated this game when it came out, but now I have to admit that playing Legend of Grimrock was an amazing experience. This is the first game in 15years that got me stuck on puzzles, it reminded me of the time when puzzle games where among the most played, and well made, games. For those of you who played games like "Eye of the Beholder", Legend of Grimrock will probably hit you in the feelings like a 1/2 ton truck.
***GAMEPLAY 9/10
The gameplay is really simple, you move as if you're on a grid one step at time (up,down,left,right and rotate 90° L or R)
You have 4 characters that move together in a square formation, so you have 2 on front and 2 at the back, note that this also mean that you have 2 on the left and 2 on the right, which might seem obvious, but will become a problem if you get sandwiched between monsters. The combat mechanic is simple, but challenging. Your front row can attack any monster with any weapon, the back row can only attack monsters with ranged/missile weapons, or with spells. You can only attack monsters that are facing you, but monsters can sneak on you and easily kill your back row, so beware of how you move when fighting more than one enemy.
When you are not killing enemies, you're probably trying to solve puzzles. This is the core of the game : how to reach the end of the dungeon. Your wits will be challenged, sometimes lightly, sometimes harder, sometimes you'll find the solution to a hard puzzle in no time and some other times you'll feel the king of all dumbs by realizing you had the solution under your nose for 1 hour, but you didn't see it... true story.
Why 9/10? I need to write this down. I'd normally give 8, game controls are good, game is challenging but not impossible, however, this +1 bonus comes from the fact that Legend of Grimrock resurrected the dungeon crawler mechanics that was abandoned long time ago. It demonstrates that old school can still kick asses.
***STORY 7/10
Story is almost a MacGuffin, it's there just to set things in motion and to give you a purpose. You're thrown into this prison/dungeon to die, but some weird voice in your dreams tells you that you can escape if you reach the lowest level... and so it begins. While descending the levels you'll find some scrolls that give you information about Mount Grimrock, which add a bit of lore to the game.
When you finally reach the lowest level ... well, you'll see. I enjoyed every single bit of the story, even though it's really simple.
***GRAPHICS 7/10
Graphic isn't great, but it's good enough. A bit more variety for what concerns the levels wouldn't have hurt, but I admit it's not necessary. I mean, Mount Grimrock is a prison and a prison isn't supposed to be about beautiful hallways and rooms, so it doesn't feel weird roaming 4 levels that look the same. No glitches whatsoever.
***SOUND 7/10
Game is almost silent, music is just a feeble echo in the background. The monsters grunts and steps are what you'll hear most of the time. When you play at harder difficulties it creates an effect on the player, hearing wierd noises behind walls and corner almost make you fear for the lives of your characters.
3) TL;DR
Overall score 7.5/10
Legend of Grimrock resurrects the dungeon crawler genre. If you are old enough to have played this kind of games before, you should buy this game, and even if you weren't old enough, and puzzle game are your thing, you won't get disappointed.
