Jotun, the name should fill you with dread: it's is norse for giant. It is also the name of a new title on Steam. Jotun is a beautiful hand-drawn single player game from Thunder Lotus Games. The visuals are absolutely amazing, it looks like you are playing a cartoon.  What Dragon’s Lair promised back in the 80’s Jotun delivers.
You play as Thora, a female viking who dies by drowning. To preserve her place in Valhalla, she must make her way through Viking purgatory. With a two handed axe, you must push your way through five jotun in order to impress the gods.  Succeed, and you will have a seat at the table within the hall in Asgard.
The game is an exploration action game.  There are several levels in the game which do not require you to kill a single enemy.  In these levels you must explore the area and find the available items all while progressing further into purgatory. Exploration is part of every level, but some levels do have enemies, and plenty of them.  When you enter the dwarven location, at first the dwarves run away from you.  They quickly gang up and you must face a horde of little hammer-wielding builders who want you out of their space.
Each area involves you collecting runes. The runes are used to unlock the doors to the Jotun’s area, which is where the boss fights are located.  Each of the five Jotun you face is unique. They present a significant challenge and each fight becomes more difficult as you do more damage to the boss. One downfall, however, is that the bosses are a bit predictable.  They have set moves that, while not performed in the exact order each time,  do become predictable when you are fighting the same fight for the fifteenth time. That being said, the fights are fun and invigorating when you do finally defeat the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
One of other items you collect are blessings from the gods.  Each area, including the introductory area, has a shrine to one of the Norse gods. When you approach it, you gain their power to use in the game.  So far I have collected four such blessings. Loki allows you to place an illusion of yourself that enemies will attack, after a while it explodes. Frigga gives you the ability to heal. Freyja gives you a speed boost. Thor gives you the power of Mjolnir in your attacks.  I am sure there are more as I still have two areas to complete, and I am looking forward to receiving those abilities.
Thora has only a few moves outside of her god abilities. She walks rather slowly around the map. Her basic attack feels slow when you compare it to something like Assassin’s Creed’s combat. But it does fit nicely in game’s environment. Thora also has a power swing. It is extremely slow but awesomely powerful. The best part about it is that once started, you aren’t stuck finishing the swing.  You can cancel it by doing her last ability, a roll. This has saved my life several times as I started the swing and suddenly didn’t have the time to finish it before an enemy attacked.
The hand drawn animation of the game immediately put me back into the 80s, though my wife says it looks more like the 90s era cartoons. The face of the first Jotun you face, the plant boss, immediately reminded me of Mumm-ra from Thundercats. The vistas you experience were awe inspiring enough that I made sure to stop and take screenshots so I can use them as wallpaper.
The story of the games is told through Thora’s narrative as you progress through the five areas. It is all spoken in Norse, with English subtitles. She tells you of her childhood and how she became a warrior. It's a great way to experience the story, especially since the game is so laid back.  I get enough of the story that I am interested in knowing more, but not enough to take away from the gameplay.
This game is something that young kids or casual gamers could play.  There is no blood, no gore, and no sex. But it is fun and interesting enough that adults used to mainstream games will enjoy it too. Jotun will challenge you and make you want some of the original art.  I give the game an 89. It's a great game and deserves a place in your backlog, but I would recommend playing it immediately.

Jotun is an action adventure game with hand drawn graphics in which you play the fallen Viking Thora, who has been killed at sea and must prove to the gods that she is worthy to enter Valhalla even though she died a dishonorable death. Your only weapon is your giant axe, which has a basic and heavy attack. While you will probably want to explore the game without being prompted, the game rewards exploration by hiding additional abilities throughout the game including healing, speed, shield, decoy, and damage. You have the freedom to choose whether to explore or not, but since the Jotun bosses are incredibly hard, you better have great technical skill if you choose to forgo the exploration. The unique hand drawn aesthetic provides the characters with a cinematic feel that enhances both the expression and beauty throughout the entire game, and is definitely the defining feature of Jotun. The game is also fully narrated in authentic Icelandic which is extremely close to Old Norse, the actual language of Vikings. The game lasts about 6-8 hours depending on how much exploration you do and how good you are, but due to the variety of worlds and unique mechanics presented in each world, those 6-8 hours are jam packed with content. The only real criticism I have of the game is that Thora seems unnecessarily slow without the speed boost ability, which can be frustrating since dodging attacks requires an already quick reaction time. If you aren’t good at this style of game or are a casual gamer, I recommend that you watch a playthrough instead because while I think everyone should enjoy the beautiful game that is Jotun, it’s definitely a game that you will be ripping your hair out over even at the first boss. For those who ARE looking for a challenge, I highly recommend you buy Jotun.

An indie exploration game with difficult bossfights inspired by Viking mythology. It feels a lot like Shadow of The Colossus with some Dark Souls and Blood Omen: Legacy of Kain elements. You play as Thora, a Viking warrior trying to prove herself to Gods in order to be allowed into Valhalla. To impress them, Thora needs to find all runes scattered in mysterious realms and defeat jotuns - giant elemental warriors from Norse mythology.
You spend most of the time on exploring vast and dangerous realms. Every single on of them not only looks different, but also plays different. In some you solve simple riddles, like lighting up correct crystals to create animal images, or use boats and fallen trees to get to seemingly unreachable islands. In others you try to make your way through a labirynth of branches or frozen rocks, dodging attacks of a giant eagle and hiding from gusts of northern wind. There are poisonous swamps full of traps as well as caves filled with lava and giants throwing rocks at you. There's a frozen lake with a giant snake poping from beneath the ice. This variety ensures, that exploration never gets boring and requires you to be extremely cautious at all times.
Traveling through levels not only allows you to collect runes required to face jotuns, but gives you the opportunity to develop your character a bit. Finding monumental statues gives you new skills, such as healing or ability to do electrical damage with your axe. Eating golden apples makes your health bar longer whereas drinking water from mysterious fountains recharges your health and skills. Sometimes they are well hidden, so you need to explore every corner.
When you collect all runes (usually two of them) in each realm, you get to fight with its boss. Jotuns are giant and deadly just like bosses in Dark Souls. They have many attacks and require you to work out when and how to evade them. You cannot block anything, so you have to dodge, run between their legs, get away when they charge or come close when it's safe. Each fight is different and its conditions change as soon as you deplete some of the creatures health. Some of them clone themselves, others turn floor into ice making it harder to move or make giant tentacles appear around you. It's very easy to make a mistake and die since jotuns' hits take out most of your health. You will repeat some of the fights many, many times before you succeed.
All characters are drawn and animated by hand, making the game really beautiful and unique. Most of the environments look lovely as well. In some scenes the camera zooms out allowing you to see breathtaking backgrounds. This, combined with beautiful, emotional music and Icelanding voice-overs, creates an experience, that's hard to forget. Personally I wish the game was a little bit longer, but about 6 hours of gameplay is not a bad result these days.
If you value the atmosphere and are not easily scared by high difficulty boss fights, you'll love Jotun just like I did. It's melancholic, mysterious and beautiful at the same time. A true gem.

Get it? Because Jotun are… giants. Yes.
Jotun, being developed by Thunder Lotus Games, does feature the Norse giants, but its main focus is on Thora, a Norse warrior who died disgracefully, and thus must make it through Viking Purgatory before she can finally reach Valhalla. In order to get to the land of eternal fighting though, she’ll have to do a bunch of, well, fighting.
Thora wields an enormous battle axe – seriously, it’s almost bigger than she is – and has to collect Runes, which she uses to summon the Jotun. The Jotun are described as elemental creatures, which fits well with their original Norse background. In addition, to give the game a bit more mystery (and replay value), each level will be procedurally generated. The combat is advertised as being “fast-paced and brutally hard,” with the Jotun requiring skill and strategy if Thora is to have any hope of defeating them. These Norse giants are huge, to the point that the camera has to zoom out quite a lot to even place a single Jotun on-screen with Thora. The Jotun are so huge, in fact, that a single finger would easily dwarf Thora.

What a beautiful game. The art is all hand drawn and is complemented extremely well with the music and narration.
Strangely the game is more focussed on exploration and discovery than combat, and you rarely have to fight lots of enemies, except for during boss fight. Boss fights which are grand and large, along with being very difficult.
The Giants do not go down easily, and their mechanics get more complex as you continue your adventure. The same can be said for the puzzles during exploration. This is where you'll spend the majority of your time. Exploring the new lands, and searching for the Seals to unlock the chambers for the giants. During this you can find golden apples that increase your health, and shrines to the gods. Here you'll be granted a special ability, and finding similar shrines means you get an extra charge of said power.
Along with these are the ones dedicated to Mimir, which will replenish your health and powers. Don't waste these willinilly, as they can only be used once.
Combat is the main problem for me. Despite your character being a seasoned warrior and leader of her village; she's very slow and cumbersome. Especially with her broadaxe. Basic swings do little damage and you mainly need to use your heavy attack to damage a giant. This however is the slow part, she lifts the axe and then you have to wait a bit for it to glint, then you can strike.
This pause slows the combat flow, and is usually the time when you'll get hit, swatted, smashed, or the giant simply mouse out of your attack area. It can be rather frustrating at times.
Even so the battles are very exciting as you know a simple mistake means you die. You're just a little mortal trying to prove your worth and impress the gods after all. The powers of the giants range quite a bit, from spawning thorny tendrils, to creating dwarves straight from the earth.
For some the game might seem rather short, there aren't many giants. Although I think the meat of the game is the beautiful world, exploration and puzzles with the giant battles thrown in for fun.
I've certainly been enjoying it, and I'm sure many others will as well.

This game is awesome. Its not you're usual point and click RTS. You really have to learn the tactics and make the right choices when building your division. OlliOlli strips trick-based skateboarding down to its most exhilarating, addicting elements.
It’s the practice and lead up to a perfect run; the repeated failure and experimentation over and over until finally you nail that perfect combo and the multipliers go crazy. OlliOlli takes that key moment and feeling that was pioneered, refined, and then beaten into the ground by Tony Hawk Pro-Skater, and removes all the fluff and needless bloat that began to weigh the series down the further it went on.
Some of this is accomplished inherently by moving from a 3D sandbox to an always moving sidescroller, which immediately gives OlliOlli a great deal of originality. But developer Roll7 clearly knows and loves the games that built (and subsequently largely destroyed) the extreme sports genre, and borrows liberally the pieces that worked best from them to make a new, disturbingly addictive blend of mechanics.
It’s Tony Hawk’s eccentricity, Skate’s organic trick system, and a whole lot of intelligent endless runner progression design. Performing tricks is as simple as flicking the analogue stick, but having to time your landings adds a considerable amount of risk versus reward to performing longer tricks when your movement speed is largely out of your control and it’s not always easy to predict what’s going to meet you later on in the level.
OlliOlli can be absurdly difficult at parts, but it’s a challenge that I always felt prepared for. The goals for each level gradually introduce new moves into your skillset, and then gave me the perfect area to learn them. There’s a feeling of constant growth as you clear each level and the gradually climbs to counteract it, but also an understanding that for some players certain challenges will be out of their reach. OlliOlli never forced me to clear a goal or spend more time on a certain level than I wanted to, but it was so successful at instilling confidence in my ability to overcome whatever it threw at me that I rarely had any desire to move on before showing the game how capable I was.
I did eventually abandon some levels, surrendering that I wasn’t quite as skilled as I pretended to be, but unlike a lot of games my experience wasn’t tarnished in any way for doing so. OlliOlli seems designed from the ground up to be as much as you want to put into it, and providing an awesome time whatever that is. The short levels are perfect for picking off in small bursts, and the addition of a daily grind which changes daily and gives a you only one chance to hit your best score, gave even more reason to return to the game instead of trying to plow through it all at once.
My biggest frustration with OlliOlli actually doesn’t have anything to do with what’s here, but the disappointing absence of a convenient leaderboard. You can track your score and compare it with others in any level you choose, but instead of being prominently displayed it’s put on a separate screen completely removed from gameplay. For a game so perfectly designed for chasing high scores (you even unlock score focused “spots” after clearing each level once), having something like Geometry Wars 2’s immediate tracking of leaderboard positioning and your next score to beat would have been far more compelling a motivator for me to chase my friend’s best scores.
That may matter more or not at all depending on your feelings toward competing on leaderboards, but it’s at least telling that my only major issue with OlliOlli is in something it lacks (and even then, it’s more the implementation than complete absence of a feature). It’s a game so precisely tuned and refined that I found myself becoming lost for hours at a time repeating levels attempting to best my prior run. It gave me a sense of accomplishment and elation at expertly executing a sequence of tricks I haven’t felt in a decade, and reminded me why I’m so sad games of this nature were killed off by their own insistence on flooding the market and deluding themselves with features nobody wanted. OlliOlli suffers from none of that. It’s pure, sublime skating perfection.
While the PC version of OlliOlli is content complete to its Playstation 4 and Vita counterparts, the port has sadly suffered a great deal in the transition. I experience a significant amount of technical issues, from dropped frames, persistent slowdown, leaderboards crashing the game, and a generally lower level of responsiveness than a game so reliant on timing needs. It wasn’t so bad I was unable to enjoy the game or play it successfully, but if you have the ability to play it on another platform it might be advisable to do so.

Dang.... Emily is Away took me on an emotional rollercoaster, and helped me travel back in time a bit too. I relived thiis experience which was really not too far fetched, because i related to a lot of the things going on. The choices i made seemed to fit in exactly with what i would've said in the situation, and it felt like i actually had an impact on what was going on. It tugged at my heart strings and visited experiences that i am familiar with through a lense of wonderful AOL messenger nostalgia.

"Emily is away" is based on a very interesting concept: a simulated chat conversation between two young people and yet very old friends that are undoubtedly attracted towards each other but won't let it happen.
You start by writing your name and choosing a profil picture amongst the ones proposed (most are related to cultural hits of the year) before entering the chat session and Emily starts chatting with you. You'll talk with her one time per year for 5 years during which your relationship will change until it withers.
Its cleverness is in the chit-chat, especially when you're trying to tell more about your feelings and then suddenly see that the answers you chose aren't always the ones you write because the character you're playing is too afraid to lose his friend.
Overall, "Emily is away" is not as good as it could have been considering its evident potential, and definitely not as ambitious as something like "Her Story" if you were looking for a game like that. But at least it's very short, which is good because Emily can quickly get on your nerves as the years go by, letting you wishing for the game to end soon. This is obviously the worst con of this game: adults might not enjoy it as much as teenagers.
If you were in highschool/college in the early 2000 era and you wished you could go back in time and relive it.  Play this game.

Star Wars: The Force Unleashed is a hack and slash third person action game where you play as Galen Marek otherwise known as Starkiller or simply the apprentice. After witnessing your father killed by Darth Vader at a young age you are taken by him to be his secret apprentice and tasked to kill the remaining jedi in the galaxy. Over the course of the story you experience betrayal and side with an early Rebel Alliance. The game tells a pretty solid story, but the gameplay gets repetitive overtime. The game makes you feel like a badass as you kill multiple enemy types and are given multiple force powers like force lightening and repulse.
Pros:
- wide variety of force powers and upgrades
- skins and lightsaber crystals
- excellent story
- range of planets you visit that are each distinct and feel star wars
- great voice acting
Cons
- sometimes repetitive combat
- mixed quality in level design
verdict:
Overall this game has stuck with me for a long time and the characters like starkiller have been very memorable. This is a game that I would highly recommend for the story and has decent enough combat to keep you entertained for hours.

Papers Please is a lot of things.
First: It's a work of aesthetic genius. The thumping mounrful soundtrack and gray muted graphics of the game serve the bleak and desperate tone supremely well. It feels like living in an oppressive police state.
Second: It's a work of narrative decency. The whole 1984 (bit on the nose) tack is a bit played out, but the events that occur during each day of public service are what makes the game worth playing. The player is offered many chances to determine what determines their morality: the welfare of a complete stranger or the safety of the family they've left at home.
Finally: It's just a super intuitive game. It's essentially Instruction-following Simulator but everything is so clear that any person could pick it up and play to the end. It's an excellent challenge to the player's attention-paying skills and patience as they sort through paperwork to pick up even the TINIEST discrepancy.

Getting lost in this huge dungeon is so great. Even in the age of Witcher 3, this game shows that grid-based movement can still be fun. I have a hard time explaining why but here are some possible factors:
- Enemies feel more menacing because you can't circle-strafe them, play with aggro range or exploit pathfinding bugs against them like in most free movement rpgs/fpss. So the dungeon feels more claustrophobic and menacing... I definitely don't feel that in Skyrim dungeons.
- Mapping out the dungeon square by square and paying close attention to your environment for secret buttons and switches feels great, and it's not the typical modern RPG experience. A free movement game can hardly hide a button somewhere on a wall and expect you to find it, here with the constrained views it works.
- The grid system allows for some very smart puzzles, I have to admit I sometimes give up and consult a walkthrough, but I enjoy their presence nonetheless!
And you get to control (read: juggle) 4 characters, so four times the RPG goodness!
All in all, you'll like it if you liked old-school RPGs like Dungeon Master, Eye of the Beholder and Lands of Lore: Throne of Chaos. But if you haven't played those games you should try it anyways! You might very well find that grid-based movement is a bit like pixel art: originally born of technical limitations, it can still bring a unique and interesting twist to a game.
Once you're done with this one check out Grimrock 2! It's bigger, more varied visually and less linear. The modding scene is also flourishing for both games, though I suspect mods for the second game must be better, modders have more material and a more advanced engine to work with.

This is another game that I had on a CD in which my little brother used to throw around as a frisbee. Which therein made me buy a virtual copy so he couldn't touch it.
I have spent countless upon countless hours on this game. My oldest brother who rarely played video games played this. My sister who never plays video games played this. Even my dad spent half an hour trying to figure the game out before saying he had something better to do. RollerCoaster Tycoon may have been the first park simulator game (arguably).
RollerCoaster Tycoon is a park simulator game (an old one I should add). You are a manager of a park and call all the shots. When you first start on a map, there may be trees in your way or uneven land preventing you from building properly. Not a problem. Trees can be removed and dirt can be manipulated at your whim (for a nice price of course :)! Alternatively, you may build underground. Basic rides such as a merry go round, track-carts and a pirate ship may be available. You may further your parks research and choose specifically what you want to be researched.
I personally go after the thrill rides first and try to acquire go-karts as they are a money maker! My first piece of advice would be to go to the research tab and ensure that you are maximizing (the research) and choose what you would like to be discovered. If you don't like my idea, heck makes some new roller coaster, scenery or even a new food kiosk! The rides get pretty crazy after some research and some new insane roller coasters (like suspended ones) come out. Be mindful of your designs. Some guests don't like rides that cost too much, are too long, are too short, are too intense or not intense enough. I haven't quite figured out the scheme to build a successful roller coaster but I found simple concepts that use gravity instead of using manual rails to get your roller coaster to a height is preferred. Some types of roller coasters (or rides like the log flume for instance) give only a certain amount of flexibility regarding their construction. Some coasters allow for tight turns while some need extra wide turns. Some (like the steel roller coasters) can do helix's and loops! Information kiosks are also available to sell your customers umbrellas and maps of your park.
Additional scenery items can also be placed by the player (and unlocked as mentioned) such as trees, gardens, statues, fountains, benches and even garbage cans. Benches by exits of thrilling rides are exceptionally needed as some guests may have to puke. While sitting down, they slowly recover and you don't have to pay as much for an extra handy man. There are service staff that can be hired, most notably mechanics and handymen. Handymen will keep your park clean and will water the gardens whereas mechanics do inspections on rides and fix them as needed. Guests and rides in the park can be clicked on to get feedback (as in was it fun, what is this person thinking, what is this person thinking about this particular ride etc...). Almost anything can also be renamed (including guests) and admission costs to get into the park can be modified. Parks come in different sizes, shapes, colors and location. RCT works off a grid system making it quite easy to build what you need to build.

are not quite outdated but will be bothersome to a few. A full screen resolution is available and should work on most to all monitors. I think the game play will outweigh the graphics on this one.

In the beginning there was just VOID, which was incredibly blasé farie. Flanking the VOID was a fire realm and ice realm. It was inevitable then that ice and fire would have a fated meeting, star crossed lovers that they are. Sprung forth from their, ahem, unprotected meeting was Ymir, a frost giant and generally unlikable dude.
Then there was a cow and some heavy licking that resulted in more gods and giants and that all lead to a very crowded VOID.
Things went downhill quickly from here and, following some heated disagreements, Odin and his brothers created the known world from Ymir's corpse. Much bonding was done among the survivors. The last of the frost giant, finding the whole situation rather distasteful, escaped on a raft (presumably made from Ymir's all-purpose building corpse).
It was a rough Monday to say the least.
But this is all good, because without all this intergenerational conflict we wouldn't have Jotun today!
Jotun is an action/adventure indie title... I know, I know – there are a LOT of those. This one, however, is special. Diligently, lovingly hand drawn to Disney animation pedigree, narrated entirely in enchanting Icelandic, and sporting (for this reviewer's money) the most striking, stirring, and impressive game soundtrack of 2015, Jotun is a GOTY contender and should belong in any sensible gamer's library. Does it have issues? Sure, a trivial few. But not enough to dissuade me from enjoying the ever-loving ♥♥♥♥ out of this game.
You play as Thora (George Foreman Naming Syndrome?), shieldmaiden and generally badass viking lady who's been cruelly denied a seat in the beer n' blood splattered halls of Valhalla. After taking umbrage and calling Norse Afterlife Support she's given a second chance in Norse purgatory: Gingaggagap...
Ginnungapgap...
The Gap, let's just call it the Gap. Thora is trapped at the Gap presumably until Ragnarok – unless she is able to defeat the Jotun, a race of elemental giants that have literally nothing better to do.
And that's the crux of the game! Beat five elemental giants, get plucked up by the Valkyries and taken to Valhalla to watch Game of Thrones for the rest of eternity (really need to brush up on my Norse mythology).
Easier said than done.
Each Jotun encounter is broken up by two levels... you have to find their two respective runes, learn some godly powers you can call upon Kratos-style, and improve your overall health while exploring the strange and fantastical settings of Norse mythology. Each level is a little different – some have basic combat, some are puzzle focused – all require exploration. All you need to progress is the two runes but I'd recommend finding those aforementioned god powers and health ups... you'll need them.
After you've gotten your viking chores and♥♥♥♥♥♥squared away you're off to face a Jotun – arguably the highlight of the game; like if Disney's Hercules animation made a shame baby with Shadow of the Colossus/Dark Souls boss gameplay. Thora is a small fry compared to the Jotun and will have to use her god powers, wit, and axe to defeat them all. And it isn't easy, let me tell you. I died at least two, three times to each and every boss in the game (the last two I just kind of lost count after all the screaming and crying and vomiting and passing out). You have to learn their movesets, their weaknesses, and their favorite colors defeat them! When you finally bring one down it's exhilarating, the same feeling I experienced figuring out a Souls' boss coupled with the sadness of bringing down a Colossus. It's epic and my written words just won't do the event justice.
“But Spirit, didn't you mention that the game had issues – a trivial few?”
Don't – don't take me to task in my own ♥♥♥♥ing review. Jesus.
But yes, there are a few annoyances. As awesomely epic as the boss fights are, the sheer size of the Jotun can cause issues – of the hitbox variety. Sometimes you'll clearly strike the enemy and miss for whatever reason, and sometimes (worse-still) you'll get clobbered when you were clearly out of the way (two boss fights in particular are guilty of this). I also found myself getting lost a dozen times during big fights. If you end up behind a Jotun you can see your silhouette but... sometimes there's just so much action on screen it's hard to keep up with everything happening.
Jotun is also a little... formulaic. Explore two levels, defeat Jotun, rinse and repeat. Each level is captivating visually and usually does its own thaaaang, but... that's going to be an issue for some people. The story is okay, doesn't really break the mold. It's very similar to this year's other awesome indie mythology action/adventure, Apotheon. That isn't necessarily a bad point, and I still enjoyed Thora's story, just don't come into this expecting Lou Ferigno's Hercules (I'm here to write reviews and punch bears to the moon... and I'm all out of reviews).
But in spite of all that, Jotun is one of my favorite games of 2015 – definitely top FIVE. It's beautiful, it's epic, it's a tour de force for developers Thunder Lotus Games – one that has surely impressed those captious, cantankerous gods.
I don't usually find myself grinning ear-to-ear after beating a game but... I did for Jotun.
Here's hoping it impresses gamers.

Jotun tells the story of a fallen viking warrior named Thora. Battling through the depths of purgatory in order to impress the gods and gain access to Valhalla.
Waking lost in a forest dazed and confused, direction guided by your subconscious which is spoken through subtitled Icelandic dialog. From the outset it's a strange beautiful world, all handrawn and animated akin to a disney film or some of the better anime series. Revolving around Norse Mythology, if not at all familiar the game does a good job of explaining each reference.
Nine levels are spread across 5 different regions which all varied wildly, depicting different aspects of the culture and culminating with fighting a
. Without giving too much away, will be climbing giant trees, forging star constellations and all sorts of other strangeness.  Focus is around the boss fights though was plenty to do between. Each region containing 2 areas with light puzzle elements and environmental challenges. Main tasks were finding runes for further progression, god shrines that grant powers to Thora and optional hidden Ithunns Apples which increased your healthbar length.
Screen resolutions of 4k+ were available. Keyboard had full remapping support and both kb+mouse and gamepad were responsive. Perhaps the biggest flaw to some will be the walking speed. Ultimately Jotun is more about the journey then the destination. Still one worth taking that I've thoroughly enjoyed. Playthrough should take around 5hrs+, can find the rest of mine below though I would suggest checking it out firsthand. Cheers folks.

I've got mixed emotions about Choice of Robots.  Mixed because, while I ultimately cannot recommend its purchase, it OOZES of potential.  Potential that was, unfortunately, not realized.
The first half, arguably the first two thirds, are a delight.  The pacing is fantastic, and the writing is superb.  I felt a genuine attachment to the characters, and the tight, personal focus helped make my decisions feel impactful.  Maybe not on a global scale, but on a tight, individual level that mattered to me.
All that falls apart as the game goes on and the scope of the story expands.  As the game goes on, several years at a time pass at the same rate a single year passed earlier on.  The pacing jump feels jarring, at best, alarming at worst.  As the story wore on, I found myself growing less and less attached to the characters involved, even those I had previously cared about, simply because my interactions with them were often separated by in-universe years at a time.
Though Choice of Robots has its merits, ultimately the experience does not warrant its price tag, in my opinion.  It tries to be too much too quick, and loses itself in the process.  It's cheap, sure, so if you REALLY wish to try it, you'll get something from the experience.  But there's better interactive fiction out there for free.
A great idea with poor execution.  Rather appropriate, given the subject matter.

Yep... I see the hate comments... And i see what they try to get at. But let's say. Just for a minute... Get those comments out of your head and listen here, from the perspective of someone who never played the game when it was in its glory days, who only played the game when it was pronounced 'dead' by most of it's playerbase... My account of Victory: The Age of Racing.
We'll get the bad parts out of the way first, of which I could only find two prominent bad points. The first being that the developer ditched the game to try to get a 'fresh restart' with a new game, with a new engine... (that ends up being pretty bad, ♥♥♥♥ off, racecraft). The game is in a really stable state as it is, so even If the game was never updated I can't see it being plagued by any horrible bugs for a while to come.
Second and last bad point being that the Newer playerbase is dwindling, for first timers it's hard to get around and understand it, but keep in mind most games are weird to get a hang of when you first dive in. Ill get back to this point later.

*The Graphics/Playability*
Graphically, it's nothing special, but nothing horrible or something I would have discomfort with. A good point of this, though, is that a suprising amount of older machines can play this to an extent (Don't use cockpit view if you are playing on a potato, that shaves off alot of fps) Newer Intel HD graphics Laptops and even older laptops with good CPUs can run this game. NO bugs have ruined my playing experience to this point.
*The Community*
This is what's really nice, you'll find alot of good player who will help the new playerbase because of good sake, they know that If they scare away the new playerbase and never get them comfortable this game will be doomed.[There are two-and-a-half types of players in this game, the Really good Level-cap who've been playing forever (about 3 online at any given time) The I-just-intalled-this-an-hour-ago (About 4 to 7 on at any given time) and the in-the-middle-pretty-good-but-not-really-level-capped players (about 1 to 3 on at any given time).

Alright, look.
This is a great game.
If you enjoy dungeon crawling in the slightest, this will probably be the ebst dungeon crawler you will have played, at least in a very long while.
It is a grid-based system with a party of four sitting in one square, and the party members are hit depending on where they are standing in said square, so which way you face is important when in combat, along with party orientation.
I normally go around with two tanky warrior-types in the front, with a wizard and a rogue-type in the back. There is a lot of customization when it comes to using each class, and to be honest you could definately beat the game with a party of all only one class. There are also a nice selection of races to choose from, that have benifits similar to something of Dungeons and Dragons. There is also a hunger system that adds stress to how much time you spend on puzzles and walking around, while food does become somewhat plentiful, spending too much time in an area can deplete your food supply quickly.
The graphics look great, even on low-end PC's like mine, which helps set the eerie mood with a looming mystery the entire dungeon. The lighting is based mostly on torches and magic blue light spells either cast by a party wizard or just sitting in the dungeon. The player can put any grabbable torch into one of the four character's hands to carry around a light until it runs out. However, sometimes the torch placement is used in some puzzles throughout the game, which is very creative.
The dungeon layout itself is amazing, with hidden passages that can be easily found by looking at a specific spot on the wall. There is a distinctive tileset that is used throughout the entire dungeon, which helps you become familiar with what you can look for to help you survive. However this is also something of a downside, being that the areas can sort of look the same at times. They do change up the lighting which can dramatically change the feeling of different floors, as the tileset is slowly revealed thoughout the entire dungeon.
There is plenty of enemy diversity, including spiders. If you have arachnaphobia I reccommend getting someone else to play for you at certain points in the game. The developers did not hold back in making these spiders scary as they jump towards the party and cover the screen with their...spider face? Also they poison you, which is probably some of the most stressful times I have had with this game.
The story in this game is most certainly not thrust upon you, and you will have to search for it. It is not incredibly intense up until the end. It is discovered from notes of previous criminals that most likely died in the dungeon, and through these text-dreams that can occur when the player makes the party rest to recover health and mana. Honestly the gameplay and the graphics do more than make up for the story.
I am currently reviewing this game while it is 3$, I bought it for around 20$ and it has had far more value than most games that I have put over 60$ into, so it is incredibly worth it. If it makes it even MORE worth it, the game has a dungeon creator and is supported by the Steam Workshop, there is limitless time that can be put into it, and I believe someone even made an endless random dungeon or something. Even more, you can replace the icons of your party to be any small image, and have a party of anyone run through, which can be entertaining, especially for those who like to stream games. This game also has touch-support and can be played with just the mouse, or both the mouse and keyboard, which I know can be very helpful for some. So just buy it already and have a blast!

SHORT REVIEW INCOMING:

This is a decent flight simulator.  However, it has a few problems that are a direct result of its rather unconventional history.  This was originally developed and released by 1C, but they did not provide much further support for it.  During the past few years, a group known as Team Fusion has been providing community-made modifications to improve the simulator.
As far as community modifiers, Team Fusion is wonderful.  However, they are not a professional design studio, and they are not publishers.  This is where problems occur with this software.  The documentation is basically non-existent.  There is a changelog, which is great, but there is not the sort of solid flight manuals that you would expect from a serious developer.  There are "flight manuals" on a third-party website that have a list of keyboard bindings for each plane, but this is very bare-bones.
Ultimately this is the problem with Il-2 Sturmovik: Cliffs of Dover Blitz.  It is a poorly-designed flight simulator that was hacked into a usable state by community modders.  Do not expect that this will be a professionally-developed, fully functional, well-documented flight simulator.  Team Fusion is not 777 or 1C or Eagle Dynamics.  And ultimately, the blame for this does not lie with Team Fusion, but with 1C for failing to improve this simulator after its initial release and leaving it in the care of a community modding team, and then bringing the community modding team into the fold and pretending to the world that this is the same as providing professional development for this simulator.
It is possible that in the future, with an influx of funding and support from 1C, this simulator will eventually become a professional quality product.  At the moment, if you want to experience WWII combat over Britain and France, DCS has a Normandy map and four WWII planes.  This will be far more expensive than ClOD Blitz, but you will get a serious simulator from a dedicated developer with extensive documentation and constant updates and improvement.

Written after my fifth playthrough.
In interactive novels the writing is (literally) everything. And on that merit alone this one succeeds with flying colours. It's just so well written, I really can't praise author Kevin Gold enough. His real-world technical understanding of the concepts involved make Choice of Robots emminently immersive and believable without going (too far) over your head. And beyond the technical details, this is just good old fashioned great storytelling. Whether you choose to roleplay the asocial genius with only robots for friends, a cuthroat captain of industry, a devoted lover, an artist, a power hungry tyrant, or any other of the myriad life paths Choice of Robots presents, this game will tell you a story that is fundamentally about being human. And it's a compelling one at that.
Every time I sit down to play, I'm choosing to reinvest my precious time in a game that I know is going to make me really feel something, and often it's something completely different from the last playthrough. I feel thrilled when a long term goal comes to fruition, and conversely the way things spiral out of control sometimes can be genuinely upsetting. Whether I achieve my starting goals or not, almost every playthrough prompts me to redefine what it means to win. Because five playthroughs in, I'm still finding myself becoming attached to the small cast of characters in new ways. I can't say that about many other games.
Although the replay value of this game is quite high because of all of that, there is one caveat. I'll call it the Taris Effect (KOTOR players will already know what I mean). The story will always start the same way, and there are only a limited number of ways out. The choices in these first big branches can become familiar, and the immediate results start to lose their impact after only a few plays. In Choice of Robots' defense, the number of smaller and more unique branches quickly multiply once you get
out of school. Not really a dealbreaker I'd say.
Overall, if you're looking to try something new or even if you just liked choose your own adventure stories as a kid, then I highly recommend Choice of Robots.

This game is for the hardcore player with an IQ 120+ and incredible multitasking skills. For the causal player it will strain your brain with all the small micromanagement adjustments and cat like reflexes you will have to preform with your mouse while predicting in the back of your head how the rest of the flanks are going. These elements are crucial to be competitive in most games to the point where the game is simply not enjoyable and your are counting number rather then watching the battle and your commands unfold.
The campaign is a rush due to time limits and to the insane amount of units the game expects you to command against ever increasing AI counter attacks. The game at this point becomes about luck as you throw units all over the map in a rush to deploy them and thus never have enough time to actually execute complex commands. Either the enemy will overwhelm you or you will overwhelm them and you will have no idea how it happened because you were barely watching and it does not feel satisfying.
Avoid this game if you are not a hardcore RTS player or Jordan Peterson. This game requires a lot of learning, tedious micromanagement and intelligence. (Also the very few players on multiplayer will kick your♥♥♥♥♥)

First and foremost, I don't really like twin stick shooters all that much and if I didn't know who this guy who created this is, I probably would have passed on this. That said...
A lot of people who see this game do not understand what this man has done for the indie community. He is an inspiration and a visionary who takes his time and creates tutorial classes and I guarantee a lot of indie developers would not have released their games had it not been for him. Anyone who has seen his work on Youtube, C Sharp Accent Tutorials need to buy this game and support what he is doing. I'm glad people like him are in this world. Now, as for the game. It's initial humor is pretty hilarious and a creative loading screen. A great exercise how to make a fun game from a basic premise with low-fi graphics. The gameplay is actually enjoyable and suitably challenging with the ever-evolving ruleset. There is at least replay value for a second run-through of the campaign of about 6 hours.
The world is simple, yet immersive. It's easy to find yourself attached to a son you never even get to see. The ingame geopolitics have a surprising amount of coherence and depth, given that you just get snippets of history from newspaper headlines and conversations. Most entrants you process are just numbers, but a not insignificant amount comes with unique personalities.
The moral implications of your in-game job are most interesting. By the end of the game you get to push around absurd stacks of paper to fit the whims of a kafkaesque immigration ruleset. And yet each individual rule somewhat makes perfect sense. These are dire times, there are frequent terrorist attacks, there are subversive elements from within, there is rampant drug and weapon smuggling. It's actually completely sensible for a government to crack down in this situation. And yet there are individual tales of hardship, hope and love as people yearn to escape, find a better life or be reunited with their loved ones. There are no easy answers and the game does not dumb down this dilemma.
And then you find yourself thinking, "I could deny the entrant, stamp a reason and hand them back their 4 documents one-by-one - or I could just press the 'detain' button and have all my problems go away with a single click". In that moment you realize the banality of evil and how it is in each and every one of us and the game turns from a great experience to a brilliant masterpiece.

A dystopian hell where every single error you make in cross-referencing trivial details will result in dire punishments for you and your family.
Reminds me a lot of my first job.
All joking aside, Papers, Please is a fine piece of work. An almost flawless marriage of tone and mechanics; a simulation of a bureaucratic nightmare in which you are responsible for imposing half-mad arcane rules on living, breathing humanity.
I expect everyone who'd be interested in this game owns it by now, but still, a damn fine demonstration of how videogames can be art (yes, I am a ponce). Artistic intent made real by crafty design, a gem of the indie genre.

I'm going to offer a dissenting opinion on this one, because it seems all the other grognards can't seem to take off their rose-tinted glasses and put on their real prescription lenses. Furthermore, this review is going to be different from most of the others, in that I'm going to focus on the controls. Read on and you'll see why.
Essentially, this is the most awkward-controlling dungeon crawl I've ever played. It shouldn't be actively
to get my characters to do what I want. A lot of people defending the control scheme will say that this is how the old games played. Which old games, exactly, had controls like this? I played the old Wizardry. I played the old Might and Magic. I played the old Ultima. Those are the first in the CRPG genre, and they all managed to be much easier to handle than this. FFS, the old Wizardry games made you
! No, scrambling to manage a UI during real-time combat doesn't simulate the rush of combat--it just serves to frustrate me. Having to click on a small area of the screen with speed and accuracy isn't nostalgic, since all the firsts of the genre didn't have mouse input. It's scientifically-proven bad design. Yes, there's real science behind it: it's called Fits's Law. Maybe if you're a twitch gamer you'll like this, but I just found it frustrating and tiresome.
I grew up playing the firsts of the genre, and Grimrock doesn't resemble them at all--or if it does, I wasn't able to get to a point where I could appreciate it, because the controls are so bloody difficult. This game was an exercise in awkwardness and frustration that I haven't felt while gaming in a very long time. Don't confuse bad game design with challenge: the two are distinctly different.

OlliOlli is a skill and timing based 2D side scrolling runner with a skateboarding theme. I say runner, because even though you're riding a skateboard, you can't stop. You're always moving to the right. Its an original take on the genre and a fresh skateboarder. I'm not sure this game is for everyone because of the genre and control scheme.
The goal is simple, make it to the end of each level without falling off your board. You'll grind, jump and ride your board to the end. Just you. Getting to the end unlocks the next level. Each career level has five optional goals. Things like get X score or X combo. Jump gaps, collect spray cans, do a kick flip, only use one push or grind everything that needs girding. When you accomplish all five goals in an amateur level, it unlocks a pro level. Not only do the goals keep you in the relatively short levels, but you're rewarded for playing completing them. Outside of the career half of the game there is a "spot" half, with 25 more armature levels. These spots require you to do one long trick combination to the end of the level. There are 25 pro spot levels to compliment the amateurs.
The challenge isn't avoiding obstacles, its the unique control scheme. To get speed, you need to push with the simple tap of a button. Two taps gets you up to top speed. Now for the tricky part. Instead of having a jump button, you use the analog stick to hold in one direction to charge the jump and release. So you flick the stick to jump. The direction you flick the stick determines the trick in the jump. There is a trictionary if you're looking for a specific trip, but I don't think it matters what trick you do. Your momentum determines the distance of the jump. You can even do quarter circles, half circles and so on to perform bigger tricks. Its elegant and simple yet complex and difficult to time because of how unique it is.
When you are about to land the jump, you need to hit the land button, which is the same as the push button. If you don't push the land button, you'll land a "sloppy" which briefly stuns your rider by making him unbalanced. Getting stunned makes you vulnerable to falling off your board because you can't jump. Hitting obstacles or falling down a flight of stairs sends your rider tumbling a comical distance. In a way its a funny bit to tell you that you've failed, but in another way its a time wasting punishment. There are several grades to your landing depending how close to the ground you hit the button. A sloppy landing can make 20 trick combination worthless for point value. The grade of your landing not only determines the score you get for the combination, but it changes your momentum. A sloppy landing slows you down while a perfect landing will make you speed up.
Outside of pushes, jumps and landings, there are grinds and twists. Twisting in air requires you to hold the button before you jump so your rider gets into position. I didn't find these necessary, but if you want a bigger score, you'll twist like its the 1950s. Twists are true risks and rewards, because you can fail the level if you mess up. Grinds are much easier. If there's a wall, railing or rooftop, just push the analog stick and hold it. Releasing it makes the rider jump as he normally would. Getting big combos relies on your ability to grind. Like with landings, you can score perfect grinds too, depending on how late you time your grind. Some of the later levels rely on your ability to make perfect grinds, because they keep your momentum going. Just know this is what you're getting yourself into.
There is an easy to use, optional tutorial that explains all the controls. Everything gets explained one by one before the game makes you do them.
There are five themes in OlliOlli each has its own color pallet. A grey urban, a brown pallet junkyard, a blue port, a snowy white base reminiscent of Rush'n Attack and finally the bright neon city. They are all beautiful, but they go by in an unnoticeable blur. I couldn't pay attention to anything other than was there a grind or a landing coming? As the levels get higher, the challenge grows. The base has safe pavement to land on, but a lot of it is snow that sends you tumbling. Its fun to grind over helicopter blades and statues instead of simple railings and walls. Neon city is mostly rooftops and railings to grind on, because the ground is either pink spikes or wide stairways.
To keep you in the game there are daily challenges that let you practice as much as you want, but you only have one real attempt. Each level has its own leader boards after every attempt.  The game keeps track of your high score of each level and your best trick combination for that run. Truth be told, the game did freeze and twice crash in four hours after some completed runs. I assume because it was loading leader board standings and couldn't.
The soundtrack is also a real standout. The lo fi electronic beats fit the art style. For the most part it felt like all mellow songs, but there is an eclectic mix of tunes. No matter what the beat, nothing got in the way and just added to the feeling of zoning out that I had while playing. The game became all timing with no thought. I just knew from playing that was the millisecond I needed to do something. After spending 20 - 30 minutes on some of the later levels of the amateur career, I could might be able to do them blindfolded.
In the future I'd like to see different riders to unlock. Not that the rider was anything bad, but it was just him for the 4 hours I played. I am thankful for him having a red hat, otherwise he may have gotten lost in the blur of the background.
In conclusion, its a fantastic presentation and a test of skill, but I'm not sure how fun the game actually is. I found my mind not as engaged as my reflexes were. I wasn't having any joy going through the motions. Although I did get a few laughs seeing my rider tumble down flights of staircases and seeing just how many meters he could go. Its still a good game, but after going through the armature career and spots, I'm just not that willing to unlock all the pro levels.

The last skateboarding game that I played other than 'Tony Hawk's Pro Skater' was 'Skate or Die' for the original Nintendo. That was about twenty years ago. So long ago in fact, that I pretty much forgot skateboarding games existed outside of Pro Skater at all. And then I found 'OlliOlli' and had about two hours of fun before I inevitably grew bored of this board...skating game. Don't get me wrong, those two hours were pretty fun and if you get the chance to pick this up for a low price then I'd say that you should. But on the other hand, you may want to keep away.
The first thing I noticed about this game was the soundtrack, it's diverse and the songs fit into the gameplay and style extremely well. The second thing I noticed was how weird and unnatural the controls on a 360 controller initially felt. It took me a good half an hour to get used to them, and even after that I still got tripped up from time to time. They're definitely tolerable enough to enjoy the game though, so don't worry about that being that big of an issue. The third thing I noticed was that there really aren't that many tricks, and the levels mostly consist of grinding from rail to rail in search of a large enough combo to unlock the next one. As you can imagine this gets quite repetitive after a while.
So basically, after a few hours, if you aren't completely terrible, you've pretty much unlocked every level, heard every song, and collected every item. And unless you're someone who constantly feels the need to beat the highest score, there really isn't much of a reason to come back to this one. So like I said, if you get the chance to pick this up for cheap then check it out, but anything more than $5 and I'd pass. And $5 might even be asking too much.

This is the only flight sim I play anymore. It's the only one to give me the thrill of what it may actually have been like to pilot these glorious planes during those dark days of the second World War. To truly master the fine mechanics of getting a Spit I 100 octane in the air and into combat without nosing over at takeoff, or blowing a radiator on the climb-out takes real perseverance and practice. This is not War Thunder. It's a highly sophisticated simulation involving complex physics models and meticulous attention to the historical details of each aircraft represented. The joy in this type of sim is truly mastering your aircraft and learning the personalities of their engines and aerodynamic properties. It's about getting your butt handed to you by ace pilots who have put in their time, until the magic moment things click, and it's you on their six now lighting up their leaking fuel until they're a fireball spiraling into the North Sea.
In this context Team Fusion took tarnished bronze (all respect to 1C) and turned it into shining gold. Through tireless hours of their own free time spent gathering feedback, discussing, designing, coding, testing, debugging, and retesting fixes they've given the community the game it deserved. They sacrificed family time, days off, even their own money to see these enhancements through. The newest version, Blitz is the culmination of their tireless effort and sacrifice, and it deserves a huge round of applause. And all we've had to pay for is the CORE GAME. All the enhancements to date have been free of charge!
Unfortunately, flight sims have become a very niche market in the overall gaming industry and the number of fully funded development teams making high quality sims can be counted on one hand. We are fortunate to even have a group like Team Fusion who are active participants in community and doing their utmost to deliver a product that gives us hours (way too many hours some days) of endless enjoyment and camaraderie with fellow aviation and simulation buffs.
I apologize, but if you can't overlook some of the little quirks and bugs natural to a complex sim then you should probably go play a simpler game. However, if you like having a blast meeting the challenge of a sophisticated flight sim, download the current version (Blitz), mic up on Teamspeak, join us on the ATAG server and come fly with a bunch of truly great folks in one of the finest simulations ever produced. We're a super friendly bunch, we'll talk you through the learning curve, teach you how to get off the ground, and watch your back when you get in the mix. The game itself is stellar, but it's the solid community of people involved that keeps me flying for hours and will keep me coming back for more.
A big THANK YOU again to Team Fusion.

I was never a "Cliffs of Dover" fanboi. Quite the contrary: I was so disappointed by the initial release that I gave up on the game completely, in disgust, mostly over the bad FPS but also a host of other big and small issues, never touching it for years. (I played the classic "IL-2 1946" instead.) Then I heard rumors of improvements made by a modder community - Team Fusion - and eventually (and grudgingly) I tested it. That was version 4.3. And I was really impressed! Not least by seeing the performance issues solved: I got far better FPS on this state of the art combat flight simulator (with much more detailed aircraft and vehicles and equipment models, much richer terrain, much nicer effects, including dynamic shadows etc) than ever on my old and beloved "IL-2 1946". Now I have clocked some 127 hours on the 4.3 version by Team Fusion. So I know this game pretty well.
Now the 4.5 version has arrived, in the guise of "Cliffs of Dover Blitz". And this is yet another big, BIG step forward! As I understand it this is no longer a modding venture. These guys have been given the source code, and have been implementing a large number of mods and tweaks directly. This means that the performance FPS-wise it is better still! Smooth as silk on my rig, but with even better graphics! A lot of small issues have been solved - some I haven't even noticed, but some, including some real eye-sores on the map, I really have. The effects are in general better, there are a number of new variants of existing aircraft (two new Bf 110's, an improved Blennie, a bomb carrying Hurri etc) but also a new flyable: the Beaufighter in both day- and nightfighter versions. And the Beau is a real joy to fly, and not least to fight with: the armament on this beauty can rip anything apart! I've had no problems in running it.
"Cliffs of Dover Blitz" is IMHO the best WW2 Combat Flight Simulator out there. Which may come to as a surprise to you as we have now the new, sleek and MOST impressive "IL-2 Sturmovik" series (which BTW I also have). What settles the thing for me, is firstly the period and place (1939-40, Battle of Britain, NW Europe) and secondly that "Cliffs of Dover Blitz" have a much simpler and more readily available Full Mission Builder - the "Sturmovik" one being VERY tricky to use.
What is the real icing on the cake is that "Blitz" is just a stepping-stone to the next patch, or next game, which will cover the war in North Africa. And judging from this version of the game it will be very good.
Highly recommended!

Dungeon Journey is a simple concept of a tile uncovering game mixed with RPG elements and turn-based combat. By far the best $0.49 I ever spent on steam. If you like stat crunching, loot and decent challenge I think you will have lots of fun. Surprisingly enough it has a good amount of depth and variety.
For $0.49-2.00 you really can't go wrong with it but if you must have more detail please read below .
You can learn basic mechanics in about 2 minutes but there is a lot of decision making beyond that. The best way to describe the gameplay is -Risk vs Reward+Lots of Grinding. You constantly choosing between exploration and saving your health. However, grinding is a big part of this game. You may find that yourself stuck in the same dungeon for a long time until you can level up enough. Make sure you go to your inventory and right click on items to put gems inside. I have 3 unlocked playable characters but it looks like there are 5 in total. Each has 2 unique abilities and 2 passive abilities which you can level up.
If you die you loose nothing except dungeon progress. Eventually, you should have no problem beating it .There is Endless mode so if you get maxed out you can certainly go for personal goals. Loot and Crafting system is pretty fair. You can upgrade items and craft smaller gems into bigger gems to increase bonuses ( very similar to the way Diablo 2-3 did it )
Technically combat is turn-based. That means if you hit the enemy they will hit you once too. So you should not click a lot because block animation won't be able to keep up .
How to use shield properly? You will see enemies "shoot lasers" toward you and you may notice that block is not working. Well you actually have to block the animation that comes after that. When laser touches you you will see claw marks,axes,bites etc. (that is what you have to block) There are a lot of unique enemies in the game and most require different block timing. There are some that shoot projectiles that you have to block right away . Blocking also will probably not reduce damage completely.
How to do counter attack ? You just have to block at the perfect time. You will see enemy icon turn gold . Hit them to get one free hit that may trigger unique abilities.
Decent music and sound effects . Good monster variety .  I like animation style even if 3D models look a bit unfinished. Several playable characters. Map with progression and endless option. Overall pretty well put together game and I do not have much to complain about. Personally I find the aesthetics enjoyable but the game settings are barebones if that matters.
. Very good value if you like grinding loot and stats. Perhaps some people may find it repetitive but I actually think there is enough variety. Always a pleasure to find a game that is more enjoyable than some AAA games . I was pleasantly surprised to get a decent game for $0.49, lets leave it at that .

This is my first review on Steam, and I must say that I'm extremely impressed by this game. The level of details and sophistication is over the top. The consequences of your choices are never dull and always exciting and full of emotions. I just love this game and the maker for this experience.
Pros:
+ The story itself is not linear but very open to your choices so that you can have freedom to decide your own fate in this game.
+ The maker knows what he's talking about about various topics including robotics, artificial intelligence, computer science, and even legal aspects of human rights.
+ The characters are very unique and personal. They are never the same people but are unique in their views and beliefs.
+ The robots you create respond to you according to your decisions.
+ The political aspect of war and moral dilemma was superbly done. I had to pause the game for a moment to decide which choice would be 'right' for me.
+ As a player, you can be emotionally attached to your robot and it feels as though she(or he) is really alive.
+ I just finished the game but I've only unlocked 14 percent of the achievements. There's definitely replayability for this game.
+ Personally, it is far better than your typically 'wifu' games that have shallow stories and charcters. This game allows you to interact with your robots on deeper level.
Cons:
- I really can't think of any. I hope the game would have been longer, but I'm not really complaining.
- No graphics or sound effects, BUT I actually prefer it that way because it forces you to use your imagination. And come on, this game was made by ONE person if I'm not mistaken. I'm still very impressed by the fact that one person was able to write this lengthy scenario of a game.
- More 'war' scenarios with China or other countries would have been nicer.
Bottom Line:
This is an extraordinary game and the maker of this game is brilliant.
Your robots can be as fun and interesting as you make them to be.
It all depends on your choice.
But you might not like this game if you believe that graphics and action are a must in a game.
Personally, I appreciate deep story and memorable characters (I'm also a fan of FF games).

A great exercise how to make a fun game from a basic premise with low-fi graphics. The gameplay is actually enjoyable and suitably challenging with the ever-evolving ruleset. There is at least replay value for a second run-through of the campaign of about 6 hours.
The world is simple, yet immersive. It's easy to find yourself attached to a son you never even get to see. The ingame geopolitics have a surprising amount of coherence and depth, given that you just get snippets of history from newspaper headlines and conversations. Most entrants you process are just numbers, but a not insignificant amount comes with unique personalities.
The moral implications of your in-game job are most interesting. By the end of the game you get to push around absurd stacks of paper to fit the whims of a kafkaesque immigration ruleset. And yet each individual rule somewhat makes perfect sense. These are dire times, there are frequent terrorist attacks, there are subversive elements from within, there is rampant drug and weapon smuggling. It's actually completely sensible for a government to crack down in this situation. And yet there are individual tales of hardship, hope and love as people yearn to escape, find a better life or be reunited with their loved ones. There are no easy answers and the game does not dumb down this dilemma.
And then you find yourself thinking, "I could deny the entrant, stamp a reason and hand them back their 4 documents one-by-one - or I could just press the 'detain' button and have all my problems go away with a single click". In that moment you realize the banality of evil and how it is in each and every one of us and the game turns from a great experience to a brilliant masterpiece.

A dystopian hell where every single error you make in cross-referencing trivial details will result in dire punishments for you and your family.
Reminds me a lot of my first job.
All joking aside, Papers, Please is a fine piece of work. An almost flawless marriage of tone and mechanics; a simulation of a bureaucratic nightmare in which you are responsible for imposing half-mad arcane rules on living, breathing humanity.
I expect everyone who'd be interested in this game owns it by now, but still, a damn fine demonstration of how videogames can be art (yes, I am a ponce). Artistic intent made real by crafty design, a gem of the indie genre.

Have you ever thought how it would feel like to be a border guard, checking passports and various documents all day, deciding whether people you never met before are honest or lying right in your face? This is the premise of this game.
Add to that a bit of intrigue and an eastern-block type of country and higher ups and you have Papers, Please.

Victory: The Age Of Racing, A Very nice but utterly flawed and Fallen game. Today, I will go over the Pros and Cons of this Free Racing Game.
Some Pros:
-Obviously that it's free, and along with that, we have more for that.
-It's not Money-Hungry like the Free Race-Room Racing Experience,
where almost all relevant content is DLC, not to mention VERY EXPENSIVE DLC.
-It Has a simple, but great Car Creation concept, where there are Performance Index Points, you can customize the look in Any way, to Mufflers, MudGuards, Rims, Wheels, and 3 Sections of the car that you can interchange for the ultimate combination.
-After building the car, you get to tune it in any way you want, with Power, Braking, Grip, Traction, Downforce, and Aerodynamics (Aero in-game), and you use Performance Points in these catagories for the greatest tuning concept ever in a free game.
-Before building the car, you can choose the Opposing THREE vehicle classes to choose, Legend, Classic, and Formula, despite being in a time loophole of the past and present, Oldest, Old, to Newest cars are available. Also after picking the car class, you will also choose between 40, 50, to 60 Performance points to tune the car, more points is at more expense of GEARS (The Currency of the game)
-Very nice Graphics, even though I do run them on the lowest to run it the fastest possible, even at that I do really like the Graphics engine.
-Lots of races to choose from, including automatically Generated Events and Dedicated Server races for the game, so there is absolutely no wait for a server.
-The Racing engine is sweet, the Performance Index changes the experience and movement of the car Entirely.
-The Controls are easily interchangable, just like most games
-And finally, the Settings in General like Driving Assistance, Manual or Automatic (Auto at Default) Transmission, and much more.
Now I will go into the Cons of the flawed game concept:
-For some reason the game isn't really being played much anymore, there are very few drivers out there when I'm in-game, and the game has lots of bad reviews saying that no one ever should or does play, So even with the dedicated servers, it is very hard to play.
-Victory: Age Of Racing is an Online-Only concept, there is no way to play in a race by yourself (Or with Bots) without any Opposition, like bots, which makes it scarce that you will find someone to play, since most Dedicated servers are always empty, including Events.
-All Dedicated Servers are also Ported online from Europe, also making it very hard to get a decent connection for anyone in the US or anywhere out of that country.
-There is some strange thing that happens whenever I play a race with anyone,
where while my car PI (performance Index) Is supposed to tackle this problem,
No matter at what tune, At the start of a race, the car in First gear always seems to be stuck at a weird speed that is below the point where your supposed to shift, and Doesn't accelerate any further for five seconds, then starts accelerating to the top of first gear instantly, after that, it doesn't ever happen again until the start of the next race, making it impossible for me to win, and just about gets me in last every time. While everyone else can speed ahead and accelerate instantly, I have to wait that time before I can accelerate properly and try to catch up, which usually doesn't happen when this occurs.
-The Game is very time hungry and wants to consume every single day you play on it, it has the same old "Reward System", where when you play and complete an online race everyday, you will earn one point towards a reward that will progress to a higher payoff the more points, however, the reason this is a flaw is that for every day that you DON'T Play, it takes away 2 Points, which pretty much ruins any possible streak you have on the system.
-Along with the Time Hungry part, completing a race gives you barely anything, maybe about 250/450 per race, which is a flaw because building a new car or resetting and retuning a custom car is very expensive, with the MINIMUM performance Index being Any Class at "G3" (The worst performance Class, from G3,G2, to G1) is 4500 Gears, making it very time consuming to make the dream ride you've had your heart set on from the beginning.

It's a good concept, and has good music. It is fun. However, it has some serious flaws that make it a terribly annoying game to play.
1 = The game is actually broken. You'll just get a black screen of death if you don't disable Steam overlay. I know it's a small problem, but they've released a game that DOESN'T WORK and then people pay for it. This should be illegal, no matter how easy the fix is.
2 = The controls are unresponsive. You push the buttons to do a certain trick, and you just ollie. You want to do a spin trick, and do EXACTLY what you're supposed to do, and yet you don't spin. It's really annoying to just keep doing ollies and flying through the air doing absolutely nothing, just because the game sucks at reading your controller. The game is built to use a controller, and yet they don't work properly.
3 = Sometimes the game breaks your computer. I've had a couple of times now where it will do the old NES thing where the screen freezes and makes a hum. It's also worse than normal crashes, because you can't force quit. You have to manually power down your computer.... I haven't had to do that in years...
4 = There are times when your skater crashes for no good reason. Like, I'll flick the stick to jump, and he doesn't jump, he just crashes... And no, I don't suck at the game, I've almost beaten everything in this, and yet I still have these stupid things happening, which shouldn't even be possible. Like, I can't even replicate this if I'm trying to. It's just a flat out bug that happens often, and ruins the game.
5 = The whole game is a pretty good pace, good achievments that are fun to get, except for the very last one... rad mode... It's incredibly frustrating, and takes an extremely long time. It's not even fun. You have to do every level over again, but flawlessly. I'm decent at the game, and I can play one level for half an hour before I get it flawless. It makes the game not even worth playing, and I honestly don't even want to play it anymore, even though there's only this one achievement left. Terrible design.
It could be a fun little game, and even if you look past the brokeness and crashings, the controls are still very unresponsive, making the game terribly annoying rather than fun.
EDIT: As I play more, the non-responsive controls just get worse and worse. There are parts in levels that just will not accept a jump command. You'll flick the stick to jump, way before the edge, and the guy will just stop crouching (which means it KNOWS you released the stick), and yet he won't jump. So you fall and crash and have to start over. Get to that spot again, same thing happens. I'm playing a level right now that has TWO spots like this, in the same level... It's honestly one of the most frustrating games I've ever played, which is too bad, because it's a great concept.

Most every veteran gamer can appreciate a game, which can ultimately keep the entertainment level consistant, and not have to pay a single penny to reap the enjoyment. Alien Swarm has achieved this by combining aspects of a third person scroller, and a fast paced, action packed shooter into one game platform. There is a game campaign, offering a chance to play with up to four total classes, and a character selection to choose from, selecting the best option to accomodate the squads needs. There are multiple weapon unlocks for each level up achieved, keeping the initial gameplay fresh, by throwing out multiple options to kill the deadly swarms as you progress through the campaign. When your character is maxed, the player can opt to prestige, gaining a class rank, and restarting the unlock process all over again. Once the campaign is completed, there is still a loyal fan base, which has developed a solid modding community. This arguably has erased any deficites which I had intially about Alien Swarm, and has brought me back to the game on multiple occasions with the release of new mods from the community. If you havent already downloaded this game from steam, you are truly missing out.
