Another Minesweeper-style dungeon exploration game, with added QTE/timing-based combat. The game itself simply doesn't seem particularly good, feeling very much as if little to no thought or effort were put into it.
Despite having a "tutorial", a five page help screen, and the ability to right click on nearly everything to see details, the game doesn't bother to ever explain basic information to the player.  The game tells you how to block, but never bothers to teach the timing of either blocking or the counter attack.  You can socket gems into equipment for bonuses, but the game never tells you this.  You just have to happen to click on a piece of equipment and then click on the non-descript empty block that appears to just be menu decoration to bring up the socketing menu.
Game mechanics just don't seem particularly well balanced.   Being able to block near perfectly is king.  You probably can't even beat the second dungeon without excellent blocking or taking advantage of the ill-explained checkpoint system.  It looks like you can min-max your stats, or easily waste your level up points if you don't know what you are doing.  Luck plays perhaps too much a part in exploration.
Not much thought or effort seems to be put into enemy design.  No enemies feel particularly special or memorable, in part due to the generically bad CG art and in part because abilities seem almost randomly assigned at times.  Multiple enemies have the ability where they get stronger every three turns.
Ultimately, the game just isn't that much fun to play. It ends up being less than the sum of its parts.
Finished the game in a single sitting, in 4 hours. Absolutely no regrets - if one wants a great atmosphere, great soundtrack, and a challenging but not obtrusive gameplay, this is the right game.
Whenever people say that games can't be works of art, I show them Transistor.

Oh where do I begin? This is my favourite game and I think it always will be. The music is the best in any game ever made, the graphics are excellent (albeit repetitive) and the story, my God the story kept me awake from how heart-wrenchingly bittersweet it is. I have never felt so sad for a main character nor do I think I ever will. This game is an absolute masterclass in weaving a rich tapestry of story-driven gameplay and evoking emotion from the player.
The game itself revolves around you traversing Cloudbank and killing robotic creatures with your sword. You have an arsenal of abilities and each ability can be used as either an active ability (used to attack with) an upgrade to an active ability (improvement on an attack) or as a passive (health up, better dodge etc). This leads to a lot of customization and adds depth to the game. Enemies also get progressively harder as well.
You play as Red, a singer from Cloudbank who has had her voice stolen and her lover killed. She is on a mission to track down the people who stole her voice but as you play you realise things aren't that simple.
As you play you'll find people deceased and you'll have the chance to absorb their trace into the Transistor. You'll see what I mean if you play it. In short, this gives you new abilities that you can use. Each ability is tied quite deeply to the personality of the person from whom it came and, when you use it as either a passive, active or upgrade, you can learn more about that person. Each person has a history behind them that is worth exploring.
The music is done by Darren Korb and Ashley Barrett. It is beautiful. I have the soundtrack on my computer and phone and listen to it at least thrice a week. The sadness contained within the vocals combined with the heavy beat of the ambient tracks is exceptional. I hope Supergiant never stop choosing Korb for their music.
Overall I may be slightly biased as this is my favourite game but this game made me love Supergiant and acquire Pyre so I hold it dear to my heart.

LoG is a grid style dungeon crawler that has revived the genre from its dying lineage from such games like 80's Dungeon Master.  This 13 floor, heavy puzzled, medium combat gameplay title does an excellent job at presenting new comers and old to the maze like dungeon of the Mountain of Grimrock.  Most of the puzzles work around pushing lose stones that protrude out from the walls and the combat style is of dancing around in a grid motion around the enemy.  There is no tank and spank strategy here unless playing on easy difficulty.
The game will take 20+ hours to complete depending on whether or not you spend the time to do the puzzles and/or find all the missing treasures that can be used for achievements or just upgrading you characters with better equipment.  The graphics are well done and the animation is quite well too.  There is an unlockable character that you must find in the dungeon which will let you run a new game once found with all new traits that will be different compared to the games regular 4 person party you've played with.  If enjoyed this alone is great replay value that extends the life even further to this gem.
Looking for a great grid style dungeon crawler look no further to The Legend of Grimrock!

I waited some time to get some experience with the new version of my beloved Cliffs of Dover.
After about 15 hours of flying I am still very impressed by the wonderful work TFS did with this sim.
Landscape details are much better now (and they were good to start with). The rivers that looked much too wide from a distance are now corrected, making navigation easier.  The ridiculous number of golf courses in England was reduced, trees grass ... everything looks just fantastic now.
Before I forget, the effects (fires, explosions, gun hits etc.) are also improved.
And the new birds ... I immediately fell in love with the Beaufighter!
I am very sorry to see that some new pilots seem to be frustrated because they can't get immediate success or find it difficult to map their flight sticks and so on. CloD was never easy, it never was meant to be easy, and that's all the fun about it. Different planes behave different (and highly realistic!) and need different controls. Thats no reason to complain, that just shows the quality of the sim!
A few people initially had problems to start the game. It was most impressive how the members of TFS cared about each and every single case on ATAG forums and (as far as I know) found solutions for almost every one.
There was some issue with lags and rubber-banding on online servers. Again TFS indefatigably (and let's not forget: it is the week before christams and none of these guys ever saw a single cent for their work!) searched for solutions and right now I come from a flight on ATAG, as smooth as silk with more than 100 players on the server.
It is good to see lots of new player in the forums and on the servers. I am sure the majority is there to stay.

I`ve been playing Cliffs of Dover for around a year and I enjoy it very much. Realistic flight sim which reflects the pro and cons of the different airplanes of that era very well. Looking forward for further patches / expansions.

Lately this game has utterly captured my attention since the days spent playing Roller Coaster Tycoon when I was around 10 years old. I love how simple it is to play and it is incredibly easy to get started.
The early, mid, and late game all have me thinking in different ways to keep me engaged for many hours. The beginning is all about gathering your first batch of resources as well as creating the primary setup for bringing it all together. It's slow at first, but in my opinion it's perfect for new players just getting into the game. As I learned the game more thouroughly, the early game takes less and less time becaue I learned better ways to get going.
The mid game is about growing the facotory, ramping up resource extraction using automated mining, ramping up production of science and factory components in parallel, and solving logistical trouble. The logistics of where to put what is part of what reminds me a lot of RCT.
The late game is all about optimizing what you have, expanding even further with railroads, and creating a mega idustrial complex, possibly with numerous satelite outposts. Optionally, it can get even more complicated (or simpler when you get the hang of it) with robots that transport things between points by air and with the circuit network, with can handle logic and is programmable to operating machines on conditions. It's not totally unlike redstone circuitry in Minecraft, if you're familiar. Uranium processing is a fun side-goal to get power from nuclear reactors  or to create powerful weapons.
About weapons - there are enemies in the game, but you can change in the settings to make them however much of a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥you want them to be. You'll have to advance millitary assests to defend yourself if you play default settings. There is a peaceful option that makes them never attack first, but if you're achievement huntring and can't use that option, you can still set them to take up less of the map, not expand so much, etc. You'll still have to deal with them to some extent or as least know how to prevent attacks by managing pollution (they hate pollution), but I only found it burdonsome on one map I made and that was my fault for setting a particular resource to be too few and far between and I got stuck.
I really look forward to deveolping the map I'm working on now. I've played through on a few maps now, but now that I know the game much better, I'm ready to put many more hours to build my first mega factory with 4+ lanes of train tracks for my main line, thousands of robots, fields of solar panels, miles of belts, dozens of outpots, arrays of information  handled by the circuit network, help me.

Worth the full price? Yes
Why play this game? If you like the skateboarding theme and like "arcady" games give it a try. Has replayability, fastpaced gameplay and a simple yet cool artstyle (pixelated). Soundtrack is awesome too!
Problems: Keyboard and mouse is annoying to play with. I recommend a gamepad controller which feels much more natural.
Story: No story, you don't play this for a story.
Mechanics: It's a 2d sidescrolling skateboardgame. It's pretty technical when it comes to the tricks almost like EA Skate (flick stick) more than Tony Hawkes (press button-combinations). The game is about pulling off tricks and timing your landing for better score. There's like 5 different acts with 10 levels each (5 normal and 5 pro-levels). In the levels there are stairs, rails, ledges and objects that make you fall. On each level there are a few goals you have to achieve before you can proceed to the next one. If you make them all you unlock the corresponding pro-level which is harder.
Playtime/replayability: Room for replayability since there are leaderboards. Depending on your skill level it will take different amounts of time to play through all level (probably around 5 hours). If you decide to complete all goals on all levels you're probably looking at 20+ hours of gametime.
Why I recommend it: Simple artstyle, AMAZING soundtrack, responsive arcade game, the pricetag is worth the money. If you like skateboarding and wanna play a fun game ever once in a while, buy this! Just a heads up, there is a lot of trial and error, you might become angry or frustrated with the game if you play for too long.

Leave it to Devolver to take another great, simple concept, with run-away potential and screw it up. The controls in this game are so stupidly done it almost seems as if they made a bet with the staff to see who could create the most counter-intuitive operations possible for a fast-paced action/sports game. Last Devolver game I buy. After Hotline Miami I said the same thing and I honestly didnt even see that this was Devolver when I bought it on sale. When I saw the logo pop up when I started the game I said "&$#@, cant believe I missed that".
Since they wanted to rely so heavily on the analog sticks (which I totally approve) they shouldve never made a requirement of using "A" to land every single trick. Since "A" is also used to pump for speed it should only be used for transitioning between rails...if even that. Setting up for tricks and activating them didnt need to be dependant on 1/4, 1/2, 3/4, etc rotations and then releasing when using the D-pad is much more precise and you can get a longer trick list if you incorporate the diagonals as a defined direction.
Thyeve made blasting out tricks between grinds unecessarily difficult...even on the first levels. The tutorial will tell you to grind everything because that wil give you more speed. Except for when it doesnt and it stops you dead, causes you to fall, and you have to restart your run. Dumb dumb dumb dumb dumb
Anyway, trick execution is abnormally stupid. And I know how this happens. One person came up with the control scheme. It felt natural to them and they implemented it (this is someone who was just mediocre at the original Tony Hawk games and was mad that their friends were able to score higher than them). The rest of the staff thought that since the game itself wouldnt really be challenging or fun, they could just roll with the control scheme being counter-intuitive and that would suffice for a game that was well thought out. Using "A" to land is so wildly stupid that I cant even fathom how that stayed in for the final version. First of all, landing your tricks in real life is totally dependant on your prior execution. They couldve easily done one of two things to incorprate a skill/timing based landing function. Either use "down" on the analog stick or make your landing dependant on your execution. Too little speed and you may land wobbly, too much and you may not be able to set up for the next execution. Their levels are laid out perfectly for the latter.
Its amazing how well Devolver is getting at taking something that is different, fresh, and has tons of potential and just smashing it into pieces and then taking a hot steaming dump right on top of it. Thank god I only paid $6 for this. Uninstalled!

With Supergiant Games about to release a new title of which I was completely unaware, I realized I should actually get to playing Transistor.   Given that I am a big fan of Bastion, I was concerned about some kind of ‘sophomore slump’ when it came to Supergiant’s next title and it gave me just enough of a pause to end up forgetting about it.  However, after completing the game, I’m disappointed I didn’t jump in to it as soon as possible.  The consistency in quality at every level is something that you don’t see in many other developers, Indie or otherwise.
Without going too far in comparisons between Transistor and Bastion, I did get the sense that the gameplay is relatively similar, at least in the very core of the combat system.  Much like it’s predecessor, you can move around in real time bashing away at your enemies with attacks that vary in range – much like any ARPG.  That is pretty much the end of the similarities in that department though.  Transistor gives you the option of freezing time to plan a blazing fast volley of attacks once you’ve finished planning them out.  If I had to make a mechanical comparison, it’s very similar to the VATS system in Fallout games, where you trigger the time freeze and aim your weapons to fire away quickly once finished.  This design is the real meat of how you’re supposed to play as it allows to you take on and defeat multiple enemies, combo different attack effects, and dodge the enemy assault without having to navigate this all in real time.  However, in using the ability, you are forced to run around (without abilities available) in real time, waiting for a timer to refill so you can use it again.  While this is designed to be a tradeoff, the timer isn’t particularly lengthy and you ultimately get some tweaks that allow you to use some abilities even in this cooldown period.  The abilities you gain function as attacks, spells, and movement skills, which can be used individually, as modifiers to other abilities, or as passive buffs – all with unique effects.  These features work extremely well to create a deep skill system that may have you employing completely different strategies than your friends.
While Transistor has a strong gameplay loop, it seems underwhelming when you compare it to the incredible art style and sound design of the game.  I generally avoid any lengthy mention of visual design and music since perspectives on it can be distinctly different, but in cases where one or both are truly exceptional, it must be included.  The 2D isometric view may feel a bit limiting, but the excellent use of color and the unique hyper-futuristic circuit board-like design in the environment makes it wonderful to experience.  Character and enemy designs are detailed and fold seamlessly into the background – which can sometimes make it easy to lose track of one or the other, but really speaks to how cohesive the art style is.  The soundtrack, much like in Bastion, takes center stage on several occasions and does everything you would expect and more to drive home the emotion and impact of the events in the story.  It’s rare in any game that a soundtrack can take even the most simple moments and make them seem magical.  Transistor does it so well that it made me wonder why most games, including, AAA titles, don’t achieve this more often.  You really owe it to your ears to at least give the soundtrack a shot on its own, even if you don’t want to play the game.  It may be a little less guitar driven than the Bastion soundtrack, opting for a softer jazz and electronic feel, but it features the same strong rhythms and incredible vocals.
Transistor has a few minor issues that are worth mentioning.  The elephant in the room is that it’s short, maybe even slightly shorter than Bastion.  Yet, with how cohesive and involving it is, it feels like it’s more significant than the six hours I put in to it.  On top of that, it offers both optional content in the form of challenges (which can benefit you in game) and a new game plus mode.  There were also a couple of issues I had toward the end involving the mechanics of some of the later enemies in the game.  While it is not a difficult game, late game enemies seem to have a little spike in difficulty and the frequency you encounter them gets tiring.  When you lose your health in an encounter, either you go into the frozen time mode (if it’s available) or you lose one of your abilities and regain your health.  That ability is locked out until you access two new save points, so that can be frustrating if you enjoy using a particular skill.  It does actually coerce the player to try different abilities and combinations, but there may have been a better way to include a “life” system.  Overall, though, these issues are minor and I don’t think they detract enough to warrant any red flags.
I feel a little stupid for playing a game so wonderful more than three years after it came out, but I suppose this is definitely a case of “better late than never.”  If you were, for whatever reason, holding out on purchasing this, do it as soon as possible.  It has been as cheap at $3 USD on Steam, so there’s not really an excuse as far as money is involved.  I fully recommend this game along with the thousands of people who already did before me.  We can’t *all* be wrong, right?

I'll say it straight: this isn't necessarily a game that most people would enjoy; it has no visuals and, while in general is short, is a long read for someone who isn't willing to sit still and stay focused for approximately an hour for one play through.
However, for someone who is looking for a good story, Choice of Robots is worth the money you spend on it and is a wonderful narrative. I blog about stuff like this all the time, and am always looking for a good read. Choice of Robots was far better than I could have imagined and was worth every penny, as well as will be worth all the time it will take in order to get each and every achievement.
The story is interesting on it's own; make a robot, decide who to work for if anyone, go through a war, maybe even find love. The choices you're able to make through the game is really what puts the cherry on top of this game; the game's mechanics follow a normal choice based game, but the choices you choose are relevant throughout the story; depending on what you choose at the beginning alters the ending(which is where some choose your own story games lack, and instead, your choice is more relevant between different sections of the story). It's interesting to choose what you would like to do and see all the concequences this leads to.
I won't spoil any of the actual game because it's so worth it to check out the whole thing, but I highly recommend this game. As I said, it was short; for a fast reader like myself, it took a little over one half hour to go through one ending of the game, but it's very touching and you fall in love with the characters you meet/create.

Very engaging thus far.
No music, no pictures, just text. A "Choose Your Own Adventure" game apparently. You are a robotic engineer in Sillicon Valley building a robotic companion and shaping the world along the way over the course of your life. Each section of text comes with you making a decision potentially altering your path - what you are doing with your life, how the people around you will react and what will happen with the world as a whole (or not, as being passive is usually an option too).
There are several values regarding your life and the character of your robotic companion that you'll influence with your choices through the entire game and which will affect the choices you can make later on decisively. For example you can build a humanoid-looking robot and teach him (or her, or it, or whatever - you are given freedom in naming and adressing things) to get along with people increasing his "Empathy" and "Grace" values or, on the contrary, shape him to clearly stand apart from humans and handle guns and stuff increasing "Military" and "Autonomy". This value-play can sometimes feel a bit like a guessing game, and how it will affect your later course is hardly predictable, which can be seen as a good or bad thing I guess, but then I suppose that's just how life works too.
Perhaps at times the game feels a little bit too much like a dating simulator or relationship juggling. Maybe this comes natural with such games and with them trying to resemble life and how choices affect it. I can't say I remember having played anything like this before ("Cinders" maybe), so I don't know. Still: There is a "Romance: ..." placeholder at all times and the game doesn't hesitate to question your inner self quickly whether you have romantic feelings towards a just recently introduced character of either gender, or make them burst out with acts or words of affection towards you right away, which felt a bit unrealistic and forced or at the very least awkward to me at times.
Sometimes events are pressed on too quickly for my taste. There are some happenings and characters I would love to see elaborated more, but the game can be unforgiving there, making you lose track of them rather quickly pressing onward towards new things and situations. Even some greater time leaps of multiple years it doesn't hesitate to do where a little more patience might have served better. I haven't finished the game yet though so I don't want to fully judge that yet. I don't claim to know better in terms of writing. Perhaps I'm wrong and it's just right, elaborating more could end up losing track of things and aims and such and bloat things up artificially. I just sometimes felt sad and unhappy about the turn of events and how I lost touch to some characters or screwed up in geopolitical questions with no chances of undoing my mistakes. But I guess I can try better in additional playthroughs, as there seems replay value aplenty for all the choices you can make.

If you're looking at this game and you're wondering why it's so highly rated, you probably never played this as a kid, so you don't have nostalgia enhancing the experience. That's probably the biggest reason, and I'll admit that my review will likely be tinged with it.
RollerCoaster Tycoon is an old game. It's older than one of my teenage younger sisters, which is actually not as old as I thought. (I was pretty sure I was only a year or two old when this came out. I guess I was five, at least when the deluxe version came out.) The graphics are dated, the gameplay is very simple, and money is apparently a million times more valuable because it's the late 90's. (I'm kidding. Sort of. I mean, you do start out with only $10k, and you still have enough to buy a few rides, so clearly something is off with the value.)
I didn't actually grow up with this game, as far as I can remember. My parents were big on the Tycoon and Sims franchises, but I either wasn't allowed to play them or didn't care about them. But when I found the CD a few years ago, I decided to boot it up and give it a try. I was not disappointed.
The game is really easy to pick up. You get some money, you get a clear objective (usually a number of guests and a certain park rating), and you get to work. The game is all about managing both your finances and guest happiness. The game makes it very easy to figure out what you need to do via guest feedback, and it's up to you to actually do it.
Just because the game is simple, though, that doesn't mean it's boring or easy. Some of the later objectives get quite challenging, especially the park with no room for new rides. But even after you complete the challenges, it's still tons of fun to go back and continue to build up your park. You can have some pretty awesome parks going after four or five in-game years. Just sit back and watch the awards and the cash come flowing in!
Oh, and if guests don't like you, you can drown them. No one else notices or helps, either, which is both amusing and disturbing. But it's a great way to boost park rating in small doses, and it's a sick sort of amusement.
So, even if this game has no relevance to your childhood or your inner child, this still can be a fun game to go back to time and time again. Just make sure you set aside three hours or so for it. You will sit down, open the game, look at the clock, and realize that hours have gone by without you realizing it. That's why my playtime is so low on here--I've only gone back to it once, and I still accumulated over two hours of playtime. You can bet that I'll be playing it once the semester is over, however.
P.S. As I mentioned, I still have the CD, but I saw this on here for under three bucks, so I decided to buy it. I didn't have the deluxe edition, so I got a bit more content, and the devs got some more money. It was a win-win.

So I always hired one more than I needed, and made his only job being to mow grass. 35$ monthly, earned solely through his sweat and his lawnmower. Off in the unexplored regions of the park, where nobody can even see the grass he's mowing. I always made sure to give him a absurd name.
Around 10 years later, I find myself tracking Dorkle's adventure through the wilderness, chronicling his neverending battle against the grass, as I try to find a good spot for the next ferris wheel.
10/10 would relive cherised childhood memories again.

For those of us who remember spending rainy Sunday afternoons playing games like Dungeon Hack or Shadow Caster this is a welcomed re-awakening of a genre.  The graphics are superb, the controls are tight and the interface is simple enough while maintaining the desired level of PC complexity that many of us wish was still prevalent today in gaming.
The combat is fun although tactical a tad simplistic.  I have found that the most effective strategy is to lure enemies one at a time into a 2 x 2 or larger area and simply strafe around while your attack recharge.  The game does do an effective job of complicating this simple strategic by throwing multiple enemies at you at once which leads to some wonderfully frantic fights but these are (thankfully) not too common.
The puzzles are challenging while remaining logical and almost every puzzle hint that I found proved both valuable in discovering the solution without being too obvious while also adding to both the story and the atmosphere.  Also the reward of finding many of the game's secrets is very fulfilling!
All in all well worth the price of admission for those looking for a modern take on a classic genre.  I am hopeful that the sequel carries on with this level of fun and frustration as the dungeon crawler rises again!

Cliffs of Dover "Blitz" (v4.5) edition has fixed some of the problems of the previous Cliffs of Dover (v4.312). However, performance is now worse and the game is still desperately lacking in key areas (esp. AI behaviour).
There are two fundamental flaws in "Blitz".
The first is the performance. Overall, "Blitz" is worse than the previous version. The frames-per-second are lower and the servers now have major stutters. We have seen multi-crew aircraft de-synchronising (the gunner sees one thing and the pilot something totally different). Clouds and trees are client-dependent. The graphics are a bit different, but are hardly an improvement. There are still "swampy rivers" at long distance and the tree-rendering bubble is now blatantly obvious. Targets remain either invisible or as black-dots that can be seen at 20+km. The clouds look poor and some are only half-rendered (bottom half only). Trees rotate as you fly past them. There is no good graphical consistency between the cockpits, aircraft and surrounding environment. It simply looks broken. Compared to more recent titles, it looks very tired and old.
The second area is AI-behaviour. How the computer-controlled units react has not changed one bit, and remains utterly woeful. Aircraft can be shot-at and don't react, gunners are either snipers or are incapable of hitting anything at point-blank-range. AI aircraft will "bounce" and "rubber-band" and fail to land. Taxiing aircraft will run into each other and ground obstacles and explode. Formation flights will fly at maximum-parameters, making formation flying with AI impossible. With failed AI, it makes single-player missions and campaigns from a co-operative perspective unworkable. Which brings me on to the last point...
Some will say that "Blitz" is the only Battle-of-Britain simulator. I would say it is not even that. The multiplayer scene is hardly the "Battle of Britain", it is merely furballs between Dover and Calais. The single-player missions are broken and there are no enduring campaigns. You will not get
.. with the bombing of Andover, Bristol, Southampton, as well RAF Dishforth, Worthy Down, Bibury, Gosport, Farnborough, Warmwell, North Weald, Biggin Hill, Kenley and all the others. And, you can forget the real Blitz too... despite the name, the "Blitz" edition does not cover that either. In fact, "Cliffs of Dover" is accurate... both in altitude and location.
If you are new to combat flight simming, then this is not the place to start... you are much better off with, for example, War Thunder (casual-level) or IL-2: Battle of Stalingrad (intermediate-level). With broken tutorials, shabby manuals, and a mess of confusing online information, it is a nightmare for a new user. If you are a flight-sim enthusiast, chances are that you already had the earlier Cliffs-of-Dover, in which case the Blitz edition is free. And if you are looking for a study-level sim, then DCS or A2A are vastly superior.
Poor graphics performance and dire AI are the killers.

Blitz is an excellent upgrade to IL-2 Cliffs of Dover which was horrible at release. This new version is much more stable, for me at least, and looks much better as welll as improved flight models.
TF has have unofficially allowed a small fix so 3rd party campaigns now work which is a big thing for me as I only fly offline and the stock campaigns are anemic.
Hopefully TF will continue to devlop this sim as it has great potential. One would hope to see better offline campaigns as most of the people I know don't fly online and we just don't have the time to practice at the level needed to be useful against human opponents online.
The biggest problem facing any of these sims nowadays is the lack of Dynamic campaigns. Back in the days of BoB TFH, SWOTL, European Air War, BoB and so on, campaigns gave the feeling of a struggle going on around you. Your mission made an impact on the struggle and losses of pilots and material made each mission unique. Some sims allowed players to change production and strategy.
Modern sims IMO have become like Callof Duty, run at each other, shoot until shot, rinse repeat. Luckily Cliffs of Dover online campaigns do give the feeling of realism and struggle with strategy. Again, hopefully that level of feeling engaged can be brought to the offline player who has not seen such a thing in many years.
This is a great sim that has great potential. Hopefully it will continue to evolve.

I like flight simulators from the WWI/II periods. I've been flying and buying since sometime in the eighties, so I was interested in COD. But I read about the problems with the initial version so wasn't about to buy it. But, still, I followed it. Reviews seemed to improve to the point I risked buying it, and was I glad I did. It was great. I've been through more updates to the version I bought than I can remember, and each one improved the game. If you're interested in the period, BUY IT!
An amazingly good sim (thanks to Team Fusion) just got 100% better with Blitz.  Absolutely a 'must' for any flight sim fans.

Owned since original release. Always loved the concept, but released in rough state. Current developers (TFS) have sorted much of the kinks (and were fans before they were developers, so sincere enthusiam for getting it right). Atmosphere and sense of flight are excellent. Still lacks something in the dynamic weather department--a must for English Channel ops--but that is being looked at as well. I love this theater, so I may be a bit biased. I'm not British, but I feel like I'm defending my home. A look at some videos will show a mature and freindly on-line fan base. No, I'm not paid to say this. just my impressions.

Finally, after some three years of oblivion, we see an update for Cliffs of Dover. Team Fusion must be commended for their perseverance and dedication to this wily old beast. Cliffs really did not have the best start in life and, for the most part, has survived on the life-support of Team Fusion's diligence. I feel it is unfortunate to say that it all leaves a somewhat sour taste in the mouth; a negative review for a somewhat positive release.
---
There has been improvement.
Finally, the client has been updated to 64-bit and theoretically should be providing superior performance for most clients. It is excellent to see that the terrain has had a much required facelift. Gone are the endless repeated fields of northern France, and the ardent gardens of England seem now to have a greater vibrancy about them - truly does this feel like that hazy summer of 1940.
The atmospherical bugs have been quashed and, in turn, we see a tangible change to the flight models of the aircraft involved. Whether this is a true positive or not (affected FMs) I am not sure, however the meta has surely been shaken a little. The addition of the Beaufighter is also very welcome, although I cannot say much for the needless work that went in to making an armed Tiger Moth.
It's difficult for me to write much else that is positive beyond this point. Yes, it looks much nicer, there are beefier sounds and the aircraft feel satisfying to fly but I struggle to find positives beyond this - it's just all very superficial.
Very little seems to actually have been fixed on the campaign map, TF are notoriously evasive on reporting fixed errors through their publicised bug-tracker. Things that have been claimed as fixed (such as tree collision and certain German ammo rounds) have certainly been not. It was much lauded that trees were finally given their correct dues and were now solid objects. Unfortunately, TF have sorely miscalculated the application. Where both users have trees set to 'High', the collisions are made possible. However, if the client is set to 'Low', the user may fly through the invisible forests without ever colliding. In short; you may turn down the forests and enjoy an easy-flight. The menus are pig-ugly to navigate and read, I pity the novice Cliffs pilot who must negotiate their way through this game.
I feel as if 4.5 has not lived up to the expectation. Three years since the last patch and over a year since the acquisition of the source code shows for relatively little. The AI is functional at best, broken at worst. A player may fly through a formation of BF-109 aircraft, engage and escape for little punishment - they maintain a straight and ignorant flightpath. Efforts to fix up Cliffs for online play seems to have had minimal thought, unless you are an ATAG participant and enjoy senseless low-altitude scrapping over French Point. You won't find a dynamic offline campaign here, or an engaging single-player experience.
Save your money.
Purchase Cliffs outside of Steam for the usual price of £9.99 or invest in the BoX series.

About:
Papers, Please is a game where you play as an immigration officer for the fictional state of Artztotska. This may sound boring, but it is actually good.
Plot:
The game is set in 1982. [1983 in endless mode.] The war between Kolechia and Artztotska has ended. The border is now open. You get drawn from a raffle to work at the immigration office. You and your family move to a section 8 apartment. You must check immigrants' passports and papers day to day.
Gameplay:
You check people's papers, passports, ID cards, etc. You make 5 dollars for every person you process. At the end of the day, you have to manage your expenses for your family. Should you feed them, and have no heat? Or vice versa? As the game progresses, it starts getting harder. You have to check more papers. People try to fake their passport to get in. It takes longer to process people. If you make a mistake, you get a citation. If you get 3, you get a penalty of -5 dollars. Every citation onwards increases the penalty. Some people won't have the right papers, but beg you to let them in, and tell you their sob stories. You have to decide, should you help them, and get cited? Or reject them, so you can feed your family? Choices like these make this game amazing. Also, the next morning, there's a newspaper reminding you of your actions, which instills a feeling of guilt.
TL;DR
Papers, Please is a good game for the price. The choices you have to make make you think. For only 10 dollars, pick up this game.

For how much flak some reviewers give this game, I for one find it to be one of the best Serious Sam game, just a hair behind Serious Sam The Second Encounter.
+Great artstyle, even though less "serious" than it's predecesors, benefits the game in the long run, and helped it age beautifully, even after 10 years.
+Stage and enemy variety, easily trumping The First and Second Encounter by a large margin.
+Addition of a secondary fire mode (grenades) which was unfortunately scrapped in Serious Sam 3 BFE.
+Addition of vehicles such as the hovercraft and UFO, a human-sized hamster ball with spikes, as well as turrets, which prove quite useful in some battles.
+Lots of enemies on screen at once just like the good old classics.
+Fun boss battles.
+Funny cutscenes.
+You have a flying parrot with a bomb attached to its claws as a weapon.
+/- Most of the levels are shorter and more linear compared to The First and Second Encounter, although there are some open areas for the huge battles from time to time. However there are 52 levels in Serious Sam 2 which, combined with the enemy and stage variety, keep the pace going.
+/- Some weapons have been nerfed (Rocket Launcher/ Dual Uzis which replace the Tommy Gun ) while others have been buffed ( single and double barrelled shotgun).
- Sound effects for some weapons sound weak (Dual Uzis, Single-barrelled shotgun, Rocket Launcher).
Overall I give this game a 9/10.
P.S.: Play this game on Serious Difficulty for the ultimate Serious Sam experience.

These are easy enough to make, using only one herb and a refundable bottle.
From the moment I started up until the first spider encounter I saved the herb to make the Anti-venom, which lasted me a good 8/9 poisonings. Considering the front two party members can both be poisoned, on the same attack, you burn through the potions incredibly fast. That wouldn't be a problem had they made the herb a common find. What is the point in the potion, if it only lasts you 5/6 spider encounters, and then your running back and fourth just to remove poisoning? Great "time killer" at the junction of genres roguelite and a clicker.
Dungeon jorney is a small, not demanding on the computer and quite an exciting time, representing a mix of clicker and bagel. The player assuming control of one of several typical characters (mage, knight, hunter and so on), is sent to investigate one of the dungeons in search of treasure, artifacts and bonuses. The gameplay is alternately open squares — sectors dungeons, each of which may be hiding the treasure, a trap or enemy. When meeting with the enemy, a lot depends on your reaction and speed with the mouse, since all battles occur in real time, and in fact are zaklikivanie enemy attacks or abilities of the hero. The enemy also attacks, and only the timely press of the block (spacebar) saves him from most of the damage. After the death of the hero loses all accumulated in the dungeon artifacts and returns to the main map, and the dungeon will be reset, which leads to the need to re-open the map floors. The same hero can be "pumped", raising its characteristics, dressing and arming, learning skills and spells and improving equipment special stones..
So the game is easy, quite fun and simple in concept a hybrid of several genres, among which are role-playing slasher, and explore the dungeons and clicker. Despite their obvious "mobile" roots of it quite well looks and plays on the computer.
(Русский)
Отличный «убийца времени» на стыке жанров roguelite и кликера.
Dungeon jorney - небольшая, не требовательная к компьютеру и достаточно увлекательная убивалка времени, представляющая из себя смесь кликера и рогалика. Игрок, взяв на себя управление одним из нескольких типичных героев (маг, рыцарь, охотник и так далее), отправляется исследовать одно из подземелий в поисках сокровищ, артефактов и сильных противников. Игровой процесс представляет из себя поочередное открывание квадратов — секторов подземелья, за каждым из которых может скрываться сокровище, ловушка или противник. При встрече с противником многое зависит от вашей реакции и скорости работы с мышкой, так как все бои происходят в реальном времени и по сути представляют из себя закликивание противника ударами или способностями героя. Противник тоже атакует, и только своевременное нажатие блока (клавиша пробел) спасает героя от большей части повреждений. После смерти герой теряет все накопленные в подземелье артефакты и возвращается на главную карту, а подземелье «обнуляется», что приводит к необходимости заново открывать карту этажей. Так же героя можно «прокачивать», поднимая его характеристики, одевая и вооружая, изучая умения и заклинания и улучшая экипировку специальными камнями..
Таким образом игра представляет из себя легкую, вполне увлекательную и простую по концепции помесь нескольких жанров, среди которых есть и ролевой слэшер, и исследование подземелий и кликер. Не смотря на свои явные «мобильные» корни она вполне хорошо смотрится и играется на компьютере.

LoG is based off the old school RPG’s from early PC days and I think there may have even been a few on consoles. I never played much in this FPS style when I was younger but that doesn’t take away how much fun this game was to play.
You have a team of 4 characters and move through a grid based dungeon you were locked up in. You can create your characters with a variety of classes, powers, and skills to whatever playstyle fits you best. There are many floors to travel through and many secrets to find on the way. There are plenty of great challenging puzzles and enemies to keep you occupied for a good time.
There is also plenty of replay value with different difficulties and even an old-school mode where you lose the AutoMap and you can pull out some grid paper and make your own. Then there is also the added Steam Workshop where you can install mods to give you more challenges and fun to last you a long time.
The game is fantastic looking with some cool character design and great sound to go along with it. Going through the tunnels when your torch is flickering out and you can hear the skittering of an enemy somewhere nearby made for some cool moments in the game.
I played through on easy mode as I’m new to this style of RPG and figured I could get the hang of it better. It was still a decent challenge and enjoyable for me. I would highly recommend Legend of Grimrock if you like the old-school RPGs or even just want to play a well-made fantastic game. This is Almost Human’s first game and you can tell they put a lot of love into it and it was only a 4 man team too. Don’t pass this game up.

Meh... not much to say about this. It's a fairly simple RPG in which you uncover tiles which have loot, potions, spells, monsters, or nothing behind them. Loot you pick up, potions you pick up if you need them or at the end of the stage, spells you cast if you need to (so, basically never in my experience), and monsters you have to fight.
The combat system is based on timing, insofar as you have to press the spacebar when the enemy swings at you in order to reduce damage, and then click on the enemy immediately after to do a critical hit for massive damage. By the middle of the game I had nearly 100% damage reduction on a successful block, and at the end of the game I had a full 100%, so "block correctly and then attack again right away for massive damage" was the entirety of the strategy in the game, with me almost never using spells found on the ground and rarely using my character skills - only against the few types of enemies where I wasn't very good at timing their attacks. If you're better than me at it, even that wouldn't be necessary.
It still wasn't all that easy, because failing to block an attack could easily cost half of my life instantly, and the checkpoint system made the final dungeon occasionally frustrating, in that there's a checkpoint every five levels... but if you die and respawn at the checkpoint, you need to reach the next checkpoint before dying or be sent back to the start of the dungeon. This isn't so bad until you consider that each dungeon is five floors longer than the last, culminating in a 50-floor dungeon.
Furthermore, the mechanics for your stats are... weird. You first find dropped items that barely do much, and gems you can socket in your items that give small bonuses that are still the equivalent of the entire item's bonuses due to how little the items do. Then you unlock the merchant, who sells items... except they still don't do much, and its catalog expanding throughout the game basically means you'll never be able to afford them. And then you unlock the mystic and the ability to fuse gems, and suddenly your items still don't do much, but have gems in them that give gigantic stat bonuses, bigger than both the base items and your levelups. And then, near the end of the game, you unlock the blacksmith and the ability to upgrade items, and suddenly your items also give huge bonuses... two maps or so before the end of the game.
Anyway, ultimately... well, it's a $2 game. It not having much depth - not even an ending or anything once I beat the final boss - is to be expected to some degree, but I also felt it didn't have much of a point, either, and it was more tedious than fun. It's definitely not going to show up on any "worst game of 2016"-style lists, but I don't think it's worth your time to play.

Thanks to incorporating DX11 and the latest advances in graphics cards, the improved graphics are amazing, and the sound effects are much improved in many respects as well. And for those looking for a compromise between the "BoX" games' auto-start/auto-fly features and DCS' level of detail, CloD continues to feature clickable cockpits and complex engine management. In short, everything that made Cliffs of Dover so much fun to fly under previous versions of Team Fusion patches, has only been enhanced and upgraded in Blitz Edition.
Yes, there were significant problems with server lag upon initial rollout, but that issue has been pretty well resolved. And Team Fusion Simulations is already aggressively addressing other (mostly minor) bugs that have been reported by players. These should not dissude WWII flight sim enthusiasts from purchasing and playing Blitz Edition in the least. I consider it to now be the premier WWII combat flight simulator on the market, and I very much recommend that those who enjoy flying and fighting in the classic early-war aircraft of the era give it a try. is a game that took me a while to get into.  It's probably the sort of game where you should play a bit to figure out the rules, then restart.  There were several elements of the interface I found unclear at first, which made my first playthrough a bit painful.  However, I do recommend sticking with it.
The gameplay is essentially puzzle-based under a time limit, where the puzzle is "are these documents valid".  This does involve a lot of comparing two text strings to see if they match.  It's more interesting than it sounds, thanks to the context provided by the immigrant's desire to enter and your character's desire to make money and avoid fines.  Still, it won't be to everyone's taste.  The time pressure and the need to earn enough money each day provides a robust but fair challenge.  The continually changing requirements keep things interesting for the duration of the main storyline, as do the various extra ways to earn money that become available later on.
The story consists of one main overarching plot, with many little side-stories along the way.  The central narrative is simple enough but interestingly told, and offers choices that affect the final ending.  The little arcs of a few recurring characters are in some ways more interesting, and offer good variety; humour, heartwarming, and oppressive, among others.
There's also the potential to learn something about yourself; I learnt that I would be corrupt as all hell!
This is a fairly short game.  The art style serves the setting but isn't especially pretty, and there's really only one screen.  But this is a case where the whole is more than the sum of its parts.  Recommended for puzzle fans.

This game scratches a certain itch like no other I've played. The developer has made implementing logistics as easy and enjoyable as I can imagine.
At seemingly every turn there is a way to FURTHER automate the way you build your base.
For example: At first your character will craft some key items manually. A bit later, you'll build a supply chain so that items are built in a factory. Later you can build factories that make not only all resources in the supply chain, but the infrastructure for the supply chain itself (assembly machines, transport belts, inserters) and lay down blueprints for construction robots to the dirty work.
At each stage you zoom out a level and further scale-up your ability to build up your base as you march forward.

This is one of the best 2D Platformers I’ve played in a long time! It’s part Super Meat Boy with Binding of Isaac Quirkiness put into one wackily challenging tower. However, Even though I loved this game soo much, there are still some things which could be added, fixed or improved to make it even better which I will list below in my Pros and Cons.
Pros:
♦ Many hours of Challenging Fun
♦ Awesome number of level variations per death/run
♦ Lots of Replayability (Beating Friends, Global or even your own Highscores and getting Achievements makes this endlessly repayable)
♦ Music that just fits perfectly and isn’t too repetitive (Can mute and put on your own music on in a media player in the background if it annoys you)
♦ Amazing Super Meat Boy style Graphics (Which always look stunning)
♦ Easy Achievements Concept as they unlock for just playing (But this said you won’t be able to unlock them easily as beating the game is challenging in itself)
♦ Nice variety of traps and enemies
♦ Cheap and pays for itself ($5 and I’ve gotten 11 hours out of it so far)
♦ Awesome Steam Trading Cards, Emoticons and Backgrounds
♦ Great number of unique unlockables per level (This is an interesting feature)
♦ Highscores that seem to just work (This is a good aspect as you can challenge your friends to speed runs or just try and beat the global players and become Abomination Tower Champion!)
♦ Awesome Controls with Amazing Jump Box (I rarely noticed a problem jumping)
Cons:
♦ Doesn’t list all achievements In Personal Achievements (The two death achievements and the level difficulty achievements are not listed)
♦ Story is lacking (The failed Science experiement is a good start to the story but the ending could have been better and had a cinematic or something as I don't see the point in climbing up the tower only to jump off and die?)
♦ No way to know how many times you’ve died as you can’t see your progress on the death achievements due to not all Achievements showing in Personal Achievements (This is annoying if you are like me and want to get all the achievements)
♦ Easy, Normal Hard and Very Hard Difficulty Achievements are pointless as once you’ve beaten easy and unlocked the “Already Dead” head, you can just wear it and beat the other difficulties (This is bad as it means anyone can easily get some of the hardest achievements whereas others would have worked towards it. I personally think you should make the “Already Dead” head not be able to unlock achievements).
♦ No way to select a level once beaten and timed (This is annoying as you can’t just play any level to try and beat your previous time or someone elses, you have to beat every level from level 1 to get to the level).
Things I’d like to see added:
♦ Level Select (Once you beat and register a time in the Highscores for a level, it should unlock in Level Select and you should be able to play it with unlimited lives for the purpose of beating yours or someone elses highscore. As mentioned above it’s annoying having to beat 8 levels everytime just to get level 9 for example to try and beat my previous highscore.
♦ Steam Workshop Content. This would be awesome as you could easily put in a level editor, head editor and skin editor. (This would allow people to create custom heads, skins and levels for others to compete in and register their time against. This would give the game another edge, making it just that little bit more awesome!)
Overall, what other game can you put a butt on your head… this alone should make you want to buy this awesome game! However, in all seriousness, as there is only minor cons and suggestions to improve the game and as the Pros are 100% awesome… I recommend you buy this game as for the cheap price you’ll get many, many fun replaybale hours out of the game!
I give this 4/5 Smurfs (Would be 5 if it had a few less cons, level select and steam Workshop as I mentioned/suggested)

I feel slightly bad giving this game a "no" for recommendation. This isn't unplayable garbage, nor is it mindless. However, its attempts at intelligence only set it to a higher standard, which it fails to live up to.
First, a story is a lot shorter than I thought it would be-both of the two endings I reached took less than half an hour to get to. This means it's not nearly as deep as the promised "300,000 word epic"-oh, even if it has that many in its files, you'll see just a tiny portion of it. So that's one problem. The second is that while my first playthrough was genuinely "in-character" and ended up with me getting a "bad" (though not unexpected) ending, my second had me actively trying to munchkin my way to a good one (and being at least partially successful).
That I resorted to this was not a good sign. The game is too complex and has too many outcomes for one to just follow a strict "Do X to see Outcome Y", like in some similar "choose your own adventure"-style games. But the differences in outcomes themselves aren't great enough for the complexity to be worth it. Nor is the story great or intellectually stimulating enough-though it tries- to be worth repeating many times.
Ending up as neither robo-fish nor robo-fowl, Choice of Robots disappointed me.

Man, this game.
Seeing as Supergiant's third game, Pyre, will be released a couple of days after this review, I thought it might be a good time to review Supergiant's other games as well. Transistor is the second game made by this studio, released in 2014, and after playing it on and off for a couple of years, it remains one of the games closest to my heart for a multitude of reasons.
Transistor takes place in the fictional utopia of Cloudbank, which recently has had a string of incidents leading up to the spread of a robotic "plague" called The Process. You play as Red, a singer whose voice has been stolen literally and metaphorically by this upper "secret society" called the Camerata. You go around the city of cloudbank, attempting to end the spread of the Process and bring justice to the group of people who made it. This story is the best I have ever played through. It made me laugh, worry, and even cry. The story is fantastically written and got me attached to the characters. Even if you feel like you can’t get enough of the regular story, each ability has a little bit of lore tied to it that you can unlock by using the abilities differently.
The gameplay itself is innovative and immersive (while feeling maybe a bit repetitive at times – as will be explained later). You wield a sword-type object called the Transistor. The Transistor can download the consciousness of deceased people to upgrade itself and create new abilities for the user. The primary combat mechanic is that of interchangeable and stackable abilities that can be combined in hundreds of ways as offensive or defensive. This allows for heavy replayability, trying new combinations of abilities to do different things. Similarly to supergiant’s previous game, Bastion, there are ways to make the game more difficult to add to replayability- these challenges are called limiters and, for example, make enemies stronger, limit your abilities, and the like. The game can play two ways interchangeably- a turn-based strategy game, or a real time ability-based brawler using this time-stopping mechanic called Turn(). The two seamlessly combine in and out of each other, feeling balanced, and still difficult.
The art direction of this game is stunning. Similar to Bastion, the handdrawn visuals are beautiful and cinematic. They immerse the player in the world and make it feel alive. The menus all feel like they belong there, which is a level of detail that many games neglect. What Initially drew me to this game, however, was the superb soundtrack composed by Darren Korb-who also worked on Bastion's soundtrack. I found it on Supergiant's Bandcamp page after listening to Bastion's soundtrack there. The developers at Supergiant know that this is one of the strengths of their game, and added a button in this game that just allows Red to sit there and hum along with the soundtrack. That in itself is fantastic. The vocals of Red by Ashely Barrett breathe a new life into this game that I've rarely seen in other games. The voice acting in this game is rich and compelling, from the members of the Camerata, to the Transistor itself.
As previously mentioned, there is some feeling of repetition. I mostly experienced this while replaying the game, but I also experienced this feeling in some of the combat parts of my initial playthrough. The problem of potential lack of replayability appears to have been recognized by Supergiant, however, and the team has created new challenges that some players would just run past like I did initially. The story overall is on the shorter side time-wise (as compared to triple a games), but the game definitely makes up for it with beautiful story- and worldcrafting. The final boss is innovative as well, but feels a bit clunky due to some mechanics choices.
Transistor definitely a game worth the price. It is a game close to my heart due to the attachment it builds in the player. As Supergiant's second game, it made a leap forward in production value, and I hope this trend will continue with Pyre. I wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone and everyone- it has something to offer in all fields.
As a side note, the soundtrack (which is stupendous) is available to listen to online at their Bandcamp page:
.
But I recommend that if you want to support the developers, you should purchase it on Steam or buy one of the hard copies at their website. They have it in vinyl, CD, or digital.

Super Giant games must have an individual who pulls on past experiences and envisions ways to improve.
From the story, to the music, to the action, Transistor is nearly flawless. The sci-fi themed action RPG borrows elements from bastion, streamlines them into an approachable and addicting combat system with exquisite story telling.
A step away from the dwarf approached artwork in bastion, the look and feel of the stunning futuristic city is mind blowing, with several spots and scenes worthy of a wallpaper or piece of art.
Controlling "Red", most of the narrative comes from a unusual powerful weapon taking its name from the title of the game. Transistor operates as the main form of attack against a variety of amazing sprite monsters that rarely are duplicated.
Voice activing is quite superb, Logan Cunningham returns from Bastion, lending his deep smooth voice to the narrative while Ashley Lynn Barrett (runner up to Quiet\Stefanie Jootsen impersonator) offers vocals that beautifully reflect the hymn of the city.
Little is wasted and spoiling the ending on wikipedia or walk throughs takes away from the experience. although the fighting can be extremely unforgiving; planning and focus contribute to success in defeating bosses. the rpg elements aside, little interferes with the forward momentum to the story and the game is an acceptable 10+ hours of time before a thrilling conclusion.
Either on sale or full price, collect the soundtrack; I can garuntee at least one tune that will stick with you for awhile.

As an original fan of the Dungeon Master Series Legend of Grimrock held quite a bit of appeal for me. The game almost perfectly emulates  the gameplay of the classic series while bringing the visuals nicely up to date.
GAMEPLAY
Similar to another Classic Series (Elder Scrolls), LoG casts you in the role of Prisoners being exiled for unknown reasons into the catacombs of Mount Grimrock. The focus of the gameplay is on combat and puzzle solving, the latter of which can sometimes be maddeningly frustrating, but very satisfying when you finally work it through.
While you have complete freedom to go anywhere you want within the dungeon movement is grid based and fixed to the cardinal directions, up, down, left, right, and turning.  Some people (mostly new school gamers) find this limitation madden and arbitrary, but it plays an important role in gameplay and tactics.
STORY
The story is there, but is very, very light. There are lots of little bits and pieces of info scatterd throughout (esp the story of former dungeon Denzien Toorum). You're ultimately left with more questions than answers, but you don't walk away feeling unsatisfied, and that's what the expanded Story in Grimrock 2 is for as well.
In general if you are fan of or think you will enjoy the old grid based style then you'll like this game. But if you're not, pass

Still, a great game for an old school type dungeon crawler RPG.  Highly recommended.

Dungeon Journey is very clearly a ported smartphone game. That said, it does work as a PC game—if your screen is very small, or you're willing to do some registry fiddling to change the resolution of the game window. (For information on how to do this, look
.)
The game itself is a simple, casual roguelike. It's enjoyable and engaging enough to be worthwhile, although hardly unique or very memorable. Strategy-wise, there is some (if not very much) depth here, and although the practical use of some elements (such as Perception) don't become apparent until you've sunk quite a few points into them, most of the gameplay is fairly intuitive and presents itself well.
There is a hitch, however. The entire point of a casual game is to be noncommittal and not require total focus, but one of the core elements of Dungeon Journey (the shield block) is reaction-based, and thus repeatedly forces the player to concentrate entirely on playing rather than treating the game as the casual distraction it is clearly intended to be. This is unlikely to be an issue for everyone, but it can get highly frustrating for some of us.
The audio side is passable. The UI and game sounds are pretty professional. The music does sometimes get rather annoying (mostly, I think, because it's badly compressed) but then it's a casual game. For my part, I simply turned all sound off once I realised that none of it gives any gameplay advantage.
Dungeon Journey is not a bad little game, and for the low price, it is easy to forgive the lack of polish (poor English, incomplete tutorial, subpar graphics, and so on.) If you're looking for a hardcore, involving and comprehensively strategic roguelike, look elsewhere—but if like me you're simply looking for something to mess around with when your concentration isn't strictly needed elsewhere, then Dungeon Journey might well be the ticket.
Maybe it gets repetitive but it's quite relaxing - a game where you can destroy all humanity? Yes, please.

A review on a modern system:
I know with older games there is always a small worry that it won't work on a newer system. I'm happy to report that I at least didn't have any issues getting this to run in W10, on a gtx 980. Only small detractors in that area, the game doesn't support 1440p or above resolutions natively. Also be sure to get the 60fps unlocker, its an unofficial patch that's easily findable and makes quite a difference if your used to playing at 60 fps whereas 30 can seen choppy if your not accustomed to it.
Now on to the game itself. Its starting to show its age, you can tell its crossgen title between ps2/ps3 or xbox and xbox 360. There are alot of low resolution textures to be found, also details and animations look a bit old. On the upshot it controls great, responsive, and while I'm only played a couple levels, its fun using even the early force powers.  Add to that the low price the Ultimate Sith Edtion and it wass a hard offer to pass up. Overall I'd reccomend it, just don't go in expecting shiny graphics and you won't be dissapointed

A lot of people dream of hearing the pitter-patter of little feet in their house. I myself dream about the pitter-patter of undead feet. You save so much money on groceries with undead kids, and they never grow up into smelly hairy horrible teenagers. Amethyst Quarter granted my wish with a procedurally generated platformer called Abomination Tower. You play as a headless corpse named uhh… Headless. A short intro cinema shows him being thrown in the trash by the mad scientist who gave him life. Or unlife. Is Headless out for revenge? Does he just want to give his daddy a hug? Is he even capable of cognitive thought? I don’t think these questions will ever be answered. The tower is dastardly difficult, and seems to continue on forever. I suppose the journey is all part of the experience, and there are plenty of scoreboards and unlockables to motivate you on your way. I enjoyed my time with Abomination Tower, however it does fall short in a few areas. What are they? Read on, and lets take a closer look at Abomination Tower.
There is a lot of wall-jumping in this game. The gameplay is quite similar to a certain popular meat boy, however the levels focus on traveling vertically rather than horizontally. I found the controls to be tight, though it does lose a point for being slightly floaty. As you wall-jump your way past the many obstacles, you will collect eyes which are used to unlock heads for Headless. Not only do the heads make him slightly less headless, they all add their own unique powers. This, combined with a global high-score table, make replayability Abomination Tower’s strongest aspect. Speed-running the levels isn’t easy, especially when you can only take one hit, but if you’re up to the challenge you can try and run through a level as fast as possible for a shot at fame and fortune. I didn’t find the traps or enemies to be extremely innovative, but they certainly are placed in a way that cranks up the difficulty. This game requires almost pixel perfect platforming.
Most of your deaths in Abomination Tower will be your own doing. The game does fling some stuff at you, but I found most deaths were simply due to crashing into an enemy or miscalculating a jump. While I didn’t find the game to be very innovative, aside from the swapping of heads, it is still a great example of the lost art of platforming. I appreciate that the focus is solely on the platforming. You don’t even get a weapon to strike back against the enemies. You’re simply a misshapen creation on the run from larger abominations. Abomination Tower doesn’t try to be anything that it isn’t, it works well and knows what it wants to do, and for that I applaud it heartily. While the sound FX are certainly decent (I especially like the gross sloppy slapping that wall-jumping makes), I found that the music consisted of only one song. The song is creepy, has a nice progression, and fits the aesthetic however only having one song means that extended play sessions can be the equivalent of psychological warfare.
While I enjoyed Abomination Tower, my main points of criticism are due to the aesthetics. The graphics are decent, but remind me of a flash game. If you’re going to go low-res, I’d suggest going full retro. This game would’ve looked super in 16-bit. There is not really a story besides the opening scene of a scientist dumping a corpse in the trash. Perhaps the story is resolved at some point, but I painstakingly worked my way up to level six without so much as a boss fight. The only changes in the stages was a palette swap every 4 or 5 levels, which I guess makes sense because you’re climbing the same castle, but it certainly left me wanting for more. Level design also loses out because many obstacles can be avoided. Overall though, Abomination Tower is a great way to kill 10 minutes. Then you can reanimate some of those killed minutes and replace their head with a butt. Oh yea, it has a great sense of humor too which is a great accomplishment for a game having such a dark theme. Kudos. Big thanks to Amethyst Quarter for the review copy. I hope to see more from you guys in the near future.

Absolutely my favorite game. There's nothing as satisfying as finishing a game put together as well as this. Amazing art design with beautiful graphics and an unforgettable soundtrack is enough to make a game a masterpiece, but Transistor includes the miniscule details and an emotional ending that leaves a gaping hole in your heart.
Since SuperGiantGames is coming out with their third game, I ran through Transistor for a second time and it was another beautiful experience even on second play through.

Super Giant games must have an individual who pulls on past experiences and envisions ways to improve.
From the story, to the music, to the action, Transistor is nearly flawless. The sci-fi themed action RPG borrows elements from bastion, streamlines them into an approachable and addicting combat system with exquisite story telling.
A step away from the dwarf approached artwork in bastion, the look and feel of the stunning futuristic city is mind blowing, with several spots and scenes worthy of a wallpaper or piece of art.
Controlling "Red", most of the narrative comes from a unusual powerful weapon taking its name from the title of the game. Transistor operates as the main form of attack against a variety of amazing sprite monsters that rarely are duplicated.
Voice activing is quite superb, Logan Cunningham returns from Bastion, lending his deep smooth voice to the narrative while Ashley Lynn Barrett (runner up to Quiet\Stefanie Jootsen impersonator) offers vocals that beautifully reflect the hymn of the city.
Little is wasted and spoiling the ending on wikipedia or walk throughs takes away from the experience. although the fighting can be extremely unforgiving; planning and focus contribute to success in defeating bosses. the rpg elements aside, little interferes with the forward momentum to the story and the game is an acceptable 10+ hours of time before a thrilling conclusion.
Either on sale or full price, collect the soundtrack; I can garuntee at least one tune that will stick with you for awhile.

Note : I do not recommend this game for most people, but i do recommend it if you're a perfectionist, who like to replay the same level over and over again until it's perfect. Read below for more explanation.
OlliOlli frustrates me greatly. I was expecting a fun skateboard game where i could mess around a bit and do some crazy tricks. And though OlliOlli is all about unreal tricks that make you fly high into the air, it is not designed for casual fun. OlliOlli is a game for perfectionists only.
The game requires you to always perform flawlessly. If you mess up a trick, then there is a high chance you will crash, which ends the level immediately. So there is no casual fun in OlliOlli, because you have to know the levels by heart, and constantly chain tricks correctly to avoid crashing.
This merciless system is compounded by an unusual control scheme. The majority of skateboard/snowboard games have a jump button, and simply ask you to have a stabilize your board before landing. OlliOlli does the opposite : there is no dedicated jump button, but there is a landing button.
It takes a while to get used to press a button to land. Moreover, the timing is very strict, so if you mess it up you're gonna be screwed right away. If you fail a landing, 2 things may happen : best case scenario, your combo score is cut severely, to the point that the 10x or 50x combo you got is useless, and your speed is cut down. Worst case scenario, your skater loses his balance, and doesn't get back in time to avoid the next obstacle: instant crash, level is over.
So, the game is really unforgiving. But it also doesn't help players to learn how to play correctly, the game does a poor job at explaining itself. Though a tutorial will guide through the basics, the game doesnt tell you how it scores combo. For example it doesnt tell you whether it's important to get different tricks in the same combo, whether it's important to get a long grind or just hitting the grind and jumping again is enough, etc. All this means you're gonna have to figure out by trial and error if you want to achieve a score objectives or get a highscore on the leaderboards.
In the end, everything in OlliOlli is meant for people that enjoy doing things over and over again until they perform it perfectly well and reach the highest scores. I'm not one of theses people, and hence i get frustrated by the game. If you're one of these people, I think you will enjoy the game. Otherwise, stay clear of it.
One redeeming feature of the game for me : the sound design and the soundtrack, both of these are excellent and i enjoy them very much.
