If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

I have well over 2K hours in the original version of CLOD...CLOD has been my go to game/sim for the past 5 years...You can not recommend a game/sim any better than that...
CLOD had a bumpy start on release in 2011...Those days are well behind now...After patches and updates in the first couple years it became playable and very quickly the definitive WW2 flight sim....CLOD has been the one to beat since then!
The most striking differences from CLOD to Blitz for me have been the new aircraft, sounds, damage models, flight models and ground textures...Blitz is a worthy tweak to the original and make it a very exciting prospect for the future...It has been patched and re-worked by a very dedicated team (TFS) of boffins and historians over the past 4 to 5 years to make the sim you see today and that is abundantly clear when you play it...Many of us have great belief in this sim...In the future we are looking forward to more patches and a new desert theatre which is being worked as we speak...I can't thank those guys enough for their work...
You can see screenshots and discussion on up coming patches and theatre on the TFS facebook (link below)
For any of you that put the effort and time in to fly this excellent flight sim the rewards are considerable...If you join the community you will benefit from the help that will get you up and running and could well establish long term friendships that enhance what we witness in the CLOD and Blitz community today...The community we have here is one of the most friendly and welcoming you will experience in the gaming/sim community...I can't enphasize that enough...You can talk directly to the guys who have put the work into this sim...and talk with folks who have thousands of hours in CLOD...The guys that have put the hours in are the guys you need to talk with if you need help...You'll find many of them in the ATAG forums together with the TFS (link below)...
Many of us believe that the online play (multiplayer) is where this sim really excells...Thats where you get to play alongside and against real players...There is nothing quite like joining TeamSpeak and talking to the folks worldwide who instanly become your wingmen and squadmates to fly against the enemy who are doing the same...Many servers are now mission based so there are objectives to be completed even in multiplayer...Read the briefs and try complete them or simply mash it up in dogfights with other real players for fun...
So my conclusion is...If you come here from another WW2 combat flight sim, then your collection is incomplete without this...If you come from WarThunder and are looking for something more realistic as many do then this is a must for you...if you just upgraded to Blitz from many hours in CLOD then you already know...and if you are a new player looking for a WW2 combat flight sim then you won't go far wrong getting Blitz!

The game itself is okay. The controls are a bit sluggish, the camera isn't always where you want it, but it's playable.
But the gem and the real reason you should play this game is the new lore: an interesting chapter in the Star Wars saga, and a character that would have deserved his own trilogy. And the actor who played him in the game (and the basis for the character's face in the game) would have been perfect for the role. Think of this game and its sequel, Force Unleashed II, in the same way as the animated Clone Wars series. They both fill in gaps in the story. The only difference is that the game fills in gaps that you didn't know existed.

This game is fantastic. Not sure what the negative reviews are about; the controls are a little loose and tough to master but all it takes is a little practice.
Gameplay: Really fun and immersive. It does get slightly repetitive, since about half-way through the game you've already met all the enemies. I did find three bugs and I had to restart the level to fix them but overall a decent port. The Force powers are varying and really fun to use. You're supposed to use combos to kill enemies but you only need to know one or two main combos to deal a lot of damage. Apart from 3PS murder there's quicktime events for takedowns (which are fun and at the perfect level of difficutly, since you'd land a perfect one about 50% of the time and towards the end of the game you have them memorized for easy killing) and one sidescrolling level that was a pain to do but enjoyable.
The customization is one of the strong points of this game (even though the menus take forever to load). You can change costumes into droids, stormtroopers, clones, a variety of Sith or Jedi, and about ten alternate Starkiller costumes.  You can change lightsaber colors and also pick a passive effect for the lightsaber, such as health drain or added crit.
The boss battle are fun for the most part. I had to restart the Star Destroyer boss level multiple times because of a reoccurring bug, but I encountered no other issues. Honestly, most of them were slightly too easy; I beat them in one or two tries.
Graphics: Outdated; it's an old game. Still, they're not bad looking. In the cutscenes especially, the level of detail on Starkiller's face is amazing. Yes the graphics are old; no they are not bad nor do they deter from the game.
Music: Really fantastic. A good mix of the classic soundtrack and totally new, dark themes full of powerful swells that really make you feel awesome. There were a few spots in the game where there was no music and that didn't feel right; the sounds of slaughter DO need accompaniment.
Story: The story itself is quite good. Unfortunately, it's really low on character development; you can tell everything you need to know about a character simply from looking at them. The Force Unleashed books really fixed that; if you love the story its a good read and a slight improvement over the game's story. Still, its an epic saga and it really gets good towards the end as it becomes less mindless Jedi killing and there's actually emotion. The ending is fantastic.
Overall, it's made its way into one of my favorite games off all time.

What more can be said about this game, that hasn't been said a thousand times before?  This is an incredible game that is easily worth the six dollars that it currently cost.  Even if you are not big into simulation games (like myself), this game will quickly catch your attention and it will not surrender it for quite some time.  Before you realize it, 4 hours have passed.  If anything this game is dangerous for how easily it erases massive amounts of time.
I was going to write up another big, long review for this game but as I stated before, everything that could be said about how incredible this game is, has been said.  So I'll keep it short and sweet.
Very seemingly simplistic gameplay, but with oh so much depth.  Enough to keep coming back to for days, weeks, months, years....  you get the idea.  Build a park.  Aim for the objective (# of customers, customer approval rating, etc.).  Win the game.  Play forever if you wish.  The UI that is implemented here is very user-friendly and makes building even the most ridiculous elaborate parks very simplistic.
Great graphics for the time when it was released (1999).  Runs perfectly on even the oldest of machines with no fps drops.  This game was made so incredibly stable because Chris Sawyer sat it fit to program the entire game in Assembly language.  Which is ridiculously awesome and very, VERY difficult to do, but in doing so, made the game incredibly efficient and available to a massive audience.  The game does run on every Windows OS up to Windows 10 x64 (because that's what I played it on).  Might have to mess with the resolution though.
The park guests' sounds of approval, or of wretching on the sidewalk, does fit perfectly into the game, and it does give off the theme park vibe very adequately.  However, the music that can be played from the rides gets repetitive very quickly.
Holy lord don't even get me started on the lasting appeal of this game.  Not only is there the ability to play the parks forever, but in this deluxe package with the two expansions, there are over 70 FREAKING PARKS.  THAT'S value.  To give an example of how much time would be sunk into the game in that time, it would be close to 250 hours.  And that's only if you somehow manage to beat every scenario first try.  So yeah, it's got some lasting appeal.
This game is incredible.  It was amazing in 1999, and it's amazing in 2015.  And it will be amazing in 2025.

Final note: This game is a wonderful romp as any tycoon game should be.

tl;dr: Overall a pretty solid game, if a little rough around the edges. Definitely looking forward to OlliOlli 2.
The Good:
This game has both the charm and challenge of the old Tony Hawk's Pro Skater games, distilled down into a 2D sidescroller / platformer. Moment-to-moment gameplay is absolutely solid. Aside from a handful of cases (due to unfriendly camerawork), all failures are truly your own, making success that much more gratifying. The controls are pretty unconventional, but are by no means bad. Once you get comfortable with them, pulling off elaborate combos is incredibly satisfying. There's definitely at least 10 hours of wonderfully crafted content aside from the eternal leaderboard climb & daily challenges.
The Bad:
The first thing that is likely to irk new players is the controls. There are very few analogues for players to draw from, and the gameplay is pretty unforgiving, which results in a fairly frustrating introduction if you elect to skip the tutorial. The camera is fairly static, centered on the player at all times, leading to some frustrating conflicts with the level design. In the junkyard stage especially, you'll be pitched against obstacles that you will have to have anticipated in advance because the camera placement does not offer you enough information to act before it is too late. This results in a fair bit of trial and error based play as you get a better feel for the levels, which is pretty poor design. Although all stages have a distinct visual style, the minimalist mechanics force their design to feel very same-y. The largest difference between stages is increasing obstacle density and slimming the margin for error, which works OK, but leaves the overal experience feel somewhat bland.
The Ugly:
Fairly bug-ridden. Not to the point where it's unplayable, but if you're not completely taken with the game early on, it'll be frustrating enough for this to sit in your library relatively untouched.

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

Ok, I had some time to try it.
Graphics: The new map is really good I like a lot the new colours, the tree lines the new runways and so on; I liked also the new effects (venting is really good) and the bigger visibility of the clouds. But... I was expecting more. Especially from the shaders' modification.
It looks pretty much like the old clod generally speaking. Especially the lighting system.
UI: Larry's photos are great but they are still game photos so no huge resolution, lot's of different colours etc. At least now you can read the menu (comparing with the steam 4.3) but I think that the original UI was the best.
Sounds: The German ones are really good. DB601 sounds are surely improved and the new MG/cannons sounds are really really nice, same for the landing gear.
But the Merlin sound and the 303 mgs are worse than before IMHO. There is almost no sound change at high RPMs, all feels so flat. And the 303 mg feels so slow and strange. I prefer the previous sounds a lot.
Also, the carburator cut-out sound is now missing, as well as the "closed canopy" soft engine sound effect and there is a strange wind sound when you fly with the canopy closed.
FM: The ground handling is improved. No more lightweight aircraft that fly away by the wind and no more useless spit's brakes. But I noticed a big wobbling effect sometimes and taxi and brake turns are improved even if not perfect but is good enough.
About the FMs. They surely are improved. No more extreme gliding landing effect for the spit.
I really like them. FMs feels improved.
Warm-ups are now longer. For a fighter is not a big problem but I heard bombers guys that have to wait too much. Considering that IRL engine where pre-heated before pilots would get in the cockpit maybe a "pre-warm" option for bigger planes that need too many times could have been introduced.
This only encourages voulching.
Visibility: Spotting feels a hugely improved, especially against the ground, but was already good in clod (it's the best in gaming out there). Aircraft sometimes disappear I think because of the bubble in visibility so no big problem. This is one of the things that I like most of 4.5.
Performance:This is the big problem. It's almost unplayable to me online. That's what makes negative 4.5 to me.
Also considering that I can play Box at medium-high settings with absolutely no problem with 80+ players.
Conclusion: I don't know if it was by the fact that we waited so long for new content, but my expectations were higher. The product has been in beta testing for 2 months but it still has lots of CTD, no-starting problem etc. I thought the 4.5 was a sort big bug fixing but lots of old bugs are still there looking at the bug tracker, and now there are newer ones.
The bigger problem with the current version of the game (4.5) is the performance when played online. That makes the game unplayable to me. A real pity considering how much this game stayed in beta testing.
If they can solve the performance and lags problems than the game will totally change imho.
P.s. Developers that are giving themselves positive reviews? Come on guys. Let the community speaks.

Reminiscing the age of Tony Hawk's Pro skater, OlliOlli is an objective based skateboarding game that re-imagines the 3D formulae into a retro 2D side-scroller. Originally developed for the PS Vita by Roll7 – the windows port up-scales the game whilst offering a similar experience. But does it grind past its contemporaries or face-plant into failure?

The games primary feature is a single player career mode. This is split across 5 distinct areas each divided into 5 courses. Your tasked with completing each course to unlock the next with increasing difficulty as you progress.
There are also a list of 5 objectives within each course, and if completed you unlock a 'Pro' variation of the same course. Each run is fairly short and can be successfully completed within a few minutes.
To supplement this once you've unlocked a course, they can then be revisited as skating 'spots', allowing you to compete on a score board, ranking players across the globe.
The final mode is a challenge variant called 'Daily Grind' which challenges the player to grind the entirety of a run. You can practice as many times as you want but you can only compete once. Your score is also ranked, however this resets with a new course every day.
Although OlliOlli is a fairly compact game – the polish and refinement to the gameplay and mechanics makes it easy to jump in and out of. Its highly satisfying to pull off a series of tricks and slide down a rail to 100% a course, and although it can be frustrating when your stuck on a run at times, its easy to step away for a few hours and pick up where you left off later. There is also the option to skip through the levels.
The gradual increase in difficulty is the perfect means to encourage players to perfect their timing. It also encourages the revisit of past levels, as new skills are picked up that will allow previously impossible objectives to be overcome. The game can feel intimidating at first but through familiarising yourself with the tutorials and the 'tricktionary' the player can steadily progresses through the game – never becoming too hard or too easy.
Although the game is primarily single player there is a thrill with trying to out-do players on the scoreboards, and its easy to go back to a run that you've had much success and find you've been out done. The daily grind is also another great incentive to try boast you timing and trick combinations.
The games biggest weakness is perhaps its controls, as a handheld port – the instant response of controller buttons is required. A keyboard can hinder the players timing and weakens the core mechanics of the game. There were also occasions where the keys would not register a move resulting in a sloppy landing or bail. However a controller solved all these problems. On the rare occasion the game suffered from glitches that allowed us to grind through obstacles or bail on a perfect landing.

Although there isn't anything particularly impressive about the aesthetics of the game the art style is very charming. Particularly the animated background environments, and the skater himself, who has unique animations for each trick which can be viewed within the 'tricktionary'. However the contrast between the slow background and fast character can sometimes be disorientating, drawing focus away from the speed of the foreground.
OlliOlli has a subtle electronic score which really suits the retro feel of the game. Although you hear the same tracks multiple times, they can come in at just the right moment to spur you on to victory.
The game manages to avoid feeling repetitive through remaining a challenge. Rather than testing the patient of the player, there is the ability to restart at any point in a run and progressively improve over an individual course. OlliOlli is a great example of when less is more,  but with a sequel announced for next year promising to expand on its successes, we can't wait to get back on ours board.

Legend of Grimrock is best summarized in its manual: "The game features dungeon exploration, puzzles, secrets, combat, magic and role playing elements."
The game's enjoyment comes from navigating the dungeon, avoiding traps, finding hidden switches and looting treasures. Combat is fairly simple, it consists of avoiding attacks by maneuvering around your adversaries, and the only tactical element is picking a place with enough room to do so (also being mindful of pits and other enemies cornering you). All in all combat is just another puzzle element in this game, the experience points and skills you earn a different form of reward.
The game's overall difficulty is rather involved but lenient, it requires patience and attention to detail. There is a lot of diversity in puzzles, I've never come across two identical ones. They will test your memory, reflexes, and creativity, so you are bound to appreciate some of them while finding other tedious or unremarkable. Only in two instances did I get stuck. On the other hand the designers can be quite devious at times when it comes to traps, especially towards the end of the game. Some might find it frustrating, but I see it rather as playfulness and awareness of the exploits used in that genre of games.
The game's visual and sound design, while polished, lacks diversity. Being quite lengthy (20-30 hours depending on difficulty/old school mode settings), but only comprised of two different kinds of environment (with a third on the tiny last two levels), the game can seem quite bleak after a while. The loot also becomes more scarce and less exciting, supplies more numerous, making it less rewarding to search for secrets. The lack of new enemies and puzzle elements adds to an overall fatigue building up until the two bottom floors. The final boss requires mobility and precision, also some ingenuity but most of all calm. It reinvigorated my enjoyment of the game, as the end fight was unexpectedly innovative.

I started Legend of Grimrock 'cause it was on a friends pc and he hadn't tried it. I finished Grimrock because the game balances action and puzzle in the grid based movement style of older rpgs. This is a game that can be very easy and yet also rather difficult.
The plot is that you and your colleagues are tossed into a dungeon for crimes unknown with a simple objective: escape and be free. As you go deeper however the true purpose of the building becomes a growing mystery. Through puzzles, traps and battles you must reach your objective at the bottom of the dungeon where lies your escape and possibly some answers.
The game uses a tile based movement system where you and your group of four move in real time but only in the four cardinal directions. You control each of your party individualy, managing each of their separate inventories, attacking with each in their own time and chosing what spells (if any ) they will cast.
I enjoyed this game, but I don't believe it is for everyone. Though I think the grid system worked well in the claustrophobic enviroment, many may not like the idea of not having full three dimensional movement. The game also ramps up in challenge rather quickly and can be unforgiving, especially if you dont save frequently. The challenge motivated me but it may turn others off. Others may not like the fact that many of the secrets are almost invisable or will require a few trips to the wiki to get but I found them fun to guess at.

Playing this with the sequel in mind, it's a much simpler, more confined experience, but that's not necessarily a bad thing. Where the sequel is much more open and encourages exploration, this one's more about overcoming the dungeon before you, going deeper and deeper, floor by floor, as challenges and rewards alike escalate. You won't get lost, but you'll find plenty of secrets if you poke around a little. It's shorter, but there's much less time spent wandering.
Played without the sequel in mind, this is God's gift to dungeon-crawl fans, taking all the old-school things you enjoyed and decorating them in modern graphics and sound. It's not as hard, even on hard, as those older games, but it captures the spirit of them perfectly with solid mechanics and atmosphere. It's a fantastic adventure, even if the final act is a bit of a letdown, and well worth playing even if you've already played the fancier second game.

Never in the field of Flight Simulation, has so much been done for so many, by so few.
The few, Team Fusion, have turned this once-forlorn title into a top notch piece of sheer passionate endeavour. Taking it from a derelict state of it's 2011 release to a new level of excellence, upping the bar for combat flight sims everywhere.
This newly rebuilt simulator now features what I can confidently say are the very best depictions in any simulator series, of the features that follow (amongst many others):
- Flak effects.  It is actually FUN to get shot at by flak, when it looks and sounds so dramatically awesome.  Tracers wizz by menacingly and explode like it's Fourth of July in Hell.
- G forces.  No other sim has as realistic G-LoC representation as this, closely matching veteran accounts of the onset of "grayout" and "tunnel vision" leading to blackout.
- The Feeling of Flight.  It really feels like you're cutting through the air, every motion of your plane produces a thoroughly authentic sensation of being airborne.
I could go on, but I'd be just repeating the obvious...
Yet above all else, one thing stands topmost as the main feature of this sim:
It is quite possibly the best multiplayer experience you'll ever have.  In any game.   The community is absolutely top-notch. Nowhere else one can find a warmer, more friendly bunch.  Join in the ATAG server for a flight you'll never forget!
I cannot recommend this game enough.  Team Fusion has done an almost miraculous job at delivering the simulator we have longed for all these years.   Let alone that it was made purely by volunteer work!
This game now stands proudly among the leading air combat series of our day.  A fantastic simulator, if there ever was one.
A major upgrade to one of the very best combat flight simulators available.

Another very well made game created by Supergiant Games, Transistor is the second in series of games they made and it totally lives up to the expectations of all. I personally enjoyed their first game, Bastion, but this one took me beyond my expectations and I found myself loving this game more.
Pros:
- Spectacular Graphics
The company totally went all out on their graphic department because this game is so gorgeous to look at and play through. Unlike Bastion with it water-colored details, this game has a more Cyberpunk feeling to it, still retaining it original water concept, but has a mix of bright and out-going colors, to more subtle and depressing colors, which goes very well with the story. Different scenes throughout the story shows you how magnificent the art is and you have all the time in the world to take it in. All I can say is that the graphics are very unique and are unforgettable.
- Fascinating Story
Right from the beginning, your thrown into the game with no knowledge of anything and its your job to figure out the story. It makes you feel like its your duty to piece this story together and figure out what the heck is going on. The game did a great job of luring people to press forward into the story and be enveloped with its lore it has to offer. The game has a unique way of revealing the story by allowing you to using different actions to reveal more of the story, but that's is entirely up to you to discover it. The story is filled with sorrow, tragedy, trust, and mystery, which Red, the main chracter, has to dive into it and sort it all out before its too late.
- Personalized Gameplay
One of the main reasons why I fell in love with this game was the fact that you have the ability to customized your gameplay in many different ways, which is similar to their first game, Bastion. Red has different abilities that are unlocked by progressing through the story or by leveling up that can be used in your gameplay. Each function can be used in different ways to enhance your gameplay, they can be used as one of your action keys (which you only have 4 active one), they can be used as a upgrade to make your other action keys more powerful, or they can be used as a passive ability, which can enhance your characters potential in battle and out. With a variaty of ablilites to choose from, you will have varies combinations of ablities to experiment with and this is one of the ways you can discover more of the story. The game encourages you to try different combinations of ablilites to find out more of the backstory of the game. Not only that, but if the game kind of gets too easy for you, there are functions called Limiters that will make your game hell, quite literally. You unlock them while leveling up throughout the game and if you activate them, you will get more EXP in every battle. But this is like a doubled-edged blade because it will enhance your enemies in different ways. For example, some limiters might give the enemies more health or give them stronger attacks, thats up to you if you want to risk it all. The enemy also level up throughout the game, giving them more ablilites to one-up you in battle and make each battle more difficult. There are also bonus missions or levels you can discover throughout the game, which if you do complete them, you will be awarded with more EXP and unlockables. The options that the game gives to you is immersive and this truly make Transistor a game you will never forget.
- Beautiful Soundtrack
The other main reason why I fell in love with this game was their incrediable soundtrack, it was just wondrous. The music somehow flows perfectly throughout the game in and out of battles, making them more intense and emotional. The music changes as the story shifts from different tones, making it acceptable in every situation. If their is an intense battle coming up, it builds on it and goes with the flow, if there is scenes where you see the destruction of what you loved, the music builds on it with soft and emotional tunes. Supergiant Games did an outstanding job with their soundtrack and I believe they should be praised by it.
With so many good pros about this game, surely there shouldn't be any cons. Sadly, it does have some cons, but barely any and most of them people can relate too while they played this game.
Cons:
- Brief Game
I was saddened by the fact that with so much it offered, I ended up finishing the game rather too quickly than I expected. You can probably finish the game is less than a day, maybe even half a day, if you have the right builds and strategies. I was really drawn in by the story and wished their could have been more of it, but that never happened and I was quite bummed about it.
- Miscellaneous and Small Problems
Hopefully, I wasn't the only one who kind of noticed it, but sometimes when I was in battle, the enemies would sometime go behind a building or go out of my sight and I wasn't able to see them properly or fight them properly. It might not seem too bad, but it did hinder my progress a little bit, espceially when I played the New Game+ with the enemies at their maximum potential. Other than that though, there wasn't anything too major to point out or actually confirm.
My Verdict of the Game
9.5/10
Much of the game mistakes (which there were very few mistakes) were practically overwhelmed by the amount of masterpieces that were made in this game. The soundtrack was spot on, the graphics were jaw-dropping and astonishing, the story was creative and alluring, but most of all, the gameplay mechanics were open and free, giving you the power to customize them and change how you want to play the game. It totally worth your money buying this game and you won't feel any regret at all. Overall, another masterpiece created by Supergiant Games, and I can't wait for their new game, Pyre, to come out. They created two masterpieces as it is, and I have a good feeling their next game will be their third.

Where Battlefield 2 was about that slower paced Squad based Teamwork, Battlefield: Bad Company 2 went in the complete opposite direction. Sure if you work as a team you'll overcome and win as you'd expect, but the pace is ramped up and the craziness is all the way up to 11!
The singleplayer campaign has it's moments, but as with any Battlefield game that has a singleplayer campaign it's not what you'll ultimately be buying the game for. It's the multiplayer - as it should be and as it always should be. Whereas the original Bad Company was tongue-in-cheek and entirely selfaware of how over the top the franchise was at times (as well as the FPS genre in a post-Modern Warfare world), Bad Company 2 tones it down slightly (much to my own personal disappointment).
I personally didn't mind the Bad Company spinoff from the Battlefield series, it was it's own thing and that was entirely fine with me. However, it appears as if Bad Company 2 is almost ashamed of it's original brother and returns to a more 'grounded' root, and almost tries to ape Call of Duty: Modern Warfare's fast paced Michael Bay OTT action... while keeping a straight face.
Which is a shame.
However... that's not what you're interested in in this game... to the multiplayer!
The multiplayer aspect offers you almost everything you'd ask for in a Battlefield game - big maps, crazy weapons, tons of Armor and memorible moments of madness. This was one of the first Battlefield games to really try and push the envelope visually as they ramped up the Frostbite Engine to a whole new level of insanity. I remember feeling 'My PC can actually play this?!' to great surprise and glee too.
So don't undersell your PC if you're unsure on the specs. The minimum specs will still give you a good visual experience.
As for the gameplay, I think this was my favourite. I can't really put my finger on what it was exactly, but everything just seemed to work well together. Teamwork, classes, weapons - land mines. Land Mines. C4. Land mines. Airstrike. Land minds. C4...
OK, so it's the explosions. Planting landmines, hiding around the corner and giggling like a Japanese schoolgirl as that big burley tank came lumbering around the corner to go down the narrow street time and time again. Yup, it's the land mines.
Buy this game.
Plant land mines.
Laugh like Japanese Schoolgirl.

I bought this arcade skateboarding game as part of HumbleBundle. Your objective is skating as far as you can along short, but somewhat demanding levels featuring stairs, grinds, vehicles, obstacles. Along the level you get scores for tricks, grinds and combos.
With 8 key controls the game seems to be easy, but it is relatively unforgiving, which makes you wanna beat it. I mean, how many times can you smash your face into the floor just after landing an epic 20x combo?! After a few minutes you can play the game and after 1-2 hours you get to know more tricks and are able to get quite impressive scores.
The game features classic 8-bit arcade graphics style and urban music floating between trance, hip-hop and dubstep (no vocals).
Is it fun? Yes it is. You want to win the level. You want to land the combo. You want to beat your friends' score online (there are leaderboards). The graphics is retro-cool (but at times too simplistic and repetitive) and the music creates right skateboarding mood. At the same time it is a little annoying, especially after multiple failures. Despite easy controls I tend to mix up the keys in the heat of the moment. Music is good, but it just runs in the background, isn't related to levels or your activity/performance. Some levels are repetive, but the in-game achievements vary from level to level. There are multiple themes including city, port and junkyard. Some are better than others, for example in port the lack of detail on the floor makes it difficult to estimate your current speed. There are some bugs. The game crashed for me once.
It is a nice little game definitely worth getting in some bundle. Depending on how much you like arcade games you will have 5-20 hours of fun until it gets a little boring.
GRAPHICS: 6/10
AUDIO: 7/10
GAMEPLAY: 7/10

Grimrock is a modern dungeon crawler that puts age old mechanics to good use. Your goal is very simple. Guide a party through a nasty dungeon while avoiding traps, fighting monsters, collecting better equipment and leveling up.
The game is comfortable and easy to play despite the difficulty ramping up after the first few levels. For those who enjoy exploring and getting lost there's an option to switch off the automap. There are secret areas aplenty and some puzzles require a bit of thinking. Most of the time it's enough to just look everywhere and figure out how to make use of things like pressure plates, teleports or timing mechanisms.
The enemies are quite cruel and your party will become overmatched pretty quickly. Fortunately it's possible to close gates and block off some areas, and it's not necessary to kill everything. If you must kill things to progress, usually there's a way to make use of the dungeon itself and make it easier.
I have played a lot of dungeon crawlers and have liked some of them. Ishar 3 was good though i never finished it. I loved Captive but finished it even less... Albion was interesting, though not exactly a classic example, and neither was Whale's Voyage. Hired Guns was incredible for it's time and hard as hell for good measure. Never could get into Dungeon Master or Eye of the Beholder much, though EoB was ok. Anvil of Dawn was pretty impressive. I think there's a few games i forgot, but anyway...
Maybe i'm weak for Hired Guns a bit more but Legend of Grimrock is the most awesome of the bunch!

The Serious Sam series is for some reason one of those that seem to fly under most people's radar despite being fantastically solid and fun. Essentially it's over-the-top FPS with hundreds of enemies being thrown at you in arena-like levels with the odds seemingly insurmountably stacked against you.
But you are Serious Sam! Forget about Duke Nukem, the Doom space Marine or any other FPS protagonist - no-one relishes    the challenge of facing off against hordes of enemies charging at you from all directions like Sam does. It helps having a satisfying arsenal  of good-looking and sounding weapons to do said work - from the standard but effective double-barrel shotgun to ammo-melting mini-guns and the rare but powerful homing parrot Klodivik bombs.
What separates Serious Sam from the rest is that nothing is serious. You wont find drab, brown levels or laborious plot twists. Everything is bright, bold, loud , silly and the humour in the storyline somewhat ridiculous but fitting. Graphics are good for the time - Croteam likes pretty textures and bright colours in their games and there's a lot to look at and many secrets to discover in the few moments you have between mowing down hordes of enemies. It's also of decent lnegth for an FPS.
Few FPS games are as unpretentious and downright fun as Serious Sam 2. It's currently ridiculously cheap over at Humblebundle. Get a copy for yourself and a few friends - it's perfect for co-op play!

Warning, long post ahead. TL; DR - don't buy this game.
As one of the admin for Storm of War (a large multiplayer server running a persistent campaign with many unique and bespoke featres) I am unimpressed with this latest patch. Considering the hours I've spent in CLOD and running a server, I'm hugely let down.  For me, the sounds are meh, performance is worse with many players experiencing less FPS and more latency/desync online and visually while some things are nicer, we seem to have gotten a much more obvious visual bubble, worse building rendering delays, disappearing aircraft markings, overworked effects and the native anti aliasing is not great despite the move to DX11.
To be honest I'm less than impressed that bugs raised over two years ago on their internal bug tracker which should have been easy to address have not been. It’s also embarrassing that they ask the players to report bugs on this tracker but never use it to feedback what is and isn’t fixed. To do that players have had to retest their own bugs and work out whether it’s fixed or not themselves.
Personally the addition of new aircraft while impressive is not really that important to me. The priority should always have been to fix the game we had before adding new content to it IMO. In fairness there are a number of things which have been fixed for which credit should be due, the “swimming pools” of mid France are no more, the visual issue for rivers appearing much larger than they should and “marshy horizons” has also been resolved and the change of land textures to a brighter less saturated palette is also a massive improvement. I’m led to understand that the texture repetition of France has also been addressed.
Another focus of change has been the elimination of the altitude/air density bug which meant that ahistorical and inaccurate engine power calculations were a compromise in TF4.312. This has meant that the engine calculations have been redone, and the performances corrected as well as other Flight Model attributes. I’m not qualified to judge as I’ve never flown a real plane but to me the FM’s don’t feel hugely dissimilar to what they did before but I’ve not thoroughly tested them. I’m more interested in relative strengths and being able to recognise traits from the period quotes. For example using the boost cut out in the spitfire now renders a noticeable bit of “oomph” initially which I don’t remember before and which matches the Pilot recollections I’ve read.
The AI have had zero work, both in ability and giving orders, so are still essentially useless and bug ridden thereby continuing to render single player a horrible experience and difficult to employ effectively in Multiplayer to add ambience and atmosphere.
The sounds, specifically in the Hurricane and Spitfire are much worse than before. The engine noise has very little variation and while before you could essentially fly by ear, now you don’t know if you’re at full throttle or half way. Additionally we seem to have got a new addition of wind noise within the cockpit even with the canopy closed. This may be historic, I’m sure that the cockpits of 1940’s aircraft weren’t hermetically sealed, but the pilots did wear helmets and headphones so I’m not sure it’s very realistic. The worst change for some has been to the gun sounds, personally I preferred the old ones but I don’t hate the new ones, they’re just…different but I can understand the criticism, they certainly sound nothing like the “tearing calico” that you read about.
Overall, CLOD Blitz is IMO a retrograde from where we were with TF4.312 and one which has taken an inordinate amount of time to develop. Anyone seriously thinking that TF were going to meet their own timescales in releasing TF5.0 in 2017 is going to be in for a shock. They’re already suggesting it will be Christmas 2018 before the next patch and my understanding of the agreement suggests that except for obvious bug fixes to correct TF4.5, they will not be able to put out any further free patches.
Compared to the options on the market (BoX and DCS) I think Blitz will suffer and I very much doubt TF5,0 will ever see the light of day. Apart from a few absolute die hards, I think most people have moved on. Had the patch been released in 2015 or 2016 (performance issues not withstanding) I think it would have met with a different reception. However, we have waited three and a half years since the last patch. The progress made quite frankly is not reflective of this time and while I’m sure many will defend the volunteer/unpaid status of Team Fusion as an excuse, the fact remains that they are responsible for their own endeavours. Plenty of offers have been made to help which have been refused out of hand. They have consistently made bad decisions and the evidence of poor project management is now available for everyone to behold.
Ultimately, I think Jason Williams should be congratulated. He seems to have played an absolute blinder in giving TFS enough rope to hang themselves while gaining a huge amount of good will by allowing them to have the source code. He’s also benefitted by delaying the release of the original TF5 patch slated for 2016/2017 while they struggled to organise themselves into a corporate structure and then recode already accomplished hacks into the source code. In the interim he's turned BoX around and is getting regular updates, meets schedules and has a clear vision communicated in advance. It may not have the absolute capabilities that Oleg’s original had but for me, it’s now the better bet and likely the future of Combat flight sim gaming, while DCS focusses on the study sim aspect.

When it comes to the RTS (Real-Time Strategy) gaming genre, there are quite a few games that have left their mark. From the Command and Conquer series to Blizzard greats like Starcraft, or Warcraft, there are plenty of options when it comes to combat-style RTS games. Roller Coaster Tycoon, however, took things in a whole new direction and this is why it's in the spotlight for this BTN Gaming Review.
Now Roller Coaster Tycoon, upon arrival, totally reshaped the way people look at RTS games. In fact, it really created a whole new sub-genre in the Real-Time category. While the player doesn't necessarily control every aspect of the game, they do have control over the most key features. This is just one of the many details that makes Roller Coaster Tycoon stand out from its predecessors. Another key aspect, and quite possibly the one that carried the most impact, is the simple yet detail-oriented style of play. It's a very relaxed game in the fact that there isn't an enemy on the map who is ready to pillage and plunder you for everything you've got, but that's not to say that it doesn't have its own edge. Roller Coaster Tycoon delivers its thrills in a much more intricate and subtle way. It's these exact features that make it a great game, while at the same time might give a newcomer some frustrations.
For starters, Roller Coaster Tycoon's maps (campaign?) is a series of challenging theme parks that all have a certain goal that must be obtained. Whether it's building a brand new park from scratch, obtaining a specific park value, or even just to up the rating of an already thriving theme park, every single level in Roller Coaster Tycoon is wrapped around achieving these goals. Once these goals are achieved, a new map is opened up and the player can progress further on down the line. This is a great feature because it keeps the player interested with new scenes, new objectives, and really fills out the experience with the many different types of obstacles that can be overcome. However, it's this exact reason that might deter the more "casual" player. The reason for this is the simple fact that there is no sandbox mode. Not only is there the void of sandboxing but there is also this... nagging urge to just quit a park once the objective has been completed. If the player decides to save the current progress on any park once achieving the goal, they can return to it at any point in time.... but there really isn't much of a need to do so. This can severely cut the replay value of the game short, and while it isn't the biggest problem in the world, it can still be considered when arriving at the decision to purchase the game.
While the goal-oriented gameplay of Roller Coaster Tycoon is great, jaded only by the lack of a sandbox freeplay mode, we can't forget the details. Literally, the details. Roller Coaster Tycoon is absolutely FILLED to the brim with detail-oriented time management, and it's in these details that Roller Coaster Tycoon really thrives. From being able to design the roller coaster of your dreams, down the simplest detail as simply painting every ice cream shop a different color, it's these little intricacies that drive the game. That said, it's also these very minute, albeit important, features can become daunting at certain points in the game. For instance, when it comes to building said "Dream Roller Coaster" the game will not allow it to be built unless all of the brakes and speedups are in the right place. Prices too high for ice cream? Well that will drive potential patrons away before you even get the chance to fix it. So with that said, it's quite easy to get lost in the details and if things start getting to difficult to understand, just remember: breathe and if all else fails, RESTART!
On that note, however, there is also lack of any sort of tutorial or information that is in-game to help the player, should they feel lost. Don't get me wrong, I completely enjoy playing a game and feeling it out without any sort of help system at all. That's why I do what I do! But there are other players out there who don't want to mess around with understanding the mechanics or explore and experiment... simply put they want to achieve that goal for the next map. This is why some sort of help system within the actual framework of the game would be a huge help. For instance, your rating is dropping too low and you are just two months away from getting that coveted pat on the back for achieving an overall rating of 875 and you are sitting on 725. How do you get that rating up? Do you build more attractions? Do you lower the gate price? Do you run promotions? None of these answers are found directly in the game, not even in the help section. Thankfully though, there are pioneers out there who are willing and ready to write guides on issues such as this! That said, at least this information shouldn't be hard to find.
Overall, Roller Coaster Tycoon is a great little game, especially if the player is just looking to relax and chill out with a non-stressful game. All of its features can be seen as a double-edged sword so to speak, and if you are planning on buying the game, just make sure to take these things into consideration.

The Force Unleashed is a miracle of bad game design. Poor explanation of controls? Check. A tutorial (for throwing stuff with the Force, at least) that comes after the prologue level? Check. Bosses- and regular enemies- that can block attacks, knock you down, use attacks that you can't avoid or block, and make you forget all those neat combos in favor of button-mashing? Check. Seriously, one of the later levels gives you two or three purge troopers (who can knock you down), an AT-ST (which can also knock you down) and an assortment of stormtroopers (who can't knock you down but will constantly interrupt you by shooting you). Any difficulty above Apprentice, on which I still got killed by the aforementioned spam, is unthinkably nightmarish during or after the second boss. Not that the second boss is ever anything but.
There are also insultingly pointless quick-time events. You're given a surprisingly long window for each button press, and if by some perverse miracle you press the wrong button... either you can immediately initiate the QTE again or, if it's in a boss fight, you just get to press the right button. I failed to press X at a moment when doing so would prevent Starkiller from being fatally beaten in a saber lock... and I was just asked to do it again as the saber lock continued. Just let me kill the boss and watch the finisher or something. Sheesh.
The camera is rather irritating to control, though in my experience that's nothing new. Some people have complained about the fact that most of the boss fights have  a fixed camera, and while I understand that it's annoying, I'm actually somewhat glad that for once I don't have to bother with rotating the camera.  You can lock on to enemies, though, so that's a plus.
The game also only has three tilesets. We see Kashyyk in the prologue and in the story proper, we go to Felucia (how I hate Felucia) twice, and two different planets have the junkyard tileset. There might be more instances of this, though. I haven't finished the game.
To try to tie together the disparate complaints in this review, let me tell you about my favorite area in the game: a certain open area on Felucia. It's a clearing with some islands of foliage and weird tentacles that react violently when you shock them (this is probably meant to help you clear out enemies, but it didn't seem too helpful to me), loads of obnoxious Felucian warriors, some large, explosive fruits surrounding the clearing, and not one, not two, but THREE Rancors.
Quick rundown of Felucians: they have bone swords with forcefields that can block your attacks, they have forcefield shields that can block your attacks, they have shamans that can render them invincible, and they have another variant that shoot lasers at you from a staff. There are, as I mentioned, loads of them in this particular stretch of jungle, and they make it nearly impossible to take the necessary time to grab and throw fruits at the Rancors. They also seem to spawn continuously, though I could be wrong about that. Note this: the rushed, out-of-touch or downright sadistic people who made this game give the player an efficient means of dealing with the dangerous enemies in an area and then make that means essentially useless. I had to downgrade from Sith Lord (regular) difficulty to Apprentice (easy) to get through that area. At the point in the game I'm at the player is frequently pit against AT-STs, which are essentially Rancors that can consistently hit from a distance, and either not given any obvious throwables (not that they help against an AT-ST in firing range) or mobbed with stormtroopers.
This is all very tragic, really, because TFU had the potential to be a good game. There are points in the game where I've felt like the overpowered Sith I'm supposed to be, but these are few and far between when all sorts of enemies can block my lightsaber, force push or lightning and then repeatedly knock me over.

Most of all, I feel bitter about how the Camerata were portrayed. They were interesting characters that presented Red with moral dilemmas. "The Journey Back" is a short first-person adventure about the aftermath of a car crash. The game does tell a complete story despite its brevity, and I enjoyed it, but it's very straightforward. The game sports 4 different environments and a small multi-stage puzzle in each. Puzzles are pretty easy, as there are very clear cues for each solution, so it's unlikely for players to get stuck.
Soft, slow music creates a relaxing, thoughtful atmosphere. The game's graphics are highly stylized and remind me of the very early 3d era, when even the ground was made of distinct mono-colored polygons. I don't really like this particular style (I think it accentuates the imperfections of early 3d implementations in an unfavorable way), but it did not bother me much in this game, the graphics are serviceable.
I played through the full game in an hour, so it's definitely a very short experience, but the price is completely adequate for that. If you're looking for a calm, relaxing, easy first-person adventure game that doesn't require a $1000 PC to run, give it a shot.
Edit: Seeing that other reviewers reported some bugs and glitches, I should perhaps mention that I did not encounter a single one. I'm not sure if the issues were fixed in the meantime, or if I just got lucky, all I can say is that the experience was completely bug- and glitch-free for me.

If you like puzzle-centric RPGs this is for you. It's satisfying to solve a difficult challenge or find a new hidden area, and even on a second playthrough I was uncovering tons of stuff I'd missed the first time. Highly recommended.

This is my first ever review so bare with me if it's a little bit rubbish.
I bought this game because I had £2 left in my bank account (living the poor student life as you can see) and I had the option of either buying this game, or spending it on a pack of sausage rolls before work. And as much as I love sausage rolls, I feel like this was the better investment. Although not a ground-breaking game, I did quite enjoy playing through it. It takes about an hour to finish, maybe less but I'm actually really terrible at puzzles so I got stuck on a couple of occasions. The story was okay I guess, but it's pretty obvious what the big conclusion is gonna be within about ten minutes of playing. The graphics confused me to begin with, the stylisation just looked to me as a bit lazy but I soon grew to actually find the environment charming in its own way. Although, I put a strong emphasis on 'environment', as the only character model within the whole game isn't exactly up to the same standard...you'll see what I mean.
I would just like to say that my biggest issue with this game, apart from a few bugs here and there, was the sound. Some of the sound effects for doors opening etc. were so over the top and quite often didn't even really sound like what they were supposed to. And there is a weird breathing that's hardly noticeable all throughout the audio which I'm not sure whether it's accidental or intentional but once I noticed it it really put me off.
My main judging criteria is whether I had fun playing this game, and I can whole-heartedly say yes. At less than £2, it's worth the price, and I feel like a lot of love went into making it despite its imperfections which make it a rather charming and enjoyable game to play. Leave the sausage rolls for now, buy this instead.

Pros:
I really like the campaign missions. Having an allied AI fighting for another objective is really cool and refreshing to see in a strategy game.
Cons:
I really hate the fallingback mechanic. Units can just decide to fall back and never return or follow orders if it gets too tough for them. I'm all for falling back if needed for maintenance and ammo but the fact that they desert their post is just unnacceptable. Insubordination and desertion are the 2 most unbelievable things, especially in a WW2 setting. I realize that if you keep the units supplied they'll be happier but I wish then either supply units were automanaged or would follow units.
Another thing I really hate is that there's no unit formation. If your artillery units are faster than your tanks and infantry, then they can end up on the frontline and get slughtered.
The final item I dislike is how unoptimized the game feels for larger battles. If you try to go all out for a 6v6 match the game will grind to a slog once too many units are on screen.

Il-2 Battle of Stalingrad/Moscow/Kuban is undoubtedly the finest WWII flight simulator ever. However, Cliffs of Dover Blitz edition has many unique features that makes it equal or greater in some regards. The two simulators also model different parts of the world - so you really need to get both.
The Blitz edition fixes almost all of the problems that plagued the original release in 2011. Performance is considerably improved as are most of the previously unfinished features.
The graphics are likely the weakest point: The control animations still are unsmoothed, the land textures have been replaced with more vibrant but much less immersive ones (for me), and the special effects are lacking in 2017 (and possibly worse than the original ones). However, the graphics are still remarkable for a flight simulator. Otherwise, the flight models, damage models, AI, content, and numerous other features are enhanced. It is remarkably immersive and I'm looking forward to the upcoming DLC.
This was to be Oleg Maddox's masterpiece, after playing a role in saving the flight simulator genre and years working on Russian focussed flight simulators this was to be his entry into Western European simulators. It had numerous ground breaking technologies - many of which remain unique to this day. The inclusion of flyable biplanes, Blenheim light bombers for the British were nice touches. However, it was rushed out the door and most of the features couldn't be finished on time. So, teams of modders saved it! They've done a stunning job!
I appreciate the time and effort trying to revamp this game but i cannot recommend it. Save your money and spend it else where.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Was skeptical of buying this game but it gives you exactly what you would expect - An RTS (a tiny bit more strategy heavy) in a WW2 setting.  Game plays flawlessly, runs flawlessly, and is a ton of fun.

You’ll be ordering troops, tanks, artillery and other assorted machines of bloody warfare around the lovingly rendered maps of Normandy in a bid to win.
Unlike other RTS games you won’t be building bases or any other structures. Instead, you’ll have an initial amount of points to spend on deploying your first batch of troops and armor onto your portion of the map. Here you also have a chance to give them their starting orders before the match starts, examining the map for points you’d like to assault straight away or perhaps even setting up a full-blown rush for enemy territory. Once you hit the launch button you’ll begin acquiring more requisition points every minute, and the number of these depends entirely on the division you’re playing as. With these you can bring new units onto the field, although they’ll always enter from your starting area so if you’ve captured a huge chunk of the map it can take some time for reinforcements to trundle across the road network to your position.
As the battle progresses you’ll move through three phases, with new units becoming available in each phase. Sometimes these will simply be more powerful and expensive troops, tanks and weapons, but other times it may simply be MORE of the same units since you have a limited amount of each to chuck into the fight.
The most difficult part of the entire game can be understanding the subtle differences between the staggering 400 units available to you across all of the various divisions. The user interface is generally pretty good, but when you begin staring at the various stats it’s easy to feel like you’ve stepped into a maths lesson half way through and have no idea what the hell is going on.
caters to a particular audience of hardcore strategy fans,  but this difficult to master game won’t be for everyone.
- Fantastic level of detail and historical accuracy
- Clever use of extensive Battlegroup system
- Realism has a positive effect on gameplay
- Steep learning curve
- Imbalances with certain unit types
- Much micro-management

A gripping, challenging dungeon-crawler of the highest calibre. Don't play this expecting an easy ride, prepare yourself for plenty of reloads as your party gets slaughtered to a man/woman/minotaur, prepare yourself to be frustrated as you struggle again and again to solve that one puzzle or defeat that single enemy that seems unbeatable. But go into this game knowing that the sense of relief and achievement you get when you *finally* complete each level is worth the struggle!
It is a struggle, and there will be times when you'll probably just want to quit in frustration, but you won't want the dungeon to defeat you and so you'll persevere. That's the real drive of this game - you're not striving for reward or achievements; you've just trying to stay alive and escape, and that's a much more powerful motivator to see the game through.

It got off to a fairly rough start balance and bug-wise, but it's been in really great shape for the past few patches/DLCs and is now a very enjoyable WW2 tactical title.

Transistor is an isometric action RPG with combat that is a mix of both real-time and turn-based. You play as Red, an ex-singer who has lost her voice and now wields the titular sword Transistor. You explore the cyberpunk city of Cloudbank and try to stop the Process invasion and the shady Camerata who have unleashed it.
While the game has some similarities to the developer's earlier game Bastion, both the setting and the gameplay are quite different in Transistor.
The game has a stunning art style and the presentation overall is superb. One thing I wasn't a massive fan of was the enemy designs. Most of the enemies look little boring compared to the rest of the visuals.
The game has an excellent soundtrack and the ability to hum along with the music is a great touch. The voice acting is pretty solid too (Red herself is silent but Transistor will provide constant commentary) and the sound effects are well done.
The combat in Transistor is a mix of real-time action and turn-based planning. Every time your turn bar is filled, you can pause the game and take your time planning a series of actions (called functions in the game) that will then be activated in a rapid-fire fashion. This will obviously allow you to queue up some big combos or easily deal with multiple enemies.
While the combat system is clever enough, I never found it particularly fun. Personally I would have preferred a pure turn-based system or alternatively a more action-oriented real-time combat. This hybrid-system just wasn't that enjoyable for me.
On a positive note the combat system has lots of depth at least. While you only have 4 active function slots available, each function can be further upgraded with up to two other functions leading to massive amount of interesting combinations.
Transistor is a also very linear experience. You simply proceed from one area to the next and fight groups of enemies in closed-off arenas. There are some optional side-paths too, but these generally just provide some additional background lore. I definitely wasn't expecting a fully non-linear game, but a little more choice would have still been nice.
In addition to the main story the game has some optional challenge rooms that test you in various combat scenarios. I wasn't a huge fan of the combat system so I didn't care too much for these either.
Transistor uses a similar difficulty system as Bastion. There are no difficulty levels as such but uou can activate as many limiters as you like for additional challenge. The limiters make the combat more difficult in various ways and also provide you with a small XP boost. Overall I found the system pretty good, even if several of the limiters are bit tedious to play with. In practice I had just one or two limiters enabled for most of the game.
The controls work quite well with mouse and keyboard. Occasionally objects can block visibility, however, and clicking the exact right spot on the ground can be touch tricky at times. At least in planning mode this isn't a big issue since you can freely cancel orders.
The writing is quite strong but the story itself has some issues. The plot is interesting enough but suffers from rather serious pacing issues. The way the game throws you in the middle of action makes the early game rather confusing too. Bastion employed some similar storytelling techniques, but certainly did a much better job with a story that was revealed piece-by-piece.
The game felt quite polished and I didn't encounter any major bugs or issues.
Transistor is one of those games I wish I liked more than I actually did. The presentation is certainly superb and the function system has a lot of depth. It's just that the actual combat never clicked with me and I found the story little lacking too. Transistor is still a good game and something I'd recommend to most people.

Star Wars: The Force Unleashed is a 3rd person Hack and Slash game based in teh Star Wars universe. It is very similar to games such as DMC, Ninja Gaiden, and God of War. The story takes place in between episodes 3 and 4 and you play as Starkiller, Darth Vader's secret apprentice. The story is actually really good and has tons of set pieces throughout the 9 main story levels and the 3 DLC levels. You're tasked with assassinating several Jedi that survived Order 66, but later wonder if working for the empire is the right thing to do. The story has two endings, one that is the good/right ending and the other is the bad/wrong ending. The DLC continues off of the bad ending in which Starkiller goes full Sith and is tasked with hunting down several of the original trilogy's cast members, including Obi-Wan and Luke. The gameplay is pretty standard for a Hand and Slash/ Spectacle fighter game. The only new thing it has to offer is the force powers you can use in between Lightsaber combat. You get force powers such as force lightning and grapple. You can also throw your lightsaber later on. The game is locked at 30 frames per second and it does have a few bugs here and there such as the sound from blasters not playing or certain characters having textures that makes them look like the're covered by some sort of shadow. Overall though this is my favorite Star Wars game, yes even better than Knights of the Old Republic and Battlefront 2. I highly recommend you pick it up regardless of the price as it is well worth every penny if you are a big Star Wars or just looking for a fun action game with a good story.

Papers, Please is essentially a work simulator, one that is actually quite enjoyable. As an employee working for the Arstzokan government, you preside over immigration and ensure that only qualified individuals are allowed to enter the country. The game has a sort of dystopian feel, tensions are high as the nation of Kolechia is combatant with your home territoy of Arstozka. Similar to the USSR, Arstozka seems to be controlled by a totalitarian government. Your job, as an employee of the government, is to decide where your allegiance lies. Although you were provided a career by the government, you may soon find that corruption is prevalent and it is your decision to accept it or refute the current leadership.

You also have a family to manage, which takes up much of the salary you earn from your job. The game might not have big explosions and PEW PEW PEW gunfights, but it is an interesting, enjoyable and highly replayable game nontheless. By making you scan documents and use your brains immensly, Papers, Please creates a unique and reccomendable gameplay mechanic for the player.

Do you like free games that are easy to 100%? Are you afraid of forgetting how Windows XP and AIM looked/sounded? Would you like to be temporarily transported back to ~2002-2006 on a nostalgia-fueled roller coaster ride? If you answered yes to any of those questions, you're in the right place.
This game tells the story of your friendship with Emily, which you explore through yearly chat sessions over AIM. The story itself is pretty linear; choosing different dialogue options pretty much just changes some flavor text. But at the end, it left me silent and wondering how everything went so wrong with my real-life friendships. What happened to those friends I used to be so close to? Why did they seem to just disappear before my very eyes? Was there anything I could have done to stop it? Or were these relationships doomed to fail from the very start?
There is also references and memes, and I'm always a sucker for those. On top of that, something that so closely resembles Windows XP looks really funny (in a good way) on a Mac.
The game is free, and one playthrough takes maybe thirty minutes, so it's definitely worth a shot.

IL-2 Sturmovik: Cliffs of Dover Blitz Edition is remastered edition of Cliffs of Dover from 2011 by
Team Fusion Simulations. So it's not a new game from 2017, don't expect graphic from IL-2 Battle of Stalingrad.
It's also a simulator! Don't buy it if you don't look for this kind of experience, it has nothing to do with War Thunder action style. During combat your heart will beat like crazy and your armpits will sweat...

For now, it's mostly multiplayer experience, there are still 2 official scripted campaigns but lack of carrier mode hurts.. I hope it will be added one day. In my opinion multiplayer is better than IL-2 BoX series, missions are amazing and many are historical, for example Dunkirk where Wehrmacht is close to city defended by British, on the beach there is bunch of equipment and ships on the sea, even civilian wooden boats. While in BoX you have mirrored battles, Germans and Soviets have the same objectives. For example "Bomb Russian factory - defend German factory" and other way around for Russians.
For this price, it's the best sim, personally I love it more than Battle of Stalingrad. Depends on what you are looking for, Cliffs of Dover is good game for low price, BoX is something you must spend lots of money on. It's also focused on eastern front, if you want some early war on the west this is game for you. (It's the best to own all of them ;)
Keep in mind that this game will be improved, and we will get more expansions, first one will focus on Tobruk in North Africa.
I highly recommend this game!
