Note: this review is a copy of my old review from the 4.3 TF version but with added info about 4.5.
Cliffs of Dover was probably one of the worst flight sims ever when it first released. Don't let that scare you, however. It's now in my opinion just as good or better than any of its current competition. CloD (as Cliffs of Dover is usually called) is a fantastic WWII combat flight simulator. This new edition is simply fantastic. Hats off to TF!
The original developers have long since abandoned the game. However, a community patch from Team Fusion (now Team Fusion Simulations, Inc.) has turned the game from a lump of dirty coal into a diamond. The game is unrecognisable from it's initial state. Graphics have been totally improved. Sounds are fantastic. The flight models and damage models are some of the best in the genre. And the community is hands down the best one I've ever been a part of.
4.5, aka "Blitz", is a welcome new update to CloD. After years of playing 4.3 (a great game already) Blitz brings DX11 support, bug fixes, a whole new engine model system (overheating is totally reworked now), and much more. Tracers look better, you can hear flak bursts and bullet impacts much better now, ground textures are great, aircraft skins are great, and BULLET HOLES ACTUALLY SHOW UP ON THE 109!
However it's not without its downsides. The gun sounds are just terrible. The .303s went from sounding like awesome machines of doom spewing out lead at 1200 rpm in 4.3 to little dinkly 750rpm pea shooters in 4.5. The MG17s sound like a playing card in bicycle spokes. The MG-FFs sound much shallower. The new fire smoke effects are a downgrade for sure, they look more like War Thunder rather than the excellent effects in Battle of Stalingrad. Also, in my experience there was a slight performance hit, and server performance is not as good as before. I expect that give it a bit of time and the server operators will solve the problems, but for now there are frequent stutters and rubber banding.
Anyway, here are some pros and cons about CloD in general:
Pros:
+ Fun Battle of Britian map and planeset. 109s, Spitfires, Hurricanes, Heinkels, flying from France, over the Cliffs of Dover, and up to London. Quite a big map, too, that allows for many different scenarios including Battle of France, Dunkirk, Kanalkampf, the Battle of Britain, and the Blitz. The new plane options in 4.5, while not that many more, are very interesting, such as the Beaufighter, the Bf.110 C-6, and the late model Blenheim IV with the extra bombs and twin gun turret.
+ High fidelity flight models. The FMs in CloD are not the best ever, or up to say DCS standards, but they are pretty damn good. The planes fly nicely, and you have to watch your engine settings as to not push your plane too hard. The clickable cockpits are great as well. 4.5 added extra depth to the FMs, and the engine models as well. Overheating and damaging your engine isn't as simple as it was before.
+ Fantastic damage models. The DMs are in my opinion the best in WWII flight sims. While BoS has better modelled collisions and over-stress of the airframes, CloD DMs are second to none in all other aspects.
+ Amazing community. While there are some split up groups across the community, in general, everyone I've met on CloD has been a great guy, and I'm never not having fun on TeamSpeak. There are always fun events coming up and those are always a blast to take part of.
+ Good graphics. Not amazing, but the draw distance and clarity of the game is pretty darn good. 4.5 has improved this a lot as well.
+ Amazing customisability for loadouts online. You can set the horizontal and vertical convergence for each gun, and customise the ammo belt for each gun as well. Bombs and fuses have great options as well.
+ Cheap! Even at $25 it's a great deal. You'll surely get more than 25 hours out of it. Probably more than 250. I know plenty of people who've got more than 2500. And runs well on lower end machines.
Cons:
- Graphics aren't really up to par with say BoX when it comes to effects or details. Smokes, fires, leaks, clouds, water - these all look a little dated. The new 4.5 fire and leak effects are a downgrade compared to 4.3.
- The amazing sounds from 4.3 have been removed and replaced with the original vanilla sounds, which are simply garbage compared to 4.3.
- Bugs - there are more than you'd find in comparable sims - but most aren't that big of a deal.
- Singleplayer is lacking - this is a primariy multiplayer sim.
- Mediocre AI.
- Not a huge playerbase. Hard to find fights late at night on the west coast of NA, or in AUS/NZ. European evenings are the top times.
Overall, CloD is my go-to WWII flight sim. It really is a fantastic game, and absolutely worth the price. 4.5 has breathed new life into this great sim.
If you have any questions, don't be afraid to ask on the Steam discussion boards or on the ATAG forums.

We've all waited quite a long time for this patch, or to be fair, we have waited a very long time for 5.0, but got this instead in the meantime. While it certainly disappoints in terms of additional content (planes, gameplay additions of any kind), this was well known beforehand.
What was not known to me would be the severe downsides to this patch, which are in all honesty a downgrade from 4.13. And that list is quite long for my taste. Some of it absolutely boils down to personal opinion, like some of the fire/smoke effects, the (in all honesty objectively terrible) new gunsounds, the new ground textures which are fairly mixed and other visual "enhancements". Other things are just an observable fact, like the performance hit quite a few people experience, the warping of enemy planes in MP that I and a few others observed, the buggy UI and menus and the crashes people experience.
Now obviously it's not all bad, some textures definitely got better, some of the cockpits especially and a few parts of the groundwork. The remodeling of the flightmodels will have to be tested over time in-depth, before a judgement can be made, but the feeling for me and a few mates I asked didn't really change all that much. The meat of the changes might be more in the performance in certain situations, which time (and some testing) will show.
All in all I just feel like this patch removed even more polish from the game, and it couldn't really afford to lose it in the first place. Obviously this may be subject to change and I will definitely change this review if this comes to pass. But after checking this patch out, I really cannot help but wonder: Is this really the big bang that was supposed to bring Cliffs back into the game and relaunch it into a sellable product? The patch that we waited years for? Obviously I understand that 5.0 was supposed to be that, with all the new planes, the new theatre, the revamp of basically everything and all the good stuff...but right now that feels like it felt for years: a distant future. Especially now that this came along to replace it.
I just hope that Cliffs can survive long enough to actually see it come to fruition and that there is enough of a playerbase left to actually buy and play it at that time, because I do not see this patch bringing back all the people that left Cliffs by now.

I've been playing this series for well over 5 years now, and there's a reason for that. I'm sure I've logged at least over a thousand-five-hundred hours on the wargame series alone, and over two-fifty on this. There are no rts's out there like it, and it's a shame, because this game, and the series before it, are great, if you can give it the time and patience to get past what is a rather steep learning curve.
Regarding that curve; if you are new to this series, and this game in particular, prepare your bumhole if you decide to venture into multiplayer too early. Eugen doesn't coddle it's players, i.e. the tutorial and singleplayer campaign are utterly insufficient to prepare you for multiplayer. You need to learn on your own, through youtube videos from folks like VulcanHD. Better, find a mentor on teamspeak or discord - the reddit forums have links. Seriously. To get good at this game, you need to understand the mechanics, besides having a mind for tactics.
That's the shame about this game; it's hard, and doesn't have the community it deserves because of that. Because once you get into it, it's fantastic.
Also, one more thing; this game is not designed for the 10v10 servers that run it. Start with small games to learn properly. 10v10 is cancer for newbs.
challenging, mostly realistic, and complex enough to keep me coming back

An interesting return to the RUSE aesthetic with the core mechanics of the War Game series, albeit simplified some. Though I do wish there was a little more variety to the units or that the company had decided to start in and around the earlier 1940s, I believe this Eugen System's best title yet. I look forward to the DLCs which promise much, including co-op play.

+Authentic (almost) realistic compelling combat system (case and point, tank on tank battles)
+Great sense of scale
+Challenging smart AI making the campaign, compstomp and just offline games more enjoyable than most RTS nowadays
+Well designed Campaign that forces you to be on the offensive AND defensive, while offering secondary objectives and persistency. More RTS campaigns like this (and Ardennes Assault), please.
-Production values a tad lacking such as the voice acting and music and also the campaign (compare SD44 to CoH1 and the latter had cutscenes, set piece moments, etc.)
-No strategic map mode like in Wargame Airland Battle and Red Dragon
-No Co Op yet
OVERALL
+Definitely recommend it to RTS players who want that challenging authentic WWII strategic-tactical experience that mixes arcade-y and authenticity nearly flawlessly. Just hope the next Steel Division ups its production values and adds things like coop and a Total War-esque campaign map.
PS A minor complaint: I would like every division to speak in English even with accents since playing as France, Poland, and Germany can be a tad hard when your units are trying to tell you something in their own language.

Fixes many of the cheesy and counterintutive tactics from the Wargame series, while forming it own complex and rewarding combat situations.  There is something very rewarding about the combined arms tactics that, it seems to me, many other games are missing.  Even the skirmish remains fun for dozens of hours if the stress of multiplayer is not your cup of tea.
There is a steep learning curve. Learning to push only when you can put overwhelming fire on an enemy and how to assemble an in depth defense takes a bit of time, but feels great when it works out.  Nothing like watching an enemy tank turn a corner right into an ambush and get absolutely spanked by several units at once.
On the negative side, determining line of sight on maps with elevation differences can be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥since the sight line tool which is very useful does not take elevation into account.  Also, sometimes your units can take strange and downtright suicidal paths.  Sometimes online games will be determined in a matter of minutes, which can be frustrating as well.
9/10 best tactical rts I have played in years.

Steel Division is, essentially, the fourth entry in the Wargame series. If you're familiar with Wargame, you can skip this part. If not, read on. Steel Division is a multiplayer-focused RTS. There is a single-player experience, but I am not very familiar with it. You can also skirmish with bots, which is fine.
Notably, Steel Division also includes a deckbuilding element, as in games like Magic: The Gathering, or Android: Netrunner, meaning that you are impacted by choices you make before a match even begins. The deckbuilding is quite enjoyable in my view, as I enjoy tinkering with and tuning my decks to make them as effective as possible. If you're not interested in that sort of thing, you can use premade decks, though as is tradition for the Wargame series, they are pretty naff.
Another thing that new players should know going in is that Steel Division is a difficult game. It has a steep learning curve and requires both astute macro and precise micro. This can feel quite frustrating as you are just starting out, but is very rewarding with practice.
For those who have played the Wargame series, Steel Division is essentially Wargame 4, retaining most of the series' signature mechanics and adding a few new ones.
The most obvious of these is the frontline system, where there is a projection of the frontline of the battle projected onto the map. This shows to all players which team controls what territory, even if neither side necessarily knows what units their opponents have placed where. Furthermore, it is an excellent replacement of the old command zones system from Wargame. It rids the game of the gamey CVs and renders the entire map valuable, whereas in WG:RD, for instance, only small sections were fought over and these were therefore drenched in artillery and airstrikes.
The game is now split into three phases, A, B, and C. You get more income as the game progresses through phases, and more interestingly, gain access to heavier units. Phase A is thus mostly fought between infantry and light fire support, whereas C tends to be an absolute ♥♥♥♥♥how of heavy armor, artillery barrages, and waves of air support. I absolutely love the idea of this mechanic, though I think the implementation of it is fairly flawed. In particular, the Allies tend to be dominant in A phase, while the Axis dominates in C. This is mostly because the effectiveness of Allied armor in general is almost flat across the game, whereas Axis tanks start out terribly outmached and (in armored decks) go on to terribly outmach the allied tanks in return. This is far from a deal-breaker, but I think it's more than a nitpick as well.
Another refinement is the morale system. WG:RD had morale, of course, but in general Steel Division is more interested in modeling it convincingly. Infantry which comes under heavy fire will go to ground, greatly increasing their survivability but leaving them unable to maneuver or return fire. They can instead be commanded to fall back, giving up the defensive benefit of staying still in hopes of retreating to a safer position. Likewise, vehicles which are panicked will reverse away from the frontline, meaning that an effective way of fighting heavy armor is to frighten it off. (A relevant side note is that units of all kinds will seek cover when left to their own devices and vehicles will drive away from artillery strikes if not given other orders. This gives a pleasant impression that the units under your command have some life of their own)
Infantry is also modeled in much more detail than in other Wargames. Squads have varied loadouts, including mixtures of bolt-action rifles, submachine guns, anti-tank weapons, grenades, and so on. Strong infantry play is important to every deck.
The other major mechanical difference between Steel Division is its armor-penetration system. Unlike in the Wargame series, where vehicles have (usually) 10 HP and suffer damage when shot, in Steel Division a shot either penetrates the defender's armor or it doesn't. If the shot bounces off, it does (usually) nothing but scare the defender. If it penetrates, the defender either is destroyed or suffers some terrible effect such as its engine being destroyed. This mechanic is controversial, but I enjoy it greatly as it mirrors how WWII-era tank combat actually functioned.
Now, let's talk about some bad parts:
The playerbase is small. It's bigger than it was when I started playing, so that's great! But it's still small, and it can be difficult to find a game if it's not primetime.
Speaking of the community, it can be pretty unpleasant. It's nowhere near the levels of WG:RD's Warchat, but there are plenty of trolls and flamers. Also of note is that there is no real penalty for quitting a game early, so most games don't go all the way to the end before one side surrenders. This isn't a bad thing in itself, but it means that many players will simply quit as soon as things start going against tham.
The UI can be pretty poor, and the lack of an armory as in previous WG titles as well as the general lack of clarity in the unit statistics cards is honestly inexcusable. This is probably not something that you'll notice when you're new, though.
As I mentioned above, I think the phase system could do with further refinement. Hopefully Eugen will continue to work it out as time goes on.
Now let's mention some good things!
Balance, as a whole, is pretty good. Certainly far better than in WG:RD. People may complain about certain decks, and they would be justified in it, but basically every deck is viable in multiplayer, which is great.
The unit barks have been scrupulously recorded in the units' native languages. This might sound minor, because it is, but I think it's a lovely touch to hear my Ostruppen conscripts freaking out in Czech instead of German, and hearing the Free Polish speak, well, Polish.
There are a healthy number of maps and lots of units. Plenty of variety in the game overall, which is great.
The frontline system greatly reduces map-related confusion and essentially spells the death of old WG cheese strats like sneaking infantry into a player's backline.
The vehicle models are lovely (though the infantry are questionable). You won't see them closely for the most part in battle, but they're fun to admire while making your deck.
All in all, I can wholeheartedly recommend Steel Division if you're interested in a multiplayer strategy game that demands patience and commitment. If you're not interested in that, which is fair, then probably give this one a pass.

I bought this game at launch and it runs very well.
If you're new to the genre then you have quite a lot to look forward to and if you're familiar with the Wargame series then this will all feel very familiar to you.
The tutorial is quite basic but it does go and teach you the mechanics of the game and pushes you to you combined arms, cover mechanics, surrender systems and more.
The game's different systems that they have used are a welcome change from the wargame series, the use of tiered vehicles and 3 phase system works quite well and adds quite a lot of strategy to an already intricate game.
The campaign provides a constant challenge and certain units from previous missions carry over to the next for you depending on how well you perfromed, the only downside here is that there are very few missions. 12 in total split between Allied and Axis.
The multiplayer is where this game really shines, it allows 1v1 games up to 10v10 games and communcation is key in everything! You can choose from either Allied or Axis decks and each side has a number of divisions to choose from that dictate the type of units you can bring to the field. Each division will have a focus e.g. infantry, mechanized or armored that will add unique units to their respective decks.
This allows quite a lot of customisation and different strategies to employ.
Overall it's a fantastic RTS with quite a lot of depth and challenge.
Beware a lot of the negative reviews from people in the wargame community that are upset that Eugen aren't adding any new content to that game (Wargame: Red Dragon released in April 2014) and the developers themselves commenting how they are constantly abused from particular community members regardless of what they do.

Choice of Robots is a very emotional game, with a lot diversity of content. Now, there are a few paths that basically lead towards the same directions and the same events that happen no matter of your choices in game. In other words it is the same skeleton, but the skin differs based on your choices.
Now I wish I could say more, but experimenting with different paths is too time consuming as there is no save-game feature. I mean the game saves when you exit, but if you make a mistake, it means you must restart the game. So experimenting with different branches after the initial playthrough is discouraged, due to the tediousness of having to go through the same choices everytime to get to a divergent point that you are interested in.
I have few hours on record due to the fact that I completed the game twice in a relax reading session, but again, the lack of a Back option or of a Save feature, discouraged me, as I do not like tedious activities. As such I couldn't experiment more with it.
I would rate it at a pleasant 8/10, good content, diverse storytelling based on your choices, you actually get to care for your actions. If it had a save feature so I can easily play other divergen paths, I would've rated this 10/10

The only bad thing I can think about this game is a lack of saving or being able to redo a choice. Which is not too bad, if you remember all the choices you made it only takes a minute to quickly do them over.
A great game for fans of text-based adventure games and an interest in robotics.

I wish there was a rating in between "recommend" and "not recommended" here. The "I recommend it" goes for when the game is on sale... if you can get it for like 2-3 bucks, like I did while it was on sale, then go right ahead.
Here is the reasoning behind this:
- The game HAS some things going for it. You do feel pretty powerful, and throwing around big containers and stuff, causing explosions, force-throwing them into groups of enemies etc... all that is FUN. It really is.
- However, there isn't much depth to it. It's basically hack, slash and force-throw stuff, kill everything that moves, and do the objectives. I can imagine that rather quickly, even with upgrades and unlocking more powers or stronger versions, the gameplay will become dull.
- The graphics are ok. Keep in mind this game is a couple of years old. That doesn't bother me usually, so I don't mind that the graphics certainly aren't up to date.
- However, the performance is... ridiculous. I played this on a system that can, without problems, run GTAV, Witcher III, MGSV, Fallout 4, AK, AC Unity at good to ultra levels. However, this game is so badly optimized (which might explain the 30 GB!!!) that even on that PC, even today, the framerate has frequent drops. I don't even WANNA know how bad this was back when the game was new, and I find it rather unacceptable to have such a bad performance from a, what, six year old game on a modern, decent PC. It's not game-breaking, but it's annoying how badly this performs several years after its release.
So, my verdict:
Pros:
- Decent SW vibe to it (setting, graphics, force powers)
- A lot of fun especially early on to throw stuff, blow open doors with the force etc.
- Decently down force control system (throwing items)
- graphics are ok for an older game
Cons:
- Lack of depth, both to fighting and to the story
- Saberfighting is basically just spam a button type slashing. Other games have done this better
- Terrible performance even today on a modern system that can run much more recent and much more advanced games more easily
Rating: 6/10 if at sale, 4/10 if not

Grimrock is a hard sell to anyone who isn't already interested in it.  A game of a different era, its roots go way back to days of grid based dungeoneering that was defined by the limits of the hardware that pioneered the genre, i.e. pseudo-3D adventuring on what is essentially a 2D grid.  This type of gameplay, and the puzzles/challenges it created are mostly archaic and obsolete in this time and age.  As a result, one goes into it expecting fond nostalgia and fearing quick burnout, as it often happens with most retroclones, but the experience is truly fantastic.  This is mostly because Grimrock excels at everything that made the genre so fun: It's clever, challenging, punishing and intriguing.  It made me go back and finish Eye of the Beholder 1 & 2 back to back.  It also passibly has the most catchy menu music since Civilization 4 (Baba Yetu).

It's incredible to see a sim that was once dead in the water brought back to life so dramatically. Team Fusion truly deserves the utmost respect for turning CloD into the sim it was always meant to be.
While it still has minor issues, and could use a little more polish, CloD now stands shoulder to shoulder with other high class sims such as IL-2: BoX and DCS as one of the best choices on the market, especially for the price it offers.
While some would consider it outmoded by the newer entries in the IL-2 series, the excellent damage modelling and clickable cockpits keep it competetive in this area.
If the Battle of Britain is also of interest to you specifically, I struggle to think of any sim that even comes close to CloD in attempting to portary it.
The only downside to this newer version is that the gun sounds from the previous version of the Team Fusion patch have been removed, as Team Fusion lacks the rights to include them in this full paid product. While sad, there is currently no way around this, the current sounds are acceptable but the old ones were most certainly better. Hopefully new ones will be added in the future.
Since updating to Blitz edition some major graphical issues I was previously experiencing have also been resolved, which was certainly a nice surprise.
My favourite flight sim out there, hats off to Team Fusion!
[Note: if you are experiencing low FPS at low altitudes, disable Far Static Shadows and Extended Clouds in video options.]

Initially I gave this game a score of thumbs down but after finishing it I realized that all in all it was a really good game. But I think that the game only gets really good at the Elvis and planet and onward. M'Digbo to Kleer had some pretty subpar action. It’s when I fought hordes of enemies in a large field in Elliner when I heard in my mind “Now that’s what I’m talking about Mr. Wayne.”
After finishing it I can conclude it still has some cons:
The explosion radius for enemy attacks is ridiculously OP. Neither Sam nor his vehicles cannot get away from bombs fast enough to dodge them. On Mental Institution with the Seagull Fighters (bombers), you will see how helpless you feel. Of course it is doable; you have to shoot most if not all of the seagull fighters in Mental Institution to survive.
The scoring system is still bad for the reasons I said before: Instead of the difficulty level multiplying your score it adds a small amount of points to it. The lives system messes it up too. You get 100 pts for every life you have and you get another one every 10,000 pts. When you die your point counter doesn't reset or go back to the points you had on your last checkpoint. You can abuse the scoring system on certain levels. On the 2nd to last level of the Chinese planet you can gain more than 10000 points easily within the first 5 minutes. Just die and repeat till you reach the max. This could help some people who hate the lives system except that at the start of every level your lives reset back to 3.
And the first four planets are subpar, but playable. You don’t get large hordes of enemies in big open spaces until Elliner.
It has some pros though:
The graphics are an acquired taste. You’ll hate them at first but you will grow to like them, especially in Elliner and the final level.
The story is hilarious and some jokes in the game are too. Although I can imagine that some people were mad at the ending.
The music is very good. Some tracks have me bobbing my head.
It definitely is different from the other Serious Sam games but it definitely is a Serious Sam game. It has large hordes of enemies, great graphics, and great music. Some would prefer the absence of the NPCs but they don’t get in the way of the gameplay and it makes more sense story wise to have them.
A gem that often goes on sale for a dollar. Worth your time.

A tremendously fun game and a worthy spin off to the Wargames franchise. Eugen have managed to deliver an engrossing tactical strategy game which rewards preparation, planning and thought along with quick reactions. Steel Division has a steep learning curve in many respects and requires patience with a willingness to learn.
The campaign is well presented with a focus on accomplishing objectives within a set amount of time as opposed to simply comp-stomping at your luxury. This approach to the single-player offers a different experience to other games which makes a welcome break from tradition when you consider the setting and the objectives at play.
Multiplayer is were you will find the true star of the show. It will take time for you to learn the nuance of each division available along with their strengths and weaknesses but mastering your division of choice is half the fun. There's nothing like setting up the perfect ambush with the Red Devils, stopping a German tank advance in its tracks. Or smashing through the lines with your German armoured formations, breaking through an advancing American tank division and driving onto victory.
If you're looking for a wargame which rewards patience and you're willing to learn, the Steel Division might be for you.

My personal impressions of the various modes after playing through most of the game.
Single player is more of a limited-resources strategy game with a bit of randomness and time constraints thrown in.
Versus Multiplayer is a Optimization war that's equal parts strategy and luck in your opponent's starting moves not countering yours.
Co-op MP seems like a somewhat harder and far more chaotic version of SP.
Scenarios are mostly the main part of SP with various modifiers thrown in, or recreating historical plagues.
The Tutorial is exactly what it should be.
Overall, I'd give the game a 9/10, mainly because SP mostly relies on Workshop support or achievement hunting for replayability, but there's enough content in the game to last quite a while without even touching MP, so it's not too big of a deal.

Legend of Grimrock is a first person RPG dungeon crawler reminescent of old school RPG of the same genre. It takes what was good of those old games while taking almost nothing of the bad, clunky stuff in the process.
The story is kept really short: 4 criminals (your party) are brought by soldiers at the top of Mount Grimrock and sent to die in its dungeon. They fall into a huge pit that leads to the first level of the maze itself, and they can't go back. And that's basically it for the story. I mean sure, there is some kind of plot - for example there's a guy that talks in your sleep that is trying to help you get out, and there are some documents around the dungeon that fill in some details about the place - but you don't really care about it and the game doesn't really make you care for it. It's absolutely not the main focus of the game and it's perfectly fine in my opinion. This is a game that is mostly played for the gameplay aspect and the adventure.
At the start of the game you can create your party of characters (with a good amount of options for stats and abilities, and even different races) or take premade ones, but whichever you choose everyone starts the same. No equipment, not even some clothing: you have to find things as you go through the maze. There's also some kind of survival mechanic, as you need to keep your characters fed with the food that you find in the dungeon, but it's not that big of a deal really.
The combat is pretty straightforward: you just click the weapons that your character has in possession in one of his hands, then you have to wait a while to recharge its attack. But you also need to be aware of how to move in this game: you can't just stand still while you fight. You have to circle around the enemy, try to not get stuck in a corner and so on. Fights can be pretty tense, and they only get more tense as you go on through the game.
Exploration is probably my favourite part though. Each level (that is each floor that you're exploring) in the game has increasingly difficult puzzles, and they are kept smart enough and interesting throughout the adventure. It's especially fun and exciting to find secrets when you carefully explore the environment and find out that you can open a passage in a wall by pressing this hidden button and find awesome equipment for your characters. By the way, a lot of the secrets you find in this game are actually useful in some way, so finding new gear is always very exciting.  You can take notes in the map if you need and, if you feel hardcore, you can draw the map yourself by choosing "old-school mode" at the start of the game.
It's easy to learn its mechanics, but hard enough in general so it keeps you on your toes while you crawl in this maze full of monsters, traps, treasures and secrets. The scaling of difficulty is pretty well crafted, as is the level design and the enemy strength, and nothing is ever too hard for your party of four.
What I did not like, though, is that the levels in the dungeons are quite weak in the variety department, so things could feel a bit repetitive after the first few levels. You kinda always see the same textures and scenarios over and over, albeit some exceptions in a couple of levels. Also, there are almost no bosses, or not many that you can call a boss, and I felt that it would've been a cool thing to add, so that's a bit disappointing. The final boss is also a bit underwhelming: without spoilers, I felt like it was really dumb. The ending too, it's not that great really.
In summary, this is a rewarding and challenging experience, even if it is a bit repetitive. I still recommend it though, because there's not a lot of stuff like it.

Let's go in steps here.
First of all,
, even the game tells you that when you're opening it without your controller plugged in. I haven't tried playing with my keyboard, but with the controller you use your analog stick to do tricks, so it involves a lot of spinning it around in multiple ways and pressing buttons along to do all the complex stunts you need without really having to think too much about it. Simple to learn, challenging (in a fun way!) to master, as it offers a fulfilling variety of stunts of different levels that you can perform.
It involves distance, but it isn't endless. The game is comprised of "stages" with a number of goals you can accomplish in each of those. Each stage has a certain distance, to go to the next one, usually all you need to do is finish the stage in one piece. However, you also have the option of completing one or more of those multiple goals that each stage offers. Completing all goals in a level unlocks a new difficulty of that level, with even more challenges. So it's a bit different of the boring endless distance games that have been crowding the game market lately.
Sorry, not really, but even though I love games with stories, I didn't miss in this case because the game mechanics keep you hooked init. It's actually very easy to completely forget about your goals even, just because you got so excited that you got like 10 perfects in a row and you want to see how far you can go.
As you're playing, you learn with your mistakes, so even when you fail it doesn't get frustrating, because you get that feeling that in just a few more tries you'll get it right. Some times you'll have to stop doing the stunts you tend to overuse, and pull different strategies and combos to get the objects in the field that you need to collect to complete a challenge. There's also a big variety of stunts you can perform, as well as the techniques you need to develop to get perfect landings, nosegrinds, to get better speed without having to put your foot on the ground to push your skate faster, etc.
Yeah, it's a casual game, but I tell you, it's addictive. (I just spent 2 hours playing it nonstop, and had to stop myself because I had work to do, otherwise I would've kept going - even just writing this review makes me want to go back and play it a bit more!) My only sadness so far? I wish it had more steam achievs, I feel like this game has a lot of cool achievement possibilities, but sadly that wasn't well explored. At least we get cool in-game coals to achieve, though!

Before you buy this game, ask yourself some Serious (No pun intended) questions.....Do I really love mindless action? Do I really love senseless killing? Do I really like straight forward, no fooling around, linear maps and repetitive tasks?
If you answered yes to those, then this game is for you.
I remember that my cousin used to own this game, I saw the cover, but I never got to play it, until now.
Now...
+ The humour of this game might be corny at times, but at least I feel like it's well executed, it did make me laugh more than one time.
+The controls are fluid enough, you can jump and aim with ease, handling the guns itself is simple and self explanatory.
? The music gets kinda repetitive after a while, mostly because the combat music seems to be the same between each stage of each chapter, it drills your brain and stays there like dental caries.
+ The visuals, for an old game like this, are pretty good. The skybox are those dreaded "Far away, yet leaning towards you" buildings and mountains. Everything looks rather smooth, to be honest, no slowdown, no matter how many enemies there are on my screen.
-/+ Difficulty wise, it might be unforgiving for noobs at times, like me. But eh, I don't really think about this as a flaw if you love a great challenge.
- This is a fatal flaw in my opinion, that kinda makes the experience a bit lacking for me. I dunno about the other Serious Sam games, because this is the first one I get to play. But this game, is monotonous as all hell. Basically, you move to a room, fight 40 enemies in an open area, move into the next one, fight 60 in an open area, move into yet another room, fight 50 more again. Over, and over, and over, and over. Occasionally, you get to mow down enemies with a machine gun or something like that, but guess what? Open area, enemy wave. Over. And over. And over. Make it stop.
I wouldn't mind fighting 20 or so enemies per room, but sometimes, it gets ridiculous, what's worse, there are some areas full of helicopters, demons with missile launchers, headless kamikazes or orc football players, you get your♥♥♥♥♥blasted from every single direction. I actually had to move and reach the checkpoint, because the enemies wouldn't stop coming. As soon as I was dead, I respawned, there were no enemies to be found. Give me a break.
All in all, it's one of those games that, even if I do not like them that much, I'd still recommend it to people who are into mindless action packed shooters. It's a good game, just doesn't hit the nail on the head for me. And it's waaaaaay too repetitive. Give it a try, and judge for yourself.

Choice of Robots shows that text-based CYOA games can be fun and addicting. In CoR, your choices define the story; there is no illusion of choice. Your choices have impact and they will make a difference. As such, CoR is definitely worth two or more playthroughs because you'll get vastly different situations and events each time.
The choices you get are interesting and thought-provoking enough that it's almost always guaranteed you'll find one you like. Oftentimes, they are just downright tough. However, CoR is very forgiving in that if you do happen to make a less-than optimal decision, you can just continue right on because the resulting consequences are just as interesting. I would not recommend you to restart the game because that is unnecessary. You'll also get many backdoor options that you can fall back on if you choose to.
For your first playthrough, you shouldn't be paying too much attention to the stats. And don't try to guess what the author wants or what the "right" answer is, because this is your story. Just sit back and enjoy the ride by making choices as you see fit.

"A very, very deep game, and the less you know about it, the more you'll enjoy it" Yeah, thanks Me, way to be vague.
So, funny story, I played through this game several times a few months back, I enjoyed my time, exhausted enough content to make me feel I'd seen it all, then moved onto some other things. I came back recently and discovered I'd barely burned through three quarters of the content. The appeal of "Choice of robots" (which, i would like to add, sounds like the name of an intelligent drone catologue "hint hint") is that there are a mind boggling amount of ways the story can go, but I won't spoil anything.
Ok, bad stuff. The "choice of" games are often criticised for the lack of a save feature, I can go either way with that, make your own mind up. A large chunk of the difference applied in "Choice of robots" comes down to the girl (or guy) you've got in your crosshairs if ya know what im sayin'. And speaking of which, the game can carry a very "Mass effect 3" feel, in the sense that "You can and will sleep with any of these characters if you perform the right action". Slight exaggeration, but you get the idea.
But the story actually pulls you in succesfully, the system works by making choices that affect the story, as you would imagine, but while most of the "choice of" games have your own stats monitered depending on your choices, your choices instead mainly affect your robot creation. The 4 stats are: Empathy, Autonomy, Grace and Military, and your choices can either raise or lower your robots "efficiency" for want of a better word, in each category. A slight problem with this system, how am I supposed to KNOW IF MY STATS ARE ENOUGH FOR THIS CHALLENGE? This happens very rarely but i remember at one point where I was told I was applying for funding, and my highest stat (Empathy) was automatically chosen to measure the test, turns out I was spreading my decisions out too far, and my stat wasnt high enough, it wasn't "Game over" or anything like that, and in the end, it didn't result in Bad Ending omega where everyone dies in a freak robot uprising accident, but the point is, I was given absolutely no warning that I should have been focusing on one stat, or I would be failing a challenge. Granted: This event was put in place to subtly hint to the player that things aren't going to be very dandy for you and your robot if you try to do everything, but that was dashed when my character LITERALY SAID: "Do you want to do everything? (insert robot name)" Obviously the robot says yes.
Alright, rant over. Do NOT go into this game looking for a multitude of massively different endings, there isn't. It isn't mass effect 3 levels of anti climactic where a different filter gets put over one ending, and the endings are all (mostly) sufficiently climactic ,but the story is about the journey, not the endings. And that journey is a damn absorbing one.

It also displays a message when you do not have a controller attached that the game was designed for using one, so it might be a good idea to connect yours if you have one.

Of course I shouldn't have expected this game to be as deep as the Skate series, but as that's what it tries to emulate in 2D form by having to rotate the analogue stick to do flip tricks, it's hard not to compare them. First of all, the trick list seems incomplete, a lot of the movement of the left stick just end up doing ollies, and having to let the stick go back to neutral position feels like a really unnecessary step. Secondly, the most important thing to keep a run going is perfect landings, and all my video gaming instincts lead me to try hitting the landing button at the point of impact with the ground. However, it seems you have to hit the button quite a bit of time BEFORE you land, and HOLD IT until the point of landing. This just feels really unintuitive and breaks the flow of play.
I don't understand how anyone can get several hours out of this. I have played at least two more in-depth and enjoyable skateboarding games that were made in Flash. I'm not that miffed, as I got it from the Humble Bundle, but if I had spent full price on this game I would be very disappointed.

TL;DR version: This game has been all I can think about for the last week, it’s exactly what I desire in a game about automation and resource management, to make things better it has a lot of content that just doesn’t seem to get old, no matter how many times you start over. I've had this game for just about a week now. I've absolutely enjoyed every second of the already 63 hours I've put into it at this time of creating this review. (This review is for the 0.14.23 version of the game, which at this time is the current stable release)

To begin, the game mechanics are very intuitive and nicely thought out: Say you want to craft this advanced piece of technology but it requires you to craft several things to get to that point, simply click on it and the game will go through the hierarchy of components required and craft them in sequence to eventually get to the desired product. That concept alone makes the game much more enjoyable as it removes a lot of tedious time spent in the crafting menu.

You have several shortcuts and hot bars at your disposal that have been designed in a way that can really hasten the creation of your factory.. Want a specific hot bar setup to only allow certain items in those slots? No problem. Want to quickly create a cluster of machines that make the same thing? There’s a shortcut for that. You can tell they’ve put a lot of work into the game mechanics to streamline the gameplay so you’re not so overwhelmed by everything. Unfortunately, the game can be overwhelming due to the sheer amount of content (don’t even get me started on mod content), but I believe that because of how much work they’ve put into the design of the menus and controls, it makes it more fun than overwhelming.

Next, the graphics: Everything just fits so well, nothing feels out of place, and everything seems to have a appealing look to it, maybe minus the rusty factories. If I had to pull a con out of the graphics I would say that the game seems a bit dark/grim in the regards of the art style but I think it suits this game well. I don’t have much to say about the graphics as for me the gameplay is what really counts for a game like this, but the game is overall aesthetically pleasing to me, so take from that what you will.

Also, the aliens add a nice idea of conflict and challenge to the game, you can’t (unless you disable them in the options) simply build a factory without the idea of protection, which makes the game a little more interesting. Currently they’re a little too easy, even once they’ve evolved to be bigger and harder to kill, they don’t really cause too much of an issue once you’ve set up some turrets.

As of this moment I have yet to even touch trains or logistics robots, but I have heard of them and seen what they can do. I’m still yet to beat the game just because I’ve been enjoying trying to streamline my factory and maximize resource production in a nice clean way. I’ve been playing with my friend and I have to say the, seemingly perfect, online play has been a huge bonus in this game. It’s amazing to think that once I do beat this game, I can still play to further optimize my factory or simply start again and experience everything over again. Or download mods and have an entirely new experience over and over again. With this game still being in early access and already having this much content and seemingly weekly updates, I would say this game was well worth the price and I hope they continue with the wonderful content. I love this game so much.

Very competent adventure game, exquisitely written.
The script puts most games in the entire Steam library to shame. Delicious period writing, entertaining and modernised just enough to read easily. The path through the game is linear, but it's such a good yarn, and manages to grip and move you from its earliest scenes; quite a feat since you don't know the characters yet. Characterization goes from witty caricature to subtle, sometimes chilling subtext, with a few good laughs in the mix.
And there are some grotesque, disturbing passages in here. This game was not made for kids, that is for sure.
The music is very good and sets a great ambience, I'm tempted to buy it from Bandcamp.
All of the usual pitfalls were avoided:
- no waiting around for the character to move excruciatingly slowly to another screen: you can double-click the exit.
- no unskippable dialogue unfolding at a snail's pace, you can click through text once you've read it and there's no voice acting. A better choice than in, say, Technobabylon, where it was mostly wasted resources.
Even so the runtime exceeds 3 hours and those are packed with good adventuring.
- no fixed resolution, the art looks great even in full-screen at 1440p.
- no stupid button to display every clickable item in the scene, a design shortcut that often points to faulty design and makes up for bad signposting or an overwhelming number of futile interactions.
- no frustrating pixel hunt or inventory absurdity. Some leaps of logic but they are amusing and don't halt you for long.
TLDR: A perfect game for All Hallows' Eve, suitable all year long of course if you are, like me, ever susceptible to the titillation of late-Victorian gloom and Ripper fiction. I hope to play through Act II before autumn next.

I've owned this game for almost 2 months and still haven't finished it.  The Slaughter started off very strong.  Witty dialog is off the charts; great characterization.  Interesting side characters and situations.  Graphics are ok.  Not the best pixel art, but it gets the job done.  I got stuck maybe once initially and I think I had to resort to the hint system, but after that the game went well.
Until it stopped being a point and click adventure and served up a mini-game.  I knew something was up, the story stalled, there was no direction, I ended up at the right location only out of a process of elimination.  And I ended up at the mini-game only because there was nothing else to do (still haven't a clue why my character is playing though).  The mini-game is half-penny where you are supposed to slide half-pennies across a board to certain distances.  It's mind numbingly boring.  Pong is more interesting and I hate those types of games.  But you either have to win, or play 3 rounds (last I heard) to progress.  Honestly, I'd rather do housework.  So, I have a clean house, but haven't finished this episode, and will probably never bother with another one.  Sad, really, this looked like a delightfully entertaining game.  And it was, until it wasn't.
I tried to get myself to refund the game, but the writing was so good that I put it off.  Now it's too late.  Perhaps I'll try to suffer past the half-penny game some day.  Maybe I'll make my own mini-game out of it:  buy some beer and take a drink every time I don't get a half-penny in a column.  Maybe that will get me through 3 rounds.  And afterwards I'll actually feel like the main character to boot!  Alas, there are so many other good games to play.
TL;DR:  Great writing, ok graphics.  Story screeches to a dead halt with an tortuous mini-game that comes out of nowhere and doesn't appear to serve any purpose since there is no context to why you are wasting your time with it.  If you can get this at a steep sale....have you tried hidden object games?  Some of those are actually a lot of fun, and cheap too.

A unique RTS with low APM requirements and focus on unit positioning.
I've played Wargame: Red Dragon a bit so here's a view from that perspective: I found Red Dragon extremely lacking in the way it conveyed the information you needed to make strategic and tactical decisions. No LOS, hit %, penetration % or even distance indicators. Not to mention that to know the key info about units, like armor, AP, AT, or AA capabilities you had to either memorize the units or dive into the stats sheets. Additionally the huge max range of many weapons (especially AA) made all kinds of scouting very difficult and costly. Together with the game mode that didn't really incentivize aggression this let into situations where doing almost nothing seemed like the most beneficial thing to do. Combine with artillery that can shoot across the map and you got yourself a recepie for some extremely passive, and truth to be told, rather booring matches.
Fortunately, Steel Division seems to do a great job in fixing pretty much all of these issues. All of the info you need is right there, you can actually play decently with units you've never seen before (tried that by accidently entering a game with a random deck..). I consider it a huge plus for a RTS if you don't need to memorize a whole lot of stuff before you can get into the strategy part of the game. The matches should be decided by wit, not by the amount of stats you've memorized, and I feel like Steel Division does a great job on this. I'd go as far as to say that it does this better than any RTS I've ever played. Only thing I think it could do better regarding this is showing the max ranges for weapons. For that you actually need to go to the unit stats sheet.
Steel Division also adds some nice quality of life improvements over Red Dragon, like: ability to make idle units automatically seek cover, units automatically dismounting attacked transports, and visual command queues. Additionally, the pin down + fallback + surrender mechanics not only adds depth, but also even further reduce the APM requirements of the game. Combine all of this with the extremely simple 'economy' management and you got an extremely  approachable RTS game, yet one with respectable strategic depth.
Now one thing I liked more in Red Dragon was the supply trucks system. In Steel Division the supply logistics play quite a bit lesser role. It seems that generally the units don't run out of ammunition as quickly and you're not able to fully repair vehicles or replenish units in a squad with supply trucks. The trucks also seem to carry way more ammunitions, and you can't refill them at all. Maybe repairing and replenishing units was a a bit too easy and quick in Red Dragon, but the fact that you had to, and had a motive to have kind of a supply line between your base and the frontline played an interesting part in the game. Admittedly it was pretty brain dead stuff micro management -wise, but with a good command queue system it would be an interesting aspect in Steel Division as well. Also, as a WW2 game Steel Divison doesn't have helicopters, which is a shame.
Even if I can't really recommend Red Dragon to anyone, I can easily recommend trying out Steel Division to everyone - Even to those who generally find multiplayer RTS games too daunting and overwhelming. As a nice bonus Steel Division seems to have a decent AI which gives you a somewhat human like opponent to practice with. Something that can't really be said about the Red Dragon AI.

I wish Steam gave you a 'sit-on-the-fence' option than necessarily a Yes or No recommendation. :P
I'll admit - I'm struggling with Steel Division. As if I'm a glutton for punishment - I bought all of the previous Wargame franchise and haven't really managed to get into any of them. This is not Company of Heroes, but in a way I'm trying to convince myself that it's an interesting alternative. I just don't think I'm there yet.
Fundamentally, all wars focus on territory - you owning and having control over land and sea that the enemy does not. How you go about vying for that control is dependant upon using varied units to the best of their capabilities and at the right time. This is where Steel Division (and its predecessors) really shine. The unit variation is wide and varied - matched with good animation and believable behaviour. I personally like calling in the aircraft and seeing the small bombs arc downwards to their target. All fun and engaging.
However, such actions are superfluous as the game centres around the territory you hold. This is represented by a snaking coloured band that matches the too and fro of the battle upon it - with seemingly little focus spent on the actual units doing the fighting.
The brutal truth about Steel Division is that I simply don't care about any of the units. Do they survive? Do they die? Does it matter? The game makes me churn out units through the drip-feed of requisition points - to prop up the fighting front in a process of attrition. Another two tanks have bought it? No worries - I have enough points to send a couple more back unto the breach.
If an accountant and tactician merged their gaming DNA - this would be a perfect title for them. Steel Division feels soulless and without any form of attachment to the chaos and carnage that you're overseeing. Take the first mission in the campaign and pan over to the AI-controlled beach area. The number of units, what they are, where they are heading, etc - is all but a blur. Granted, it may reflect to some extent the complexity of a real life beach invasion..... but for a fun game, it does not make.
For those unfamiliar with any of the previous series - there is no base building. There are no strategic placement of defences to halt the enemy's advance. There is you, your map and a deployment zone to drop units into like the end of a production line. If you like to get stuck in with the actual action, then Steel Division may appeal - but if you prefer the likes of Company of Heroes and the way that game plays - I think you'll be disappointed.
I'll vote for recommending this game...... but only just. It's play-style doesn't really appeal to me and there are other interpretations of the RTS formula that I much prefer. However, I see what Eugen Systems have tried to do with the game and at times, it does feel involving. For me however, it's just not personally involving enough.
Overall - 5/10

I was dared to play this game to completion, and I regret it immensely. While I successfully completed the game, I feel as though a part of me is now missing.
This game is soul crushingly boring and tedious, and while that is part of the Serious Sam style of game play, it entirely misses the point of what made the first two games fun.
This game makes you feel small, slow, and generally not very powerful. The enemies soak up huge amounts of damage even on lower difficulty levels and while the previous game had specific weapons to use against specific enemies, this one has several enemies that seem to have no weaknesses, and they enjoy throwing them at you in huge quantities(Footballers)
While there are sometimes big open areas and arenas in this game, you are often specifically confined to much smaller arenas than the previous game, and the designers just toss enemies one by one at you for 5-10 minutes. The developers even seem to realize that this is annoying because there are several voice callouts that Sam makes that emphasis that they are just tossing fodder at you in a padded fashion.
The game is split up into 7 distinct sections, the worst of them being the TV challenge series section and the ice world levels, where they introduce a resource mechanic where Sam will freeze to death, yes, Serious Sam will freeze to death, the man who can walk in lava. There are long auto scroller sections often with downtime or enemies on all sides, while confining you to extremely small areas and giving you very little in the way of dodging room. At one point there is a sewer level and the developers thought they were clever by saying all games had sewer levels and making it a maze, but it only calls out how much everyone hates these levels and it drags on far too long to be humorous.
While the developers added many new enemies to this game, they all behave as re-skins of existing enemies and don't add to the variety in play styles. Many of the enemies that people lamented from the previous games are back and more annoying than ever, almost as though they thought it would be a good idea to harass players of the existing games for having the audacity to question their design decisions. The flying enemies move around waaaay too much and too fast, and while you can usually lead them around, they tend to cluster directly above you where you can't easily aim, or stay way off in the distance where very few of the weapons they give you are effective.
They added turrets and vehicles to the game this time around, and it was a huge mistake. While the turrets are typically optional to use, the quantity and rate at which they throw enemies at you implies that they expect you to use them. Anchoring the player down is in stark contrast to the run around at the speed of light I loved in the previous game. The vehicles are typically overpowered and you just hold down mouse one and abuse the infinite ammo until it forces you to get back out of the vehicle. On rare occasions you get out to pull out the minigun and shoot down the flying enemies that you can't hit with the vehicle weapons.
The audio comes off as polished, but wears thin quickly. With as much as you hear the weapons sounds and musical tracks that don't fit with what you're doing, you grow tired of them, and I eventually turned off the music and turned down the sound effects to listen to something that wasn't going to put me into a coma.
The game while generally technically competent and feels polished, has a glaring technical flaw. For a game where almost every enemy runs straight at the player, the pathfinding in this game is horrendously broken if there are any obstacles. The enemies often spread out and run in the opposite direction of you, don't notice you at all, or get stuck behind objects that really should have been accounted for in the levels. This leads to parts of the game where you hunt around for several minutes trying to find the last few enemies that have become stuck in the level before the game lets you continue on. (You must kill all enemies to continue through the level.)
The pacing of the game is rather poor, and it takes away your weapons at the start of each of the 7 distinct sections and makes you run around collecting them, creating a saw wave difficulty curve, and ends up simply annoying more than interesting. They knew they didn't have enough content to make the game the 8.5 hours that it enforces on you, and it shows everywhere, leading to long drawn out sections that are neither harder, nor easier than the previous, just more of the same. If you finished the first three sections of the game, you've seen the rest. It's just another set piece behind the same tedious actions.
The boss design is typical Serious Sam, where you don't shoot the boss yourself, but play some gimmick that hurts the boss. Most bosses are invincible to player weapons(not technically but you could shoot them for an hours, run out of ammo and still not kill them), and they don't feel particularly rewarding to defeat. The first boss is possibly the most insulting boss I've ever seen in a game. If you take no action, the boss dies within 1-2 minutes, with no involvement. It's a "protect the AI while the AI kills the boss" battle, and I'm astonished they even put it in the game.
I'm giving the last level a special section because of how much I hated it. The last level is a one hour slog through 1200+ enemies while the game showers you in armor and health, and then throws an extremely tedious boss fight at you that will make you question your life, unless you exploit the terrible pathfinding on the AI fighters and hold down the fire button on the vehicle until the boss dies. In comparison with the typical level, it has nothing to offer that is new, just more of the same that you'd grown tired several sections back, and is more than 6 times as long as the typical level.
I cannot reccomend this game in any fashion. If you liked Serious Sam, pick up one of the others in the series, and avoid this one like the plague.

TD;LR:  Epitomizing the idea that video games can be and are an art form, Transistor blends a unique art style with narrative-driven gameplay.  Being well-crafted, stunning to look at, and engaging to play, the game sets a standard and goes beyond that standard without failing to impress and amaze the player.  Whether you choose a single playthrough or the game's recursion mode, Transistor is a perfect example of video game art done right and an experience players should choose to have.
I must admit that, at first, I had a hard time finishing this game.  It wasn't that the story or gameplay was bad or that I found it boring, but rather I was having difficulty getting immersed in the game.  Immersion is a big factor for me, and I will talk about it in a bit with respect to this game, but long story short I managed to find my footing and ended up loving this game.  I'm also not entirely sure what genre it falls unded (other than indie, of course), so I will do my best to describe it.
Transistor is a sci-fi hack-n-slash indie game (could have been longer lol) with some minor turn-based elements mixed into the gameplay.  The game's story follows Red as she seeks out those who have unleashed the "Process" on her home-city and have attacked her and her friends as well.  As the story progresses, the player finds out more about Red, her friends, the city, and the antagonists as well as the mysterious Transistor Red uses to combat the Process.
I must start with the story because that is the primary element of the game.  If you take the time to look around, read the OVC terminals scattered throughout the world, unlock each of the characters' bios, and listen to the dialogue throughout the game, a very intricate story comes together in a very neat way.  Much like any good mystery, only small details are given to the player at any one time, and it isn't until the end that the pieces start to match up.  There are not any "I am your father" moments in the game, per se, but the details given can lead to some interesting twists and demonstrate that a great deal of time was spent perfecting the plot of the game.
Gameplay is simple and ties in with the narrative style of the game nicely.  The Transistor is your primary weapon and is customizable with functions and limiters you can find and unlock.  Functions can be active, meaning they can be used by the player via the attack button, upgrades, meaning that they bolster active functions, or passive, meaning they affect the player.  This ranges from focused long-range attacks, to speed upgrades, to even a personal (but limited) shield.  All functions can act in the categories allowing the player many options to create an ability build that they like.  Limiters, as their name suggests, make the game harder to play but give more XP to the player.  Both limiters and functions are characters you come across and their bios can be unlocked by using them in different ways.  When in combat, the player can enter a "turn-phase" where they can plan a certain number of attacks and movements to inflict maximum damage to enemies.  Once out of this turn-phase, that plan is executed and the player is returned to real-time.  Combat can also be done in real-time allowing for a different play style entirely.
Now about that immersion thing I was talking about:  Originally, I had a hard time caring about the characters or the plot.  It may have been simply because it was presented in a different way than I was used to, but going back through the game made me feel really dumb for stopping in the first place.  Immersion for this game, as best as I can describe it, is sort of like a lucid dream.  You sort of don't realize it at first, but all at once things start to make sense.  Once I started playing it again and I started to grasp some of the deeper concepts of it, I was hooked.  And the music, oh my gosh, the music.  I finished the rest of the game within a few hours and the snap back to reality threw me off (I guess I'll call it The Transistor Effect).  I'm not saying this is how it is for everyone or how it will be for you, but I am glad the game was able to immerse me like it did.
Transistor is one of those games you have to experience because it is one of the few games that can offer such an experience and do it well.  I wouldn't worry too much about any technical issues detracting from that experience as the game is very well optimized.  All I can really say from here is Transistor is a one-of-a-kind game that, hopefully, you will consider.....oh, and of course, GG and Good Hunting.

But really, the story behind this was really well written and thought out. Its also nice to see how your actions IMMEDIATELY affect how your story will be.  You'd think a narrative like this would get boring, but it didn't.

Choice of Robots is, at its core, a choose your own adventure book - and a well written one, at that. The stories available to the player are interesting and, most importantly, immersive - I got carried away in several playthroughs as events occurred and I was swept up not in how I should react according to the choices provided, but how
would react myself. When any story - book or movie or videogame - gets me invested to that point, I can give it a full recommendation.
The only thing I particularly have grief with is the lack of a save system, which makes replays arbitrarily longer, especially considering how the first chapter is largely stats-building with fewer (relatively) plot-influencing choices. If you want to retry a choice to see how it turns out - or worse, misclick at any point - the only recourse is to restart the entire game. While there are arguably reasons that justify this limitation, I personally dislike them, as it makes end-game content much more difficult to explore due to the exponential increase in time commitment.

Olli Olli is a loveletter to things like the original generation playstation 1 skateboarding games. You remember everything you loved about Tony Hawks Pro Skater on the playstation 1? What Thrasher: Skate and Destroy made you feel as you aced trick after trick in a huge combo?
Well it's not quite on the par with those games, obviously, because they are 3d and kinda open world... but in a way, this is something of a purer experience. OlliOlli is two dimentional, and ... well basically combine Canabalt with THPS and you pretty much have what the game is gameplay wise. You are always moving forwards, you can't go back and redo a trick without restarting entirely. The course is always to the right and there's no going back.
Because it's a "simpler" control system, where your left stick controls what trick you're doing and timing that landing button (A on your controller) perfectly is key to getting huge combos, you will quickly find yourself struggling a little. It's a hard game to control! Especially when grinds come into the mixture because it seems the devs, to increase challenge and keep you on your toes, deliberately made sure that landing a grind perfectly means using the Left Stick instead of the A button. Honestly though, I don't mind. The cognitive dissonance it causes is a little frustrating, but it's possible to overcome it.
Graphics wise, it's full of wonderful, colourful pixels. I'm pretty early on into the game so the game isn't hugely detailed yet, the trailer seems to imply that later levels will be bigger, grander, more complex and more exciting though, which is nice. It's not hugely graphically intensive, so the game runs at a fantastic speed regardless of your rig, so it's got that going for it, but the pixel style really isn't going to be for everyone. Pixelly graphics is something that appeals to a particular niche... granted a fairly LARGE niche but still a niche none the less. I am part of said niche but I recognise the validity of the opinions of people who prefer more graphical fidelity than chunky low-res sprites. That's fair. Not everything needs to be pixel graphics, or low-poly chunky-ness, or mired in nostalgia.
Music? Incredible. I love it. A fantasic mix of techno-hiphop-trance and a bunch of other electronic styles. It's very listenable and very very good to get you in the mood for the game. It mixes perfectly. My only gripe is that I can't get the soundtrack as one package, which is a terrible shame but understandable because, just like the old THPS games, the soundtrack is a collection of various tracks from various artists, each of which were released not specifically for this game, but as part of said artists' own albums and record labels. So yeah. Gotta go get the tracks individually. THANKFULLY the devs put in a tracklist in the credits, which is nice!
The price of this game is £9.99 or regional equivalent, and I think personally that it's very reasonably priced. A lot of work has gone into making this game playable and fun, and not overly frustrating, the soundtrack's great, the mechanics are rock solid, so yes, £9.99 is a great price for this game and well worth it. You'll get well over 10 hours of gameplay from this and will most likely keep coming back to it, so that's totally worth the price.
Okay so, in summary, here's the good and bad parts of this little gem:
GOOD:
Solid, engaging and fun mechanics
Great soundtrack
Very well tuned twitch gameplay
Very reasonable price
BAD:
Missing manuals! But that's coming in the sequel
Graphical style MAY NOT appeal to everyone (again though the sequel is not pixelly by the looks of things!)
Challlenging control system may frustrate people to begin with.
For those wanting the complexity and depth of THPS, this game may well disappoint.
Overall rating:
A good solid 8/10
