Transistor is the BEST indie game which I have ever played so far.
Everything is so perfect with everything I mean Story, Gameplay, Game mechanics, Game Design, Soundtrack and I still can't belive it's indie game.
Developers did great job that they connected everything so nicely in one game.
Story is very nice created and story has nice connect with gameplay, that transistor is your sword that talk and guide you through the game is so interesting and he is feeling like he is human being
. You are controlling Red, a singer in the city of Cloudbank, who uses Transistor to the Process, and to bring the Camerata (Group of 4 members and they are reposnible for the disappearances of high profile people in Cloudbank) to justice.
The Game action is happening in future and everything is robotic around you (specially enemies).
In gameplay you are controlling character "Red" and you are eliminating enemies with your Transistor (Big Sword) that has a lot of Functions (abilities) and you are getting new Functions from leveling up and for finding them from dead bodies of some important Characters (Bosses etc.).
Also every Function (ability) has 3 forms that can be used for and it's:
There is in total of 16 Functions and every Function has diffrent cost that can be used from 1 to 4 MEM (MEM short of Memory is an in-game resource that determines how many Functions can be equipped.)
Leveling up you are not just choosing what new ability will you pick up, you also choose what will you unlcok (More MEM or new Upgrade slot or new Passive slot) and what Limiter will you pick (Limiters are like passive functions).
There is excelent created game mechanic and it's that you create a Turn() in which you freeze the time of enemies and you can cast Functions and move in the battlefield. You have limited usable space to walk/run and to cast Functions, and good thing about this game mechanic you can undo previous walk path or function; you also can see what area will Function hit and how much damage will it done.
After you make a Turn() there is cooldown for other Turn().
Game mechanic about your life is that you have regular Life points (100%) and when it get to fatality (near 0%) you automaticlly create a Turn() and you don't die, but if Turn() is on cooldown and u get fatality damage you dont lose life like in other games, you lose one of your usable Functions and that Function is like broken and can't be usable for upgrade or passive until you get level up and refersh it; After you lose all 4 Usable Functions it's game over and u start from last save.
In-game you are saving on special locations (like checkpoints) in which you also customize your Functions.
When you kill the enemy they leave some kind of capsule that you have time to pick it up, if you dont pick it up (in 10sec) new enemy would have been created.
In-game there is "Backdoor" that is beach room for practicing and for completing Tests (challenges).
In New Game Plus (NG+) you get same functions but that make customization even bigger so you can have same Passive and Usable Function, but you can't upgrade one usable Function with 2 same Functions.
My favorite Function is "Void", that Function has 4 MEM usage and it can be casted max 3 times on the enemy (it's stacking), basiclly what Function do is that it make enemy weaker so you can one shot any enemy with some good finisher Function (actually any damage Function). Passive part is that increase your base damage.
Background city is well done designed, also robotic enemies, all human characters and Transistor. Transistor is story for himself, it's designed so nicely with that green sword and that red circle that symbolize like an eye.
Function effect design, also Turn() design is perfectlly designed that you can clearly see where is it going and how is pathing going.
Cutscenes are minimalist designed with only pictures or sometimes some animations when you are traveling, but overall that make game even better.
Soundtrack is connected with the story and it's basiclly some electro/robotic music, but the protagonist (Red) is also singing in some part of the game and at the end of the game some classic/jazz song.
And Backdoor beach room has some beachy music.
Soundtrack is changing throught the game and it's so beautiful. With sound you will know when it's time to fight and when is time too chill to listen story and to watch some background graphics.
Also with completing Tests you are unlocking new songs that can be playable through the Sandbox on the Record Player so you can change music in backdoor room. i think it's pretty cool.
I recommended Transistor (RPG indie game) for really every gamer who like sci-fi RPG, but also who doesn't like sci-fi or RPG in-general. At least give it try and I can guarantee you will not regret it.
P.S. It cost only 2,84€ on Summer sale, so it's must buy.

7/10, vaguely reminiscent of a hybrid of Close Combat, Blitzkrieg and World in Conflict. Winning is about looking ahead and bringing the right unit to the right part of the front in the right moment (as well as microing adequately).
Plus:
+ No healthbars! (So sick of those.) Tanks/vehicles are either fully alive, have some specific sort of damage, or are destroyed.
+ Units can be pinned down and even forced to retreat or surrender. I find this works well once you get acquainted with this game's specific rules for this.
+ Battles look beautifully violent. Game looks OK if you zoom in (then again, why should you?), if "somewhat derpy" to cite my friend running on highest graphics settings.
+ Tanks/vehicles/guns are reasonably accurate to their historical counterparts. You will even see exactly what weapons and ammo they have, etc.
+ Light vehicles actually have a role to play in this game instead of being completely worthless. You will finally see massed German halftracks, etc.
Minus:
- I have my doubts about replayability, for me 100-200 h will stretch it. This due to the fact the game is about repeatedly fighting battles... and not much else. Close Combat 3-4 at least has a developed campaign/operational layer.
- Some of the audio could use more variation and better mixing.
- I realized it's for balance reasons, but rock-scissor-papers take precedence over sheer armor. Expect your Tigers to go poof quickly if you expose them to AT guns. This will likely annoy some players.

I'm into building and survival games. I like for example Terraria, ARK Survival Evolved and Astroneer.
You crash on a planet. You build stuff with the goal to make a rocket silo and get the heck out of there.
It's all in top-down perspective.
The unique property of this game is of course the automation. You automate the mining and the production. But, you automate as much or as little as you want.
The resources are limited. There are bug-like enemies that possibly make your struggle worse. It all depends on what type of game you choose to play; easy, hard, sandbox etc.
One important aspect is that you never lose material. You build, demolish and rebuild without losing anything. (Actually this is true for everything except for wires used in the circuit network.)
Personally I've played single player only. I ended up not using the circuit network, nor the logistics network, but of course automated as much as I could or found necessary anyway. I simply grinded my way through, producing the bare minimum of most resources, to finally win the game. I had a lot left in the development tree when I finished the game. (The thing is, I've tried to learn the logics of the circuit network but so far it's just not for me; I think I need more active brain cells.)
Apparently there's co-op and PvP aswell. I have not tried these modes yet.
Great game if you're into skill based games. There's not much randomness here (other than where resources are located). Just you, the resources and the production development tree. You can use your imagination and create your own beatiful assembly lines. You'll build, make mistakes, learn, demolish, rebuild, expand, make mistakes again and so on many times. You'll be inspired to create the perfect factory and perhaps you'll manage.

Steel division, normandy 44 review.
First things off, I'm not a strategy-games player, and I didn't play wargame, so I won't be comparing this game to others.
I'm gonna start by putting a list of what I think is good and it's bad about this game:
The good:
-Realistic game setting, maps are almost a copy of real-life locations, vehicles all have plausible resistance/penetration values, infantry stealth dynamics are pretty good too.
-Big units/divisions variety, big array of divisions and units into them.
-I never felt as if the game was discouraging any kind of gamestyle, further beneffitting variety.
-Alive developement, despite this game not being a great must-have success, devs are still improving it constantly.
-No ''censorship'', this game is not afraid to let you play with young SS soldiers or to give you a german-side campain, however it has to be said that there's really few to censor in a mulitplayer strategy game.
-Stable platform, I don't think this game ever crashed on me.
The bad:
-Awfull campain, all 3 of them are just 3 missions, usually with ridicolously short timers that kill strategic gameplay and force a mindless swarm of A-moved units.
-Some divisions are DLC only, not saying it's pay to win, as these divisions are carefully balanced, however it is really frustrating to pay 40 bucks for a game and just get a portion of it.
-Repetitive maps, most of them feel the same, and the only different ones are often kicked aside in favor of a few community-favourite ones that you will start getting bored of really soon. I know that this is '' Normandy 44 '', and thus we get Normandy maps, but man is it boring to see the same woods, bushes and fields over and over.
-Percentage-based hit chanche on many units, altough handled quite realistically ( closer = more accurate, different guns have different accuracies, experienced crews are more accurate ... ), it still leads to some '' 90% hit chanche and still you miss '' situations, and it can be frustrating.
-Dead matchmaking, go to custom, you won't be finding ranked even if you wait 30 minutes.
-Somewhat expensive, I didn't expect such a game to be 40 bucks, especially without the DLCs.
The game is not cheap enough to say '' Il'l buy it, even if I'm not sure I will like it '', especially if you add-in DLCs, so when should you buy it ? Id say in these cases:
-You want to get started into strategy games but don't want something harcore even in his basics ( starcraft 2 )
-You have some friends that you can reliably play with. This because you can both get serious with em ( and thus exploit the competitive nature of the game ) or you can just have fun ( and jerk around A-moving 20 shermans ).
-You are a strategy-games player that wants to try something different.

Playing a rogue for example, putting points into Missile weapons gains you Dex points, which affect your ability to hit in Melee, but not from a distance. Ranged attacks always hit something in front of you. Dex does not increase your damage with ranged atacks so by extension if you focus on using a bow for one of your characters, you'll build a stat that is nearly useless to them. This is by definition bad game design.
Furthermore, I admire loot being hard to comeby, but not supporting all builds from the outset is dumb. If you're doing the above and making one of your characters an archer, then I hope to god you find the secret bow on level 3 or else you've been literally screwed. This is a game that should promote and reward exploration with better and special equipment but instead twists your arm into looking up secrets online to get the most basic of equipment.
Overall, if you love the concept of this game then buy the sequel or stick to user made dungeons.

A vast improvement over Breath of Death VII.
Even though these two games are virtually the same, Cthulhu Saves the World is somehow drastically superior. This is yet another title from Zeboyd Games that is straight out of the RPG Maker, but thematically it has something that drives it forward that its predecessor, Breath of Death, does not. Although this game does not inherently present its own innovative mythos, it does attach itself to a universe that is semi-well known amongst readers of the victorian distopian author, H.P. Lovecraft. With a moderate level of wit, you (the player) are charged with the task of making a fallen Lovecraftian god into a hero of the realm. It's an interesting concept... I will give it that. And much like in Breath of Death, it is apparent that the writing for this game has a certain lightheartedness about the commonplace RPG absurdity. Jokes about you searching each drawer and bookshelf are made to inform you that your actions are nothing more than a foolhearty attempt to get that one extra potion that ulitmately will not provide you any advantage within the game. These jokes, as such, are a welcome attention to detail. Even though there is no reward for your diligence in searching for some secret gem, Its good to know that they could have just as easily put a potion in the drawer but refused to do so for the sole opportunity to tell you what's what. I kind of like that.
There is really nothing significant about this game that sets it apart from any other RPG Maker title, but I did have fun playing it. There is more substance to this game than what i was expecting, and I found myself wanting to come back to it to complete the story. It was not challenging and it only took about 10 hours of my time; which means it did not feel like an inconvenience to play. There is a minor improvement on replayability for this game compared to Breath of Death VII in that there are different combat mechanics and a small party selection capability.  This means you can create a team that is effective for the situations wherein you find yourself. Its not a vast overhaul, but it is something. Its a simple game and doesnt require a lot of thought. If that is what you are looking for, I would recommend it.

Serious Sam 2 doesn't take itself seriously on the surface, but as a hardcore fan of tough slaughterfest FPS bullet/melee hell gameplay that this franchise is known for, I give this game a serious thumbs up.
I am by no means an inexperienced player so trust me, if I say a game is hard it's probably tougher than what you'd expect and SS2 is surprisingly difficult which is a refreshing revamp of the series that delivers exactly what real fans wanted. Normal in SS2 feels more like hard in SS1 a lot of the time and the tricks up the dev's sleeves perform nicely and will have you strategizing more than shooting on various occasions.
The weapons have a pleasant, balanced feel to them that encourages you to get creative and never have an ultimate go-to. Yes some weapons are of course better for certain situations than others, but seldom will you feel like you'd be screwed if you didn't have ammo for a specific weapon. The Devs are good about giving you the ammo you need, and you see ammo packs, large health and powerups much more often in this installation of the series making way for big fights equally more often.
Enemies are what you'd expect, but there's some awesome additions especially ranged enemies. In the first game, most of the ranged attacks were projectiles but in SS2 there's more rockets and more bullets to force you to kill fast, fast fast and prioritize targets effectively if you want to stay alive for long. Also, there's more strategy involved in taking down enemies this time around. One of the first enemies has a shield that it'll drop when you shoot it, but I'm pretty sure making contact while before it drops the shield does more damage. I'm not positive about that though. Either way, more strategy difficulty and satisfaction.
The environments are pretty epic and vary just enough to keep you happy without getting overly obnoxious. There's moments where you say "Damn, this game had amazing graphics for it's time" and it did, not only that, but the engine is super optimized. I have a pretty aweful system and I'm very impressed by how well I can run the game.
Serious Sam 2 has stupid humor that made me laugh and facepalm simultaniously. You have to not take it seriously, and with the massive amount of bloodshed that goes into this game, the comic style of the game and it's visual design is commendable on the part of the Dev's. I will say that I prefered the darker style of SS1 but where this game lacks in any area for me it makes up for in gameplay. The gameplay is just awesome.
This game is satisfyingly challenging, fun, surprisingly not repetetive for the very basic concept behind it, and goes down in my book as a must-have for fans of games like oldschool doom, painkiller, and other doom clones including serious sam 1.
I'd pay $20 for this game, and I paid $10. Maybe I'm a sucker for games like these, but if I am then I gladly sucked this game right up and I give this a total of 7/10. Not bad for a game that's literally like: Here's baddies, here's gun, here's excuse oops I mean story, go kill. *Pounds chest*.

It's not a terrible game, but it falls short of its predecessors. The Dungeon Master and Eye of the Beholder series were much better games than this one. Let me list the good and bad  points:
-- Good --
- The graphics are sharp. Thumbs up in this department.
- The monsters actually behave differently depending on their type, giving you the idea that they aren't just sacks of hitpoints charging at you.
- A lot of secrets to uncover.
- Most levels have a healing crystal that will instantly heal your party and resurrect fallen members.
-- Bad --
- The magic system is terrible. Both DM and EOB had a rich magic system with a lot of useful spells, both combat and utility. This game has essentially 6 or 7 spells. (There are actually more than this, but in essence a fire arrow spell is the exact same as a lighting/poison/frost arrow, so I am calling it one spell.) Of these, the only real utility spell is a light spell. No healing spells, no create food spells, no detect secrets spells - nothing. This was my #1 biggest complaint with this game.
- The puzzles are mostly of the 'hit a switch and race to this location to hit another one' variety. I want puzzles that test my cunning, not my reflexes.
- Most of the monsters in the game are about impossible to stand toe-to-toe with. The game relies heavily on the 'attack and sidestep' school of combat. It's wasn't fun in EOB, and it isn't fun here. I understand it for a boss fight, but here it is necessary with most monsters, at least until you are way over their level.
- THERE ARE NO HOTKEYS! You have to use your mouse to manually click each party member's weapon in order to attack. Come on guys - even Might and Magic had combat hotkeys! This is annoying with melee attacks, but downright aggravating when it comes to magic. To cast a spell, you have to right-click your wand, select the runes (up to 3), and then click again. Want to cast that spell again? Ok, 5 more clicks coming right up. All this while trying to sidestep and manage 3 other party members' melee attacks.
My recommendation is go back and play DM or EOB. They are much better (although uglier) games.

Legend of Grimrock is a first person, dungeon crawling, puzzle solving, RPG featuring 4 prisoners cast into the ancient dungeon of Grimrock in order to atone for their crimes.
This is a great game, a very simple but great game.  When I say simple, I mean it’s easy to pick up and start, but difficult to master.  You can be as good as you can be at an RPG, but you still eventually make a mistake in combat, and this game capitalizes and punishes mistakes with heavy damage and/or death.  However, this doesn't detract from the simple fun of this game.
As I said in the beginning, you are controlling four prisoners (or less, you can go solo, but I seriously DONT recommend that) cast into the ancient dungeon/prison in the mountain of Grimrock, a mysterious and eerie mountain surrounded in death.  While it seems weird to control 4 people, while in first person, its actually not that bad, it’s actually quite interesting.
The movement is tile based, as in each move, moves you a whole tile.  I personally like that change from the usual RPGs.
The combat is cooldown and turn based, the front two party members can attack a target and must wait (based on the weapon and their DEX) to attack again.  There are 3 classes (as per usual) Fighter, Rogue, and Mage. Fighters are you usual warriors, utilizing swords, axes or maces and armor, I usually keep them in the front row as they are usually tougher.  Rogues use speed and timed strikes and ranged weapons, if you put skill points in Evasion you can eventually make it so all weapons they use are "reach" weapons, meaning a dagger can attack from the back row.  Mages are arcane users that utilize Air, Fire, Ice, and Earth magic, put enough points in one of those skills and the whole party learns to resist that type of damage.  Personally I found Fire and Earth to be the most dangerous early on, but that’s your choice.   I recommend balance, don't go using a whole team of Rogues for example, they are just too squishy.
The game is also quite tough and unforgiving, as I said.  You can win battle after battle, but sooner or later you are going to get obliterated by some stupid mistake or a powerful enemy or a meanass trap, just be careful.
The graphics are a bit dated, but I personally don't care that they are, I still loved the game.
The puzzle solving mechanics are tricky, and definitely increase based on your game progress, heavy learning curve.  There are dozens of secret areas, hidden objects and treasures, and quite a few weapons.  Lots to find using the puzzle solving mechanics.
An interesting feature, that I actually didn't do my first playthrough but will next time, is Old School Mode.   Put simply, no map at all.  You "must" use a pen and paper and manually put down the dungeons in order to remember them, or just google them, I think of that as cheating but near the end I did use google, so whatevs.
The game also has a "food" mechanic, you aren't required to feed your party, but you get serious negs if you don't and they are starving.  Mainly, they don’t regenerate health or energy at all, unless you trek back to a Life Crystal (largeass blue crystals that fully restore and revive fallen party members must wait a bit after each use).  Obviously being in an abandoned prison/dungeon, food is a little scarce, but you'll usually find food when you need it.
EXPLORE! If you are one of those people who burn through games as quickly as possible without exploring, DON'T! Go off the beaten the path often, that's where a majority of the treasure and loot and armor sets lie.
My only kind of gripe is the a little overpowered enemies, a few of them.  Most of the enemies are fairly balanced and scale with you, but some are a little TOO good.  My biggest annoyance was the annoyingass giant crabs; yes GIANT crabs.  They have a ♥♥♥♥ ton of health and almost never miss and hit hard, TWICE! Just a little overpowered imo.  At higher levels, they hit pretty hard but so do you, but when you first run into them, they wipe the floor with your face, just be careful, they appear on the 4th level if my memory serves me right.
A fun, exciting, tough and moddable game with a dungeon creator tossed into the game, decent graphics a little dated (granted this came out in 2010 but still), fun combat, lots of loot and monsters. The closed environment and a bit of lack of replay value and a few overpowered enemies are annoying.  However, I recommend everyone to play this game at least once.

From Horizon Studio comes Elsewhere High, a visual novel about a school for kids who were expelled from... everywhere else. You play as Derek, a boy expelled for writing horrible messages to another student, sent to Elsewhere High to become a better student.
This is for all intent and purposes, a book. Your choices don't change the course of the story at all, it all still leads to the same place. The achievements are all really easy to get. The characters don't pull me in. The background noises are much more distracting than they help with the ambience. There's nothing about this that really pulled me into it and I was just playing to complete.
And then the twist happened and my interest is definitely peeked. At first, I wasn't going to bother getting the second chapter, but after the twist, I definitely want to. I wouldn't really recommend this for anyone who doesn't enjoy sitting down and just reading a visual novel, especially because it doesn't have much to it. The story line as well, it's just not that gripping.
However, the twist? It definitely makes chapter two worth looking at for me. Unfortunately, chapter one just went a little too long on for my own personal tastes. For what this is, a lot of filler could have been removed before it was released to the public.

Transistor is the BEST indie game which I have ever played so far.
Everything is so perfect with everything I mean Story, Gameplay, Game mechanics, Game Design, Soundtrack and I still can't belive it's indie game.
Developers did great job that they connected everything so nicely in one game.
Story is very nice created and story has nice connect with gameplay, that transistor is your sword that talk and guide you through the game is so interesting and he is feeling like he is human being
. You are controlling Red, a singer in the city of Cloudbank, who uses Transistor to the Process, and to bring the Camerata (Group of 4 members and they are reposnible for the disappearances of high profile people in Cloudbank) to justice.
The Game action is happening in future and everything is robotic around you (specially enemies).
In gameplay you are controlling character "Red" and you are eliminating enemies with your Transistor (Big Sword) that has a lot of Functions (abilities) and you are getting new Functions from leveling up and for finding them from dead bodies of some important Characters (Bosses etc.).
Also every Function (ability) has 3 forms that can be used for and it's:
There is in total of 16 Functions and every Function has diffrent cost that can be used from 1 to 4 MEM (MEM short of Memory is an in-game resource that determines how many Functions can be equipped.)
Leveling up you are not just choosing what new ability will you pick up, you also choose what will you unlcok (More MEM or new Upgrade slot or new Passive slot) and what Limiter will you pick (Limiters are like passive functions).
There is excelent created game mechanic and it's that you create a Turn() in which you freeze the time of enemies and you can cast Functions and move in the battlefield. You have limited usable space to walk/run and to cast Functions, and good thing about this game mechanic you can undo previous walk path or function; you also can see what area will Function hit and how much damage will it done.
After you make a Turn() there is cooldown for other Turn().
Game mechanic about your life is that you have regular Life points (100%) and when it get to fatality (near 0%) you automaticlly create a Turn() and you don't die, but if Turn() is on cooldown and u get fatality damage you dont lose life like in other games, you lose one of your usable Functions and that Function is like broken and can't be usable for upgrade or passive until you get level up and refersh it; After you lose all 4 Usable Functions it's game over and u start from last save.
In-game you are saving on special locations (like checkpoints) in which you also customize your Functions.
When you kill the enemy they leave some kind of capsule that you have time to pick it up, if you dont pick it up (in 10sec) new enemy would have been created.
In-game there is "Backdoor" that is beach room for practicing and for completing Tests (challenges).
In New Game Plus (NG+) you get same functions but that make customization even bigger so you can have same Passive and Usable Function, but you can't upgrade one usable Function with 2 same Functions.
My favorite Function is "Void", that Function has 4 MEM usage and it can be casted max 3 times on the enemy (it's stacking), basiclly what Function do is that it make enemy weaker so you can one shot any enemy with some good finisher Function (actually any damage Function). Passive part is that increase your base damage.
Background city is well done designed, also robotic enemies, all human characters and Transistor. Transistor is story for himself, it's designed so nicely with that green sword and that red circle that symbolize like an eye.
Function effect design, also Turn() design is perfectlly designed that you can clearly see where is it going and how is pathing going.
Cutscenes are minimalist designed with only pictures or sometimes some animations when you are traveling, but overall that make game even better.
Soundtrack is connected with the story and it's basiclly some electro/robotic music, but the protagonist (Red) is also singing in some part of the game and at the end of the game some classic/jazz song.
And Backdoor beach room has some beachy music.
Soundtrack is changing throught the game and it's so beautiful. With sound you will know when it's time to fight and when is time too chill to listen story and to watch some background graphics.
Also with completing Tests you are unlocking new songs that can be playable through the Sandbox on the Record Player so you can change music in backdoor room. i think it's pretty cool.
I recommended Transistor (RPG indie game) for really every gamer who like sci-fi RPG, but also who doesn't like sci-fi or RPG in-general. At least give it try and I can guarantee you will not regret it.
P.S. It cost only 2,84€ on Summer sale, so it's must buy.

The most immersive adventure game I played these last years.
What Legend of Grimrock will do:
- Reward you for exploring
- Confront you with many situation and puzzles that will make use of your instinct and brainpower to resolve
- Give you a strong sense of accomplishment when you figure out a puzzle, and feel superhuman for doing so at times
- Make you feel incredibly immersed in an oppressing claustrophobic experience
What it definitely won't do:
- Insult your intelligence by holding your hand unnecessarily through puzzles, but instead cleverly hint you in unexpected ways
This game is not for everyone though, as it's more or less a revival of an old genre not much represented anymore these days: tile-based dungeon crawling adventure. But what a treat is it if you decide to get it.
I don't doubt that new gamers will enjoy the amount of work that was put into that little gem though.

The lord of insanity, Cthulhu was all set to plunge the world into insanity and destruction when his powers were sealed by a mysterious sorcerer. The only way for him to break the curse is to become a true hero. Save the world to destroy it in an epic parody RPG journey of redemption, romance, and insanity!
Pretty typical JRPG as far as gameplay goes. You have your party and you explore dungeons, towns, and the overworld. As with most JRPG’s you can find a wide variety of armour and weapons, each with their own special abilities. The only feature that separates this game from any other JRPG is its combat. It is turn based, with the unique twist; after each turn the monsters slowly get more powerful. Ultimately all this normally does is forces you to use the spells that cause the most damage, and subsequently use up the most of your magic points. After the battle is over your characters will regain full health and a portion of their magic points back. This at first is pretty fun, however after a few hours you will only be playing this game for its storyline, as it is pretty repetitive. Also, each area has a predefined amount of monsters you can fight, which for me really encouraged exploration as I wouldn’t have to fight endless enemies. So, back in 1996, George Lucas, creator of Star Wars wanted to know whether the world was ready for more Star Wars. After all, it had been 13 years since the last film had been released. To gauge the public’s opinion, Lucas launched a massive multimedia project quite unlike anything seen before. The entire Lucasfilm marketing engine would produce and publish everything that would tie in with a feature film release, but without actually releasing a film. The result was the
chapter. Basically Star Wars 5,5; rich in plot, lore, characters and other elements you’d expect from a Star Wars feature. The project was such a success that it motivated the release of the Special Editions one year later, and finally the prequels.

When you consider that project’s success, it isn’t hard to imagine why Lucas would revisit the concept to continue the Star Wars line, even after the release of
. Once again, the marketing machine was awoken and the fires of the multimedia forge flared to give shape to:

bridges the gap between episodes three and four. It tells the story of the founding of the Rebellion and the uneasy relationship between the Emperor and Darth Vader. The story is compelling enough to keep you playing. At the same time the game boasts an interesting three-way of physics engines that create a spectacular environment to test your mettle. The package is rounded out with great concepts and art direction, but it is stained with severe cosmetic glitches.
The game’s story, and the project’s main plotline follows the exploits of Galen “Starkiller” Marek, who is taken by Vader to be trained in the ways of the Sith after he killed Starkiller’s father himself. Darth Vader raises and trains the boy in secret until he is ready for trials. Vader then sends Starkiller out test his mettle against a number of Jedi who escaped the purge with the ultimate goal of preparing him for a showdown with the Emperor whom Darth Vader seeks to overthrow. The plot ultimately leads to betrayal, rebellion and finally a test of resolve that either leads the universe into the natural course of the larger Star Wars line, or you can derail the entire plot and force the premature end of the rebellion.
While strictly linear and with hardly any exploring to do in both gameplay and lore, the game does offer an interesting bridge between the prequels and original trilogy. Both as an explanation for the founding of Rebellion, as well as Vader’s old personality still seeking revenge against the man who turned him a mechanical monster. The newcomer Galen is a rather disappointing affair. He is your typical bald space marine and communicates through whispers and shouting, but no measure in between. He merits more exploration, because the game makes him out to be stronger in the force than any Jedi seen before. The game makes a set piece out of this by having you drag a mile-long, gargantuan, Imperial Star Destroyer out of orbit with the Force just to draw the Emperor’s attention.
The story is compelling, and certainly interesting for Star Wars fans, but it also introduces some awkward subjects. Like the robot Proxy, who is programmed to both train and kill Galen, while also appearing at the most impossible locations to provide some gratuitous fan service. Or the character of Juno Eclipse, Galen’s love interest, who seems to be just an accessory. All in all though, the story is interesting and enthralling enough to warrant a good romp. The included DLC chapters play a fun “what-if?” game with the original trilogy events, but they’re short, and unsurprisingly, non-canon*.
is a technological show stopper with some very clever design, but also riddled with clichéd traits and other gameplay substitutes. It runs a total of three physics engines at the same to time govern a set of parameters. The first engine, Havoc, controls ragdolls and other jiggle bones to give the game its organic aesthetic. Alongside runs Euphoria, the engine that controls the enemy AI to interact with the environment. That way, enemies with grab on to objects to prevent being thrown away with the force. Lastly, the DMM engine governs the world’s materials and their reaction to collision and impacts. Glass shatters realistically when you send a poor sod hurtling through it into deep space. Everything comes together in LucasArts’ own Ronin engine where you basically play like Kratos from
, but with significantly more lightning.
As Force prodigy, your abilities stretch far beyond your regular Jedi. Force push isn’t just a shove; it’s more like a hadouken. Force lightning now lights up the night sky. You can weaponise the environment by throwing everything and the kitchen sink at you enemies. It is inviting and fun to rip off the walls to toss at your enemies in every new room. However, the multitude options has its limits. A lot of enemies are still dealt with through boring and poorly executed quick-time events. While the physics generally hold up well, they can get buggy at times. It wouldn’t be the first time a boss would sink through the floor after zapping him. Or that the ground suddenly stretches to insane lengths. If you’re entirely unlucky, the game can even give up on you and crash. However, as a PC port, it holds up reasonably well. Don’t expect the illustrious 60fps or 4K resolution. It’s a 2009 game.
While its age does show, the art makes up for it. Although not as stylised as
or the
cartoons, the game does a good job looking like a technically advanced version of the original trilogy. The bedlam around you is well married to the fine-tuned art of the levels and characters. Electricity arcs convincingly, characters recoil and writhe in accordance. Air rushes out of rooms as you break the windows; explosions blow enemies away. Trees move and sway in the wind and shockwaves. Some bosses have seen a very stylish makeover from their film versions. Everything is accentuated with John Williams’ impeccable score to heighten the mood.
However, that is where the problems arise. The game shows cracks in the veneer. The music suddenly stops and doesn’t come back on until after a reboot. Or that the sound effects are horribly out of synch with the cut-scenes. Last time, my lightsabre didn’t deactivate during a cut-scene; resulting in a hilarious display of senseless eye-poking. However, it’s such a mess at times you just want to stop playing.
In the end though, the game is enjoyable to Star Wars fans. Especially people who got involved during the original era will get a kick out of the focus on the empire over the clones. Interesting characters and satisfying storyline make it worth at least one romp at a good discount. The tech is a thing behold when it doesn’t bug itself out too much. The same goes for the visuals; while a little dated, they use the source material in a dignified and well adapted manner for a more brutal game. This media project paid off my opinion. Give it a go if you like Star Wars.

I am an absolute hardcore fan of the farming simulator series, and FS17 is a worthy successor to FS15.
Is it worth to spend the money on? Yes, it is hours and hours of fun. There are so many different things to do for everyone, from fieldwork to animal husbandry or logging.
FS17 has a lot more base vehicles than FS15 and there are some really shiny and nice new addittions to the game.
The game has a lot more to offer, with the new way objects are handled and even trains that can be actually used and driven by players in the game.
The FS series has a very large and active modding community, which provides for tons of new vehicles, scripts, buildings, animals etc. etc. and even more importantly new maps.
Is it all glorious? No, there are some things that really irritate me personally. A couple of bugs that have been here in FS15 and some new bugs that still have not been solved by the dev team.
One of the biggest bugs that currently is bothering a lot of people, is the handling of trees when they are cut down and logs. Trees do not fall down after cutting them, but due to the new scripting of Giants, you have to push them with a vehicle or crane to actually fall down. Also are there still problems with the bounding-boxes of the woodlogs, which provided for some interesting jumping around of units when trying to grab hold or loading the logs onto any vehicle.

Initially, OlliOlli appears to be another running game like Canabalt with a skateboarding gimmick. Nevertheless, it turns out to be a fun little ride while it lasts. It lacks the diversity of Skate or Die and the fluidity of Thrilla's Surfari, and most virtual skaters won't bother to figuratively catch 'em all like they would in Tony Hawk's Pro Skater or Skate, because ultimately it does feel more like a running game successor than a skateboarding game.

Stop waiting for a new tony hawk game and just buy this.
At first glance OlliOlli looks like a runner but it has much more depth than that but it does borrow things like auto-moving character and instant reload times. The gameplay is somewhat a mix between skate and tony hawk's pro skater. The tricks are done by flicking the left stick in a specifc direction i.e. skate but unlike skate you have to press A to stick your landing(a perfect timing will get you more points).
At first the challenge is to finish the stages but once you master the control scheme the stages become fairly easy and then you have challenges to complete on each level. Like in the pro skater games you have to complete the challenge within the run. There are 25 amateur levels and a pro variant on each level (completing all challenges will unlock the pro level) and also includes a daily generated level for you to compete for the best score. This game has a lot for the price if you want a challenge and/or like to score chase then this game is for you.

Factorio is amazing.
I'm sure if you're reading this review, you've seen a few others. People joke about it being like crack, and I can understand why. The first day I bought this game, I played for an hour or two. Then I couldn't get to sleep because I was thinking about it. Then I decided to hell with it, since I can't sleep anyways, I may as well play more. Next thing I know it's 8AM and my wife is waking up for work. Then the next *next* thing I know, it's past 6pm and she's getting home from work. All told, I ended up spending nearly 20 hours playing this game straight, day one.
Thankfully I've managed to ease off since then, but I still spend roughly half as much time playing Factorio as I do working at my actual job. This isn't something you can fire up for a few minutes before work or on your lunch break because it's SO engaging that you will lose track of time.
About the game. Factorio is an open-world sandbox game where you start with nothing more than some iron plates (which you can use to make some pickaxes) and have to work your way up until you can eventually launch a rocket into space. The main focus of the game is to build and automate your factory so that it does all (or at least the vast majority) of the hard work for you.
Above all else, Factorio is a game of logistics. Getting resources from point A to point B, setting up power networks, figuring out ideal ratios for efficient production. All while defending your base and yourself from the aliens who would much rather you stop messing with their planet.
Each new map brings a new set of logistic challenges, with a proceduarlly generated map placing resources of different sizes, richness and location on the map for you to find, gather, and use. If you like problem-solving and logistical challenges, this is absolutely the game for you.
Just make sure you don't fire it up before work.

Heroic Dungeon is an addictive puzzle game with nice artstyle combination between minesweeper and a "3 in a row" connect game. The minesweeper part is that you click tiles on a playing field and under them there is extra health, extra damage and other goodies or a monster. (or the key that lets you progress to the next playing field). If you clear out all the tiles you also get to spin the wheel for more goodies of the kind you can find on the playing field/in the chests.
Another thing is that you can not click the tiles next to a monster without killing it and it can block more than one tile.
The connect game is very much like Ironcast so you do not get the bombastic chain reaction style of a connect game, there also appears some things that'll make you take all the monster heads in a square pattern across the board. (plus some other variants). You need to connect enough of them to be able to attack and the first round in a battle has you connecting twice so you're fairly likely to get the first attack in a game, the monsters you fight only attacks with their attack value.
Music's fairly bombastic in the battle sequence and prob. very suited for the inbetweens as well as I never really thought about it. (which generally is a good thing).It's a great timekiller. Cthulhu Saves the World is a fun 16-bit JRPG-style game with a neat system for leveling.  Each time a character gains a level, you get two choices for what to improve. How the heck did I spend 23 hours playing this? Well, it's been a while since I've played, but I have fond memories of playing Cthulhu Saves the World, and found it to be an enjoyable experience that quickly passed the time and didn't bore me or waste my time. Most JRPG-styled games require countless hours of grinding unless you're incredibly skilled and knowledgeable about upcoming bosses and such, as JRPGs are typically deliberately designed take up time running around in the same area to trigger more fights, as if extending playtime is a good solution to a shortage of content in terms of number of maps/locations developers bothered to put into the game.
Cthulhu Saves the World doesn't eat your time up and need long periods of grinding. When you complete it, there's a bonus playthrough with different characters as well, which I had a nice time playing through, too. I wish more JRPG-style games were like this and their other game which preceded this one, Breath of Death VII. Just because some developers are lazy and don't want to create many maps doesn't mean all of them have to do that and cram grinding in to hide that fact.
Some day, I need to grab Cosmic Star Heroine since the same developer made it. It looks pretty spiffy from the trailer, and name-dropping Chrono Trigger in inspirations they list on the store page was an easy way to get my attention.
Want a old school FF style game with modern jokes? Play this game then!

The Force Unleashed is a game where you take... hold, on, let me start over, I've already ♥♥♥♥ed this up and called it a game. The Force Unleashed is a franchise-themed BDSM simulator where you play the part of a hapless consumer who pays a monolithic giant to hold you down against the floor and violate you repeatedly.
The Force Unleashed is a great example of what happens when none of the developers communicate in any way. First you have the nerdy tech people like myself who start drooling in their trousers when they think of all of the things you could do with a physics-heavy engine designed around the use of Force powers. They brought ground-breaking technology like Digital Molecular Matter, which allows materials like metal or wood to deform or shatter in dynamic, realistic ways when you do something like Force-push them or slam a stormtrooper into them, or Euphoria, an AI engine which allows those stormtroopers to reach out and grab on to nearby objects in a vain attempt to stop you from flinging them around like a screaming hackey-sack. Unfortunately, the tech people never communicated with the rest of the team, so their fancy tech doesn't really get used at all and the engine is essentially wasted. The tech people also didn't communicate with REALITY, and actually told the general public that
. Somehow this didn't stop them from releasing the game on the Wii.
Next are the level designers, who were busy constructing their linear set pieces. Apparently they were too caught up trying to make outdoor environments feel like narrow hallways to speak with the tech team, and didn't even find out about the fancy Digital Molecular Matter system until just before release, the result being that there is about one conspicuously-placed object that actually uses the system in each level. We can also see that the level designers didn't actually watch the films, because in The Force Unleashed the Death Star consists entirely of an interlocking grid of gigantic hangar bays.
The gameplay designers were apparently never told that they were working on a Star Wars property at all, and so they worked from the offset under the model that every enemy should have exactly one weakness, and that each enemy should have a different weakness, apparently not knowing that your character is always holding a ♥♥♥♥ING LIGHTSABER.
Let's look at this lightsaber issue further. One of the core game design problems faced by every team designing a Star Wars game that includes lightsabers is that the lightsaber quite obviously should be a one-hit kill weapon, but unlimited-use one-hit kill weapons don't usually make for the best game design. Therefore, the designers always have to find some way not to let lightsabers effortlessly carve through all opposition, either by encouraging ranged combat or by limiting the damage of lightsabers for gameplay purposes.
TFU, however, is set between the three Star Wars films and George Lucas's parody prequels; we see claerly in the films that no one has lightsaber-proof armor. In TFU, every later enemy has a sword or shield or armor that is
. In TFU the only difference between a lightsaber and a pointy stick is that a stick doesn't require batteries. Well, I suppose there is also the fact that a lightsaber never gets dull; I wish I could say the same of the gameplay.
It's ironic that in a game where it seems that 100% of the effort went into graphics and gameplay, the gameplay is really quite terrible. As previously mentioned, the lightsaber is really quite useless and you are only able to kill enemies with Force powers. While this doesn't sound bad on paper, in reality each enemy is only weak to exactly one thing, and so for the most part combat alternates between guessing which power is going to kill a new type of enemy, and long sections of fighting that same type of enemy over and over and over in the same exact way. Wait a minute, I thought this game was supposed to encourage creativity?
The only enemies you are given true freedom against are the hapless standard stormtroopers, who fart their blasters ineffectually at you until you go barelling through them or pick them up with Force grip and bash them around a bit. Since the basic stormtrooper is the only opportunity you have to really have fun with grip and push, they are actually given quite a lot of durability, so you can sadistically bash them back and forth between two walls like a future serial killer swinging a squirrel between two trees by the tail. This is fun at first, but if you aren't actually a future serial killer, after a while you actually start to feel bad for the poor stormtrooper who was just doing his job until you decided to smack him around like an unwanted baby at a post-delivery abortion clinic.
Of course, making you scream in rage at all of the enemies who are immune to ♥♥♥♥ING LIGHTSABERS wasn't sufficiently sadistic for these developers. As the game goes on, you start running into more and more enemies whose primary weapon is a homing blast that knocks you over, and whose rate of fire is exactly equal to the amount of time it takes you to stand back up. "A long time ago in a galaxy far, far away...."
Taking place between Episodes III and IV (Revenge of the Sith and A New Hope), Star Wars - The Force Unleashed ties the two trilogies nicely together. Not diverging from the main story canon but actually expanding it, while giving the player a sense that you are part of something bigger.
In the beginning, as the title of the game implies, you can't help but "unleash the force" left right and center - while merrily giggling as storm troopers are sent flying off cliffs or picking up objects and propelling them into somebody's face.  But then after a while that can get a bit repetitive, as the AI of npc's seem to be - "oh the main protagonist is coming, let me get into his way by lying in front of him while he pummels his way through".  Then there is another "but" - even when you progress to a higher level with your skills, you characters execution of those skills is sluggish at best, allowing the enemy to actually hurt you or kill you.
The main drawback of this game is spotty camera control, or lack there of. Example - When entering into a fight (boss fights), suddenly you have no control and it turns into a side scrolling 'Beat 'em up" - so if you already cant perform you sluggish skills, you can get beat into a corner by Darth Maul... :)
The character and environment design is beautiful. I can envision this a bit more polished but when visiting Felucia, you can't help but to take it in, taking a few screen shots and wishing there was more to explore.
I definitely grew attached to the main protagonist as the story developed, but I felt that sometimes the developers rushed the story - throwing action sequences at you or cutting some of the story and leaving you wondering how the relationship between some of the characters developed.  The game felt a bit short, could have been longer - to allow more character growth and story development.
Star Wars - The Force unleashed is a flawed game, yes - but has a solid story, mostly fun and a great way to burn a few hours.

This game is adorable: light-hearted, briskly paced, sarcastic, and while not at all thougtful in itself, inspiring a little thought in the player. The gameplay and your opponents are a kitchen sink of first-person shooters, with characters from everything from /Doom/ to /Halo/ (just the Covenant), as well as the occasional Conan the Barbarian reference; the settings of the game are various cliche game settings, from the /Far Cry/ planet to the /Doom/ planet to the /Big Trouble in Little China/ and /World of Warcraft/ planets. The effect is not to be missed; there's something unique, beautiful, even haunting about driving a light tank and fighting helicopters in front of the gates of a fairy-tale castle.
Why do these planets retain their distinctive character, despite Mental's occupation? _How_ do they do so, given that Mental's homeworld is gleaming and hyper-modern, and surely produces the sort of abundant, cheap consumer goods that have caused the Middle East and East Asia to lose their distinctive visual character? Perhaps Mental doesn't permit free trade between his own planet and his colonies, but this seems unlikely; more likely, perhaps his homeworld is a command economy (Mental is an AI, after all), and just doesn't produce enough of a surplus of anything -- or have enough interest in peaceful trade -- to provide blue jeans and televisions cheap enough for the people of the Far Cry world to afford...
Mental's manpower also doesn't appear to be as good as it could be; he's dependent on local levies to keep order, and his regular troops -- Warhammer-style orcs supported by heavy military hardware -- seldom show up in large numbers outside of small numbers of major bases and garrisons. This despite the orcs having access to antibiotics and vaccination, Green Revolution agriculture, computerized manufacturing, and all sorts of other things that should be keeping their numbers up relative to their enemies... but command economies aren't really known for high population growth.
It's an interesting puzzle; it certainly produces a memorably combined visual character; and it does seem to have an answer in the end. I doubt that the writers knew that Serious Sam is fighting the AI Soviet Union, but the internal evidence does point that way...
I wonder what inspired this company to write this game. They certainly make some amusing points about how there's a shared culture of video games that shouldn't exist, looking at the matter a priori -- there's no reason why everyone should use the same types of characters and settings. But they satirize it with a great deal of flair, and in a way that turns out to have a surprisingly hefty inner logic.

The units on both sides are varied enough, and although, as historically, they have counterparts on both sides (the german stostruppen and allied assault teams), playing different divisions and either axis or allies brings a different feel to it. Vehicles drive, shoot and withstand damage differently, various infantry units bring in different weapons, levels of discipline and results. It is a welcome change to dynamics of the game, that I would say are more nuanced than in previous instances of Wargame series. I imagine they could improve this still, but it works.

OlliOlli is a 2d skateboarding game that bares similarities to the gameplay of now defunct developer Black Box skateboarding game "Skate". The basic control scheme is all there, you have your left analog stick quarter circles, full circles and point analog at said direction to pull off a variety of combo skateboarding tricks and grinds. Sure it doesn't have any of the crazy stunts of a Tony Hawk like 720 shove it-to -superman-heelflip-whatever but pulling off chain combo in OlliOlli has just the degree of difficult and requires just the amount of skill that pulling them off will give players an equal amount of gratification when done properly. Players progress in challenge latened levels where either collecting, pulling off x amount of combos, or reaching a certain amount of score will progress you to the next level and ultimately to more difficult challenges.
When it comes to presentation OlliOlli 2d pixelated art style helps sets it apart from the more well known 3D skateboarding franchises by giving the game a indie feel very reminiscent of underground skateboarding back in the day. This feeling is reinforced by the music that not only helps set the tone but remind players the variety and diversity skateboarding is. There's a level of cool brought to this game simply by choosing these aesthetics.
A few issues I had with this game was primarily on the mechanics side where the initial timing for the landing of tricks require players to press a button at the right time to pull it off perfectly. This window to press the button is fairly short and requires you to pay attention to how far your board is to the ground. This can prove an issue because like other 2d endless runners before it if you aren't paying attention to the screen correctly your character may blend into the background which can prove troublesome.  Failing to pull off the perfect landing on a trick can be the difference between getting 100k score on a perfectly run level to 20k score on a poorly runned one.

Based on the game "3 in a row" and made in its own way. The game has 7 levels. The passage of the level is to open all the tiles on the map and find the key to the door to the next level. It is pretty much what the blurb says, a combination between minesweeper and a connect game, the minesweeper part is that you click tiles on a playing field and under them there is extra health, extra damage and other goodies or a monster. (or the key that lets you progress to the next playing field)
If you clear out all the tiles you also get to spin the wheel for more goodies of the kind you can find on the playing field/in the chests.
Another thing is that you can not click the tiles next to a monster without killing it and it can block more than one tile.
The connect game is very much like Ironcast so you do not get the bombastic chain reaction style of a connect game, there also appears some things that'll make you take all the monster heads in a square pattern across the board. (plus some other variants)
You need to connect enough of them to be able to attack and the first round in a battle has you connecting twice so you're fairly likely to get the first attack in a game, the monsters you fight only attacks with their attack value.
Music's fairly bombastic in the battle sequence and prob. very suited for the inbetweens as well as I never really thought about it. (which generally is a good thing)
Graphics are simplistic and nice, I like the artstyle personally.
The bad would be the english, it could do with some proof reading but the game doesn't make you read a lot, it's mostly fleeting text so I can live with it, it's far from a game breaker.
The conclusion would be; if you liked Ironcast you might want to give this a go, I think you'll like it. (I certainly do and I like Ironcast quite a lot, this has a lot less RNG in it in that the enemies damage and health is known and set in stone...at least so far...)

Here's what I remember about the campaign: I couldn't beat it. It was really, really hard. The AI seemed too smart, too capable, too deadly. And then, because Windows 7 64-bit was giving me trouble at the time, I downgraded, switched back to good old Vista, and lo and behold, suddenly, I beat the campaign with no issues. Since then, I have played on Windows 7, which has none of the teething problems it used to, and not experienced this problem.
Weird, right?
I have no explanation for this. None whatsoever.
The campaign is short--you know how people always accuse multiplayer campaigns of being like four hours long? Well, me, I generally play them in two to three times that much. Only a small handful of games have ever proven to me to be super short, and Bad Company 2 is one of them. It's not a particularly well-designed campaign, either. Fun, I guess, but limited.
The multiplayer was where I spent all my time. Never before or since has a game gripped me as much. I'd be willing to argue it's the best multiplayer in the Battlefield series--it doesn't use that stupid web-based Battlelog like BF3 and BF4 do, after all.
Other than a lack of maps--that were eventually added in, a lack of multiplayer modes (people only ever seem to play Rush or Conquest, a far cry from the dozens of multiplayer modes that ship with other games, like Unreal Tournament or Call of Duty), and a frequent re-use of map assets (which were first seen in BFBC1 and reused in BF3), it's just... the best. It's tweaked right, the classes feel balanced, and the maps themselves are my favorites. I wouldn't say everyone should play this game, but I will say that if you like team-based multiplayer shooters, Battlefield: Bad Company 2 is something you'll enjoy.
The Vietnam expansion was pretty cool, by the way.

The plot is comparable to mediocre fan fiction. 1) Use a controller.
2) Find no flaws in the prequel trilogy.
3) Forget that good storytelling exists.

Greatest game EVER! It is set after order 66 and before episode IV which means you get to see characters from both the prequels and the original films. You get to see the remenants of the Clone Wars and the rise of the Empire. The levels are quite long and gameplay can get repetitive but for me, because of the vast array of abilties, every time I pkay I discover something new. There's also two ending to the game which adds to relay value, Jedi Holocrons to collect in each mission (and other secondary objectives to complete), not forgetting this Sith Editions' extra missions which I have yet to play. You can customise the colour and crystal type and upgrade unlocking new combos. There s only 10 missions in the main game (the first of which you play as Darth Vader but cannot replay for some reason) but they all take time and have a difficult boss at the end.

In my first playthrough, I wasn't sure exactly what I was expected so I played how I would probably do in real life and ended up with a personable robot that became so autonomous it started demanding additional wages for it and its fellow robots.  My second playthough I took the role of a typical "profits first" CEO and ended up with a race of robots determined to take over the planet.   With a gun pointed at my head I either had the choice of helping them achieve singularity or I would be killed.
The amount of work put into this book is rather amazing.  The beginning is repetitious in subsequent playthroughs because the time is spent designing and building your robot.  After this point, however, your story can vary wildly.  A lot of philosophical questions are addressed throughout your life.  It's reminiscent of Asimov in a number of ways.  Occasionally, you are limited to choices that differ from what you want to do, but not often.
For completionists, there are a number of achievements to get depending on what you've done or who you've become.  The game suggests you look through them, I suggest you avoid doing so unless you have played through many times.
Make no mistake, this is a book, but I couldn't put it down.  Plus, the digital format helps avoid the temptation to cheat skipping ahead to the results.  Recommended.

God… where to start with this game… Just be warned that this is a Thriller-esque type of narrative, where you’re going to have zero idea about what is going on at the beginning. Even at the end nothing will be completely written in stone and high levels of interpretation will shape your view of characters, the world and events. It is done well though and keeps enough information flowing as you progress to keep you interested in what’s happening.
The main content of gameplay is mostly within the fight mechanics. It starts off slow as one would expect but takes a while to really ramp up. Once you get most of your abilities though things are fluid within the game. Balance within the move sets I found slightly lacking. There is a move or two you’ll never touch after trialing them out. Then there’s one you’ll be guaranteed to use, Breach() being the obvious example.
This game also uses a fluid difficulty structure that adds layers of depth to the game. There is no set difficulty marker, and you’ll receive Limiters that, imagine this, limit your abilities in fights. This is where the difficulty slider comes in and it works fairly well for this game. Anytime I felt like the game was getting too easy, I simply slapped on a new limiter and usually I was met with resistance once again. Without this the game, would have been far too easy. I rather enjoyed this variable difficulty and found it to be fair.
The total story/world package is the strong point of this game. As you play a sort of revenge laden detective. This requires you to read the info that gets from using certain functions in specific terms. Every little detail matters in the story as it provides clues as to how the world worked before this adventure began.
The music and artwork really add to the final world product.  Giving a deeper immersion into the experience and on some level allowing an emotional connection to be established between you and a character that is unable to speak. It adds to the world a unique feeling that allows the world to breathe in and out as its body is revealed.
There are a few negatives to this game though. The menu to check what function does what when coupled with another. Sometimes the ability won’t seem to match the original function of when used by itself, though this is rare.  Going through each individual function and then what each corresponding function that amplifies it can get monotonous. I said screw the reading and basically threw stuff together and tried it out in practice mode. The beginning is so confusing that it almost immediately throws you off balance in a bad way, such is the nature of a thriller though.
In the end, though, everything turned out to be fun, interesting and slightly emotional. You’ll need to keep a relatively open mind as you go into this one as the opening is rather jarring.

Ok, I just marathoned through Grimrock 1 and 2 and thought I would conclude that with a concise review.
In short : the games are unbelievably good. Admittedly, this was the first time I've ever played a first person dungeon crawler with classic grid-based movement, but there is very little I can actually criticize.
The puzzles are extremely well designed. Even though it usually took me few minutes to go from "This♥♥♥♥♥♥makes no sense at all, what the hell!" to "ohhhh, I get it!", it felt all the more rewarding when I finally managed to solve a particularly difficult puzzle all on my own.
The first game manages to create a great gloomy atmosphere, when you delve into pitch black dungeons, devoid of any other human being, and when you can hear the various critters crawl somewhere on the other side of a wall. I would even say, it's not too far off from what a horror game feels like.
The successor has a much more open and interconnected world, with differently themed areas, both above and below the surface, similar to how the first Dark Souls approached level design (including the bit where you aimlessly wander around in already cleared areas, looking for the entrance to the next dungeon). It may not be quite as eerie as the first Grimrock game, but the first mimic you encounter in the game will make sure to give you a heart attack regardless.
The only thing left to say is : Don't play them on hard mode on your first play through, like I did, or else you're in for a lot of frustration. The games do have a few really cheap moments, the second one even more so than the first one.
Because if there's one thing the developers really like, it's trying to make you fall down into a monster infested trap pit, which spells inevitable death. Few things are more infuriating than finding and activating a hidden switch on a wall, only to be mauled by a dozen monsters crawling in from all directions a few seconds later. Now, combine that with an incredibly clunky combat system (Grid-based attacks and movement. In real time. Why...?) which in itself poses enough of a challenge, when enemies can kill your front line in two hits, and you'll find yourself dangerously close to throwing something valuable out of the window. I'm pretty sure I'm not the only one who would have loved to have turn based battles, like in Wizardry 8 for example, in these games.

Assault Android Cactus is a wolf in sheep's clothing. It may look like a cute game for kids, but beating this arcade, bullet hell, twin-stick shooter is no joke. Be prepared to be utterly destroyed when it comes to the last boss battle.
High fidelity audio and visuals paired with tight, fast gameplay make this title a fun party game not only for kids. The pushing techno beats, pew pew sound effects and lively voice acting build up this games' galvanizing, energetic mood. Due to its easily distinguishable colour cues and bright graphic effects on plain backgrounds, the game provides the visual clarity needed within a bullet hell.
Boosting the action and putting further pressure on the player is the need to keep the android's battery up. This underlines the importance of speed: the faster enemies die, the faster the next battery drop occurs. With that internalised, it's an overall easy to learn game with a manageable selection of consecutively unlocked android girls, each with their own weapon loadouts.
Different game modes, unlockable lore, art and game options and multiplayer add onto the otherwise quite short single player campaign. All in all, Assault Android Cactus is a fantastic twin-stick shooter.

The graphics are excellent, however the controls, combat and general game play are nothing amazing. Same with the customizations that you can apply to your character, I personally found that they make very little to no difference (except one or two).
Difficulty wise its fairly easy and my feeling is that it was intentionally made to not be too challenging so that the story arc flows without long gaps.
Would I recommend it ? If you are a fan of Star Wars = absolutely... but view it as an interactive movie/story that you will go through once and never play again. Still, its an enjoyable experience, just keep in mind what it is, so you don't get disappointed after a full playthrough.

Possibly the greatest shooter of its time.
BFBC2 was and still is an excellent shooter.
The game is built on the classic and well done squad based shooter. There are 4 different classes, Assault, Engineer, Medic and Recon. Each class has it's own specific weaponry and perks which it can use to alter the way the class plays. For example, do you want to be a long range support sniper? Choose a high calibre rifle and mortat strike. Want to play close recon? Choose an SMG or a sniper with a red dot scope, tracking orbs and something like C4. This is viable for all classes.
One thing that this game is excellent is, is weapon balance. Yes there are still standout choices, but every gun has a niche that it can sit in nicely. I mainly play Medic, and loved playing the Spas12 with long range SS shells, and magnum ammo. Medics can also easily play with the non-class specific SMGs or rifles, or play as a heavy support class with LMGs, all of which are equally balanced depending on how you want to play; up close with the M60, or further back with a lower recoil like MG9 for example.
The whole shooter is balanced excellently. The vehicles are somewhat difficult to counter at times, but this is normally because they are played by good pilots or drivers. An Apache chopper with a skilled gunner will cause havoc, unless your team can club together, tag the chopper and RPG it; or maybe a sniper can take it down.
The whole game is based on team co-operation; in stark contrast to dumb shooters like CoD, which rely on pounding as many kills from spawn trapping and kill streaks. These don't exist in BFBC2, and the game is hugely more enjoyable from it.
The game is still active even with the release of BF3 and BF4, and that is because the game is fun, balanced and enjoyable, and Hardcore is a must.

God… where to start with this game… Just be warned that this is a Thriller-esque type of narrative, where you’re going to have zero idea about what is going on at the beginning. Even at the end nothing will be completely written in stone and high levels of interpretation will shape your view of characters, the world and events. It is done well though and keeps enough information flowing as you progress to keep you interested in what’s happening.
The main content of gameplay is mostly within the fight mechanics. It starts off slow as one would expect but takes a while to really ramp up. Once you get most of your abilities though things are fluid within the game. Balance within the move sets I found slightly lacking. There is a move or two you’ll never touch after trialing them out. Then there’s one you’ll be guaranteed to use, Breach() being the obvious example.
This game also uses a fluid difficulty structure that adds layers of depth to the game. There is no set difficulty marker, and you’ll receive Limiters that, imagine this, limit your abilities in fights. This is where the difficulty slider comes in and it works fairly well for this game. Anytime I felt like the game was getting too easy, I simply slapped on a new limiter and usually I was met with resistance once again. Without this the game, would have been far too easy. I rather enjoyed this variable difficulty and found it to be fair.
The total story/world package is the strong point of this game. As you play a sort of revenge laden detective. This requires you to read the info that gets from using certain functions in specific terms. Every little detail matters in the story as it provides clues as to how the world worked before this adventure began.
The music and artwork really add to the final world product.  Giving a deeper immersion into the experience and on some level allowing an emotional connection to be established between you and a character that is unable to speak. It adds to the world a unique feeling that allows the world to breathe in and out as its body is revealed.
There are a few negatives to this game though. The menu to check what function does what when coupled with another. Sometimes the ability won’t seem to match the original function of when used by itself, though this is rare.  Going through each individual function and then what each corresponding function that amplifies it can get monotonous. I said screw the reading and basically threw stuff together and tried it out in practice mode. The beginning is so confusing that it almost immediately throws you off balance in a bad way, such is the nature of a thriller though.
In the end, though, everything turned out to be fun, interesting and slightly emotional. You’ll need to keep a relatively open mind as you go into this one as the opening is rather jarring.

Wargame veteran here! And more importantly a die-hard Paradox Interactive fan (Their games, not DLC practice). I’m here to tell you why this is a dream match made in heaven.
The Wargame series made by Eugen Systems is fantastic. However there are two big aspects that bother me personally. First of all there’s way too many different type of units and transports, overcomplicating the process of making good decks. More importantly however is the extremely fast type of combat as one would come to expect of modern warfare. You for example just use the plane as a single artillery strike that practically teleports in and out, while the enemy if they have AA shoot out a single missile taking it out or not.
And then we have Steel Division. BOOM. Simple decks but with great unit variety per division! Actual plane warfare! Bombers are slow and take time getting into the battlefield and out, allowing you to react by sending in fighters. Okay they might bullet sponge way too many AA rounds but still better than the opposite. This point is further enhanced with infantry, how vital they are within Steel Division and dynamic to use.
My point is that the slower pace of Steel Division truly does result in a fantastic and enriched experience. I just read another review complaining about the micromanagement.. Ha-ha.. Trust me on the note that in the Wargame series merely blinking robs you of the opportunity to consider micromanaging your AA and getting destroyed by enemy anti-radar missiles (SEAD). A micromanagement nightmare in comparison.
In conclusion the game is best played multiplayer. Of course that does not necessarily mean PvP but Coop missions are coming and skirmishing against A.I is just as rewarding. This is a rather niche developer that will hopefully thrive under the Paradox Interactive publishing into more renown that it deserves.
TL;DR!
Without a doubt a phenomenal strategy game. The best Eugen Systems game to start playing, in time if you’re up for more intensive micromanagement and faster paced combat see the Wargame series for Cold War-era warfare. Steel is my personal favorite for its perfect slower pace.
