First off let me start by saying this game is bug ridden and I personally got so many bugs and crashes that drove me insane but I stuck with it and beat the game. Ok now that's out of the way let me start by saying this is a great game but a really crappy PC port.
The story revolves around an orphaned that Darth Vader made and raised ultimately taking him as an apprentice by the name of starkiller (I know theres a nod there to the films but I'm not such a star wars geek so I won't touch on that). This game is a hack and slash with light puzzle elements. Its more a kin to God of war than in the vain of such greats as Devil may cry with all the quick time events and boy there sure are a lot of QTE's. The QTE's aren't as annoying as in other games though I really wished they'd give more of a reward for going for them instead of just regualr health and points and a death finishing animation. That's cool and all but I just skipped a lot of them to save time on some of the bigger enemies and just killed them the old fashion way to avoid the long animations. Once you see them you get the gist. The combat isn't all that complicated but its not that simply either there are a bunch of moves to unlock to break up the monotomy of button mashing but most the time you're gonna go back to those few trusty and easy to pull off combos instead of the finicky longer moves that require you to press this and then hold that for x amount of seconds.
The story is  the driving point for this game imo. It had me invested from the start where they let you play as Vader just blowing the crap up in the prologue in side a wookie village. And damn is Vader a bad♥♥♥♥♥ He just walks like he's the♥♥♥♥♥♥and he's so OP that everything dies with one hit of his dark force powers. Starkiller on the other hand is kind of one dimensional but the story between him and the commrades he meets along his journey is what keeps you invested. Its nothing to write home about but near the end you actually cared about him and Juno. I wished they'd just get past the "hey I like you but I know you're going to die so I won't be romantic with you" act and just let them get closer to the point where when you go and face the last battle the player would be emotional torn of which side to go with. (A nod to the last battle that I won't spoil)
Overall its a good game but the countless crashes makes it an average PC port. I admit though the most of my problems stem from me trying to better the gfx with third party sweetfx. I highly suggest giving this a playthrough and only buy it if its on sale don't waste your money on a almost 10 yr old game now but if you have it then play it! if your a starwars fan or a fan of this genre then you owe it to yourself to enjoy this short and sweet game.

Already beat the game fully on vita, but had to buy it again because of how quality and polished it is. The basic premise is that it's a runner game similar to Bit.Trip runner except you have a wide variety of tricks you can pull off the ground and a variety of grinds you can pull off on rails you find on the stage.
The game has a strong focus on timing as you gain maximum speed by pressing a button just as you land on the ground or on a rail for a perfect landing and harder stages have huge gaps after a series of rails that require you to perfect land on one, off it and perfect land onto another.
The trick/grind system can also be compared to moves in ARPGs like DMC. There is a wide variety of them and in order to build up a good score, you have to use a variety of each throughout the stage.
In order to unlock stages, you just have to beat the previous, but there are optional objectives in each one that you can shoot for for 100% completion. Usually there's 1 for achieving at least a certain high score for the whole stage, 1 for achieving at least a certain high score for a combo, and the other 3 involve a variety of objects like collecting hard to reach collectibles in the stage, reaching high places in the stage which requires a set of perfect grinds, pulling off a certain move or a combination of trick/grind, restrictions like not pushing for more speed on ground, no grinding, etc. They're all fun to get.
When you've beaten the initial 25 stages which will take you a hell of a long time especially starting out, there are 25 additional harder stages. After that, there is rad mode where you have to beat all 50 stages with only perfect landings, and while you can get used to it, some stages are incredibly brutal because some gaps seem only passable if you slow down and not perfect land to hit a closer platform before a huge gap.
There is a lot to do in this small, high skill ceiling game, and if you like runner games like Bit.Trip runner, I would reccomend this♥♥♥♥♥♥with the force of a thousand suns. The aesthetics are varied and simple enough to focus on gameplay, and the music is beautiful and fitting that you'll have no problems with it while you 100% it.
I'd give it at least an 8 out of 10, and it probably deserves higher than that.

It's hard not to notice that 2017 has seen a resurgence in World War Two films and video games alike. Just during summer, Blitzkrieg 3 and Sudden Strike 4 were released while the game I’m writing about today, launched at the end of May. “Dunkirk” opened in cinemas as a true summer blockbuster. You get my point, WW2 is back in the saddle. Even the upcoming Call of Duty, shall be a well deserved return to the series’ historic roots. Not a moment too soon. I first heard of the developer, Eugen Systems when I played their Act of War: Direct Action, close to 12 years ago.
I was impressed by the amount of details and information poured into a strategy game, in a time when RTS titles were emphasizing on generic base building mechanics, churning equally generic units. In 2009, R.U.S.E. (no longer on Steam, sadly) introduced the developer’s signature style & proprietary graphics engine, IRISZOOM to the delight of most armchair generals wishing for a quality compromise between eye candy and in-depth strategy. Steel Division: Normandy 44 is proudly carrying the torch of its spiritual and technical predecessors. In more ways than one, it has surpassed them all.
Steel Division: Normandy 44 as its name suggests, focuses on a very specific WW2 campaign. The turning point for the entire war and the event which truly signaled, the inevitable end of the Third Reich. The Invasion of Normandy, D-Day,  Operation Overlord, The Normandy Landings. Many names, a single great event in human history. The greatest seaborne invasion, in fact and Nazi Germany would slowly begin to crumble once the second, Western front would open in war-torn Europe. Steel Division features three distinct singleplayer campaigns for the United States of America, Third Reich and the United Kingdom. In that order, based on the difficulty rating of the missions themselves. More on that below, but for now I shall focus on the raw numbers.
There are four missions for each aforementioned nation. I have to agree that they seem like quite a few, even if the amount of planning they involved, is visible even to the untrained eye. Everything from historically accurate maps, unit placement and sheer amount of intel, all point out towards the developer’s efforts in creating a D-Day video game unlike anything which came before it. I should know, since I’ve been an avid Osprey Publishing reader long before I even owned a gaming-capable PC or knew about the existence of Wikipedia. Ironically, for someone who pretty much abhors warfare and its innate violence, I like to keep myself informed about anything from tactics, to seemingly “useless trivia” about caliber sizes and off road speeds of tanks from many decades ago. We all have our quirks, right?
Don’t expect a story. You get full interaction with history, in a title which brings the stress of managing a war room, back to life. And the rewarding aspects of it all, should your plans come to fruition. Saving the lives of your troops and hopefully forcing the enemy to surrender lest they suffer total annihilation. The US and UK campaigns are deeply imbedded into historical facts, names and places, while the German missions take some minor artistic liberties. So, you shall first take full command of the US 82nd Airborne Division, providing support from behind enemy lines, in what Steel Division: Normandy 44 deems as the “Normal” difficulty of Mission Boston. I can assure you though, that pitting paratroopers against machine gun nests and light tanks, is anything but normal in terms of actual difficulty.
The “Hard” ones, within Atlantikwall, are from Germany’s 21st Panzer Division (veterans of Afrika Korps), which the game wishes to debate and imagine as a swift response from Field Marshall Erwin Rommel to the D-Day landings. A true “what if” the elite German units would have managed to counter-attack the Allies instead of failing to even predict the location or scale of the invasion. Almost as expected, leave it to the Scots, to face and overcome insurmountable odds. The “Very Hard” campaign missions in Steel Division: Normandy 44, focus on the heroic exploits of the 15th (Scottish) Infantry Division in Operation Epsom and the bloodbath which ensued around German-occupied Caen before its subsequent liberation.
Powered by the developer’s own graphics engine, Steel Division: Normandy 44 looks better than any title in the Close Combat series or similar and recently released WW2-focused RTS. The engine itself would be regarded as IRISZOOM V5 since it was called V4 in the latest Wargame iteration,  2014’s Red Dragon. Eugen Systems specialized in offering battle maps which shine both in a bird's eye view and zoomed in perspectives. To put it in contemporary terms, it would resemble the support offered nowadays by UAVs (unmanned aerial vehicles, also known as “drones”) and convert that accurate, real time intel into the technology available 70 years ago. Keep in mind that even long-range and portable radio communication wasn’t available to the military until the Vietnam War, some 20 years after WW2 ended.
Steel Division: Normandy 44 leaves very few details amiss. Apart from the resource-hungry graphical details, which I could only run maxed out at 2K resolution if I wanted close to 50fps, the players get access to a whole lot of information, relating to the units and the divisions present in-game along with short biographies for their commanders. How can I not love and respect strategy games, when they taught and piqued my interest in history back when school was doing the exact opposite? Stability through constant 60 frames per second can be achieved at 1080p, in case you’re wondering. No RTS game should be played at 30fps or less.
I’ve always been fond of the soundtracks from the strategic titles I’ve played over the years. From Age of Empires and Cossacks/American Conquest, to Company of Heroes and Blitzkrieg 2. Steel Division doesn’t disappoint with its audio assets. Voice acting is present in briefings and throughout the missions themselves while the units don’t suffer from repetitive spoken lines, a sin that was more prevalent in past RTS’. Sound effects are adequate and I really can’t think of another method in which all that shooting and engine noises, could have been rendered better. The OST has yet to surface online as separate songs, but I shall still link below a small audio sample which I prefer regarding as the game’s main theme since it’s also featured in Steel Division: Normandy 44’s Main Menu.

Okay, I'm a massive Paper and Pen RPG nerd, and I grew up on D&D.
The preceding statement may have made me a little biased here, but onward! Legend of Grimrock (LoG) is a great game. You control a party of Adventurers through the maze-like bowels of a great mountain called Grimrock. You upgrade their skills, attributes, and equipment as you go to allow them to better survive the monsters that exist within the darkness.
Though there are beasts and monsters within Grimrock, it is the puzzles and lack of consumables that will probably cost you dearly, as the challenges put infront of you can be devious indeed, and food is extremely scarce.
The history of the Grimrock, told through flashbacks, notes, etc is intriguing, and add to the already gloomy, oppressive atmosphere of dread and desperation.
The Community has made a LOT of Steam Workshop stuff for LoG, and it is really worth a look, some of the modules people have created are fantastic, and will extend the enjoyment of this game indefinitely.
If you like fantasy gaming, RPG's or are more used to Tabletop RPG/Wargames then give this game a go. It won't be for everyone, but it is definitely hitting all the right marks with the crowd it was intended for.

I have been trying to decide what my favorite twin-stick shooter is. Tormentor X for it crazy frantic, balls to the wall gameplay? Nuclear Throne for its insane presentation, killer soundtrack, and tight mechanics? Binding of Isaac for its random craziness and replayablilty?  Monilith for upping the Isaac formula by adding faster and tighter gameplay? Nex Machina for its beauty and the desire to 100% a level at all costs? Full Mojo Rampage for is sheer visuals and difficulty or Geometey Wars 3 for....well, a lot of the above? No. After a ton of time will all the mentioned titles I decided Cactus was the winner.
No game on my list nails everything so well. The presentation is the highest I know of in this genre. The graphics, gameplay, control, unlockable character, unlockable "mods", and flow of this game are perfect...and the music, the MUSIC.
Every unlockable character plays very diffrently from the others and changes the core mechanics. The levels are clever in their design from a sheer visual aspect, and demand revisiting just to get a high rank and a position on the leaderboards, and the infinity drives just that, a battle arena that goes on forever and keeps the high standards main game, even a daily for an added bonus.
I know some people don't like the battery aspect ( you have to kill quicky and wait for a battery to drop to keep on playing), but this is why I chose this game over all the others. This one added element keeps the game frantic and fun. The battery system is fair. Do well and they drop at a constant pace, don't and the game becomes heart pounding experience where its a race to do better in hopes of getting a drop. This mechanic never felt cheap, and in the end made me a better player.

Lovecraftian lore or the Cthulhu mythos, for those who are blissfully unaware, is a terrifying series of books created by author H.P. Lovecraft. These horror books explore monsters known as Eldritch beings, powerful and godlike demons each taking on a warped and sickening form. Chances are that if you haven’t heard of Lovecraft, you have at least heard of one of these Eldritch beings: Cthulhu. One of the most well-known Eldritch beings in mainstream media, Cthulhu is a winged demon with the visage of a squid. It is said that simply being in his presence can cause a man to go insane. So what happens when this monstrous abomination is put in a humorous light? Cthulhu saves the world, that’s what!
In this classic turn-based RPG, Cthulhu rises from the sea only to have his demonic powers stripped by a mysterious wizard before he can start conquering the world. The only way Cthulhu can regain his powers is if he becomes a true hero and saves the world. So, Cthulhu sets out to save the world in an epic quest… just so he can conquer it when he breaks the curse! On paper, the concept sounds ridiculous… and is even more so in the actual game! The story doesn’t do anything special; most of the time you just work your way through the nearest dungeon for some reason given by a nearby town such as a strange illness or a dragon and sometimes even just to progress to the next place on the map. The game doesn’t really need a special and epic story though, the writing for each of the party members that join you throughout the game ensures a big story isn’t needed.
Over time, Cthulhu is joined by several companions: seven in total each with their own unique personalities. You can only have four members in your party at one time however and Cthulhu always has to be the first member because otherwise he wouldn’t be the one doing the heroic deeds and wouldn’t be able to get rid of the curse. Thankfully all party members gain experience and level up regardless of whether they take part in battles or not.  Some of my favourites party members are the goth mage October, the alien cat Paws and the old yet clueless Dacre. It is amusing seeing all these radically different characters interact with one another and there is a chat option in the menu just so you can watch them talk among themselves at several points in the game. Almost every bit of dialogue in the game is filled with some joke or reference and you can’t help smiling at every single one.
The gameplay is taken out of a classic turn-based fantasy RPG such as Final Fantasy but with a few unique twists. One of these is the ability to build up a combo. As you attack enemies you add to your combo for every individual strike. Certain moves known as combo breakers have the capability to deal massive damage depending on how high your combo is and I found myself building my combo up until I could deal enough damage to finish off a boss with a final epic strike. They felt almost useless however in normal random battles and I only really used them in boss fights. This brings me to the next twist. After a certain amount of battles you will stop getting randomly assaulted by normal enemies every few steps in a dungeon. I was incredibly thankful for this feature because as someone who likes exploring every inch of a dungeon and collecting everything in it, this made it much more bearable, especially in the more maze-like dungeons. You can still choose to manually fight some normal enemies by manually selecting the fight option in the menu meaning grinding is still possible if you are having trouble with a boss. Finally, there is the unite techniques. Depending on the members you have in your party and the order they are in you can perform various “unite” techniques that use up the turn of two of your members but have the capability for colossal damage and punishing status effects. This encourages experimentation and means you can find a use for all of the party members.
Unfortunately, the base game is woefully short at around 7-10 hours but the generous helping of bonus content more than make up for this. First is the Cthulhu’s Angels bonus campaign. Cthulhu is too lazy to save the world and break the curse himself so he just gets a group of girls to do it for him. I say “bonus campaign” but it is more like a modded base game with a new story(kind of) with new dialogue, bosses, music and playable characters as well as a harder difficulty. Most things remain the same however such as the map, areas towns, most of the dungeons and normal enemies within them making for relatively the same experience with a different story. Nevertheless, it was fun to play through and will probably take a little less time than the main campaign due to the prior knowledge of the world and dungeon layout. There are also a few bonus modes and features such as a bestiary, highlander mode(only one person in a party at a time), score attack mode, overkill mode and a developers commentary which was quite interesting to read as I worked through the game. Finally, you also get a second game: Breath of Death VII which I will cover at another time.
Overall, Cthulhu Saves the World is a refreshing addition to the turn-based RPG genre with its great writing, unique twists to the genre and awesome music.Despite being short, the large amount of bonus content lengthen the playtime quite a bit and for the cheap, cheap price of £2 it is MORE than worth it. I highly recommend it.

It's hard to say more than what's already said. It's a twin stick shooter, the characters are cute, and it's really, really good. Instead, we'll address the common negative comments for the game:
"Game is too hard": there are unlockable EX options to make the game easier; they disable high scores but that shouldn't matter if your goal is to just have fun.
"Game is too hard": There are many different playable characters; if you're having trouble with one character, try another. The character you unlock first is extremely good against bosses, and against the first boss Cactus is pretty servicable. For normal stages (and the Licorice fight), Holly and Lemon are probably the easiest to handle, while characters with narrow shot patterns that don't penetrate (like Cactus) aren't quite as good. Also seriously use your secondary weapons.
"Game is too hard": I'm 35 with old man hands and a crappy trackball mouse, and I found the game a little on the easy side, since weapon switching makes you invulnerable for a really long time (probably .75 seconds).
In other words, if you see a review that claims the game is too hard, chances are that reviewer is bad at video games.

Absolutely excellent little game.
One of the most common things you'll read about it elsewhere on the internet is that it's
This is true-- but OlliOlli's difficulty is fair, fun, and rewarding. Landing tricks is legitimately difficult and feels great. After a few play sessions, you should really start to feel yourself improving.
The controls are extremely simple-- left analog stick to line up a trick, 'A' button to push against the ground or land the end of a trick combo. Tricks are controlled by the directions you push the left analog stick. Releasing the stick causes your character to jump in the air and attempt the trick. Sweeping the stick around in a circle will line up a more complicated trick, based on the distance and direction you sweeped it. The only way to get credit for a trick or a combo is to tap the 'A'button quickly just before you hit the ground. The closer to the ground, the better multiplier you get.
Overall, the system is simple and rewards practice. Chaining together a long combo is quite difficult, and you'll have to chain some pretty ridiculous ones to complete all the objectives in each campaign level.
Speaking of levels-- the "Career" campaign has several "acts" with eight tracks each-- four easy, four hard. Each act has its own art style. There's also a "Spots" mode, where you get to execute precisely one combo before the level ends. Extending that combo gets you more points and a better spot on the leaderboards. The final game mode is the "Daily Grind." It provides a single randomly-generated track that you only get one chance to set a score on. So far, the Daily Grind I've tried has been quite hard.
I'd recommend this game to anyone who enjoys twitchy, timing-based platformers or arcadey, combo-centric skill games. Not for the weak of heart, but ultimately accessible to anyone with a gamepad and the will to improve.
It's also worth mentioning that the soundtrack is excellent.

I really want to give this game a recommendation, I really do. When the game works, you feel like a true Sith. Throwing things at enemies, firing Force Lightning at them or just flat out throwing them off ledges/into walls is immensely satisfying. You feel like a god among men. The problem, though is that the times the game works are few and far between.
Overall, the game just feels wrong on PC. The combat controls are loose and the camera is painful, even with an Xbox 360 controller. Several enemies have way more melee range than you do and are guaranteed a knock down. Their animations are also hard to interrupt, meaning the fastest way to defeat them is actually to use Force Grab and throw them off the nearest cliff/down the closest pit. Using Force Grab to throw things at enemies just does not work most of the time. It sort of works with a controller and about 30% of the time, you'll throw it at an enemy. The other 70% of the time, you'll either throw it off a cliff or into a wall about 30 feet to the side of the enemy. Trying to do it with keyboard/mouse is even more impossible.
Force Lightning is satisfying, but only with the second upgrade where you can actually hold the button and fire lightning for as long as you have Force energy. The first level is useless for the most part as it only affects one or two enemies, though it's nice for stunning them.
I won't comment on the combos because I'm terrible at combos in any game I play and thus consider them stupid in all games.
The quick-time events (and there are a lot of them) are far too quick. You will have to repeat them at least once unless you have above average reaction time. This would be alright except that failing a quick-time often will heal the boss/miniboss, which is a terrible but effective way to pad out a fight's length.
The biggest complaint I have, though, is that the game is riddled with bugs. The game crashed for me three times in the same boss fight. The only time it didn't crash, the boss' attack knocked me out of the world, trapping me outside the boss arena and making the fight impossible to complete. There are numerous other bugs I could add to this list, but those are the worst offenders. Having to restart a boss fight four times because of bugs/crashing is unacceptable and frustrating.

Serious Sam 2 is not the best of the series it is definitely the worst of the 4 main games. But it's still a good game. Yes, I admit, I was turned off by the graphics and decided to never touch it, until it was on sale for a $1.50. And after playing it, I wouldn't spend too much money to buy it, but I think $10 isn't a half bad price for this game. It took me about 16 hours to complete and that's pretty much the length of every Serious Sam game, for me at least. In the way of level design it's mixed. Some levels are very interesting and keep me looking around and then some aren't as well designed. For example, the sewer level is pretty much just a bunch of hallways. But at least the game makes fun of the level, saying that every game has one. And that's why I think some of the bad parts work towards Serious Sam 2's favour. The game acts self aware, so when something stupid happens, it's supposed to be stupid. Now the games have always been self aware about the cheesy humour, but Serious Sam 2 manages to be self aware about pretty much everything in the game. It manages to be self aware about the badly animated cutscenes, not bad but silly sound effects and voice acting, unrealistic characters, enemies, weapons and universe in general, plot and ending. And yes, I don't like the ending either, but at least it's not supposed to be a good ending. They know they don't have the budget to polish everything, so they don't and then use it for the game's humour.
In terms of gameplay, the normal gunfights are no different from the other Serious Sam games, but they manage to change it up with simple but interesting vehicle segments. In a game where you strafe in every single fight, I thought that the vehicle segments might be just taken from any other game around the time, but when in the vehicles, you actually continue strafing in the vehicle which while not completely different from the rest of the game, made it fresh whenever you got one.
All the weapons are the same from the previous games, with the addition of a Zap Gun (which is just a charge up gun to replace the single colt pistol) and Klawdovic which is a bird the flies towards the closest enemy and blows them up. And to replace the Thompson theres double uzis. But besides that the new weapons are pretty much the same except for their design. I might consider this a problem but the aresenal is already sound from the previous 2 encounters that I don't mind how similar they are.
In terms of Boss battles, some were amazing and some were average. I would go into more detail, but I don't want to spoil the good fights.
A lot of the enemies from the first encounter are there, but shoved to the side, for a lot of newer ones. Some specific to the level you're playing which I thought was pretty cool. But they're very, very silly. Which isn't totally a bad thing, since this game is the silliest of the quadrilogy, but it is pretty hard to consider even real with all the stuff that's coming at you in certain parts of the game. And while I don't need to take a Serious Sam game seriously, it is hard to consider it canon with the other games. But, I know I'm probably one of the few people that actually care about the Serious Sam story, so for most people this probably won't be an issue, but it took me out of the game a little.
All in all, it's the weakest of the Serious Sam Quadrilogy, but it's still a good old school shooter. I don't recommend this game to everyone, but if you're a bit lenient about the graphics and think it looks too silly, give it a chance next time it's on sale because I dismissed it and am sorry I did. All the humorous reviews of not being able to stop playing this game are by no means untrue, but there is another side to Factorio.
The game itself is very deep, has lots of content continually added, and overall is just a great game with good mechanics.
However, in my opinion, the game does not have the best repeatability. Through the use of mods the game can be expanded, but only to a certain extent. Everytime you start a new save, everything is the same. There are optimal setups for everything that cannot be improved upon, and since the blueprint library was introduced in beta version 0.15, any factory of yours can and most likely will be cookie cutter. There is no incentive to change designs at all, so the only variability of the game is resources, biters, and spawn locations.
That said, the game itself is very fun and immersive, and by no means should you not spend an easy 20 dollars for hours of content. The actual game itself is an amazing game, and I recommend it, but bear in mind that it may not be easy to repeat without growing bored or tired.

Some of the WONDERFUL Infocom games, such as "Suspended: A Cryogenic Nightmare" actually benefited from being purely text.
I've read many pages of science fiction. Between my two favorite catagories, science fiction and fantasy, the pages literally number well over a million, so there aren't many speculative fiction concepts I've not encountered.
But we're here to discuss "Choice of Robots". First off, on the basis of cost/hour this is among the MOST expensive, shortest computer games I have ever played. True, it was less than $3 (on sale), but lasted under 2 hours (even with starting over on PC #2), most of the time spent in thought. There was nothing new in this game, beyond perhaps some of the more recent concepts not devised yet when I was doing the bulk  of my reading. As far as robotics, Asimov has already said pretty much everything encountered in this story, better. While Dr. Gold has allowed the reader/gamer to create his own character, or explore themselves (however briefly), a writer as good as Asimov (or numerous others) creates a world so real you believe yourself a part of it. As far as feelings of reality, I prefer the latter.
I began it a second time, but only a few pages, so I'm not sure if I "achieved" further. I'd presume I received around 1/10th of the achievements. This presumably means one of two things: 1) either the story branched so often that, even with substantial overlap in story, there were perhaps in excess of 20 endings (seemingly too many to consider equally), or 2) the story was far more fleshed out for a prefered reader/gamer type, and I was not among them. (I don't understand the purpose behind having achievements in this game, except as a selling tool. Why create a "loser" scenario (OR winner) in a game marketed as being an individualistic world? "Personal choice"="wrong choice"?)
This felt less to me a story OR game, and more like a personality test, perhaps as component of a thesis. I admit, by far the majority of the time I spent was in contemplation of what the character I created might actually do if he were real. While the other characters I was given were extremely superficial, I still felt a strong obligation to create as real, AND as good, a world as possible for them to participate in. But despite MY agonizing over choices, I felt the writer rapidly lost interest in my character as I made less "literary" choices. He simply ended the story with no resolution of any kind, leaving the lead character to complete his participation several short paragraphs after life-extending, life-affirming choices. While I anticipated fighting for life using robotics as tool/metaphor, the majority of the story remaining as life choices are considered/corrected, instead I was reading the last paragraph on the final page. The overwhelming feeling was one of abandonment, much like Mary Shelley wrote of Dr. Frankenstein feeling for his creation. Except that the abandonment was of OUR jointly created world.
Quite possibly this game/story simply wasn't written for me. Perhaps if I were educated or intelligent, or imagined greatness, there might have been some AMAZING stories in this game. Instead I'm just a regular guy with personal dreams of home, hearth and health (albeit, while dealing with greatness would be for me, a GREAT story to create, or better still, to participate in.) I've read those other people's accounts lived out THOUSANDS of times in other stories. This time I wanted it to be my story. Perhaps there are choices that would have made it longer or more interesting, but then it would not have been MY story. And after all, wasn't that the whole point?

Transistor is a story-driven RPG with a unique combat style. When in an encounter, you can pause the game and plan your moves (up to a certain cost). The planned moves will be executed afterwards pretty much instantaneously. This enables taking a more strategic approach and setting up satisfying combos. The game features pretty, hand-drawn, graphics.
You can gear yourself with functions. Functions can be abilities, passives applied to abilities and global passives. Every function can be combined with other functions to have a different effect, so the combat will stay fun as long as you have the mindset to keep changing your kit.
The game is pretty fleshed out and definitely worth your time, but there were a few things that I didn't like about it:
The game is linear. You move from encounter to encounter with walking and storytelling in between. I don't think a level progression system is really needed in this game, as you gain levels at a pretty much predefined rate. You can choose to do challenges to boost your level, but these are only available in a predetermined amount in specific places. You can enable limiters to gain levels (perks) earlier but you will gain disadvantageous perks. I personally don't think that this is worth it in the slightest, but it helped increase the game difficulty once I noticed that certain combos were just too strong for the enemies to deal with.
The planned combat does not account for movement of the enemy in any way, therefore you miss a lot of attacks that initially show as having registered. This was quite frustrating before I noticed what was going on.
And then there is one big issue I had with the plot (spoilers):
I just couldn't get into the plot, which I think is pretty important for RPGs.

Legend of Grimrock: a classic dungeon crawling role-playing game. Legend of Grimrock gets it right by keeping the premise simple and making the game easy and interactive while making sure to put the challenge in the combat and the puzzle solving.
You were four prisoners who were shoved into the depths of Mount Grimrock to atone for your crimes, you are free the moment you fall, however you have to escape Grimrock if you want to enjoy your freedom, and that’s the story. There are tidbits of lore and story in scroll, text on walls and various objects you find throughout Grimrock, its simple and that’s honestly for the best.
The game plays up the survival part well with needing to keep your guys fed or risk of getting hungry, health and energy regenerate although slowly, you can rest but risk getting attacked while resting.
Graphics weren’t top notch for the time it came out, but they don’t feel dated or old, they’re more than adequate and the style of the dungeon and its inhabitants is very realistic in tone.  There is no music throughout most of the game; instead you get this creepy ambiance similar to Amnesia or Penumbra games. It isn’t meant to scare as much as it is to create a tone of dread from  hearing ‘things’ in the distance, again the game feels like it’s going more for a realistic immersion.
Combat is much more interesting and tactical, your team is in a 2x2 formation, two in front and back, the two in front are taking the brunt of the damage while the two in back are support, you can switch these positions easily and you often will in order to save companions from death or to rotate dealing damage, spells are cast by selecting the correct rune sequence, you can do this as long as your skill level lets you and you know the combination, you can find scrolls that tell you correct rune combinations, but these aren’t required, you can find them through experimentation, or if you don’t care about finding it out, the internet.
You can also craft in this game various potions from the reagents you find in Grimrock, potions can be simple healing or energizing potions to better damage or even invisibility, again you can find the correct combination through experimentation or scroll and recipes.
Finally the puzzles in the game are much more challenging, there are a few simple and easy ones to begin with, but, even in the first room you start in there are various secret switch to hidden treasures, and as you progress the game starts putting more challenging riddles up for you to solve, some necessary to progress others to great treasures to help you survive. Overall, I felt the puzzle solving in this game was a good balance between challenging while also not needing to be overly difficult.
Legend of Grimrock is a great throwback to dungeon crawling RPGs, it shows that this type of game can easily be done and be fun if done well, it’s simple and easy to get into and actually gave me quite a challenge and I was really impressed once I finished the game, it took me about 20 hours to beat the game, and for $14.99 USD that is not bad at all. I highly recommend this game if you’re looking for good ole fashioned role-playing games, or just something different from the standard fair now-a-days, if you need that more action oriented role-playing game, Grimrock may not be for you, although I still feel it’s just as fun, if not more.
TL/DL; Legend of Grimrock is a classic dungeon crawling RPG with up to 20 hours of gameplay at only $14.99 USD, it’s a steal and well worth the price, its challenging, creepy, and interesting, it’s simple in its gameplay and story making it easy to jump in, it’s worth checking it out of you enjoy RPGs in general, if you need more action oriented RPGs, it may not be for you, but, I encourage you to check it out, you won’t regret it.
-Double Thumbs Up from Royial

TL;DR: The best farming simulator out today.
With that out of the way, I honestly didn't want this game, even though I absolutely love the Farming Simulator series. Check my time played in FS 13 & 15 if you don't believe me. I was very happy with FS 15 and didn't want to chase that carrot of constantly having to replace it every year or so anymore. Seriously.
And even recieving FS 17 as a gift for the holdays I resisted downloading it and playing it til today, Jan. 8th. I did though, hoping it was too close to FS 15, so I could just refund it and put the money in my Steam wallet for some future game or DLC.
Well...after playing it for six hours straight, I logged out, and uninstalled FS 15 without a second thought to all my work there. FS 17 really is that much better than the previous games in the series, in every single way except one. Where the frick is my potato and sugar beet storage!?!
Anyway...with more crop choices (which I've wanted forever), more animal choices (including breeding), the fact the base game has pretty much all the DLCs of FS 15 included,
better ground textures (which my old eyes have been needing),
higher detailed and animated machines...heck they even have working radio's,
a more vibrant, living community now that all of the other plots of land are owned by other farmers that you can work for both money and to get on their good side for better land purchases....geeze....I could go on and on..
So yeah, after playing FS 17 for just one day I knew that this version so far outpaced FS 15 that there was just not going to be any going back and so I removed 15. All that work, but it just didn't matter once I saw all that was available and improved on with 17.
So if you're still on the fence and reading reviews to see if you want to finally make the switch, take it from me, someone who didn't actually want to play this game and was very happy where I was in FS 15...it's worth it.... Geeze, can't believe I'm saying this, but yeah, it is....

I`ve played all wargames franchise (780hrs playing wargame red dragon), and after playing playing this game for a while ( like 350 hours ), i think that this game is "AWESOME".
In my opinion, there are so many improvements on this game that it saddens me to read negative critics that comes from people that had a couple of hours ( not enought to understand the game in my opinion)
Since the begining i had access to the vip beta, and  i have to admit that my first impression was dissapointment. But after giving a lot of chances and time to the game u just fall in love.
First of all, the damage system and the phases. These are the most important differentiating factor between Steel division and Wargame. On Red Dragon the damage is cumulative, so you are able to destroy a unit for example a heavy tank with an Atgm team(antitank guide misile) and destroy the enemy unit with 1 or a couple of misiles, or send  a rush of many many light tanks (cavalry style), so theres always a ways to destroy and enemy even if it is eficient or ineficient .
On Normandy 44 the  damage system its binari, that means that a unit is enabled or not enabled to destroy an enemy unit, as a consecuence of this, on Steel division you units have more value and at the same time are scarce. This encourage a more tactical micromanagent of your units, especially playing as an ally, you will protect at all costs your firefly, your achilles or your 17pdr because its your only chance to deal with a king tiger or even a tige E.
On Gameplay mechanics there are a lot of improvements, even to the point that i  can prefer Steel Division over Wargame just because its more comfortable to manage your troops.For example you can presset the units route, destination and even where the have to unload, this is very usefull when you are deploying units at the begining of the match. There are tools that allowed you to determine area of ​​vision and distance, making more easy to deploy recon units, canons and ambushes.
All this allowe you to have more focus on your tactics an strategies, and not just on your "micro".
By last, i`ve been reading a lot of coments that says that the "game is dead", or "theres no one playing anymore".  Before those comments i want to say that I do not agree with these. I have been playing Wargame Red Dragon for a few years, and think it is an amazing type of stratergy. So I looked forward to Steel Division 44 with excitement.
It's not a terrible game, and it isn't buggy. But it also isn't anywhere as good as Wargame Red Dragon.
The new features added to the game, actually have taken away from the fun and stratergy found in the previous title. The dynamic frontline looks great, and is really clever. Except it follows the position of all your troops, not just command units. So it is impossible to penetrate, flank or ambush with troops, as the dyanmic battle front immediately tells your opposition where you are moving troops forward, or lying them in wait. This removes a huge amount of stratergy from the game. And it is disaster because it makes destroying heavy tanks near impossible, as their front armour is so strong. They need to be ambushed.
There is also some serious balancing issues between Allies and Axis it seems to me. Balancing wasn't perfect in Red Dragon, but you had a good chance with a good deck from any side. But in this it heavily favours the Axis. The Allieds air power should overcome this, but planes seem to panic and flee as soon as they hit heavy AA, before even dropping a single bomb or rocket.
Which brings me to the fear factor. Troops seem to fall back and get pinned way too easily. And when they do, all you can do is watch, whilst a terrible AI model makes them flap around like civilians at a go kart course. I enjoy the idea of the new feature, but it really once again has removed any stratergy and chance of winning against the odds, or unbalances. Making advancing very very hard, a less you happen to have the exact right units at the right place against a n00bish opposition.
So as you would of read on other reviews, this turns the whole game in to a clicking game, of just chucking units in to hold the line. And really having to look hard to find a whole to exploit, if you have the right units, at the right time, in the right place. Too rarely this seems to occur. It feels more like a WW1 game, then WW2 with the lack of tactics able to be played.
Oh also, because of all this, hardly anyone seems to be palying it, despite being a new game. The servers are as empty as Red Dragon was after 2 years. Not so soon after release.
So if your not sure, I'd save your money, as the longevity of this game is very limited, due to the nature of not being able to be tactile, losing any real feel of achievement and excitement of different out comes and situations.

This is another game by Supergiant Games, and like their previous game Bastion, it has great visuals, one of my favorite soundtracks courtesy of Darren Korb, that same gravelly voice (this time as a talking sword instead of a narrator), and a good story (although I admit I had trouble following said story at times, it's a bit more complex than Bastion's post-apocalyptic tale). Basically, it's stylish as heck, even more so than Bastion. Super customizable combat, but I kinda hated how they gated bits of lore behind said combat system, requiring you to try out every single ability in every possible configuration to read it all. Seriously though, go play this game (and Bastion, go play that too).

inb4: I didn't like Bastion.
I didn't like how the developers threw a dark theme, a fantasy world with bright colors, a modern oriental soundtrack and a cliché cowboy narrator into one pot. I didn't like the stupid story where you create crystal shards to save the world and some dumbass destroys the crystal again because he argued with a girl. I didn't like how the narration took the immerson from the game. I didn't like the gameplay which could have come straight out of a flash game.
Initially, I didn't want to try Transistor because of my experience with Bastion. But it's very cheap during the current sale (-85%), so I took a closer look at it and I figured that the setting looks really interesting and more coherent than Bastion's. The gameplay looks better, too.
However, this is only partly true.
Alright, the combat system is quite cool. You can customize your funcions (skills) from scratch, you can pause the combat and program a short sequence of functions like in the VATS system of Fallout. However, it's easy. Upgrade your ranged attack with additional backstab damage. Pause the combat, jump behind the enemy, spam the ranged attack. Done. For weaker enemies, just spam the area effect bomb circle.
This tactic worked in the beginning of the game and after 1 hour I still won every battle (even boss fights) without ever losing more than 50% HP.
Pathfinding is somewhat buggy, especially on short distances.
But alright. The combat works. What's more interesting are the story and the world. And here is where the game fails in my opinion.
Look at the screenshots. The world is beautiful. It's even more beautiful ingame. But the ♥♥♥♥ing narrator can't ♥♥♥♥ing shut his ♥♥♥♥ing mouth. ♥♥♥♥.

Play it on the Wii just for the novelty of it. It's fun. Don't even bother with any other edition. To begin: they're not all the same. Making separate versions of games for different platforms? When did we start doing this again? Each version has different levels. Also: it's not a very good game. It's fun at first but it gets tedious VERY quickly.
Playing it on the Wii was cool just for the fun of swinging my Wiimote around like a lightsaber (which I stopped doing once I figured out I could make the teeniest wrist flicks to perform any of the same actions as swinging for the fence). Playing with a gamepad is boring and playing with (*shudder*) keyboard and mouse is just god-awful.
Like I said: it's just tedious. The boss battles are boring, the level designs aren't very intriguing and there just isn't much to do. You run through some maps, swinging your lightsaber at people and force-pushing a lot. This is Jedi Knight Lite. Actually, porting JK2 or JA into this engine would be awesome.
One of the big drawbacks to those games was the clunky method of switching between active force powers (or the clunky method of having every individual force power mapped onto a keyboard/mouse button). TFU gets rid of all that by (about damn time) consolidating all your force powers into essentially push/pull, lightning and choke/grab. You mean I don't have to push an extra button to activate Force Jump? I'm simply able to jump higher? Why did it take twenty years for a developer to figure out how stupid it was for "jump high" to be a different button push from "jump?"
But I digress. Game mechanics and play: fun. Variation in levels, enemies, bosses, etc: nonexistent. This is a very cool game that gets boring very quickly.

But if you liked Jedi Outcast or Jedi Academy or Star Wars in general then this game is for you! All the classic force powers, the lightsaber moves, characters and the environments combined with a fairly decent story make it worth picking up if you see it on sale. Just avoid the Force Unleashed 2; a half baked follow up that does the franchise no favours.

I would describe the game as a great start.
It's a twin-stick shooter with bullet hell elements where the character shot-type design is pretty varied. It has
animations and a camera that rather impressively captures long-ranged and/or fast abilities that most games would have trouble with. It runs on a potato and usually looks nice.
The main problems with the game are that the difficulty curve is totally ecletic, and that the bosses are very bland and uninteresting. That is a huge let-down in a genre where the bosses are usually the main attraction. The game is never particularly difficult, due to the interesting "Battery" mechanic where you can only die by failing to score a certain amount over time, instead of dying when your health depletes. I'm generally positive about this mechanic but my god does the game tend to use it as a crutch for completely negligent enemy and area design. The main source of difficulty is the sheer amount of enemies spawning at any given time, which can get very difficult to handle in stages with gimmicks. Despite the zone-based design, the difficulty of each stage appears to be totally arbitrary since in nearly all cases, smaller stages are harder than larger stages. This means that I managed to S+ rank three levels on the open-ended final zone on my first try, but I struggled to even get a C rank on a second zone level with tight corridor design and a rotating flamethrower.
The bosses similarly seem to defy a curve. the second boss has an expanding and retracting swarm of insects protecting it with extremely little room to move once they retract on you. But the fourth boss's
attack is a curtain of bullets with obvious character-size holes inbetween them.
Then there is the extremely bizarre decision of having barely two frames of invulnerablility after getting hit...in a bullet hell. This is what I mean by the game using the battery mechanic as a crutch. In any other twin-stick bullet hell this would be absolutely inexcusable, but because you can never "die" as a result of the time-attack design, I can't say I'm bothered about it. Batteries are a
interesting mechanic, but it's obvious that they were used here to prevent people from whining about the difficulty.
Pretty much the definition of "points for trying". I would have been much harder on the game if it wasn't an independent project.

I didn't know what to expect from this game, I only knew it belonged to a genre that diverges from what I usually play, but a few minutes in and I was in love with it. The secrets, the combat, the atmosphere, it sucked me in and I just had to complete it, and so I did. I'll share my experience now.
About it's mechanics, you control a party of 4 characters. You're able customize their race, class, attributes and set custom portraits, I myself made an epic party with my closest friends. The battle formation is a square, so 2 characters lead and the others stay in the back, this encouraged me to balance my party members with melee or ranged attacks. The combat happens in real time and you can only move in tiles, each character have two available slots that you can place weapons, potions or other items into, you click these slots to perform actions, ones that depending on your char skills may "cool-down" faster. ( One of my chars had max level sword ability, so he could strike twice as fast ). I enjoyed the combat A LOT, and after a while getting used to, you'll be predicting enemies actions and flanking them. Just be careful not to end up cornered, I can still.. hear.. their.. screams.. *arghhhhhh*.
There are potions to be crafted, magic to be discovered, secret areas which may grant you powerful unique weapons or a headache in case you didn't save often. Puzzles are well crafted, I didn't feel the need to "google" my way trough the game, though one or two times I was stuck searching for a solution.
The graphics are Okay considering you spend all your game time inside of a dungeon, there will be variety as of three or four ambient styles for about 10 levels and another metal based theme at the end game. It does a good job making you believe that you're really trapped inside a place and there is no way out, they nailed atmosphere! Sound is of good quality as well.
I don't have anything bad to say about this game, honestly. The dungeon's ambiance may get repetitive for some people, or the combat may be hard to get used to, but I enjoyed the whole game since each level is clever and has it's own set of characteristics, puzzles, etc... Can't wait to play the second game now!
tl;dr
+ Puzzles and more puzzles
+ Replay value ( try new builds or custom maps! )
+ Length, not too long, not too short
+ Nostalgia aspect for some people
- Managing consumable items during combat can be a painfull thing

Wow.
This is a WOW game.
This game doesn't have cutting edge graphics, the audio is slightly better than average, and the genre is as old as, what, the 1980s?
This game isn't great because of some stupid parlor trick. It's good because it's a near-perfect implementation of a specific class of game; the old PC dungeon crawler.
If you love finding secret wall switches, solving puzzles and finding loot, and eating a giant roasted maggot-on-a-stick because you're desperate to eat, then this is the game for you.
If you want a fantasy FPS with lots of jumping and airducking, this isn't for you, GTFO.
Legend of Grimrock doesn't try and improve much on the old classic dungeon crawler game design, I think that works well for it, and I don't think they do anything really new or crazy that hasn't been done in dungeon crawlers before. They just put modern graphics and sound together into a game and implemented it well.
The game doesn't have any music beyond the title screen, but the ambient background through the game is pleasant and detailed. Turn the volume up, because sounds of the dungeon will alert you to nearby foul beasts and secrets.
The background story is compelling and interesting, but nothing too deep. Secrets are found in the dungeon, and a reason for being is evident, but they leave the details up to your imagination, which is probably for the best. You can't climb back up. Your only way out is down. The story is your journey along the way.
The last few levels are spooky and the game has a very fulfilling final battle.
Secrets are plentiful, so pay attention. There were a couple of puzzles which had me really baffled, including two that were required to proceed with the story. I don't recomend ruining the challenge for yourself by reading a walkthrough online, but if you get stuck in the story, it's there for you. The best thing to do is sit and think. With two specific exceptions that I can mention, most of the puzzles are evident if you just use your brain for more than thirty seconds.
I do have a complaint regarding the final puzzle in the game (Minor spoiler warning): There are four items which need to be placed around a single block in a room. Two of them are pretty easy to figure out, but the small gear in particular has a non-obvious arbitrary placement location which should be fixed. Even if you have the right item on the right wall, you have to click it on a very specific small area that doesn't offer any clue that it's the right part to go in the right place.
Also, the level 9 riddle room had me really stuck for awhile. I just didn't get the clues and had to randomly guess at it until I figured it out.

This game is great! And yet I give it thumbs down. Why?
The game uses good game mechanics. Choosing your battlegroup is fantastic. The battle itself feels great and in my opinion looks great as well.
The major downfall of the game however is it's lack of variety and the many opportunities that have been lost. There is so much potential in the game mechanics but they are barely being used. The game could offer an epic campaign possibly even in cooperative mode. What we got however  seems like a campaign that was developed last minute in order to promote it as a single player game as well and to justify the full price tag.
It's not that the campaign missions are too hard. Yes, they are hard but they're also annoying as hell. Being forced to micromanage at several frontlines at the same time is just no fun under pressure of timers. It becomes tedious work and the only way to manage it is to slow down time which makes the whole concept of a real time strategy game absurd.
Then there is the lack of variety in maps. Almost every map feels and looks the same. I understand that this is the landscape in Normandy however maybe that was a bad decision by the development team to call the the game Normandy 44.
This point of criticism however could have been avoided by allowing modders to create their own maps. I suppose they will be coming as paid DLC. And from what I have read the modability of this game seems to be pretty complicated as well.
I have not played that much multiplayer. I kind of enjoyed the Co-operative side but when I did play multiplayer it seemed plagued by connectivity issues.
In conclusion and to put it in a simple sentence to review the game:
Great concepts, great game mechanics but very very poor execution by the developers when it comes to the actual game.

** Tiny, tiny spoilers. But nothing plot related! **
"Hey, Red. We're not gonna get away with this, are we?"
You are Red, a lounge singer, who, for reasons unknown at the start of the game, is missing her voice. Coupled with your talking sword, you pick yourself up, and wander into a seemingly desolate world...
Having only just finished the game, I am still finding it hard to put my experience into words. There is this nagging yearning to return to the beautifully vivid cyberpunk landscape, which reveals its secrets to you slowly, through varied means as the game progresses. I found myself scouring every area, worried that I would miss something! Because of how the story is told, I was hungry for every tidbit of information, be on the terminal machines (which would reveal anything from the local weather forecast, to current opinion polls!) to discarded items I would come across - for me, this added a certain depth and realism to the world.
From the opening scene, I found myself delving deeper into the mysterious city, looking for clues to help me try and piece together what had happened. The game offers no explanations at the outset about who you are, what your motivations are, what is happening in the ever shifting environment and why oh why, you have such a sexy sounding sentient sword quipping in with his conversational commentary every now and then!
I'll come back to the sword in a moment!
Transistor has so much going for it, the game is a slick, sophisticated masterpiece, that just oozes coolness. Put the gorgeous hand drawn artwork together with the catchy techno music, and occasional soulful piece by Red herself, and you have the makings of something that looks and sounds great-- but wait, did I mention the addictive combat system?
Personally, I am a fan of being allowed to plan out my combat strategy and moves, so the fact that I was able to effectively freeze time so that I could plot my moves and combinations, and then bring up the battle to normal speed, made for some very satisfying combat! Not only that, the game encourages you to experiment with abilities, offering them one by one as you level up. The mixing and matching can be very rewarding, as you have the freedom to enhance existing abilities (want to nip around super speedy-like, while making a decoy copy of yourself each time you stop!?) or to create new abilities altogether!
Alongside the unfurling mysteriousness outside, are secret backdoors, allowing Red into her own personal space, this is where I'd send her to relax, to lay on her hammock and talk to her sexy sword.. or force her through extra doors to try and beat the various and quickly escalating challenges! This experimenting area helped me realise the full potential of certain abilities and better grasp the combat mechanics, away from the main story. And well, who doesn't like ticking off achievements too?!
Now! Back to the sword! I have to be honest, I could have sat here, with Red standing in one place, shifting wayward strands of hair out of her face, and listened to her sentient sword talking alllllll night! His voice! His comments! I won't give too much away, but I appreciated the voice carrying me through what could be a very lonely environment, he added some heart, and an insight into Red's life prior to the events of the game.
In short, buy this game! Whether it is on sale or full priced, it is worth every penny. The slight draw back is that it is relatively short, but this is to be expected with many indie games. There is plenty of replay value with the New game plus, which allows you to revisit the world, and pick up on things  you have missed, as well as additional dialogue, and of course, it gives you more time with the sword! Yees!

One of the best PC games ever made. I originally got this game back in 1999 when it was first released, and 16 years later it's still fun to play. The Steam version also comes with both expansion packs.
The game had amazing optimization for its time. It ran smooth on a 400 MHz Celeron, even with a huge park. Chris Sawyer is a programming genius for making the game run so well. It still works on modern systems too, and runs flawless on Windows 8.1 and Windows 10.
There is a large variety of different rides to build, and you can build your own roller coaster designs. There are also lots of different scenarios to play and unlock, each with their own goals.
The only downsides to this game are the lack of mod support, and that there is no sandbox mode. There are, however, a few scenarios with unlimited money, though they still have goals you have to reach, and failing them will result in your park being permanently closed.
Still, it's an amazing game, even to this day. I would recommend if you enjoy building simulators and/or theme park management games, or just for the nostalgia if you played it years ago.

This game offers an opportunity that only creativity games can offer. Your only limits are your imagination...... and amount of land..... and money. Okay, yes, there are limits. But the opportunity that it gives is everyone's fantasy, be it large, or small, to make their own rollercoaster and run their own theme park. The game is a massive time sponge, you WILL end up spending more time making just one rollercoaster than you thought, and it really takes into consideration about momentum and intertia so that when the coaster goes up a hill to create more intensity and fun for the guests, you're not going to lose momentum and roll all the way back down and hit the train behind the first one, and potentially kill someone.
Go ahead and buy the first RCT to learn the ropes of theme park management, but I'd recommend you buy the third one afterwards. It's in 3-D and you can intentionally kill someone.

I am primarily writing this review due to nominating “Cthulhu Saves the World” for the Steam Award’s custom category “Best use of an Lovecraftian Mythos in a Turn Based Comedy”. This little gem is a top down turn based rpg reminiscent of NES/SNES generation RPGs. The game opens with Cthulhu rising from the depths of the ocean with the intention of destroying the world. Unfortunately for Cthulhu a mysterious stranger seals his power away until he proves himself a true hero. This sets Cthulhu on his quest to nobily regain his powers so he can then complete his initial goal of destroying the world. All of the side characters are very entertaining including: “Sharp” a talking sword, a cat from outer space named “Paws”, the ever optimistic “Umi” who wants to marry Cthulhu, “Goth” an edgy necromancer who can’t control the dead, and a couple others who were not in my party. The dialogue between these characters is very tongue n cheek with some genuinely funny moments making the story very amusing at times. Another great bonus to this 6 to 10 hour games is the price. It retails for $2.99 bundled with”Breath of Death VII”, but I think I bought it for $0.99 on sale. The only downside is the turn based combat does become a little repetitive by the end. All in all, it is a dirt cheap funny RPG that harkens back to the classics NES titles like Final Fantasy and Zelda. So join Cthulhu quest to save the world, so he can regain his power, so he can well destroy the world.

It's alright for a free-to-play game. However, I was expecting to receive more than what I actually got.
First of all, the typing mechanism is pretty much useless. You just mash random buttons to spell out pre-determined words when conversing with Emily. Either just have the dialogue choices be a simple click and that's it, or let the users get to type in their own questions for Emily.
Second, your choices DO NOT MATTER. There are only two endings, one of which is Emily ending the discussion in Chapter 5 very abruptly if you treated her terribly in Chapter 4. The other one, which most of you will probably get on your first try, is pretty much the standard ending to this game. You and Emily's friendship ceases to exist. She goes back to dating her ex-boyfriend, so there is no way for your character and Emily to end up together. Then your "friend" Mike starts dating this girl Emma that you meet at college (you'll meet Mike and Emma at whatever college you choose to go to), so there is no way to end up with Emma. In the end, no matter how nicely you might have treated Emily, your kindness goes unappreciated. Emily comes off as a real manipulative ♥♥♥♥♥ who takes out all of her frustrations on you for no good reason. She asks to come over and see you and then later accuses you of taking advantage of her when she was in a very vulnerable emotional state.
Third, why couldn't the player message anybody else on their friends list? The player gets to see other people's profiles, such as Mike and Emma, and yet there is no option to even just send a quick "hello". That's some missed potential right there.
If this wasn't a free-to-play game, I'd strongly suggest you all to not purchase this game. Since it is free however, play it if you want, but there is no replay value.

Steel Division: Normandy 44.  I've never felt so conflicted by a game in a genre that I admire such as this one.
When it was first announced, the hype I had was great, made by Eugen Systems, the same publishers of the incredible 'Wargame' series.  Now instead of a Cold War period, it was WWII, which was something I had often wished for in a game, I mean there's Men of War AS2, but I wanted something on a much larger scale.
When I finally got it pre-release I was expecting a very similar set up to the Wargame UI.  But, when I played it for the first couple of times, and saw it's features, I was somewhat disappointed, I know that was the pre-release, however my pros and cons list still continue to be relavent since the official release date.  Cool new features were added like new divisions and maps but I still felt that it had fallen a tad short.  Here are my reasons why: Note - a lot of my comparisons will be linked to Wargame, specifically Wargame: Red Dragon.
1 - Deck building - Steel Division: Normandy 44 uses the same battlegroup builder as the Wagame series is known for.  I would spend hours in the Armoury screen on Wargame, but purusing through and seeing the enormous options and availability you had to customise a battlegroup for any nation or alliance you wanted.  SD:N44 has this feature, but it's a huge downgrade, that you can't view the entire armoury like you could in Wargame, you can only see the available units for a specific historic division.  I get that Wargame is based on hyerthetical Cold War conflict and SD:N44 is based on real events, but it would be lovely just to have everything available on one screen.
2 - Graphics - The graphics in SD:N44 are much lower quality than that of Wargame.  Wargame was made in 2014, Steel Division was made in 2017.  Which game would you assume to have better graphics?
The details of the models themselves are nice, yet it feels as if there's something missing.  The terrain and environment graphics are standard.  This leads me onto the explosions and munitions effects..... If the game had any!!  The game seems to be completely void of any kind of large explosion or fireball effects that Wargame showcased beautifully.  The feature of a flare line following mortar fire / tank rounds are weird and unrealistic.  Wargame was loved because it was so realistic.
3 - Obsticles / Hedgerows - I get that the Allied invasion of Normandy was hindered by the masses of hedgerows and farms, and the game includes these nicely.  The problem is, pretty much every map is identical.  You face hardly no new challenge from map to map.  No new terrain to negotiate, no new hinderences, just fields and hedgerows and some settlements here and there.  The hedgerows present an unrealistic block to your ranged LOS.  Infantry and vehicles are unable to shoot through them, not even in Fire at Position mode.  I get that this represents the sheer challenge of fighting from field to field, but after a while becomes tedious.
I think I've slated the game enough now.  There are plenty of things that I do like.
1- Moral - I like the advanced moral system.  When a unit is under intense fire, it'll get 'Pinned Down' and will be unable to move or return fire.  This is especially great when it's not happening to you.  If a unit is overwhelmed it'll Fall Back.  I really like this, you rarely see a RTS that incorporates a realistic moral mechanic.  Wargame's moral system (built into SD:N44) based units at four different moral stages; Calm, Worried, Shaken and Panicked.  There is a routing mechanic mentioned on the Wiki, but in my playtime have never witnessed a routing unit, this has somewhat been replaced by the Falling Back feature and the surrender feature, which enemy forces will give in if your forces get too close.  Some targets, particularly unarmed, such as supply trucks can be captured.  Something I wish could be done on Wargame.
2 - New Conquest - I think the biggest thing I like is the Front Line feature, that shows how much land control is being lost or won, this is a nice alternative to the sectors system in Wargame, and is more accurate to the battle in question.  It makes the Conquest game mode a lot more challenging, by constantly moving up and taking more ground.  Better than Wargame's capture and defend feel.
3 - Numbers - WWII campaigns in other games all too often seem to be a few guys against an onstaught of enemies, which are often controlled by very thick AI.  SD:N44 campaign features hundreds of units on the map, both allied and axis forces.  Just like Wargame, the AI is pretty decent, and puts up a fight.  It's tricky, strategically demanding and can be so demoralising if you lose, but it's such a boost when you win, and that's something I absolutely love about a game.
As the game was 'co-piloted' by Paradox, I'm assuming that there'll be a ton of DLC that will come out soon, as is Paradox's way...  I'm hoping they'll include features that I feel have been left out.
I would love to think that Steel Division: Normany 44 is the beginning of a whole series of games spanning the WWII theatres.  Could there be plans for a Pacific, African, Italian or Soviet theatre etc?  I sure hope so.
I have to conclude, that as this game has only been out for a few months, there will probably be various updates.  As Eugen is the developer, and because of the time period, as well as how much effort has gone into this game, dispite it's draw backs.  I will recommend this game.

This is my favourite "modern warfare" RTS of all time, and I have played quite a few. I have long ago realized that I cannot write a short review , but I will try. I give this game a 9.5/10, because the sounds and graphics could use a little work.
Gameplay: Very good tactical gameplay, no base building, more realistic ranges and pretty much everything (e.x. rifles have a range of 300 meters, CoH rifles have a range of 30). Maps are tens of square miles in size. There is no Fog of War, but there is a very realistic Line of Sight system that takes into account the surrounding terrain and the "optics" of your units. Vehicles have a special damage system, no health, instead every attack that can penetrate armor has a chance to inflict a status effect (driver stunned, transmision damaged) or insta-kill. There are no repairs. Infantry is exposed in the open. All units have a "stress" level that increases when fired upon, maximum stress leads to pinned infantry or retreating vehicles. You can manually retreat pinned infantry.
Graphics: Nothing special, the vehicles are detailed but the human figures are "blurry" and don't have too many animations (no crouching or falling prone for example) but at least they are not holding MP40s and Sten Guns by the magazine. Also, most of the time you will only be seeing "ants on the ground" because of the map sizes.
Sound: The sound is not very good, the firearms don't sound as they do in reality, but the sounds do convey a basic message, where there is a firefight, where the enemy vehicles are (roughly) and so on.
Voice Acting: I'm a sucker for good voice acting. I stayed with Company of Heroes 2 long after the fun stopped just for the voices (and other sound effects). The voice acting here is controversial. For me, it sounds as if the soldiers themselves were trying to sound epic, it has that sort of "untrained actor" feel. At first I thought it was just plain bad, but it very quickly grew on me. No other game has troops actually singing a line (Gory Gory for the Airborne, Sturm Oder Schnei for Panzers, We'll Hang Out the Washing on the SIegfried Line and of course "It's a Long Way to Tipperary for the Brits). Also, all nationalities speak in their own language (including the French and Polish).
Finally, the game has a distinct problem with a lack of players, which is one of the reasons I'm writing this review. Many players quit because they found the balance was off (I haven't noticed, pretty much all of the units have authentic stats and the game plays well), and that this game is not Wargame: Normandy (the other Eugen title). I played Wargame after playing this, and to me, this is a better, more streamlined (but not dumbed down) game.
I honestly hope you will purchase this game and join the player base. Every regular player is of great value to this great game, and while the single player AI is quite good, the game still shines best when played with other humans.
EDIT: The singleplayer is still great, I have 70  fun hours of singleplayer alone.

Probably the best recent Battlefield game out there. Battlefield 3 was alright but the look and feel of this game beats it by far. The sound design is amazing, gunfire can be heard across the battlefield and reverberates deafeningly when firing indoors. The guns have rich, deep sound, and while not entirely realistic, they don't sound tinny like in Battlefield 3. You'll notice that if you stop shooting in BF3, everything is pretty much quiet if you aren't in the middle of a fight. In Bad Company 2, you can hear the sounds of firefights raging in the distance and can often locate them purely through sound. It really adds to the action and makes it feel like you're just one soldier in the middle of a huge warzone. This also has more destructibility than Battlefield 3. Pretty much every building can be leveled with grenades, C4 or other explosives. The maps are very varied with lots of possible routes and positions for different classes. All in all, an excellent game, and my favorite multiplayer shooter. Consider getting the Vietnam expansion, it includes period weapons, armor, and even music, which really helps set the mood.
