FIRST OFF: Victory, to me,  is NOT a racing SIM. IT IS NOT PAY TO WIN to the best of my knowledge. This game seems like a hybrid...very customizable, but you don't have to count every tooth on every gear in your car. Yet, every change I make to my car, no matter how small, affects it's performance. I like that.
With all the control options, I must say that Victory is the most accessable/intuitive racing game I have ever played and the community is extremely helpful towards new players. My steering wheel I use (MS Sidewinder FF Wheel)* can be adjusted in game. I would recommend enabling "Reverse force feedback" for those having issues with the "feel" of your wheel. Worked for me. Graphics are good. The scenery isn't as alive as some racing games. I haven't seen huge crowds or sponsors I recognize. You'll forget about that the moment a race starts.
The Sound, to me, is spectacular! I can hear the audible whine of gears straining in the transmission as the engine approaches 12000rpm. I can hear the realistic "WHOOSH!" of the wind getting louder and louder as I pass 200mph! THAT CORNER IS COMING UP FAST!      WHAM!
You will learn every day that you are getting a bit faster with each lap. You'll find yourself starting a server of your own and inviting people to your race. And you can set up a race that will temporarily degrade the performance of seasoned drivers. It levels the playing field. People flock to these "handicap" races! That's my experience.
Sooooo...............
OLD FOGIE'S BEWARE! KEEP YOUR HEART MEDICATION HANDY! XD
YOUNGSTER'S, STOP LAUGHING AND WATCH OUT! OLD FOGIE'S WILL KICK YOUR A**!
OLD FOGIE'S! HELP OUT YOUNGSTERS! GIVE THEM ADVICE AND GUIDANCE! RAISE THEIR FRAGILE SELF-ESTEEM! LET'EM WIN, ONCE!
YOUNGSTER'S! THEY BOUGHT IT! NOW, IT'S ON! THE SECRET TO WINNING IS OUT! HA HA!
Truth is, I haven't found the "secret" to winning. My experience is that skill and practice, along with the community exchanging ideas for the betterment of whoever is asking for assistance....THAT is most important to me having fun in this game.
Again, all I have to say is WOW! The sense of speed while driving in Victory and the excitement of racing others online...and losing to them...again and again...can be matched only when you win your first race! AWESOME!
I've played a lot of mostly EA(tm)'s Formula and NASCAR(R) series and appreciate the vast mechanical customization available in these games. I would spend hours and hours fine tuning and customizing my car. The pre-race practice, tuning again, qualifying and racing on actual real-world tracks was awesome! (Customization on the car bodies used to be great. Over time, I've noticed that I'm having to buy "custom cars" as DLC....hmmm.) Anyway....
Then I got a job. And a relationship. Then the military. Back to school...again! Where did all my time go?
I accept now that my alone time is at a premium and micromanagement of every tooth of every gear in the tranny is not feasable at this time. Man! What a bummer!
Victory: The Age of Racing has enabled me to use a system of simple* sliders to adjust each of the major mechanical  groups on my car....gears, suspension, downforce, brakes, etc. I am up and on the track in moments. And, yes, the in-game customization is, in my view, the best in the biz. Check out some user made cars online. Yep, most are created by ppl like you and me. A very, very intuitive system with too many combination to go into. I love the customization in Victory. The only thing that beats it WAS early NASCAR(R) Sims where I could practically create a car skin with my face on it! As I mentioned earlier, it seems I gotta buy many cars from EA(tm), now.
PLEASE, I have never spent any more $$$ than the original purchase price on this game! As far as I know, and I'm approaching 700 hours of game time, all purchases through "gear credits".  "Gear credits" are awarded by driving hotlaps for the best time, or racing humans from around the world. Believe me, there are good drivers out there! Few are playing at this time, that's what I'm seeing.
I believe there is an anticipation in the community of major news. The standard events are down, but I can create a server and people who are in "stealth mode", where players can  choose to appear offline to do personal stuff (creating cars, practicing, etc) suddenly join my race. It appears many times that the servers are dead. Only a very few times have I put out the "bait" and sat there on my track and no one joins. Some people don't want to be interrupted while they are perfecting their car. Sometimes I am busy and don't necessarily want to race....I'm in the middle of finishing my next Formula Car!
BTW: Races are restricted to cars of the same point class. The amount of points you put into your car will have a great influence on it's performance. These 0-60/70 points are put into YOUR OWN CAR, CREATED BY YOU. The points are allocated to your own preference. You can customize aerodynamics, downforce, braking, grip, etc and,  more importantly, EVERY car is different, in my opinion. AND I CANT, NO MATTER HOW HARD I TRY, FIND ANYTHING REMOTELY "PAY-TO-WIN" HERE! BELIEVE ME, I'M A HUGE FAN OF PAY-TO-WIN AND VICTORY IS NO "PAY-TO-WIN"!
Victory: Age of Racing will make your hair stand on end.
If you think you're not getting anything out of it, like me...losing a lot more than winning, ask someone in game to give you some advice on a generic set up for your car. You will be amazed at the level of control you'll gain when you understand what the points and sliders do to your car.

I've played this game for 25 hours as of this review, but AAC is already one of my favorite games.  It's extremely addictive, and this game caused the first time I've ever had strain in my directional key fingers in my ~25 years of PC gaming.  It was a subtle ache that felt so good because it reminded me how much fun I'd been having.
The art style is modern futuristic.  The music is pumpin' and really gets you into the game.  The sound effects are absolutely perfect.  The characters are simultaneously cute and cool in every way, and each has their own unique style.  I love them.  The simultaneously cute and cool style of this game sets it apart from any other futuristic game I've ever played.
This is a game with an example of a perfect difficulty curve.  It starts out very easy and increases in difficulty at steady rate.  It took me about 8 hours to beat the game the first time, and 4 or 5 of those hours were spent on the last boss.
While I think this game is incredibly good, there are a few minor technical flaws I encountered that I'll cover in the next few paragraphs.
I found that disabling vsync for lower input latency helped me, as their vsync implementation seems to add quite a lot of input latency.  With the frame rate I'm getting, I barely notice any tearing.  Also, the isometric camera mode makes the game a little easier for me, and I was able to start getting some very high scores using it, as it just aligns with my brain.
This game does have multiplayer, but it is local co-op only (not even LAN, unfortunately).  It does not support multiple keyboards and mice, so at least one of the players must use a gamepad.  My brother and I played it together and it was quite an enjoyable experience, but there is one major flaw with the multiplayer camera.  The camera is so zoomed in that often, one player or the other goes off the screen, making it much more difficult for that player temporarily.  I hope this is fixed in any sequels, expansions, or patches of this game.
The player character is not locked to the center of the camera, which makes mouse aiming require a bit of extra effort to know where your character is on the screen, making leading shots and close-range angles more difficult than they could be if the player was always centered.  This is an extremely minor complaint to me, but one I figured I should address in my review for completion.  The bullets are fast enough that simply mousing over most enemies gets the job done.  Obviously, this does not affect gamepad users.  I hope an option to enable a locked camera with a more distant zoom level is added, as it would make the game even more enjoyable for mouse users like me.
I am a Dvorak keyboard layout user, and I also use qwerty's ESDF key positions for movement in other games.  This game doesn't support other layouts than qwerty, unfortunately, so I had to switch my keyboard layout to qwerty.  It also doesn't support rebinding controls, but the in-game binds are only directional movement (WASD), fire weapons (LMB), and switch weapons (RMB).  I was annoyed and confused for the first few seconds of gameplay, but I switched my keyboard layout to qwerty and wasn't bothered any more.  It's not a big deal, though it would be kind of nice if it was keyboard-layout-agnostic by using keycodes instead of letters internally, like many other games do.
Overall, excellent game, and a new favorite.  I would recommend it to almost anyone.  If there was a rating system, I'd rate it 9/10, with the 1 off only being due to the small technical drawbacks I experienced.
Edit: I've now earned 100% of the achievements in this game.  This is the first game that made me want to do so, because it's so fun.  It took me 107 hours, though I was earning S+ rank on the first 18 levels with every android for a large portion of that time.
While I still love the game, I've discovered several more issues that if fixed, could really improve the game.  While I don't remember all of them, I'll describe the most bothersome one.
The player character's aim lags behind the cursor.  The crosshair cursor is already a software cursor, so it is already slightly delayed behind the mouse movement.  However, even after pointing it to the right spot, the character's gun is not pointed to the same spot if it has moved in the last frame.  This is most noticeable when playing the sniper android, Shiitake. Why doesn't someone make a game like that again?!!
No seriously, let me know if you see one, because that's what this game seems to be going for but it sadly misses the mark.
I would be more forgiving and I would even give this game a positive except that the mis-steps they took are downright bewildering.
First what do I love about this title...
It really is incredibly challenging.  The puzzles, battles, and resource management is unforgiving which is a nice throwback to the "good old days".  I love that they took that risk here, because usually it makes the difference between a grind and compelling, rewarding gameplay.  Grimrock is a nice reminder of the days when games weren't all just an endurance contest, and not everyone could beat every game given enough time.
The first thing you'll notice is that this game is fun. Actually, really fun.  You can jump right in without any help and start adventuring.  The puzzles feel like first-person zelda and the written "clues" are a great homage to the first-generation of PC rpg titles.  I love the creepy dream sequences, and the customizable party pics are a great touch that is long overdue.  The biggest issue this game struggles with slowly becomes apparent with the combat system.
There is a gaping hole in what should be simple mechanics and functionality of the UI and especially combat.  The spellcasting system is pretty original, but the act of casting like other actions just doesn't jive with "real-time" battle.  Every battle quickly devolves into a scramble to CLICK ALL THE THINGS and it often leaves the player feeling cheated when things go wrong, especially considering how clunky the menus can be.  The frenzy of battle becomes a tedium of switching gear, passing potions around, and constantly equipping new projectiles.
There are no hot keys, you pretty much have to rely on the mouse for everything.  The cerebral aspects of the game (puzzles, carefully managing resources, distributing skill points) is lost every time you encounter an enemy, because battle feels too much like a chore rather than fun.  To excel in this combat system you have to play a perpetual game of hopscotch with your enemies as you desperately try to click the next action square that lights up at the right time.  In addition, the characters here can't seem to hit the broad side of a barn.   Had this game incorporated turn-based combat or at least an option for it, this game still wouldn't be a home run but this would be a positive review.
I love that these devs dusted off an sadly neglected style of RPG, but other than a nice facelift there's not much else to see here.  I respect the risks they took here but the potential here is tragically lost in the tedium of the clunky and frenzied comat system and a general lack of polish.
You get 4 party members and there are 3 classes.
Scarce resources is one thing I respect, but for an RPG the equipment is so scarce that your characters are still half-naked 8 hours into the game.
Thrown weapons, torches, and food all need to be perpetually "maintained", and inventory management becomes a chore.
There seem to be no status icons, save for "over-encumbered", which doesn't even seem to function properly as the numbers don't make sense.  Maybe as part of the homage to old games they decided to add a dash of "WTF" just for good measure I don't know what else to chalk some of this up to.
There's something here for those of us who remember this classic style, but this just feels like a poorly designed RPG reluctantly wedged into a brilliant dungeon puzzler.  Maybe it would be great on a tablet for poop breaks, but as a PC title it feels half-baked.  I haven't played the sequel yet but I'm hopeful that they learned some things from this release and improved on what is an intriguing foundation here.  I'm not giving up on this series.  Don't get me wrong, despite the mis-steps there really is a lot of potential here.

This game has gotten a lot of flack that has little to do with the actual game itself in my opinion. This is by far my favorite Eugen game to date, and also an excellent spiritual successor for the close combat series. If you want a modern game of "close combat" this is your game.  A lot of my gripes with the war game series were fixed in Steel Division. The detractors tend to fall into two camps.
1. Lack of player base. This is a valid reason, but it is not a knock against the game itself. This has the ability to become a cult classic or if it gets the right exposure, it can really grow. Honestly, this game fulfills so many wants in a realistic Company/Battalion level tactical game that I am some what baffled by how small the player base is. I have my theories however, which I will explain with point 2.
2. Unhappy "War Game" crowd. Eugen made the popular war game series. It is a great game in a lot of ways. I also had issues with the game that created a lot of tactical and strategic "game-isms". Don't mis-interpret what I am saying. There is some game-ism's in Steel Division too (or any "game" for that matter. No game, no matter how realistic, is going to show the realism of being dog tired by humping that ruck on a long patrol to an ORP, to then conduct a raid on an enemy position.) But the gameisms in Steel Division affect individual units rather then an entire strategy that would have no actual basis in reality. (CV sniping is the most glaring example.)
Almost all of the negative reviews (not all) for Steel Division have come from someone expressing their dislike that this game is not "War Game: WW2". It is slower paced. Units in general are not as easily replaced. Vehicles are slower, and less frequent, thus making them more valuable. Since it is slower, you can't expect to just keep throwing guys into the meet grinder and expect to brute force your way through. They will get pinned and fall back. Don't let the fact that those in the war game crowd are not happy they did not get a new version of War Game steer you away from what is an excellent ww2 company/battalion level game. For you Grognards, this is the closest you are going to get to a computerized version of your old Squad Leader board games.

Short review to Steel Division: Normandy 44
Well, what is there to say, except that his game is a
decent RTS game. And honestly I think it's underrated and deserves more credit and more player base.
The game has very nice visuals as well as sound design. There are a absolute TON of different units to play with, all scattered across a large number of different battlegroups on both allies and axis side of war, which you can customize to your very own liking. And while many of the German units aren't fully historically accurate in their looks, they still managed to put effort and detail in how the units look. I also appreciate the fact that they found a workaround for having historical symbolism in the game which otherwise would have been forbidden.
The major focus of the game is clearly the multiplayer, but unfortunately a lot of people don't see that, since even when the game still had a higher player count, there would always be a lot of people who did not play this game for multiplayer. (juding from the steam current player count and amout of lobbies going on.)
The multiplayer is plaigued by people with sh-itty internert unfortunately, which often results in lag, but most games have that unfortunately.
There are 2 different game modes, which are both good, and the game doesn't really need more game modes, since there's really no need for it. There are a lot of different maps, which are all cut-outs of a even bigger map, depending on size of the map you play on a certain section of the overal-map. And who's starting from which side of the map always is randomized, so there's a lot of variety in the maps and the match play itself, it always feels different.
The singleplayer is GREAT. And I honestly wish that there would have been more. There's 3 campaigns, each with 4 missions which get increasingly more difficult. They have some nice cinematics in the beginning of each campaign, and the missions itself are callenging and really fun to play. But as I said, very short unfortunately, I would have loved to have many more of these mission.
Overall, it's a great game with minor flaws. But you have a lot of content within this game, and for multiplayer it will keep you plenty busy. (which is what everybody should play)

I was a longtime Wargame and R.U.S.E. player and Steel Division was a title that really excited me. I even got access to the close "VIP" beta and played the hell out of it. I obviously pre-ordered to get access to the open beta and played the hell out of that too. I eagerly awaited what I presumed to be a giant patch on release day that would've fixed all of the open beta problems.
The sad reality is that Steel Division has been a trainwreck from the day it released. A lot of the problems would be gone and the community would likely be thriving if the game would have had a much longer closed beta and a full-featured open beta to iron out the bugs. Eugen is not an early access developer, they have never been. They have traditionally released full-featured games with excellent support and with Red Dragon, free and paid DLC. Steel Division was not adequately tested in either beta so the release was a balance nightmare where divisions that had never been tested immediately became the meta and it was a really terrible meta at that. The patches since then have largely been targeted at trying to fix the horribly imbalanced airborne divisions. There have been various tweaks to AAA and planes and veterancy and infantry in general, all of these have to do with Airborne Divisions. Meanwhile, the rest of the game languishes.
The best Allied Armored Division is the French one and it is completely ahistorical and more or less cancerous because it thrives on cheap, high-vet units with ridiculous income. The Germans can counter this spammy quick rush stuff with their own like half track and armored car spam. Couple these spam "fast" divisions with the airborne spam and you've got yourself a proper rush based game, except that isn't what they sold the game as at all. Good players can end a match against even competent players before Phase C ever really gets started. This makes some of the most interesting and varied decks all but useless in multiplayer. Yes, you can do a lot of work with Panzer Lehr in Phase A and B, but that's because you can spam armored cars and half tracks and then in Phase B, roll out some nice high vet Panthers, but you're still using the deck as a rush deck. What you get from this is a bunch of players fighting to grab 51% of the territory and then grinding until the clock runs out. The better players can push this further and win sooner. But all they're good at is the initial rush, which is fine, good on them, but that is not what the game was sold as. They don't have to be good at Phase C because Phase C is irrelevant.
Eugen knows this, they built this into the game. They billed Phase A as a recon phase, but for some reason filled it with unicorn units like the Beute Firefly and cancerous high vet light tank and armored car spam. Phase A has nothing to do with recon, it's just "drive fast and win the merge".
And that's just the inherently terrible design of Conquest + the Phase System + certain decks being OP in Phase A. Nevermind the fact that destruction is effectively unplayable once German heavy units start rolling out. Wehraboos talk about Ronsons needing to outnumber a Tiger or Panther 5 or 10 to 1 but you won't see that in this game. At most you'll see maybe 10 Shermans fighting 3 King Tigers. Guess who wins that? And people aren't stupid so what do you do since you can't spam Shermans all over the place? Just bomb and shell the King Tigers and ignore them with your tanks.
How fun is it to get bombed and shelled all game? How fun is it to know that you really don't have a chance to kill that King Tiger with your armor because you'll never get close enough so you just sit there, bombing and shelling? It just isn't good gameplay.
Nevermind the fact that you've got a terrible off-map artillery mechanic that they've tweaked twice now and it's still terrible, but rather than fix the decks that really need the off-map artillery, they just let everyone have access to it. Why not scrap this terrible mechanic and fix decks like 6th Airborne and 91st Luftlande? Eugen won't do that, they never take anything out of their games, they just waste time nerfing it over a period of years. Just ax it already.
The machinegun meta is trash. The mortars are still cancerous. The MLRS is still cancerous. Plane trains are still cancerous. Availabilities are nonsensical and ahistorical. Come to think of it, really the game is just flat out ahistorical and grossly favors the German side, however, since the Allies have a couple decks that are really good at Phase A, they prevent the game from going too far to the Germans. But let's be real here. Eugen gives all German decks access to nice planes, some of them have a lot of planes which is not at all historical. Fine, that's for gameplay, I get it. But then they don't make the same adjustment for the Allies by giving them a weapon they would've used in real life had they worried about the Luftwaffe.
So you see, Eugen can rationalize putting the entire complement of Jagpanthers used in Normandy because they were there in the TO&E. And then they can give the Germans a fully fledged straight out of 1940 Luftwaffe terror force because of balance and "flavor". But they won't give the Allies access to heavy AAA because while it was part of the TO&E of every single unit, they stopped using stuff like the 90mm because they didn't need to shoot at planes.... but instead used them as AT weapons and indirect fire. But the Allies can't have this because you know, Eugen has never given a good reason. The fact is that the 90mm AAA was there in theater and would have been deployed against this mythical Luftwaffe Eugen has put in game, but again, who cares about authenticity for all.
At least when it came to the M18, Eugen admitted that they simply glossed over the fact that it was in Normandy.
What you've got is a game that appears to be a slow, methodical grind that should cater to more cautious players, but the game doesn't. It is 100% about grabbing as much territory as you can early on and then sitting on your hardpoints while you constrict the rest of the map. Then you've got all these odd decisions in card allocation, pricing, availability, veterancy, it's just a mess. Even the suppression mechanic is infuriating at times. Personally, I like the penetration mechanic.........but the way they implemented it is just childish. Really Eugen? 2 six sided dice that's what you've come up with? In 2017?

I come from a group of 12-15 regular Wargame: Red Dragon players (we don't play anymore) and to a man, other than myself, they basically all hated Steel Division after a few hours of playing it. There's too many hidden stats, too many tricks you have to learn, too much that goes against even layman WW2 convention that players have learned over the years. Couple these difficulties with the server instability, the return of lobby simulator, broken promises from the beta and overall just a really bad experience in most games, and I can say that this is probably the biggest flop I've ever been a part of in gaming.
And this is really sad because going back to the beginning of this review, in the closed beta and the start of the open beta, it really looked like Eugen was taking community requests under advisement. They gave us several changes the community has wanted for years. They even acted like they were making really big changes based on our feedback. Since then, Eugen has gone silent. The player count has cratered and recently the servers aren't even on.
The game is dead, and it won't be coming back. Not without some massive DLC that changes the fundamentals of the game.

Coming from an avid player of Wargame (Cough Red Dragon alone was like 400 hours), SD44 is a far cry from what Eugen is capable of. So far in fact that SD44 comes across as a pocket project for the other games theyve wasted thier time on.
First of all, i bought the entire edition, with artwork, and commentary as well. That said, the understanding that the campaign and maps where intentionally built around historically accurate photos of Normandy is very admirable. But that only stretches so far. The campaigns as compared to WG RD are minimal. While they're oneshot wonders, the replayability of it means nothing in the long run. For people who are either masochists or expert RTS players, the campaign is a lot of fun, or a nice challenge. That said, the fact that less than 90% have beaten the majority of german campaign missions implies that almost everyone who purchases the game will never even play HALF of the campaign thats available. Why? Because its damn near unplayable. The units you are given are the dregs that the NPC's haven't already lost, and you are assigned isn't much more flexible. That is a complete 180 turn from WG RD where you could literally compose entire armies from purchasable army groups. There is no naval units, nor is there any decisive air application.
Next is multiplayer. The former issue of pub stacking is gone, which is awesome, but the next issue thats equally as bad is that NO ONE PLAYS THE GAME. It's dead after 6pm until 8am. I work as well, meaning the majority of the time, multiplayer isnt multiplayable. Next, it easily takes half an hour to fill a lobby when people do play. That doesnt even go to say that the multiplayer will have anyone in it within a few months. The multiplayer isnt worth the game.
Lastly, the battlegroup system is bland. I spent a good amount of time maping out unique units per each battlegroup to figure out what was even available. The jist boils down to germans= expensive reliable units, allies = cheap and plentiful units. Worse is the fact that the allies lack unique units that make any allied BG standout, whereas the germans have decks good for artillery, armor, and infantry individually. Its not fun to play as allies in a nutshell. Nothing they have is clearly better than the germans, and its not bias.
Graphics, i have maxed out, and it looks good, but its not exceptionally noteable. Sound, is also subpar - why do howitzer sounds litterally sound like *pew* when they impact? Thats almost laughable. Why do tanks lack base in thier rumble? Why doesnt a field gun sound like its slinging quarter ton shells? Red Dragon had this issue, so does SD.
In the end, is the game fun? Yes it is, and i still play it. Could Eugen do better, yes, very much so. Would i have bought it knowing what i know now? Probably on the discount sale.

Alright. So, this game - in my opinion - is a great game. And I am not going to compare it to the Wargame titles.
The gameplay is fluid, and plays out nicely. The units are responsive and does what they're told, and they have a bit of conciousness, as they go into cover automatically and can actually hold a defensive, which is nice.
The phased systen kills off early bum-rushing and gives a place for lighter units, such as light tanks and tank guns. This is well thought out to balance out the game.
The specialized battlegroups are nice. They each have varying playstyles and my favorite is the Pz. Lehr-Div., due to it's late-game striking capabilities.
The maps have little variety, as one could assume from the fields and bocages of Normandy, and this is a bit of a downer, that they all play the same - BUT - they don't. They can play similarly, but an Infantry BG plays differently on Point du Hoc than an Armoured would do.
The graphics are stunning, and is a step forward from Eugene, and I love the fact that the game world turns into a paper map when you soom out.
The UI is a step backwards, though, with the menues being simple but the overall aesthics being mediocre.
Overall, a good game, which has a steep learning curve but nice gameplay.

For these Choice of Games CYOAs, which I tend to find pretty limited over many playthroughs, Choice of Robots has a lot of choices and a great deal of different ways that your game can end up.
First, a note of warning, you cannot save AT ALL. It's one go every time and if you die, you're gone.
I don't feel like putting out a long review, as there are many that get the job done better than I will, but I will say this:
If you want a game that will make you think some over ethical and personal ramifications of an alternate future, buy this game.

Wow. That was such an unexpectedly wonderful experience.
As this is a CYOA (Choose Your Own Adventure), your experience may vary, but, I say with little hesitation that
experience with the story is the most meaningful experience I've had with a game - ever.
Although wonderful in their own right, choice oriented games like The Walking Dead and Mass Effect don't even come close to what this game accomplishes.
CoR gives you choices.
CoR gives you lots of choices that make the story feel like your own, fostering immersion in a way that traditional literature cannot.
CoR gives you lots of difficult choices that may have you thinking hard and agonizing about the potential consequences. The game has no manual save function. If you make choices that lead to a premature ending, you can't undo and must start over. (such branches seem rare, though, and replaying doesn't take much time once you're familiar with the text)
CoR gives you lots of difficult choices that have a real impact. Something that is uniquely possible when the creator is unconstrained by the need to create full art assets for every possibility.
This "game" has no graphics at all except for the cover image, which is exactly akin to a book cover illustration. Is it a game or a book? I say it is most certainly a game. Graphics is not a requirement of a game. Interactivity is. A series of choices that impact the experience do a game comprise.
CoR's language is competent, but not "literary". It reads like a matter-of-fact narrative of events that might actually happen in your life if the stars align in just the right way. Initially, I got an "amateur" vibe from the writing, but later realized that the experience may actually benefit from the simple, contemporary writing style. As the story progressed and sucked me in deeper, I became much too busy thinking about what was going on to criticize the writing style.
CoR is (mostly) accessible. Although the fact that it was written by somebody with a Ph.D. in Computer Science does show. Having a CS degree myself, I certainly appreciated that perspective. Although lots of artistic license is taken for the sake of plot, there is lots of grounding in contemporary technology.
The story makes mostly "reasonable" extrapolations starting from the near future forward several decades. Like all good science (or 'speculative', if you prefer) fiction, the story poignantly references the present while writing about the future, framing the timeless human condition in extrapolated contexts.
To elaborate about why I put "reasonable" in quotation marks above, the story explores the future in ways that could, for the most part, conceivably happen, and many futurists would even claim that CoR's extrapolation towards the Singularity doesn't go far enough. However, the author is not afraid to explore fantastic scenarios that probably won't happen, at least not soon, and in some cases, hopefully never.
The scope of the story is indeed quite epic, following the main decades of a lifetime of the character you control. I do have to object to the game description's categorization of this as a "novel", though, as it is not nearly long enough to count as one. At best, it is the length of a (very) short story (a single playthrough takes a matter of hours). On the other hand, the sheer amount of content of all possible branches easily exceed the length of a long novel (50% longer than Moby♥♥♥♥♥♥. It's quite an accomplishment.
And, if you are worried about this being a boring, technical slog, don't be. Despite the apparently sterile subject matter of robots, there is plenty of emotion in this game - or, at least, there can be, depending on your choices.
I've only explored one of the many, distinct branches of CoR. I will probably be going back to explore the others.
I heartily recommend CoR to anyone who can read English, especially those with an interest in technology and/or science fiction.
Note that there is also a free demo where you can play through the first 2 chapters (out of 7), either via Steam, or on the developer's web site.
Having now explored a few other branches and having made more "optimal" choices, I feel that choosing less optimally for the first playthrough does make for a better experience.
My first playthrough involved an above average number of failures and tragedies, which amounted to a much more poignant experience than when everything basically goes well.
I do suggest playing the game "organically". Perhaps it is unlikely to play optimally the first time around anyway. Certainly I would discourage any attempts to "cheat" by looking up optimal choices beforehand. That would truly ruin the experience. You can always go back later and "fix mistakes" on subsequent playthroughs.

I was recommended (and later gifted) Choice of Robots by a friend.  I'm a huge Transformers fan, so a game entirely revolving around the idea of playing a character that creates robots and the impact/influence that has on the world immediately grabbed my attention.  I tried the demo, and was hooked.
I'd never heard of the developer, "Choice of Games" before now, but their other works are of a similar vein.  All of them are basically text-based CYOA (Choose Your Own Adventure) games, much like the old CYOA books of our childhood.  You play a character is can be like, or unlike yourself, and progress through a series of choices that can have a variety of branches, leading the story's eventual conclusion.
"Choice of Robots" follows the life of a young college student, trying to build their own robot.  It starts with a cryptic dream sequence (an excellent plot hook I might add), before going into 'character creation', which consists of selecting a name (either a custom one, or chosen from a list), and your gender.  (I should note, you can only select 'boy' or 'girl', so NB people don't get an option, sorry!)  From there, you make choices which influence a variety of stats (which can be easily checked), including your Fame, Wealth, status of your relationship with the NPCs, and other numerical values.  The status screen even gives you a summary of all the completed chapters so far, sort of an abridged version of your story.
The writing is well done.  It's vague enough that you can easily imagine events or people in your head as you would want them to be, while still giving them enough detail that it's not a complete blank space.  There's a template, and you can fill the gaps.  The way the game interprets your choices is quite fascinating too.  Even small, seemingly insignificant choices can influence future areas.  Not all influences turn out to be significant, but it does address and acknowledge choices you've made, so it feels like you're having a greater push on the story.
However, for all of the game's interactivity and originality, it falls (sometimes painfully) flat in a few areas.  The biggest and probably most damning thing, is the lack of a save/load function.  It autosaves your progress, so if you need to take a break, you can shut it down, go do something else, come back, and immediately jump back in.  And with the summary in status, you can easily determine where you're at.  But without a hard save function, you literally have to start completely over to experiment with new branches and decisions.  This does give a sense of finality and weight to the story, since you can't save-scum for an "ideal" outcome (to whatever degree a player would consider 'ideal anyway), but it makes trying out different decisions painfully tedious, as you have to start over totally anew each time.
This leads to the second issue, and one that most adventure games always fall into, and was the trap of the CYOA-genre: replayability.  While Choice of Robots has a LOT of variation, after a while you do start to notice the patterns.  You'll start to know which options lead to what future choices.  Eventually, it probably becomes second-nature what sort of paths lead to a particular ending.
Which ironically enough, leads to a sub-issue of this problem.  While some of the patterns are obvious, others are not.  Painfully not.  There's a few branches I have NO idea how to access, because the options you'd need aren't very obvious, and the achievement descriptions don't help at ALL.  And as there's no guides, it's a constant stream of trial and error.  This also hurts in-game.  It's not always obvious how good (or bad) a stat should be to elicit a particular response, or to enable particular choices, which again, can only be determined through trial and error, and a LOT of it.  So be prepared that if you're someone who really wants to earn/unlock everything, it'll take some time.
The NPCs tend to suffer as well.  As the story focuses on your avatar and his creation, the NPCs, while recieving a modicum of development, don't really tend to be more than accessories to the overall story.  There's a variety of them, and story does do justice to fleshing them out at times, but after a point they sort of fall into scripted roles and don't really contribute to the story beyond being names.  And scripting can be a problem as well.  There's a few milestones you simply cannot avoid, and a few events where you would think there should be a third option or a way to avoid having to go A or B, but none exist.
Even with these issues, Choice of Robots is an excellent game considering you can get it for under 3 dollars right now (until the sale ends after New Years anyway).  I would highly recommend it to anyone who:
- Wants a fun little diversion from the madness of Triple-A games
- Loves robots
- Enjoys the CYOA genre
- Has a few bucks to spare

Ive seen alot of reviews stating that this game is "dead" because there is simply no one online to race against. While this is true MOST of the time, (just recently raced against 6 other racers in a major event) those leaning on this one flaw in the game are missing out on alot of what Victory has to offer.
Victory: The Age of Racing is simply the best racing game I've played on Steam. Hands down. The blistering sense of speed is better than all but one of the many racing games I've experienced, F-Zero GX being the best in that category. The three classes of cars: Legend, Classic, and Formula, each have thier own handling characteristics and quirks, and each reqiring a different skillset to be brought to thier fullest racing potential. Combine that with probably some of the most fun and frustrating original tracks in a racing game (Mario Kart notwithstanding) and you have one hell of a racing experience. That, quite honestly, only gets better with the addition of rival racers. When they're on of course.
Car customization is another thing Victory has down. The paint room is very Forza-esque in it's function, but one thing I like about it better than Forza is the fact your graphics don't get warped on curved sections of your car. The decals curve with your cars curves, which makes painting replicas pretty satisfying. Plus the fact you can MAKE YOUR CAR LOOK HOWEVER YOU WANT IT TO. You want a crazy front wing that looks like it wont even work aerodynamically? Slap it on there! You want a two story tall rear wing on that Classic car? Go for it! Dont want wings at all? Who da heck needs downforce!? The styles of car are endless, and it's very interesting to see all the custom cars drivers make. From F1 replicas to "How is that even working?"
Also, well, going back to the point that there arent alot of people playing this game. The few who do, at least the ones that I know, are all really friendly. If you come in and see some one on, dont be afraid to ask questions. From what I know, the community in Victory recognize the lack in number of players and will help any newbie who needs help in anything. I will definitely answer any questions asked to me if im on. As you can see with my hours on record, I'm on quite a bit.
So dont let the "Mixed" reviews on this game turn you off to it. Ive had so much fun with this game in the near 10 months I've owned it, even made a few really good friends. If you see video games as an investment and not as an opportunity to have some fun, I can't help you there. But if you're looking for a well made racing experience in a fantasy setting, look no further. Come on in, theres a car with your name on it waiting to be driven.
No seriously, the cars have your name on them. It's pretty cool.
-------------------------
P.S. Forgot to mention. It's small, but probably one of the coolest features in this game is the fact that you are still in control of your car after you cross the finish line. Adds a level of immersion I haven't experienced in any racing game I've played before.

This is one of my favorite Indie RPG's because it knows when to borrow from formula and when to depart from it.
Chiefly -- the battle system is actually interesting. Enemies get stronger each round, so you have a built-in timer that keeps you from just turtling and healing. Another cool thing is that Cthulhu has an "insane" status he can inflict with one of his attacks, that makes enemies more vulnerable but also makes them more dangerous, which is a cool risk tradeoff.
Outside of battle, you have a a random encounter quota that caps out, so if you clear a dungeon of enemies, you don't have to fight any more and can freely explore. Also, you can trigger fights at any time if you want to grind a bit, so you don't even have to waste time running around waiting for them to happen. Very streamlined, in a good way.
And of course the goofy characters and premise are really enjoyable. Basically this little gem is a master class in how to update a classic formula into something that's appetizing to the modern gaming palate.

(reviewed after 85 hours of play on my brother’s steam account)
When a random 15$ indie game is one of the best games I've ever played…
I picked this game up casually, hoping for a fun little diversion to play with my bro to for a few days.  It looked good enough...What I got is a masterpiece I am going to sink hundreds of hours into.
————————————
Assault Android Cactus is one of those fabled relics of gaming magic.  You know, when all of the mechanics, design, gameplay, and programming all come together to achieve pure bliss; this is a game for the real, core gamer.
…Oddly, the above is perhaps partially to blame for its lack of commercial fame.  The game is not well known or played, as you can see from the leaderboards.  What will you *Will* also see is that many of the few who have picked up Cactus hold it in very high esteem.  This is a testament to the goal of the developer: A lot of time and love was put into the game to ensure the experience is as good as it could be.  It is not a game primarily made to sell.
—
AAC is a twin-stick shooting game (like geometry wars), but it is, in my opinion, the best the genre has to offer.  Unlike other twin stick shooters where you frequently must run away and back yourself into corners to survive, Cactus has the opposite mentality- You are forced to dish out as much damage and kill as many things as fast as possible by dashing headfirst into giant hordes of enemies. The reason for this is that you do not lose by dying.  You have infinite lives.  You lose by running out of battery meter, which is constantly draining as you play.  New batteries spawn after killing a certain amount of enemies, which is expertly programmed in a very in-depth way, if you are interested in that sort of information.  This means that trying to sit back and pick off enemies won’t work, not only because the battery will be too far away to recover when it appears, but also because you will not deal damage fast enough, since practically every character must get in close to the crowd to deal their damage the fastest.  The correct mentality to mastering Cactus is to be as aggressive as you can.  Think of yourself like an evil terminator android, relentlessly rushing down your foes with calculating precision.   The meta of Cactus is fine-tuning your ability to be as efficient as possible at dealing damage.
——
I could go into a lengthy discussion of what makes the mechanics and the game itself so good, but no one wants to read through all of that.
——
Cactus experience #1:  Trying to S+ a level with Shi itake (sniper character) on a level with escalator floors and changeable walls.  Zipping around at high speed, twirling (a dodge mechanic) through moshes and waves of crawlers, drones, bullets, bombs, rockets, drones, bees, lasers etc. while dropping mines before I lose my kill chain, picking off multiple enemies at once by lining up my shots to snipe the edges of enemy hitboxes while dashing atop escalators and around cover, chaining power ups so I can stay afloat while also trying to kill everything as quick as possible…All at the same time...Losing literally 100+ times (never stops being fun) but pushing harder and harder to be my best.  It is mad, sweaty gaming zen.
Cactus experience #2: Playing on endless mode (infinity drive) with my brother and trying to coordinate attack patterns and coordinating the effects of our different androids’ primary and secondary weapons.  Changing our tactics on the fly while racking up 800 kill streaks, while the frame rate blazes along at 140 fps. shooting and rushing down, blowing everything up, and sucking everything into a black whole as the level and music continues to warp and bend before our battery runs out.
Cactus experience #3: Trying to complete each level on VPC4 (virtual player count 4), which basically scales enemy spawns as if 4 people are playing, yet you are by yourself.  Being swarmed by impossible odds, yet strategically thinking your way to victory, by choosing the right android and figuring out just the right strategy for the level’s specific challenges.  It’s like a puzzle.  And yet, even though it acts as a puzzle game, you are challenged by a high need for skill as well as a high ability to adapt, since you can’t completely rely on memorizing enemy patterns.  You can’t perfectly predict all of the enemy spawns and power ups, so you must be able to shoot and think on your feet in addition to planning ahead.
Cactus experience #4: Earning #1 in daily drive (daily score chase mode) CO-OP, only to realize no one plays this game, then being sharked by 200,000 points right before the day ends.
Cactus experience #5: watching the best players speed run levels and the campaign in awe.
Cactus experience #6: Being mindblown at how geniusly programmed the following are: The game is impossibly fun and balanced no matter whether you’re playing solo or up to 3 buddies or 3 AI partners…There is challenge for the casual gamer all the way to the hardest of hardcore, without ever compromising the core metagame!  There’s a variety of challenges to shake up the meta and keep you going for hundreds of hours. Every one of the 9 droids has insane potential and very different play styles, yet are all balanced and excel under varying situations.  Some droids are very friendly to those who aren't the best at aiming, while some characters demand nothing less than perfection.
———————
Verdict: if any of this sounds remotely intriguing, pick this up or try the demo.  Do you live for the edge of your seat, hands sweating, heart pounding feeling when you can feel yourself on the verge of beating an impossible challenge?  Are you craving a bat-sh*t insane, high octane arcade game that requires a staggering amount of skill, concentration and strategic thinking?  If so, just buy this and thank me later.
This is a game to master, and with 9 droids to master for every stage and changeable play conditions/challenges, an infinity mode that is literally near impossible to beat, and daily score challenges, you can easily sink hundreds of hours into this game either alone or with friends as a party type game.   Oh, and good luck trying to S+ every level with every droid... But can you do it on VPC2-4?
Negatives: I wish the campaign was slightly longer (a few more levels to master)….it’s just too f***ing good, especially with how much variety and originality is in the stages, whether it’s on a moving train car or a giant convection oven with changing heat patterns.  I also wish the UI was slightly better designed.  It isn’t necessary to look at the UI during intense moments, but it would be nice if it were quicker to read.  The audio cues for certain situations should also have been explained to the player.  Basically, you will hear things like dings and chimes to notify the player of recharging health etc.  It can be really useful to pay attention to.
Bonus: the soundtrack is also very good and crazy and will get you in the zen mode and pump up your jams.  You’re gonna need to be in that zone.
9.5/10  (I don’t give high scores lightly)

So, Assault Andriod Cactus is a game that I can see myself playing for at least another 40 hours, if not more.
It has some of the smoothest rewarding twin-stick action I've played, because it has a very strong focus on getting you into the aim/dodge groove. Some people talk about how DOOM can put you in the "shooter trance", I've found that this does the same for twin-sticks.
It's very polished, has more than enough of a campaign (getting to the last level takes about 6 hours, but I have yet to beat the final boss), and then revisting the levels to try and S+ or get good scores on them is fun, as it's very satisfying to beat a level with an unbroken chain of kills. I also enjoy the characters of each of the andriods, even though they aren't 100% voice acted (which would have been fun, but it doesn't get in the way of the game)
If you like twin-stick shooters at all, you *really* need to pick this up.

This game follows in the footsteps of games like Eye of the Beholder, yet gets lost along the way.
Mainly this game is trying to take an RPG and make it a strategy/ puzzle crawler, instead of a dungeon crawler.  In order to succeed at this game you can't fight monsters toe to toe.  The game seems to be designed in a way that you must exploit the game mechanics (taking a swing at a monster then retreating before it can attack) in order to survive.  This combined with constant puzzles instead of exploring, make this game a poor choice for anyone looking for a true RPG dungeon crawler game.
Party creation is also mediocre, with a minimum selection of classes, and non dynamic races.  You also only get a 4 person party instead of 6 which also limits experience.
The game also has a combat interface that is clunkier than I remember the Eye of the Beholder games to be.  You can equip two weapons on a chanracter, but can't use them at the same time.  Also the spell system tried to be inovative with a rune selection process to make spell casting more of a challenge in the heat of battle.  However, the spell interface needs to be opened each time and has some issues.
Also food seems to be unevenly distributed in the dungeons, making me wonder if food was initially and after thought of the game, and then made into a major mechanic at the last minute.  It seems to be laid out that if you try and 'clean' the dungeon by exploring every inch of a level, your party will starve to death.  However since the game is based on puzzles to unlock the next dungeon, complete exploration is usually a must.

One word: Functions.
Functions are kinda sorta your "skills" in Transistor--and it's one of the most interesting skill systems I've ever seem. I like figuring out a good build of my own in anything I play, and Transistor's Functions allow just that.  What the Devs came up with here is brilliant.
The game's story is weirdly intriguing. Its graphics and soundtrack are also very charming--but these things are secondary for me. The actual gameplay is what matters, and the game did not disappoint in that regard. To sum up:
- You can either fight in real time, or pause, issue Red (your character) commands, watch as she executes it, and then play in real time for a few seconds while your ability to pause and issue orders recharges.
- The Functions system, like I said before, is awesome.
- The game is adequately challenging: it's hard, but not too much.
- The final boss fight is quite interesting as well, rather unique.
This is a very well thought-out game--you can feel the love that went into it. It doesn't copy anyone, it's none of that crap of "hey, everyone's doing zombies or crafting games now, so let's do the same!" Transistor is different, its refreshing, and its GOOD.
The only downside is that it lasts only 7-8 hours. I got through it in one day. On the other hand, it's the only game I've played in 25 years or so of videogames that was very satisfactory even being so short--and there's also a New Game+ mode that let's you keep all your Functions and finally put together that dream build while fighting more and tougher enemies.
In as few words as possible: although short, Transistor is totally worth your money.

This game requires a decent amount of time to truly grasp the complex gameplay. After you understand it, combat is a lot of fun.
The frontline mechanic makes this game more fun as you are trying to hold territory instead of just killing units(there is a mode for that in destruction). The morale bar makes units more realistic in terms of combat. The combat phases and point system are great for differentiating divisions' strengths and weaknesses throughout each match.
Many people complain about over powered divisions and artillery spam, but they don't seem to grasp the true essence of the game. Yes the game could be better balanced and the developers are working on that. But that doesn't mean non meta divisions can't win. There are different playstyles for each division and every division can win. Also, people who over invest into artillery tend to not have enough units to hold ground, so they can lose even if they spam artillery as it is not cheap.
The only real negative in my opinion is the matchmaking system is raw and not polished enough for a fully released game. 1v1 tends to use the queue while team battles of 2v2 3v3 4v4 and 10v10 are mostly on the custom game browser. Hopefully the developers take the time to fix this issue.
Overall,this game has a steep learning curve and some may not have the patience for it. But if you are willing to take the time to learn the complex style of RTS gameplay, it is very rewarding in the end.

By all means, this game should not be as good as it is. You play as a border crossing immigration officer working under a hostile government and all you do is check the documents of everyone who is trying to get into the country. On paper, this sounds like one of the most boring games ever made, but it is expertly designed making it very interesting and captivating, and is easily one of the most original games I have ever come across.
Having to balance your family life and bills with moral decisions and strict rules starts to take its toll on you. You have just denied a person to go see their dying mother in another country just so you can afford to pay for food for your family. You start putting your family’s health in jeopardy so that you can save money to buy a new flat for yourself. You do start feeling mentally drained as the requirements to enter the country start getting bigger and bigger, and soon you start letting wanted murderers through the border and getting fined for it.
The background stories going on are incredible as well. You can help a bunch of freedom fighters to overthrow the government, or work diligently to please your supervisors and stay out of trouble. The border gets attacked all the time, with you having to take down some crazy suicide bomber who might have killed your friend if you weren't quick enough. The relationships you start to have with some of the characters can be extremely funny or incredibly dark. Murderers, dealers, smugglers, terrorists, freedom fighters, border patrol guards and supervisors are just some of the people you will meet. It makes a world that should be drab or lethargic full of life and an engaging to the players.
Until I started writing this, I didn't really realize just how much stuff there was to talk about. There are lots of little tid bits in this game hidden under the surface that make it soooo good. At the beginning you might find it a bit dull, but once the ball starts rolling, it gets very interesting. I am definitely going to keep my eye out for other Lucas Pope games and you should too. If this game is anything to go by, then his next games will hopefully be just as fantastic.
8/10

TL;DR
It's a good game, but there are quite a few problems with it. Buy it at a reduced cost, if possible.
The full review contains MILD SPOILERS. Caution advised.
Star Wars: The Force Unleashed was one of my favorite games on my old PS2 when I was younger, and decided to pick this up after feeling a bit nostalgic. This is actually a port of the PS3 / Xbox 360 versions of the game, which disappointed me somewhat, though it's the same game for the most part. (It may just be nostalgia, but I find the PS2 / Wii version better than this version)
The Story is good, probably 6.5 stars. It's nothing spectacular, but it gets the job done. Taking place in between Episodes III and IV, you play as Galen Marek, the son of a Jedi, turned Vader's Apprentice at a young age. Now known as Starkiller, your training is almost complete, with the end goal being to help Vader overthrow the Emperor. However,
The gameplay is absolutely where the game shines. While it does fall into that same problem that every Star Wars game has, where lightsabers geel way too weak, it's still fun when you don't think about the fact that they're supposed to cut through just about everything. Starkiller is also a master of the Force, however, which is what makes this Beat-em-Up different from other Beat-em-Ups. You can pick things up, throw people and things, shock them, throw your lightsaber, push them, everything you'd expect from a Force prodigy. The boss fights are quite a lot of fun, and regular combat is great hoards of Troopers and Rebels alike.
The game suffers from a few major problems, however. The level design is not very good. It asks for some way-too-specific jumps for the game's floaty physics engine, and failing generally results in instant death. Quick Time Events are very frequent, and break up the flow of combat when you fight larger enemies, such as Rancors or AT-ATs. Load times are ridiculous, and far too frequent. Lastly, the game has a 30 FPS cap, though there are fixes for that available on the Internet.
(Also the Star Destroyer mission is atrocious. The PS2 / Wii version may be better simply because it's not there.)
Overall, I'd probably give the game a 6 / 10. Above average, but not by much. Pick it up on sale, if you can.

It's a very nice addition to the Star Wars universe. The story is nice, the characters are good and the graphics are really nice, but you don't have access to the "advanced" configurations, limiting you to choose between low, medium or high graphics without changing things like texture quality or anti-aliasing. It has an FPS cap on it, but there are mods made to cap it higher or uncap it. Gameplay is good and combat is pretty decent, but the force usage is clunky. For example, if you grab a trooper and wants to throw it at a wall that is in front of you, there's a high chance you end up just throwing him up the air, because it's weird like that, but when it works as intended, it's really satisfying. Overall, it is a pretty good game.

It’s called the Force Unleashed because you’ll get to use force powers in full overdrive. That means force blasts that push entire armies over cliffs, lightning that electrifies everything, and super high force jumps. The pinnacle of the game is crashing down a Star Destroyer into a planet using nothing but the force.  If this is enough to win you over, you will definitely have a blast playing this game.
The force’s not the only thing unleashed though: the illogical over-the-top story and level and gameplay design are all over the place.
The story’s decent, you hunt down hidden Jedi as Darth Vader’s assassin. It’s a pretty dark story, with a predictable redemption arc. Most Star Wars games offer you a light and a dark choice, here confined to a single choice as to which final boss you fight. It would have been much more interesting if the story had followed the dark route, evidenced by 2/3 of the 3 DLC (included in this edition) following the alternative dark ending.
The biggest problem is the ambivalent nature of the game. There’s some dark nightmarish stuff, definitely unsuited for younger players. You get to kill legions of enemies, but to keep the age rating in check there’s no blood or dismemberment:  the gameplay is a tame, almost cartoony version of God of War, which contrast heavily with the dark story.
While all the levels are good looking, they’re plagued by some odd design issues. You’ll repeatedly fall, jump, or get pushed to your death in one of the game’s many abysses, sending you back to the last save point, forcing you to replay part of the level. Often irritating, especially in connection with the unskippable CGI scenes. The many legions of enemies are too easily defeated, the only challenges posed by the game’s Jedi bosses. Those boss fights are generally fun, but all come down to using the same tactics, and are often plagued by a second adversary: the camera.
In short, it’s fun to play around with the force powers and to fight iconic bosses, but the gameplay and level design are not good enough to make you want to come back for more.
There’s far better games out there where you can play with the force, the Jedi Knight series chief among them.

You have all different ways of farming such a farming crops, woodchopping, mowing, silage, animals. So today we are going to break it down to the pros and the cons.
Pros:
Let's start with the woodchopping bit, as you can see the cons of woodchopping are, you can woodchop in this game and it isn't really that hard, there is a variety of woodchopping which is a very nice feature as you can use woodchippers, use a chainsaw and cut it down and put it in your pickup truck by cutting individual pieces that are not to heavy or you can use a skid steer loader with a log fork and pick it up and take it to the sawmill, and you earn a nice bit of money. There is also planting trees with saplings which I find not the biggest feature seen but a very nice smaller feature, especially as you could have a tree farm on a field. There are also trains which can transport logs when you fasten the tension belts as well as these logging machines that are big and can chop trees, transport trees etc. Moving on now, I like they added more crops so it doesn't fell like your doing the same thing every time and all you do is cultivate, sow, harvest and then sell. There is way more purpose for the existence of crops as you can feed pigs with it and I think cows may also need crops because it says "power food". Now here is the bit where it can be interesting for you, you can increase your field yield many ways, such as manure, fertilizer spreaders, sprayer and plowing which can be a big bonus, so in the end there is a good use for it and is like a cycle. Now onto animals, this year they added pigs, which is a good way to make money but not the best as in my opinion I think that cows and sheep make you some decent money, so sheep aren't actually that hard to deal with, all you do is get a water tank, fill it up and then grow grass or just go anywhere where there is grass (not unowned fields) and start mowing, then under the loading wagons in the shop, get a forage wagon and pickup the dark greenish area and take the silage to the sheep area and you will start producing wool, another feature is how the let the sheep in like in real life which makes it very realistic. Moving on to cows which I wouldn't be surprised is a bit complicated but soon you should get the hang of it, anyways the game claims it is "advanced farming", so don't be worried, even if you played this game for years like me. There are also more features for me which adds a bit of a "More than just being a farmer with no life" experience to the game: you have houses and on Goldcrest Valley you have a Pickup parked in a parking area near this house, it would be cool if you had a bit more of a life apart from farming like a house. They also have a feature which allows you to clean dirty vehicles which is pretty interesting and fun, there is also gas/fuel, places to park your cars and different views and other small features like the gold coins on singleplayer which give you Bill Gates money and lots of other features.
Cons:
This is a very hard one but some of the physics in the game get questionable, but the ability to fly with a log is very questionable and also have your logs all out of the trailer and see a pickup fly in the air when it was on the ground.
Overall this is the best Farming Simulation sort of game in the universe and if I rated this bad, I would have to rate all the other Farming Simulation games that compete as bad. Thanks for tuning into my review today! Peace Out!

RollerCoaster Tycoon is one of the first games that I've ever played in my life and is essentially part of my childhood, so when I saw this game on Steam, I became exited and bought it a couple of days later. All I can say is that this game brings back so many nostalgic memories and is still as great as I remembered. Truly a classic that needs to be bought by every person on the planet.

Rollercoaster Tycoon: Deluxe is a classic. A classic that I grew up with, and was amongst the very first games I've played in my life, so it was an instant buy for me, alongside RCT2.
Here, like the games after it, you manage a theme park, and try to keep the rating as high as possible, and basically keep your visitors happy. (And if you so wish drown those who don't like your park, just to set an example)
It's a fairly simple, and straight forward game that you can sink many, many hours into trying to manage your park, create the ultimate rollercoasters, and keep profit up at the same time.
This game, unlike it's successor Rollercoaster Tycoon 2, has unlockable scenario's. You start with several scenario's, and work your way up (or down) from that, trying to get to the very bottom of the list. There's three lists of unlockable scenario's. One for the vanilla game, and the other two are from the expansions Corkscrew Follies and Loopy Landscapes, so if you're a completionist; you'll be sinking many, many hours into it!
Other than that, the game has aged very well since when it was released back in 1999. So do you like managing parks, creating rollercoasters, completing scenario's to progress and having countless of hours of fun? Then throw your money at the screen and buy this game already!
I give this game a definite 9/10, truly a wonderous game!

Probably my most favorite 'Choice of Games' game yet, right beside
. To be honest, I started the game off not too into it, disliking how the game opened up and unsure of what to expect and whether I'd enjoy the story. After a few pages into it, I fell in love with it, and consequently my little robot child.
As other reviewers have said already said, it's hard not to give away any story spoilers while discussing PROs and CONs, but I'll give it a shot.
The game does a great job of giving you several ways to navigate throughout the story, while making each story "branch" or "path" just as detailed as the others you passed over. While some of these CYOA games feel like choosing one option over the other is only to gain/change some stat, with little variance in the rest of the story,
does not do this. It's also incredibly written, with just enough detail to help you envision the story, while giving your brain the freedom to "fill in the holes" to your desire on how something/someone looks. For example, you design a robot specifically pick out certain components/aspects of it that give you a general basis of how it looks. However, someone else may have picked the same exact makeup of their robot but imagine it differntly in their head because the writing leaves things purposefuly open for you to imagine.
In short, if you really enjoy scifi writing and the idea of advanced robots in the near future, you'll absolutely love this game. Even if you don't, like me, you'll probably still end up enjoying it and admire it for the plot and detailed writing.
If you hate CYOA games, which is totally fine, .... yeah you probably won't enjoy it. But you wouldn't be reading this review if you absolutely hated them would you? I don't know. I'm done.
